status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Finding a combinatorial interpretation of the Kronecker coefficients is a classical open problem, posed by Murnaghan in 1938 and widely cited as one of the central open problems in algebraic combinatorics and geometric complexity theory. Partial results are known (e.g., Blasiak's interpretation when one partition is a hook, and various two-row / near-rectangular cases by Blasiak, Mulmuley, Sohoni, Pak, Panova, Tewari and others), but the general problem remains unsolved as of 2026; the problem is not even known to be in the complexity class #P.

Consider an N-electron quantum system whose state is described by a sequence of reduced density matrices (RDMs). For p = 1, 2, the p-body reduced density matrix γ_p(t) is the trace over N − p particles of the full N-fermion density operator, regarded as a self-adjoint operator on the antisymmetric p-particle Hilbert space. The exact time evolution of {γ_p}_{p=1,...,N} is governed by the BBGKY hierarchy

  i ∂_t γ_p(t) = [H_p, γ_p(t)] + Tr_{p+1}[V_{p,p+1}, γ_{p+1}(t)],

which couples γ_p to γ_{p+1}. A "closure" at the two-body level is any prescription γ_3 ≈ Φ[γ_1, γ_2] that produces a closed system of evolution equations for (γ_1(t), γ_2(t)).

Required physical constraints to be preserved for all t ≥ 0 along the closed evolution:

(i) Positive semidefiniteness: γ_1(t) ⪰ 0 and γ_2(t) ⪰ 0 as operators.
(ii) Fermionic occupation bounds: every eigenvalue n_i(t) of γ_1(t) (the natural occupation number) satisfies 0 ≤ n_i(t) ≤ 1.
(iii) Physical local densities: the diagonal ρ(x,t) := γ_1(x,x;t) remains nonnegative and finite (no negative or divergent local densities) throughout the dynamics.
(iv) Consistency between γ_1 and γ_2: γ_1(t) = (N − 1)^{-1} Tr_2 γ_2(t) and the appropriate trace normalization is preserved.

Problem. Construct a nontrivial closure functional Φ[γ_1, γ_2] (going beyond the trivial mean-field/Hartree–Fock factorization) such that the resulting closed evolution equations for (γ_1(t), γ_2(t)) provably preserve conditions (i)–(iv) for arbitrary admissible initial data and for general one- and two-body Hamiltonian terms describing electron dynamics. Equivalently, identify structural conditions on Φ that are sufficient to guarantee these preservation properties, or prove that no such closure exists within a specified class.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No closure approximation for the time-dependent BBGKY hierarchy at the 1- and 2-RDM level is known to provably preserve positive semidefiniteness together with the fermionic occupation-number bounds 0 ≤ n_i ≤ 1 and nonnegative local densities throughout electron dynamics. Recent literature on N-representability and 2-RDM methods (variational SDP-based ground-state methods, machine-learning approaches, and contracted Schrödinger-equation methods) addresses related representability constraints but does not provide a general dynamical closure with these guarantees, indicating the problem remains open.

Consider a nonrelativistic many-body quantum system of N identical fermions (or bosons) governed by a Hamiltonian H = T + V, where T is a one-body kinetic operator and V is a two-body interaction. Define the reduced p-particle density matrices (p-RDM) ρ_p(t) by partial trace of the full density operator ρ(t) = e^{-iHt/ħ} ρ(0) e^{iHt/ħ} over N − p particles. The time-dependent BBGKY-type hierarchy for the {ρ_p} couples ρ_p to ρ_{p+1}, and any practical numerical scheme must close this hierarchy by approximating ρ_{p+1} as a functional of {ρ_1, …, ρ_p}. Standard closures include cluster (cumulant) expansions and closures motivated by nonequilibrium Green's-function (Φ-derivable / conserving) approximations such as Hartree–Fock, second Born, GW, and T-matrix approximations.

Empirically, when one integrates the resulting truncated equations of motion forward in time, the dynamics may exhibit unphysical behavior including loss of N-representability of ρ_1 (eigenvalues escaping the interval [0,1] for fermions), violation of positivity or trace conditions on ρ_p, and finite-time blow-up of matrix elements, despite the fact that the truncated equations exactly preserve the total particle number Tr ρ_1(t) = N and the total energy E(t) = Tr(T ρ_1(t)) + (1/2) Tr(V ρ_2(t)).

Problem. Identify and rigorously characterize the mathematical mechanism by which truncated BBGKY closures — in particular those derived from Green's-function-based conserving approximations — can produce solutions that violate N-representability and/or diverge in finite time, even when the closure manifestly conserves total particle number and total energy. Specifically:

(a) Determine necessary and sufficient structural conditions on a closure functional ρ_{p+1} = F[ρ_1,…,ρ_p] under which the resulting truncated hierarchy preserves the cone of N-representable reduced density matrices for all t ≥ 0.

(b) Show whether any closure that is conserving (in the Baym–Kadanoff sense) and that exactly conserves N and E necessarily preserves N-representability, or exhibit an explicit obstruction proving it need not.

(c) Explain why the divergence observed in numerical simulations is independent of the initial state (provided ρ(0) is a valid N-representable density matrix) and must be attributed to the structure of the approximated equations themselves.

The question of how to truncate the BBGKY / time-dependent reduced-density-matrix hierarchy in a way that simultaneously conserves particle number and energy and preserves N-representability remains an active and unresolved problem in nonequilibrium many-body theory. Subsequent work by Lackner, Brezinová, Kreibich, Stefanucci, Bonitz, and others has identified purity/contraction violations and finite-time instabilities in standard cumulant and Green's-function-based closures, and has proposed partial remedies (e.g., purification schemes, contraction-consistent closures), but no general structural characterization that rules out divergence under conservation of N and E has been established.

Consider a polling system with a single server and two queues $Q_1, Q_2$ operating in continuous time. Customers arrive at $Q_i$ according to a Poisson process with rate $\lambda_i > 0$, $i = 1, 2$, and the two arrival processes are independent. Service times at $Q_i$ are i.i.d. with distribution $B_i$ (Laplace–Stieltjes transform $\beta_i$ and finite mean), independent across queues and of the arrival processes. The server visits the queues in cyclic order $Q_1, Q_2, Q_1, Q_2, \ldots$ . Between a visit to $Q_i$ and the next visit to $Q_{i+1 \bmod 2}$, the server incurs an i.i.d. switch-over time with distribution $S_i$ (LST $\sigma_i$, finite mean), independent of everything else.

The service disciplines are mixed:
- $Q_1$ uses the gated discipline: upon arrival of the server at $Q_1$, exactly those customers present at that polling instant are served, while customers arriving during the visit are deferred to the next cycle.
- $Q_2$ uses the 1-limited discipline: at each visit to $Q_2$, the server serves exactly one customer if $Q_2$ is non-empty, and otherwise leaves immediately.

Assume the system is stable. Let $(X_1^{(i)}, X_2^{(i)})$ denote the steady-state vector of queue lengths at the polling instant of $Q_i$ ($i = 1, 2$), and define the joint probability generating functions
$$F_i(z_1, z_2) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ z_1^{X_1^{(i)}} z_2^{X_2^{(i)}} \right], \qquad |z_1|, |z_2| \le 1, \quad i = 1, 2.$$

Determine $F_1(z_1, z_2)$ and $F_2(z_1, z_2)$ in closed form (or as the explicit solution of a tractable functional/boundary value problem) for this two-queue gated/1-limited polling system with general service and switch-over time distributions.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is identified as an open problem in the polling-systems literature: while the joint queue-length PGF is known for two queues both under 1-limited (via boundary-value-problem techniques) and for branching-type disciplines (gated, exhaustive), the mixed gated/1-limited case does not satisfy the branching property and has not been resolved. No published solution was located in the search.

For each permutation $w$ of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ (regarded as an element of the symmetric group $S_n$, embedded in $S_\infty=\bigcup_n S_n$), the Schubert polynomial $\mathfrak{S}_w \in \mathbb{Z}[x_1,x_2,\ldots]$ is defined as follows. Let $w_0=(n,n-1,\ldots,1)$ be the longest element of $S_n$, and set $\mathfrak{S}_{w_0}=x_1^{n-1}x_2^{n-2}\cdots x_{n-1}$. For any permutation $w \ne w_0$, there exists $i$ such that $w(i)<w(i+1)$, and one defines $\mathfrak{S}_w = \partial_i \mathfrak{S}_{ws_i}$, where $s_i=(i,i+1)$ and the divided difference operator $\partial_i$ acts on polynomials $f$ by
$$\partial_i f = \frac{f - s_i f}{x_i - x_{i+1}},$$
with $s_i$ exchanging $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$. The polynomials $\{\mathfrak{S}_w : w \in S_\infty\}$ form a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of $\mathbb{Z}[x_1,x_2,\ldots]$, so for any permutations $u,v$ there are unique integers $c_{uv}^w$ such that
$$\mathfrak{S}_u \cdot \mathfrak{S}_v = \sum_{w} c_{uv}^w\, \mathfrak{S}_w.$$
It is known from geometry that $c_{uv}^w \ge 0$ for all $u,v,w$.

Provide an explicit combinatorial interpretation of the coefficients $c_{uv}^w$ — that is, exhibit a family of combinatorial objects depending on $u,v,w$ whose cardinality equals $c_{uv}^w$ — thereby giving a combinatorial proof that $c_{uv}^w \ge 0$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Finding a manifestly nonnegative combinatorial rule for the Schubert structure constants $c_{uv}^w$ remains a central open problem in algebraic combinatorics. Recent 2024–2025 work has produced only partial progress: signed puzzle rules (Pak–Robichaux, 2025), explicit formulas in special cases such as boolean elements (2024), and complexity-theoretic results about vanishing and #P-hardness questions. No general positive combinatorial rule is known.

Consider a cyclic polling system with $N \geq 2$ queues $Q_1, \dots, Q_N$ served by a single server that visits the queues in the fixed cyclic order $Q_1 \to Q_2 \to \cdots \to Q_N \to Q_1 \to \cdots$. Customers arrive at $Q_i$ according to an independent renewal process with finite mean inter-arrival time $1/\lambda_i$ and a generally distributed service requirement with finite mean. The server uses a fixed work-conserving service discipline (e.g. exhaustive or gated) at each queue. Between completing service at $Q_i$ and starting service at $Q_{i+1}$, the server incurs a deterministic switch-over time $s_i > 0$. Assume the system is stable, i.e. $\rho := \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i \mathbb{E}[B_i] < 1$, where $B_i$ is the service time at $Q_i$.

Fix positive constants $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N$ with $\sum_i \alpha_i = 1$, and consider the family of systems indexed by $S > 0$ in which the switch-over times are $s_i = s_i(S) = \alpha_i S$. Let the corresponding stationary cycle behavior (e.g. the joint distribution of cycle lengths, visit times, and queue lengths at polling instants, suitably normalized by $S$) be denoted $\mathcal{P}(S)$.

Prove rigorously that as $S \to \infty$, $\mathcal{P}(S)$ converges (in an appropriate distributional sense) to the behavior of the corresponding "deterministic cyclic system" — namely the limiting cyclic system in which inter-arrival times act as their means and all randomness in the polling dynamics vanishes, yielding a deterministic periodic schedule of visit times, cycle lengths, and workload trajectories determined solely by the means $1/\lambda_i$, $\mathbb{E}[B_i]$, and the ratios $\alpha_i$.

Consider a cyclic polling system with $N \geq 2$ queues $Q_1, \dots, Q_N$ served by a single server that visits the queues in the fixed cyclic order $Q_1 \to Q_2 \to \cdots \to Q_N \to Q_1 \to \cdots$. Customers arrive at $Q_i$ according to an independent renewal process with finite mean inter-arrival time $1/\lambda_i$ and a generally distributed service requirement with finite mean. The server uses a fixed work-conserving service discipline (e.g. exhaustive or gated) at each queue. Between completing service at $Q_i$ and starting service at $Q_{i+1}$, the server incurs a deterministic switch-over time $s_i > 0$. Assume the system is stable, i.e. $\rho := \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i \mathbb{E}[B_i] < 1$, where $B_i$ is the service time at $Q_i$.

Fix positive constants $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N$ with $\sum_i \alpha_i = 1$, and consider the family of systems indexed by $S > 0$ in which the switch-over times are $s_i = s_i(S) = \alpha_i S$. Let the corresponding stationary cycle behavior (e.g. the joint distribution of cycle lengths, visit times, and queue lengths at polling instants, suitably normalized by $S$) be denoted $\mathcal{P}(S)$.

Prove rigorously that as $S \to \infty$, $\mathcal{P}(S)$ converges (in an appropriate distributional sense) to the behavior of the corresponding "deterministic cyclic system" — namely the limiting cyclic system in which inter-arrival times act as their means and all randomness in the polling dynamics vanishes, yielding a deterministic periodic schedule of visit times, cycle lengths, and workload trajectories determined solely by the means $1/\lambda_i$, $\mathbb{E}[B_i]$, and the ratios $\alpha_i$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is posed as an open problem (a conjecture asking for a rigorous proof) in the polling systems literature. A targeted web search did not surface any subsequent paper providing a rigorous proof of this convergence result for general renewal arrivals as deterministic switch-over times tend to infinity, so it appears to remain open.

Let $S_n$ be the symmetric group on $n$ letters. The irreducible complex characters of $S_n$ are indexed by partitions $\lambda$ of $n$, and the conjugacy classes are indexed by partitions $\mu$ of $n$ (where $\mu$ records the cycle type of any element of the class). Let $\chi^\lambda(\mu)$ denote the value of the irreducible character $\chi^\lambda$ on the conjugacy class of cycle type $\mu$. For each partition $\lambda$ of $n$, define the row sum
$$ R_\lambda \;=\; \sum_{\mu \,\vdash\, n} \chi^\lambda(\mu). $$
It is known (via Frobenius–Schur indicator considerations, since every irreducible representation of $S_n$ is defined over the rationals) that $R_\lambda$ equals the number of elements $w \in S_n$ of cycle type $\lambda$ that are squares, divided by appropriate centralizer data; equivalently $R_\lambda \ge 0$ for all $\lambda \vdash n$.

Problem: Give an explicit combinatorial interpretation of $R_\lambda$, i.e. exhibit a family $\mathcal{F}_\lambda$ of combinatorial objects (depending naturally on $\lambda$) such that $R_\lambda = \#\mathcal{F}_\lambda$ for every partition $\lambda$ of $n$, and use this interpretation to give a combinatorial proof that $R_\lambda \ge 0$.

The problem of giving a combinatorial interpretation of the row sums of the character table of S_n appears still open. Frumkin showed nonnegativity (indeed positivity for n>2) using representation theory (these row sums equal multiplicities in the conjugation representation), and partial combinatorial results have appeared (e.g., Early's work on character polynomials, and recent identities involving Riordan numbers by Hemmer–Straub–Westrem, 2025), but no general combinatorial interpretation yielding a bijective proof of nonnegativity has been established.

Consider a system of N identical fermions evolving under a time-dependent many-body Hamiltonian. For each time t, let Γ^{(p)}(t) denote the p-body reduced density matrix (p-RDM), defined as the partial trace over N−p particles of the full N-body density operator, with normalization Tr Γ^{(p)} = N!/(N−p)!. Write γ := Γ^{(1)} and Γ := Γ^{(2)}. The time evolutions of γ, Γ, and Γ^{(3)} are linked by the BBGKY-type hierarchy, in which the equation of motion for Γ^{(p)} depends on Γ^{(p+1)}. Truncating this hierarchy at the three-body level requires approximating Γ^{(3)} as a functional of γ and Γ; such approximations generically break the exact contraction (trace) identities

  Tr_{p+1} Γ^{(p+1)} = (N−p) Γ^{(p)},

so that even if the approximate Γ^{(3)} is positive semidefinite, the propagated γ and Γ need not be.

Problem. Devise a variational (or otherwise constrained) time-propagation scheme for the truncated BBGKY hierarchy at the three-body level which, for all t ≥ 0, maintains simultaneously:

 (i) Γ^{(3)}(t) ⪰ 0,
 (ii) Γ(t) ⪰ 0, and
 (iii) γ(t) ⪰ 0,

despite the fact that the contraction identities relating Γ^{(3)}, Γ, and γ may fail under the chosen truncation. Equivalently, determine whether positive semidefiniteness of all three reduced density matrices can be enforced as a dynamical constraint along the evolution, and exhibit such a method, or prove that no such scheme can exist within a specified class of approximations.

Subsequent work on time-dependent 2RDM methods has addressed the positive-semidefiniteness/N-representability issue partially via purification schemes (e.g., projective purification of correlated RDMs and TD2RDM stabilization), which restore N-representability of the 2RDM in many regimes. Consider a system of identical fermions described by the time-dependent reduced density matrices (RDMs) γ^{(k)} of order k = 1, 2, 3, …, satisfying the BBGKY hierarchy. Introduce the cumulant (cluster) expansion of the two- and three-body RDMs:

  Γ^{(2)} = A[γ ⊗ γ] + Δ^{(2)},
  Γ^{(3)} = S[γ ⊗ γ ⊗ γ] + A[γ ⊗ Δ^{(2)}] + Δ^{(3)},

where A and S denote the appropriate antisymmetrization/symmetrization operators acting on tensor products, Δ^{(2)} is the genuine two-body correlation function, and Δ^{(3)} is the residual (irreducible) three-body correlation function.

To close the BBGKY hierarchy at the level of γ and Δ^{(2)}, one must specify Δ^{(3)} as a functional of the lower-order objects (γ, Δ^{(2)}). Three standard truncations are:

 (i) the three-body collision-integral-free closure, in which the contribution of Δ^{(3)} to the equation of motion of Γ^{(2)} is set to zero;
 (ii) the three-body noninteracting closure, in which Δ^{(3)} ≡ 0;
 (iii) the Wang–Cassing-style closure, in which Δ^{(3)} is approximated by a specific antisymmetrized product structure built from γ and Δ^{(2)}.

Problem. Construct an approximation Δ^{(3)} ≈ F[γ, Δ^{(2)}] which goes beyond (i)–(iii), is consistent with the symmetry, trace, hermiticity, and contraction (sum-rule) properties required of a three-body cumulant, preserves conservation of energy, momentum, particle number, and (where applicable) total spin under the resulting closed equations of motion for (γ, Δ^{(2)}), and yields a more reliable closure of the BBGKY hierarchy than (i)–(iii) for time-dependent fermionic many-body dynamics.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general problem of approximating the irreducible three-body cumulant Δ^{(3)} in time-dependent reduced-density-matrix theory is a long-standing challenge in many-body physics. Various proposals (e.g., reconstruction functionals via Green's-function/RDM connections, Nakatsuji–Yasuda and Mazziotti reconstructions in contracted Schrödinger equation theory) exist, but no universally accepted, conservation-preserving and reliable closure is known. The question is regarded as open.

The (q,t)-Kostka positivity conjecture was proved by Mark Haiman in 2001 ("Hilbert schemes, polygraphs and the Macdonald positivity conjecture", J. Amer. Math. Soc. 14 (2001), 941–1006), by establishing the n! conjecture via the geometry of the Hilbert scheme of points in the plane. Combinatorial formulas (e.g., Haglund–Haiman–Loehr) have since given explicit positive expansions, though a manifestly positive combinatorial formula in general remains an active area.

For a vector $x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)^	op \in \mathbb{R}^n$, define the map $T_A : \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R}^n$ by
$$ igl(T_A(x) igr)_i \;=\; \sum_{i_2,\dots,i_m=1}^n a_{i\,i_2\cdots i_m}\, x_{i_2}\, x_{i_3}\cdots x_{i_m}, \qquad i=1,\dots,n,$$
and let $T_A^r$ denote the $r$-fold composition of $T_A$ with itself. The tensor $A$ is called primitive if there exists a positive integer $r$ such that $T_A^r(x) > 0$ (componentwise) for every nonnegative nonzero vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. $$\gamma(A) \;\le\; (n-1)^2 + 1.$$

Fix an integer k ≥ 1. A k-ribbon is a connected skew shape of size k containing no 2×2 square. Given partitions μ ⊆ λ such that |λ/μ| is divisible by k, a k-ribbon tableau T of shape λ/μ is a sequence of partitions μ = λ^(0) ⊂ λ^(1) ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ λ^(n) = λ such that each λ^(i)/λ^(i−1) is a k-ribbon, together with a labeling of these ribbons by positive integers that is weakly increasing along rows and strictly increasing down columns in the natural sense. For a k-ribbon tableau T, let x^T = ∏ x_{T(R)} where the product runs over the ribbons R of T, and let spin(T) be one-half of the sum, over all ribbons R in T, of (height(R) − 1), where height(R) is the number of rows R occupies. Define the ribbon polynomial
   G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) = ∑_T q^{spin(T)} x^T,
the sum being over all k-ribbon tableaux T of shape λ/μ.

(a) Give a combinatorial proof that G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) is a symmetric function in x = (x_1, x_2, …).

(b) When G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) is expanded in the basis of Schur functions s_ν(x), determine whether all coefficients lie in ℤ_{≥0}[q]; that is, decide whether
   G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) = ∑_ν c_{λ/μ,ν}^{(k)}(q) s_ν(x)

Given partitions μ ⊆ λ such that |λ/μ| is divisible by k, a k-ribbon tableau T of shape λ/μ is a sequence of partitions μ = λ^(0) ⊂ λ^(1) ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ λ^(n) = λ such that each λ^(i)/λ^(i−1) is a k-ribbon, together with a labeling of these ribbons by positive integers that is weakly increasing along rows and strictly increasing down columns in the natural sense. For a k-ribbon tableau T, let x^T = ∏ x_{T(R)} where the product runs over the ribbons R of T, and let spin(T) be one-half of the sum, over all ribbons R in T, of (height(R) − 1), where height(R) is the number of rows R occupies. Define the ribbon polynomial
   G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) = ∑_T q^{spin(T)} x^T,
the sum being over all k-ribbon tableaux T of shape λ/μ.

(a) Give a combinatorial proof that G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) is a symmetric function in x = (x_1, x_2, …).

(b) When G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) is expanded in the basis of Schur functions s_ν(x), determine whether all coefficients lie in ℤ_{≥0}[q]; that is, decide whether
   G_{λ/μ}^{(k)}(x; q) = ∑_ν c_{λ/μ,ν}^{(k)}(q) s_ν(x)
with each c_{λ/μ,ν}^{(k)}(q) a polynomial in q with nonnegative integer coefficients.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Schur positivity (part b) of the ribbon/LLT polynomials was established by Grojnowski and Haiman using affine Hecke algebras and Kazhdan–Lusztig theory, a non-combinatorial proof. A combinatorial proof of Schur positivity (and hence of symmetry, part a) for LLT polynomials was later given by Assaf via dual equivalence graphs, though it does not produce an explicit positive combinatorial formula for the Schur coefficients in full generality. Explicit combinatorial Schur expansions remain known only in special cases (e.g., small numbers of ribbons or unicellular LLT polynomials). Thus part (a) is solved combinatorially, part (b)'s positivity is solved, but a combinatorial formula for the coefficients is still open in general.

representations.normalized:
Consider a system of N interacting fermions evolving under a (possibly time-dependent) Hamiltonian, and let ρ_p(t) denote the p-body reduced density matrix at time t. The exact dynamics is governed by the BBGKY hierarchy, in which the time evolution of ρ_p couples to ρ_{p+1}. A standard truncation closes the hierarchy at second order by approximating ρ_3 as a functional of ρ_1 and ρ_2 (e.g., via cluster-expansion-type ansätze that preserve particle number and total energy), yielding coupled equations of motion for ρ_1(t) and ρ_2(t).

When this truncated scheme is applied to the few-site Hubbard model (a finite lattice with on-site Coulomb repulsion U and nearest-neighbor hopping), three pathologies have been documented:
(i) numerical/dynamical instability of the propagation;
(ii) divergence of local densities at finite times;
(iii) violation of the N-representability/fermionic constraints, namely the requirement that ρ_2 (and the contracted ρ_1) remain Hermitian, antisymmetric, positive semidefinite, and satisfy the correct partial-trace and eigenvalue bounds (0 ≤ eigenvalues of ρ_1 ≤ 1).

Several partial remedies have been proposed, including purification/positivity-restoration projections of ρ_2 during propagation and modified closure functionals designed to enforce contraction consistency.

Question: Do the three pathologies (i)–(iii) above persist when the same BBGKY truncation schemes are applied to genuine small-molecule electronic systems (i.e., ab initio Hamiltonians for atoms and small molecules with realistic Coulomb interactions and basis sets) and to other complex correlated-electron systems beyond the Hubbard test case? Furthermore, can the proposed partial remedies be rigorously validated as cures (or systematic mitigations) of these pathologies in those more general settings?

representations.normalized:
Consider an N-fermion quantum system with antisymmetric, normalized time-dependent wave function Ψ(t) ∈ ⋀^N H, where H is a one-particle Hilbert space, evolving under a Hamiltonian of the form H = ∑_i h(i) + ∑_{i<j} v(i,j). For each k = 1, …, N define the k-particle reduced density matrix (k-RDM) by

  γ_k(t; x_1,…,x_k; x'_1,…,x'_k) = (N choose k) ∫ Ψ(t; x_1,…,x_k, y_{k+1},…,y_N) Ψ*(t; x'_1,…,x'_k, y_{k+1},…,y_N) dy_{k+1}…dy_N.

These satisfy the time-dependent BBGKY hierarchy

  i ∂_t γ_k = [H_k, γ_k] + Tr_{k+1}[ V_{k,k+1}, γ_{k+1} ],   k = 1, …, N,

where H_k is the k-particle part of H and V_{k,k+1} couples particles 1,…,k to particle k+1.

A truncation of the hierarchy at level k consists of replacing γ_{k+1} on the right-hand side of the k-th equation by a functional Φ_k(γ_1,…,γ_k) (a closure), producing a closed evolution for (γ_1,…,γ_k). The eigenvalues of γ_1, called natural occupation numbers, are required by N-representability to lie in [0,1]; a truncation is said to preserve physicality of natural occupation numbers if, along its evolution, the eigenvalues of γ_1(t) remain in [0,1] for all t ≥ 0.

In the special case of time-dependent Hartree–Fock (the truncation γ_2 = γ_1 ∧ γ_1), there always exists a Slater-determinant wave function whose 1-RDM equals γ_1(t), and consequently the natural occupation numbers are automatically physical.

Problem. Identify and characterize a precise relationship between truncated BBGKY equations and (approximate) N-particle wave functions that yields, beyond the Hartree–Fock level, time-dependent truncation schemes Φ_k for which the evolved 1-RDM γ_1(t) corresponds (exactly or via an explicit construction) to some antisymmetric wave function and whose natural occupation numbers therefore remain in [0,1] for all times.

The question concerns constructing wave-function-consistent truncations of the time-dependent BBGKY hierarchy that preserve physical natural occupation numbers. This is recognized as an outstanding open problem in time-dependent reduced-density-matrix theory; later work on TD-RDM and TD-density-matrix functional methods (e.g., contracted Schrödinger equations, purification schemes) addresses N-representability violations heuristically, but no general construction tying truncated BBGKY equations to an underlying approximate wave function (beyond TDHF) appears to have been established. No definitive solution was found in the search.

Let $A=(a_{i_1 i_2\cdots i_m})$ be a nonnegative tensor of order $m\ge 2$ and dimension $n$, i.e. $a_{i_1\cdots i_m}\ge 0$ with each index in $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$. The product of two such tensors is defined coordinatewise so that powers $A^k$ are again nonnegative tensors of order $m$ and dimension $n$ (using the standard tensor product that yields, for each $k\ge 1$, an $m$th-order $n$-dimensional tensor $A^k$). The majorization matrix $M(A)$ of $A$ is the $n\times n$ matrix with entries
\[ M(A)_{ij} = a_{ij j\cdots j}, \qquad i,j\in[n]. \]
The tensor $A$ is called primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that every entry of $M(A^k)$ is positive; the least such $k$ is the primitive degree $\gamma(A)$. For a fixed $j\in[n]$, $A$ is called $j$-primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that $(M(A^k))_{uj}>0$ for all $u\in[n]$, and the least such $k$ is denoted $\gamma_j(A)$.

Question: Let $A$ be a nonnegative primitive tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$. Must there exist positive integers $a<b$ such that
\[ \{\gamma_1(A),\gamma_2(A),\dots,\gamma_n(A)\} = \{a,a+1,\dots,b\}, \]
i.e. the set of $j$-primitive degrees is always a consecutive interval of integers?

Let (W, S) be a Coxeter system, with length function ℓ : W → ℤ_{≥0} and Bruhat order ≤. The Hecke algebra H(W) is the free ℤ[q^{1/2}, q^{-1/2}]-module with basis {T_w : w ∈ W} and multiplication determined by T_s T_w = T_{sw} if ℓ(sw) > ℓ(w) and T_s T_w = (q−1) T_w + q T_{sw} if ℓ(sw) < ℓ(w), for s ∈ S. There is a unique ℤ[q^{1/2}, q^{-1/2}]-basis {C'_w : w ∈ W} of H(W) characterized by the conditions that C'_w is invariant under the bar involution (sending q^{1/2} ↦ q^{−1/2} and T_w ↦ T_{w^{−1}}^{−1}) and that
   C'_w = q^{−ℓ(w)/2} ∑_{u ≤ w} P_{u,w}(q) T_u,
where P_{u,w}(q) ∈ ℤ[q] satisfies P_{w,w}(q) = 1 and deg P_{u,w}(q) ≤ (ℓ(w) − ℓ(u) − 1)/2 for u < w. The polynomials P_{u,w}(q) are the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials of W.

Question: For every Coxeter system (W, S) and every pair u ≤ v in W under the Bruhat order, are all coefficients of P_{u,v}(q) nonnegative integers?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The nonnegativity of coefficients of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials for arbitrary Coxeter groups was proved by Ben Elias and Geordie Williamson via their proof of Soergel's conjecture and the Hodge theory of Soergel bimodules (Annals of Mathematics, 2014). Prior to this, positivity was known only in special (e.g., crystallographic) cases. The general case is now considered settled.

Let $m \ge 2$ and $n \ge 2$ be integers, and let $[n] = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. A tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$ is an array $A = (a_{i_1 i_2 \cdots i_m})$ with entries indexed by $i_1, \ldots, i_m \in [n]$. Such a tensor is called nonnegative if all entries $a_{i_1 \cdots i_m}$ are nonnegative real numbers.

For a nonnegative tensor $A$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$, define the majorization matrix $M(A)$ to be the $n \times n$ matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry is
$$M(A)_{ij} = a_{i j j \cdots j}, \qquad i, j \in [n].$$

The tensor product $A^k$ is defined recursively so that $A^k$ is again a nonnegative tensor of order $m$ and dimension $n$ via the standard tensor product associated with the Perron–Frobenius theory of nonnegative tensors: the entries of $A^k$ are the iterated polynomial expressions in the entries of $A$ obtained from $k$-fold composition (equivalently, from the map $x \mapsto Ax^{m-1}$).

The tensor $A$ is said to be primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that every entry of $A^k$ is strictly positive. For a fixed $j \in [n]$, the tensor $A$ is said to be $j$-primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that
$$\bigl(M(A^k)\bigr)_{u j} > 0 \quad \text{for every } u \in [n].$$

The tensor $A$ is said to be reducible if there exists a nonempty proper subset $I \subsetneq [n]$ such that
$$a_{i_1 i_2 \cdots i_m} = 0 \quad \text{whenever } i_1 \in I \text{ and } i_2, \ldots, i_m \in [n] \setminus I.$$
Otherwise $A$ is called irreducible.

Prove or disprove: a nonnegative tensor $A$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$ is primitive if and only if $A$ is irreducible and there exists some $j \in [n]$ such that $A$ is $j$-primitive.

The problem of building linear-response BBGKY truncations for optical spectra that avoid the divergences known in nonlinear time-dependent reduced-density-matrix propagation is a programmatic open research direction. Standard low-order linear-response schemes (RPA, second RPA) exist, but a systematic linear-response BBGKY truncation with proven boundedness, sum-rule preservation, and a controlled spectrum at general order p_0 has not been established in the literature, and work in this direction is described as ongoing without a definitive resolution.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The construction of nonadiabatic, memory-dependent, energy-conserving exchange–correlation functionals for time-dependent DFT and TDRDMFT is a long-standing open problem. While partial progress has been made (e.g., Vignale–Kohn current-functional approximation, phase-including natural orbital (PINO) functionals by Giesbertz–Gritsenko–Baerends, and various memory-kernel constructions), no functional is known that simultaneously satisfies nonlocality, full memory dependence, phase dependence enabling time-dependent occupation numbers, and exact energy conservation while reducing to an accurate ground-state limit. Reviews and recent works through the mid-2020s continue to list this as an outstanding challenge.

Fix integers $m \ge 3$ and $n \ge 2$. A tensor $A = (a_{i_1 i_2 \ldots i_m})$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$ has entries indexed by $i_1, \ldots, i_m \in [n] := \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, and is called nonnegative if all entries are $\ge 0$. For two order-$m$ dimension-$n$ tensors $A$ and $B$, their product $A B$ is the order-$m$ dimension-$n$ tensor whose $(i, i_2, \ldots, i_m)$ entry is
$$ (AB)_{i\, i_2 \cdots i_m} \;=\; \sum_{j_2,\ldots,j_m \in [n]} a_{i\, j_2 \cdots j_m}\, b_{j_2\, i_2 \cdots i_m} \cdot \mathbf{1}[j_3=\cdots=j_m]\text{ along the standard tensor product convention,} $$
so that powers $A^k$ are defined recursively by $A^1 = A$ and $A^{k+1} = A \cdot A^k$ in the standard way used for nonnegative tensors. The majorization matrix $M(A)$ of $A$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with entries
$$ (M(A))_{ij} \;=\; a_{i\, j\, j\, \cdots\, j}, \qquad i,j \in [n]. $$
The tensor $A$ is called primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that every entry of $M(A^k)$ is positive. For a fixed $j \in [n]$, $A$ is called $j$-primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that $(M(A^k))_{u\, j} > 0$ for every $u \in [n]$; the smallest such $k$ is the $j$-primitive degree $\gamma_j(A)$.

Define
$$ r(m, n) \;=\; \max\bigl\{\, \gamma_j(A) \,:\, A \text{ is a nonnegative order-}m\text{ dimension-}n\text{ tensor},\ A \text{ is not primitive},\ \exists\, j \in [n] \text{ with } A \text{ being } j\text{-primitive} \,\bigr\}. $$

Determine $r(m, n)$ in closed form, and characterize all tensors that attain this maximum.

For a partition $\lambda \vdash n$, let $\chi^\lambda$ denote the irreducible character of the symmetric group $S_n$ corresponding to $\lambda$. The (irreducible-character) immanant of an $n\times n$ matrix $X = (x_{ij})$ is defined by
$$\operatorname{Imm}_\lambda(X) \;=\; \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \chi^\lambda(\sigma)\, \prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}.$$
A real $n\times n$ matrix $X$ is called totally nonnegative if every minor (the determinant of every square submatrix) is nonnegative.

Prove or disprove: for every totally nonnegative $n\times n$ matrix $X$ and every partition $\lambda \vdash n$,
$$\operatorname{Imm}_\lambda(X) \;\ge\; 0.$$

This nonnegativity statement (Stembridge's immanant conjecture) was proved by Mark Haiman in his 1993 paper "Hecke algebra characters and immanant conjectures" (J. Amer. Math. Soc. 6, 1993), where the immanants of totally nonnegative matrices are shown to be nonnegative via Kazhdan–Lusztig/Hecke algebra character theory. The problem is therefore considered solved.

Consider a finite, non-relativistic many-fermion quantum system whose state is described by a time-dependent density matrix on Fock space. For each integer $p\ge 1$, let $ho_p(t)$ denote the $p$-body reduced density matrix obtained by partial trace, normalized so that $\mathrm{Tr}\,ho_p =  inom{N}{p}$ where $N$ is the particle number. With a Hamiltonian containing one-body kinetic terms and a two-body interaction, the time-dependent reduced density matrices satisfy the BBGKY hierarchy
$$ i\hbar\,\partial_t ho_p(t) = [H_p,ho_p(t)] + \mathrm{Tr}_{p+1} igl[V_{p,p+1},ho_{p+1}(t) igr], $$
which couples $ho_p$ to $ho_{p+1}$. A "second-equation propagation scheme" consists of choosing a closure functional $ho_3[ho_1,ho_2]$ (e.g. cumulant expansions, the 3b-NIA approximation, or weak-coupling/WC truncations) and then evolving only $ho_2(t)$ via
$$ i\hbar\,\partial_t ho_2(t) = [H_2,ho_2(t)] + \mathrm{Tr}_{3} igl[V_{2,3},\,ho_3[ho_1(t),ho_2(t)] igr], $$
with $ho_1(t)$ obtained by contraction from $ho_2(t)$.

It is known that for typical closures (i) the total energy $E(t)=\mathrm{Tr}(Hho(t))$, while formally conserved, can in numerical simulations exhibit large fluctuations in time, and (ii) the propagated $ho_2(t)$ may fail to remain positive semidefinite or representable, leading to divergences in finite time, even in regimes where the compatibility relation $ho_1 = 	frac{1}{N-1}\mathrm{Tr}_2 ho_2$ between the first and second hierarchy levels is not violated.

Problem. Determine whether there exists a closure $ho_3[ho_1,ho_2]$ such that the resulting second-equation propagation scheme is generally reliable, in the sense that for a broad class of finite fermionic systems and initial data the propagated $ho_2(t)$ (a) remains positive semidefinite and $N$-representable for all $t\ge 0$, (b) conserves total energy with bounded long-time fluctuations, and (c) does not diverge in finite time. Equivalently, either construct such a closure together with a proof of these properties, or prove that no closure depending only on $ho_1$ and $ho_2$ can simultaneously satisfy (a)–(c) uniformly.

For an order-$m$, dimension-$n$ tensor $A=(a_{i_1 i_2\cdots i_m})$ with $1\le i_j\le n$, define the tensor product $A\cdot B$ and the powers $A^k$ via the standard multilinear (Shao-type) product on nonnegative tensors, so that $A^k$ is again a nonnegative tensor of the same order and dimension. Call $A$ nonnegative if every entry is $\ge 0$, and call $A$ positive (write $A>0$) if every entry is $>0$.

Say that a nonnegative tensor $A$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$ is strongly primitive if there exists a positive integer $k$ such that $A^k>0$. When $A$ is strongly primitive, define the strongly primitive degree
$$\eta(A)\;=\;\min\{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\,:\,A^k>0\}.$$
Define the strongly exponent set of order $m$ and dimension $n$ as
$$E_s(m,n)\;=\;\{\eta(A)\,:\,A\text{ is a strongly primitive nonnegative tensor of order }m\text{ and dimension }n\}.$$
For an integer $j\ge 1$, call a nonnegative tensor $A$ of order $m$ and dimension $n$ $j$-strongly primitive if $A$ is strongly primitive and exactly $j$ entries of $A^{\eta(A)-1}$ are zero (equivalently, $A^{\eta(A)-1}$ has exactly $j$ zero entries while $A^{\eta(A)}>0$).

Develop the theory of these notions. In particular:

Let $n\geq 1$ and let $H_n(q)$ denote the Iwahori–Hecke algebra of the symmetric group $S_n$ over $\mathbb{Z}[q^{1/2},q^{-1/2}]$, with standard basis $\{T_w : w\in S_n\}$ satisfying the relations $(T_{s_i}-q)(T_{s_i}+1)=0$ for each simple transposition $s_i$, and $T_uT_v=T_{uv}$ when $\ell(uv)=\ell(u)+\ell(v)$, where $\ell$ denotes the Coxeter length. Let $\{C'_w : w\in S_n\}$ be the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of $H_n(q)$, normalized so that
$$C'_w \;=\; q^{-\ell(w)/2}\sum_{v\le w} P_{v,w}(q)\, T_v,$$
where $P_{v,w}(q)$ are the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials and $\le$ is the Bruhat order.

For each composition $\lambda\models n$ (or partition of $n$), the induced sign character of the corresponding Young (parabolic) subalgebra extends to a class function on $H_n(q)$; the resulting characters $\varphi_\lambda : H_n(q)\to \mathbb{Z}[q^{1/2},q^{-1/2}]$ are called the monomial characters of $H_n(q)$.

Question: Is it true that for every monomial character $\varphi$ of $H_n(q)$ and every Kazhdan–Lusztig basis element $C'_w$, the Laurent polynomial
$$\varphi\!\left(q^{-\ell(w)/2}\,C'_w\right) \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{1/2},q^{-1/2}]$$
is a polynomial in $q$ with nonnegative integer coefficients, whose coefficient sequence is unimodal and palindromic (symmetric) about $q^{\ell(w)/2}$?

Background and definitions. A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose vertices are decorated as either classical crossings (with over/under information) or virtual crossings (drawn as a small circle). Two virtual knot diagrams are equivalent if they are related by a finite sequence of planar isotopies, the three classical Reidemeister moves, the three virtual Reidemeister moves, and the mixed (semi-virtual) move. A virtual knot is an equivalence class of virtual knot diagrams. The unknot is the equivalence class of the diagram with no crossings.

A long virtual knot diagram is a virtual knot diagram in which one strand is cut at a generic point to produce two free ends going to infinity (a 1-1 tangle in the plane); equivalence of long virtual knot diagrams is generated by all the moves above performed away from the two ends. The closure of a long virtual knot is the (closed) virtual knot obtained by reconnecting the two ends in the plane.

The connected sum of two closed virtual knots K_1 and K_2 is defined by cutting each at a chosen arc and splicing them; in general this operation depends on the chosen arcs. For long virtual knots, concatenation gives a well-defined (but in general non-commutative) connected sum.

Problems.
(a) Classify all non-trivial virtual knots K that arise as a connected sum K = K_1 # K_2 in which both K_1 and K_2 are equivalent to the unknot.
(b) Classify all long virtual knots whose closure is equivalent to the (closed) unknot, up to equivalence of long virtual knots, and use this classification to describe precisely which choices of cutting arcs in two unknotted closed virtual knots can yield a non-trivial closed virtual connected sum.

The phenomenon that a non-trivial virtual knot (e.g., the Kishino knot) can be a connected sum of two unknotted virtual knots is well known, and many invariants (surface bracket, biquandle, parity, arrow polynomials) detect specific examples of non-triviality. However, no general classification of such virtual knots, nor of the long virtual knots whose closure is the unknot, appears in the literature; the question is listed among unsolved problems in virtual knot theory and remains open.

Let $P$ be a finite poset on the vertex set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ that is naturally labeled, meaning that whenever $i <_P j$ in $P$ one has $i < j$ as integers. A linear extension of $P$ is a permutation $\pi = \pi_1 \pi_2 \cdots \pi_n$ of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ such that if $i <_P j$ then $i$ appears before $j$ in $\pi$; let $\mathcal{L}(P)$ denote the set of all linear extensions of $P$. For a permutation $\pi$, let $\mathrm{des}(\pi) = \#\{i : \pi_i > \pi_{i+1}\}$ be the number of descents. Define the $P$-Eulerian polynomial
$$W(P,t) \;=\; \sum_{\pi \in \mathcal{L}(P)} t^{\mathrm{des}(\pi)+1}.$$
Question: Is it true that for every naturally labeled finite poset $P$, all complex zeros of $W(P,t)$ are real?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The statement is the Neggers conjecture (1978) for naturally labeled posets, a special case of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture. Brändén (2004) disproved Stanley's general (non-naturally labeled) version, and Stembridge subsequently produced naturally labeled counterexamples; the smallest naturally labeled narrow poset whose $W$-polynomial has non-real zeros has 17 vertices. Hence the answer is no in general.

A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent plane graph whose vertices are decorated as either classical crossings (with over/under information) or virtual crossings (drawn as a small circle), considered up to the generalized Reidemeister moves (the three classical Reidemeister moves, the three purely virtual moves, and the mixed semivirtual move). A flat virtual knot (equivalently, a virtual string) is the equivalence class of a virtual knot diagram in which the over/under information at every classical crossing is forgotten, so that classical crossings are simply transverse double points; the equivalence relation is generated by the corresponding flat versions of the generalized Reidemeister moves.

The flat biquandle algebra is the unital associative algebra generated by two invertible elements A and B subject to the relations obtained from the flat Reidemeister moves; it is known to be isomorphic to the Weyl algebra (the algebra generated by x, y with [x, y] = 1 over a field of characteristic zero), and consequently it admits no nontrivial finite-dimensional representations.

To date, the principal nontrivial combinatorial invariant of flat virtual knots is the mod 2 linking number (and small refinements thereof).

Problem: Construct new combinatorial invariants of flat virtual knots that distinguish pairs of flat virtual knots not separated by mod 2 linking numbers, and identify richer algebraic structures (beyond the flat biquandle / Weyl algebra) capable of detecting flat virtual-knot phenomena despite the absence of nontrivial finite-dimensional representations of the Weyl algebra.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The real-rootedness of the chain polynomial of a finite distributive lattice is equivalent to the Neggers–Stanley conjecture for naturally labeled posets. This conjecture was disproved: Stembridge and Brändén produced counterexamples (around 2004–2007), so in general the chain polynomial of a finite distributive lattice need not be real-rooted. Various special cases (face lattices of simplicial and cubical polytopes, noncrossing partition lattices, etc.) remain known to be real-rooted.

Fix an ordinal $\alpha$. Define the *flat $\alpha$-hierarchy of diagrams* as follows. A diagram is a 4-valent planar graph (with the usual virtual-crossing convention) whose classical-type crossings are flat (i.e. unsigned, with no over/under information) and each such flat crossing carries a label drawn from $\alpha$. Two diagrams are considered equivalent if they are related by a finite sequence of the following local moves, performed in any region of the plane:

(i) Planar isotopy and the standard detour move for virtual crossings (so virtual crossings behave as in flat virtual knot theory).

(ii) A flat first Reidemeister move that adds or removes a flat kink with an arbitrary label from $\alpha$.

(iii) A flat second Reidemeister move that creates or destroys a bigon whose two flat crossings carry the same label.

(iv) A *labeled flat third Reidemeister move*: a strand both of whose crossings on the boundary of a triangular region are labeled by the same element $a \in \alpha$ may be slid across a flat crossing labeled $b \in \alpha$ to the opposite side of that crossing if and only if $a > b$ in $\alpha$.

When $\alpha = 1$ this reduces to ordinary flat virtual knot theory (virtual strings).

Problem: Classify the equivalence classes of diagrams under these moves for an arbitrary ordinal $\alpha$, and describe in what precise sense the resulting theory generalizes flat virtual knot theory (e.g., construct complete or computable invariants distinguishing the classes, identify nontrivial elements arising at each level $a \in \alpha$, and determine the relationship between the hierarchies for $\alpha < \alpha'$).

Let $P$ be a finite poset. Say that $P$ is $(\mathbf{3}+\mathbf{1})$-free if $P$ contains no induced subposet isomorphic to the disjoint union of a 3-element chain and a 1-element chain. The incomparability graph $G=\operatorname{inc}(P)$ has vertex set equal to the elements of $P$, with two distinct vertices joined by an edge if and only if the corresponding elements are incomparable in $P$.

For a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$, the chromatic symmetric function is
$$X_G(x_1,x_2,\dots)=\sum_{\kappa}\prod_{v\in V}x_{\kappa(v)},$$
where the sum is over all proper colorings $\kappa:V\to\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ (i.e., $\kappa(u)\neq\kappa(v)$ whenever $\{u,v\}\in E$). For a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$, let $e_\lambda=e_{\lambda_1}e_{\lambda_2}\cdots$ where $e_k=\sum_{i_1<i_2<\cdots<i_k}x_{i_1}x_{i_2}\cdots x_{i_k}$ is the $k$-th elementary symmetric function. We say $X_G$ is $e$-positive if, when expanded in the basis $\{e_\lambda\}$, all coefficients are nonnegative.

Prove or disprove: for every $(\mathbf{3}+\mathbf{1})$-free finite poset $P$, the chromatic symmetric function $X_{\operatorname{inc}(P)}$ is $e$-positive.

This is the Stanley–Stembridge conjecture. A proof was announced by Tatsuyuki Hikita in October 2024 (arXiv:2410.12758), giving a probabilistic interpretation of the coefficients in the elementary symmetric function expansion of the chromatic (quasi)symmetric function for unit interval graphs, equivalent to the conjecture for incomparability graphs of (3+1)-free posets via results of Guay-Paquet.

Background and definitions.

(a) A flat virtual knot/link diagram is a 4-valent planar diagram whose crossings are of two kinds: flat (unoriented, undecorated) crossings and virtual crossings (drawn with a small circle). Two diagrams are equivalent as flat virtual links if they are related by a finite sequence of: (i) the flat Reidemeister moves on flat crossings, (ii) the virtual Reidemeister moves on virtual crossings, and (iii) the mixed "detour" move that allows an arc passing only through virtual crossings to be replaced by any other such arc with the same endpoints. (Crucially, the detour move is allowed for virtual crossings relative to flat crossings, but not vice versa.)

(b) A doodle is a finite collection of closed curves immersed in the 2-sphere (or in a closed oriented surface) having only transverse double points and no triple points, considered up to ambient isotopy and the doodle Reidemeister moves that exclude any move creating or destroying a triple point. One may also enlarge this category to "virtual doodles" by allowing, in addition to ordinary double points, virtual crossings subject to the virtual Reidemeister moves and the detour move.

(c) A cobordism between two doodles D_0 and D_1 is a compact immersed surface S in (surface)×[0,1] whose boundary is D_0⊔D_1, whose singular set consists only of double-point curves (i.e. S has no triple points and no branch points). Doodle cobordism is an equivalence relation, and the set of cobordism classes of doodles forms an abelian group under disjoint union; this group is conjectured/observed to be free abelian.

Problem. Develop a precise dictionary between the theory of flat virtual knots and links and the theory of (possibly virtual) doodles. Specifically:

1. Construct a well-defined map (or pair of mutually inverse maps) between equivalence classes of flat virtual links and equivalence classes of (virtual) doodles, and determine its kernel and image.

2. Define cobordism in both categories so that the dictionary of (1) descends to a homomorphism between the corresponding cobordism groups, and identify this homomorphism.

3. Determine the structure of the free-abelian cobordism group of doodles whose cobordisms are immersed surfaces without triple points: produce an explicit set of free generators (e.g. in terms of double-point–count invariants or homotopy classes of immersions), and compute the analogous group for virtual doodles.

4. For each of the categories above (flat virtual links, doodles, virtual doodles), describe the naturally associated group invariant (the analogue of the knot group / fundamental group of the complement / quandle-type group), and exhibit how these groups correspond under the dictionary of (1).

The problem of relating flat virtual knot theory to doodle theory (with or without virtual crossings) and describing the associated cobordism groups and group invariants appears in collections of unsolved problems on virtual knot theory and is the subject of ongoing research. Recent works (e.g. on free-knot invariants by Manturov, on doodle groups and twin groups, and on virtual knot cobordism) develop pieces of the picture but no complete dictionary or full computation of the free-abelian doodle-cobordism group has been established.

For a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$, a proper coloring is a function $\kappa: V\to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ with $\kappa(u)\neq \kappa(v)$ whenever $uv\in E$. The chromatic symmetric function of $G$ is
$$X_G(x_1,x_2,\dots) \;=\; \sum_{\kappa \text{ proper}} \prod_{v\in V} x_{\kappa(v)},$$
a symmetric function in the variables $x_1,x_2,\dots$ . For a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$, let $e_\lambda = e_{\lambda_1}e_{\lambda_2}\cdots$ where $e_k$ denotes the $k$-th elementary symmetric function. We say $X_G$ is $e$-positive if, when expanded in the basis $\{e_\lambda\}$, every coefficient is a nonnegative real number.

A graph $G$ is called claw-free if $G$ has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $K_{1,3}$, i.e., no vertex of $G$ has three pairwise non-adjacent neighbors.

Question: Is it true that for every finite claw-free graph $G$, the chromatic symmetric function $X_G$ is $e$-positive?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been answered in the negative. Dahlberg, She and van Willigenburg exhibited an infinite family of claw-free graphs (the "triangular tower" graphs $TT_{n,n,n}$ for $n\ge 3$) whose chromatic symmetric functions are not $e$-positive, refuting the conjecture that claw-freeness implies $e$-positivity.

Background. A classical closed orientable 3-manifold can be presented by integral Dehn surgery on a framed link in S^3, and two such links present homeomorphic 3-manifolds if and only if they are related by a finite sequence of Kirby moves (handle slides and stabilizations). A virtual link diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose crossings are labeled as classical (over/under) or virtual, considered up to the classical Reidemeister moves and the virtual Reidemeister moves. By extending the Kirby calculus to framed virtual link diagrams via "generalized Kirby moves," one obtains an equivalence relation on framed virtual links; the equivalence classes are called virtual 3-manifolds. Every classical framed link is in particular a virtual one, so this gives an equivalence relation on classical (ordinary) 3-manifolds (two ordinary 3-manifolds are virtually equivalent if their framed-link presentations are related through the virtual Kirby calculus).

Alternatively, for each closed orientable surface Σ_g one may consider framed links in the thickened surface Σ_g × ℝ and perform Dehn surgery on them; identifying surfaces and links under stabilization (adding a handle to Σ_g together with the corresponding inclusion of links) produces another candidate notion of "virtual 3-manifold."

Problems.
(a) Do the two equivalence relations on ordinary closed orientable 3-manifolds — homeomorphism, and virtual equivalence via generalized Kirby moves — coincide? Equivalently, if two framed links K, L ⊂ S^3 are equivalent via the virtual Kirby calculus, must they be equivalent via the classical Kirby calculus?

(b) Give a geometric-topological interpretation of the equivalence classes of framed virtual links under the virtual Kirby calculus: that is, identify what kind of geometric object a "virtual 3-manifold" is.

(c) Does the theory of virtual 3-manifolds defined via surgery on framed links in thickened surfaces Σ_g × ℝ, taken up to surface stabilization, coincide with the theory defined by virtual Kirby calculus on framed virtual link diagrams?

Web search did not surface a published resolution. The notion of virtual 3-manifolds via virtual Kirby calculus is established in work of Dye and Kauffman, and a thickened-surface/stabilization viewpoint is well known in virtual knot theory, but no source found explicitly proves that virtual Kirby equivalence of classical links implies classical Kirby equivalence, gives a definitive geometric-topological interpretation of virtual 3-manifolds, or proves equivalence of the two constructions. Status appears to remain open, but this could not be conclusively verified.

A graph G = (V, E) is called claw-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to the complete bipartite graph K_{1,3} (the "claw"). For a finite simple graph G, an independent (stable) set is a subset of V whose vertices are pairwise non-adjacent. Let s_i = s_i(G) denote the number of independent sets of G of cardinality exactly i (with s_0 = 1), and define the stable set (independence) polynomial
   I(G, t) = Σ_{i ≥ 0} s_i t^i.

Prove or disprove: for every finite claw-free graph G, all zeros of I(G, t) are real numbers.

Background and definitions.

A welded knot diagram is a generic immersion of a circle in the plane whose double points are decorated as either classical crossings (with over/under information) or welded (virtual) crossings. Two welded knot diagrams are equivalent if they are related by a finite sequence of the classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3, the virtual Reidemeister moves V1, V2, V3, the mixed move M (a classical strand passes through a welded crossing), and the over-commute (forbidden-overpass, F1) move in which an over-strand may slide past a virtual crossing. (The under-commute move F2 is NOT allowed.) A welded knot is an equivalence class of welded knot diagrams under these moves; welded links are defined analogously with several components.

The welded knot group of a welded knot K is the group with Wirtinger presentation read off from any of its diagrams (one generator per arc, one relation per classical crossing); this is a welded invariant.

Satoh's Tube map Tube assigns to every welded knot K an ambient isotopy class Tube(K) of an oriented embedded ribbon torus in S^4, by "inflating" each arc of a diagram into an annulus and resolving classical and welded crossings as ribbon singularities in 4-space. The map is well defined on welded equivalence classes, surjects onto ambient-isotopy classes of ribbon torus knots, and induces an isomorphism between the welded knot group of K and the fundamental group π_1(S^4 ∖ Tube(K)).

Problems. Provide answers to each of the following.

(a) Construct effective invariants of welded knots that, ideally, suffice to classify them up to welded equivalence.

(b) Decide whether the Tube map
      Tube : { welded knots } / (welded equivalence)  →  { ribbon torus knots in S^4 } / (ambient isotopy)
(and its analogue for welded links) is injective.

(c) Decide whether every welded knot K with trivial welded knot group (i.e. π_1 isomorphic to Z) is welded-equivalent to the unknot.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Recent work shows Satoh's Tube map is not injective: there exist non-trivial welded knots and links mapped to the same ribbon torus knot, and Y-type local moves on welded links have been identified as part of the kernel, though the kernel of Tube is not yet completely understood. It is also known that having welded knot group Z does not force a welded knot to be trivial; non-trivial welded knots with trivial group exist. The broader problem of constructing a complete set of invariants and a full classification of welded knots remains open.

Let $J$ denote the $n\times n$ matrix all of whose entries equal $1$, and for an $n\times n$ matrix $B=(b_{ij})$ let
$$\operatorname{per}(B)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n b_{i,\sigma(i)}$$
denote its permanent. Consider the univariate polynomial
$$P_A(t)=\operatorname{per}(A+tJ)\in\mathbb{R}[t].$$

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with real entries such that every column of $A$ is weakly increasing, i.e. $a_{1j}\le a_{2j}\le\cdots\le a_{nj}$ for each $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $J$ denote the $n\times n$ matrix all of whose entries equal $1$, and for an $n\times n$ matrix $B=(b_{ij})$ let 
$$\operatorname{per}(B)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n b_{i,\sigma(i)}$$
denote its permanent. Consider the univariate polynomial 
$$P_A(t)=\operatorname{per}(A+tJ)\in\mathbb{R}[t].$$
Prove or disprove: $P_A(t)$ has only real zeros.

A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent plane graph whose vertices are decorated as classical crossings (with over/under information) or as virtual crossings (drawn with a small circle), considered up to the generalized Reidemeister moves (the classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3 together with the virtual moves V1, V2, V3 and the mixed move M). A long virtual knot is the analogous object for a properly embedded oriented arc with a generic projection to the plane (one input and one output strand at infinity), again considered up to generalized Reidemeister moves performed in a compact region. A long flat virtual knot is obtained by forgetting the over/under information at every classical crossing, so that classical crossings are replaced by transverse double points and one works modulo the flat versions of R2, R3 and the virtual/mixed moves.

A biquandle is a set X equipped with two binary operations (a,b) ↦ a^b and (a,b) ↦ a_b satisfying the axioms ensuring invariance under the classical and virtual Reidemeister moves: each map x ↦ x^y and x ↦ x_y is a bijection, the "sideways" map S(a,b) = (b^a, a_b) is invertible, and the operations satisfy the exchange laws making the biquandle coloring of any virtual knot diagram well defined.

For a long flat virtual knot F, one may form its descending diagram D(F): traverse the long arc from input to output and at each double point encountered for the first time declare the strand to pass over the strand met later, producing a long virtual (non-flat) knot D(F).

Solve the following research program:

(a) Construct a strengthened invariant theory for long virtual knots that unifies the long-knot invariant framework (in which a long virtual knot is encoded by the algebraic word read along its strand, modulo relations corresponding to long-knot Reidemeister moves) with the biquandle coloring construction, and produce invariants of long virtual knots strictly stronger than those obtained from either framework alone.

(b) From this combined framework, extract new invariants of classical knots (long classical knots, viewed as long virtual knots whose diagrams have no virtual crossings) that are not equivalent to previously known classical invariants, or prove that no such new classical invariants arise.

(c) Using the descending-diagram assignment F ↦ D(F), give a complete classification of long flat virtual knots: namely, decide whether two long flat virtual knots F1 and F2 are equivalent if and only if D(F1) and D(F2) are equivalent as long virtual knots, and if not, determine the precise equivalence relation on long virtual knots induced by this assignment so as to obtain a full set of invariants classifying long flat virtual knots.

Let M be a matroid on a finite ground set E, with rank function r and rank n = r(E). Recall:

(i) The characteristic polynomial of M is χ_M(t) = Σ_{F flat} μ(̂0,F) t^{n−r(F)}, where μ is the Möbius function of the lattice of flats L(M). If G is a graph, the chromatic polynomial of G equals (up to a factor t^c, where c is the number of connected components) the characteristic polynomial of its cycle matroid.

(ii) Let f_i(M) denote the number of independent sets of M of size i (so f_0 = 1, and f_i = 0 for i > n). If G is a graph, f_i of its cycle matroid is the number of spanning forests of G with i edges.

(iii) A geometric lattice is a finite, atomistic, semimodular lattice; equivalently, the lattice of flats of a matroid. For a geometric lattice L of rank n, let W_i denote the number of elements of L of rank i.

A finite sequence a_0, a_1, …, a_n of nonnegative reals is called unimodal if there exists j with a_0 ≤ a_1 ≤ … ≤ a_j ≥ a_{j+1} ≥ … ≥ a_n, and log-concave if a_i^2 ≥ a_{i−1} a_{i+1} for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n−1.

Determine whether each of the following sequences is always unimodal, and whether it is always log-concave, as M (respectively L) ranges over all matroids (respectively geometric lattices):

(a) the absolute values |w_i| of the coefficients of χ_M(t) = Σ_{i=0}^n w_i t^{n−i};

(b) the sequence (f_0(M), f_1(M), …, f_n(M)) of numbers of independent sets of M of each size;

(c) the rank-level sequence (W_0, W_1, …, W_n) of a geometric lattice L.

Parts (a) and (b) have been resolved: log-concavity (hence unimodality) of the absolute coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of a matroid was proved by Adiprasito–Huh–Katz (Annals of Math., 2018), settling the Heron–Rota–Welsh conjecture. Log-concavity of the independent-set numbers (and even Mason's ultra-log-concavity conjecture) was proved by Brändén–Huh and independently Anari–Liu–Oveis Gharan–Vinzant (2018). Part (c), the long-standing Rota–Heron conjecture on whitney numbers of the second kind (W_i) of a geometric lattice, remains open in general; only partial results (e.g., for small ranks, certain classes, and recent partial progress via the combinatorial atlas of Chan–Pak) are known.

Setup. Let $R = k[x_1,\dots,x_r]$ be a polynomial ring over a field $k$. A finite, nonempty set $X$ of monomials in $R$ is called an order ideal (or "downset") if, whenever $m \in X$ and $m'$ divides $m$, then $m' \in X$. The order ideal $X$ is pure if all its maximal monomials (under divisibility) have the same degree. The pure O-sequence of $X$ is the vector $h = (h_0, h_1, \dots, h_e)$, where $h_i$ counts the number of monomials of degree $i$ in $X$ and $e$ is the common degree of the maximal monomials. A vector $(h_0,\dots,h_e)$ of nonnegative integers is called a pure O-sequence if it arises in this way for some pure order ideal; its codimension is $h_1$ (which equals the number of variables actually used).

Interval Property (IP). A class $\mathcal{C}$ of integer sequences is said to satisfy the Interval Property if, whenever $(h_0,\dots,h_e) \in \mathcal{C}$ and $(h_0,\dots,h_{i-1},h_i+\alpha,h_{i+1},\dots,h_e) \in \mathcal{C}$ for some index $i$ and some positive integer $\alpha$, then for every integer $\beta$ with $0 \le \beta \le \alpha$ the sequence
$$(h_0,\dots,h_{i-1},h_i+\beta,h_{i+1},\dots,h_e)$$
also belongs to $\mathcal{C}$.

Interval Conjecture for Pure O-sequences (ICP). The class of pure O-sequences satisfies the Interval Property.

Pure $f$-vectors. The pure $f$-vector of a pure simplicial complex $\Delta$ on a finite vertex set is $(f_{-1},f_0,\dots,f_{d-1})$, where $f_i$ is the number of $i$-dimensional faces of $\Delta$ and all facets have the same dimension $d-1$. A vector is called a pure $f$-vector if it arises as the $f$-vector of some pure simplicial complex.

Problem. Resolve the following:

(a) Does the Interval Property hold for the class of pure O-sequences in codimension three (i.e., when $h_1 = 3$)?

(b) Does the Interval Property hold for the class of pure O-sequences in arbitrary codimension?

(c) Does the Interval Property hold for the class of pure $f$-vectors?

(d) Determine the precise scope of the Interval Property: identify natural classes of integer sequences arising in combinatorial commutative algebra and enumerative combinatorics for which the Interval Property holds, and exhibit natural classes for which it fails.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Interval Conjecture for pure O-sequences (ICP) is widely cited as open in most cases, including codimension three. Subsequent work (e.g., by Boij–Migliore–Miró-Roig–Nagel–Zanello and others) has established partial structural results such as unimodality for codimension 3, type 2 pure O-sequences via the Weak Lefschetz Property, but no full proof of the ICP in codimension three appears in the literature. The Interval Property for pure $f$-vectors is also reported as wide open with little progress, and the precise scope of the Interval Property remains unclarified.

A virtual link diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose vertices are decorated either as classical crossings (with over/under information) or as virtual crossings (drawn with a small circle). A virtual biquandle is a set X equipped with two binary operations ▷, ▷* : X×X → X (for the classical crossings) and a bijection f : X → X (for the virtual crossings), satisfying:

(i) the biquandle axioms at classical crossings, ensuring invariance under the classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3;
(ii) the conditions making f compatible with the virtual Reidemeister moves V1, V2, V3 and the mixed move M, namely that f is a bijection and that the operations ▷, ▷* commute appropriately with f so that labeling rules at virtual crossings (where the outgoing labels are obtained by applying f and f⁻¹ to the incoming labels) yield an invariant of virtual links.

Given a unital (possibly non-commutative) ring R, a linear (non-commutative) representation of the classical biquandle operations on a free R-module M is a pair of formulas of the form
   a ▷ b = α·a + β·b ,    a ▷* b = γ·a + δ·b ,
with fixed elements α, β, γ, δ ∈ R chosen so that the biquandle axioms hold; these specify how the labels in M propagate through classical crossings.

Problem. Exhibit an explicit virtual biquandle (X, ▷, ▷*, f) of the following form:
 • X = M is a free module over a (non-commutative) ring R, with classical operations ▷, ▷* given by a fixed linear formula as above (a non-commutative analogue of the Alexander/Burau-type biquandle);
 • the virtual-crossing map f : M → M is given by a non-trivial algebraic operation (i.e., not equal to the identity and not reducible to a permutation that trivializes the virtual structure) producing a genuinely informative invariant of virtual links;
 • all virtual biquandle axioms (compatibility with the classical, virtual and mixed Reidemeister moves) are verified.

Provide the ring R, the module M, the constants α, β, γ, δ, and the map f explicitly.

Background and definitions.

The virtual braid group VB_n is the group with generators σ_1, …, σ_{n−1} (classical braid generators) and τ_1, …, τ_{n−1} (virtual generators) subject to:
• σ_i σ_j = σ_j σ_i and τ_i τ_j = τ_j τ_i for |i−j| ≥ 2;
• σ_i σ_{i+1} σ_i = σ_{i+1} σ_i σ_{i+1};
• τ_i^2 = 1, τ_i τ_{i+1} τ_i = τ_{i+1} τ_i τ_{i+1};
• σ_i τ_j = τ_j σ_i for |i−j| ≥ 2;
• τ_i τ_{i+1} σ_i = σ_{i+1} τ_i τ_{i+1}.

A birack is a set X equipped with a bijection S : X × X → X × X, written S(a,b) = (b^a, a_b), satisfying the set-theoretic Yang–Baxter equation
   (S × id)(id × S)(S × id) = (id × S)(S × id)(id × S)
on X × X × X, together with the invertibility/sideways conditions that make the maps a ↦ a_b and b ↦ b^a bijections (so that S yields a well-defined assignment for each generator σ_i of the virtual braid group, with τ_i acting by the transposition).

Given a birack (X, S), the assignments σ_i ↦ id^{i−1} × S × id^{n−i−1} and τ_i ↦ id^{i−1} × T × id^{n−i−1} (where T is the swap on X × X) define a homomorphism
   ρ_{X,S} : VB_n → Sym(X^n).

A linear biquandle is a birack arising from a pair of commuting invertible linear maps on a module, giving the Burau-like (Alexander) representation of VB_n.

Problems.

(1) Does there exist a birack (X, S) (allowing X infinite) such that the induced homomorphism ρ_{X,S} : VB_n → Sym(X^n) is faithful for every n ≥ 2?

(2) For the standard birack/biquandle invariant of virtual braids defined by a generic biquandle structure (in particular the "universal" birack invariant assigning to a virtual braid the tuple of output labels as a function of input labels), determine whether this invariant distinguishes all distinct virtual braids — i.e., whether it is faithful as an invariant on VB_n.

(3) Show that every linear biquandle action on VB_n fails to be faithful precisely because the induced linear invariant of the closure (a virtual link invariant) is not a complete invariant of virtual links; equivalently, identify whether the failure of faithfulness of linear biquandle actions on virtual braids comes from, and is equivalent to, the non-faithfulness of the corresponding linear invariant of virtual knots and links.

Background and definitions.

The virtual braid group VB_n is the group with generators σ_1, …, σ_{n−1} (classical braid generators) and τ_1, …, τ_{n−1} (virtual generators) subject to:
• σ_i σ_j = σ_j σ_i and τ_i τ_j = τ_j τ_i for |i−j| ≥ 2;
• σ_i σ_{i+1} σ_i = σ_{i+1} σ_i σ_{i+1};
• τ_i^2 = 1, τ_i τ_{i+1} τ_i = τ_{i+1} τ_i τ_{i+1};
• σ_i τ_j = τ_j σ_i for |i−j| ≥ 2;
• τ_i τ_{i+1} σ_i = σ_{i+1} τ_i τ_{i+1}.

A birack is a set X equipped with a bijection S : X × X → X × X, written S(a,b) = (b^a, a_b), satisfying the set-theoretic Yang–Baxter equation
   (S × id)(id × S)(S × id) = (id × S)(S × id)(id × S)
on X × X × X, together with the invertibility/sideways conditions that make the maps a ↦ a_b and b ↦ b^a bijections (so that S yields a well-defined assignment for each generator σ_i of the virtual braid group, with τ_i acting by the transposition).

Given a birack (X, S), the assignments σ_i ↦ id^{i−1} × S × id^{n−i−1} and τ_i ↦ id^{i−1} × T × id^{n−i−1} (where T is the swap on X × X) define a homomorphism
   ρ_{X,S} : VB_n → Sym(X^n).

A linear biquandle is a birack arising from a pair of commuting invertible linear maps on a module, giving the Burau-like (Alexander) representation of VB_n.

Problems.

(1) Does there exist a birack (X, S) (allowing X infinite) such that the induced homomorphism ρ_{X,S} : VB_n → Sym(X^n) is faithful for every n ≥ 2?

(2) For the standard birack/biquandle invariant of virtual braids defined by a generic biquandle structure (in particular the "universal" birack invariant assigning to a virtual braid the tuple of output labels as a function of input labels), determine whether this invariant distinguishes all distinct virtual braids — i.e., whether it is faithful as an invariant on VB_n.

(3) Show that every linear biquandle action on VB_n fails to be faithful precisely because the induced linear invariant of the closure (a virtual link invariant) is not a complete invariant of virtual links; equivalently, identify whether the failure of faithfulness of linear biquandle actions on virtual braids comes from, and is equivalent to, the non-faithfulness of the corresponding linear invariant of virtual knots and links.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent literature (e.g., works on birack modules, switch braid quivers, and bridging biquandle colorings of virtual links) continues to develop birack/biquandle invariants of virtual braids and virtual links, with results showing certain enhancements are strictly stronger than the unenhanced birack counting invariant, but no source confirms that any birack action on virtual braids has been shown to be faithful, nor that the linear-biquandle invariant has been proven faithful or proven to fail faithfulness for a reason independent of the corresponding link invariant. The questions therefore appear to remain open.

representations.normalized:
A virtual link diagram is a 4-valent planar diagram whose crossings are marked as classical (with over/under information) or virtual (drawn with a small circle). Virtual links are equivalence classes of oriented virtual link diagrams under the generalized Reidemeister moves (the three classical Reidemeister moves together with the four virtual Reidemeister moves).

A biquandle is a set X equipped with four binary operations a^b, a_b, a^{\bar b}, a_{\bar b} (right actions) satisfying:
(i) for all a,b in X, the maps b \mapsto a^b and b \mapsto a_b are bijections, and the operations with bars are their inverses;
(ii) for every a, there exists x with x^a = a and a_x = x, and a^a = a_a;
(iii) the exchange/biquandle axioms
   (a^b)^{c^b} = (a^c)^{b_c}, \quad (a_b)_{c_b} = (a_c)_{b_c}, \quad (a^b)_{c^b} = (a_c)^{b_c},
hold for all a,b,c in X.

The fundamental biquandle FB(L) of an oriented virtual link diagram L is the biquandle presented by one generator for each semi-arc of the diagram (a semi-arc is an edge between two consecutive under/virtual breaks) together with two relations at each classical crossing encoding the biquandle operations between incoming and outgoing semi-arcs (with no relations at virtual crossings beyond the identification of semi-arcs as one passes through). Up to isomorphism, FB(L) is an invariant of the oriented virtual link.

Given a virtual link L, let L^* denote the mirror image of L (obtained, say, by switching every classical crossing). It is known that FB(L) equals FB(L^{*r}), where L^{*r} denotes the orientation-reversed mirror image obtained by reflecting the diagram in a line in the diagram plane (equivalently, reflecting in a plane perpendicular to the diagram plane and reversing orientation).

Question: Does the fundamental biquandle classify oriented virtual links up to this known mirror-image ambiguity? That is, if L_1 and L_2 are oriented virtual links with FB(L_1) \cong FB(L_2) as biquandles, must L_1 be equivalent either to L_2 or to the orientation-reversed mirror image of L_2?

A biquandle structure on a set $X$ consists of two binary operations $\underline{\triangleright}, \overline{\triangleright}: X\times X\to X$ satisfying the following axioms:

(B1) For every $a\in X$, $a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,a = a\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a$.

(B2) The maps $\alpha_b: X\to X$, $\alpha_b(a)=a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b$, and $\beta_b: X\to X$, $\beta_b(a)=a\,\overline{\triangleright}\,b$, are bijections of $X$ for every $b\in X$, and the map $S: X\times X\to X\times X$ defined by $S(a,b)=(b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a,\, a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b)$ is a bijection.

(B3, exchange / Yang–Baxter type identities) For all $a,b,c\in X$,
$$(a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b)\,\underline{\triangleright}\,(c\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b) = (a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,c)\,\underline{\triangleright}\,(b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,c),$$
$$(a\,\overline{\triangleright}\,b)\,\overline{\triangleright}\,(c\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b) = (a\,\overline{\triangleright}\,c)\,\overline{\triangleright}\,(b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,c),$$
$$(b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a)\,\underline{\triangleright}\,(c\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a) = (b\,\underline{\triangleright}\,c)\,\overline{\triangleright}\,(a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,c).$$

Call $(X,\underline{\triangleright},\overline{\triangleright})$ a weak biquandle if it satisfies (B1), (B3), and the bijectivity of $\alpha_b,\beta_b$ together with the requirement that $S$ is a bijection, but where the additional "strong" condition
$$\text{for all } a,b\in X,\ \alpha_b(a)=a \iff \beta_a(b)=b$$
(equivalently, $a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b=a$ if and only if $b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a=b$) is not required. Call it a strong biquandle if this additional condition does hold.

Problem: Construct an explicit example of a weak biquandle $(X,\underline{\triangleright},\overline{\triangleright})$ that is not a strong biquandle, i.e., exhibit a set $X$ with operations $\underline{\triangleright},\overline{\triangleright}$ satisfying the weak biquandle axioms together with elements $a,b\in X$ such that exactly one of $a\,\underline{\triangleright}\,b=a$ and $b\,\overline{\triangleright}\,a=b$ holds.

Search results indicate that explicit examples of weak biquandles that are not strong have been constructed, in particular in the work "On axioms of biquandles," where a weak biquandle (using a construction involving the Prüfer group) is shown to fail the strong-biquandle axiom.
