Background and setup. A classical knot diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose vertices are decorated with over/under crossing information. A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent graph in the plane in which each vertex is marked either as a classical crossing (with over/under information) or as a virtual crossing (drawn with a small circle). Two virtual knot diagrams are said to be virtually equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of the classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3 together with the virtual Reidemeister moves V1, V2, V3 and the mixed move (a virtual triangle move involving one classical and two virtual crossings). A classical knot is called non-trivial if it is not virtually equivalent to the unknot.

The crossing virtualization operation replaces a chosen classical crossing c in a diagram by the local tangle obtained by switching c and then surrounding the resulting crossing by two virtual crossings on the two strands; equivalently, it is the local move that replaces a classical crossing by a "virtualized" crossing. This operation is known to preserve the Jones polynomial V (defined for virtual knots via the Kauffman bracket extended by setting the bracket of virtual crossings as identity) but can change the virtual isotopy class.

Say that a virtual knot K has unit Jones polynomial if V(K) = 1.

Questions.

(a) Let K be a non-trivial classical knot, and let K̃ be the virtual knot obtained from K by virtualizing some non-empty subset of its classical crossings. Suppose K̃ is non-trivial and has V(K̃) = 1. Must K̃ be non-classical (i.e. not virtually equivalent to any classical knot diagram), or is it possible for K̃ to be virtually equivalent to a classical knot?

(b) Suppose K is an arbitrary virtual knot diagram with V(K) = 1. Is K necessarily equivalent, under the combination of virtual equivalence and crossing virtualization, to a classical knot diagram?

(c) Suppose K and K′ are two classical knots such that K can be obtained from K′ by a finite sequence of crossing virtualizations and virtual Reidemeister moves (including the classical Reidemeister moves and the mixed move). Must K and K′ then be classically equivalent (i.e. ambient isotopic as classical knots in S³)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The questions concern detecting non-classicality of virtual knots with unit Jones polynomial obtained by virtualization. Examples of virtual knots with unit Jones polynomial that are not equivalent to any classical knot have been produced (notably using Manturov's parity bracket), but the general questions—whether every virtual knot with unit Jones polynomial reduces to a classical diagram via virtualization, and whether crossing virtualization plus virtual Reidemeister moves between classical knots forces classical equivalence—appear to remain open in the surveyed literature on virtual knot theory.

Virtual quandles were introduced by Manturov and quandle cocycle invariants have been extended to virtual knots in several works (e.g., Carter–Elhamdadi–Saito on twisted quandle homology, and follow-ups computing cocycle invariants of virtual knots). However, a full homology theory specifically tailored to virtual quandles in complete parallel to classical quandle homology, together with a systematic determination of the new virtual-knot invariants it produces, does not appear to have been developed comprehensively; partial constructions and examples exist, so the program is partially carried out rather than completed.

A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent plane graph whose vertices are decorated as either classical crossings (with over/under information) or virtual crossings (drawn as a small circle), considered up to the generalized Reidemeister moves (the classical Reidemeister moves R1, R2, R3 together with the virtual moves V1, V2, V3 and the mixed move M). Classical Khovanov homology assigns to each oriented classical link diagram L a bigraded chain complex C(L) of free abelian groups whose homotopy type is a link invariant; its homology Kh(L) categorifies the Jones polynomial.

Problem. Construct, in a combinatorial and diagrammatic way, a Khovanov-type chain complex C(D) of free abelian groups associated to an arbitrary virtual knot (or link) diagram D, defined over the ring of integers Z, such that:

(a) C(D) is invariant up to chain homotopy equivalence under the generalized Reidemeister moves, so that its homology Kh(D) is a virtual link invariant;
(b) when D is a classical diagram, C(D) is chain-homotopy equivalent to the classical Khovanov complex, and Kh(D) recovers the classical Khovanov homology;
(c) the construction extends, or is compatible with, existing partial constructions of Khovanov homology defined for those virtual diagrams whose associated abstract surface (atom) is orientable.

Using such a theory, address the following structural questions. Call a virtual knot K-full (respectively Kho-full) if it attains the maximal possible rank of an associated Kauffman-bracket-based (respectively Khovanov) invariant in a suitable sense made precise by the construction. Call a diagram D of a virtual knot K optimal if it realizes the maximum possible bigraded support of Kh(K).

(i) Classify all K-full virtual knots and all Kho-full virtual knots.
(ii) Determine whether every optimal diagram of a virtual knot is minimal with respect to the number of classical crossings.
(iii) Determine which diagrammatic moves preserve optimality of a diagram.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Manturov constructed a Khovanov-type homology for virtual knots over arbitrary coefficient rings (including Z), agreeing with classical Khovanov homology on classical diagrams. Subsequent works (Dye–Kaestner–Kauffman, Tubbenhauer, Rushworth, etc.) have extended and refined such constructions. However, the full package of structural questions (classification of K-full/Kho-full knots, minimality of optimal diagrams in classical crossing number, and characterization of optimality-preserving moves) remains open in general.

Let $\mathrm{TL}_n(d)$ denote the Temperley–Lieb algebra on $n$ strands with loop value $d$, generated by identity and elements $U_1,\dots,U_{n-1}$ subject to $U_i^2 = dU_i$, $U_iU_{i\pm 1}U_i = U_i$, and $U_iU_j = U_jU_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$. Inside $\mathrm{TL}_n(d)$, the Jones–Wenzl projector $p_n$ is the unique nonzero idempotent satisfying $p_n U_i = U_i p_n = 0$ for all $1\le i\le n-1$ (when $d$ avoids the relevant roots of unity).

Adjoin to $\mathrm{TL}_n(d)$ "virtual crossing" generators $v_1,\dots,v_{n-1}$, where each $v_i$ is an involution corresponding to a transposition of strands $i$ and $i+1$, satisfying the symmetric group relations $v_i^2 = 1$, $v_iv_{i+1}v_i = v_{i+1}v_iv_{i+1}$, $v_iv_j = v_jv_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$, together with the mixed relations
$$v_i U_j = U_j v_i \quad (|i-j|\ge 2), \qquad v_i v_{i+1} U_i = U_{i+1} v_i v_{i+1}, \qquad v_i U_i = U_i v_i = U_i$$
that make the resulting algebra isomorphic to the Brauer algebra $B_n(d)$.

(a) Determine the structure of the virtual analogues of the Jones–Wenzl projectors inside $B_n(d)$: explicitly describe idempotents $\tilde p_n \in B_n(d)$ characterized by $\tilde p_n U_i = U_i \tilde p_n = 0$ and $\tilde p_n v_i = v_i \tilde p_n = \tilde p_n$ for all $i$, and give a recursive or closed-form construction analogous to the Wenzl recursion.

(b) Decide whether classical Temperley–Lieb recoupling theory (the trivalent spin network calculus producing $6j$-symbols, theta nets, and the Kauffman–Lins evaluation of closed networks) admits a useful algebraic generalization to this Brauer-algebraic setting with virtual crossings, and if so formulate the corresponding recoupling identities (orthogonality, Biedenharn–Elliott, fusion).

A virtual knot may be presented either as a virtual knot diagram (a 4-valent planar diagram whose crossings are marked as classical over/under or virtual) modulo the generalized Reidemeister moves, or equivalently as a knot in a thickened orientable surface Σ × [0,1] modulo ambient isotopy and stabilization/destabilization of Σ. A "weave" on a surface Σ is the image of an immersed circle in Σ that gives a knot diagram on Σ (i.e. a knot in Σ × [0,1] together with its projection).

(a) Give a definition of "alternating virtual knot" and classify alternating virtual knots up to equivalence.

(b) Classify all alternating weaves on closed orientable surfaces, considered up to homeomorphism of the surface and Reidemeister moves on the surface, but without allowing stabilization (adding/removing handles to the surface).

(c) Formulate a virtual analogue of the Tait flyping conjecture — i.e. a statement asserting that any two reduced alternating diagrams (in the appropriate virtual or surface sense) representing the same virtual knot are related by a sequence of flypes — and prove it.

Substantial progress has been made. Boden and Karimi developed a theory of alternating virtual knots, and Boden–Karimi–Sikora proved Tait's first two conjectures for alternating links in thickened surfaces. A "virtual flyping theorem" was established (arXiv:2210.03720), proving the virtual analogue of Tait's flyping conjecture for alternating virtual links / links in thickened surfaces. Let $A$ and $B$ be positive (semidefinite) operators on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and let $\mathrm{Tr}$ denote the usual trace. For a real parameter $q$, consider the inequality
$$\mathrm{Tr}(A+B)^{q} \;\le\; \mathrm{Tr}\,A^{q} \;+\; \mathrm{Tr}\,B^{q} \;+\; (2q-2)\,\mathrm{Tr}\!\left(A^{1/2}BA^{1/2}\right)^{q/2}.$$
(Here $X^{q}$ for a positive operator $X$ is defined via the functional calculus; when $q<0$ the operators $A$, $B$, $A+B$ are assumed invertible.)

Prove or disprove the following two assertions:
1. The inequality above holds for every pair of positive operators $A,B$ and every real $q$ with $-2 < q < 0$.
2. The reverse inequality
$$\mathrm{Tr}(A+B)^{q} \;\ge\; \mathrm{Tr}\,A^{q} \;+\; \mathrm{Tr}\,B^{q} \;+\; (2q-2)\,\mathrm{Tr}\!\left(A^{1/2}BA^{1/2}\right)^{q/2}$$
holds for every pair of positive operators $A,B$ and every real $q \ge 3$.

Let L be a virtual link, i.e., an equivalence class of virtual link diagrams (4-valent planar graphs whose vertices are either classical crossings, marked with over/under information, or virtual crossings, marked with a small circle) under the generalized Reidemeister moves. For a virtual link L define:

- C(L) = the minimum, over all diagrams of L, of the number of classical crossings;
- V(L) = the minimum, over all diagrams of L, of the number of virtual crossings;
- T(L) = the minimum, over all diagrams of L, of the total number of crossings (classical plus virtual).

Investigate the following questions:

(a) Determine the relationships among C(L), V(L), and T(L). In particular, decide whether the equality
        T(L) = C(L) + V(L)
holds for every virtual link L, or exhibit virtual links for which T(L) is strictly smaller than C(L) + V(L).

(b) Define the virtual unknotting number u_v(L) as the minimum number of classical crossing changes (in any diagram of L) needed to transform L into the unknot in the virtual category, and study its basic properties (additivity under connected sum, lower bounds in terms of invariants, computability).

(c) Every virtual knot can be represented as a knot in a thickened oriented closed surface up to stabilisation; let g(L) denote the minimal genus of such a surface representative. Determine the precise relationship between V(L) and g(L) (e.g., whether V(L) ≥ 2g(L), or sharper bounds).

(d) Provide effective algorithms or polynomial-time bounds for computing or estimating C(L), V(L), T(L), u_v(L), and g(L) from a given virtual link diagram.

The questions remain largely open. Work by Manturov and others (e.g., "On Virtual Crossing Numbers for Virtual Knots", arXiv:1107.4828) shows that V(L) can grow quadratically in C(L), refuting earlier linear conjectures, but the exact relationship among C, V, T is not determined; the virtual unknotting number is poorly understood; and no general polynomial-time algorithms for these invariants are known. Recent work (e.g., arXiv:2312.03994 on flat virtual knots) continues to study connected-sum/crossing-number relations without resolving the general problems.

A virtual link diagram is a 4-valent plane graph each of whose vertices is decorated either as a classical crossing (with over/under information) or as a virtual crossing (drawn as a small circle). Two virtual link diagrams are called tamely equivalent if they are related by a finite sequence of classical Reidemeister moves and the detour (virtual) moves; the resulting equivalence classes are the (tame) virtual links.

By analogy with the classical theory, where wild knots are obtained from tame knots by allowing limit points of "infinitely many shrinking crossings", one wishes to enlarge the class of virtual link diagrams so as to permit diagrams with infinitely many crossings accumulating at limit points (and possibly with limit points of limit points, etc.), together with a notion of "wild Reidemeister/detour equivalence" allowing infinite sequences of moves whose supports shrink to such limit points.

The problem has two parts:

(1) Define a category WVK of wild virtual knots: specify precisely the objects (a class of generalized virtual link diagrams admitting wild behavior), the morphisms or equivalence relation (a wild analogue of the classical and detour Reidemeister moves), and a complete list of axioms making this into a well-defined category that contains the category of tame virtual links as a full subcategory and that reduces to the classical theory of wild knots in the absence of virtual crossings.

(2) Within the category WVK so constructed, formulate and prove a criterion (a "tameness theorem") giving necessary and sufficient conditions on two tame virtual links L_1 and L_2 under which the existence of a wild equivalence between L_1 and L_2 in WVK implies that L_1 and L_2 are already tamely equivalent as virtual links.

Let $\mathbb{P}_n$ denote the set of $n\times n$ positive definite complex matrices. For $X,Y\in\mathbb{P}_n$ and $t\in[0,1]$, define the weighted matrix power mean of order $r\in[-1,1]\setminus\{0\}$ by
$$\mu_t^{(r)}(X,Y) = \big((1-t)X^{r} + tY^{r}\big)^{1/r},$$
with $\mu_t^{(0)}(X,Y) := X^{1/2}(X^{-1/2}YX^{-1/2})^{t}X^{1/2}$ (the weighted geometric mean) understood as the limit $r\to 0$. For $q\in[1,\infty]$, let $\|\cdot\|_q$ denote the Schatten $q$-norm on $n\times n$ matrices, and define the associated $L_q$ distance
$$\delta_q(X,Y) = \|X-Y\|_q.$$

Determine the pairs $(r,q)$ and additional hypotheses on $X,Y\in\mathbb{P}_n$ (if any) for which the function
$$t\longmapsto \delta_q\big(\mu_t^{(r)}(X,Y),\,Y\big)$$
is monotone (non-increasing) on $[0,1]$. In particular, characterize the largest range of $q\in[1,\infty]$ for which this monotonicity holds for every $X,Y\in\mathbb{P}_n$.

Background. A virtual knot diagram is a knot diagram in the plane in which each double point is labelled either as a classical crossing (over/under) or as a virtual crossing (a small circle). Virtual knots are equivalence classes of such diagrams under the generalized Reidemeister moves (the classical Reidemeister moves together with the virtual and mixed moves of Kauffman). A long virtual knot is the analogous notion for a 1-1 tangle: a virtual knot diagram with two free ends going to infinity, considered up to generalized Reidemeister moves fixing the ends.

Singular extension and finite-type (Vassiliev) invariants. A singular (virtual) knot is a (virtual) knot diagram allowed to have finitely many transverse classical double points. Any invariant v of (virtual) knots with values in an abelian group is extended to singular (virtual) knots by the Vassiliev skein relation
   v(D_×) = v(D_+) − v(D_−),
where D_+, D_− denote the two classical resolutions of a transverse double point D_×. The invariant v is said to be of finite type of order ≤ n (a Vassiliev invariant of order ≤ n) if its extension vanishes on every singular (virtual) knot with more than n double points. For long virtual knots one uses the same definition with singular long virtual diagrams.

Polynomial invariants. Let P denote the collection of polynomial-type invariants of virtual knots (for example, Kauffman's f-polynomial / bracket polynomial for virtual knots, the Sawollek / Alexander-type polynomial of a virtual knot, the arrow polynomial, and similar invariants).

Problems.
(a) Determine the precise relationship between the polynomial invariants in P and the Vassiliev (finite-type) invariants of virtual knots in Kauffman's sense: specifically, characterize which coefficients, evaluations, or derived numerical functions of these polynomials are finite-type invariants, and identify the order of each such finite-type invariant.

(b) Decide whether every finite-type (Vassiliev) invariant of classical knots extends to a finite-type invariant of long virtual knots of the same order. That is, for every Vassiliev invariant v of order ≤ n on classical knots (valued in an abelian group), does there exist a finite-type invariant V of order ≤ n on long virtual knots whose restriction to classical long knots equals v?

(c) An alternate notion of finite-type invariant for virtual knots may be formulated using moves other than the standard Vassiliev double-point resolution (for instance, by replacing the local change D_+ − D_− with a virtualization move or another local replacement on virtual diagrams). Investigate this alternate finite-type theory: compare the resulting filtration on the space of virtual-knot invariants with the Kauffman/Goussarov–Polyak–Viro filtrations, and determine which classical Vassiliev invariants extend in this alternate sense.

Background and definitions.

(a) A classical knot is a smooth embedding $K\colon S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$, considered up to ambient isotopy. Such a knot is (smoothly) slice in the classical sense if it bounds a smoothly embedded disk in the 4-ball $B^4$.

(b) A virtual knot (in Kauffman's sense) is an equivalence class of Gauss diagrams, equivalently a knot in a thickened surface $\Sigma\times[0,1]$ modulo orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $\Sigma$ and stabilization/destabilization (adding or removing handles to $\Sigma$ disjoint from the knot). A virtual knot is slice in the sense of Kauffman if its representative bounds an immersed disk realizable by a sequence of births, saddles, deaths and virtual moves whose total Euler characteristic equals $1$, equivalently if it is concordant to the unknot in the virtual concordance category.

(c) For a closed oriented surface $\Sigma$, a knot $K\subset \Sigma\times[0,1]$ is slice in the sense of Turaev if there exists a compact oriented $3$-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=\Sigma$ and a smoothly (properly) embedded disk $D\hookrightarrow W\times[0,1]$ with $\partial D=K\subset \Sigma\times\{0\}\subset \partial(W\times[0,1])$.

Stabilization. Given $K\subset \Sigma\times[0,1]$, attaching a $1$-handle to $\Sigma$ disjoint from $K$ yields a knot in $\Sigma'\times[0,1]$; the equivalence class under all such stabilizations and destabilizations is the underlying virtual knot of $K$.

Questions.
(1) Does there exist a classical knot $K\subset S^3$ that is not slice in the classical sense, but, when regarded as a virtual knot via the standard inclusion $S^2\hookrightarrow \Sigma$, is slice in the sense of Kauffman, or, when regarded as a knot in a thickened surface, is slice in the sense of Turaev?

(2) If a knot $K\subset \Sigma\times[0,1]$ is slice in the sense of Turaev, must its associated virtual knot (obtained by stabilization) be slice in the sense of Kauffman?

Let $VB_n$ denote the virtual braid group on $n$ strands, defined as the group with generators $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ (classical braid generators) and $\rho_1,\dots,\rho_{n-1}$ (virtual generators) subject to the relations:
- $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j = \sigma_j\sigma_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$;
- $\rho_i^2 = 1$, $\rho_i\rho_{i+1}\rho_i = \rho_{i+1}\rho_i\rho_{i+1}$, $\rho_i\rho_j=\rho_j\rho_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$;
- $\sigma_i\rho_j=\rho_j\sigma_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$ and $\rho_i\rho_{i+1}\sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1}\rho_i\rho_{i+1}$.

Let $F_{n+1}$ be the free group of rank $n+1$ with basis $x_1,\dots,x_n,y$, and let $\rho:VB_n\to \operatorname{Aut}(F_{n+1})$ be the homomorphism given by
$$\sigma_i:\ x_i\mapsto x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1},\ x_{i+1}\mapsto x_i,\ x_k\mapsto x_k\ (k\ne i,i+1),\ y\mapsto y,$$
$$\rho_i:\ x_i\mapsto y x_{i+1} y^{-1},\ x_{i+1}\mapsto y^{-1} x_i y,\ x_k\mapsto x_k\ (k\ne i,i+1),\ y\mapsto y.$$

Let $WB_n$ denote the welded braid group, obtained from $VB_n$ by additionally imposing the mixed relation $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\rho_i = \rho_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$, and let $\rho_A:VB_n\to WB_n$ be the natural projection. Virtual links are equivalence classes of closures of virtual braids modulo the virtual Reidemeister moves; welded links are obtained by additionally allowing the forbidden over-crossing move.

Settle the following:

(a) Is $VB_n$ a linear group (i.e., does it admit a faithful finite-dimensional representation over a field) for every $n>3$?

(b) Is the homomorphism $\rho:VB_n\to\operatorname{Aut}(F_{n+1})$ described above faithful for every $n>2$?

(c) Do there exist non-equivalent virtual links $L_v$ and $L'_v$, realized as closures of virtual braids $\beta,\beta'\in VB_n$, such that the welded links obtained as the closures of $\rho_A(\beta)$ and $\rho_A(\beta')$ in $WB_n$ are equivalent as welded links?

A long virtual knot is an equivalence class of immersed oriented arcs in the plane, with finitely many double points each marked as either a classical crossing (with over/under information) or a virtual crossing, that coincide with a fixed horizontal line outside a compact region, taken modulo planar isotopy and the generalized Reidemeister moves of virtual knot theory. The set of long virtual knots forms a monoid under the concatenation operation #, in which two long virtual knots are joined end to end; the unit is the trivial long knot. A long virtual knot K is called prime if K is non-trivial and whenever K ≅ A # B, then either A or B is trivial. A long virtual knot is called classical if it admits a diagram with no virtual crossings, and non-classical otherwise.

(a) Prove that every non-trivial long virtual knot K admits a decomposition K ≅ P₁ # P₂ # ⋯ # Pₙ as a finite concatenation of prime long virtual knots.

(b) Prove that such a prime decomposition is unique in the following sense: if P₁ # ⋯ # Pₙ ≅ Q₁ # ⋯ # Qₘ where all Pᵢ and Qⱼ are prime long virtual knots, then n = m and Pᵢ ≅ Qᵢ for every i (note that # is not commutative on long virtual knots, so the order matters).

(c) Determine whether, when A and B are prime non-classical long virtual knots, the concatenation A # B can ever admit an essentially different decomposition into the same prime factors A and B (for instance A # B ≅ B # A or any other rearrangement realized in the monoid).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

A uniqueness theorem for prime decompositions of long virtual knots in the non-classical regime was established by M. Chrisman (arXiv:1311.5748): if A, B, C, D are prime non-classical long virtual knots with A#B non-classical and A#B ≅ C#D, then A ≅ C and B ≅ D. The monoid of long virtual knots is known to be non-commutative. A complete existence-and-uniqueness theorem for prime decompositions of arbitrary long virtual knots (covering mixed classical/non-classical factors and arbitrary lengths) does not appear to have been fully established, so the problem is partially solved.

Background. Let L = K ∪ J be an oriented two-component link in S^3 with J a (possibly trivial) component such that the linking number lk(K, J) = 0. Choose a Seifert surface Σ for J, push it off to obtain a thickened surface neighborhood N(Σ) ≅ Σ × [−1, 1] disjoint from K, and let Σ_g be a closed orientable surface obtained by capping or stabilizing Σ. The "virtual cover" construction associates to (K, J) (together with a choice of Σ) a virtual knot v(K, J) ∈ Σ_g × I, well defined up to a controlled set of stabilizations and isotopies of Σ in S^3 \ K. This produces a map from a class of two-component classical links in S^3 to the set of virtual-knot types.

Problem. Develop and resolve the following items concerning the virtual-cover construction.

(a) Knot extension. Formulate an effective extension of the virtual-cover construction that takes as input a one-component link (i.e. a classical knot) K ⊂ S^3 and produces an associated virtual-knot invariant, in such a way that nontrivial classical information about K is detected.

(b) Relation to Milnor invariants. For an oriented link L = K ∪ J in S^3 with lk(K, J) = 0, exhibit an explicit relation between Milnor's μ-invariants μ_L(I) of L and invariants (e.g. polynomial, quandle, or concordance invariants) of the virtual knot v(K, J). In particular, identify which μ-invariants of L are recovered from v(K, J).

(c) Behavior under local moves. Determine how the virtual-knot type of v(K, J) changes when L is altered by each of the following local operations applied to the classical link L: (i) a single crossing change, (ii) a self-Δ-move on K, (iii) a Z-move. In each case, give a sharp description of the resulting change in v(K, J) (invariance, controlled stabilization, or specific virtual local move).

(d) Mutation. Decide whether the virtual-knot type v(K, J) can distinguish a link L = K ∪ J from any of its Conway mutants L'; equivalently, exhibit a pair (L, L') of mutant two-component classical links whose associated virtual knots are not virtually isotopic, or prove that no such pair exists.

(e) Complete move set. Find a finite list M_1, …, M_n of local moves on the class of two-component oriented links L = K ∪ J ⊂ S^3 with lk(K, J) = 0 such that, for two such links L and L', the associated virtual knots v(K, J) and v(K', J') are virtually isotopic if and only if L can be transformed into L' by a finite sequence of ambient isotopies and the moves M_1, …, M_n.

A complete solution consists of precise definitions making (a)–(e) well posed and proofs of the corresponding statements.

Let $H$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal{S}_p$ denote the Schatten $p$-class of compact operators on $H$, with norm $\|T\|_p = (\operatorname{tr}|T|^p)^{1/p}$ for $1\le p<\infty$ (and the corresponding quasi-norm for $0<p<1$). Fix an integer $n\ge 2$ and let $A_0,A_1,\dots,A_{n-1}\in\mathcal{S}_p$. Let $p$ and $q$ be conjugate exponents, $\tfrac1p+\tfrac1q=1$.

Decide whether the following Clarkson-type $n$-tuple inequalities always hold:

(i) For $2\le p<\infty$,
$$ n\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\|A_j\|_p^{\,p}\Bigr)^{q/p} \;\le\; \Bigl\|\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} A_j\Bigr\|_p^{\,q} \;+\; \sum_{0\le j<k\le n-1}\|A_j-A_k\|_p^{\,q}. $$

(ii) For $0<p\le 2$, the reversed inequality
$$ n\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\|A_j\|_p^{\,p}\Bigr)^{q/p} \;\ge\; \Bigl\|\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} A_j\Bigr\|_p^{\,q} \;+\; \sum_{0\le j<k\le n-1}\|A_j-A_k\|_p^{\,q}. $$

Prove these inequalities for all such $n$-tuples, or otherwise produce a counterexample.

For an integer $n\ge 2$ and a real number $\mu$, let $\mathcal{M}_n(\mu)$ denote the set of all probability distributions $F$ on $\mathbb{R}$ (respectively on $\mathbb{R}^d$, with $\mu\in\mathbb{R}^d$) for which there exist random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$, each having distribution $F$, such that
$$X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n = n\mu \quad \text{almost surely}.$$
A distribution $F$ is called $n$-completely mixable if $F\in\mathcal{M}_n(\mu)$ for some $\mu$, and any such $\mu$ is called a center of mixability of $F$.

Question: Is the center of mixability necessarily unique? Equivalently, prove or disprove that for every $n\ge 2$ and every pair of distinct real numbers (or vectors) $\mu\ne\nu$,
$$\mathcal{M}_n(\mu)\cap\mathcal{M}_n(\nu)=\varnothing.$$

Setup. For an integer $n\ge 2$, an $n$-tuple of one-dimensional probability distributions $(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is said to be jointly mixable if there exist random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ defined on a common probability space, with $X_i\sim F_i$ for each $i$, such that
$$P(X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n = c) = 1$$
for some constant $c\in\mathbb{R}$ (called a center of the joint mix). The realization $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ is called a joint mix. A distribution $F$ is called $n$-completely mixable if the $n$-tuple $(F,F,\ldots,F)$ is jointly mixable; the corresponding center is then necessarily $n\,\mathbb{E}_F[X]$ when the mean exists.

Known structural theorems give sufficient conditions for complete mixability and joint mixability — for example, that any distribution on $[a,b]$ with monotone density and mean satisfying the obvious necessary condition $a+(n-1)b \le n\mu \le (n-1)a+b$ is $n$-completely mixable, and analogous results for unimodal-symmetric distributions, concave/convex densities, and certain tuples of distributions. The currently available proofs proceed by discretizing the distributions, decomposing the discretizations as convex combinations of completely mixable atomic distributions established by combinatorial arguments, and then passing to a weak limit; in particular, they rely on induction on the support size of the discretization and do not exhibit an explicit description of the joint dependence structure of the resulting joint mix.

Problem. Provide a generic probabilistic or analytic proof of the principal complete-mixability and joint-mixability theorems for absolutely continuous distributions (in particular, the result for distributions on a bounded interval with monotone density, and the result for jointly mixable tuples with monotone or concave/convex densities) that:
(a) does not invoke induction on discretized approximations or a combinatorial decomposition of finitely supported measures, and
(b) renders explicit, or at least transparent, the joint dependence structure (e.g. the copula or a constructive coupling) of the random vector $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ realizing the joint mix.

Either produce such a proof and the associated explicit coupling, or show that no such generic argument with the stated properties can exist.

The question is listed as an open problem in the survey "Current open questions in complete mixability" (Probability Surveys, 2015) and is reiterated in subsequent works on joint mixability. Subsequent literature (e.g. Wang–Wang 2016 on joint mixability, papers on elliptical distributions 2017, and later surveys) provides new sufficient conditions and explicit couplings in special cases (elliptical/unimodal-symmetric families) but no generic probabilistic/analytic proof replacing the combinatorial discretization technique for the main results has been reported. The problem appears to remain open, with only partial progress in special families.

Let $\mathbb{Z}_+ = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$. A random vector $X = (X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(n)})$ taking values in $\mathbb{Z}_+^n$ is called a joint mix with joint center $N \in \mathbb{Z}_+$ if $X^{(1)} + X^{(2)} + \cdots + X^{(n)} = N$ almost surely. A binary multinomial random vector is a random vector $Y = (Y^{(1)},\dots,Y^{(n)}) \in \{0,1\}^n$ with $Y^{(1)}+\cdots+Y^{(n)} = 1$ almost surely (equivalently, multinomial with one trial and some probability vector $(p_1,\dots,p_n)$).

It is known that a $\mathbb{Z}_+^n$-valued random vector $X$ is a joint mix with joint center $N$ if and only if it admits a representation
$$X = \sum_{k=1}^{N} X_k,$$
where $X_1,\dots,X_N$ are (not necessarily independent) binary multinomial random vectors.

Recall that an $n$-tuple of one-dimensional distributions $(F_1,\dots,F_n)$ is jointly mixable (JM) if there exist random variables $Y_i \sim F_i$ such that $Y_1 + \cdots + Y_n$ is almost surely constant; if additionally $F_1 = \cdots = F_n = F$, then $F$ is called completely mixable (CM).

Problem: Determine whether the above decomposition of $\mathbb{Z}_+^n$-valued joint mixes into sums of binary multinomial random vectors can be used in a non-trivial way to characterize new classes of completely mixable or jointly mixable distributions, and if so, exhibit such a characterization.

Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and let $\mathrm{Tr}$ denote the usual matrix trace on $B(\mathcal{H})$. For a self-adjoint operator $X$, write $|X| = \sqrt{X^*X}$. There is a known multivariate trace inequality of the form
$$\mathrm{Tr}\,\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^n A_j^{\,2}} \; \le \; \sum_{j=1}^n \mathrm{Tr}\,A_j ,$$
valid whenever $A_1,\dots,A_n$ are positive semidefinite operators on $\mathcal{H}$ (so that the square root on the left is the unique positive square root of $\sum_j A_j^{\,2}$).

The problem is to determine whether this inequality admits a modification (for instance, by replacing each $A_j$ on the right-hand side with $|A_j|$, or by another natural substitute) that remains valid for arbitrary operators $A_1,\dots,A_n \in B(\mathcal{H})$, with no assumption of positivity or normality. Let $d \ge 1$ be an integer. A probability distribution $F$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is called $n$-completely mixable (for an integer $n \ge 2$) if there exist $n$ random vectors $X_1, \dots, X_n$, each with marginal distribution $F$, such that
$$X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n = n\,\mu \quad 	ext{almost surely},$$
for some constant $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (necessarily the mean of $F$ when it exists).

Let $C \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded convex set of positive Lebesgue measure, and let $F$ be the uniform distribution on $C$.

Question: Is $F$ necessarily $n$-completely mixable for every integer $n \ge d+1$? Equivalently (the property for $n=d+1$ implies it for all larger $n$ by standard arguments), is the uniform distribution on every bounded convex set $C \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ always $(d+1)$-completely mixable?

Background and definitions. Let n ≥ 2 be an integer and let F be a probability distribution on R^d with d ≥ 2. The distribution F is said to be n-completely mixable (n-CM) if there exist random vectors X_1, ..., X_n on a common probability space, each with marginal distribution F, such that the sum X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n is almost surely equal to a constant vector in R^d.

For a linear subspace V ⊆ R^d, let π_V : R^d → V denote the orthogonal projection onto V, and let π_V(F) denote the pushforward (projection) distribution of F under π_V. A subspace V ⊆ R^d is called essential for F if the projection π_V(F) is not concentrated on a proper affine subspace of V (equivalently, the support of π_V(F) affinely spans V).

Problem. Suppose that for every essential subspace V of R^d the projected distribution π_V(F) is n-completely mixable on V. Determine additional conditions on F (or on the family of its projections) under which one can conclude that F itself is n-completely mixable on R^d.

A probability distribution F on the real line is called n-completely mixable (n-CM), for an integer n ≥ 2, if there exist random variables X_1, …, X_n, each with marginal distribution F, defined on a common probability space, such that the sum X_1 + X_2 + ⋯ + X_n is almost surely constant. The distribution F is said to be asymptotically completely mixable if there exists an integer N such that F is n-CM for every n ≥ N.

It is known that any distribution F on a bounded interval [a,b] ⊂ ℝ that is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure and whose density is bounded away from zero on [a,b] (i.e. ess inf_{x∈[a,b]} f(x) > 0, where f = dF/dx) is n-CM for all sufficiently large n.

Question: Does the conclusion remain true without the lower-bound assumption on the density? Equivalently, is every absolutely continuous probability distribution supported on a bounded interval [a,b] necessarily n-completely mixable for all sufficiently large n?

Suppose that $F$ is known to be $n$-CM (for instance, because it satisfies one of the standard sufficient conditions, such as: $F$ has a symmetric and unimodal density on a bounded interval, or $F$ has a decreasing density satisfying an appropriate mean condition).

Problem. Provide an explicit description of a copula $C:[0,1]^n \to [0,1]$ such that the joint distribution
$$H(x_1,\dots,x_n) = C\bigl(F(x_1),\dots,F(x_n)\bigr)$$
has marginals $F$ and is supported on the hyperplane $\{x_1+\cdots+x_n=c\}$ (i.e., realizes an $n$-complete mix with margins $F$). More generally, for given margins $F_1,\dots,F_n$ that are jointly mixable, give an explicit copula realizing a joint mix with these margins.

Let $F$ be a probability distribution on the real line. For an integer $n\ge 2$, $F$ is called $n$-completely mixable ($n$-CM) if there exist $n$ random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$, each with distribution $F$, such that
$$X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n = n c \quad \text{almost surely}$$
for some constant $c\in\mathbb{R}$ (called a center of $F$). A distribution $F$ on a bounded interval $[a,b]$ with mean $\mu$ is said to satisfy the mean condition (for $n$-complete mixability) if
$$b-a \le n(\mu-a) \quad \text{and} \quad b-a \le n(b-\mu).$$
A density $f$ on $[a,b]$ is unimodal if there exists $m\in[a,b]$ such that $f$ is non-decreasing on $[a,m]$ and non-increasing on $[m,b]$.

It is known that:
(i) every continuous distribution with a symmetric unimodal density is $n$-CM for every $n\ge 2$;
(ii) there exist distributions with a unimodal density on a bounded interval and satisfying the mean condition that are not $n$-CM, so unimodality together with the mean condition is not sufficient in general.

Problem. Find natural additional conditions on a unimodal distribution $F$ supported on a bounded interval $[a,b]$ (beyond unimodality and the mean condition) that are sufficient to guarantee that $F$ is $n$-completely mixable for a given $n\ge 2$.

Background. Given univariate distribution functions $F_1,\ldots,F_n$, the tuple $(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ is called jointly mixable if there exist random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ defined on a common probability space, with $X_i\sim F_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$, such that the sum $X_1+\cdots+X_n$ is almost surely constant. When $F_1=\cdots=F_n=F$, $F$ is said to be $n$-completely mixable.

The Rearrangement (swapping) Algorithm operates on an $N\times n$ matrix $A=(a_{i,j})$ whose $j$-th column consists of $N$ equiprobable quantiles of $F_j$. At each step one chooses a column $j$ and rearranges its entries so as to be oppositely ordered to the row sums of the remaining $n-1$ columns; this is iterated over columns until a stopping criterion is met. The algorithm is used both to numerically detect joint mixability (by trying to drive $\max_i\sum_j a_{i,j} - \min_i\sum_j a_{i,j}$ to zero) and, more generally, to address the minimax assignment problem of permuting entries within each column of a given non-negative matrix $A=(a_{i,j})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n}$ so as to minimize $\max_{1\le i\le N}\sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,\sigma_j(i)}$, where each $\sigma_j$ is a permutation of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

Problem.
(a) Design algorithms that, given $F_1,\ldots,F_n$ (or given quantile matrices approximating them), decide whether $(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ is jointly mixable, and that compute (or approximate) the minimum of $\max_{1\le i\le N}\sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,\sigma_j(i)}$ over all column-permutations $(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n)$ of a given matrix $A$.
(b) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the input distributions $F_1,\ldots,F_n$ (respectively on the matrix $A$) under which the Rearrangement (swapping) Algorithm converges to a globally optimal arrangement, and quantify its rate of convergence.

representations.normalized:
A tuple of univariate cumulative distribution functions $(F_1, \dots, F_n)$ is said to be jointly mixable if there exist random variables $X_1, \dots, X_n$, defined on a common probability space, with $X_i \sim F_i$ for each $i$, such that the sum $X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ is almost surely equal to a constant. Such a random vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ is called a joint mix.

Now consider the following extension. Let $n \ge 3$ and partition the index set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into (possibly overlapping) subsets $S_1,\dots,S_m \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}$, each of cardinality at least $2$. For each $k \in \{1,\dots,m\}$, prescribe a multivariate distribution $H_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^{|S_k|}$. Say that a joint mix compatible with these higher-dimensional marginal constraints exists if there is a random vector $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ such that:
(i) for every $k$, the subvector $(X_i)_{i \in S_k}$ has joint distribution $H_k$; and
(ii) $X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ is almost surely constant.

Solve the following:

(a) Characterize, in terms of the prescribed multivariate marginals $\{H_k\}$, when a joint mix compatible with these constraints exists.

(b) In the special case where $m \ge 2$ subsets $S_k$ are pairs (so each $H_k$ is a bivariate distribution) with consistent univariate marginals, give necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of such a joint mix.

(c) Develop an effective numerical algorithm that, given the prescribed multivariate marginals $\{H_k\}$ (or sufficiently regular approximations thereof), decides whether a joint mix compatible with the constraints exists and, when it does, constructs one.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be an atomless probability space and let $F_1,\dots,F_n$ be univariate cumulative distribution functions. The classical notions of mixability are defined via the aggregation map $(X_1,\dots,X_n)\mapsto X_1+\cdots+X_n$:

- The tuple $(F_1,\dots,F_n)$ is called jointly mixable if there exist random variables $X_i\sim F_i$ ($i=1,\dots,n$) on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ such that $X_1+\cdots+X_n$ is almost surely constant.
- A distribution $F$ is called $n$-completely mixable if $(F,\dots,F)$ ($n$ copies) is jointly mixable.

Now let $\psi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a fixed measurable function (an "aggregation function"), and define $(F_1,\dots,F_n)$ to be $\psi$-jointly mixable if there exist $X_i\sim F_i$ such that $\psi(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ is almost surely constant, with the analogous definition of $\psi$-complete mixability.

Problem. Develop a theory of $\psi$-mixability for aggregation functions $\psi$ other than the summation $\psi(x_1,\dots,x_n)=x_1+\cdots+x_n$. Specifically:

1. Identify natural classes of multivariate functions $\psi$ (e.g. symmetric, monotone, continuous, associative, or homogeneous aggregation functions, including means, maxima, products, and copula-based aggregations) for which the resulting notion of $\psi$-(complete or joint) mixability yields a mathematically useful and nontrivial theory.
2. For such $\psi$, give characterizations (necessary and/or sufficient conditions on $F_1,\dots,F_n$) of when $(F_1,\dots,F_n)$ is $\psi$-jointly mixable, paralleling the known moment, support, and mean-type conditions in the additive case.
3. Determine which structural properties of additive mixability (such as the relation to variance reduction, optimal couplings, and the dual representation via the convex order) extend to general $\psi$, and which fail.

representations.normalized:
Let $(G,+)$ be a (topological) abelian semigroup equipped with a $\sigma$-algebra making $+$ measurable. For an integer $n\ge 2$ and probability measures $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n$ on $G$, the tuple $(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n)$ is called jointly mixable on $G$ if there exist $G$-valued random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$, defined on a common probability space, with $X_i\sim\mu_i$ for each $i$, such that the sum $X_1+\cdots+X_n$ is almost surely constant (equal to some fixed $c\in G$). A probability measure $\mu$ on $G$ is called $n$-completely mixable if $(\mu,\dots,\mu)$ ($n$ copies) is jointly mixable on $G$.

Investigate how the algebraic structure of the underlying semigroup $G$ governs joint and complete mixability. Specifically, address the following:

(a) Identify algebraic properties of $G$ (e.g., cancellativity, existence of identity, existence of inverses making $G$ a group, divisibility, torsion, being finite/finitely generated, ordering, presence of idempotents) that ensure the existence of jointly mixable or completely mixable tuples for natural classes of marginals.

(b) Identify algebraic properties of $G$ that obstruct mixability — for example, properties that force the constant sum $c$ (the "center") to be unique, or that prevent any nontrivial $\mu$ from being $n$-completely mixable.

(c) Provide characterizations of which probability measures on $G$ are $n$-completely mixable, and which $n$-tuples are jointly mixable, in terms of the algebraic structure of $G$, including the question of uniqueness of the achievable center $c$.

Let $L$ be a finite field of characteristic $p$ with $|L|=q>2$, and let $\mu\colon L\to\mathbb{C}^\times$ be the canonical additive character of $L$, that is, $\mu(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,\mathrm{Tr}_{L/\mathbb{F}_p}(x)/p)$. For an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$ (so that $x\mapsto x^s$ is a permutation of $L$), define the Weil sum
$$W_{L,s}(a)=\sum_{x\in L}\mu(x^s-ax),\qquad a\in L.$$
The exponent $s$ is called singular if there exists $a\in L^\times$ such that $W_{L,s}(a)=0$.

Prove or disprove: if $|L|>2$ and $s\equiv 1\pmod{p-1}$ (with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$), then $s$ is singular.

The Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture (1976) remains open in general. Partial results are known: it has been verified for Niho exponents and in various special cases (e.g., certain characteristic-3 settings). Recent work (e.g., Katz–Langevin–Nguyen, 2020–2021) provides new proofs in restricted families but does not establish the full conjecture.

Let p be a prime, let L be a finite field of characteristic p with q = |L| elements, and let ψ : L → ℂ^× denote the canonical additive character of L, given by ψ(x) = exp(2πi · Tr_{L/F_p}(x)/p), where Tr_{L/F_p} is the absolute trace.

For an integer s with gcd(s, q − 1) = 1 (so that x ↦ x^s is a permutation of L) and for a ∈ L, define the Walsh (Weil) transform
    W_{L,s}(a) = ∑_{x ∈ L} ψ(x^s − a x).
The exponent s is called singular (over L) if there exists a ∈ L with a ≠ 0 such that W_{L,s}(a) = 0; otherwise s is called nonsingular. The Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture asserts that whenever q > 2 and s is an invertible exponent satisfying s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1), then s is singular.

Problem. Suppose p ∈ {2, 3}, L = F_q is a finite field of characteristic p with q > 2, and s = q − 2 (so that s is the inverse exponent, i.e. x^s = x^{−1} for x ≠ 0, and s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1) in both cases). Prove, without invoking the theory of elliptic curves over finite fields, that s = q − 2 is singular over L: that is, exhibit by an alternative method a nonzero element a ∈ L such that
    W_{L,q−2}(a) = ∑_{x ∈ L} ψ(x^{q−2} − a x) = 0.

Recent literature on Helleseth's vanishing conjecture (e.g., work by Katz, Langevin, Aubry, Feng, and Nguyen on Weil sums and Niho exponents) establishes the conjecture in various cases, including for the inverse exponent s = q − 2 via reductions to point-counting on elliptic curves in characteristics 2 and 3. Let p be a prime and let L be a finite field of characteristic p such that the degree [L : F_p] is a power of two, where F_p denotes the prime field with p elements. Let q = |L|. An integer s with 1 ≤ s ≤ q-1 is called an invertible exponent on L if gcd(s, q-1) = 1, so that the map x ↦ x^s is a permutation of L. Fix a nontrivial additive character ψ: L → C^× (for example, ψ(x) = exp(2πi · Tr_{L/F_p}(x)/p)). For an invertible exponent s, define the Weil/Fourier sum
    W_s(a,b) = Σ_{x ∈ L} ψ(a x^s + b x),    a, b ∈ L,
and let the reduced Fourier spectrum of the power permutation x ↦ x^s be the set of distinct values
    Spec(s) = { W_s(a,b) : a ∈ L^×, b ∈ L }  (equivalently, the set of nontrivial values arising from this family).

Prove or disprove: for every prime p and every finite field L with [L : F_p] a power of two, and for every invertible exponent s on L, the set Spec(s) does not consist of exactly three distinct values. (The cases p = 2 and p = 3 are known; the question concerns p > 3.)

Let $p$ be a prime, let $L = \mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field of order $q = p^n > 2$ and characteristic $p$, and fix a nontrivial additive character $\psi: L \to \mathbb{C}^\times$ (e.g. $\psi(x) = \exp(2\pi i\, \mathrm{Tr}_{L/\mathbb{F}_p}(x)/p)$). For a function $f: L \to L$, define its Walsh–Fourier transform by
$$\widehat{f}(a) = \sum_{x \in L} \psi(a f(x)) \qquad (a \in L).$$
A power map $f(x) = x^s$ (with $\gcd(s, q-1) = 1$, so that $f$ is a permutation of $L$) is called a power permutation of exponent $s$.

It is known that whenever $s \equiv 1 \pmod{p-1}$, there exists $a \in L^\times$ such that $\widehat{f}(a) \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ (the Fourier values being algebraic integers in a cyclotomic ring, where divisibility by $3$ is interpreted via any prime above $3$).

Problem: Determine whether an analogous forced-divisibility phenomenon holds for some prime $\ell \neq p$ in place of $3$. Precisely, find conditions on the exponent $s$ (comparable to the congruence $s \equiv 1 \pmod{p-1}$) and a prime $\ell \neq p$ such that for every finite field $L$ of characteristic $p$ satisfying these conditions, there must exist $a \in L^\times$ with $\widehat{f}(a) \equiv 0 \pmod{\ell}$ in the ring of algebraic integers, where $f(x) = x^s$.

Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^n$. For an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s, q-1) = 1$, the map $\chi_s : \mathbb{F}_q \to \mathbb{F}_q$, $x \mapsto x^s$, is a permutation of $\mathbb{F}_q$ called a power permutation. Fix a nontrivial additive character $\psi : \mathbb{F}_q \to \mathbb{C}^\times$ (e.g. $\psi(x) = e^{2\pi i \operatorname{Tr}(x)/p}$, where $\operatorname{Tr}$ denotes the absolute trace). The Walsh (or Weil) spectrum of $\chi_s$ is the multiset
$$\mathrm{Spec}(s) = \Big\{\, W_s(a) := \sum_{x \in \mathbb{F}_q} \psi(x^s - a x) \;:\; a \in \mathbb{F}_q^\times \,\Big\}.$$
The exponent $s$ is called $k$-valued if $\mathrm{Spec}(s)$ takes exactly $k$ distinct values, and $s$ is called singular if its $p$-adic digit expansion involves fewer than $n$ nonzero digits (equivalently, $s$ is not a "generic" exponent in the sense of Katz).

A theorem of Katz (2012) asserts: if $\chi_s$ is a three-valued power permutation, then
(i) $s$ is singular,
(ii) $s \equiv 1 \pmod{p-1}$, and
(iii) the spectrum $\{0, A, B\}$ of $\chi_s$ is contained in $\mathbb{Z}$.

Problem. Establish a structural analogue of this theorem for four-valued power permutations: namely, determine which of the conclusions (singularity of $s$, the congruence $s \equiv 1 \pmod{p-1}$, and integrality/rationality of the spectrum), or suitable modifications thereof, must necessarily hold whenever $\chi_s : x \mapsto x^s$ is a power permutation of $\mathbb{F}_q$ whose Walsh spectrum takes exactly four distinct values.

$$\prod_{i=1}^{n}A_i$$
is divisible by $q$ (in the ring of algebraic integers $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$).

Fix an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$, so that $x\mapsto x^s$ is a permutation of $L$. Define
$$F(x)=\mu(x^s)\qquad(x\in L),$$
and consider the Fourier transform (Weil sum)
$$\widehat{F}(a)=\sum_{x\in L}\mu(x^s-ax),\qquad a\in L.$$
The Fourier (Walsh) spectrum of $F$ is the multiset $\{\widehat{F}(a):a\in L\}$. Let $A_1,A_2,\dots,A_n$ denote the distinct nonzero values appearing in this spectrum. 

Determine all exponents $s$ (subject to $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$) for which the product
$$\prod_{i=1}^{n}A_i$$
is divisible by $q$ (in the ring of algebraic integers $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$).

The problem is posed as an open problem in a survey on Fourier spectra of power permutations over finite fields (related to Helleseth's conjectures). No subsequent paper located via web search resolves the divisibility by $q$ of the product of nonzero spectral values of $F(x)=\mu(x^s)$ in general; related work (Aubry–Katz–Langevin, etc.) addresses individual spectral-value valuations and three-valued cases, but not the product question itself.

Let $L = \mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field of odd characteristic, and let $s$ be an integer with $\gcd(s, q-1) = 1$, so that the map $x \mapsto x^s$ is a permutation of $L$. For $u, v \in L$, define
$$N(u, v) = \#\{x \in L : (x+u)^s - x^s = v\}.$$
Call $s$ a nice exponent over $L$ if the set $\{N(1, v) : v \in L\}$ has cardinality at most $3$. Two exponents $s, s'$ are called equivalent (written $s \approx s'$) if $s' \equiv p^i s \pmod{q-1}$ or $s s' \equiv p^i \pmod{q-1}$ for some $i \geq 0$, where $p$ is the characteristic of $L$.

Two known families of nice exponents are:
(i) $s = 3$ over any finite field of odd characteristic;
(ii) $s = q - 2$ (the inversion exponent) over any finite field of odd characteristic.

Prove or disprove: every nice exponent $s$ over a finite field $L$ of odd characteristic that is not equivalent to $1$ is equivalent to either $3$ or $q-2$.

representations.normalized:
Consider a dynamical system whose state evolves stochastically (classically or quantum-mechanically) in contact with one or several thermal reservoirs, driven by an external protocol and subject to feedback control. At specified times the controller performs a measurement of the system, obtaining an outcome that is correlated with the system's microstate. The mutual information between the measurement outcome and the system state quantifies the amount of information acquired by the controller, and on the basis of this outcome the controller chooses a subsequent driving protocol from a prescribed family.

Let one of the following be a chosen performance functional:
- the average work W extracted from the system over a cycle,
- the thermodynamic efficiency η = W/Q_h of a cyclic engine operating between two reservoirs at temperatures T_c < T_h,
- the average power output P = W/τ over a cycle of duration τ, or
- a steady-state average flux J of particles, charge, or energy across the system.

Let I denote a precisely defined measure of the information available to the controller about the system (for example, the mutual information between measurement outcomes and the system state, or, more generally, an information-theoretic quantity such as the QC-mutual information that may include quantum correlations).

Problem. Determine sharp, achievable upper bounds on the performance gain due to feedback as a function of I. Concretely:

(a) For each choice of performance functional above, find a tight inequality of the form
        Φ_feedback − Φ_no-feedback ≤ B(I, system parameters),
valid over all admissible measurement-and-feedback protocols, where Φ denotes the chosen performance functional and B is an explicit function expressing the maximal improvement allowed by access to information content I.

(b) Identify the protocols (measurements and feedback rules) that saturate each such bound, or prove that the bound cannot be saturated and exhibit the optimal achievable constant.

(c) Show that each such bound is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics when the thermodynamic cost of measurement and memory erasure performed by the controller is included.

representations.normalized:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $L=\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ for some integer $n\ge 1$, and let $L^{*}=L\setminus\{0\}$. For a positive integer $s$, the map $f:L\to L$ given by $f(x)=x^{s}$ is called a power permutation of $L$ if it is a bijection (equivalently, $\gcd(s,p^{n}-1)=1$); in this case $s$ is called an invertible exponent over $L$. Two exponents $s$ and $t$ are said to be equivalent (written $s\approx t$) if $t\equiv p^{i}s\pmod{p^{n}-1}$ for some $i\ge 0$, or if $st\equiv p^{i}\pmod{p^{n}-1}$ for some $i\ge 0$ (so that $f(x)=x^{s}$ and $g(x)=x^{t}$ have the same differential properties up to Frobenius and inversion).

For each $u,v\in L$, define
$$N(u,v)=\#\{(x,y)\in L^{2}:\ x+y=u,\ x^{s}+y^{s}=v\}.$$
A positive integer $m$ is called a differential multiplicity of $s$ if there exist $u\in L^{*}$ and $v\in L$ such that $N(u,v)=m$. Equivalently (by the substitution $x\to ux,\ y\to uy$), $m$ is a differential multiplicity of $s$ if and only if there exists $v\in L$ for which the system
$$x+y=1,\qquad x^{s}+y^{s}=v$$
has exactly $m$ solutions $(x,y)\in L^{2}$.

Question: Suppose $s$ is an invertible exponent over $L=\mathbb{F}_{p^{n}}$ (with $p$ odd) and $s\not\approx 1$. Must $2$ always be a differential multiplicity of $s$? That is, must there always exist some $v\in L$ such that the system $x+y=1,\ x^{s}+y^{s}=v$ has exactly two solutions in $L^{2}$?

The "optimist" conjecture asserting that 2 is always a differential multiplicity of any non-trivial invertible exponent in odd characteristic appears to remain open. Recent literature on differential spectra of power permutations over odd-characteristic finite fields (e.g., work on Niho exponents and on specific families such as $x^{p^{n}-3}$) treats individual exponent classes but does not establish the general statement. No source located resolves the conjecture in full generality.

The Laguerre–Pólya class $\mathcal{L\!-\!P}$ consists of those real entire functions $\varphi:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ which are uniform limits, on compact subsets of $\mathbb{C}$, of real polynomials all of whose zeros are real. Equivalently, $\varphi\in\mathcal{L\!-\!P}$ if and only if it admits a Hadamard-type representation
$$\varphi(x)=c\,x^{m}e^{-\alpha x^{2}+\beta x}\prod_{k\ge 1}\Bigl(1-\tfrac{x}{x_{k}}\Bigr)e^{x/x_{k}},$$
with $c,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$, $\alpha\ge 0$, $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, $x_{k}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$, and $\sum_{k}x_{k}^{-2}<\infty$.

Let $\{\gamma_{k}\}_{k\ge 0}$ be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers such that
$$f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma_{k}\,\frac{x^{k}}{k!}$$
defines an entire function. For a parameter $p\in\mathbb{C}$ with $-p\notin\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$, define the associated generalized Bessel-type function
$$F_{p}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\gamma_{k}\,x^{k}}{k!\,\Gamma(k+p+1)}.$$

Problem. Give a complete characterization of all nonnegative sequences $\{\gamma_{k}\}_{k\ge 0}$ (with $f$ entire) for which $F_{p}\in\mathcal{L\!-\!P}$ for every parameter $p$ with $-p\notin\mathbb{N}$ (equivalently, determine the precise necessary and sufficient conditions on $\{\gamma_{k}\}$).

Consider a classical or quantum thermodynamic system in contact with one or more heat reservoirs, together with an external controller (a "demon") that performs measurements on the system and applies a feedback protocol whose form depends on the measurement outcomes. Let the joint dynamics of system and controller be specified, with the controller possessing a memory register that stores measurement outcomes and is reset between protocol runs.

Develop a consistent thermodynamic framework for such feedback-controlled systems that explicitly incorporates the thermodynamic role of information transfer between the system and the controller. Concretely, the framework should:

1. Define the relevant information-theoretic quantities (e.g., the mutual information acquired by measurement and any QC-mutual or transfer-entropy-type generalizations) entering the thermodynamic balance.

2. Derive a generalized second law of the form
   ⟨ΔS_sys⟩ + ⟨ΔS_bath⟩ ≥ −I,
   (and the corresponding bound on extractable work ⟨W_ext⟩ ≤ −ΔF + k_B T · I) that holds for arbitrary feedback protocols, where I is the chosen information measure.

3. Establish a fluctuation theorem (Jarzynski/Crooks-type identity) for trajectories that incorporates the information exchanged between system and controller.

4. Account for the thermodynamic cost of the controller's measurement and memory erasure (Landauer's principle), so that the total entropy balance over system + controller + reservoirs is consistent with the ordinary second law.

5. Define and bound the efficiency of feedback-driven heat engines (e.g., Maxwell-demon-type cycles) in terms of the information acquired, identifying when and how the conventional Carnot bound is modified.

The problem is to construct such a framework in full generality (covering classical stochastic, classical Hamiltonian, and quantum settings, with discrete or continuous measurements and feedback) and to identify the tightest universal information-thermodynamic inequalities governing entropy reduction, extractable work, and efficiency.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

A substantial information-thermodynamics framework has been developed since 2008. Sagawa and Ueda derived generalized second laws and Jarzynski-type fluctuation theorems incorporating mutual information for both classical and quantum feedback control, establishing bounds on extractable work and efficiency that account for measurement and erasure costs. Subsequent work (fluctuation theorems with information exchange, transfer-entropy bounds, experimental verification via the Maxwell-demon photon experiment, and recent results on universal validity of the second law of information thermodynamics, e.g. 2023–2024) has extended and refined these results. The core programme is thus largely realized, although fully general formulations (continuous measurement, strong coupling, non-Markovian and fully quantum regimes) remain active research areas, so the broader programme is best classified as partially solved.

Consider a feedback-controlled thermodynamic system in which a controller repeatedly performs measurements on the system and applies actuations conditioned on those measurement outcomes, with successive actuations allowed to be correlated (i.e., the controller's memory retains a record of past measurement outcomes that influences subsequent actuations). Two complementary frameworks describe the thermodynamics of such a setup:

(A) A "system" viewpoint, in which one bounds the entropy reduction of the controlled system in terms of the mutual information between system and controller and derives generalized second-law inequalities involving the work extracted, the free-energy change, and the information acquired by the controller.

(B) An "algorithmic" viewpoint based on Kolmogorov complexity, in which the physical entropy of the joint system-plus-controller is taken to be the sum of the statistical (Shannon/Boltzmann) entropy of the system conditioned on the controller's record and the algorithmic complexity K(r) of the binary string r stored in the controller's memory. In this viewpoint, Landauer's principle implies that the minimum energetic cost of erasing the record r is k_B T ln 2 · K(r), and this cost in turn imposes a thermodynamic upper bound on the achievable reduction of the system's entropy under correlated repeated actuation.

Problem. Establish the precise quantitative relationship between frameworks (A) and (B) for correlated repeated actuation. Specifically:

(i) Derive an exact identity (or, failing that, matching upper and lower bounds) connecting the maximal system entropy reduction obtainable in framework (A) to the algorithmic-complexity-based bound k_B T ln 2 · K(r) on the erasure cost in framework (B), in the regime where the controller's stored record r exhibits non-trivial temporal correlations across repeated actuations.

(ii) Identify the conditions under which the two frameworks give equivalent thermodynamic limits, and characterize the gap (if any) when they differ, in terms of the statistical properties of the measurement record and the protocol used by the controller.

(iii) Show how the minimum energetic erasure cost k_B T ln 2 · K(r) translates into the maximum entropy reduction of the controlled system, and compare this maximum with the bounds obtained from mutual-information-based generalized second laws.

(B) An "algorithmic" viewpoint based on Kolmogorov complexity, in which the physical entropy of the joint system-plus-controller is taken to be the sum of the statistical (Shannon/Boltzmann) entropy of the system conditioned on the controller's record and the algorithmic complexity K(r) of the binary string r stored in the controller's memory. In this viewpoint, Landauer's principle implies that the minimum energetic cost of erasing the record r is k_B T ln 2 · K(r), and this cost in turn imposes a thermodynamic upper bound on the achievable reduction of the system's entropy under correlated repeated actuation.

Problem. Establish the precise quantitative relationship between frameworks (A) and (B) for correlated repeated actuation. Specifically:

(i) Derive an exact identity (or, failing that, matching upper and lower bounds) connecting the maximal system entropy reduction obtainable in framework (A) to the algorithmic-complexity-based bound k_B T ln 2 · K(r) on the erasure cost in framework (B), in the regime where the controller's stored record r exhibits non-trivial temporal correlations across repeated actuations.

(ii) Identify the conditions under which the two frameworks give equivalent thermodynamic limits, and characterize the gap (if any) when they differ, in terms of the statistical properties of the measurement record and the protocol used by the controller.

(iii) Show how the minimum energetic erasure cost k_B T ln 2 · K(r) translates into the maximum entropy reduction of the controlled system, and compare this maximum with the bounds obtained from mutual-information-based generalized second laws.

Web search did not surface any work that establishes a precise quantitative bridge between mutual-information-based entropy-reduction bounds for feedback-controlled systems and Zurek's algorithmic-complexity treatment of the system-plus-controller in the correlated repeated-actuation regime. Foundational references (Zurek's algorithmic randomness/physical entropy papers and Cao–Feito-style thermodynamics of feedback) appear, but no source claims to have closed this connection, suggesting the problem remains open.

Consider a feedback-controlled stochastic system in contact with a thermal reservoir at temperature T, whose dynamics are repeatedly modulated by a controller that performs successive measurements on the system and applies control protocols based on the measurement outcomes. Let the sequence of measurement outcomes be {m_1, m_2, …, m_N}, generally correlated across time, and let H({m_i}) denote the Shannon entropy of this sequence. Within the framework of stochastic thermodynamics, the entropy reduction of the system due to feedback obeys quantitative bounds expressed in terms of the mutual information (or Shannon entropy) of the correlated measurement record, and the minimum energetic cost of erasing the controller's memory imposes a corresponding limit on the maximum extractable work.

Question: Develop quantitative thermodynamic bounds, derived from (or extending) the entropy-reduction results for correlated repeated feedback actuation, on the following performance measures of such feedback-controlled systems:

(a) the maximum attainable steady-state probability flux J (e.g., the average net particle or charge current that the feedback can sustain across the system per unit time), and

(b) the maximum attainable power P (e.g., the rate of work extraction, or the rate of free-energy production, achievable by the feedback protocol).

Specifically, express upper bounds on J and P in terms of the temperature T, the rate of information acquisition by the controller (the entropy rate of the correlated measurement sequence), and the relevant timescales of the controlled dynamics, and determine the conditions under which these bounds are saturated.

Consider a stochastic dynamical system whose state $X_t$ evolves in continuous time (e.g., according to a Langevin or Markovian stochastic differential equation), together with a feedback controller that, at each actuation step, performs a measurement of the system, gains an amount of information characterized by a mutual information $I_n$ between the measurement outcome and the system state, and applies a control action that influences subsequent dynamics. For the discrete repeated feedback setting, suppose one has established a generalized second law of thermodynamics of the form
$$\langle W_{\mathrm{ext}}\rangle \;\le\; -\Delta F + k_B T \sum_{n} I_n,$$
where $\langle W_{\mathrm{ext}}\rangle$ is the average extracted work, $\Delta F$ is the free-energy change, $T$ is the bath temperature, and $I_n$ are the (discrete) Shannon mutual informations gathered at each of the discrete actuation times $t_n = n\,\Delta t$.

Now define the continuous-actuation limit as $\Delta t \to 0$, in which the controller's actuation period is shorter than every characteristic time scale of the system dynamics. In this limit, discrete Shannon entropies of the measured and controlled variables generically diverge, and the appropriate information measures become differential entropies (or mutual informations between continuous-time processes), whose relationship to the discrete Shannon entropies is nontrivial (e.g., $H(X_\varepsilon) = h(X) - \log\varepsilon + o(1)$ for an $\varepsilon$-quantization of a continuous random variable $X$ with differential entropy $h(X)$).

Problem: Formulate and prove a generalized second law for the continuous-actuation limit of feedback-controlled stochastic systems that:

(a) extends the discrete inequality above to a well-defined bound involving an information-theoretic functional of the joint continuous-time process of measurements and system trajectories;
(b) yields a finite, physically meaningful information term as $\Delta t \to 0$, despite the divergence of the individual discrete mutual informations $I_n$ and the nontrivial relation between Shannon and differential entropies; and
(c) reduces to the discrete result in the limit of large actuation period.

Equivalently, identify the correct continuous-time information-theoretic quantity (such as a transfer-entropy rate or mutual-information rate between the measurement record and the controlled trajectory) that bounds the extractable work in continuous feedback control, and rigorously establish the corresponding inequality.

Subsequent work has made substantial progress on this question. Continuous-time generalizations of the second law of feedback-controlled systems have been formulated using information rates (notably transfer entropy and mutual information rates), and the thermodynamics of continuous, non-Markovian feedback control has been developed and experimentally tested with levitated microparticles (Debiossac et al., Nature Communications 2020). Recent works (e.g., 2025 entropic-balance and quantum-classical transfer-entropy results) further refine these inequalities. Nevertheless, a fully general framework matching the discrete results in the strict continuous-actuation limit for arbitrary feedback protocols remains an active research direction, so the problem is best classified as partially solved.

The sequence is called a complex zero decreasing sequence (CZDS) if for every real polynomial $f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^m c_k x^k$ one has $Z_c(T[f]) \leq Z_c(f)$, where $Z_c(g)$ denotes the number of nonreal zeros of $g$ counted with multiplicity.

Let $p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n a_j x^j$ be a polynomial with real coefficients satisfying $a_j\geq 0$ for all $0\leq j\leq n$. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the coefficients of $p(x)$ such that:
(a) the sequence $\{p(k)/k!\}_{k\geq 0}$ is a multiplier sequence;
(b) the sequence $\{p(k)/k!\}_{k\geq 0}$ is a complex zero decreasing sequence.

representations.normalized:
Consider a feedback-controlled flashing ratchet: a Brownian particle in contact with a thermal bath at temperature $T$ moves in one dimension under a spatially periodic, asymmetric potential $V(x)$ that can be switched on and off in time. A controller observes the position of the particle (either continuously or at discrete sampling times) and, based on the measurement outcomes, decides whether to keep the potential on or off, with the aim of rectifying thermal fluctuations into directed motion.

Within the framework of stochastic thermodynamics for feedback-controlled systems, the second law must be modified to incorporate the information acquired by the controller: for a feedback protocol acting on a stochastic system, one has a generalized inequality of the form
$$\langle W_{\mathrm{ext}}\rangle \le -\Delta F + k_B T\, I,$$
where $\langle W_{\mathrm{ext}}\rangle$ is the mean work extracted, $\Delta F$ is the free-energy change, and $I$ is an information-theoretic quantity (a mutual information / entropy reduction) characterizing the controller's measurements and actions. Equivalently, the entropy production of the controlled system is bounded below by $-I$, so $I$ plays the role of a maximum attainable "entropy reduction" induced by the feedback protocol.

Problem. Apply this general thermodynamic framework explicitly to the feedback flashing ratchet:
(a) Define the appropriate information quantity $I$ for an arbitrary measurement-and-switching protocol (continuous or discrete-time) acting on a flashing ratchet, taking into account the non-Markovian sequence of control actions generated by the controller.
(b) Determine the maximum entropy reduction $I_{\max}$ achievable by any such feedback protocol on the flashing ratchet, and exhibit (or bound) protocols saturating it.
(c) Use the result to give a complete thermodynamic description of feedback flashing ratchets, including tight upper bounds on extracted work, output power, and efficiency in terms of $I$, and identify the protocols that saturate these bounds.

Subsequent work has substantially developed the thermodynamic and information-theoretic description of feedback flashing ratchets. In particular, "Information in feedback ratchets" (Phys. Rev. representations.normalized:
Consider a feedback-controlled flashing ratchet: a Brownian particle (or ensemble of particles) moves in one dimension in an asymmetric periodic potential V(x) that can be switched on or off by a controller. The controller measures the particle positions at discrete actuation times and, based on these measurements, decides whether the potential is on or off, producing a directed mean flux ⟨J⟩ and extractable mechanical power ⟨P⟩ when an external load is applied.

For such systems there exist known bounds on the flux improvement Δ⟨J⟩ and on the power improvement Δ⟨P⟩ over the corresponding open-loop ratchet, expressed in terms of the Shannon information I_act used by the controller per actuation event (i.e., the mutual information between the measurement outcome and the chosen action at a single actuation step).

Separately, in the general thermodynamic framework of feedback-controlled systems, the relevant quantity is the rate Ï of non-redundant information acquired per unit time, defined as the entropy-reduction rate of the (generally non-Markovian) sequence of control actions, that is
   Ï = lim_{N→∞} (1/(NÏ„)) [ H(A_1,…,A_N) − redundant correlations ],
where A_k are the successive control actions, Ï„ is the actuation period, and only genuinely new information beyond what is already implied by previous actions is counted.

Problem. Reformulate the known per-actuation bounds on Δ⟨J⟩ and Δ⟨P⟩ for a feedback flashing ratchet as bounds expressed in terms of the non-redundant information rate Ï (information per unit time) rather than the per-actuation information I_act. In particular, derive explicit inequalities of the form
   Δ⟨J⟩ ≤ F_J(Ï),    Δ⟨P⟩ ≤ F_P(Ï),
that remain valid when successive measurements are correlated, and that connect directly to the entropy-reduction / second-law inequality for general feedback-controlled systems.

Background and definitions.

The Laguerre–Pólya class, denoted LP, is the set of entire functions that are uniform limits, on compact subsets of the complex plane, of sequences of real polynomials all of whose zeros are real. The subclass LP^+ consists of those f in LP whose Taylor coefficients at 0 are all nonnegative; equivalently, f in LP^+ if and only if f can be written as
  f(x) = c x^m e^{a x} ∏_{n} (1 + α_n x),
with c ≥ 0, m ∈ Z_{≥0}, a ≥ 0, α_n ≥ 0, and ∑ α_n < ∞.

A real sequence {γ_k}_{k≥0} is called a multiplier sequence if, for every real polynomial p(x) = ∑_{k=0}^n a_k x^k whose zeros are all real, the polynomial
  Γ[p](x) := ∑_{k=0}^n γ_k a_k x^k
also has only real zeros. By the Pólya–Schur theorem, a sequence of nonnegative real numbers {γ_k} is a multiplier sequence if and only if the formal power series
  Φ_Γ(x) := ∑_{k=0}^∞ γ_k x^k / k!
represents an entire function in LP^+.

A real sequence {γ_k}_{k≥0} is called a complex zero decreasing sequence (CZDS) if, for every real polynomial p(x) = ∑_{k=0}^n a_k x^k,
  Z_c(Γ[p]) ≤ Z_c(p),
where Z_c(q) denotes the number of nonreal zeros of the polynomial q (counted with multiplicity).

Problem. Consider the sequence
  γ_k = √k / k!,  k = 0, 1, 2, ….

(a) Determine whether {γ_k}_{k≥0} is a multiplier sequence. Equivalently, decide whether the entire function
  φ(x) = ∑_{k=0}^∞ (√k / (k! k!)) x^k
belongs to the Laguerre–Pólya class LP^+.

(b) Determine whether {γ_k}_{k≥0} is a complex zero decreasing sequence (CZDS).

Consider a composite stochastic system consisting of two interacting subsystems A and B, where B acts as a controller that observes A through a noisy measurement channel and applies a feedback action to A in order to improve some performance measure of A (for example, to extract work, reduce entropy, or stabilize a target state). Let I denote the mutual information acquired by B about A per unit time, let W denote the average work extracted (or analogous performance gain) by the feedback protocol, let ΔS denote the entropy production of the joint system, and let kT be the thermal energy scale. Generalized second-law inequalities of the Sagawa–Ueda type assert that the achievable performance is bounded by information-theoretic quantities, e.g. ⟨W⟩ ≤ −ΔF + kT·I, with related bounds on entropy reduction and control accuracy.

Problem: Derive the concrete, quantitative limitations that such information-theoretic and thermodynamic bounds for bidirectional feedback-controlled systems place on the operation and achievable performance of physical realizations relevant to nanotechnology devices and biological systems (e.g., molecular motors, ion channels, sensory adaptation networks, single-electron transistors with feedback). Specifically, identify the optimal trade-offs between (i) the rate of information acquisition by the controller, (ii) the energetic/dissipative cost of measurement and feedback, and (iii) the resulting performance gain of the controlled subsystem, and characterize attainability of these bounds in concrete model classes.

$$\Gamma[p](x) := \sum_{k=0}^{n} \gamma_k a_k x^k$$

$$T_k := \frac{\gamma_k}{k!} = \frac{1}{(k+1)^{k+1}\, k!}, \qquad k = 0,1,2,\dots.$$

Determine:
(a) whether $\{T_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ is a multiplier sequence;
(b) whether $\{T_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ is a complex zero decreasing sequence.
