Let $\{P_n(x)\}_{n\ge 0}$ be a sequence of monic orthogonal polynomials defined by the three-term recurrence
$$P_n(x) = (x-c_n)P_{n-1}(x) - \lambda_n P_{n-2}(x), \qquad n\ge 1,$$
with $P_{-1}(x)=0$, $P_0(x)=1$, where $c_n\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\lambda_n>0$ for all $n$. Assume that
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} c_n = +\infty \quad\text{and}\quad \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\lambda_{n+1}}{c_n c_{n+1}} = \frac{1}{4};$$
sequences satisfying these conditions are said to belong to the "one-quarter class".

For each $n$, denote the zeros of $P_n$ by $x_{n,1}<x_{n,2}<\cdots<x_{n,n}$, and define, when these limits exist,
$$\xi_i = \lim_{n\to\infty} x_{n,i},\quad \eta_j = \lim_{n\to\infty} x_{n,n-j+1}, \quad \sigma = \lim_{i\to\infty}\xi_i,\quad \tau = \lim_{j\to\infty}\eta_j.$$
In the one-quarter class one always has $\tau = +\infty$.

The classical theorem of Blumenthal asserts, for sequences with $c_n\to c$ and $\lambda_n\to\lambda>0$, that the true interval of orthogonality is $[c-2\sqrt{\lambda},\,c+2\sqrt{\lambda}]$ together with at most countably many isolated points outside it whose only possible accumulation points are the endpoints. The problem is the following:

Formulate and prove an analogue of Blumenthal's theorem describing the true interval (or unbounded interval) of orthogonality, and the location of the spectrum of the associated Jacobi matrix, for one-quarter class orthogonal polynomial sequences in the case $\sigma = -\infty$ (so that the smallest zeros tend to $-\infty$ while the largest tend to $+\infty$).

Consider the class of linear quantum networks defined as follows. A linear quantum system consists of a finite collection of bosonic modes with canonical operators (a_1, ..., a_n) (equivalently quadratures (q_i, p_i) with [q_j, p_k] = i δ_{jk}) whose internal Hamiltonian is at most quadratic in the canonical operators. The system is coupled irreversibly to a finite collection of external bosonic quantum field channels (input/output fields satisfying quantum stochastic differential equations) through coupling operators that are linear in the mode operators. Such a system is called a quantum linear network; its Heisenberg-picture dynamics map linear combinations of canonical operators to linear combinations of canonical operators (with added field noise), and its (S, L, H) parameters have S unitary, L linear in the modes, and H quadratic.

A quantum error-correction procedure is a process that, for an arbitrary unknown pure state |ψ⟩ encoded in some subsystem, recovers |ψ⟩ (with arbitrarily high fidelity) after the encoded system has been subjected to errors drawn from a specified noise model acting on the encoded degrees of freedom — in particular, the recovery must succeed without prior knowledge of |ψ⟩.

Prove that no quantum linear network (in the above sense, possibly including measurement of output fields and linear feedback derived from such measurements through the same linear-network class) can implement quantum error correction for arbitrary unknown encoded quantum states against a non-trivial error model. Equivalently, show that the implementation of genuine quantum error correction necessarily requires nonlinear (non-Gaussian) resources beyond the linear-network framework.

A 97, 022324) and earlier no-go style results restricted to Gaussian states/operations (Niset–Fiurášek–Cerf 2009 showing Gaussian errors cannot be corrected by Gaussian operations on Gaussian states), but a complete proof of the general statement does not appear to be established. representations.normalized:
Consider a quantum linear network: a continuous-variable quantum system whose dynamics is generated by a Hamiltonian that is at most quadratic in the canonical mode operators (creation and annihilation operators of a finite collection of bosonic modes), possibly coupled to external bosonic reservoirs through linear (i.e. mode-operator–linear) Lindblad jump operators. Such evolutions form the class of Gaussian (linear) quantum dynamics: they map Gaussian states to Gaussian states and preserve the linear span of canonical operators in the Heisenberg picture.

A "linear noise" channel on the system is any completely positive trace-preserving map arising from coupling the system, via at most quadratic system–bath Hamiltonians, to a (possibly thermal) Gaussian environment, so that the joint reduced dynamics on the system is a Gaussian channel.

Let ρ be a fixed, known non-Gaussian state of the bosonic system (for instance a Fock state, a Schrödinger-cat state, or any state whose Wigner function is not a Gaussian). A "protection protocol using a linear network" consists of:
 (i) an encoding Gaussian channel E that embeds ρ into a (possibly larger) bosonic system,
 (ii) the action of the linear noise channel N on the encoded system, and
 (iii) a decoding Gaussian channel D,
all of which are Gaussian (linear) operations, possibly involving ancillary modes prepared in arbitrary Gaussian states, Gaussian measurements, and Gaussian feed-forward.

Prove the following statement, or exhibit a counterexample:

For every non-Gaussian state ρ and every nontrivial linear noise channel N (i.e. one that is not the identity on the relevant modes), there exist no Gaussian encoding E, ancillary Gaussian resources, and Gaussian decoding D such that
   D ∘ N ∘ E (ρ) = ρ.
Equivalently, quantum linear networks cannot perfectly protect any known non-Gaussian state from linear noise.

Let $\{P_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ be a sequence of real orthogonal polynomials defined by a three-term recurrence relation
$$P_{n+1}(x) = (x - c_n)\, P_n(x) - \lambda_n\, P_{n-1}(x), \qquad n \geq 0,$$
with $P_{-1}(x) = 0$, $P_0(x) = 1$, $c_n \in \mathbb{R}$, and $\lambda_{n+1} > 0$ for all $n \geq 0$ (so that $\{P_n\}$ is orthogonal with respect to some positive Borel measure on $\mathbb{R}$ by Favard's theorem).

Say that $\{P_n\}$ belongs to the "one-quarter class" if
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} c_n = \infty \qquad \text{and} \qquad \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\lambda_{n+1}}{c_n\, c_{n+1}} = \frac{1}{4}.$$

A known example of an OPS in the one-quarter class whose orthogonality measure has support equal to all of $\mathbb{R}$ is given by the Meixner polynomials of the second kind (the Meixner–Pollaczek polynomials).

Question: Does there exist an orthogonal polynomial sequence $\{P_n\}$ in the one-quarter class, other than (an affine equivalent of) the Meixner–Pollaczek polynomials, whose orthogonality measure has spectrum equal to the whole real line $\mathbb{R}$?

Let $\{P_n(x;\mathbf{a})\}_{n\ge 0}$ denote a family of hypergeometric (or basic-hypergeometric) orthogonal polynomials in a single variable $x$, indexed by a tuple $\mathbf{a}$ of parameters; concrete cases of interest include the Laguerre polynomials, Gegenbauer (ultraspherical) polynomials, Jacobi polynomials, the continuous $q$-ultraspherical (Rogers) polynomials, and the continuous $q$-Jacobi polynomials.

For a single parameter set $\mathbf{a}$, define the ordinary linearization coefficients $\alpha_{k,m,n}(\mathbf{a})$ by
$$P_m(x;\mathbf{a})\,P_n(x;\mathbf{a}) \;=\; \sum_{k} \alpha_{k,m,n}(\mathbf{a})\,P_k(x;\mathbf{a}).$$
For two parameter sets $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, define the connection coefficients $\beta_{k,n}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$ by
$$P_n(x;\mathbf{a}) \;=\; \sum_{k} \beta_{k,n}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\,P_k(x;\mathbf{b}).$$
Define the generalized linearization coefficients $\gamma_{k,m,n}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$ by
$$P_m(x;\mathbf{a})\,P_n(x;\mathbf{a}) \;=\; \sum_{k} \gamma_{k,m,n}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\,P_k(x;\mathbf{b}).$$

Problem: For each of the polynomial families listed above (Laguerre, Gegenbauer, continuous $q$-ultraspherical/Rogers, Jacobi, and continuous $q$-Jacobi), obtain closed-form expressions — preferably as (basic-)hypergeometric series with explicit Pochhammer/$q$-Pochhammer symbol arguments — for the generalized linearization coefficients $\gamma_{k,m,n}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$.

Let $\{P_n(x;\mathbf{a})\}_{n\ge 0}$ denote a family of hypergeometric (or basic-hypergeometric) orthogonal polynomials in a single variable $x$, indexed by a tuple $\mathbf{a}$ of parameters; concrete cases of interest include the Laguerre polynomials, Gegenbauer (ultraspherical) polynomials, Jacobi polynomials, the continuous $q$-ultraspherical (Rogers) polynomials, and the continuous $q$-Jacobi polynomials.

For a single parameter set $\mathbf{a}$, define the ordinary linearization coefficients $\alpha_{k,m,n}(\mathbf{a})$ by
$$P_m(x;\mathbf{a})\,P_n(x;\mathbf{a}) \;=\; \sum_{k} \alpha_{k,m,n}(\mathbf{a})\,P_k(x;\mathbf{a}).$$
For two parameter sets $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, define the connection coefficients $\beta_{k,n}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$ by
$$P_n(x;\mathbf{a}) \;=\; \sum_{k} \beta_{k,n}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\,P_k(x;\mathbf{b}).$$
Define the generalized linearization coefficients $\gamma_{k,m,n}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$ by
$$P_m(x;\mathbf{a})\,P_n(x;\mathbf{a}) \;=\; \sum_{k} \gamma_{k,m,n}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\,P_k(x;\mathbf{b}).$$

Problem: For each of the polynomial families listed above (Laguerre, Gegenbauer, continuous $q$-ultraspherical/Rogers, Jacobi, and continuous $q$-Jacobi), obtain closed-form expressions — preferably as (basic-)hypergeometric series with explicit Pochhammer/$q$-Pochhammer symbol arguments — for the generalized linearization coefficients $\gamma_{k,m,n}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$.

Closed-form generalized linearization formulas have been obtained for Gegenbauer and continuous q-ultraspherical/Rogers polynomials (and certain Jacobi/Laguerre cases) as (basic-)hypergeometric series, but a uniform closed-form treatment for all classical and basic-hypergeometric families in the (q-)Askey scheme is not established. Subsequent work (e.g., two-dimensional contiguous relations for linearization coefficients) has extended results, but the general program remains only partially completed.

Consider linear feedback networks in quantum control: networks of quantum systems whose dynamics are governed by quadratic Hamiltonians and linear couplings (including measurement-based or coherent feedback links), with the controlled variables being either Gaussian states of bosonic modes or analogous linear-Gaussian degrees of freedom. Traditionally, such networks are studied with time-independent system Hamiltonians and time-independent inter-system couplings.

Allow now the introduction of time-dependent external control: i.e., let the system Hamiltonians and/or the coupling parameters of the network be modulated as functions of time according to an externally chosen control protocol.

For a given control task on the network (for example, state preparation, stabilization of a target Gaussian state, cooling of a mode, generation or distribution of entanglement, noise suppression, parameter estimation, or disturbance rejection), define a performance functional P that quantifies how well the task is accomplished (e.g., asymptotic fidelity, steady-state variance, entanglement measure, or estimation precision). Let P_static denote the optimal value of P over all admissible time-independent network configurations, and P_dyn the optimal value over all admissible time-dependent control protocols (subject to the same energy or bandwidth constraints).

(a) Quantify the gain G = P_dyn − P_static (or an appropriate ratio) achievable by introducing time-dependent control into linear feedback networks. Provide bounds, explicit formulas, or scaling laws for G.

(b) Determine how G varies across different classes of quantum control problems on linear feedback networks (state preparation vs. stabilization vs. estimation vs. entanglement generation, etc.), and identify which classes of problems benefit most from time-dependent control.

representations.normalized:
Consider linear quantum feedback networks consisting of interconnected open quantum harmonic oscillators. Two interconnection mechanisms are available:

(i) Direct (reversible) coupling, modeled by a bilinear interaction Hamiltonian of the form H_int = i(a^† K b − b^† K^* a) between the canonical mode operators of the component systems, which preserves unitarity and introduces no additional bath.

(ii) Field-mediated (irreversible) coupling, in which subsystems are connected via bosonic quantum field channels in the (S,L,H) / SLH framework, so that any such connection necessarily comes with coupling to a vacuum bath via Lindblad/quantum-stochastic terms.

For a fixed target class of input–output linear quantum stochastic systems and a fixed performance measure (e.g. coherent H^∞ disturbance attenuation, coherent LQG cost, or fidelity of a desired Gaussian input–output map), let

P_direct := the optimal performance achievable using a network in which both direct and field-mediated couplings are permitted,
P_field  := the optimal performance achievable using a network restricted to field-mediated couplings only,

each evaluated under two regimes:
(a) static, time-invariant interconnections only;
(b) augmented by arbitrary external time-dependent classical control inputs applied to each component.

Problem. Quantify the gap between P_direct and P_field in regimes (a) and (b). Specifically:

1. Provide a sharp, explicit bound (or exact formula) for the performance improvement that admitting direct coupling provides over restricting to field-mediated coupling, in terms of intrinsic parameters of the target linear network (e.g. system matrices, number of modes, channel dimensions).

2. Determine how this gap changes when external time-dependent control is allowed versus disallowed, and identify whether time-dependent control can fully or partially compensate for the absence of direct coupling.

3. Characterize the class of target linear quantum input–output maps that are realizable with field-mediated coupling alone versus those requiring direct coupling, and relate this realizability gap to the quantitative performance advantage in (1).

The problem appears to remain open.

Notation. For a non-negative integer $m$, set $(q)_m=\prod_{i=1}^m(1-q^i)$ with $(q)_0=1$, and let $(q)_\infty=\prod_{i=1}^\infty(1-q^i)$. For non-negative integers $a,b$, the Gaussian $q$-binomial coefficient is
$$\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{a}{b}_q=\begin{cases}\dfrac{(q)_a}{(q)_b\,(q)_{a-b}}&\text{if }0\le b\le a,\\[4pt]0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Consider the $A_2$ Rogers–Ramanujan identity
$$(q)_\infty\sum_{r_1,r_2\ge 0}\frac{q^{r_1^2-r_1r_2+r_2^2}}{(q)_{r_1}(q)_{r_2}(q)_{r_1+r_2}}\;=\;\sum_{r_1,r_2\ge 0}\frac{q^{r_1^2-r_1r_2+r_2^2}}{(q)_{r_1}}\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{2r_1}{r_2}_q\;=\;\prod_{n\ge 0}\frac{1}{(1-q^{7n+1})^2(1-q^{7n+3})(1-q^{7n+4})(1-q^{7n+6})^2}.$$

Tasks:
(a) Express the left-hand side as a $q$-series that is simultaneously (i) manifestly of $A_2$ type (its summand reflects the $A_2$ root-system structure, e.g.\ involves the quadratic form $r_1^2-r_1r_2+r_2^2$ in an essential way) and (ii) manifestly coefficient-wise positive (each coefficient in the $q$-expansion is visibly a non-negative integer, with no need for cancellation).

(b) Give a partition-theoretic interpretation of the middle sum
$$\sum_{r_1,r_2\ge 0}\frac{q^{r_1^2-r_1r_2+r_2^2}}{(q)_{r_1}}\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{2r_1}{r_2}_q,$$
i.e.\ exhibit a class $\mathcal P$ of partitions (or coloured/multi-partitions) together with a statistic such that the generating function of $\mathcal P$ equals this sum, and such that $\mathcal P$ is naturally in bijection with the partitions enumerated by the infinite product on the right-hand side.

Let $S^2$ denote the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and let $\{Y_\ell^m : \ell \ge 0,\ |m|\le\ell\}$ be the standard orthonormal basis of spherical harmonics in $L^2(S^2)$. For a band-limited function $f:S^2\to\mathbb{C}$ with expansion
$$f(\theta,\varphi) = \sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell} \widehat{f}_\ell^m\, Y_\ell^m(\theta,\varphi),$$
the forward spherical harmonic transform produces the coefficients $\{\widehat{f}_\ell^m\}$ from samples of $f$ on a suitable grid of $n = \Theta(L^2)$ points on $S^2$, and the inverse transform reconstructs the samples from the coefficients.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm (numerically stable, with provable accuracy guarantees) that performs both the forward and inverse spherical harmonic transforms in time $O(n \log n)$, or more generally $O(n (\log n)^c)$ for some absolute constant $c$, on a grid of $n$ points on the sphere?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Several asymptotically fast algorithms exist for spherical harmonic transforms, achieving complexities such as O(n (log n)^2) (Mohlenkamp; Healy–Rockmore et al.) and O(n^{5/4} log n) variants, with butterfly-scheme and HEALPix-based methods widely used in practice. A fully O(n log n), provably stable, and practically competitive algorithm matching the FFT analogue is generally regarded as still not achieved; the question remains an active research area rather than a fully closed problem.

Let $C=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ be the $A_2$ Cartan matrix. For a vector $v=(v_1,v_2)\in\mathbb Z^2$ write $(q)_v=(q)_{v_1}(q)_{v_2}$, where $(q)_n=\prod_{i=1}^n(1-q^i)$ for $n\ge0$ and $(q)_n=\infty$ for $n<0$. Define the Gaussian $q$-binomial coefficient $\binom{a}{b}_q=(q)_a/((q)_b(q)_{a-b})$ for $0\le b\le a$ and $0$ otherwise.

For an integer triple $\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3)$ with $\mu_i\ge0$ and a triple $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)\in\mathbb Z^3_{\ge0}$ with $|\mu|=|\lambda|$, let the (completely antisymmetric) $A_2$ supernomial $T(\mu;\lambda)$ be the finite sum over chains of Young diagrams encoded by Gaussian $q$-binomials in the standard way (a Kostka-type generating function which is nonzero exactly when $\mu$ dominates the conjugate partition associated to $\lambda$).

For $L=(L_1,L_2)\in\mathbb Z^2_{\ge0}$ and $k=(k_1,k_2,k_3)\in\mathbb Z^3$ with $k_1+k_2+k_3=0$, define the normalized $A_2$ supernomial
$$S(L,k)=\frac{1}{(q)_{CL}}\, T\big((CL)_+;\, L_2(1,1,1)-k\big),$$
where the antisymmetric supernomial with top vector $CL$ and lower vector $L_2(1,1,1)-k$ is meant. Restrict $k$ to the dominant chamber $k_1\ge k_2\ge k_3$, and parametrize it by $K=(K_1,K_2)=(k_1+k_2,\,k_1)$. Then $S(L,K)\ne0$ exactly when
$$K_1\le L_1,\ K_2\le L_2,\ 2K_1\ge K_2,\ 2K_2\ge K_1,\ 2L_1\ge L_2,\ 2L_2\ge L_1.$$

Find an explicit closed-form expression $\bar S(K,L)$ such that, simultaneously,
$$\sum_{L_1,L_2\ge0}\bar S(K,L)\,S(L,K')=\delta_{K,K'}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{\substack{k\text{ dominant}\\|k|=0}}S(L,k)\,\bar S(k,L')=\delta_{L,L'},$$
valid for all admissible $K=(K_1,K_2)$ (not only for the previously known partial cases $K=(r,2r-p)$ with $p\in\{0,1,2,3\}$).

where the antisymmetric supernomial with top vector $CL$ and lower vector $L_2(1,1,1)-k$ is meant. Restrict $k$ to the dominant chamber $k_1\ge k_2\ge k_3$, and parametrize it by $K=(K_1,K_2)=(k_1+k_2,\,k_1)$. Then $S(L,K)\ne0$ exactly when
$$K_1\le L_1,\ K_2\le L_2,\ 2K_1\ge K_2,\ 2K_2\ge K_1,\ 2L_1\ge L_2,\ 2L_2\ge L_1.$$

$$\sum_{L_1,L_2\ge0}\bar S(K,L)\,S(L,K')=\delta_{K,K'}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{\substack{k\text{ dominant}\\|k|=0}}S(L,k)\,\bar S(k,L')=\delta_{L,L'},$$
valid for all admissible $K=(K_1,K_2)$ (not only for the previously known partial cases $K=(r,2r-p)$ with $p\in\{0,1,2,3\}$).

Consider a quantum control setup in which a target quantum system $S$ (with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_S$ and free Hamiltonian $H_S$) is controlled by coupling it to an auxiliary quantum system $C$ (the "controller", with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_C$ and free Hamiltonian $H_C$) through a tunable interaction Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{int}}(u(t))$ depending on classical control parameters $u(t)$. The joint evolution is taken to be Markovian and is generated by a Lindblad master equation
$$\dot{\rho}_{SC} = -i[H_S+H_C+H_{\mathrm{int}}(u(t)),\rho_{SC}] + \mathcal{D}_S[\rho_{SC}] + \gamma\,\mathcal{D}_C[\rho_{SC}],$$
where $\mathcal{D}_S$ collects the (weak) dissipators acting on $S$ and $\mathcal{D}_C$ collects dissipators acting on the controller $C$ with damping rate $\gamma>0$ that is not negligible (so $C$ is not an ideal noiseless ancilla). Assume the "good control" regime, i.e.\ the coherent coupling strengths in $H_{\mathrm{int}}$ are large compared with the dissipation rates of $S$ but the controller damping $\gamma$ remains significant.

Given a control task specified by an initial state $\rho_{SC}(0)$, a target functional $J[\rho_{SC}(\cdot),u(\cdot)]$ (for example, fidelity to a target state of $S$, or a gate fidelity on $S$, at a final time $T$), determine the optimal control protocol $u^\star(t)$ — together with the optimal choice of controller parameters and coupling — that extremizes $J$ in this regime. Characterize the structure of optimal protocols and the achievable performance as a function of $\gamma$ and the system–controller coupling.

Consider a quantum system S (the "target") undergoing open-system dynamics generated by some Hamiltonian together with a noise process (e.g., a Lindblad master equation with dissipators of a fixed strength). One attempts to control S by coupling it to an auxiliary quantum system A (the "controller"), and the joint system S+A evolves under some controllable Hamiltonian interaction. Assume that the auxiliary controller A is itself subject to noise of the same type and strength as the noise acting on S (so that, per degree of freedom, the controller is just as noisy as the system).

Define a control task by a target operation or target state on S, and define the achievable control error as the infimum, over all admissible joint Hamiltonians and initial states of A, of a suitable distance (e.g., diamond-norm or fidelity-based error) between the realized reduced dynamics on S and the target.

Questions:
(a) Determine the fundamental lower bound on the achievable control error for S as a function of the noise strength, given that the auxiliary A is subject to noise of equal strength per subsystem.
(b) Determine how this lower bound scales with the size (Hilbert-space dimension, or number of qubits/degrees of freedom) of the auxiliary A relative to the size of S. In particular, can the control error be driven to zero by enlarging A while keeping the per-subsystem noise rate fixed, and if so at what rate; if not, what is the asymptotic floor?

Let $w:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$ be a weight function with finite moments $\int x^n w(x)\,dx<\infty$ for all $n\ge 0$, and let $\{p_n(x;w)\}_{n\ge 0}$ denote the associated sequence of orthonormal polynomials, defined by $\deg p_n = n$ and $\int p_m(x;w)p_n(x;w)w(x)\,dx=\delta_{mn}$. By a uniform asymptotic expansion of $p_n(x;w)$ we mean an expression of the form
$$p_n(x;w) = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} A_k(x,n;w) + R_K(x,n;w),$$
together with explicit, computable functions $A_k$ (typically built from elementary or special functions arising in Riemann–Hilbert / steepest-descent analysis) and an explicit, rigorously verified bound $|R_K(x,n;w)|\le E_K(x,n;w)$ that holds uniformly for $x$ in the entire real line (or in a prescribed family of regions covering the whole line, including the bulk, edge, and exterior of the spectrum) and for all $n$ sufficiently large.

Problem. Construct a general algorithm and an accompanying software implementation which, given as input a sufficiently regular weight $w$ (for instance, a positive weight on $\mathbb{R}$ of the form $w(x)=e^{-Q(x)}$ for a real-analytic external field $Q$ with appropriate growth, or a weight on a bounded interval with Jacobi-type endpoint behavior) and integers $n$ and $K$, outputs:
(i) the explicit leading terms $A_0,\dots,A_{K-1}$ of a uniform asymptotic expansion of the orthonormal polynomial $p_n(\,\cdot\,;w)$ valid uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$, and
(ii) a rigorous, computable error bound $E_K(x,n;w)$ for the remainder $R_K$.

Equivalently: determine whether uniform asymptotic expansions with rigorous error bounds for orthogonal polynomials with respect to a general weight can be produced in a fully automated way.

For each integer $n\geq 2$, the normalized $A_{n-1}$ supernomial coefficient $S(L,k)$ is a $q$-series-valued function of $L=(L_1,\dots,L_{n-1})\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{n-1}$ and $k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ subject to $|k|:=k_1+\cdots+k_n=0$; for $n=2$ it reduces to the usual normalized $q$-binomial coefficient, and for $n=3$ it coincides with the $A_2$ supernomial. Let $C=(C_{ij})$ denote the Cartan matrix of $A_{n-1}$ and write $LCL = \sum_{i,j} C_{ij} L_i L_j$. The "weak" $A_{n-1}$ summation
$$\sum_{L\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{n-1}} q^{LCL/2}\, S(L,k) \;=\; \frac{q^{(k_1^2+\cdots+k_n^2)/2}}{(q;q)_\infty^{\,n-1}}$$
is known but is insufficient to iterate Bailey-type chains of identities.

Problem. Find and prove an arbitrary-rank $A_{n-1}$ Bailey-type summation theorem involving the supernomials $S(L,k)$ that simultaneously generalizes:
(i) the $A_1$ $q$-binomial invariance summation, and
(ii) the two known $A_2$ supernomial summations used in the Bailey iteration,
and is strong enough to admit indefinite iteration, thereby producing infinite families of Rogers–Ramanujan-type identities of higher rank rather than only the single identity yielded by the weak form above.

Let $n\geq 2$ and $N\geq 1$ be integers. Let $C=(C_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq n-1}$ be the Cartan matrix of type $A_{n-1}$, i.e. $C_{ii}=2$, $C_{i,i\pm 1}=-1$, and $C_{ij}=0$ otherwise. For $k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$ with $|k|=k_1+\cdots+k_n=0$, define:

(i) the normalized $A_{n-1}$ supernomial $S(L,k)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ associated with a composition $L\in\mathbb Z_+^{n-1}$ and the weight encoded by $k$ (the standard $q$-supernomial coefficient of type $A_{n-1}$);

(ii) the level-$N$ $A_{n-1}$ string function $C_k(q)$, expressed via a sum
$$C_k(q)=\sum_{\eta\in\mathbb Z^{n-1}\otimes\mathbb Z^{N-1}} (\text{standard summand})\,,$$
which is the normalized branching/string function of the level-$N$ vacuum module of $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n$ at weight $k$.

For $L\in\mathbb Z_+^{n-1}$ and $\eta\in\mathbb Z^{n-1}\otimes\mathbb Z^{N-1}$, let $\mu\in\mathbb Z^{n-1}\otimes\mathbb Z^{N-1}$ be determined by the linear constraint
$$(C\otimes I)\eta + (I\otimes C)\mu = (CL)\otimes e_{N-1},$$
where $e_{N-1}$ is the last standard basis vector in $\mathbb Z^{N-1}$, with the integrality requirements that make $\mu$ a well-defined nonnegative integer vector.

Define the $q$-binomial coefficient $\binom{a+b}{b}_q$ in the usual way. Prove that
$$\sum_{L\in\mathbb Z_+^{n-1}}\sum_{\eta} q^{\tfrac{1}{2N}\,L^{T}CL+\tfrac{1}{2}\eta^{T}(C\otimes C^{-1})\eta}\binom{\mu+\eta}{\eta}_q S(L,k) \;=\; q^{(k_1^2+\cdots+k_n^2)/(2N)}\,C_k(q).$$

The case $n=2$ is established; prove the identity for all $n\geq 2$.

Setup. Let $S$ be a quantum system (the target) coupled to an auxiliary quantum system $A$ (the controller/ancilla). The joint system evolves on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_S\otimes\mathcal{H}_A$ under a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(t)$ whose role is to drive $S$ toward a desired target unitary or state. Suppose a control protocol has been designed to achieve a target operation with ideal fidelity $F_0$ when $H(t)$ is implemented exactly and when the auxiliary $A$ is noiseless.

Now perturb the control Hamiltonian by a stochastic process: replace $H(t)$ by
$$\tilde H(t) = H(t) + \delta H(t),$$
where $\delta H(t)$ is a (possibly time-correlated) random Hermitian operator modelling imperfections in the implementation of the control fields (e.g. amplitude, phase, or timing noise on the classical drives that generate $H(t)$). Let $F[\delta H]$ denote the average fidelity (over realisations of $\delta H$) of the realised protocol with respect to the intended target.

Questions.
(i) Derive a quantitative description of how the deviation $F_0 - \mathbb{E}\,F[\delta H]$ depends on the statistics (mean, covariance, spectral density) of $\delta H(t)$ and on the structure of the ideal $H(t)$.
(ii) Compare this to the case where the only noise is decoherence/noise acting on the auxiliary system $A$ (e.g. a Lindblad dissipator on $A$). Determine whether noise on the control Hamiltonian $H(t)$ can be modelled, suppressed, or compensated by the same mathematical and algorithmic methods (e.g. dynamical decoupling, robust/composite pulses, ensemble optimal control, filter-function formalism) used to handle noise on the auxiliary controller, or whether genuinely different techniques are required.

Provide either a unified framework that treats the two noise sources on equal footing, or identify a structural obstruction showing that they must be treated separately.

Consider a quantum feedback-control setup in which a quantum "plant" system $P$ is to be regulated (e.g., stabilized to a target state, cooled, or have a target observable optimized) by a controller $C$. Two paradigms are to be compared:

(a) Measurement-based feedback (MBF): the plant is continuously monitored by a measuring device, producing a classical record on which a classical controller acts to apply control fields back on the plant.

(b) Coherent feedback control (CFC): the controller $C$ is itself an auxiliary quantum system, coherently coupled to the plant through quantum channels (no measurement is performed); control is implemented via Hamiltonian and dissipative interaction between $P$ and $C$.

Model the controller $C$ as an open quantum system that is itself subject to damping and noise. Concretely, suppose in case (b) the joint plant–controller dynamics are described by a Lindblad master equation
$$\dot\rho_{PC} = -i[H_{PC},\rho_{PC}] + \mathcal{D}[L_{\text{ctrl}}]\rho_{PC} + \kappa\,\mathcal{D}[a_C]\rho_{PC} + \gamma\,(\bar n+1)\mathcal{D}[a_C]\rho_{PC} + \gamma\,\bar n\,\mathcal{D}[a_C^\dagger]\rho_{PC},$$
where $\kappa$ parameterizes controller damping and $(\gamma,\bar n)$ parameterize controller thermal noise; in case (a) the analogous noise is absent on the (now classical) controller but the plant suffers measurement back-action and detector inefficiency.

For a fixed control task (e.g., minimization of steady-state plant entropy, minimization of an observable variance, or maximization of fidelity to a target pure state), do the following:

1. Determine, as a function of the controller noise parameters $(\kappa,\gamma,\bar n)$, the comparative performance of optimal MBF and optimal CFC protocols.

2. Identify the threshold values of the controller noise level at which any performance advantage of CFC over MBF is eliminated.

3. Characterize whether such thresholds occur in regimes that are physically relevant for realistic experimental implementations.

Several works since 2013 have begun to address the comparison. Hamerly and Mabuchi, and later studies including a unified collision-model framework (Phys. Rev. A 108, 042413, 2023) and recent works on atoms coupled to semi-infinite waveguides (arXiv:2307.16876), provide partial results: coherent feedback tends to be superior at low temperatures and weak coupling and for operator control, while measurement-based feedback can outperform coherent feedback in strong-coupling/noisy regimes and for state stabilization; controllers in the maximally mixed state nullify any CFC advantage. However, a general quantitative threshold answer for arbitrary noisy controllers and tasks of practical relevance remains incomplete, so the problem is best regarded as partially solved.

Background and definitions.

(1) An invariant random-matrix ensemble on the space of N×N Hermitian matrices is a probability measure of the form
   dP_N(H) = (1/Z_N) exp(-N Tr V(H)) dH,
where V: ℝ → ℝ is a (sufficiently regular, confining) potential, dH is Lebesgue measure on Hermitian matrices, and Z_N is the normalizing constant. Such measures are invariant under unitary conjugation H ↦ U H U*. The empirical spectral distribution μ_N = (1/N) Σ_{i=1}^N δ_{λ_i(H)} converges, as N → ∞, to a deterministic compactly supported probability measure μ_V on ℝ (the equilibrium measure associated with V), called the limiting spectral density of the ensemble.

(2) A Wigner-type ensemble is an ensemble of N×N Hermitian matrices W = (W_{ij}) whose entries are independent (up to the Hermitian symmetry W_{ji} = conjugate(W_{ij})) and centered, with variances scaled so that an N → ∞ limiting spectral density exists. The classical Wigner ensembles share the semicircle law as their limiting spectral density with the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE), the invariant ensemble corresponding to V(x) = x²/2. Similarly, Wishart-type ensembles (sample covariance matrices with i.i.d. entries) share the Marchenko–Pastur law as their limiting spectral density with the Laguerre Unitary Ensemble (LUE), an invariant ensemble built from a quadratic potential on positive matrices.

Problem. Given an arbitrary confining potential V (or, more generally, an arbitrary invariant ensemble) with limiting spectral density μ_V, does there exist a corresponding Wigner-type family — that is, an ensemble of Hermitian random matrices with independent entries (subject to Hermitian symmetry), centered, with appropriately scaled variances — whose empirical spectral distribution also converges almost surely (or in probability) to μ_V as N → ∞? In other words, for every limiting spectral density μ_V arising from an invariant ensemble, construct a Wigner-type ensemble realizing the same limiting spectral density, or else prove that no such Wigner-type family exists for some μ_V.

Let $q$ be a formal variable and use the standard $q$-Pochhammer notation $(q)_n = \prod_{j=1}^n (1-q^j)$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, with $(q)_n = 0$ for $n<0$ and the convention $1/(q)_{n}=0$ when $n<0$. For a vector $L=(L_1,L_2,L_3)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^3$ and $M=(M_1,M_2,M_3)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^3$, write $1/(q)_{M-L} = \prod_{i=1}^3 1/(q)_{M_i-L_i}$.

Let $C$ be the Cartan matrix of type $A_3$,
$$C=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&2\end{pmatrix},$$
and define the quadratic form $LCL/2 = \tfrac12\sum_{i,j}C_{ij}L_iL_j$.

For $L\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^3$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, let $S(L,k)$ denote the normalized $A_3$ supernomial coefficient: with $|L| = L_1+2L_2+3L_3$ assumed $\equiv 0\pmod{4}$ (otherwise $S(L,k)=0$),
$$S(L,k) = \sum_{\substack{a,b,c,d\ge 0\\ a+b=L_1,\ c+d=L_2,\\ \text{(standard }A_3\text{ supernomial constraints)}}} \prod (\text{Gaussian }q\text{-binomials})$$
i.e. the $q$-supernomial associated with the symmetric power representation of weight $(k,k,k,\dots)$ for $\mathfrak{sl}_4$, normalized so that for the rank-one truncation it reduces to the Andrews--Bressoud $q$-supernomial.

Find a closed-form evaluation, simple enough that (after extracting common factors) it can be iterated as a Bailey-type recursion, of the multi-sum
$$F(M,k;q) \;=\; \sum_{L\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^3} \frac{q^{LCL/2}\, S(L,k)}{(q)_{M_1-L_1}(q)_{M_2-L_2}(q)_{M_3-L_3}}, \qquad M=(M_1,M_2,M_3)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^3.$$

The known case in which the denominator contains only the single factor $(q)_{M_2-L_2}$ (with no restriction on $L_1$ or $L_3$) admits a closed form; the problem is to obtain the analogous closed form for the full three-parameter sum above.

For a real parameter $\lambda > 0$ and a nonnegative integer $n$, let $C_n^{\lambda}$ denote the Gegenbauer (ultraspherical) polynomial of degree $n$ and parameter $\lambda$, defined by the generating function
$$\frac{1}{(1-2xr+r^2)^{\lambda}} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} C_n^{\lambda}(x)\, r^n, \qquad |r|<1,\ x\in[-1,1].$$
For real parameters $\delta>0$, $\lambda>0$, and $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$, define
$$F_n^{\lambda,\delta}(t) \;=\; \int_0^t (t-\theta)^{\delta}\, C_n^{\lambda}(\cos\theta)\, (\sin\theta)^{2\lambda}\, d\theta, \qquad 0<t\le \pi.$$
Decide whether the following statement is true: $F_n^{\lambda,\delta}(t) > 0$ for every $t\in(0,\pi]$ and every $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$ if and only if $\delta \ge \lambda+1$.

Let $n\ge 2$ and $p\ge n$ be integers. Let $C=(C_{ij})$ be the Cartan matrix of type $A_{n-1}$, i.e. $C_{ii}=2$, $C_{i,i\pm1}=-1$, and $C_{ij}=0$ otherwise, and let $I$ denote the identity matrix of size $p-1$. For $L\in\mathbb Z_+^{n-1}$, define
$$F_{p,L}(q)=\sum_{\mu} q^{\frac12\,\mu^{T}(C^{-1}\otimes C)\mu - \mu^{T}(\,\text{shift}\,)}\,\prod\frac{1}{(q)_{\eta}},$$
where the sum is over all $\mu$ in the appropriate tensor lattice satisfying the integrality condition that $(C^{-1}\otimes I)\mu$ has integer entries, and
$$\eta=L\otimes e_1-(C^{-1}\otimes C)\mu.$$
(Here $e_1$ is the first standard basis vector of $\mathbb Z^{p-1}$ and the bosonic factor is the standard Kac–Peterson type sum normalised so that, in the limit $L\to\infty$, $F_{p,L}(q)$ becomes the level-$(p-n)$ string function of the affine Lie algebra $\widehat{sl}_n$.)

Let $S(L,N)$ denote the normalised $A_{n-1}$ supernomial coefficient associated with weights $L\in\mathbb Z_+^{n-1}$ and composition $N\in\mathbb Z_+^n$, defined as the $q$-analogue of the multiplicity of the symmetric $L$-power Schur polynomial in the product of elementary symmetric functions indexed by $N$, normalised in the standard way.

For $k\in\mathbb Z^n$ with $|k|=k_1+\cdots+k_n=0$, $\rho=(1,2,\dots,n)$, and $S_n$ the symmetric group on $n$ letters with sign $\varepsilon(\sigma)$, prove the identity
$$\sum_{\substack{k\in\mathbb Z^n\\|k|=0}}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\varepsilon(\sigma)\,q^{\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(p k_i-2\sigma_i)k_i}\,S\bigl(L,\,p k-\sigma+\rho\bigr)=F_{p,L}(q).$$

Let $n\ge 2$ and $p\ge n$ be integers. Let $C=(C_{ij})$ be the Cartan matrix of type $A_{n-1}$, i.e. $C_{ii}=2$, $C_{i,i\pm1}=-1$, and $C_{ij}=0$ otherwise, and let $I$ denote the identity matrix of size $p-1$. For $L\in\mathbb Z_+^{n-1}$, define
$$F_{p,L}(q)=\sum_{\mu} q^{\frac12\,\mu^{T}(C^{-1}\otimes C)\mu - \mu^{T}(\,\text{shift}\,)}\,\prod\frac{1}{(q)_{\eta}},$$
where the sum is over all $\mu$ in the appropriate tensor lattice satisfying the integrality condition that $(C^{-1}\otimes I)\mu$ has integer entries, and 
$$\eta=L\otimes e_1-(C^{-1}\otimes C)\mu.$$
(Here $e_1$ is the first standard basis vector of $\mathbb Z^{p-1}$ and the bosonic factor is the standard Kac–Peterson type sum normalised so that, in the limit $L\to\infty$, $F_{p,L}(q)$ becomes the level-$(p-n)$ string function of the affine Lie algebra $\widehat{sl}_n$.)

Let $S(L,N)$ denote the normalised $A_{n-1}$ supernomial coefficient associated with weights $L\in\mathbb Z_+^{n-1}$ and composition $N\in\mathbb Z_+^n$, defined as the $q$-analogue of the multiplicity of the symmetric $L$-power Schur polynomial in the product of elementary symmetric functions indexed by $N$, normalised in the standard way.

For $k\in\mathbb Z^n$ with $|k|=k_1+\cdots+k_n=0$, $\rho=(1,2,\dots,n)$, and $S_n$ the symmetric group on $n$ letters with sign $\varepsilon(\sigma)$, prove the identity
$$\sum_{\substack{k\in\mathbb Z^n\\|k|=0}}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\varepsilon(\sigma)\,q^{\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(p k_i-2\sigma_i)k_i}\,S\bigl(L,\,p k-\sigma+\rho\bigr)=F_{p,L}(q).$$

The cases $p=n$ and $p=n+1$ are known. Prove the identity for all remaining $p\ge n+2$.

Consider an open-loop quantum control setting in which the controller drives a finite-dimensional quantum system of Hilbert-space dimension N via a time-dependent Hamiltonian of the form
   H(t) = Σ_n c_n(t) H_n,
where {H_n} is a fixed finite set of available control Hamiltonians and the classical control coefficients c_n(t) may be varied (essentially) arbitrarily as functions of time. Given a control objective (for example, preparing a specified target state from a fixed initial state, or implementing a specified unitary on the system, up to a prescribed error tolerance), define the time-dependent-control complexity of the objective to be the minimal description complexity (e.g., number of bits or piecewise-constant control segments) of a control schedule {c_n(t)} that achieves the objective. Call the control problem "easy" for the pair (objective, {H_n}) if this complexity scales as a polynomial in log N as N grows along a natural family of systems.

(a) Characterize the pairs consisting of a control objective and a set of available control Hamiltonians {H_n} for which the open-loop control problem is easy in the sense above.

(b) Determine whether the class of easy objectives depends nontrivially on the choice of the set {H_n}: that is, exhibit objectives that are easy for some admissible sets of control Hamiltonians but not for others, or prove that the class of easy objectives is independent of the choice of {H_n} within a suitable family.

Consider a small open quantum system $S$ (for example, a single qubit with Hilbert space $\mathbb{C}^2$) coupled to an environment and subject to a continuous quantum measurement whose record is fed back, in real time, into the system's Hamiltonian and/or into the choice of measurement itself. Formally, the conditional state $\rho_t$ evolves according to a stochastic master equation
$$d\rho_t = -i[H(u_t),\rho_t]\,dt + \mathcal{D}[L(v_t)]\rho_t\,dt + \mathcal{H}[L(v_t)]\rho_t\,dW_t,$$
where $\mathcal{D}[L]\rho = L\rho L^\dagger - \tfrac{1}{2}\{L^\dagger L,\rho\}$, $\mathcal{H}[L]\rho = L\rho + \rho L^\dagger - \mathrm{Tr}[(L+L^\dagger)\rho]\rho$, $dW_t$ is a Wiener increment associated with the measurement record, and the control parameters $u_t$ (Hamiltonian control) and $v_t$ (measurement-basis/operator control) are causal functionals of the past measurement record. Fix a control objective such as the steady-state fidelity with a target pure state $|\psi\rangle$, i.e.\ maximize
$$J[u,v] = \liminf_{T\to\infty}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T \langle\psi|\rho_t|\psi\rangle\,dt\right].$$

(a) Construct continuous-measurement-based feedback protocols for such small systems—in particular for a single qubit—that are strictly more general than those considered to date by allowing the measurement operator $L(v_t)$ itself to be modified in feedback, and determine whether such protocols can strictly improve $J[u,v]$ over the best known protocols that use only a fixed measurement and Hamiltonian feedback.

(b) For any protocol that does yield such an enhancement, determine what the structure of the enhancement implies about coherent feedback control, in which the controller is itself a quantum system coupled to $S$ without any classical measurement step.

Identify, where possible, the optimal feedback protocol for the single-qubit case under physically natural noise models and control constraints.

Define a sequence of polynomials $\{A_n(t)\}_{n\ge 0}$ in a variable $t$ by the initial conditions $A_0(t)=1$, $A_1(t)=0$, and the three-term recurrence
$$(n^3-(-1)^n t^3)\,A_n(t)+(n+1)^2(2n+1)\,A_{n+1}(t)+\frac{(n+2)^2}{n+1}\,A_{n+2}(t)=0,\qquad n\ge 0.$$
Set $\widetilde A_n(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n} A_k(t)$. It is known that this partial-sum sequence satisfies the three-term recurrence
$$(n^3-(-1)^n t^3)\,\widetilde A_{n-1}(t)+(2n+1)n\,\widetilde A_n(t)-(n+1)^2 n\,\widetilde A_{n+1}(t)=0,\qquad n\ge 1,$$
and that
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\widetilde A_n(t)=\prod_{j=1}^{\infty}\left(1+\frac{t^3}{8j^3}\right).$$
Provide a proof of this limit identity that proceeds directly from the three-term recurrence satisfied by $\widetilde A_n(t)$, i.e., deduce the value of $\lim_{n\to\infty}\widetilde A_n(t)$ from this recurrence alone, without recourse to the closed-form/combinatorial expressions for $A_n(t)$.

Setup. Fix integers $n\ge 2$ and $p\ge n$. Let $C$ denote the Cartan matrix of type $A_{n-1}$, with inverse $C^{-1}$. Let $\rho=(n-1,n-2,\dots,1,0)\in\mathbb Z^n$, and let $e_1=(1,0,\dots,0)\in\mathbb Z^n$. For a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$ let $\ell(\sigma)$ denote its length, and write $\sigma\cdot v$ for the natural action of $S_n$ on $\mathbb Z^n$ by coordinate permutation.

For $L,M\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$ and zero–sum vectors $k=(k_1,\dots,k_n),\ k'=(k'_1,\dots,k'_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$ with $\sum_i k_i=\sum_i k'_i=0$, define
$$T''(L,M,k,k')\ :=\ \prod_{i=1}^{n}\binom{M+L-k_i+k'_i}{L-k_i}_q,$$
where $\binom{a}{b}_q=\frac{(q)_a}{(q)_b(q)_{a-b}}$ when $0\le b\le a$ and zero otherwise, with $(q)_m=\prod_{j=1}^m(1-q^j)$.

For each $k\in\mathbb Z^n$ with $|k|:=\sum_i k_i=0$ and $\sigma\in S_n$, define an integer exponent $\phi_{p,k,\sigma}$ by
$$\phi_{p,k,\sigma}\ =\ \tfrac{p(p-1)}{2}\,k\cdot C\,k\ -\ k\cdot(p\rho-(p-1)\sigma\cdot\rho)\ +\ \ell(\sigma).$$

On the other side, let $\mu=(\mu^{(1)},\dots,\mu^{(n-1)})$ range over tuples of compositions (with the usual integrality/length restriction of the $A_{n-1}$ supernomial hierarchy: $\mu^{(b)}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{N}$ for a fixed large $N$, satisfying the standard congruence conditions making all subsequent $q$-binomials nonzero). Put
$$\eta\ :=\ nL\,(C^{-1}e_1\otimes e_1)\ -\ (C^{-1}\otimes C)\,\mu,$$
and define
$$\binom{\mu+\eta}{\mu}_q\ :=\ \prod_{b=1}^{n-1}\prod_{j\ge 1}\binom{\mu^{(b)}_j+\eta^{(b)}_j}{\mu^{(b)}_j}_q.$$

Conjecture (to be proved). For all $L,M\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$ and all $p\ge n$,
$$\sum_{\substack{k\in\mathbb Z^n\\ |k|=0}}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}(-1)^{\ell(\sigma)}q^{\phi_{p,k,\sigma}}\,T''\!\bigl(L,M,\,pk-\sigma\cdot\rho+\rho,\,(p-1)k-\sigma\cdot\rho+\rho\bigr)$$
$$=\ \sum_{\mu}q^{\,\tfrac12\,\mu\,(C^{-1}\otimes C)\,\mu}\ \binom{M+nL-\sum_{b=1}^{n-1}C^{-1}_{1,b}\mu^{(b)}_1}{nL}_q\ \binom{\mu+\eta}{\mu}_q.$$

Prove this identity. (The case $p=n+1$ is known from a Gessel–Krattenthaler-type cylindric-partition identity; establish the general case.)

Define two sequences of polynomials $\{A_n(t)\}_{n\ge 0}$ and $\{\widetilde{A}_n(t)\}_{n\ge 0}$ in the variable $t$ by the following recurrences.

The polynomials $A_n(t)$ are determined by the three-term recurrence
$$(n^3-(-1)^n t^3)\,A_n(t) + (n+1)^2(2n+1)\,A_{n+1}(t) + (n+2)^2(n+1)\,A_{n+2}(t) = 0,$$
with initial conditions $A_0(t)=1$ and $A_1(t)=0$.

The polynomials $\widetilde{A}_n(t)$ are determined by the recurrence
$$(n^3-(-1)^n t^3)\,\widetilde{A}_{n-1}(t) + (2n+1)n\,\widetilde{A}_n(t) - (n+1)^2 n\,\widetilde{A}_{n+1}(t) = 0,$$
with appropriate initial conditions ensuring the limit
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \widetilde{A}_n(t) = \prod_{j=1}^{\infty}\left(1+\frac{t^3}{8j^3}\right).$$

Question: Can the polynomials $A_n(t)$ and $\widetilde{A}_n(t)$ be expressed in explicit closed form as (generalized) hypergeometric functions, i.e., as ${}_pF_q$-type series with parameters and argument depending on $n$ and $t$?

(a) (Cylindric/product limit) In an appropriate limit, $T$ reduces to the cylindric-partition product expression $T''(L_1,M_1,k,k';q)$ for $A_{n-1}$.

(b) (Reciprocal-supernomial limit) In another limit, $T$ reduces to the reciprocal supernomial $T'(L,k;q)$.

(c) ($A_1$ specialization) For $n=2$, $T$ reduces to $T((M_1,M_2),k;q)/(q)_{M_1+M_2}$, recovering the known $A_1$ generalized supernomial.

(d) (Reciprocal-$q$ symmetry) $T$ satisfies
$$\frac{T(L,M,k,k';1/q)}{T(L,M,k,k';q)} = q^{-\,M\,C\,L \;+\; \sum_i k_i k'_i},$$
where $C$ is the Cartan matrix of $A_{n-1}$.

Consider a mesoscopic quantum system (e.g., a superconducting circuit, quantum dot, optomechanical resonator, or ultracold atomic ensemble) modeled as an open quantum system whose dynamics are governed by a controlled master equation or stochastic Schrödinger equation, and which is subject to a classical or quantum noise process N(t) generated by an identifiable environment.

Define two control paradigms:

1. Feedback control: the controller obtains information about the system only by performing measurements on the system itself (or on its output fields), and uses the measurement record to choose control inputs applied back to the system.

2. Feedforward control: the controller obtains information about the realization of the noise N(t) without interacting with the system — for example, by directly probing the noise source or environment before (or independently of) the noise's action on the system — and uses this information to apply a control input to the system designed to compensate for the upcoming noise.

The problem is the following:

(a) Identify physically meaningful situations in mesoscopic quantum systems for which feedforward control, in the sense above, is useful — that is, situations where access to the noise realization (without measuring the system) provides a control advantage with respect to relevant figures of merit such as fidelity, decoherence suppression, gate error, or state transfer efficiency.

(b) Construct explicit example models (with concrete Hamiltonians, noise sources, and control inputs) demonstrating the feedforward-control paradigm in such systems.

(c) For each such example, quantitatively compare feedforward control with feedback control on the same system and noise model, identifying the regimes (in terms of noise statistics, bandwidth, measurement back-action, accessibility of the environment, and control resources) in which feedforward outperforms feedback, and vice versa.

Work in the framework of algebraic logic. For a countably infinite ordinal α, let CA_α denote the variety of cylindric algebras of dimension α. A representation of an algebra 𝔄 ∈ CA_α on a square unit is an embedding into a cylindric set algebra whose unit is a Cartesian power ^αU for some non-empty set U. A representation on a weak unit (also called a weak representation, or representation on a weak space) is an embedding into a generalized cylindric set algebra whose unit is a weak space ^αU^{(p)} = { s ∈ ^αU : |{ i ∈ α : s(i) ≠ p(i) }| < ω } for some fixed p ∈ ^αU. Such a representation is called complete if it preserves all existing infinitary suprema and infima of the algebra.

Let CRCA_α^w denote the class of all atomic algebras 𝔄 ∈ CA_α that admit a complete representation on a weak unit, where α is countably infinite and 𝔄 is countable.

Question: Is CRCA_α^w an elementary class? Equivalently, can membership in CRCA_α^w be characterized by a set of first-order sentences in the signature of CA_α, so that CRCA_α^w is closed under elementary equivalence?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

It is known (Hirsch–Hodkinson) that the class of completely representable cylindric algebras of dimension ≥ 3 with square units is non-elementary, and that for infinite-dimensional polyadic algebras the class of completely representable algebras is elementary. The variant for weak units (weak representations) in countably infinite dimension does not have a clearly identified resolution in the available sources; the Hirsch–Hodkinson cardinality argument is noted not to transfer to weak units, and no later paper located in the search definitively settles whether the weak-unit version is elementary. Status is therefore reported as unknown.

Let $1 < p < \infty$ with $p \neq 2$, and let $\mu$ be a finite (positive) measure such that the Banach space $L^p(\mu)$ is non-separable. Recall that a sequence $(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in a Banach space $X$ is called an unconditional (Schauder) basis if every $x \in X$ has a unique representation $x = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n e_n$ that converges unconditionally (i.e., the convergence is independent of the order of summation).

Question: Does there exist a Banach space $Y$ which possesses an unconditional basis and contains $L^p(\mu)$ as a (closed linear) subspace?

Equivalently, can a non-separable $L^p(\mu)$ space (with $1 < p < \infty$, $p \neq 2$) be embedded isomorphically into a Banach space having an unconditional basis?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Enflo and Rosenthal proved that the answer is "no" when the density character of $L^p(\mu)$ is at least $\aleph_\omega$, and conjectured the same conclusion in the entire non-separable range. Subsequent work (e.g., by Johnson and Schechtman) has obtained partial results on non-separable $L^p$ spaces, but the problem in full generality (for all non-separable densities, in particular $\aleph_1$) appears to remain open.

The problem has been solved in the negative. Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a star graph consisting of $N\ge 3$ half-lines joined at a common vertex $v$. For $\Psi=(\psi_j)_{j=1}^N\in L^2(\mathcal{G})=\bigoplus_{j=1}^N L^2(\mathbb{R}^+)$, denote the mass by $M(\Psi)=\sum_j\int_0^\infty|\psi_j(x)|^2\,dx$. Fix a coupling constant $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ and a focusing power $p>2$. Consider on $\mathcal{G}$ the nonlinear Schrödinger problem with an attractive $\delta$-interaction of strength $\alpha$ at $v$: functions are continuous at $v$, $\psi_1(0)=\cdots=\psi_N(0)$, and the Kirchhoff-type condition $\sum_j\psi_j'(0)=\alpha\psi_1(0)$ holds. Define the energy
$$E(\Psi)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^N\int_0^\infty|\psi_j'|^2\,dx+\frac{\alpha}{2}|\Psi(v)|^2-\frac{1}{p}\sum_{j=1}^N\int_0^\infty|\psi_j|^p\,dx,$$
on the form domain $H^1(\mathcal{G})$, and, for $\omega>0$, the action
$$S_\omega(\Psi)=E(\Psi)+\frac{\omega}{2}M(\Psi).$$
There is a known threshold $\alpha^\ast<0$ (depending on $N$ and $p$) such that:

(i) for every $\omega>0$ with $-N\sqrt{\omega}<\alpha<\alpha^\ast$, the action $S_\omega$ admits an absolute minimizer on the natural Nehari-type constraint;

(a) When the condition $-N\sqrt{\omega}<\alpha<\alpha^\ast$ in (i) fails, the action $S_\omega$ still possesses, on the constrained set, a local minimizer whose action value is strictly greater than the infimum.

Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a star graph consisting of $N\ge 3$ half-lines joined at a common vertex $v$. For $\Psi=(\psi_j)_{j=1}^N\in L^2(\mathcal{G})=\bigoplus_{j=1}^N L^2(\mathbb{R}^+)$, denote the mass by $M(\Psi)=\sum_j\int_0^\infty|\psi_j(x)|^2\,dx$. Fix a coupling constant $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ and a focusing power $p>2$. Consider on $\mathcal{G}$ the nonlinear Schrödinger problem with an attractive $\delta$-interaction of strength $\alpha$ at $v$: functions are continuous at $v$, $\psi_1(0)=\cdots=\psi_N(0)$, and the Kirchhoff-type condition $\sum_j\psi_j'(0)=\alpha\psi_1(0)$ holds. Define the energy
$$E(\Psi)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^N\int_0^\infty|\psi_j'|^2\,dx+\frac{\alpha}{2}|\Psi(v)|^2-\frac{1}{p}\sum_{j=1}^N\int_0^\infty|\psi_j|^p\,dx,$$
on the form domain $H^1(\mathcal{G})$, and, for $\omega>0$, the action
$$S_\omega(\Psi)=E(\Psi)+\frac{\omega}{2}M(\Psi).$$
There is a known threshold $\alpha^\ast<0$ (depending on $N$ and $p$) such that:

(i) for every $\omega>0$ with $-N\sqrt{\omega}<\alpha<\alpha^\ast$, the action $S_\omega$ admits an absolute minimizer on the natural Nehari-type constraint;

(ii) for every $\alpha<0$, the energy $E$ admits an absolute minimizer at fixed mass $M(\Psi)=m$ for all $m$ below an explicit critical value $m^\ast(\alpha)$.

Prove or disprove the following:

(a) When the condition $-N\sqrt{\omega}<\alpha<\alpha^\ast$ in (i) fails, the action $S_\omega$ still possesses, on the constrained set, a local minimizer whose action value is strictly greater than the infimum.

(b) When the analogous mass condition $m<m^\ast(\alpha)$ in (ii) fails, the energy $E$ at fixed mass $m$ still possesses a local minimizer on $\{M(\Psi)=m\}$ whose energy value is strictly greater than the infimum.

The energy part (b) of the conjecture has been addressed by Adami, Cacciapuoti, Finco, and Noja in "Stable standing waves for a NLS on star graphs as local minimizers of the constrained energy" (arXiv:1509.01810, 2016), where they prove that on a star graph with attractive delta interaction the symmetric standing wave is a local minimizer of the constrained energy at fixed mass for all admissible masses, even when the absolute-minimum threshold fails, yielding orbital stability. The corresponding statement for the action functional (part (a)) does not appear to be explicitly resolved in the same generality, so the full conjecture is at least partially solved.

representations.normalized:
Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a connected metric graph (i.e., a finite or countable collection of edges, each identified isometrically with an interval of $\mathbb{R}$ or with a half-line, glued at vertices), and consider the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation
$$ i \partial_t \psi(t,x) = -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}} \psi(t,x) - |\psi(t,x)|^{2\mu}\psi(t,x), \qquad x \in \mathcal{G},\ t \in \mathbb{R}, $$
where $\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$ is the Laplacian on $\mathcal{G}$ defined edgewise as $\partial_x^2$ with Kirchhoff (free) boundary conditions at each vertex, and $\mu>0$ is the focusing power. A standing wave is a solution of the form $\psi(t,x) = e^{i\omega t}\Phi_\omega(x)$, where $\Phi_\omega \in H^1(\mathcal{G})$ solves the stationary equation
$$ -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}\Phi_\omega + \omega \Phi_\omega - |\Phi_\omega|^{2\mu}\Phi_\omega = 0. $$
A standing wave is called orbitally stable if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that any solution with initial data within $\delta$ (in $H^1$-norm) of $\Phi_\omega$ remains within $\varepsilon$ of the orbit $\{e^{i\theta}\Phi_\omega : \theta \in \mathbb{R}\}$ for all time; otherwise it is orbitally unstable.

For star graphs (finite collections of half-lines joined at a single vertex), explicit formulas for the stationary states $\Phi_\omega$ are available, and orbital stability/instability has been analyzed via variational and spectral methods.

Problem: Extend the orbital stability and instability analysis of standing waves to more complex metric graphs $\mathcal{G}$, such as metric trees or graphs containing loops (e.g., tadpole, dumbbell, or bubble-tower graphs), where explicit closed-form expressions for the stationary states are generally unavailable. Specifically, identify branches $\omega \mapsto \Phi_\omega$ of standing-wave solutions on such graphs and establish the spectral conditions (on the linearized operator around $\Phi_\omega$) and variational/energy conditions sufficient to determine the orbital stability or instability of these branches.

Let X be a (real) Banach space and X* its topological dual. Recall that the Mackey topology μ(X*, X) on X* is the topology of uniform convergence on weakly compact, absolutely convex subsets of X. Given a sequence (x*_n) in X*, a convex block subsequence of (x*_n) is a sequence (y*_k) of the form
   y*_k = Σ_{n ∈ I_k} a_n^{(k)} x*_n,
where I_1 < I_2 < ⋯ are nonempty finite subsets of ℕ (with max I_k < min I_{k+1}), a_n^{(k)} ≥ 0, and Σ_{n ∈ I_k} a_n^{(k)} = 1 for every k.

The Banach space X is said to have property (K) if every weak*-null sequence in X* admits a convex block subsequence that converges to 0 in the Mackey topology μ(X*, X).

For an index set Γ and a family {X_γ : γ ∈ Γ} of Banach spaces, the ℓ^1-direct sum is
   (⨁_{γ ∈ Γ} X_γ)_{ℓ^1} = { (x_γ)_{γ ∈ Γ} : x_γ ∈ X_γ, Σ_{γ ∈ Γ} ‖x_γ‖ < ∞ },
endowed with the norm ‖(x_γ)‖ = Σ_{γ ∈ Γ} ‖x_γ‖.

Determine the least cardinal κ such that there exists a family {X_γ : γ ∈ Γ} of Banach spaces with |Γ| = κ, where each X_γ has property (K), but the ℓ^1-direct sum (⨁_{γ ∈ Γ} X_γ)_{ℓ^1} fails property (K).

Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a metric graph (a finite or locally finite collection of vertices joined by edges, each edge identified isometrically with an interval of $\mathbb{R}$ or a half-line). On $\mathcal{G}$ consider the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation
$$ i\,\partial_t \psi = -\Delta_V \psi - |\psi|^{2\mu}\psi, \qquad \mu>0, $$
where $\psi:\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{C}$ and $-\Delta_V$ denotes the self-adjoint Laplacian on $L^2(\mathcal{G})$ associated with a chosen family $V$ of linear vertex (boundary) conditions. Standing waves are solutions of the form $\psi(t,x)=e^{i\omega t}\phi(x)$ with $\phi$ satisfying
$$ -\Delta_V \phi - |\phi|^{2\mu}\phi = -\omega\phi. $$
Ground states are minimizers of the energy
$$ E_V(\phi) = \tfrac{1}{2}\langle \phi, -\Delta_V\phi\rangle - \tfrac{1}{2\mu+2}\int_{\mathcal{G}}|\phi|^{2\mu+2}\,dx $$
restricted to the mass constraint $\|\phi\|_{L^2(\mathcal{G})}^2 = m$.

For the standard Kirchhoff (free) vertex conditions and $\delta$-type vertex conditions the existence, structure, and stability of ground states have been investigated. The question concerns alternative vertex couplings, in particular $\delta'$-type vertex conditions (defined, on each vertex of degree $d$, by continuity of the normal derivatives and a jump in the values weighted by a coupling constant, generalizing the $\delta'$ point interaction on the line).

Problem. For metric graphs $\mathcal{G}$ equipped with non-standard vertex couplings (e.g., $\delta'$-type or other self-adjoint couplings beyond Kirchhoff and $\delta$-type), determine:
(i) whether new families/branches of standing waves $e^{i\omega t}\phi(x)$ exist that are not present in the Kirchhoff or $\delta$ cases;
(ii) whether bifurcations of constrained ground states occur as the mass $m$, the nonlinearity exponent $\mu$, or the coupling strength varies;
(iii) whether spontaneous symmetry-breaking phenomena occur for ground states, in analogy with the symmetry-breaking pitchfork bifurcation established for the NLS on $\mathbb{R}$ with a $\delta'$ point interaction.

Provide existence/nonexistence theorems, identify bifurcation thresholds, and describe the resulting symmetry-broken ground state profiles.

Let G be a connected metric graph with nontrivial topology beyond a star graph — for instance, a finite or infinite tree with bounded vertex degrees, or a network containing internal edges and/or loops. Each edge e of G is identified with an interval (of finite or infinite length), and a function u on G is a collection {u_e}_{e∈E(G)} of functions on the edges. On each edge consider the focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation
   i ∂_t u_e = −∂_{xx} u_e − |u_e|^2 u_e,
coupled at every vertex v by Kirchhoff (free) boundary conditions: continuity of u across v, and vanishing of the signed sum of outgoing derivatives ∑_{e∋v} ∂_x u_e(v) = 0. Let H = −Δ_G denote the corresponding self-adjoint Kirchhoff Laplacian on L^2(G).

A soliton on a single edge (viewed as a line) is the standard NLS profile φ_{c,v}(x,t) = √(2c) sech(√c (x−vt)) e^{i(vx/2 − (v^2/4 − c)t)} with speed v ∈ ℝ and amplitude parameter c > 0.

(a) Establish dispersive and Strichartz-type estimates for the linear propagator e^{−itH} on G that are sufficient to develop a local and global well-posedness theory for the cubic NLS on G in an appropriate energy space.

(b) Using such estimates, prove a rigorous scattering theorem for incoming solitons: given a high-velocity soliton ψ_0 ≈ φ_{c,v}(·,0) initially supported far from the vertex set on a chosen incoming edge, describe the asymptotic behavior of the solution u(t) as t → +∞, in particular decompose u(t) along each outgoing edge into a sum of transmitted/reflected soliton-like profiles plus a dispersive remainder, and compute the corresponding transmission and reflection coefficients in terms of the topology (vertex degrees, edge lengths, internal cycles) of G.

(c) Determine how the topology of G — e.g. branching of trees, presence of bounded internal edges, or loops — quantitatively affects the dispersive decay rates, the validity of Strichartz inequalities, and the resulting soliton dynamics.

The known general implications are: weak*-separability of $B_{X^*}$ implies weak Baire measurability of the norm, which in turn implies weak*-separability of $X^*$; the reverse implications fail in general Banach spaces. For the specific case $X = C(K)$, whether these properties are equivalent is stated as an open problem, and recent literature on weak Baire measurability of balls in Banach spaces and on weak*-separability of $C(K)^*$ does not appear to resolve it.

Let $\mathcal{G}=(V,E)$ be a metric graph: a connected combinatorial graph in which each edge $e\in E$ is identified with a real interval (either $[0,\ell_e]$ for finite edges or a half-line $[0,\infty)$ for unbounded edges), with edges glued at their endpoints according to the vertex structure of $\mathcal{G}$. A function $u:\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{C}$ is a tuple $(u_e)_{e\in E}$ of functions on the corresponding intervals. On $\mathcal{G}$ consider the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation
$$ i\,\partial_t u_e(t,x) = -\partial_{xx} u_e(t,x) - |u_e(t,x)|^{p-1} u_e(t,x), \qquad e\in E,$$
with $p>1$, equipped at every vertex $v\in V$ with Kirchhoff (free) boundary conditions: continuity of $u$ across $v$ and vanishing of the sum of outgoing derivatives at $v$. The mass $M(u)=\int_{\mathcal{G}} |u|^2\,dx$ and energy
$$E(u)=\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{\mathcal{G}} |\partial_x u|^2\,dx-\tfrac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathcal{G}}|u|^{p+1}\,dx$$
are conserved. By a soliton on a half-line $[0,\infty)\subset\mathcal{G}$ we mean the standard NLS soliton profile
$$ \phi_{c,v}(t,x)=A\,\operatorname{sech}\!\big(\kappa(x-vt-x_0)\big)\,e^{i(\frac{v}{2}x-\omega t)} $$
of the line, suitably translated and modulated, where the parameters $A,\kappa,\omega$ are determined by $p$ and the soliton speed $v$. Two extreme dynamical regimes are well understood: the standing-wave regime, in which $u(t,\cdot)=e^{-i\omega t}\Phi(\cdot)$ for a bound state $\Phi$ on $\mathcal{G}$, and the fast-soliton-scattering regime, in which an incoming soliton with $|v|\gg 1$ on a half-edge approaches a vertex and is scattered into outgoing solitons on the other half-edges with effective transmission/reflection coefficients given, to leading order in $1/|v|$, by the linear scattering matrix at the vertex.

The problem is to develop a rigorous mathematical theory describing intermediate regimes (moderate soliton speeds, finite size of localized structures relative to graph features) for the NLS equation on metric graphs. Specifically, formulate and prove theorems giving necessary and/or sufficient conditions, in terms of the graph geometry (edge lengths, topology, vertex structure), the nonlinearity exponent $p$, and the initial data, under which the dynamics:
(a) traps an incoming soliton at a vertex or in a compact subgraph (capture), producing a long-time localized coherent structure;
(b) generates one or more new solitons emerging from a junction after the interaction (generation);

representations.original:
Let $\mathcal{G}=(V,E)$ be a metric graph: a connected combinatorial graph in which each edge $e\in E$ is identified with a real interval (either $[0,\ell_e]$ for finite edges or a half-line $[0,\infty)$ for unbounded edges), with edges glued at their endpoints according to the vertex structure of $\mathcal{G}$. A function $u:\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{C}$ is a tuple $(u_e)_{e\in E}$ of functions on the corresponding intervals. On $\mathcal{G}$ consider the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation
$$ i\,\partial_t u_e(t,x) = -\partial_{xx} u_e(t,x) - |u_e(t,x)|^{p-1} u_e(t,x), \qquad e\in E,$$
with $p>1$, equipped at every vertex $v\in V$ with Kirchhoff (free) boundary conditions: continuity of $u$ across $v$ and vanishing of the sum of outgoing derivatives at $v$. The mass $M(u)=\int_{\mathcal{G}} |u|^2\,dx$ and energy
$$E(u)=\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{\mathcal{G}} |\partial_x u|^2\,dx-\tfrac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathcal{G}}|u|^{p+1}\,dx$$
are conserved. By a soliton on a half-line $[0,\infty)\subset\mathcal{G}$ we mean the standard NLS soliton profile
$$ \phi_{c,v}(t,x)=A\,\operatorname{sech}\!\big(\kappa(x-vt-x_0)\big)\,e^{i(\frac{v}{2}x-\omega t)} $$
of the line, suitably translated and modulated, where the parameters $A,\kappa,\omega$ are determined by $p$ and the soliton speed $v$. Two extreme dynamical regimes are well understood: the standing-wave regime, in which $u(t,\cdot)=e^{-i\omega t}\Phi(\cdot)$ for a bound state $\Phi$ on $\mathcal{G}$, and the fast-soliton-scattering regime, in which an incoming soliton with $|v|\gg 1$ on a half-edge approaches a vertex and is scattered into outgoing solitons on the other half-edges with effective transmission/reflection coefficients given, to leading order in $1/|v|$, by the linear scattering matrix at the vertex.

The problem is to develop a rigorous mathematical theory describing intermediate regimes (moderate soliton speeds, finite size of localized structures relative to graph features) for the NLS equation on metric graphs. Specifically, formulate and prove theorems giving necessary and/or sufficient conditions, in terms of the graph geometry (edge lengths, topology, vertex structure), the nonlinearity exponent $p$, and the initial data, under which the dynamics:
(a) traps an incoming soliton at a vertex or in a compact subgraph (capture), producing a long-time localized coherent structure;
(b) generates one or more new solitons emerging from a junction after the interaction (generation);
(c) transfers a quantitatively controlled portion of the mass $M(u)$ from a propagating soliton into a localized bound-state-like coherent structure supported near a vertex or compact subgraph.

Provide a rigorous framework (e.g., modulation analysis, effective dynamics for soliton parameters, asymptotic stability statements, or scattering-type results) that quantifies these phenomena in the intermediate regime between the standing-wave and fast-scattering limits.

Existing rigorous results concern bound states/standing waves (Adami–Cacciapuoti–Finco–Noja and others) and fast-soliton scattering at vertices, but the intermediate dynamical regime appears to remain open with no published resolution found.

Let $(\Omega, \Sigma, \mu)$ be a complete probability space and let $X$ be a (real) Banach space. Denote by $\mathcal{P}_0(X)$ the family of nonempty subsets of $X$. A multifunction $F:\Omega \to \mathcal{P}_0(X)$ is called scalarly measurable if for every open half-space $H \subseteq X$ (equivalently, for every $x^* \in X^*$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, taking $H = \{x \in X : x^*(x) < \alpha\}$), the lower inverse image
$$F^{-}(H) = \{\omega \in \Omega : F(\omega) \cap H \ne \emptyset\}$$
belongs to $\Sigma$. Equivalently, this means that for each $x^* \in X^*$ the support function $\omega \mapsto \sup_{x \in F(\omega)} x^*(x)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable as an extended real-valued function. A function $f:\Omega \to X$ is called a selector of $F$ if $f(\omega) \in F(\omega)$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$, and it is called scalarly measurable if $\omega \mapsto x^*(f(\omega))$ is $\Sigma$-measurable for every $x^* \in X^*$.

Question: Suppose $F:\Omega \to \mathcal{P}_0(X)$ is a scalarly measurable multifunction whose values $F(\omega)$ are convex and closed subsets of $X$. Must $F$ admit a scalarly measurable selector $f:\Omega \to X$?

A celebrated result of Cascales–Kadets–Rodríguez (2009) establishes that every scalarly measurable multifunction with weakly compact (not necessarily convex) values in an arbitrary Banach space admits a scalarly measurable selector. The general case of closed convex (possibly unbounded, not weakly compact) values appears to remain open in the literature; recent works (e.g., Di Piazza–Sambucini 2025 on selections of integrable multifunctions in arbitrary Banach spaces, and surveys on Pettis integration of multifunctions) discuss closely related selection problems but do not provide a definitive resolution of this specific question. No source found explicitly claims a solution.

Let X be a Banach space with dual X*. A multifunction F : Ω → 2^X defined on a measurable space (Ω, Σ) is called scalarly measurable if for every x* ∈ X* the real-valued function ω ↦ sup{x*(x) : x ∈ F(ω)} is Σ-measurable. Let wk(X) denote the family of all nonempty weakly compact subsets of X. A set selector on wk(X) is a map ψ : wk(X) → X such that ψ(C) ∈ C for every C ∈ wk(X). The family wk(X) is said to have property (SC) if there exists a set selector ψ on wk(X) such that, for every scalarly measurable multifunction F : Ω → wk(X) defined on any measurable space (Ω, Σ), the composition ψ ∘ F : Ω → X is scalarly measurable (i.e. x* ∘ ψ ∘ F is Σ-measurable for every x* ∈ X*).

Question: Assume that the density character of X equals ω₁. Does wk(X) necessarily have property (SC)?

Consider a real analytic time-optimal control problem of the form
  ẋ(t) = f(x(t), u(t)),  x(t) ∈ M,  u(t) ∈ U,
where M is a real analytic manifold, U ⊂ ℝ^m is a control set (e.g. a compact polytope), and f is real analytic in x and (in standard formulations) affine in u. A time-optimal trajectory is an absolutely continuous curve x(·) : [0, T] → M, generated by a measurable control u(·) : [0, T] → U, that joins two given points x(0) = p and x(T) = q in minimum time among all admissible trajectories.

For an admissible control u(·), define its switching set to be the set of times t ∈ [0, T] at which u is not locally constant (equivalently, every neighborhood of t contains points where u takes at least two distinct values). Call this the switching set of the corresponding trajectory.

Question: Is it true that whenever two points p, q ∈ M can be joined by a time-optimal trajectory, there exists a time-optimal trajectory from p to q whose switching set has Lebesgue measure zero? Equivalently, can time-optimal trajectories whose switching sets have positive Lebesgue measure always be avoided?

A function $f:[0,1]\to X$ with values in a Banach space $X$ is called Riemann integrable if there exists $v\in X$ such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with the property that for every tagged partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=1$ of $[0,1]$ with $\max_i(t_i-t_{i-1})<\delta$ and every choice of tags $s_i\in[t_{i-1},t_i]$, one has $\bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}(t_i-t_{i-1})f(s_i)-v\bigr\|<\varepsilon$. A Banach space $X$ is said to have the Lebesgue property (LP) if every Riemann integrable function $f:[0,1]\to X$ is continuous at almost every point of $[0,1]$ with respect to Lebesgue measure.

Problem: Give an intrinsic characterization of those Banach spaces $X$ that have the Lebesgue property.

Recent work (2023–2024) provides a characterization of the Lebesgue property in terms of a new sequential asymptotic structure lying strictly between spreading models and asymptotic models, and shows that a subspace $X\subset L_1[0,1]$ has LP iff every spreading model of $X$ is equivalent to the unit vector basis of $\ell_1$. Let κ be an infinite cardinal and let ℓ₂(κ) denote the Hilbert space of all functions x : κ → ℝ such that {γ ∈ κ : x(γ) ≠ 0} is countable and ∑_{γ∈κ} |x(γ)|² < ∞, equipped with the inner product ⟨x, y⟩ = ∑_{γ∈κ} x(γ)y(γ).

A function f : [0, 1] → X with values in a Banach space X is said to be Riemann integrable if there exists v ∈ X such that for every ε > 0 there is a partition 0 = t₀ < t₁ < ⋯ < tₙ = 1 of [0, 1] with the property that ‖∑_{i=1}^{n} f(s_i)(t_i − t_{i−1}) − v‖ < ε for every choice of points s_i ∈ [t_{i−1}, t_i]. The function f is called weakly continuous at a point t ∈ [0, 1] if for every continuous linear functional x* ∈ X*, the scalar function x* ∘ f is continuous at t.

A Banach space X is said to have the weak Lebesgue property (WLP) if every Riemann integrable function f : [0, 1] → X is weakly continuous at almost every point of [0, 1] with respect to the Lebesgue measure.

Determine the cardinals κ for which the Hilbert space ℓ₂(κ) has the weak Lebesgue property.

Question: For every bounded function $f:[0,1]\to c_0$, must the set $I(f)\subseteq c_0$ be convex?

Let $c_0$ denote the Banach space of real sequences converging to $0$, equipped with the supremum norm. For a bounded function $f:[0,1]\to c_0$, a Riemann sum of $f$ associated with a tagged partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=1$ with tags $\xi_i\in[t_{i-1},t_i]$ is the vector
$$S(f,\{t_i,\xi_i\})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(\xi_i)\,(t_i-t_{i-1})\in c_0,$$
and the diameter of the partition is $\max_i(t_i-t_{i-1})$. Define
$$I(f)=\bigl\{x\in c_0 : \text{there exist tagged partitions }P_k\text{ with diameter}\to 0\text{ such that }S(f,P_k)\to x\bigr\}.$$
Question: For every bounded function $f:[0,1]\to c_0$, must the set $I(f)\subseteq c_0$ be convex?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Kadets–Kadets question on convexity of the set of limits of Riemann sums for bounded $c_0$-valued functions appears to remain open. Convexity of $I(f)$ is known for finite-dimensional target spaces (Halperin–Miller for Hilbert; finite-dimensional case of more recent work) and for B-convex spaces, but $c_0$ is not B-convex, and a 2023 arXiv preprint on the topic does not claim a resolution for $c_0$.

Let $(\Omega, \Sigma, \mu)$ be a complete probability space and let $X$ be a Banach space with topological dual $X^*$. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is said to be scalarly measurable if $x^*\circ f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ is $\Sigma$-measurable for every $x^*\in X^*$, and scalarly bounded if there exists a constant $M$ such that for every $x^*\in X^*$ with $\|x^*\|\le 1$ one has $|x^*(f(\omega))|\le M$ for $\mu$-almost every $\omega\in\Omega$ (the exceptional null set may depend on $x^*$). The function $f$ is called Pettis integrable if $x^*\circ f\in L^1(\mu)$ for every $x^*\in X^*$ and if for every $A\in\Sigma$ there exists a vector $\int_A f\,d\mu\in X$ satisfying
$$x^*\!\left(\int_A f\,d\mu\right)=\int_A x^*\circ f\,d\mu\qquad\text{for all }x^*\in X^*.$$
Associated with such $f$ is the vector measure $\nu_f:\Sigma\to X$ given by $\nu_f(A)=\int_A f\,d\mu$, with range
$$R(\nu_f)=\{\nu_f(A):A\in\Sigma\}\subset X.$$
The Banach space $X$ is said to have the Pettis Integrability Property (PIP) if, for every complete probability space $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)$, every scalarly bounded and scalarly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is Pettis integrable.

Question: Suppose $X$ has the PIP. Must $R(\nu_f)$ be a separable subset of $X$ for every Pettis integrable function $f:\Omega\to X$ defined on every complete probability space $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)$?

Let $\mathcal{U}$ denote the class of Banach spaces $X$ with the property that every Pettis integrable function $f\colon [0,1]\to X$ (with respect to Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$) is McShane integrable. Recall that:

- A function $f\colon [0,1]\to X$ is Pettis integrable if $x^*\circ f$ is Lebesgue integrable for every $x^*\in X^*$ and, for each measurable $E\subseteq[0,1]$, there exists $x_E\in X$ such that $x^*(x_E)=\int_E x^*\circ f\,d\lambda$ for all $x^*\in X^*$.
- $f$ is McShane integrable with integral $x\in X$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a gauge $\delta\colon[0,1]\to(0,\infty)$ such that $\bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^n f(t_i)(b_i-a_i)-x\bigr\|<\varepsilon$ for every $\delta$-fine McShane partition $\{(t_i,[a_i,b_i])\}_{i=1}^n$ of $[0,1]$.

A compact Hausdorff space $K$ is called Eberlein compact if it is homeomorphic to a weakly compact subset of some Banach space, and uniform Eberlein compact if it is homeomorphic to a weakly compact subset of a Hilbert space (equivalently, $C(K)$ is Hilbert generated).

Let $\mathcal{K}=\{K \text{ compact Hausdorff} : C(K)\in\mathcal{U}\}$. It is known that every uniform Eberlein compact belongs to $\mathcal{K}$, while some Eberlein compacta do not.

Question: Does there exist a non-uniform Eberlein compact space $K$ that belongs to $\mathcal{K}$?
