Let $\Gamma$ be a group and let $\rho_1, \rho_2 : \Gamma \to \mathrm{Diff}^2_+(S^1)$ be two representations of $\Gamma$ into the group of orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphisms of the circle $S^1$. The Godbillon–Vey class of $\mathrm{Diff}^2_+(S^1)$ is the bounded 2-cocycle (Bott–Thurston cocycle)
$$ gv(f,g) \;=\; \int_{S^1} \log(f\circ g)' \, d\!\log g' , $$
which defines a class $[gv] \in H^2(\mathrm{Diff}^2_+(S^1); \mathbb{R})$. Pulling back via $\rho_i$ gives a class $\rho_i^*[gv] \in H^2(\Gamma; \mathbb{R})$.

Say that $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ are topologically conjugate if there exists a homeomorphism $h: S^1 \to S^1$ such that $\rho_2(\gamma) = h \circ \rho_1(\gamma) \circ h^{-1}$ for every $\gamma \in \Gamma$.

Question: Is the pulled-back Godbillon–Vey class invariant under topological conjugacy? That is, does $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ being topologically conjugate (by some homeomorphism $h$ of $S^1$, not assumed to be smooth) imply
$$ \rho_1^*[gv] \;=\; \rho_2^*[gv] \quad \text{in } H^2(\Gamma; \mathbb{R}) \,? $$

$$ gv(f,g) \;=\; \int_{S^1} \log(f\circ g)' \, d\!\log g' , $$

Question: Is the pulled-back Godbillon–Vey class invariant under topological conjugacy? That is, does $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ being topologically conjugate (by some homeomorphism $h$ of $S^1$, not assumed to be smooth) imply
$$ \rho_1^*[gv] \;=\; \rho_2^*[gv] \quad \text{in } H^2(\Gamma; \mathbb{R}) \,? $$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The classical foliation analogue of this question (topological invariance of the Godbillon–Vey class for codimension-one C^2 foliations) was settled affirmatively by Hurder–Katok (under absolute continuity) and Ghys–Tsuboi gave related results, but the discrete-group/circle-diffeomorphism version remains a recognized open problem; in the broader piecewise-C^2 category the invariant is known to fail to be a topological invariant. No source found establishing or refuting topological invariance of the restricted Godbillon–Vey class for arbitrary groups of C^2 circle diffeomorphisms.

Let $S^1 = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ denote the circle. An orientation-preserving homeomorphism $f : S^1 \to S^1$ is said to have a real-analytic graph if the set $\{(x, f(x)) : x \in S^1\} \subset S^1 \times S^1$ is a real-analytic subvariety of $S^1 \times S^1$ (so $f$ may fail to be a real-analytic function in the usual sense, since both $f$ and its inverse $f^{-1}$ are allowed to have singularities, e.g., points with vertical or horizontal tangencies in the graph). Recall Denjoy's classical theorem: every orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphism of $S^1$ with irrational rotation number is topologically conjugate to the rigid rotation by that rotation number.

Question: Does the conclusion of Denjoy's theorem persist in this enlarged class? That is, is every orientation-preserving homeomorphism $f : S^1 \to S^1$ whose graph is a real-analytic subvariety of $S^1 \times S^1$, and whose rotation number is irrational, topologically conjugate to the corresponding rigid rotation, even when the graph admits singular points (so that $f$ or $f^{-1}$ need not be smooth at every point)?

For a finite word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n$ over a finite alphabet, a factor of $w$ is any contiguous block $w_i w_{i+1} \cdots w_j$. The Parikh vector of a finite word over an alphabet $\Sigma$ is the vector indexed by $\Sigma$ whose $a$-th entry is the number of occurrences of the letter $a$. An abelian square is a nonempty word of the form $uv$ where $u$ and $v$ have the same Parikh vector (i.e., $v$ is a permutation of $u$). The number of distinct abelian-square factors of $w$ is the cardinality of the set $\{x : x \text{ is a factor of } w \text{ and } x \text{ is an abelian square}\}$, where factors are compared as strings.

Prove or disprove: for every positive integer $n$ and every finite word $w$ of length $n$ over an arbitrary finite alphabet, if $w$ contains exactly $k$ distinct abelian-square factors, then there exists a word $w'$ of length $n$ over the binary alphabet $\{0,1\}$ that contains at least $k$ distinct abelian-square factors.

Let $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n$ be a finite word over the binary alphabet $\{0,1\}$. A factor of $w$ is a contiguous subword $w_i w_{i+1} \cdots w_j$. The Parikh vector of a binary word $u$ is the pair $(|u|_0, |u|_1)$ counting the occurrences of $0$ and $1$ in $u$. A factor of the form $uv$, where $u$ and $v$ have the same length and the same Parikh vector, is called an abelian square; its associated Parikh vector is $(|u|_0, |u|_1)$. Two abelian-square factors of $w$ are said to be equivalent if they have the same Parikh vector, and non-equivalent otherwise.

For each integer $n \geq 1$, define
$$\mathrm{XNL}(n) = \max_{w \in \{0,1\}^n} \#\{\text{Parikh vectors } (a,b) : w \text{ has an abelian-square factor with Parikh vector } (a,b)\},$$
the maximum, over all binary words of length $n$, of the number of pairwise non-equivalent abelian-square factors.

Determine whether
$$\mathrm{XNL}(n) = O(n^{3/2}),$$
i.e.\ whether there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that $\mathrm{XNL}(n) \leq C n^{3/2}$ for all $n$.

Let $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n$ be a binary word over the alphabet $\{a,b\}$, viewed as a circular word, i.e., indices are taken modulo $n$. A factor of $w$ of length $\ell \le n$ is any string $w_i w_{i+1} \cdots w_{i+\ell-1}$ (indices mod $n$). An abelian square is a nonempty word of the form $u v$ where $|u|=|v|$ and $v$ is a permutation of $u$ (equivalently, $u$ and $v$ have the same number of $a$'s and the same number of $b$'s). For a circular word $w$ of length $n$, count only factors of length at most $n$, and call two abelian-square factors distinct if they are different as strings.

The conjugates of $w$ are all cyclic rotations of $w$, and the complement is obtained by swapping $a \leftrightarrow b$.

Prove or disprove the following:
(a) If $n$ is odd, then the minimum, over all binary circular words of length $n$, of the number of distinct abelian-square factors equals $(n-1)/2$, and this minimum is attained exactly by the conjugates and complements of $a^n$ and $a^{n-1}b$.
(b) If $n$ is even, then this minimum equals $(n-2)/2$, and it is attained exactly by the conjugates and complements of the words $a^k b^{n-k}$ with $k$ odd, $k \in \{1,3,5,\dots,n-1\}$.

Let $F \in \mathbb{C}\{z_1,\dots,z_n\}$ be the germ of a holomorphic function defining an isolated hypersurface singularity at the origin of $\mathbb{C}^n$ (so that $F(0)=0$ and the partial derivatives $F_{z_1},\dots,F_{z_n}$ generate an ideal of finite colength in $\mathbb{C}\{z_1,\dots,z_n\}$). Define the Tjurina algebra of $F$ by
$$T_F \;:=\; \mathbb{C}[[z_1,\dots,z_n]]\big/\bigl(F,\,F_{z_1},\dots,F_{z_n}\bigr),$$
which is a finite-dimensional local $\mathbb{C}$-algebra. The Mather–Yau theorem asserts that the pair $(n, T_F)$ determines the germ $(V(F),0) \subset (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ up to biholomorphism, but its proof is non-constructive.

Problem (Reconstruction Problem): Give an explicit algorithmic procedure that, taking as input the integer $n$ and the isomorphism class of the finite-dimensional local $\mathbb{C}$-algebra $T_F$, produces a defining holomorphic germ $F' \in \mathbb{C}\{z_1,\dots,z_n\}$ such that the hypersurface germ $(V(F'),0)$ is biholomorphic to $(V(F),0)$.

The reconstruction problem dates to the 1980s and remains a long-standing problem in singularity theory. Explicit reconstruction has been achieved in special cases: e.g., for homogeneous (and quasi-homogeneous) isolated hypersurface singularities from their Milnor/Tjurina algebras (Eastwood–Isaev and others, ~2012), and a 2022 preprint (arXiv:2212.00566) claims a constructive procedure for reconstruction from the moduli algebra in further generality. Let $n \ge 2$ and $d \ge 3$ be integers. Denote by $\mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]_d$ the vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ in $n$ complex variables, and let $X_n^d \subset \mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]_d$ be the Zariski open subset of forms with nonzero discriminant. For $f \in X_n^d$, the partial derivatives $\partial f/\partial z_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial z_n$ form a regular sequence and define a graded Artinian Gorenstein algebra $M_f := \mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]/(\partial f/\partial z_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial z_n)$ whose socle lies in degree $n(d-2)$. Via Macaulay's inverse system, $M_f$ corresponds to a homogeneous polynomial $\overline{f}$ of degree $n(d-2)$ in the dual variables $e_1,\dots,e_n$, called the associated form of $f$. This construction defines a morphism of affine algebraic varieties
$$\Phi : X_n^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}[e_1,\dots,e_n]_{n(d-2)}, \qquad f \mapsto \overline{f},$$
which is equivariant with respect to the standard $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$-actions (with appropriate characters) on source and target.

Prove or disprove: for every regular $\mathrm{GL}_n$-invariant function $S$ on $X_n^d$ there exists a rational $\mathrm{GL}_n$-invariant function $R$ on $\mathbb{C}[e_1,\dots,e_n]_{n(d-2)}$, defined at every point of the image $\Phi(X_n^d)$, such that $R \circ \Phi = S$ on $X_n^d$.

Fix integers $n\ge 2$ and $d\ge 3$, and work over $\mathbb{C}$. Let $V=\mathbb{C}^n$ with coordinates $x_1,\dots,x_n$, and let $\mathbb{C}[x_1,\dots,x_n]_d$ denote the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$. Let
$$X_n^d=\{f\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,\dots,x_n]_d : f \text{ defines a smooth hypersurface in } \mathbb{P}(V)\},$$
i.e. the locus of forms whose partial derivatives $\partial f/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial x_n$ have no common nontrivial zero. For $f\in X_n^d$ the Milnor algebra
$$M_f=\mathbb{C}[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(\partial f/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial x_n)$$
is a graded Gorenstein Artinian $\mathbb{C}$-algebra with socle in degree $n(d-2)$, and dualising one obtains the "associated form" $\mathbf{A}(f)\in\mathbb{C}[e_1,\dots,e_n]_{n(d-2)}$ on the dual space, where $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is the dual basis. This construction extends to a morphism
$$\nabla : X_n^d \longrightarrow Z_n^{d-1}, \qquad f\longmapsto (\partial f/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial x_n),$$
with $Z_n^{d-1}\subset(\mathbb{C}[x_1,\dots,x_n]_{d-1})^{\oplus n}$ the open subset of $n$-tuples of degree-$(d-1)$ forms with no common nontrivial zero, and to a morphism
$$\Psi : Z_n^{d-1} \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}[e_1,\dots,e_n]_{n(d-2)}$$
sending such a regular sequence to the corresponding associated form. The natural $\mathrm{SL}_n$-actions on $V$ and $V^\vee$ make $\nabla$ and $\Psi$ equivariant, and after passing to $\mathrm{SL}_n$-quotients of the projectivisations one obtains induced morphisms
$$\mathbb{P}\nabla|_{\mathbb{P}X_n^d}: \mathbb{P}X_n^d /\!/\mathrm{SL}_n \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}Z_n^{d-1}/\!/\mathrm{SL}_n,$$
$$\mathbb{P}\Psi : \mathbb{P}Z_n^{d-1}/\!/\mathrm{SL}_n \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}\mathbb{C}[e_1,\dots,e_n]_{n(d-2)}^{ss}/\!/\mathrm{SL}_n,$$
where $(-)^{ss}$ denotes the GIT-semistable locus.

Prove, for every $n\ge 2$ and $d\ge 3$, that:

(C1) $\mathbb{P}\nabla|_{\mathbb{P}X_n^d}$ is a closed immersion, i.e. an isomorphism onto a closed subset of $\mathbb{P}Z_n^{d-1}/\!/\mathrm{SL}_n$.

(C2) $\mathbb{P}\Psi$ is an isomorphism onto a closed subset of an affine open subset of $\mathbb{P}\mathbb{C}[e_1,\dots,e_n]_{n(d-2)}^{ss}/\!/\mathrm{SL}_n$.

Fix integers $n \ge 2$ and $d \ge 3$. Let $W^d_n = \mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]_d$ denote the vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ in $n$ variables over $\mathbb{C}$, and let $\mathbb{P}W^d_n$ denote its projectivization. The natural action of $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ induces an action on $W^d_n$ and on $\mathbb{P}W^d_n$.

For $f \in W^d_n$, the gradient map sends $f$ to the linear span $\langle f_{z_1},\dots,f_{z_n}\rangle$ of its first partial derivatives, viewed as an element of the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(n,\, \mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]_{d-1})$ (well-defined for $f$ such that the partials are linearly independent). This induces an $\mathrm{SL}_n$-equivariant morphism
$$\mathbb{P}\nabla : \mathbb{P}W^d_n \dashrightarrow \mathrm{Gr}(n,\, \mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]_{d-1}),$$
defined on the open locus where the partial derivatives are linearly independent. Let $\mathbb{P}X^d_n \subset \mathbb{P}W^d_n$ be the locus of forms $f$ whose Jacobian ideal $(f_{z_1},\dots,f_{z_n})$ is $\mathfrak{m}$-primary (equivalently, $f$ defines an isolated singularity at the origin when viewed as a function), so that $\mathbb{P}\nabla$ is regular on $\mathbb{P}X^d_n$. Pass to GIT quotients by $\mathrm{SL}_n$ on both source and target.

Question: Is the (closure of the) image of the restriction $\mathbb{P}\nabla\big|_{\mathbb{P}X^d_n}$, after taking the GIT quotient by $\mathrm{SL}_n$, a normal variety for all $n \ge 2$ and $d \ge 3$?

Fix integers $n\ge 2$ and $d\ge 3$. Let $\mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]_d$ denote the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ in $n$ variables, and let $X^d_n\subset\mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]_d$ be the affine open subvariety of forms with nonzero discriminant (the nondegenerate forms). For $f\in X^d_n$, the Milnor (Jacobian) algebra $M(f):=\mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]/(\partial f/\partial z_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial z_n)$ is a graded Gorenstein Artinian $\mathbb{C}$-algebra of socle degree $\nu:=n(d-2)$. Choose any linear form $\omega:M(f)_\nu\to\mathbb{C}$ that generates the socle; then the Macaulay inverse system / Gorenstein duality produces a homogeneous polynomial $\widetilde{f}$ of degree $\nu=n(d-2)$ in the $n$ dual variables $e_1,\dots,e_n$, well defined up to the action of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ on the target. This defines a morphism of affine algebraic varieties
$$\Phi:X^d_n\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}[e_1,\dots,e_n]_{n(d-2)},\qquad f\mapsto \widetilde{f},$$
called the associated-form map.

Whenever $\Phi(f)$ has nonzero discriminant, one may apply $\Phi$ again (with the parameters $(n,d)$ replaced by $(n,n(d-2))$), obtaining the iterate $\Phi^2$ as a rational map between the corresponding spaces of forms. More generally, define $\Phi^k$ recursively as a rational map between the relevant spaces of forms.

Question: Is $\Phi^k$ a well-defined rational map for every positive integer $k$? Equivalently, is it the case that for every $k\ge 1$ there exists at least one nondegenerate form $f\in X^d_n$ such that $\Phi(f),\Phi^2(f),\dots,\Phi^{k-1}(f)$ all have nonzero discriminant?

Let $n \geq 2$ and $d \geq 3$ be integers. Denote by $V_d := \mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]_d$ the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ in $n$ variables, and by $X_n^d \subset V_d$ the nondegenerate locus, i.e., the set of forms $f \in V_d$ whose discriminant $\Delta(f)$ is nonzero (equivalently, the projective hypersurface $\{f=0\}$ is smooth, or, working affinely, $f$ has an isolated singularity only at the origin).

For $f \in X_n^d$, the Milnor algebra $M(f) := \mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]/(\partial f/\partial z_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial z_n)$ is a finite-dimensional graded Gorenstein $\mathbb{C}$-algebra whose socle is concentrated in degree $n(d-2)$. Choosing the standard volume form, one obtains a canonically defined nondegenerate symmetric $n(d-2)$-linear form on $M(f)_1 \cong \mathbb{C}\langle z_1,\dots,z_n\rangle$, hence a homogeneous polynomial $\Phi(f)$ of degree $n(d-2)$ on the dual space, called the associated form of $f$. This defines the associated-form morphism
$$\Phi : X_n^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}[z_1^*,\dots,z_n^*]_{n(d-2)}, \qquad f \mapsto \Phi(f).$$

Let $p$ be the smallest positive integer such that the map
$$\Delta^p \, \Phi : X_n^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}[z_1^*,\dots,z_n^*]_{n(d-2)}, \qquad f \mapsto \Delta(f)^p \, \Phi(f),$$
extends to a morphism defined on the whole affine space $V_d = \mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]_d$.

Determine this integer $p$ as an explicit function of $n$ and $d$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of computing the minimal exponent $p$ such that $\Delta^p \Phi$ extends to the full space of degree-$d$ forms is stated as an open problem in the literature on the associated-form morphism. An upper bound $p \le \max\{\pi_{i_1\dots i_n}\}$ is known, and partial results exist for small cases (e.g. binary forms), but no general closed-form expression for $p$ has been established. Subsequent works on the associated form morphism do not appear to resolve it.

A graph $G=(V,E)$ is called a block graph if every block (i.e., every maximal 2-connected subgraph, or bridge) of $G$ is a complete graph. The (0,1)-adjacency matrix $A(G)$ of $G$ is the symmetric $|V|\times|V|$ matrix whose $(u,v)$ entry equals $1$ if $\{u,v\}\in E$ and $0$ otherwise. The graph $G$ is said to be nonsingular if $A(G)$ is invertible (equivalently, $\det A(G)\neq 0$, or the nullity $\eta(G)=\dim\ker A(G)$ equals $0$), and singular otherwise.

Problem: Give a combinatorial characterization, in terms of the structural arrangement and sizes of the blocks of $G$, of exactly which block graphs $G$ are nonsingular.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of characterizing nonsingular block graphs, posed by Bapat and Roy in 2013, appears to remain open. Subsequent work has produced partial results: classes of nonsingular/singular block graphs, related conjectures, a linear-time algorithm to test singularity of block graphs, and a characterization in the more general vertex-weighted setting via deletion/contraction of pendant blocks. No source found provides a complete combinatorial characterization in the unweighted case.

Let $G$ be a finite simple connected graph. A block of $G$ is a maximal connected subgraph of $G$ that has no cut vertex; equivalently, blocks are the maximal 2-connected subgraphs together with the bridge edges and isolated vertices. A graph $G$ is called a block graph if every block of $G$ is a complete graph. The order of a block is its number of vertices. Let $A(G)$ denote the adjacency matrix of $G$, and define the nullity $\eta(G)$ to be the multiplicity of $0$ as an eigenvalue of $A(G)$.

Question: Is it true that for every connected block graph $G$ in which every block has order at least $3$, the nullity satisfies $\eta(G)\le 1$?

Let $(M^{2n}, \omega)$ be a symplectic manifold and let $F = (f_1, \dots, f_n) : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be the moment map of a completely integrable Hamiltonian system, so that $f_1, \dots, f_n$ are smooth functions on $M$ that pairwise Poisson-commute and are functionally independent on a dense open set. The level sets of $F$ define a singular Lagrangian fibration on $M$. A point $p \in M$ is called a singular point of the fibration if $df_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge df_n$ vanishes at $p$, and it is called a degenerate singularity if the quadratic parts of $f_1, \dots, f_n$ at $p$ do not span a Cartan subalgebra of the symplectic Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sp}(T_p M, \omega_p)$ (i.e., $p$ fails to be a non-degenerate singularity in the sense of Williamson).

Two germs of singular Lagrangian fibrations $(M_1, \omega_1, F_1, p_1)$ and $(M_2, \omega_2, F_2, p_2)$ are called fiber-wise diffeomorphic if there exists a germ of diffeomorphism $\varphi : (M_1, p_1) \to (M_2, p_2)$ that maps the fibers of $F_1$ to the fibers of $F_2$ (no compatibility with the symplectic forms is required). They are called symplectically equivalent if such a $\varphi$ can additionally be chosen to satisfy $\varphi^* \omega_2 = \omega_1$.

Question. For germs of degenerate singular points of completely integrable Hamiltonian systems, do there exist nontrivial local symplectic invariants distinguishing fiber-wise diffeomorphic germs that are not symplectically equivalent? If so, classify them: how many independent invariants occur and what is their nature (functional moduli, formal series, numerical invariants, etc.)? Address this question already in the simplest setting of one-degree-of-freedom systems ($n = 1$), where $M$ is a surface, $\omega$ is an area form, and $F = f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is a smooth function with a degenerate critical point at $p$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The general question is still open, but partial results exist. For cusp (parabolic-type) singularities in one degree of freedom, normal forms and symplectic classifications have been obtained: a real-analytic Lagrangian fibration near a cusp $H = y^3 - x^2$ has been classified, with the symplectic form reducible to $dx\wedge dy + f(H)\, dx\wedge dy$ for a functional invariant $f$. A complete answer for general degenerate singularities is not available.

Two singular points (or singular fibers) of such systems are said to have the same topological type if there is a fiber-preserving homeomorphism between saturated neighborhoods of them, and the same symplectic type if this homeomorphism can be chosen to be a symplectomorphism.

Carry out the following two tasks for $n \le 3$:

(a) Provide a complete classification, up to topological equivalence, of all singularities (singular points and singular fibers, including their saturated neighborhoods) that can occur in algebraically integrable Hamiltonian systems with $n$ degrees of freedom, $n \in \{1,2,3\}$.

(b) For each such topological type, determine a complete set of symplectic invariants that classifies these singularities up to symplectic equivalence in a saturated neighborhood.

Let $(M,\omega)$ be a symplectic manifold of dimension $2n$ equipped with a completely integrable Hamiltonian system, that is, a smooth map $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ whose components are functionally independent and pairwise Poisson-commute, $\{f_i,f_j\}=0$. Suppose that $F$ is obtained by a toric degeneration procedure: there exists a flat family $\pi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{C}$ of complex projective varieties whose generic fiber is isomorphic to a smooth projective variety $X$ (with a chosen Kähler form pulling back to $\omega$) and whose central fiber $X_0=\pi^{-1}(0)$ is a (possibly singular) toric variety with moment map $\mu_0:X_0\to\Delta\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ for the residual torus action. The map $F:X\to\Delta$ is then constructed by transporting $\mu_0$ via a gradient-Hamiltonian flow associated with the degeneration, yielding a continuous map whose restriction to a dense open subset is a smooth Lagrangian torus fibration over the interior of $\Delta$, but which acquires singular fibers over a codimension-at-least-one subset of $\Delta$ coming from the singularities of $X_0$ and from points where the gradient-Hamiltonian flow fails to be defined.

Problem. Describe the topology and geometry of the singular fibers $F^{-1}(b)$ of such an integrable system $F$ obtained by toric degeneration, and of small open neighbourhoods of these singular fibers in $M$. In particular:

(a) Determine the homeomorphism (and, where possible, diffeomorphism) type of each singular fiber, including whether it is a smooth manifold, an orbifold, or a more general stratified space, and whether it is isotropic or Lagrangian in $(M,\omega)$.

(b) Describe the symplectic germ of $F$ near such a singular fiber: identify normal forms (analogous to the Eliasson–Miranda–Zung normal forms for non-degenerate singularities) and the local monodromy and affine-structure data on the base $\Delta$ near the corresponding singular value.

(c) Classify the singular fibers that arise this way up to fiber-preserving symplectomorphism of a neighbourhood, and relate the classification to the combinatorial/algebraic data of the toric degeneration (e.g. the singularities of $X_0$ and the Newton–Okounkov body $\Delta$).

Consider a smooth Calabi–Yau 3-fold $X$ equipped with a (special) Lagrangian fibration $\pi : X \to B$ of Strominger–Yau–Zaslow type, i.e. a proper map whose generic fibers are special Lagrangian 3-tori. The discriminant locus $\Delta \subset B$ (the set of critical values of $\pi$) is a real codimension-2 graph-like subset of $B$. Along generic edges of $\Delta$ the singular fibers have a single focus–focus (nodal) singularity, so that one obtains one-parameter families of focus–focus singular fibers. At isolated points of $B$ where two or more such one-dimensional families of focus–focus singularities meet (vertices of the discriminant graph), the topology and symplectic local model of the corresponding singular fiber become more intricate.

Problem. Give a complete and explicit description of the singular Lagrangian fibers of $\pi$ that occur over these intersection points of one-dimensional families of focus–focus singularities: describe their topological type, their stratification, and a local symplectic normal form for $\pi$ near such a fiber.

Let $S^2$ denote the standard two-dimensional sphere with its round Riemannian metric, and let $T^*S^2$ be its cotangent bundle equipped with the canonical symplectic structure. A natural Hamiltonian system on $S^2$ is one whose Hamiltonian has the form
$$H(q,p) = \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^{ij}(q)\, p_i p_j + V(q),$$
where $g^{ij}$ is the inverse of the round metric and $V \in C^\infty(S^2)$ is a potential. A function $F \in C^\infty(T^*S^2)$ is called a polynomial integral of degree $n$ if $\{H,F\} = 0$ and $F$ is a polynomial in the momenta $p_i$ of degree exactly $n$ with coefficients depending on $q$. An integral is called trivial if it is a polynomial in $H$ (in particular, a constant), and nontrivial otherwise.

Problem. Exhibit a natural Hamiltonian system on $S^2$ with nonconstant potential $V$ that admits a nontrivial polynomial integral of degree $5$ in the momenta, but admits no nontrivial polynomial integral of degree less than $5$. Equivalently, construct such $(S^2, V)$ together with the integral $F$, or prove that no such system exists.

1. $(M,g)$ is an Einstein manifold, i.e. $\mathrm{Ric}(g) = \Lambda\, g$ for some constant $\Lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
2. $(M,g)$ admits two commuting Killing vector fields $\xi$ and $\eta$, where $\xi$ is timelike (generating stationarity) and $\eta$ has closed orbits with a fixed axis (generating axial symmetry); equivalently, $(M,g)$ is stationary and axially symmetric.
3. $(M,g)$ admits a Killing tensor of order (valence) $k \geq 3$, that is, a totally symmetric tensor field $K_{a_1\cdots a_k}$ satisfying $\nabla_{(a_0} K_{a_1\cdots a_k)} = 0$, which is irreducible in the sense that it cannot be expressed as a polynomial in the metric $g$, the Killing vectors $\xi,\eta$, and Killing tensors of lower order.

Either exhibit such a metric explicitly, or prove that no such metric exists.

Let H be a random N×N real symmetric matrix drawn from the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE), i.e. the probability measure on the space of real symmetric matrices is invariant under orthogonal conjugation and the entries above the diagonal are independent centered Gaussians (with off-diagonal variance equal to half the diagonal variance). The eigenvalues {E_n} of H model the energies of compound-nucleus (CN) resonances of fixed exact quantum numbers (spin, parity, isospin), and the squared overlaps of eigenvectors with fixed channel vectors model the partial reaction widths.

The GOE makes specific predictions for:
(a) the nearest-neighbour spacing distribution of the unfolded levels (Wigner surmise);
(b) long-range spectral rigidity, in particular the Dyson–Mehta Δ₃(L) statistic for sequences of L consecutive levels;
(c) the distribution of partial widths in any single channel, namely the Porter–Thomas distribution (a χ² distribution with one degree of freedom).

Question. Determine whether these GOE predictions are quantitatively consistent with the available experimental data on compound-nucleus resonances obtained from sequences of resonances with clean (well-resolved) quantum numbers. In particular:

(i) Do the measured nearest-neighbour spacings and the Δ₃(L) statistic for long sequences of levels agree, within statistical errors, with the GOE predictions?

(ii) Does the empirical distribution of reduced neutron widths in such sequences agree with the Porter–Thomas distribution?

A complete answer should either establish agreement (with quantified confidence) sufficient to justify modeling CN resonances by GOE Hamiltonians, or identify and quantify statistically significant deviations.

Spacing statistics and short-range correlations of CN resonance sequences agree well with GOE predictions, but two issues remain unsettled: the Δ₃(L) statistic for long level sequences, and the distribution of reduced neutron widths. Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian symmetric space. A symmetric tensor field $K$ of valence $r$ on $M$ is called a Killing tensor if its symmetrized covariant derivative vanishes, i.e. $\nabla_{(i_0} K_{i_1\dots i_r)} = 0$. Equivalently, the function $P_K(x,p) = K^{i_1\dots i_r}(x)\, p_{i_1}\cdots p_{i_r}$ on the cotangent bundle $T^*M$ is a polynomial first integral of the geodesic flow. Killing vector fields correspond to valence-1 Killing tensors and yield linear integrals. The set of Killing tensors of all valences forms a graded commutative algebra under the symmetric tensor product.

Question: Is every Killing tensor on a Riemannian symmetric space expressible as a sum of symmetric products of Killing vector fields? Equivalently, is the algebra of all polynomial first integrals of the geodesic flow on a Riemannian symmetric space generated by the linear integrals coming from Killing vector fields?

Equivalently, the function $P_K(x,p) = K^{i_1\dots i_r}(x)\, p_{i_1}\cdots p_{i_r}$ on the cotangent bundle $T^*M$ is a polynomial first integral of the geodesic flow. Killing vector fields correspond to valence-1 Killing tensors and yield linear integrals. The set of Killing tensors of all valences forms a graded commutative algebra under the symmetric tensor product.

Question: Is every Killing tensor on a Riemannian symmetric space expressible as a sum of symmetric products of Killing vector fields? Equivalently, is the algebra of all polynomial first integrals of the geodesic flow on a Riemannian symmetric space generated by the linear integrals coming from Killing vector fields?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been answered negatively. While the property holds for spaces of constant curvature and for complex projective spaces, explicit examples of quadratic Killing tensor fields on quaternionic projective spaces and on the Cayley projective plane that cannot be written as quadratic forms (sums of symmetric products) in Killing vector fields have been constructed (see arXiv:2312.16518). Hence the algebra of polynomial integrals of the geodesic flow on a Riemannian symmetric space is not in general generated by linear integrals.

The system is called superintegrable if it admits, in addition to $H$, two further functionally independent polynomial integrals of motion (so that the total number of functionally independent polynomial integrals is three).

Construct an explicit example of such a natural Hamiltonian system $(S^2, g, V)$ with $V$ nonconstant that is superintegrable, where the two additional functionally independent integrals can be chosen to be polynomial in the momenta of degree $\geq 3$, and which admits no nontrivial polynomial integral of motion of degree one or two (other than those obtained as constants times $H$ or trivially from $H$ itself, in the degree-two case).

Background and definitions. The Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) is the probability measure on the space of real symmetric N×N matrices H with density proportional to exp(-(N/4) tr H^2), invariant under orthogonal conjugation. Random-Matrix Theory (RMT) makes definite predictions for spectral fluctuation statistics of GOE matrices, such as the nearest-neighbor level-spacing distribution (Wigner surmise), the number variance Σ²(L), the spectral rigidity Δ₃(L), and higher correlation functions, taken in the limit N→∞ after unfolding the spectrum to unit mean level density.

The Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit (BGS) conjecture asserts: if a bounded quantum system has a classical limit whose Hamiltonian flow is fully chaotic (e.g. ergodic and mixing on the energy shell, with positive Lyapunov exponents), then in the semiclassical limit the fluctuation statistics of its quantum energy levels — after unfolding — coincide with those of the GOE (in the time-reversal–invariant case).

Consider a heavy atomic nucleus modeled as a bounded many-body quantum system with a time-reversal–invariant Hamiltonian H_nuc acting on an appropriate Hilbert space, and consider the regime of highly excited compound-nucleus states relevant to nuclear reaction theory.

Problem. Determine whether the intrinsic dynamics of H_nuc in this regime is "chaotic" in the sense required by the BGS conjecture, i.e. whether the spectral fluctuation properties of its eigenvalues (level spacing distribution, spectral rigidity, two-point correlation function) agree, after unfolding, with those of the GOE in the limit of large excitation. Equivalently, justify or refute the use of GOE statistics as the spectral-fluctuation model for compound-nucleus levels by establishing (or disproving) the chaotic-dynamics hypothesis underlying the BGS conjecture for nuclear many-body Hamiltonians.

Let $n > 2$ and let $S^n$ denote the $n$-dimensional sphere. A Riemannian metric $g$ on $S^n$ is called conformally flat if every point has a neighborhood on which $g = e^{2\varphi} g_0$ for some smooth function $\varphi$ and some flat metric $g_0$. The geodesic flow of $g$ is the Hamiltonian flow on $T^*S^n$ generated by the Hamiltonian $H(x,p) = \tfrac{1}{2} g^{ij}(x) p_i p_j$. A function $F: T^*S^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is said to be polynomial in momenta if, in any local coordinate chart, $F(x,p)$ is a polynomial in the fiber variables $p_i$ with coefficients depending smoothly on $x$. The geodesic flow is called maximally superintegrable in the class of integrals polynomial in momenta if there exist $2n-1$ functions $F_1 = H, F_2, \dots, F_{2n-1}$ on $T^*S^n$, each polynomial in momenta, that are functionally independent and Poisson-commute with $H$ (i.e., $\{H, F_i\} = 0$ for all $i$).

Question: Does there exist a Riemannian metric on $S^n$ ($n > 2$) which is not conformally flat and whose geodesic flow is maximally superintegrable in the class of integrals polynomial in momenta?

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a strictly convex bounded planar domain with smooth boundary $\gamma = \partial \Omega$. Consider the billiard dynamics inside $\Omega$, in which a point particle moves along straight lines and reflects elastically off $\gamma$ (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection). A smooth closed convex curve $\Gamma \subset \Omega$ is called a caustic of the billiard if every billiard trajectory tangent to $\Gamma$ remains tangent to $\Gamma$ after each reflection on $\gamma$.

Suppose there exists a neighbourhood $U$ of $\gamma$ inside $\Omega$ that is foliated by caustics of the billiard in $\Omega$ (i.e., $U \setminus \gamma$ is the disjoint union of a smooth one-parameter family of caustics accumulating on $\gamma$).

Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses, $\gamma$ must be an ellipse.

This is a version of the local/Birkhoff–Poritsky conjecture. Background and setup. The Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) is the probability ensemble of real symmetric N×N matrices H whose entries are independent (up to symmetry) centered Gaussian random variables, with variance v on off-diagonal entries and variance 2v on diagonal entries; the distribution is invariant under orthogonal conjugation. A spectrum is said to exhibit GOE spectral-fluctuation behavior if, after unfolding to unit mean level density, its local statistics (e.g., nearest-neighbor spacing distribution, number variance, Dyson–Mehta Δ_3 statistic, two-point correlation function) coincide in the large-N limit with those predicted by the GOE.

In the nuclear shell model, single-particle states are organized into "major shells" separated by large energy gaps. A shell-model configuration at given total angular momentum and isospin is the finite-dimensional Hilbert space obtained by distributing a fixed number of valence nucleons among the single-particle orbitals of a chosen valence space, on which an effective two-body Hamiltonian acts as a real symmetric matrix. It is empirically and theoretically established that, when the valence space is a single major shell, the eigenvalue fluctuations of realistic effective shell-model Hamiltonians, as well as the mixing of basis configurations by the residual interaction, conform to GOE predictions (with the unmixed basis-state distribution treated as a Gaussian ensemble after appropriate scaling).

Problem. Consider shell-model spaces and effective Hamiltonians describing nuclei at excitation energies that lie midway between two major shells, so that the active valence space necessarily includes single-particle orbitals from two adjacent major shells separated by a large gap, together with the two-body residual interaction connecting them. Equivalently, consider the compound-nucleus resonance spectrum at such intermediate excitation energies.

Determine whether, in this between-shells regime:
(i) the local spectral fluctuations (nearest-neighbor spacing distribution, Δ_3 statistic, two-point correlation function) of the resulting Hamiltonian still agree with the GOE predictions in the large-dimension limit; and
(ii) the mixing of basis configurations induced by the residual interaction is statistically equivalent to that produced by a GOE perturbation of the diagonal single-particle part,

or whether instead these GOE properties—known to hold within a single major shell—are modified or fail when configurations from two adjacent major shells are mixed.

Let $\gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth strictly convex closed plane curve (of positive curvature), bounding a convex region $K$. The outer (dual) billiard map $T$ is defined on the exterior $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus K$ as follows: for a point $p$ outside $K$, consider the right tangent line from $p$ to $\gamma$ (using a fixed orientation), and let $q$ be the point of tangency; then $T(p)$ is the reflection of $p$ in $q$, i.e., $q$ is the midpoint of the segment $[p, T(p)]$.

Suppose the exterior $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus K$ is foliated by a continuous family of closed curves each of which is invariant under $T$ (i.e., the outer billiard around $\gamma$ is totally integrable in this sense).

Prove that $\gamma$ must be an ellipse.

A 2024 result by M. Bialy in the Journal of Modern Dynamics ("Integrable outer billiards and rigidity") proves precisely that if the exterior of a smooth strictly convex plane curve of positive curvature is foliated by continuous curves invariant under the outer billiard map, then the curve must be an ellipse. Work in the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$. Let $\gamma \subset \mathbb{RP}^2$ be a smooth closed strictly convex curve, and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a smooth foliation by smooth closed convex curves of an exterior one-sided neighbourhood of $\gamma$, with $\gamma$ itself being a leaf of $\mathcal{F}$.

For every point $p \in \gamma$, let $\ell_p$ denote the projective tangent line to $\gamma$ at $p$. Each leaf of $\mathcal{F}$ near $\gamma$ meets $\ell_p$ in two points close to $p$, and swapping these two intersection points (with $p$ as a fixed point) defines a germ of an involution $\sigma_p : \ell_p \to \ell_p$ on the tangent line.

Assume that for every $p \in \gamma$, the involution $\sigma_p$ is the restriction of a projective transformation of $\ell_p \cong \mathbb{RP}^1$.

Prove that under these hypotheses $\gamma$ is necessarily an ellipse, and the leaves of $\mathcal{F}$ are ellipses that, together with $\gamma$, belong to a single pencil of conics (a one-parameter family of conics sharing four base points, possibly complex or with multiplicities).

Background and setup. Let a "resonance sequence" be a finite ordered list of nuclear resonance energies $E_1 < E_2 < \cdots < E_N$ for fixed quantum numbers (compound nucleus, spin, parity). After unfolding so that the local mean spacing equals 1, the Dyson–Mehta $\Delta_3$ statistic on an interval of length $L$ is
$$\Delta_3(L) \;=\; \min_{a,b} \frac{1}{L}\int_{x_0}^{x_0+L}\bigl(\mathcal{N}(x) - a x - b\bigr)^2\,dx,$$
where $\mathcal{N}(x)$ is the staircase counting function of the unfolded levels. For the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) one has the asymptotic prediction
$$\mathbb{E}[\Delta_3(L)] \;\sim\; \frac{1}{\pi^2}\bigl(\ln L - 0.0687\bigr) \quad\text{as } L\to\infty.$$

Consider the "reconstructed Nuclear Data Ensemble" (reconstructed NDE) obtained by pooling, after unfolding, a collection of experimentally measured neutron-resonance sequences of various nuclei (with the U and Th isotopes excluded), and let $\overline{\Delta_3}(L)$ denote the ensemble-averaged $\Delta_3$ statistic computed from that data.

It has been reported that $\overline{\Delta_3}(L)$ deviates increasingly from the GOE prediction as $L$ grows, with the deviation appearing significant for $L > 20$.

Problem. Determine whether this observed disagreement at $L > 20$ constitutes a genuine statistical rejection of the GOE hypothesis for the reconstructed NDE, or whether it can be quantitatively accounted for by one or more of the following effects:
(a) the sharp decrease, with growing $L$, in the number of sequences contributing to the $\Delta_3$ average, leading to underestimated statistical uncertainty in $\overline{\Delta_3}(L)$;
(b) experimentally missed narrow $s$-wave resonances whose fraction grows with distance from the neutron threshold;
(c) erroneous $p$-wave (or otherwise non-$s$-wave) assignments among resonances that were excluded from the sequences.

Specifically, give a quantitative analysis (with rigorously propagated uncertainties incorporating sequence count, missing-level fractions, and misassignment rates) that either (i) shows the observed deviation lies outside any plausible combination of (a)–(c) and therefore refutes GOE for the reconstructed NDE, or (ii) exhibits values of these systematic effects, consistent with the experimental information available, that reproduce the observed deviation while remaining compatible with the GOE hypothesis.

Let $M$ be a complete simply connected two-dimensional Riemannian manifold of constant curvature, i.e. either the round sphere $S^2$ or the hyperbolic (Lobachevsky) plane $H^2$. Let $\gamma \subset M$ be a smooth strictly convex closed curve. The outer (dual) billiard map $T_\gamma$ associated with $\gamma$ is defined on the exterior of $\gamma$ as follows: for a point $P$ outside $\gamma$, draw the (oriented) geodesic tangent line from $P$ to $\gamma$ touching $\gamma$ at a point $Q$; then $T_\gamma(P)$ is the point obtained by reflecting $P$ through $Q$ along this geodesic (so that $Q$ is the geodesic midpoint of $P$ and $T_\gamma(P)$).

The map $T_\gamma$ is said to be polynomially (algebraically) integrable if there exists a non-constant function $F$ on the exterior of $\gamma$, polynomial in the natural coordinates inherited from the ambient projective model of $M$, such that $F \circ T_\gamma = F$ on a neighborhood of $\gamma$.

Prove the algebraic version of Birkhoff's conjecture in this setting: if the outer billiard map associated with a smooth strictly convex closed curve $\gamma$ on a non-Euclidean surface of constant curvature ($S^2$ or $H^2$) admits a non-trivial polynomial integral, then $\gamma$ is a conic, i.e. a curve of the form $\{aF^2 + bG^2 + cH^2 = 0\}$ in the standard projective model — equivalently, $\gamma$ is the dual of a confocal-conic boundary on $M$.

Consider a planar billiard inside a smooth strictly convex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ that admits a 2-periodic orbit (a segment hitting the boundary perpendicularly at two points). The billiard map $T$ acts on the space of oriented chords (parametrized, e.g., by an arclength coordinate on $\partial\Omega$ and the angle of reflection), and the 2-periodic orbit corresponds to a fixed point of $T^2$. Assume this fixed point is elliptic, with the linearization of $T^2$ being a rotation by some angle $2\alpha$ (so that $T$ has, at the 2-periodic point, rotation angle $\alpha$).

Question: Does there exist a domain $\Omega$ (other than a disk) such that, in some neighborhood of the 2-periodic orbit, the billiard map $T$ is smoothly (or analytically) conjugate to the rigid rotation $R_\alpha: (x,y)\mapsto (x\cos\alpha - y\sin\alpha,\; x\sin\alpha + y\cos\alpha)$ of the plane by the angle $\alpha$?

Equivalently, does there exist a smooth (resp. analytic) diffeomorphism $h$ from a neighborhood of the fixed point to a neighborhood of the origin in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that $h \circ T = R_\alpha \circ h$ on this neighborhood, for some choice of $\Omega$ and some $\alpha$?

The conjugacy equation for billiard maps near a 2-periodic orbit was introduced by Treschev (Physica D, 2013), who showed that a formal power series solution exists when α is incommensurable with π and provided numerical evidence for convergence. Subsequent work (e.g., Steklov Inst. 2015; "Lazutkin coordinates and the conjugation problem for billiard maps", arXiv 2503.19550, 2025) continues to investigate the analytic conjugacy. As of 2025–2026, the existence of an actual (non-circular) domain with such an analytic/smooth conjugacy to a rigid rotation appears to remain an open problem, with only formal/numerical results known.

Consider the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) scattering formulation for a compound-nucleus reaction in which the scattering matrix S is expressed, on a finite energy interval, in terms of a GOE-distributed internal Hamiltonian H (an N×N real symmetric random matrix drawn from the GOE) coupled to a fixed number Λ of open channels through an energy-independent real N×Λ coupling matrix W. Concretely, write

  S_{ab}(E) = δ_{ab} − 2πi [W^T (E − H + iπ W W^T)^{−1} W]_{ab},  a,b = 1,…,Λ,

and assume W satisfies the standard orthogonality condition Σ_μ W_{μa} W_{μb} ∝ δ_{ab}. In real nuclear reactions the number of open channels grows (roughly exponentially) with energy, so the assumption that Λ and W are energy-independent can only hold over some finite energy window ΔE. This approximation is most severely violated for s-wave neutron channels, since for them no angular-momentum barrier and no Coulomb barrier suppress the coupling between the channel and the GOE-distributed internal states.

Develop a theoretical framework that extends or modifies the above GOE scattering formulation so as to provide an adequate description of s-wave neutron scattering in the regime where the fixed-Λ, energy-independent-W assumption fails. The framework should account for the unsuppressed s-wave neutron coupling to the internal GOE states and yield well-defined statistical predictions (e.g. for averaged cross sections, S-matrix correlation functions, and fluctuation properties) on energy intervals over which the number of effectively open channels and/or the coupling strengths vary significantly.

Setup. Let $\gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth strictly convex closed curve bounding a domain $D$. The (Birkhoff) billiard inside $D$ is the dynamical system on oriented chords of $D$ in which a point moves along straight lines and reflects off $\gamma$ according to the law of equal angles. A smooth convex curve $\Gamma\subset D$ is called a caustic of the billiard if every chord tangent to $\Gamma$ reflects off $\gamma$ to another chord tangent to $\Gamma$. A caustic $\Gamma$ is said to be rational with rotation number $p/q\in\mathbb{Q}$ (in lowest terms, $0<p/q<1/2$) if every billiard trajectory tangent to $\Gamma$ is a closed polygon with $q$ vertices on $\gamma$ that makes $p$ turns around $\Gamma$.

Analogously, for the outer (dual) billiard defined outside a smooth strictly convex closed curve $\gamma$ — where the map $T$ sends a point $x$ outside $\gamma$ to the reflection of $x$ in the point of tangency of the right tangent line from $x$ to $\gamma$ — a smooth closed convex curve $\Gamma$ surrounding $\gamma$ is an invariant caustic if it is invariant under $T$, and it is called rational with rotation number $p/q$ if the restriction of $T$ to $\Gamma$ is conjugate to the rotation by $2\pi p/q$, so that every orbit on $\Gamma$ closes up after $q$ steps and $p$ turns.

It is classical that an ellipse, as the boundary of an inner billiard, possesses a one-parameter family of confocal elliptic caustics, and in particular admits rational caustics for every rational rotation number in $(0,1/2)$; the analogous statement holds for the outer billiard about an ellipse.

Question. Does there exist a smooth strictly convex closed plane curve $\gamma$ that is not an ellipse such that the inner billiard inside $\gamma$ possesses rational caustics with at least two different values of the rotation number? Same question for the outer billiard about $\gamma$.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth strictly convex bounded domain, and consider the Birkhoff billiard inside $\Omega$: a point particle moves in a straight line and reflects off $\partial\Omega$ according to the law of equal angles. A smooth convex curve $\Gamma \subset \Omega$ is called a caustic of the billiard if every billiard trajectory tangent to $\Gamma$ remains tangent to $\Gamma$ after each reflection. To a convex caustic one associates a rotation number $\omega \in (0, 1/2]$.

For coprime integers $0 < p < q$, a caustic $\Gamma$ is called $(p,q)$-rationally integrable if it has rotation number $p/q$ and the billiard map admits an integral whose level sets foliate a neighborhood of the invariant curve associated to $\Gamma$ by invariant curves carrying $(p,q)$-periodic orbits.

Given an integer $q_0 \geq 2$, the billiard in $\Omega$ is said to be $q_0$-rationally integrable if for every rational $p/q \in (0, 1/q_0]$ in lowest terms, $\Omega$ admits a $(p,q)$-rationally integrable convex caustic.

Prove or disprove: if the billiard in $\Omega$ is $q_0$-rationally integrable for some $q_0 \geq 2$, then $\partial\Omega$ is an ellipse.

The conjecture remains open in full generality. Let A be a finite alphabet. The class of extended regular expressions over A is defined inductively: 0 and 1 are extended regular expressions, every letter a ∈ A is an extended regular expression, and if E and F are extended regular expressions, then so are (E ∪ F), (E · F), (¬E), and (E*). The language L(E) ⊆ A* denoted by an extended regular expression is defined as usual, where ¬E denotes the complement A* ∖ L(E) and E* denotes the Kleene star.

Define the star height of an extended regular expression E, denoted sh(E), recursively by:
- sh(0) = sh(1) = sh(a) = 0 for a ∈ A,
- sh(E ∪ F) = sh(E · F) = max(sh(E), sh(F)),
- sh(¬E) = sh(E),
- sh(E*) = sh(E) + 1.

For a regular language L ⊆ A*, define its (generalized) star height by
  h(L) = min { sh(E) : E is an extended regular expression with L(E) = L }.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input a finite description of an arbitrary regular language L (e.g., a finite automaton or a regular expression for L), computes the value h(L)?

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a strictly convex bounded domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$. Consider the Birkhoff billiard inside $\Omega$: a point particle moves along straight lines and reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) at $\partial\Omega$. The billiard map $T$ acts on the phase cylinder of inward unit vectors based at points of $\partial\Omega$, parametrized by $(s,\varphi)$ where $s$ is arclength on $\partial\Omega$ and $\varphi \in (0,\pi)$ is the angle with the boundary.

A rotational invariant circle is a $T$-invariant curve in the phase cylinder that is homotopically nontrivial (i.e., wraps around the cylinder). Each such invariant curve has a well-defined rotation number $\rho \in (0,1)$ for the restriction of $T$. By time-reversal symmetry one may restrict attention to $\rho \in (0,1/2)$.

Conjecture: If the billiard inside $\Omega$ admits a family of rotational invariant circles whose rotation numbers fill the entire interval $(0,1/2)$, then $\partial\Omega$ is an ellipse.

Prove or disprove this statement.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

This is a strong form of the Birkhoff–Poritsky integrability conjecture (Bialy's version, with foliation by invariant curves of all rotation numbers in (0,1/2)). It remains open in full generality. Significant partial results exist: Kaloshin–Sorrentino (Annals 2018) established rigidity near the boundary for rotation numbers in (0,1/4]; Bialy–Mironov (Annals of Math. 2022) proved the conjecture for centrally-symmetric C²-smooth convex tables. Subsequent works (e.g., Bialy–Tsodikovich, 2021; Bialy–Mironov 2024 survey) extend related rigidity results, but the general (non-symmetric) case stated above is not resolved.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a strictly convex bounded planar domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$. Consider the Birkhoff billiard inside $\Omega$: a point particle moves along straight lines and reflects off $\partial\Omega$ according to the law of equal angles. A smooth convex curve $\gamma \subset \Omega$ is called a (convex) caustic of the billiard if every billiard trajectory tangent to $\gamma$ remains tangent to $\gamma$ after each reflection at $\partial\Omega$. To each convex caustic $\gamma$ one associates a rotation number $\rho(\gamma) \in (0, 1/2)$, defined as the asymptotic average angular fraction of $\partial\Omega$ traversed per reflection along any trajectory tangent to $\gamma$.

Suppose that there exists a sequence $\{\gamma_n\}_{n \ge 1}$ of convex caustics of the billiard in $\Omega$ whose rotation numbers $\rho(\gamma_n)$ converge to some number $\omega \in (0, 1/2)$. Must $\partial\Omega$ be an ellipse?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is a variant of the Birkhoff–Poritsky conjecture. Known results include: if a sequence of convex caustics has rotation numbers converging to 1/2, then the table is an ellipse; local versions near ellipses, and a 2022 proof of the Birkhoff conjecture for centrally-symmetric C^2 strictly convex tables (Bialy–Mironov). Setting. Consider a model of compound-nucleus resonance reactions in which the internal Hamiltonian H of the compound nucleus is drawn from the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) of N×N real symmetric random matrices (entries Gaussian, distribution invariant under orthogonal transformations, with variance scaled so that the average level density has a finite limit as N→∞). Coupling to a finite set of open reaction channels a=1,…,Λ is described by real coupling vectors W_a∈R^N held fixed, and the scattering matrix is

   S_{ab}(E) = δ_{ab} − 2π i [W^T (E − H + iπ W W^T)^{-1} W]_{ab},

where W is the N×Λ matrix with columns W_a. Observables of interest include energy-averaged cross sections, S-matrix correlation functions ⟨S_{ab}(E) S_{cd}^*(E+ε)⟩, higher-order cross-section correlation functions ⟨σ_{ab}(E) σ_{cd}(E+ε)⟩ (and their multi-point generalizations), distributions of partial widths and of S-matrix elements, and quantities relevant in the presence of direct reactions, isospin or other symmetry breaking, and overlapping resonances.

Problem. Develop the GOE scattering model above into a viable and practically useful theory of nuclear resonance reactions by deriving, in closed analytic form (or via a tractable computational scheme exact in the GOE average), the full set of observables needed for nuclear-reaction applications. In particular:

(a) Obtain explicit expressions for the n-point S-matrix and cross-section correlation functions ⟨S_{a_1 b_1}(E_1)⋯ S_{a_n b_n}(E_n)⟩ and ⟨σ_{a_1 b_1}(E_1)⋯ σ_{a_n b_n}(E_n)⟩ for arbitrary n, valid in the regime of arbitrary channel transmission coefficients T_a=1−|⟨S_{aa}⟩|^2 (weak to strong absorption) and arbitrary degree of resonance overlap Γ/D.

(b) Extend these expressions to incorporate direct reactions (nonzero ⟨S⟩), partial symmetry breaking (e.g. isospin mixing modeled by a block GOE with coupling), and channel-channel correlations.

(c) Determine the resulting distributions of cross sections, partial widths, and resonance parameters, including deviations from Porter–Thomas, and quantify their dependence on the model parameters.

The question is whether such a comprehensive theoretical framework, with a sufficiently broad set of analytically tractable observables to be useful for practical analysis of compound-nucleus data, can be constructed.

Let $K = (K, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ be a semiring. A $K$-weighted finite automaton over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ is a tuple $\mathcal{A} = (Q, \Sigma, \mu, \lambda, \gamma)$ where $Q$ is a finite set of states, $\mu : \Sigma \to K^{Q \times Q}$ assigns to each input symbol a transition matrix with entries in $K$, $\lambda \in K^{Q}$ is an initial (row) vector, and $\gamma \in K^{Q}$ is a final (column) vector. The behavior of $\mathcal{A}$ is the function $\|\mathcal{A}\| : \Sigma^{*} \to K$ defined for every word $w = a_{1} a_{2} \cdots a_{n} \in \Sigma^{*}$ by
$$\|\mathcal{A}\|(w) = \lambda \cdot \mu(a_{1}) \cdot \mu(a_{2}) \cdots \mu(a_{n}) \cdot \gamma,$$
where the empty-word value is $\lambda \cdot \gamma$. The range of $\mathcal{A}$ is the set $\mathrm{Range}(\mathcal{A}) = \{\|\mathcal{A}\|(w) : w \in \Sigma^{*}\} \subseteq K$.

Problem. Provide an algorithm that, given as input a $K$-weighted finite automaton $\mathcal{A}$ (over a fixed semiring $K$ for which arithmetic is effective), decides whether $\mathrm{Range}(\mathcal{A})$ is a finite subset of $K$, or prove that no such algorithm exists. In particular, characterize the semirings $K$ for which this finite range problem is decidable.

The finite range (finite-image) problem's status depends on the underlying semiring. Recent work has established undecidability for the finite-image property of (deterministic) weighted finite automata over certain idempotent commutative past-finite ordered semirings, and for weighted finite automata over certain commutative past-finite monotonic ordered strong bimonoids. Decidability is known in classical restricted settings (e.g., the limitedness/finite range problem over the tropical semiring is decidable, by Hashiguchi/Leung/Simon). Thus the problem is partially resolved: decidable in some classical semirings, undecidable in others, with a complete classification still incomplete.

Setting (Birkhoff billiards). Let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, $n \ge 3$, be a smooth strictly convex bounded domain with boundary $\partial D$. The Birkhoff billiard map $T: M \to M$ is defined on the phase space
$$M = \{(q,v) : q \in \partial D,\ v \in \mathbb{R}^n,\ \|v\|=1,\ \langle v, \nu(q)\rangle \ge 0\},$$
where $\nu(q)$ denotes the inner unit normal to $\partial D$ at $q$. The map sends $(q,v)$ to $(q', v')$, where $q'$ is the next intersection of the ray $\{q+tv : t>0\}$ with $\partial D$, and $v'$ is obtained from $v$ by reflection in the tangent hyperplane $T_{q'}\partial D$ (so the tangential component of $v$ is preserved and the normal component is reversed). An invariant hypersurface is a smooth codimension-one submanifold $\Sigma \subset M$ with $T(\Sigma) = \Sigma$.

Setting (outer billiards). Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^{2n}$, $n \ge 2$, be a smooth strictly convex bounded body, and let $\omega$ be the standard symplectic form on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$. The outer billiard map $T_K$ is defined outside $K$ as follows: for a point $x$ outside $K$, there is a unique oriented support hyperplane $H$ to $K$ through $x$ (with respect to a chosen rule using $\omega$), tangent to $K$ at a point $z(x)$; then $T_K(x) := 2z(x) - x$. An invariant hypersurface is a smooth codimension-one submanifold of the domain of $T_K$ that is preserved by $T_K$.

It is classical that ellipsoids in $\mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \ge 3$) yield Birkhoff billiards possessing invariant hypersurfaces in phase space (foliated by caustics).

Questions.
(a) Does there exist a smooth strictly convex bounded domain $D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with $n \ge 3$, not an ellipsoid, such that the associated Birkhoff billiard map admits an invariant hypersurface in its phase space $M$?
(b) Does there exist a smooth strictly convex bounded body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ with $n \ge 2$, not an ellipsoid, such that the associated outer billiard map admits an invariant hypersurface?

(b) Does there exist a smooth strictly convex bounded body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ with $n \ge 2$, not an ellipsoid, such that the associated outer billiard map admits an invariant hypersurface?

For multi-dimensional Birkhoff billiards, the question appears to remain open: it is known that only ellipsoids have convex caustics in higher dimensions, but no non-ellipsoidal example of an invariant hypersurface in phase space is known, and recent surveys list this as open. Let $\Sigma_1$ and $\Sigma_2$ be two closed, smooth, strictly convex hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d \ge 2$), with $\Sigma_1$ enclosed in the bounded region bounded by $\Sigma_2$. For each $i \in \{1,2\}$, the billiard reflection $T_i$ is defined on the set of oriented lines in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that intersect $\Sigma_i$ transversally as follows: given an oriented line $\ell$ meeting $\Sigma_i$, let $p$ be the last point of intersection of $\ell$ (in the direction of $\ell$) with $\Sigma_i$; then $T_i(\ell)$ is the oriented line through $p$ obtained from $\ell$ by reflecting its direction in the tangent hyperplane to $\Sigma_i$ at $p$, oriented away from $p$. Let $\mathcal{U}$ denote the set of oriented lines that intersect both $\Sigma_1$ and $\Sigma_2$ transversally and on which both $T_1, T_2$, and their iterates relevant below, are defined.

Assume that $T_1$ and $T_2$ commute on $\mathcal{U}$, i.e., $T_1 \circ T_2(\ell) = T_2 \circ T_1(\ell)$ for every $\ell \in \mathcal{U}$ for which both sides are defined.

Prove that $\Sigma_1$ and $\Sigma_2$ are confocal ellipsoids, that is, there exist constants $a_1 > a_2 > \cdots > a_d > 0$ and parameters $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ (with $\lambda_i < a_d^2$) such that, in suitable Cartesian coordinates,
$$\Sigma_i = \left\{ x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \sum_{k=1}^d \frac{x_k^2}{a_k^2 - \lambda_i} = 1 \right\}, \qquad i=1,2.$$

Background and setup. Let H be a real symmetric Hamiltonian acting on the model space of an s-d-shell nucleus (valence nucleons restricted to the 1s_{1/2}, 0d_{3/2}, 0d_{5/2} single-particle orbits) at a filling near the middle of the shell. Restrict attention to the subspace of states with total angular momentum J = 2 and total isospin T = 0; diagonalisation in this subspace yields an ordered sequence of eigenvalues E_1 ≤ E_2 ≤ … ≤ E_N (with N of order a few thousand). After unfolding the spectrum so that the local mean level density equals 1, denote the unfolded levels by x_1 < x_2 < … < x_N and the nearest-neighbour spacings by s_i = x_{i+1} − x_i.

Two standard spectral statistics are considered:

(i) The nearest-neighbour spacing (NNS) distribution P(s), the empirical distribution of {s_i}, to be compared with the Wigner-like GOE prediction P_{GOE}(s).

(ii) The Dyson–Mehta Δ_3 statistic, defined for an interval of length L by
   Δ_3(L; α) = (1/L) min_{a,b} ∫_α^{α+L} [ N(x) − a x − b ]^2 dx,
where N(x) = #{i : x_i ≤ x} is the staircase counting function, with the average ⟨Δ_3(L)⟩ taken over starting points α along the unfolded spectrum. The GOE prediction in the large-L regime is ⟨Δ_3(L)⟩_{GOE} ≈ (1/π^2)[ln(2π L) + γ − 5/4 − π^2/8].

Empirical observation. For shell-model spectra of s-d-shell nuclei restricted to J = 2, T = 0 states near mid-shell, P(s) and ⟨Δ_3(L)⟩ both agree well with the GOE predictions for small and moderate L, but ⟨Δ_3(L)⟩ systematically lies slightly above the GOE curve when L becomes very large (a sizeable fraction of the available sequence length).

Problem. Provide a quantitative explanation of this systematic large-L excess of the Dyson–Mehta Δ_3 statistic over the GOE prediction in such shell-model spectra. Specifically, identify the mechanism (e.g. residual long-range spectral rigidity violations from approximate constants of motion, finite-N saturation effects, secular variations in the level density not removed by unfolding, or other structural features of the shell-model Hamiltonian) responsible for the deviation, and derive the leading correction to ⟨Δ_3(L)⟩ as a function of L that accounts for the observed upward drift, while remaining consistent with the agreement of P(s) and Δ_3 with GOE at smaller L.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. Define an *intermediate regular expression* over $\Sigma$ inductively as follows: $\emptyset$, $\varepsilon$, and each letter $a \in \Sigma$ are intermediate regular expressions; if $E$ and $F$ are intermediate regular expressions, then so are the union $E \cup F$, the intersection $E \cap F$, the concatenation $E \cdot F$, and the Kleene star $E^*$. (Complementation is not allowed.) Each intermediate regular expression $E$ denotes a regular language $L(E) \subseteq \Sigma^*$ in the usual way. The *intermediate star height* $h(E)$ of an intermediate regular expression is defined recursively by $h(\emptyset) = h(\varepsilon) = h(a) = 0$, $h(E \cup F) = h(E \cap F) = h(E \cdot F) = \max(h(E), h(F))$, and $h(E^*) = h(E) + 1$. The *intermediate star height* of a regular language $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ is $h(L) = \min\{h(E) : L(E) = L\}$.

Answer the following two questions:
(a) Does there exist, for every integer $n \geq 0$, a regular language $L_n \subseteq \Sigma^*$ (over some finite alphabet) with intermediate star height exactly $n$? Equivalently, is the intermediate star height hierarchy strict?
(b) Is there an algorithm that, given a regular language $L$ (e.g. via a finite automaton or regular expression), computes its intermediate star height $h(L)$?

The closely related generalized star-height problem (where complement is also allowed) is a long-standing open problem; even the question of whether star height greater than 1 is needed is unresolved. The intermediate variant, restricting the operations to union, intersection, concatenation and Kleene star (no complement), is likewise listed as an open problem in surveys of regular-language problems, with no published algorithm or hierarchy theorem. No source found announcing a solution.

Setup. Fix integers $d\ge 2$ and $n$ with $n$ sufficiently large. A twisted $n$-gon in projective space $\mathbb{RP}^d$ is a sequence $\{v_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ of points in general position in $\mathbb{RP}^d$ together with a projective transformation (the monodromy) $M\in\mathrm{PGL}_{d+1}(\mathbb{R})$ such that $v_{k+n}=M(v_k)$ for all $k$. Denote by $\mathcal{P}_n^{\,d}$ the moduli space of such twisted $n$-gons modulo projective equivalence.

Multi-indices and generalized pentagram maps. A multi-index is a tuple $I=(i_1,\dots,i_{d-1})$ of positive integers. To a pair of multi-indices $I=(i_1,\dots,i_{d-1})$ and $J=(j_1,\dots,j_{d-1})$ one associates a generalized pentagram map $T_{I,J}\colon \mathcal{P}_n^{\,d}\dashrightarrow \mathcal{P}_n^{\,d}$ as follows. For each $k$, let
$$P_k \;=\; \overline{v_k\,v_{k+i_1}}\;\cap\;\overline{v_{k+i_1}\,v_{k+i_1+i_2}}\;\cap\;\cdots\;\cap\;\overline{v_{k+i_1+\cdots+i_{d-2}}\,v_{k+i_1+\cdots+i_{d-1}}}^{\,*},$$
that is, $P_k$ is the projective subspace spanned by $d$ consecutive vertices skipping according to $I$; more precisely $P_k$ is the span of $v_k,v_{k+i_1},v_{k+i_1+i_2},\dots,v_{k+i_1+\cdots+i_{d-1}}$, a hyperplane in $\mathbb{RP}^d$. The new vertex $T_{I,J}(v)_k$ is then defined as the intersection of two consecutive such hyperplanes shifted according to $J$; namely the new vertices are obtained by intersecting $d$ consecutive hyperplanes $P_{k},P_{k+j_1},P_{k+j_1+j_2},\dots,P_{k+j_1+\cdots+j_{d-1}}$. (For $d=2$ and $I=J=(2)$ this recovers the classical pentagram map.)

The map $T_{I,J}$ is rational and well defined on a Zariski-open subset of $\mathcal{P}_n^{\,d}$.

Question. Is it true that for every dimension $d\ge 2$ and every multi-index $I=(i_1,\dots,i_{d-1})$, the generalized pentagram map $T_{I,I}$ on twisted $n$-gons in $\mathbb{RP}^d$ is completely integrable, in the sense of admitting an invariant Poisson structure together with a maximal family of functionally independent Poisson-commuting first integrals?

The conjecture that $T_{I,I}$ is integrable for every multi-index $I$ is generally regarded as open in full generality. Integrability has been established in several cases, including the "dented" pentagram maps and special instances such as $T_{(2,2),(1,1)}$, $T_{(2,1),(1,1)}$, $T_{(3,1),(1,1)}$, and integrability frameworks via Poisson–Lie groups of pseudo-difference operators (Izosimov) and refactorization mappings have given Lax representations and invariant Poisson structures for broad subfamilies, but a complete proof for all $I$ does not appear in the literature as of 2026.

representations.normalized:
Consider a low-energy neutron-scattering experiment on a heavy target nucleus that produces a sequence of compound-nucleus resonances at energies $\{E_i\}$ with partial neutron widths $\{\Gamma_i^n\}$. Each resonance carries an orbital angular momentum $\ell$; those with $\ell = 0$ are called s-wave and those with $\ell = 1$ are called p-wave. Random-matrix theory predicts that, for a fixed spin-parity sequence, the rescaled level spacings should follow the Wigner–Dyson statistics of the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE), and that the reduced neutron widths $\gamma_i = \Gamma_i^n / \langle \Gamma^n\rangle$ within a single $\ell$-channel should follow the Porter–Thomas distribution
$$P(\gamma)\,d\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\gamma}}\,e^{-\gamma/2}\,d\gamma,$$
i.e. a $\chi^2$ distribution with $\nu = 1$ degree of freedom.

In practice, the measured resonance list contains a mixture of s-wave resonances, p-wave resonances (whose mean reduced widths are systematically smaller by a factor proportional to the p-wave penetrability), and resonances of unassigned parity. Including p-wave contaminants in a putative s-wave sample biases tests of GOE level statistics and inflates the apparent low-width tail of the width distribution, leading, e.g., to fitted values $\nu < 1$.

Problem. Devise a procedure that, given only the measured energies $\{E_i\}$ and neutron widths $\{\Gamma_i^n\}$ (possibly augmented by partial parity assignments), cleanly separates the s-wave subset from the p-wave and unknown-parity resonances, so that:
(i) the resulting s-wave subset has a quantifiable, unbiased completeness and purity;
(ii) statistical tests of GOE level-spacing statistics on the extracted s-wave sequence are not confounded by missed s-wave levels or admixed p-wave levels; and
(iii) the inferred reduced-neutron-width distribution can be compared with the Porter–Thomas law in a way that is provably free from selection bias due to the small-width threshold and from p-wave contamination.

Specify both the algorithm and a rigorous statistical framework that quantifies the residual systematic uncertainty in the resulting s-wave sequence.

Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $K \subseteq A^*$ be a regular language. For a language $X \subseteq A^*$, write $X^* = \bigcup_{n \ge 0} X^n$ (with $X^0 = \{\varepsilon\}$, the language consisting of the empty word).

Consider the equation $K = XK$ in the unknown $X \subseteq A^*$. Among all solutions, there is a (unique) maximal one of the form $L^*$ for some language $L$; equivalently, $L^*$ is the largest language $Y$ with $YK \subseteq K$ that is closed under concatenation and contains $\varepsilon$. Set $L_1 := L$, so that $K = L_1^* K$.

Next, consider the equation $K = L_1^* R$ in the unknown $R \subseteq A^*$. This equation admits a minimal solution, given by
$$R = K \setminus (L_1^* \setminus \{\varepsilon\}) K.$$
Call this minimal solution $R_1$, so that $K = L_1^* R_1$.

Now iterate: having obtained a decomposition $K = L_1^* L_2^* \cdots L_k^* R_k$, apply the same procedure to $R_k$ in place of $K$, producing the maximal $L_{k+1}^*$ with $R_k = L_{k+1}^* R_k$ and the corresponding minimal remainder $R_{k+1}$, so that
$$K = L_1^* L_2^* \cdots L_k^* L_{k+1}^* R_{k+1}.$$

Question: Does this iterative star-removal process always terminate? That is, must there always exist some integer $k \ge 1$ such that $L_k^* = \{\varepsilon\}$?

Let $(M,\pi)$ be a regular Poisson manifold, i.e., a smooth manifold $M$ equipped with a bivector field $\pi \in \Gamma(\wedge^2 TM)$ satisfying $[\pi,\pi]=0$ (Schouten bracket) and such that the rank of $\pi$ is constant on $M$, so that the image of $\pi^\sharp:T^*M\to TM$ defines a regular symplectic foliation $\mathcal{F}$ of $M$. A (non-commutative) integrable system on $(M,\pi)$ is a surjective submersion $F=(f_1,\dots,f_r):M\to B$ onto an $r$-dimensional manifold whose components Poisson-commute with a chosen subset and whose level sets are connected Lagrangian-isotropic submanifolds carrying a free, transitive action of $\mathbb{R}^k$ (with $k$ equal to the rank of the leaves), with compact fibers. Locally near any compact connected fiber there exist action-angle coordinates: a neighborhood of the fiber is Poisson-diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{T}^k\times D^k\times P$ for some Poisson manifold $P$, with $\pi$ given in standard form $\sum_i \partial_{\theta_i}\wedge \partial_{a_i}+\pi_P$.

Problem. Identify and characterize the complete set of cohomological/topological obstructions to the existence of global action-angle coordinates on $(M,\pi)$, that is, to the existence of a global Poisson diffeomorphism (covering $F$) between $M$ and a model of the form $(\mathbb{T}^k\text{-bundle over }B)\times_B P$ with the standard fiberwise action-angle Poisson structure. In particular, determine all obstructions arising from (i) the monodromy and Chern class of the period lattice bundle of $F$, (ii) the action bundle and its lattice, and (iii) the interaction between the action, angle, and transverse foliations of $M$, that go beyond the obstructions known in the symplectic case.

The obstructions to global action-angle coordinates have been classically described by Duistermaat (Liouville case) and Dazord–Delzant (non-commutative case) on symplectic manifolds. For non-commutative integrable systems on regular Poisson manifolds, additional obstructions have been identified and analyzed (e.g., Laurent-Gengoux–Miranda–Vanhaecke, and subsequent work on b-symplectic manifolds), using the action bundle, action lattice bundle, and the action/angle/transverse foliations. A complete classification of obstructions for general regular Poisson manifolds is not fully settled, so the problem is partially solved.

Let $(M,\pi)$ be a Poisson manifold and let $\mu:M\to B$ be the moment map of an integrable Hamiltonian system (or, more generally, of a Poisson action) on $M$. The connected components of the regular fibers of $\mu$ form a singular foliation of $M$, and the existence of (possibly generalized) action–angle coordinates equips the base $B$ (away from singularities) with an integral affine structure; equivalently, the image of $\mu$ inherits a foliation whose leaves carry affine structures.

Conversely, consider an abstract foliation $\mathcal{F}$ on a manifold $B$ whose leaves are equipped with affine structures (i.e. each leaf carries a torsion-free flat connection, or equivalently an atlas with affine transition maps).

Characterize intrinsically those foliations $(B,\mathcal{F})$ with affine leaves that can be realized as the image of the moment map of some integrable Hamiltonian system on a Poisson manifold $(M,\pi)$. That is, give necessary and sufficient conditions on $(B,\mathcal{F})$ for there to exist a Poisson manifold $(M,\pi)$ and a moment map $\mu:M\to B$ such that the induced foliation with affine leaves on $\mu(M)$ coincides with $(B,\mathcal{F})$.

Random Matrix Theory predicts that for an isolated compound-nucleus resonance with a single open neutron channel, the reduced neutron partial width amplitude is a Gaussian random variable, so the reduced neutron widths $\Gamma_n$ follow the Porter–Thomas distribution: a chi-squared distribution with $
u = 1$ degree of freedom,
$$P(x)\,dx =  rac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}\,e^{-x/2}\,dx, \qquad x = \Gamma_n/\langle \Gamma_nangle.$$
More generally one may consider the family $P_
u(x) \propto x^{
u/2-1} e^{-
u x/2}$ (chi-squared with $
u$ degrees of freedom, suitably normalized) and treat $
u$ as a parameter to be estimated from observed resonance widths.

In practice, the data set of measured neutron widths is incomplete: very small widths fall below an experimental detection threshold, so analyses use only widths above a cutoff $c$ and apply a maximum-likelihood (ML) estimator for $
u$ on the truncated sample. Applied to s-wave neutron resonances in platinum isotopes and to a reconstructed Nuclear Data Ensemble, this procedure has yielded ML estimates of $
u$ that are small and widely spread, and apparently inconsistent (at high statistical significance) with $
u = 1$.

Question: After properly accounting for (a) the choice of cutoff $c$, (b) finite-sample bias and variance of the ML estimator, and (c) simulation-calibrated confidence intervals (e.g. Monte Carlo simulations of truncated chi-squared samples of comparable size and signal-to-noise to the data), are the observed ML estimates of $
u$ for neutron widths in Pt isotopes and for the reconstructed Nuclear Data Ensemble genuinely inconsistent with the GOE prediction $
u = 1$, or are they statistically compatible with the Porter–Thomas distribution?

The question is the Brzozowski-type conjecture on regularity of classes of the free Burnside semigroup satisfying x^n = x^{n+m}. It has been answered affirmatively for all n ≥ 3 and m ≥ 1 by work of McCammond, Guba, and especially do Lago, who proved that the classes are recognizable and the word problem is decidable. The remaining case n = 2 is still open: only partial results are known (notably Plyushchenko and Shur, 2011, treating x^2 = x^3 on a two-letter alphabet via overlap-free representatives), and Brzozowski's conjecture for n = 2 has been neither proved nor disproved.

Partial analogs of Delzant's theorem have been established in special cases. In particular, Gualtieri–Li–Pelayo–Ratiu (arXiv:1407.3300) classify compact toric Hamiltonian log-symplectic manifolds — Poisson manifolds that are symplectic away from a normal-crossing degeneracy locus — via decorated log affine polytopes ("tropical momentum map"). Beyond log-symplectic structures (e.g. arbitrary Poisson manifolds symplectic on a dense set, or b^k-Poisson and more general b-symplectic settings), the question is addressed only in further special cases (Guillemin–Miranda–Pires–Scott et al.), and a fully general Delzant analog remains open.

Let $(M^{2n},\omega)$ be a connected symplectic manifold equipped with a completely integrable Hamiltonian system, i.e. a smooth map $F=(f_1,\dots,f_n):M\to\mathbb{R}^n$ whose components are pairwise Poisson-commuting, $\{f_i,f_j\}=0$, and are functionally independent on a dense open subset. Let $B\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ denote the set of regular values of $F$ over which the fibers are compact and connected. By the Liouville–Arnold–Mineur theorem, $F^{-1}(B)\to B$ is locally a Lagrangian torus bundle and admits local action-angle coordinates. The obstructions to globalizing this structure were identified by Duistermaat: the monodromy, the Chern class of the underlying torus bundle (the "Duistermaat–Chern class" $c\in H^2(B;\mathbb{Z}^n)$), and the Lagrangian class. The Duistermaat–Chern class measures the obstruction to the topological torus bundle $F^{-1}(B)\to B$ admitting a global section.
