Consider a sparse linear system $A x = b$, with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ symmetric positive definite (or, more generally, arising from the discretization of a partial differential equation), to be solved by an algebraic multigrid (AMG) method. In bootstrap AMG (BAMG), the setup phase is driven by a small set of "test vectors" that are intended to span the algebraically smooth components of $A$ (i.e., error modes that classical relaxation reduces slowly). Three principal mechanisms are used to compute and refine these test vectors and the associated transfer operators:

1. Least-squares interpolation: given current test vectors $\{v^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}$, the interpolation operator $P$ from a coarse grid to the fine grid is defined row by row by solving, for each fine point $i$, a local least-squares problem
$$P_{i,\cdot} = \arg\min_{w} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \omega_k \, \big( v^{(k)}_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_i} w_j v^{(k)}_j \big)^2,$$
where $\mathcal{C}_i$ is a chosen set of coarse interpolatory neighbors and $\omega_k > 0$ are weights.

2. Bootstrap setup cycles: a multilevel V-cycle-like procedure in which the current multigrid hierarchy is itself applied to enrich the test set, by computing approximate eigenvectors associated with the smallest eigenvalues of $A$ on each level and feeding them back into the least-squares interpolation construction, iteratively improving $P$ and the coarse operators.

3. Adaptive cycles: an outer loop in which the current solver is applied to the homogeneous problem $A x = 0$ from random initial guesses; slowly converging error components revealed in this process are added to the test set and the hierarchy is rebuilt.

Define a setup algorithm to be "optimal in work" if its total computational cost is $O(n)$ (with constants independent of problem size and uniformly bounded across a prescribed family of problems) and yields a solver whose convergence factor is bounded below 1 independently of $n$. Call it "robust across problem classes" if it achieves this for a broad family of discrete operators including, e.g., scalar elliptic PDEs with strongly varying or anisotropic coefficients, systems of PDEs, and certain non-symmetric or indefinite problems.

Problem. Devise a self-learning bootstrap AMG setup procedure that combines least-squares interpolation, bootstrap setup cycles, and adaptive cycles—specifying how many test vectors to use, how to schedule and interleave the bootstrap and adaptive phases, and how to choose the local interpolation patterns and weights—such that the resulting algorithm is simultaneously optimal in work and robust across the problem classes above. Prove the corresponding convergence and complexity bounds.

Let $f\colon \mathbb{P}^N \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^N$ be a dominant rational map defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. Let $I_f \subset \mathbb{P}^N$ denote the indeterminacy locus of $f$, and define
$$\mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f = \{P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) : f^n(P) \notin I_f \text{ for all } n \geq 0\},$$
so that the forward orbit $\mathcal{O}_f(P) = \{P, f(P), f^2(P), \ldots\}$ is well defined for $P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f$.

Let $h\colon \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \to [0,\infty)$ denote the absolute logarithmic Weil height, and write $h^+ = \max(h, 1)$. For $P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f$, define the upper and lower arithmetic degrees
$$\overline{\alpha}_f(P) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} h^+(f^n(P))^{1/n}, \qquad \underline{\alpha}_f(P) = \liminf_{n \to \infty} h^+(f^n(P))^{1/n}.$$
Let $\delta_f = \lim_{n\to\infty}(\deg f^n)^{1/n}$ denote the (first) dynamical degree of $f$.

Prove the following four statements.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For every $P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f$, the limit $\alpha_f(P) := \lim_{n\to\infty} h^+(f^n(P))^{1/n}$ exists; equivalently, $\overline{\alpha}_f(P) = \underline{\alpha}_f(P)$.

$$\mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f = \{P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) : f^n(P) \notin I_f \text{ for all } n \geq 0\},$$
so that the forward orbit $\mathcal{O}_f(P) = \{P, f(P), f^2(P), \ldots\}$ is well defined for $P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f$.

Let $h\colon \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \to [0,\infty)$ denote the absolute logarithmic Weil height, and write $h^+ = \max(h, 1)$. For $P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f$, define the upper and lower arithmetic degrees
$$\overline{\alpha}_f(P) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} h^+(f^n(P))^{1/n}, \qquad \underline{\alpha}_f(P) = \liminf_{n \to \infty} h^+(f^n(P))^{1/n}.$$
Let $\delta_f = \lim_{n\to\infty}(\deg f^n)^{1/n}$ denote the (first) dynamical degree of $f$.

\item[(a)] For every $P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f$, the limit $\alpha_f(P) := \lim_{n\to\infty} h^+(f^n(P))^{1/n}$ exists; equivalently, $\overline{\alpha}_f(P) = \underline{\alpha}_f(P)$.
\item[(b)] The set $\{\alpha_f(P) : P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f\}$ is finite.
\item[(c)] For every $P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f$, the arithmetic degree $\alpha_f(P)$ is an algebraic integer.

The Kawaguchi–Silverman conjecture remains open in general for dominant rational self-maps of $\mathbb{P}^N$. Parts (a) (existence of the limit) is known for morphisms (Kawaguchi–Silverman) and for monomial maps (Lin), and part (d) has been established for many classes: surjective endomorphisms of projective surfaces, int-amplified endomorphisms of $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial klt varieties (Meng–Zhang and subsequent work, 2024), birational automorphisms of certain irregular varieties, and others. The question concerns the precise asymptotic form of height growth along Zariski dense orbits of dominant rational self-maps of projective space, refining the Kawaguchi–Silverman conjecture (which only asserts $\alpha_f(P)=\delta_f$). For morphisms of $\mathbb{P}^N$ a canonical height gives $h(f^n(P))=\delta_f^n\hat h_f(P)+O(1)$, and for morphisms with $\alpha_f(P)>1$ on smooth projective varieties Sano proved the analogous bound with $k_f=0$. Recent work (e.g., Matsuzawa and others, 2019–2024) has obtained partial results on arithmetic degrees and the Kawaguchi–Silverman conjecture in various cases, but the full asymptotic refinement (15.5) for general dominant rational maps of $\mathbb{P}^N$ — including the polynomial and logarithmic correction factors and the claim $k_f=0$ when $\delta_f>1$ — does not appear to be established in the literature surveyed. The problem appears to remain open.

Consider a single distinguishable impurity immersed in an ideal three-dimensional Fermi gas of N identical non-interacting fermions filling a Fermi sea up to Fermi momentum k_F, with a short-range two-body interaction acting only between the impurity and the majority fermions. The exact many-body ground state |Ψ⟩ can be expanded in sectors labeled by the number s = 0, 1, 2, … of particle–hole pairs excited out of the Fermi sea:

|Ψ⟩ = Σ_{s=0}^{∞} |Ψ_s⟩,

where |Ψ_s⟩ contains the impurity dressed by exactly s particle–hole excitations of the majority Fermi sea, with amplitudes φ_s(p; k_1,…,k_s; q_1,…,q_s) (p the impurity momentum, k_i the particle momenta above the Fermi sea, q_i the hole momenta below it).

(a) Determine the asymptotic form of |Ψ_s⟩, or equivalently of the amplitudes φ_s and of the sector weight w_s = ⟨Ψ_s|Ψ_s⟩, in the limit s → ∞ that controls the long-time / low-energy coherence properties (the quasiparticle residue and orthogonality-catastrophe-like behavior) of the impurity in the Fermi gas.

(b) Decide whether this large-s asymptotic tail can be obtained analytically by treating the s particles and s holes as an effectively non-interacting gas of excitations in which each particle and each hole scatters only from the impurity (i.e. by an independent-scatterer / single-impurity-T-matrix factorization), and either prove such a factorized asymptotic representation or exhibit corrections that invalidate it.

Let X be a smooth projective variety defined over the algebraic closure Q̄ of Q, and let f : X ⇢ X be a dominant rational self-map. Let X(Q̄)_f denote the set of Q̄-points P of X whose forward orbit O_f(P) = {P, f(P), f^2(P), ...} is well-defined (i.e., f^n(P) avoids the indeterminacy locus of f for all n ≥ 0).

Fix an ample divisor H on X, and let h_H : X(Q̄) → R be a corresponding (logarithmic) Weil height, normalized so that h_H ≥ 1. For P ∈ X(Q̄)_f define the upper and lower arithmetic degrees
   ᾱ_f(P) = limsup_{n→∞} h_H(f^n(P))^{1/n},   α_f(P) = liminf_{n→∞} h_H(f^n(P))^{1/n}.
These quantities are independent of the choice of H. Let δ_f denote the (first) dynamical degree of f, defined as
   δ_f = lim_{n→∞} ((f^n)^* H · H^{dim X − 1})^{1/n},
which is known to exist and is a birational invariant.

Prove or disprove each of the following statements:

(a) For every P ∈ X(Q̄)_f, the limit lim_{n→∞} h_H(f^n(P))^{1/n} exists (so ᾱ_f(P) = α_f(P) =: α_f(P)).

(b) The set { α_f(P) : P ∈ X(Q̄)_f } is finite.

(c) For every P ∈ X(Q̄)_f, the arithmetic degree α_f(P) is an algebraic integer.

(d) If P ∈ X(Q̄)_f has orbit O_f(P) Zariski dense in X, then α_f(P) = δ_f.

The package of statements is the Kawaguchi–Silverman arithmetic degree conjecture. Parts (b) and (c) (finiteness of the set of arithmetic degrees, and the algebraic-integrality of α_f(P)) have been disproved by counterexamples of Lesieutre–Satriano using birational self-maps on surfaces. Consider a single mobile impurity of mass $M$ immersed in an ideal three-dimensional Fermi gas of non-interacting fermions of mass $m$ at zero temperature, where the impurity interacts with the fermions via a short-range two-body potential characterized by a scattering length $a$. The total momentum $\mathbf{p}$ of the system is a good quantum number. For sufficiently weak attractive coupling, the dressed impurity ("polaron") at total momentum $\mathbf{p}$ is expected to be a long-lived quasiparticle whose true excitation energy is a complex number $\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{p}) = E(\mathbf{p}) - i\Gamma(\mathbf{p})/2$, with the real part $E(\mathbf{p})$ admitting a low-momentum expansion of the form
$$E(\mathbf{p}) = E_0 + \frac{|\mathbf{p}|^2}{2M^*} + O(|\mathbf{p}|^4),$$
where $M^*$ is the quasiparticle effective mass.

A standard procedure to estimate $M^*$ is the following variational scheme. Choose a truncated variational ansatz $|\Psi_{\mathbf{p}}\rangle$ for the polaron at total momentum $\mathbf{p}$ (for example, the Chevy ansatz containing the bare impurity plus a finite number of particle–hole excitations of the Fermi sea). For each small but nonzero $\mathbf{p}$, minimize the expectation value
$$\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{var}}(\mathbf{p}) = \min_{|\Psi_{\mathbf{p}}\rangle} \frac{\langle \Psi_{\mathbf{p}} | \hat{H} | \Psi_{\mathbf{p}}\rangle}{\langle \Psi_{\mathbf{p}} | \Psi_{\mathbf{p}}\rangle}$$
within the chosen truncated subspace, and extract a variational effective mass $M^*_{\mathrm{var}}$ by fitting $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{var}}(\mathbf{p}) = \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{var}}(\mathbf{0}) + |\mathbf{p}|^2/(2M^*_{\mathrm{var}}) + O(|\mathbf{p}|^4)$.

The questions are:

(a) Is this minimization procedure mathematically well defined at small nonzero $\mathbf{p}$? In particular, does the variational functional possess a true minimum (rather than only an infimum or a saddle point) within the truncated subspace, given that for $\mathbf{p}\neq 0$ the bare polaron state is typically embedded in a continuum of polaron-plus-particle-hole scattering states that may render the variational energy unbounded below or non-stationary?

(b) Assuming the procedure is well defined, prove or disprove that the resulting $M^*_{\mathrm{var}}$ coincides with the effective mass $M^*$ associated with the real part $E(\mathbf{p})$ of the exact complex quasiparticle energy $\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{p})$ of the long-lived dressed impurity.

Setting. Consider a sparse symmetric positive definite linear system $Au=f$ on a finite index set $\Omega=\{1,\dots,n\}$. In an algebraic multigrid framework one selects a subset $C\subset\Omega$ of "coarse variables" with complementary fine set $F=\Omega\setminus C$, and builds a coarse space via an interpolation operator $P:\mathbb{R}^{|C|}\to\mathbb{R}^n$. The quality of $C$ is measured through compatible relaxation (CR): given a smoother $M$ for $A$ and the restriction $A_{FF}$ of $A$ to the $F$–$F$ block, one performs the iteration $e_F\leftarrow (I-M_{FF}^{-1}A_{FF})e_F$ on the fine subspace and defines the CR convergence rate
$$\rho_{CR}(C)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\bigl\|(I-M_{FF}^{-1}A_{FF})^k\bigr\|^{1/k}.$$
A coarse set $C$ is regarded as adequate when $\rho_{CR}(C)\le\rho^*$ for a prescribed target $\rho^*<1$, and inadequate otherwise. The coarsening cost is measured by $|C|/n$ (or, recursively, by the operator complexity of the resulting hierarchy).

Problem. Provide a constructive procedure that, for any such $A$:

(a) selects an initial coarse set $C_0\subset\Omega$ (using only information available algebraically from $A$ and from a small set of test vectors produced by relaxation on $Au=0$);

(b) when applied iteratively, locally modifies the current coarse set $C$ by additions, removals, or replacements of indices in regions where CR is observed to converge slowly, producing an updated set $C'$ that satisfies
$$\rho_{CR}(C')\le\rho_{CR}(C)\quad\text{and ultimately}\quad \rho_{CR}(C')\le\rho^*,$$
while keeping $|C'|/n$ bounded by a prescribed coarsening ratio.

The procedure should come with a rigorous justification—in particular, identifying which local quantities derived from CR (e.g.\ pointwise errors, slow-to-converge components) reliably indicate the indices whose addition to $C$ most reduces $\rho_{CR}$—together with an analysis showing convergence of the update process to an adequate $C$ without introducing unnecessary coarse-space complexity.

Let $(C_v, |\cdot|)$ be an algebraically closed field that is complete with respect to a nontrivial non-archimedean absolute value. Let $\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathrm{Berk}}$ denote the Berkovich projective line over $C_v$, whose points are classified into Types I, II, III, and IV; the Type I points are exactly the classical points $\mathbb{P}^1(C_v) \subset \mathbb{P}^1_{\mathrm{Berk}}$.

Let $f \in C_v(z)$ be a rational function of degree $\deg(f) \geq 2$, viewed as a self-map of $\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathrm{Berk}}$ via its canonical continuous extension. Let $J_f \subset \mathbb{P}^1_{\mathrm{Berk}}$ denote the Berkovich Julia set of $f$ (the complement of the Berkovich Fatou set, defined as the largest open set on which the family of iterates is equicontinuous in a suitable sense, or equivalently as the support of the canonical $f$-invariant measure).

A point $x \in \mathbb{P}^1(C_v)$ is called a Type I repelling periodic point of $f$ if there exists an integer $n \geq 1$ such that $f^n(x) = x$ and the multiplier $(f^n)'(x)$ satisfies $|(f^n)'(x)| > 1$.

Prove or disprove: $J_f \cap \mathbb{P}^1(C_v)$ equals the closure in $\mathbb{P}^1(C_v)$ (with respect to the topology induced by $|\cdot|$) of the set of Type I repelling periodic points of $f$.

Let $(K,|\cdot|)$ be a complete, algebraically closed, non-archimedean valued field (for example $K=\mathbb{C}_v$, the completion of an algebraic closure of a complete non-archimedean field), and let $f \in K(z)$ be a rational map of degree $d \geq 2$ acting on the Berkovich projective line $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_K$. The Fatou set of $f$ is the largest open subset of $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_K$ on which the iterates $\{f^n\}$ form an equicontinuous (normal) family; its connected components are called Fatou components. A periodic Fatou component $U$ of period $n \geq 1$ (so $f^n(U) = U$) is called indifferent if the action of $f^n$ on $U$ is neither attracting nor in the basin of any attracting/super-attracting cycle, and equivalently can be characterized by the multiplier behavior on the boundary type-II points associated with $U$. A Fatou component is called a disk if it is isomorphic, as a Berkovich analytic space, to an open Berkovich disk. A periodic cycle of Fatou components is the orbit $\{U, f(U), \dots, f^{n-1}(U)\}$ of a periodic component.

Address the following questions:

(a) Can $f$ have infinitely many distinct periodic cycles of indifferent Fatou components that are not disks?

(b) If not, is there an upper bound, depending only on the degree $d$, for the number of such cycles?

(c) Do the answers to (a) and (b) depend on the particular non-archimedean field $K$ (e.g., its residue characteristic or value group)?

Setting. Consider a sparse symmetric positive (semi)definite linear system $A u = f$ on a finite index set $\Omega$ of fine-grid degrees of freedom, together with a chosen subset $\mathcal{C}\subset\Omega$ of coarse variables and complementary fine set $\mathcal{F}=\Omega\setminus\mathcal{C}$. For each $i\in\mathcal{F}$, let $\mathcal{C}_i\subset\mathcal{C}$ denote a small "interpolatory" neighborhood. A prolongation operator $P:\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}$ acts row-wise as
$$ (Pv)_i = \sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} p_{ij}\, v_j ,\qquad i\in\mathcal{F}, $$
with $(Pv)_i=v_i$ for $i\in\mathcal{C}$.

Suppose one is given a finite collection of test vectors $\{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}$, intended to represent algebraically smooth error components (i.e., components slow to be reduced by relaxation). The least-squares (LS) definition of interpolation determines the rows of $P$ by solving, for each $i\in\mathcal{F}$,
$$ \{p_{ij}\}_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} \;=\; \arg\min_{\{q_{ij}\}}\;\sum_{k=1}^{K} \omega_\kappa^{(k)}(i)\,\Big( x^{(k)}_i - \sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} q_{ij}\, x^{(k)}_j \Big)^{\!2}, $$
where $\omega_\kappa^{(k)}(i)\ge 0$ are local weights assigned to test vector $k$ at the local LS problem indexed by $i$ (or, more generally, by a local aggregate $\kappa$).

Problem. In a purely algebraic setting (i.e., without recourse to an underlying PDE, mesh, or finite-element structure), give a procedure to define the local weights $\omega_\kappa^{(k)}$, and, if needed, an associated set of local equations whose solutions provide local test vectors, with the following property:

(P) If a test vector $x^{(k)}$ is globally smooth in the sense of having small global $A$-residual $\|A x^{(k)}\|$ relative to $\|x^{(k)}\|_A$, but on some local region $\kappa$ has a large local residual (e.g., $\sum_{i\in\kappa}(Ax^{(k)})_i^2$ is large compared to a local energy measure of $x^{(k)}$ on $\kappa$), then the weights $\omega_\kappa^{(k)}$ used in the LS problems centered in $\kappa$ should not over-emphasize $x^{(k)}$ relative to other test vectors. Equivalently, the scheme should generalize the local-scaling-by-residual (LSR) idea — which is presently used only in conjunction with global weights — to a fully local weighting strategy, while still producing an interpolation $P$ that yields a convergent bootstrap algebraic multigrid method on a broad class of symmetric positive (semi)definite problems.

Provide such a definition of $\{\omega_\kappa^{(k)}\}$ (and any auxiliary local equations for local test vectors) and prove that the resulting LS interpolation satisfies a two-grid weak-approximation bound uniform in problem size on this class.

$$ (Pv)_i = \sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} p_{ij}\, v_j ,\qquad i\in\mathcal{F}, $$
with $(Pv)_i=v_i$ for $i\in\mathcal{C}$.

Suppose one is given a finite collection of test vectors $\{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}$, intended to represent algebraically smooth error components (i.e., components slow to be reduced by relaxation). The least-squares (LS) definition of interpolation determines the rows of $P$ by solving, for each $i\in\mathcal{F}$,
$$ \{p_{ij}\}_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} \;=\; \arg\min_{\{q_{ij}\}}\;\sum_{k=1}^{K} \omega_\kappa^{(k)}(i)\,\Big( x^{(k)}_i - \sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} q_{ij}\, x^{(k)}_j \Big)^{\!2}, $$
where $\omega_\kappa^{(k)}(i)\ge 0$ are local weights assigned to test vector $k$ at the local LS problem indexed by $i$ (or, more generally, by a local aggregate $\kappa$).

Problem. In a purely algebraic setting (i.e., without recourse to an underlying PDE, mesh, or finite-element structure), give a procedure to define the local weights $\omega_\kappa^{(k)}$, and, if needed, an associated set of local equations whose solutions provide local test vectors, with the following property:

(P) If a test vector $x^{(k)}$ is globally smooth in the sense of having small global $A$-residual $\|A x^{(k)}\|$ relative to $\|x^{(k)}\|_A$, but on some local region $\kappa$ has a large local residual (e.g., $\sum_{i\in\kappa}(Ax^{(k)})_i^2$ is large compared to a local energy measure of $x^{(k)}$ on $\kappa$), then the weights $\omega_\kappa^{(k)}$ used in the LS problems centered in $\kappa$ should not over-emphasize $x^{(k)}$ relative to other test vectors. Equivalently, the scheme should generalize the local-scaling-by-residual (LSR) idea — which is presently used only in conjunction with global weights — to a fully local weighting strategy, while still producing an interpolation $P$ that yields a convergent bootstrap algebraic multigrid method on a broad class of symmetric positive (semi)definite problems.

Provide such a definition of $\{\omega_\kappa^{(k)}\}$ (and any auxiliary local equations for local test vectors) and prove that the resulting LS interpolation satisfies a two-grid weak-approximation bound uniform in problem size on this class.

representations.normalized:
Consider the bootstrap algebraic multigrid (BAMG) framework for solving a large sparse linear system $A x = b$, where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is symmetric positive (semi)definite or otherwise admits a near-kernel of algebraically smooth error components. In BAMG, the prolongation operator $P$ between a fine level and a coarse level is constructed so as to fit, in a (weighted) least-squares sense, a collection of "test vectors" $\{v^{(1)}, \dots, v^{(k)}\} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ that are intended to span (or approximately span) the algebraically smooth subspace of $A$. These test vectors are themselves produced by a bootstrap setup procedure: an initial multigrid hierarchy is applied (e.g., via relaxation, multigrid eigensolves, and recursive coarse-level computations) to a set of random or problem-informed initial vectors, yielding successively more accurate approximations to slow-to-converge modes.

Let $W(k,\tau)$ denote the total computational work (in floating-point operations) expended in the setup phase to produce $k$ test vectors each computed to an accuracy $\tau$ (measured, for instance, by the $A$-norm residual of the homogeneous problem $A v = 0$ relative to the dominant smooth modes). Let $\rho(k,\tau)$ denote the asymptotic convergence factor of the resulting BAMG V-cycle (or W-cycle) when interpolation is built by least-squares fitting these test vectors, and let $C_{\mathrm{solve}}(k,\tau)$ denote the work per cycle in the solve phase.

Problem. Determine, for a given target overall solve-phase efficiency, principled criteria for choosing the number $k$ of test vectors and the accuracy $\tau$ to which each is computed in the setup phase that:
(i) guarantee that the constructed interpolation $P$ approximates the algebraically smooth subspace of $A$ accurately enough to yield a convergence factor $\rho(k,\tau)$ bounded below $1$ uniformly in problem size and parameters of interest, and
(ii) keep the setup work $W(k,\tau)$ bounded by a small multiple of the solve work, so that total cost $W(k,\tau) + N_{\text{cycles}}\cdot C_{\mathrm{solve}}(k,\tau)$ is minimized (or at least kept comparable to that of an optimally-tuned geometric multigrid method) for the class of problems considered.

In particular, give quantitative guidance, supported by analysis, on the optimal stopping accuracy $\tau$ for the bootstrap test-vector iterations and on the optimal number $k$ of test vectors as functions of the spectral properties of $A$ and the desired convergence factor.

Let $A \in \mathbb{C}^{n	imes n}$ be a (possibly non-Hermitian) nonsingular matrix arising as a fine-level discretization, and consider a two-level multigrid scheme defined by a restriction operator $R \in \mathbb{C}^{n_c 	imes n}$ and an interpolation operator $P \in \mathbb{C}^{n 	imes n_c}$, with $n_c < n$. The Galerkin coarse-grid operator is
$$A_c \;=\; R\,A\,P \in \mathbb{C}^{n_c 	imes n_c}.$$
A two-level cycle alternates a relaxation (smoothing) step with the coarse-grid correction $x \leftarrow x + P A_c^{-1} R(b - A x)$.

In the non-Hermitian setting it is possible that $A$ is nonsingular while $A_c = R A P$ is singular or has eigenvalues/singular values much smaller in modulus than those of $A$, leading to coarse-grid correction that overshoots and causes the resulting iteration to diverge.

Problem. Devise a constructive procedure that, given $A$ and a set of (approximate) algebraically smooth test vectors, produces $R$ and $P$ jointly — tying their local definitions together — such that:

(i) $A_c = R A P$ is guaranteed to be nonsingular whenever $A$ is nonsingular;

(ii) the smallest singular value (and the spectrum near $0$) of $A_c$ is not underestimated relative to that of $A$ in a quantifiable sense, so that the coarse-grid correction does not produce overcorrection;

(iii) the resulting two-level (and, recursively, multilevel) iteration converges uniformly, with a contraction factor bounded away from $1$ independently of $n$, for a useful class of non-Hermitian matrices $A$.

Provide such a coupled construction of $R$ and $P$, together with theoretical guarantees of (i)–(iii), or prove that no such local coupling can achieve all three properties simultaneously.

The construction of jointly compatible restriction and interpolation operators that guarantee a nonsingular, well-conditioned Galerkin coarse-grid operator for general non-Hermitian problems remains an active research topic in algebraic multigrid. While various heuristic and partial approaches (e.g., bootstrap AMG, AMGe, nonsymmetric smoothed aggregation, Petrov-Galerkin AMG) have been proposed, no general construction with the requested rigorous guarantees for broad non-Hermitian classes appears to be established. Status is best characterized as open.

representations.normalized:
Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid (BAMG) is an iterative linear-solver framework for large sparse linear systems $A x = b$, where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is a sparse matrix, that constructs a multilevel hierarchy of coarse spaces adaptively. Starting from an initial set of test vectors (typically random vectors smoothed by a relaxation scheme such as Gauss–Seidel), BAMG iteratively improves a multigrid hierarchy — consisting of interpolation operators $P_\ell$, coarse operators $A_{\ell+1} = P_\ell^T A_\ell P_\ell$, and relaxation schemes — by using the current multigrid cycle itself as the smoothing/improvement mechanism for the test vectors, with the goal of producing a hierarchy whose two-grid and multigrid convergence factors are uniformly bounded below 1 independently of $n$. A solver is called "genuinely fast" if the cost of computing $x$ to fixed accuracy $\varepsilon$ is $O(\mathrm{nnz}(A)\,|\log\varepsilon|)$ with constants independent of problem size and parameters.

BAMG and closely related adaptive AMG methods have been demonstrated to be genuinely fast solvers on several challenging non-elliptic problem classes, including certain Markov chain (stochastic) matrices, lattice gauge theory Dirac operators (e.g., Wilson and staggered Dirac systems in QCD), and graph Laplacians arising from anisotropic or unstructured discretizations.

Problem. Determine the maximal class $\mathcal{C}$ of sparse matrices $A$ for which a Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid–type method can be designed that is a genuinely fast solver in the sense above. In particular:

(a) Identify structural or spectral conditions on a sparse matrix $A$ (beyond ellipticity, definiteness, or M-matrix structure) that are sufficient to guarantee the existence of a BAMG hierarchy with mesh-independent convergence.

(b) Either construct a BAMG-type algorithm that is provably a genuinely fast solver for arbitrary nonsingular sparse linear systems, or exhibit a class of sparse matrices for which no BAMG-type construction (interpolation built from adaptively smoothed test vectors plus standard relaxation and Galerkin coarsening) can yield mesh-independent convergence.

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be a large sparse symmetric positive (semi)definite matrix and let $S: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ denote a fixed smoother (relaxation operator) for $A$, with error-propagation operator $E = I - M^{-1}A$ for some $M$. The "algebraically smooth" error space associated with $S$ is the subspace $\mathcal{S} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ of vectors $e$ for which the convergence factor $\|Ee\|_A / \|e\|_A$ is close to $1$, i.e. components not significantly reduced by the smoother.

For a chosen partition of the indices into a coarse set $C$ and a fine set $F = \{1,\dots,n\}\setminus C$, an interpolation operator $P:\mathbb{R}^{|C|} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is defined row-by-row (for each $i\in F$) by a weighted least-squares problem
$$
P_{i,\cdot} = \arg\min_{w} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \omega_k\,\big(v_k(i) - \textstyle\sum_{j\in C_i} w_j\, v_k(j)\big)^2,
$$
where $\{v_1,\dots,v_K\}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is a finite collection of "test vectors" (each obtained by applying several relaxation sweeps with $S$ to a random initial vector on the homogeneous system $Ax=0$), $C_i\subset C$ is a prescribed set of interpolatory neighbors of $i$, and $\omega_k>0$ are weights.

Design a procedure based on randomized range-finding / randomized low-rank approximation (such as randomized SVD, subspace iteration, or related sketching techniques) that, given access to $A$ and to $S$, produces a finite test set $V=\{v_1,\dots,v_K\}$ whose span provably approximates the dominant part of $\mathcal{S}$ (the slow-to-converge eigen-directions of $E$) to a prescribed tolerance with high probability, with $K$ as small as possible. Establish quantitative bounds showing that the resulting least-squares interpolation operator $P$ satisfies a weak approximation property of the form
$$
\min_{x_c} \|e - P x_c\|_2^2 \le \kappa\, \|e\|_A^2 \qquad \forall\, e\in\mathbb{R}^n,
$$
with a constant $\kappa$ that is independent of $n$ and depends explicitly on the sample size $K$, the number of relaxation sweeps applied to form each $v_k$, and the spectral gap of $E$.

Work in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $d \geq 2$. An algebraic curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is the zero set of a finite collection of polynomials whose common zero locus has dimension one; the curve is said to be of constant degree if its degree is bounded by a fixed constant independent of $n$. An algebraic helix is an algebraic curve $\gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ such that there exists a one-parameter group of rigid motions of $\mathbb{R}^d$ acting transitively on $\gamma$ (equivalently, a curve all of whose points are equivalent under a one-parameter family of isometries of $\mathbb{R}^d$); in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ the only algebraic helices are lines and circles.

For a finite point set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, let
$$D(P) = |\{\,\|p - q\|_2 : p,q \in P,\ p \neq q\,\}|$$
denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances spanned by $P$. Define
$$D^{(d)}_{\mathrm{curve}}(n) = \min\{\,D(P) : |P|=n,\ P \subset \gamma,\ \gamma \text{ a constant-degree algebraic curve in } \mathbb{R}^d \text{ containing no algebraic helix}\,\}.$$

Determine the asymptotic order of $D^{(d)}_{\mathrm{curve}}(n)$ as $n \to \infty$.

Fix an integer $d\ge 2$ and a positive integer $n$ such that $n^{1/d}$ is an integer. Let
$$L_d \;=\; \{0,1,\dots,n^{1/d}-1\}^d \subset \mathbb{R}^d$$
be the $d$-dimensional integer lattice cube containing $n$ points, equipped with the Euclidean metric. For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, call a subset $S\subseteq P$ a "no-repeated-distance subset" (or distance-Sidon subset) if for every positive real $r>0$ the number of unordered pairs $\{p,q\}\subseteq S$ with $\|p-q\|=r$ is at most $1$. Define
$$\mathrm{subset}(L_d) \;=\; \max\bigl\{\,|S| : S\subseteq L_d,\ S \text{ is a no-repeated-distance subset}\bigr\}.$$
It is known that $\mathrm{subset}(L_d) = \Omega(n^{2/(3d)})$ and $\mathrm{subset}(L_d) = O(n^{1/d})$. Determine the asymptotic order of $\mathrm{subset}(L_d)$ as $n\to\infty$ (with $d$ fixed).

The problem of determining the asymptotic size of the largest no-repeated-distance subset of the d-dimensional integer lattice is a classical Erdős–Guy problem. Work in the Euclidean plane R^2. For a finite set P of points in R^2, let D(P) denote the number of distinct values in the multiset { ||p - q|| : p, q ∈ P, p ≠ q } of pairwise Euclidean distances. Given two irreducible algebraic plane curves γ1 and γ2 of degree at most a fixed constant, and finite sets P1 ⊂ γ1 and P2 ⊂ γ2 with |P1| = m and |P2| = n, define
   D(P1, P2) := |{ ||p - q|| : p ∈ P1, q ∈ P2 }|.
Define
   D_curves(m, n) := min D(P1, P2),
where the minimum is taken over all such pairs (γ1, P1), (γ2, P2) excluding the following exceptional configurations: (i) γ1 and γ2 are parallel lines, (ii) γ1 and γ2 are orthogonal lines, (iii) γ1 and γ2 are concentric circles.

Determine the asymptotic order of D_curves(m, n) as m, n → ∞.

For integers n ≥ k ≥ 2 and l ≥ 2, let φ(n, k, l) denote the minimum, over all sets P of n points in the Euclidean plane such that every k-element subset of P determines at least l distinct distances, of the total number of distinct distances determined by P. (The total number of distinct distances of P is the cardinality of the set { |pq| : p, q ∈ P, p ≠ q }.)

Consider the case k = l = 4. Equivalently, P is a set of n points in the plane such that no 4-point subset of P determines fewer than 4 distinct distances; this rules out any 4 points of P forming a rhombus, a rectangle, or a "deltoid" (kite) in which one vertex is equidistant from the other three.

It is known that
   φ(n, 4, 4) = Ω(n / log n).
Determine the asymptotic order of φ(n, 4, 4): find functions f(n) such that φ(n, 4, 4) = Θ(f(n)), or improve the known lower and upper bounds.

Erdős originally asked whether φ(n,4,5) = Θ(n²). In September 2024, Tao constructed n-point planar sets with at most O(n²/√log n) distinct distances in which every 4 points determine at least 5 distinct distances, disproving the Θ(n²) conjecture and giving an upper bound matching (up to constants) the Guth–Katz upper bound for the unrestricted distinct-distances problem. The general lower bound Ω(n/log n) from Guth–Katz applies. The exact asymptotic order is still not pinned down — there remains a √log n gap between the best known lower and upper bounds — so the problem is partially solved.

For a finite planar point set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ and a point $p \in P$, let $\hat D_p(P)$ denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances from $p$ to the other points of $P$, i.e.
$$\hat D_p(P) = |\{\, \|p-q\| : q \in P,\ q \neq p\,\}|.$$
Define
$$\hat D_\Sigma(P) = \sum_{p\in P} \hat D_p(P), \qquad \hat D_\Sigma(n) = \min_{|P|=n} \hat D_\Sigma(P),$$
the minimum being taken over all $n$-point sets $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. The $\sqrt n \times \sqrt n$ section of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ shows $\hat D_\Sigma(n) = O(n^2/\sqrt{\log n})$. Determine the asymptotic order of $\hat D_\Sigma(n)$. In particular, is it true that $\hat D_\Sigma(n) = \Theta(n^2/\sqrt{\log n})$?

Consider a non-relativistic Coulomb many-electron system: a fixed configuration of static nuclei with positive charges $Z_1,\dots,Z_K$ at positions $R_1,\dots,R_K\in\mathbb{R}^3$, together with $M$ non-relativistic electrons. The Hamiltonian acting on the antisymmetric subspace of $\bigotimes^M L^2(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{C}^2)$ is
$$H_M = \sum_{i=1}^M\Big(-\tfrac12\Delta_{x_i} - \sum_{k=1}^K\frac{Z_k}{|x_i-R_k|}\Big) + \sum_{1\le i<j\le M}\frac{1}{|x_i-x_j|}.$$
Let $E(M) = \inf\sigma(H_M)$ denote the ground-state energy (with $E(0)=0$), and define the ionization energy of the $M$-electron system by
$$I[M] := E(M-1) - E(M) \ge 0.$$
Equivalently, $I[N]$ is the energy required to remove one electron from the $N$-electron ground state, while $I[N+1]$ is the electron affinity of the $N$-electron system.

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every choice of nuclear charges and positions and every integer $N\ge 1$ for which the relevant ground states exist,
$$I[N+1] < I[N],$$
i.e., the ionization energy of any Coulomb many-electron system is strictly greater than its electron affinity.

Let $L\geq 1$ and let $c_1,c_2,\dots,c_L$ be non-negative integers with $c_1\geq 1$ and $c_L\geq 1$. Define a positive linear recurrence sequence $\{H_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ by prescribed initial conditions and the recurrence
$$H_{n+1}=c_1H_n+c_2H_{n-1}+\cdots+c_LH_{n-L+1}\qquad (n\ge L).$$
Associated to such a recurrence is a notion of legal decomposition: every positive integer is written as a sum $\sum a_i H_i$ where the digit string $(a_i)$ obeys a prescribed lexicographic rule generalising Zeckendorf's rule for the Fibonacci case ($L=2$, $c_1=c_2=1$).

(a) Investigate generalised Zeckendorf-type decomposition theories in which the legality rule is relaxed so that some positive integers admit multiple legal decompositions, and theories in which some positive integers admit no legal decomposition. Describe how existence/uniqueness, the average number of summands, and Gaussian-type fluctuation results for the number of summands are modified in these regimes.

(b) For a positive integer $N$ chosen uniformly from $[H_n,H_{n+1})$ and a uniformly chosen pair of consecutive summands in the legal decomposition of $N$, let $P_n(k)$ denote the probability that the gap between their indices equals $k$. Determine, for an arbitrary positive linear recurrence with coefficients $(c_1,\dots,c_L)$, an explicit closed-form expression for the limiting gap distribution $P(k)=\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n(k)$ as a function of $(c_1,\dots,c_L)$, valid for all $k\ge 2$ (including $k\le L$, where the behaviour depends on which $c_i$ vanish).

(c) Determine the limiting distribution of the largest gap appearing in the legal decomposition of a uniformly random integer in $[H_n,H_{n+1})$, as a function of the coefficients $(c_1,\dots,c_L)$.

For positive linear recurrences, the limiting gap distribution has been shown to converge to geometric decay (with ratio given by the dominant root of the characteristic polynomial) for gaps of length larger than the recurrence length $L$, and individual gap measures and Gaussianity of summand counts have been established in several follow-up works (Beckwith–Bower–Gaudet–Insoft–Li–Miller–Tosteson 2014; Bower–Insoft–Li–Miller–Tosteson 2015; and subsequent papers including treatments of recurrences with zero coefficients up to 2026). However, fully explicit closed-form formulas for short gaps ($k\le L$) for arbitrary coefficient patterns, and a complete theory for legal rules that allow multiple representations or non-representable integers, are not available in full generality; only special cases (Fibonacci, far-difference, certain $f$-decompositions, recurrences with zero coefficients) are understood. The problem is thus partially solved.

Consider a non-relativistic interacting many-electron system described by the Hamiltonian
H = -\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\nabla_i^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{N} v(r_i) + \sum_{i<j} \frac{1}{|r_i - r_j|},
where v: R^3 -> R is a (Coulombic) external one-body potential representing the electron–nuclear attraction. Let Ψ_gs denote a normalized ground-state wave function of H (assumed to exist), with ground-state energy E_gs = ⟨Ψ_gs, H Ψ_gs⟩, and let
ρ(r) = N ∫ |Ψ_gs(r, r_2, …, r_N)|^2 dr_2 ⋯ dr_N
be the associated ground-state one-electron density.

Question: Does there exist an explicit closed-form expression (i.e., a known explicit functional, built from elementary operations, integrals, and standard analytic functions, without reference to the underlying many-body wave function or to an implicit variational/constrained-search procedure) F[ρ, v] such that
E_gs = F[ρ, v]
holds for every such interacting many-electron system? Equivalently, is there a closed-form formula expressing E_gs directly in terms of the pair (ρ, v)?

No closed-form expression for the universal Hohenberg–Kohn functional or for the ground-state energy as an explicit closed form in (ρ, v) is known for interacting electron systems. For an infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in the $d$-dimensional unit cube $[0,1)^d$, the star discrepancy of its first $N$ terms is
$$D_N^*(x) \;=\; \sup_{B} \left| \frac{\#\{1 \le n \le N : x_n \in B\}}{N} - \mathrm{vol}(B) \right|,$$
where the supremum is taken over all axis-aligned boxes $B = \prod_{i=1}^{d}[0,a_i)$ with $a_i \in [0,1]$.

Let
$$\mathcal{D}_d(N) \;=\; \inf_{(x_n) \subset [0,1)^d} N \cdot D_N^*(x),$$
where the infimum is over all infinite sequences in $[0,1)^d$. Determine the exact asymptotic order, as $N \to \infty$, of the largest function $\varphi_d(N)$ such that
$$N \cdot D_N^*(x) \;\ge\; c_d \, \varphi_d(N) \quad \text{infinitely often}$$
holds for every infinite sequence $(x_n) \subset [0,1)^d$, with a constant $c_d > 0$ depending only on $d$.

Equivalently, find the correct order of the best general lower bound for the discrepancy that is valid for every infinite sequence in $[0,1)^d$ when $d \ge 2$. (The conjectured order is $(\log N)^d / N$.)

A solar filament (also called a prominence when seen at the limb) is a structure of relatively cool, dense plasma suspended in the solar corona and supported against gravity by a magnetic flux rope: a coherent bundle of magnetic field lines that wind helically around a common axis, typically containing magnetic dips in which dense plasma can accumulate. Two competing scenarios have been proposed for how the supporting flux rope comes into existence above the photosphere (the visible solar surface):

(L) Levitation scenario: a pre-existing, twisted magnetic flux rope is bodily transported upward through the photosphere from below, emerging as an already coherent helical structure into the chromosphere and corona.

(R) Reconnection scenario: no coherent flux rope crosses the photosphere; instead, the coronal flux rope is built in situ above the photosphere through a sequence of magnetic reconnection events between sheared, initially non-twisted (or weakly twisted) magnetic field lines belonging to a bipolar arcade, which progressively reconnect to form long, helical field lines wrapping around a common axis.

Determine which of these two mechanisms is responsible for the formation of the magnetic flux rope associated with a solar filament: is the flux rope lifted up through the photosphere by a levitation process, or is it instead created above the photosphere by successive magnetic reconnections between field lines? In particular, decide whether one mechanism operates universally, or whether different filaments (e.g. quiescent versus active-region filaments) form by different mechanisms, and characterize the observational signatures that would distinguish the two cases.

A solar prominence is a cool, dense plasma structure suspended in the hot solar corona by magnetic fields. High-resolution observations frequently reveal dark "bubbles" beneath the prominence, with "rising plumes" of dark material ascending through the prominence body. Three competing physical explanations have been proposed for these features:

(A) The bubbles are filled with hot, low-density coronal plasma that gradually condenses, producing buoyantly rising plumes that subsequently fill the overlying cavity with prominence plasma before condensation.

(B) The dark rising structures arise from a thermal instability acting in the prominence-corona transition region, in which radiative cooling produces runaway condensations whose dynamics generate the observed plumes.

(C) The bubbles correspond to a magnetic separatrix surrounding a parasitic emerging bipolar flux region beneath the prominence; the bubbles and dark rising features are not distinct hot plasma at all, but rather optically thin "windows" through the prominence sheet through which one sees the background corona, with plumes generated by reconnection at the separator.

Determine, on the basis of the temperature, density, magnetic topology, and dynamical signatures inferred from coordinated multi-wavelength spectroscopic and imaging observations of prominence bubbles and plumes, which of mechanisms (A), (B), or (C) (or which combination thereof) is responsible for the observed bubbles and rising plumes in quiescent solar prominences.

Consider a three-dimensional thin junction body $\Omega_h \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ consisting of a thin plate of thickness $h>0$ glued to finitely many thin cylindrical rods of diameter $O(h)$, attached transversally to the plate. As $h \to 0$, the plate collapses to a two-dimensional domain $\omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ and the rods collapse to one-dimensional segments $\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_N$ meeting $\omega$ at points $P_1, \dots, P_N$, forming a hybrid skeleton of mixed limit dimension (parts of dimension 2 and parts of dimension 1).

On $\Omega_h$, consider the scalar Neumann problem for $-\Delta$ (or the corresponding spectral problem). The naive limit operator decouples into the two-dimensional Laplacian on $\omega$ and one-dimensional second-order operators on the segments $\gamma_j$, with no canonical way to transmit data between the 2D and 1D pieces at the junction points $P_j$.

Question: Can the theory of self-adjoint extensions of symmetric operators be used to construct, on the hybrid skeleton $\omega \cup \gamma_1 \cup \dots \cup \gamma_N$, a self-adjoint operator (obtained as a self-adjoint extension of the direct sum of the restrictions of the 2D Laplacian on $\omega$ to functions vanishing near $\{P_j\}$ and the 1D operators on $\gamma_j$ with vanishing endpoint conditions at $P_j$) that serves as an asymptotic model for the original boundary value problem on $\Omega_h$, in the sense that its spectrum and resolvent approximate those of the problem on $\Omega_h$ with controlled error as $h \to 0$? More generally, does the self-adjoint extension method apply to junctions of domains with different limit dimensions?

Consider a population of galaxies observed across a wide range of redshifts and host dark-matter halo masses. For each galaxy, suppose one has either a spectrum or a set of broadband photometric flux measurements across multiple wavelengths. Two key derived quantities of interest are: (i) the stellar mass M_*, defined as the total mass currently bound in stars within the galaxy; and (ii) the star formation rate (SFR), defined as the rate (in solar masses per year) at which new stellar mass is being produced by ongoing star formation. Standard estimation procedures fit the observed spectral energy distribution to template models built from assumed stellar population synthesis libraries, an assumed initial mass function, an assumed star formation history parameterization, an assumed dust attenuation law, and an assumed chemical enrichment history; M_* and SFR are then read off from the best-fit model.

Determine whether it is possible, in principle and in practice, to design inference techniques that meaningfully reduce the systematic uncertainties (arising from these modeling assumptions and from degeneracies among age, metallicity, and dust) in the recovered values of M_* and SFR across the full range of redshifts and halo masses, or whether these uncertainties instead represent a fundamental information-theoretic limit imposed by the available observables on how accurately M_* and SFR can be extracted and subsequently used to constrain theories of galaxy formation.

Consider the population of galaxies with stellar mass M_* < 10^9 M_⊙, where M_⊙ denotes one solar mass. This population includes two principal morphological classes: (i) dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSph), which are gas-poor and are observed to cluster preferentially as satellites around more massive host galaxies, and (ii) dwarf irregular galaxies (dIrr), whose cold-gas mass fraction f_gas = M_gas/(M_gas + M_*) ranges from nearly 0 to nearly 1, and which are typically found in relative isolation from massive hosts.

For a galaxy in this low-mass regime, define:
• its star formation history as the function SFR(t), giving the star formation rate as a function of cosmic time t since the Big Bang;
• its assembly history as the time-dependent build-up M_*(t) of its stellar mass, accounting for both in situ star formation and accretion of stars from merging subsystems.

Determine, for the full M_* < 10^9 M_⊙ population:
1. The functional form (or family of forms) of SFR(t) and M_*(t) characterizing dSph galaxies versus dIrr galaxies, including the dependence on environment (satellite vs. isolated) and on present-day gas fraction f_gas.
2. The physical mechanisms (e.g. cosmological gas accretion, supernova feedback, reionization-era UV heating, ram-pressure and tidal stripping in dense environments) that quantitatively reproduce the observed diversity of SFR(t) and f_gas across this mass range.
3. Whether dSph and dIrr galaxies belong to a single evolutionary sequence connected by environmental transformation, or constitute genuinely distinct formation channels.

Solar prominences (also called filaments when seen on the disk) are cool, dense plasma structures suspended in the much hotter and more tenuous solar corona, supported against gravity by magnetic fields above photospheric polarity inversion lines (lines separating regions of opposite line-of-sight magnetic polarity). A coronal cavity is an elongated, low-density region in the corona that often surrounds a prominence and is threaded by a flux-rope or arcade-like magnetic field consisting of long, curved magnetic flux tubes. One proposed formation mechanism — the thermal non-equilibrium / evaporation–condensation scenario — posits that localized heating concentrated near the footpoints of these coronal flux tubes drives chromospheric evaporation; the evaporated plasma accumulates near the tops of the tubes, becomes thermally unstable, and condenses into cool, dense material that constitutes the filament/prominence.

Determine whether this mechanism is the actual cause of filament formation: that is, do filaments form by condensation of coronal material along magnetic flux tubes inside coronal cavities? Specifically, identify under what magnetic and thermodynamic conditions (heating localization, flux-tube geometry, density and temperature regimes) thermal non-equilibrium produces condensations consistent in mass, lifetime, spatial distribution, and dynamics with observed prominences, and assess whether this condensation pathway accounts for the observed population of filaments as opposed to, or in combination with, alternative mechanisms such as direct injection of chromospheric plasma or levitation by emerging flux.

In the standard cosmological picture of structure formation, galaxies are hosted by dark matter halos. Define a 'central' galaxy as the galaxy located at the center of a dominant (most massive) dark matter halo, and define a 'satellite' galaxy as a galaxy residing in a gravitationally bound subhalo of a more massive host halo. Consider the partition of the galaxy population into these two classes (centrals vs. satellites) as a framework for analyzing galaxy evolution across diverse environments, including rich clusters, compact groups, Local-Group-like systems, isolated field galaxies, filaments, and voids.

Determine whether this central/satellite dichotomy constitutes an adequate framework for studying galaxy evolution. Specifically: (i) Can galaxies be reliably classified as centrals or satellites given observational tracers (e.g., stellar mass, halo membership inference, group finders), and what is the misclassification rate? In a solar prominence — a cool, dense plasma structure suspended in the hot solar corona — spectro-polarimetric measurements based on the Hanle and Zeeman effects (as obtained, for example, with instruments such as THEMIS) statistically indicate that the magnetic field threading the prominence is predominantly horizontal, with typical strengths of order 5–15 G. At the same time, high-resolution EUV and optical imagery (such as that produced by SDO/AIA and Hinode/SOT) reveals fine plasma structures (threads, barbs, "tornado"-like columns) that visually appear predominantly vertical, and Doppler observations show counter-streaming flows along these apparently vertical features.

Formulate and justify a magnetohydrostatic and/or magnetohydrodynamic model of a quiescent prominence that simultaneously accounts for the following observational constraints:

1. The large-scale magnetic field vector is mainly horizontal (parallel to the photosphere and to the underlying polarity inversion line).
2. The visible cool plasma is organised into thin, apparently vertical filamentary structures whose lengths greatly exceed their widths.
3. The plasma supports persistent vertical (upward and downward) mass flows along these apparently vertical features.
4. The configuration is consistent with quasi-static support of the dense prominence material against solar gravity by Lorentz forces.

Specifically, determine whether the apparent vertical fine structure can be reconciled with a globally horizontal field — for example via dipped, sagging, or bowed field lines that locally tilt and host plasma condensations, via line-of-sight projection effects, or via an additional small-scale vertical field component superposed on a dominant horizontal field — and identify which class of models (if any) is consistent with all of the constraints (1)–(4).

The apparent conflict has been partially addressed but is not fully resolved. Magnetostatic models with horizontal field lines that locally dip or sag to support thin vertical plasma filaments have been proposed, and analyses (e.g., Schmieder et al. 2014) suggest a weak (5–15 G) horizontal large-scale field plus a stochastic small-scale component. Studies of "atypical" prominence structures (bubbles, tornadoes, eruptions) find that field orientation can vary by structure type. Living Reviews in Solar Physics (2018) still discusses the puzzle of vertical flows in nominally horizontal-field prominences as an open theoretical issue, indicating only partial resolution.

Consider satellite galaxies evolving inside the gravitational potential of a more massive host halo. The following physical mechanisms are believed to act on such satellites: (i) ram-pressure stripping, the removal of cold and hot interstellar gas by the hydrodynamic pressure of the hot intracluster/intragroup medium; (ii) galaxy harassment, cumulative high-speed gravitational encounters with neighboring galaxies and the host potential; (iii) strangulation (also called starvation), the cutoff of fresh cold-gas accretion onto the satellite once it enters the host halo; (iv) tidal stripping, the removal of stars, gas, and dark matter by the tidal field of the host; and (v) assembly bias, the dependence of galaxy properties on the large-scale assembly history of the host halo at fixed halo mass.

Let S denote the population of satellite galaxies parameterized by stellar mass M_*, host halo mass M_h, halo-centric radius r, infall time t_inf, and orbital parameters. Let O denote the set of observed statistical trends of satellites, including the quenched fraction f_q(M_*, M_h, r), the dependence of star-formation rate, gas content, morphology, and metallicity on environment, and any residual dependence on large-scale environment at fixed (M_*, M_h).

Provide a quantitative framework that:

1. Models each of the five mechanisms (ram-pressure stripping, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, assembly bias) as an operator acting on a satellite's state vector, including their mutual interactions, back-reactions (e.g., stripping altering subsequent ram-pressure efficiency), and self-regulating feedback loops.

2. Reproduces the observed trends O across the relevant ranges of M_*, M_h, r, and cosmic time.

3. Decomposes the contribution of each mechanism so that one can quantify, for any given observable in O, the fractional relative role of ram-pressure stripping, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, and assembly bias.

Determine such a framework, or prove obstructions to its existence given current observational constraints.

Consider a solar prominence modeled as a magnetized plasma structure embedded in the solar corona. Spectro-polarimetric observations of such prominences yield Stokes parameter profiles (I, Q, U, V) of suitable spectral lines (e.g. He I D3, Mg II, Na I D), which can be inverted using the Hanle and Zeeman effects to infer the local magnetic field vector. Two distinct magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) descriptions are used to describe the prominence plasma:

(1) A large-scale, predominantly horizontal magnetic configuration, in which cool dense plasma is supported against gravity by the magnetic tension/pressure of a nearly horizontal field (as in flux-rope or sheared-arcade equilibria, with field strengths of order 5–30 G).

(2) A small-scale turbulent MHD regime, in which the magnetic field has a substantial fluctuating, isotropic-like component associated with unresolved dynamics, consistent with depolarization signatures and observed plasma motions.

Formulate a single self-consistent MHD model of a quiescent prominence — specifying the equilibrium (or quasi-equilibrium) equations, the decomposition B = B_0(x) + δB(x,t) into a mean horizontal component and a turbulent fluctuation, the statistical closure for δB, and the coupling between the two — that simultaneously accommodates both descriptions. Within this combined framework, derive the forward-modeled Stokes profiles (I, Q, U, V) as functionals of B_0 and the statistics of δB (incorporating the appropriate Hanle and Zeeman radiative transfer for an optically thin or moderately thick prominence slab), and provide an interpretation/inversion scheme that consistently extracts the mean horizontal field and the turbulent magnetic component from observed Stokes profiles.

In the standard hierarchical structure-formation framework, galaxies form at the centers of dark-matter halos and accrete gas to fuel star formation. When a halo containing a galaxy falls into a larger host halo, the galaxy becomes a "satellite" of the host's central galaxy. Observations indicate that:

(i) star-forming satellite galaxies have specific star-formation rates (sSFR ≡ SFR/M_*) statistically indistinguishable from those of central galaxies of the same stellar mass, implying that the transition from star-forming to passive must be rapid; and

(ii) the fraction of passive satellites at fixed stellar mass implies that satellites must continue forming stars at near-central rates for several Gyr after accretion before quenching.

Standard semi-analytic prescriptions assume that upon accretion the hot circumgalactic gas reservoir of the satellite is either (a) stripped instantaneously, or (b) stripped on a halo dynamical-friction or ram-pressure timescale. Both prescriptions produce too many galaxies with intermediate sSFR (so-called "green-valley" satellites) and a satellite quenched fraction that rises too quickly with time-since-infall.

Problem: Construct a physical model of gas-stripping, cold-gas consumption, and possibly internal feedback that, when embedded in a cosmological halo merger tree with realistic infall and orbital statistics, simultaneously satisfies both of the following constraints:

(1) After infall, satellites maintain a sSFR distribution matching that of centrals of the same M_* for a delay time τ_delay of order several Gyr (with appropriate dependence on M_* and host halo mass);

(2) After τ_delay, the sSFR drops to passive values (sSFR ≲ 10^{-11} yr^{-1}) on a timescale τ_fade short enough that the predicted distribution of sSFR shows the observed bimodality, with a deficit of galaxies at intermediate sSFR.

Specify the functional forms of τ_delay(M_*, M_host, z) and τ_fade(M_*, M_host, z), and identify the physical mechanism (e.g., partial hot-gas retention, delayed ram-pressure stripping, gradual starvation followed by ram-pressure stripping of the cold ISM, internal feedback in absence of accretion) that yields these timescales while remaining consistent with cosmological hydrodynamic simulations.

A "delayed-then-rapid" quenching paradigm has been developed and progressively refined since 2014. Empirical and simulation work (e.g., Oman et al. 2021, MNRAS 501, 5073) has measured delay times of ~3.5 Gyr in clusters and ~5.5 Gyr in groups between first pericenter passage and quenching, broadly matching observed sSFR bimodality but with substantial scatter. A 2025 study (arXiv:2503.15183) argues the quenching timescale is set primarily by ISM depletion via star formation and stellar/AGN feedback in the absence of fresh accretion (starvation), with ram-pressure stripping playing a modulating rather than driving role. The qualitative scenario is thus partially established, but a fully predictive model with calibrated τ_delay and τ_fade across mass and host-mass remains an active area of research.

The systematic uncertainty budget on SED-derived galaxy stellar masses remains an active and unresolved area. Comparison studies (e.g. Conroy 2013 review; Pacifici et al. 2023; Lower et al. 2020) continue to find model-dependent offsets of factors ~1.5–3 (~0.2–0.5 dex), with the TP-AGB treatment, IMF, SFH parametrization, and dust attenuation laws still debated, and additional physics (binaries via BPASS, rotation, non-universal IMFs) under ongoing investigation. No consensus quantification of the full systematic error including "unknown unknowns" exists.

Consider theoretical models of galaxy formation and evolution (e.g., semi-analytic models and hydrodynamical simulations) that track the assembly history of galaxies inside dark-matter halos, the cooling of gas, star formation, stellar feedback, and the production and recycling of metals. Existing implementations typically parametrize star formation in terms of total cold gas, treat galaxies as one-zone systems, and follow only bulk metallicity.

Develop a framework that extends such models so that they can be quantitatively confronted with upcoming observational datasets that provide (i) spatially resolved optical/IR spectroscopy of galaxies (resolved kinematics, ages, and metallicities on sub-galactic scales), (ii) resolved measurements of atomic hydrogen (HI) and molecular gas (H2/CO) content. Specifically, address the following:

1. Atomic-to-molecular transition. Formulate an explicit prescription, derivable from the local interstellar medium properties (gas surface density, metallicity, radiation field, dust shielding), that partitions cold gas into atomic and molecular components in each modeled resolution element, and tie the star-formation rate to the molecular component. Demonstrate that the prescription reproduces simultaneously the observed HI and H2 mass functions, the H2/HI ratio as a function of stellar mass, and the Kennicutt–Schmidt relation across redshift.

2. Spatially resolved galaxy properties. Extend galaxy models from one-zone descriptions to spatially resolved (e.g., axisymmetric multi-ring or full 3D) descriptions, evolving radial profiles of gas surface density, stellar mass, star-formation rate, and metallicity. Identify the minimal set of physical ingredients (gas inflow with prescribed angular momentum, radial transport, feedback-driven outflows, satellite accretion) needed to reproduce, jointly, observed radial profiles of stellar age, metallicity, and star-formation rate in galaxies of different masses and morphologies.

3. Detailed chemical evolution. Replace single-metallicity tracking with explicit, time-resolved nucleosynthetic yields for individual elements (at minimum H, He, C, N, O, Mg, Si, Fe), incorporating delay-time distributions for Type Ia supernovae, mass- and metallicity-dependent yields from core-collapse supernovae and AGB stars, and the impact of finite stellar lifetimes (no instantaneous-recycling approximation). Use abundance-ratio diagnostics (e.g., [α/Fe] vs. [Fe/H], [N/O] vs. [O/H]) of stars and gas as primary constraints, and quantify the resulting constraints on star-formation timescales, IMF, and feedback efficiencies.

Provide such an integrated extension and demonstrate, through comparison with current and forthcoming resolved spectroscopic surveys and HI/H2 surveys, that it yields a self-consistent description of galaxy evolution under these combined constraints.

Consider three independent methods used to infer the star formation history (SFH) of a low-mass galaxy (stellar mass roughly $10^7$–$10^9 \, M_\odot$):

1. Spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting, in which a galaxy's broadband photometry is fit by stellar population synthesis models that yield a parametric or non-parametric SFH and a mean stellar age.
2. Main-sequence integration, in which the observed star-formation-rate vs. stellar-mass relation at successive redshifts is integrated backward in time to reconstruct the cumulative stellar mass growth of a galaxy of given present-day mass.
3. Color–magnitude diagram (CMD) analysis of resolved stellar populations, in which the distribution of stars in the CMD is decomposed into coeval stellar populations to recover the cumulative fraction of stellar mass formed as a function of lookback time.

Empirically, for dwarf galaxies the CMD method indicates that a large fraction of the stellar mass was formed at redshifts $z > 1$, while extrapolations of SED-fitting and main-sequence-integration methods yield substantially younger mean ages and later assembly times.

Quantify and reconcile this discrepancy. Specifically:
(a) Identify the dominant sources of systematic age uncertainty in each of the three methods (e.g., age–metallicity–dust degeneracies in SED fitting, scatter and selection effects in the main sequence, isochrone and IMF assumptions in CMD fitting).
(b) Determine how these uncertainties propagate to the inferred cumulative SFH at lookback times corresponding to $z>1$.
(c) Propose a methodological framework (data, priors, modeling choices) under which the three SFH estimators become statistically consistent for galaxies in this mass range.

Consider a galaxy system analogous to the Local Group, in which two comparably massive galaxies (call them G1 and G2, playing the roles of the Milky Way and M31) each host their own bound population of smaller satellite galaxies, while G1 and G2 are themselves gravitationally interacting and will eventually merge. Suppose a group-finding algorithm enforces a strict single central / satellite hierarchy on this system, designating exactly one of {G1, G2} as the unique central halo and reclassifying the other together with all its satellites as satellites of that central.

(a) Provide a quantitative characterization of the physical and statistical information about the system that is destroyed by such a forced single-central assignment, relative to the true two-center hierarchy. Examples of information potentially lost include: the multiplicity and mass function of distinct host halos, the kinematic association of each satellite with its true host, the merger history and future dynamical evolution of the subsystems, the radial profiles and quenching environments experienced by satellites, and the conditional luminosity / stellar mass functions of secondary hosts.

(b) Define one or more measurable indicators (e.g. information-theoretic divergences between the true and assigned satellite-host probability distributions, or differences in summary statistics such as satellite kinematics, quenched fractions, and host stellar-mass functions) by which this lost information can be quantified for an ensemble of Local-Group-like systems drawn from a cosmological simulation or mock catalog.

(c) Determine which components of the lost information are the most consequential for inferring the physics of galaxy evolution (star formation histories, quenching, environmental processing, satellite accretion histories) in Local-Group-like systems, and quantify their impact.

In the standard cosmological framework, dark matter halos host a single "central" galaxy at their center together with a population of "satellite" galaxies. Galaxies are commonly classified by their star formation properties (e.g., star-forming vs. quiescent, or late-type vs. early-type morphology). Empirically, one observes the phenomenon known as galaxy conformity: at fixed halo mass, halos whose central galaxy is star-forming (late-type) host a significantly higher fraction of late-type, star-forming satellites than halos whose central galaxy is quiescent (early-type). This correlation has been reported both within single halos (one-halo conformity, on scales comparable to the virial radius) and between neighboring halos (two-halo conformity, extending well beyond the virial radius, in some cases out to several Mpc).

Identify and characterize the physical mechanism (or combination of mechanisms) responsible for galaxy conformity. Specifically, determine why the star-formation state of a central galaxy correlates with the star-formation states of its satellite galaxies and of galaxies in neighboring halos, including the dependence of this effect on halo mass, central stellar mass, environment, and spatial scale, and decide to what extent conformity reflects (i) correlated assembly histories of dark matter halos ("assembly bias"), (ii) large-scale environmental pre-heating or other intergalactic-medium effects, (iii) baryonic feedback processes coupling centrals to their surroundings, or (iv) systematic effects in the identification of central galaxies.

The origin of galaxy conformity remains an active area of research without a definitive consensus. Proposed explanations include halo assembly bias, large-scale pre-heating of intergalactic gas (especially for low-mass, gas-poor centrals), and feedback processes operating near the virial scale, while some studies have argued that two-halo conformity signals are partly contaminated by central/satellite misclassification. No single mechanism has been broadly accepted as fully explaining the observed effect across all mass and scale regimes.

Galaxy groups are gravitationally bound associations of galaxies whose typical one-dimensional velocity dispersions lie roughly in the range 100–500 km/s, intermediate between isolated field galaxies and massive clusters; they are believed to be the most common environment in which galaxies reside. Several physical processes are thought to transform satellite galaxies inside such groups, including: (i) ram-pressure stripping, the removal of a galaxy's interstellar gas by the hydrodynamic pressure of the surrounding hot intragroup medium as the galaxy moves through it; (ii) tidal effects, the gravitational stripping and heating of a satellite's stars, gas, and dark matter by the host group potential and by encounters with other group members; and (iii) the dynamical evolution of the gaseous components of satellites, including starvation/strangulation through removal of an extended hot gas reservoir, turbulent viscous stripping, and thermal evaporation. In semi-analytic and hydrodynamical models of galaxy formation, satellite galaxies are commonly found to be too red, too gas-poor, and too passive compared with observations — the so-called "satellite problem".

Quantify, at velocity dispersions characteristic of galaxy groups (rather than massive clusters), the relative importance of ram-pressure stripping, tidal effects, and gaseous-component evolution in shaping the star formation, gas content, and morphology of satellite galaxies. Determine to what degree the discrepancies between predicted and observed properties of satellite galaxies in current galaxy formation models can be attributed to inadequate modeling of these environmental processes in the group regime.

Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for an unknown velocity field $v:\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p:\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$:
\[
\partial_t v + (v\cdot\nabla)v = -\nabla p + \nu \Delta v,\qquad \nabla\cdot v = 0,
\]
with viscosity $\nu>0$ and smooth, divergence-free initial data $v(\cdot,0)=v_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ (decaying suitably at infinity, e.g., Schwartz class).

Determine the most general conditions on the initial datum $v_0$ that guarantee existence of a unique smooth solution $v\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty);\mathbb{R}^3)$ for all $t\ge 0$, as opposed to the development of a finite-time singularity.

Pose the analogous question for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations (the case $\nu=0$): identify the most general conditions on a smooth divergence-free initial datum $v_0$ that ensure a globally smooth solution exists on $\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)$.

The global regularity problem for the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations remains a famous open Clay Millennium Prize Problem. The corresponding question for the 3D incompressible Euler equations is also widely regarded as open, although significant recent progress on finite-time singularity formation for Euler (e.g., Elgindi's work on $C^{1,\alpha}$ data, and Chen–Hou's computer-assisted proof of singularity for axisymmetric Euler with boundary) shows that singularities can form from non-smooth or boundary data; the smooth, no-boundary case remains unresolved.

In the standard multi-stage description of an ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collision, the evolution of the produced matter is decomposed into successive stages: (i) a pre-equilibrium stage immediately following the collision of the two highly Lorentz-contracted nuclei, in which the produced partonic system is far from local thermal equilibrium; (ii) a relativistic hydrodynamic stage, during which the matter is modeled as a relativistic fluid governed by the conservation laws ∂_μ T^{μν} = 0 (and conserved-charge currents ∂_μ J^μ = 0) supplemented by an equation of state and, in viscous hydrodynamics, by constitutive/relaxation equations for dissipative currents; (iii) a hadronic freeze-out stage, in which the fluid converts to free-streaming hadrons that are eventually detected.

To run the hydrodynamic stage (ii) one must prescribe, on some initial Cauchy hypersurface Σ_0 (typically a constant proper-time surface τ = τ_0), the full set of fluid fields: the energy density ε(x), the flow four-velocity u^μ(x) (with u^μ u_μ = 1), any conserved-charge densities, and—if dissipative hydrodynamics is used—the initial values of the shear-stress tensor π^{μν}(x), bulk viscous pressure Π(x), and any diffusion currents. Direct experimental access to these fields is impossible: only the asymptotic hadrons produced after stage (iii) are measured.

Problem. Provide a principled, predictive prescription that determines, from the properties of the two incoming nuclei and the collision kinematics alone, the most plausible initial data {ε(x), u^μ(x), π^{μν}(x), Π(x), …} on the hypersurface Σ_0 at which relativistic hydrodynamics begins. In the standard multi-stage description of an ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collision, the evolution of the produced matter is decomposed into successive stages: (i) a pre-equilibrium stage immediately following the collision of the two highly Lorentz-contracted nuclei, in which the produced partonic system is far from local thermal equilibrium; (ii) a relativistic hydrodynamic stage, during which the matter is modeled as a relativistic fluid governed by the conservation laws ∂_μ T^{μν} = 0 (and conserved-charge currents ∂_μ J^μ = 0) supplemented by an equation of state and, in viscous hydrodynamics, by constitutive/relaxation equations for dissipative currents; (iii) a hadronic freeze-out stage, in which the fluid converts to free-streaming hadrons that are eventually detected.

To run the hydrodynamic stage (ii) one must prescribe, on some initial Cauchy hypersurface Σ_0 (typically a constant proper-time surface τ = τ_0), the full set of fluid fields: the energy density ε(x), the flow four-velocity u^μ(x) (with u^μ u_μ = 1), any conserved-charge densities, and—if dissipative hydrodynamics is used—the initial values of the shear-stress tensor π^{μν}(x), bulk viscous pressure Π(x), and any diffusion currents. Direct experimental access to these fields is impossible: only the asymptotic hadrons produced after stage (iii) are measured.

Problem. Provide a principled, predictive prescription that determines, from the properties of the two incoming nuclei and the collision kinematics alone, the most plausible initial data {ε(x), u^μ(x), π^{μν}(x), Π(x), …} on the hypersurface Σ_0 at which relativistic hydrodynamics begins. The prescription should specify the initialization time τ_0, the spatial profiles of all required fluid fields, and their dissipative components, in a way that is consistent with the underlying microscopic (quantum chromodynamic) dynamics of the pre-equilibrium stage and that yields, after hydrodynamic evolution and freeze-out, agreement with the measured hadronic observables.

Recent reviews of relativistic hydrodynamics in heavy-ion collisions (e.g., Jaiswal–Roy 2016 and subsequent literature) explicitly identify the specification of initial conditions for the hydrodynamic stage as a major source of uncertainty, with several competing models (Glauber, KLN, IP-Glasma, EKRT, dynamical initialization schemes) but no first-principles consensus. Consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for an unknown velocity field $u:\mathbb{R}^3	imes[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p:\mathbb{R}^3	imes[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}$:

$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\,\Delta u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,\qquad u(\cdot,0)=u_0,$$

where $\nu>0$ is the kinematic viscosity and $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ is divergence-free with appropriate decay at infinity (e.g., Schwartz class).

A smooth solution is said to blow up in finite time if there exists $T^*<\infty$ such that $\limsup_{t\to T^{*-}}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3)}=\infty$, and is said to be globally regular if it extends to a smooth solution on $\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)$.

Problem: Provide an explicit construction (i.e., produce concrete smooth, divergence-free, decaying initial data $u_0$ together with an explicit, verifiable description of the resulting solution) of either

(a) a solution that blows up in finite time, or
(b) a solution corresponding to large, generic initial data that remains globally regular,

in such a way that the question of whether finite-time singularities can form from smooth, finite-energy initial data is settled by direct exhibition rather than only through a priori estimates or indirect arguments.
