Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision modeled as a multi-stage process: (i) a pre-hydrodynamic stage immediately after the collision, during which the produced matter is generally far from equilibrium, followed by (ii) a hydrodynamic stage in which the evolution of the medium is described by relativistic fluid dynamics. The applicability of relativistic hydrodynamics requires the existence of local thermodynamic equilibrium, which in kinetic terms demands that the mean free path λ_mfp of the elementary constituents (quarks and gluons, or hadrons) be much smaller than a characteristic spatial scale L of the system, i.e. λ_mfp ≪ L (the Knudsen number Kn = λ_mfp/L is small).

Determine whether the pre-hydrodynamic stage (i) of a relativistic heavy-ion collision can dynamically generate a state of matter that, by the onset of stage (ii), satisfies the condition λ_mfp ≪ L characteristic of local thermodynamic equilibrium. Equivalently, show whether the microscopic interactions during the pre-equilibrium stage are frequent enough to drive the system to local thermodynamic equilibrium on the timescale at which hydrodynamics is conventionally applied, or exhibit an obstruction preventing such equilibration.

Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision modeled as a relativistic fluid. Assume that at an initial proper time $t_0$ the system is specified by initial conditions consisting of: (a) the three spatial components of a fluid velocity field $u^i(\mathbf{x}, t_0)$, (b) an energy density $\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, t_0)$, and (c) an entropy density $s(\mathbf{x}, t_0)$, all defined on a spatial slice. The subsequent dynamics is governed by the relativistic hydrodynamic equations $\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$ together with a prescribed equation of state $p = p(\varepsilon, s)$, evolved until a freeze-out hypersurface on which the fluid is converted into hadrons whose momenta and yields constitute the final-state observables (e.g. single-particle spectra and azimuthal Fourier coefficients $v_n$).

Decompose the initial transverse profile of the energy density into a "geometric" part (its shape, characterized for instance by the eccentricity moments $\varepsilon_n e^{i n \Phi_n} = -\int r^n e^{i n \phi} \varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, t_0)\, d^2x \,\big/\, \int r^n \varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, t_0)\, d^2x$) and a "non-geometric" part (overall normalization, microscopic equation-of-state-dependent details, fluctuations of the velocity field, etc.).

Establish, in a quantitative and mathematically rigorous form, the following:

1. To what extent are the final-state hadronic observables determined predominantly by the geometric component of the initial conditions, as opposed to the non-geometric components, after the full hydrodynamic evolution and freeze-out?

2. Provide an explicit reconstruction map (or prove an inversion theorem) that, given the final-state hadronic observables on the freeze-out hypersurface, recovers the geometric component of the initial conditions at time $t_0$, and characterize its stability and uniqueness.

Consider a spacetime modeled by a 4-dimensional smooth manifold M endowed with a Lorentzian metric g of signature (-,+,+,+) and an affine connection Γ on the tangent bundle TM. Two formulations of a gravitational theory on (M, g, Γ) are distinguished:

(i) Purely metric formulation: Γ is identified a priori with the Levi-Civita connection of g, i.e. the unique torsion-free connection satisfying ∇g = 0. The dynamical variable is g alone.

(ii) Palatini (metric-affine) formulation: g and Γ are treated as independent dynamical variables, with Γ a general (possibly non-metric, possibly with torsion) affine connection that need not coincide with the Levi-Civita connection of g. The relation between Γ and g is then a consequence of the field equations rather than an a priori identification.

The Einstein Equivalence Principle (EEP) asserts that (a) the trajectory of a freely falling structureless test body is independent of its internal composition (Weak Equivalence Principle / Universality of Free Fall), (b) the outcome of any local non-gravitational experiment is independent of the velocity of the freely falling reference frame in which it is performed (Local Lorentz Invariance), and (c) the outcome of any local non-gravitational experiment is independent of where and when in the universe it is performed (Local Position Invariance).

Question: Determine whether arbitrarily precise experimental tests of the Einstein Equivalence Principle can, in principle, discriminate between formulations (i) and (ii). Concretely, identify observable signatures (in the dynamics of test particles, in atomic-clock comparisons, or in other local non-gravitational experiments) by which a non-Levi-Civita independent connection Γ in formulation (ii) would produce deviations from the EEP that are absent in formulation (i), and quantify the precision required to detect or rule out such deviations; or, alternatively, prove that no EEP-based experiment can distinguish the two formulations.

Consider a modified theory of gravity formulated on a four-dimensional spacetime (M, g) with a scalar degree of freedom φ that couples to gravity. Two equivalent mathematical formulations of such a theory can be obtained by a conformal rescaling of the metric, g̃_{μν} = Ω²(φ) g_{μν}:

(a) The Jordan frame, in which the Einstein field equations are modified (the gravitational Lagrangian contains a non-trivial coupling, e.g. f(φ) R, or a function f(R) of the Ricci scalar) and matter fields are minimally coupled to the metric g_{μν}.

(b) The Einstein frame, obtained by the conformal transformation above (with a suitable redefinition of φ), in which the gravitational sector takes the standard Einstein–Hilbert form R̃ and matter fields acquire a non-minimal coupling to the rescaled metric g̃_{μν} through φ-dependent factors.

The two frames are related by a field redefinition (a conformal transformation of the metric together with a rescaling of the scalar) and are therefore mathematically equivalent at the level of the action.

Question: Determine whether the choice of conformal frame (Jordan vs. Einstein) carries genuine physical significance. Specifically, is there an observable or operationally well-defined physical quantity — at the classical level, at the semiclassical level, or at the quantum level — that distinguishes predictions made in the Jordan frame from those made in the Einstein frame, or are the two frames physically equivalent in every operational sense (so that the passage between them is merely a change of variables)?

Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) predicts that strongly interacting matter, composed of quarks and gluons, can exist in distinct thermodynamic phases parameterized by temperature T and baryon chemical potential μ_B. Two physically motivated regions of the (T, μ_B) phase diagram are: (i) the high-temperature, near-zero baryon chemical potential regime (T large, μ_B ≈ 0), believed to describe the matter present a few microseconds after the Big Bang; and (ii) the low-temperature, high baryon chemical potential regime (T small, μ_B large), believed to describe the matter in the cores of neutron stars.

Relativistic and ultra-relativistic collisions of heavy nuclei produce transient regions of strongly interacting matter at high energy densities and temperatures. Determine to what extent QCD matter states corresponding to regimes (i) and (ii) above can actually be created, controlled, and quantitatively characterized in terrestrial heavy-ion collision experiments. In particular, identify what observable signatures (collective flow, thermal radiation, particle yields, fluctuations, jet modification, etc.) and what range of collision energies and system sizes give experimental access to these regimes, and clarify which thermodynamic and transport properties of QCD matter near regime (i) and regime (ii) can be inferred from such measurements.

Consider proton–proton collisions at very high center-of-mass energies (LHC-scale and beyond) restricted to events with low impact parameter and high charged-particle multiplicity. Model the partonic activity in such events as a superposition of multiparton interactions accompanied by subsequent rescatterings of the produced partons. Assume that the resulting deconfined-phase constituents have a mean free path of order λ ≈ 0.2–0.3 fm, and that the transverse extent of the interaction region is of order the proton radius R ≈ 0.8 fm, so that R/λ is only a few.

Determine whether the following three propositions hold simultaneously in this regime:

(a) The cumulative energy transferred by the multiparton interactions and rescatterings into a volume of proton size is sufficient to reach (or exceed) the QCD deconfinement energy density, producing a close-to-equilibrium deconfined initial state.

(b) Despite the smallness of the system (only a few mean free paths across), the constituents of this initial state thermalize on a timescale shorter than the system's lifetime.

(c) The thermalized, proton-sized fireball thereafter undergoes a hydrodynamic / collective expansion describable by relativistic fluid dynamics, with collective observables (radial flow, anisotropic flow harmonics, strangeness enhancement, etc.) analogous to those seen in heavy-ion collisions.

Provide a rigorous theoretical or phenomenological resolution of (a)–(c): either establish all three within a controlled framework, or identify which fail and characterize the regime of validity.

Consider a four-dimensional smooth spacetime manifold $M$ equipped with two a priori independent geometric structures:

(i) a Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, which determines the causal structure of $M$ (in particular, the null cones along which photons propagate); and

(ii) a torsion-free linear connection $\Gamma$ on $TM$, whose autoparallel curves are postulated to describe the worldlines of freely falling test particles (free fall).

Impose only the following physical compatibility requirement: photon worldlines, which are null geodesics of $g$, must also be (unparametrized) autoparallels of $\Gamma$, i.e. the null geodesics of $g$ coincide as point sets with null autoparallels of $\Gamma$.

Question: Does this compatibility requirement, together with the standard principles of a relativistic theory of gravitation, force $\Gamma$ to be the Levi-Civita connection of $g$? Equivalently, can one consistently formulate a relativistic theory of gravitation on $(M,g,\Gamma)$ in which $\Gamma$ is a genuinely independent connection (not equal to the Levi-Civita connection of $g$), so that the geodesic structure (free fall) and the causal structure (light propagation) of spacetime are physically disentangled?

In high-energy proton-proton collisions, each event produces a set of charged particles whose transverse momenta $\vec{p}_{T,i}$ in the plane transverse to the beam axis can be measured. For an event with $N$ charged particles, define the following global event-shape observables:

(i) The transverse sphericity tensor $S^{xy}_{\alpha\beta} = \frac{\sum_i p_{T,i,\alpha}\,p_{T,i,\beta}}{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}|^2}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq 0$, and the transverse sphericity $S_T = 2\lambda_2/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2) \in [0,1]$, where $S_T \to 1$ corresponds to azimuthal isotropy and $S_T \to 0$ corresponds to a pencil-like event.

(ii) The transverse thrust $T_\perp = \max_{\hat{n}_T} \frac{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}\cdot\hat{n}_T|}{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}|}$, maximized over unit vectors $\hat{n}_T$ in the transverse plane.

(iii) The Fox–Wolfram moments $H_\ell = \sum_{i,j} \frac{|\vec p_i||\vec p_j|}{E_{vis}^2}\, P_\ell(\cos\theta_{ij})$ for $\ell=0,1,2,\dots$, where $P_\ell$ are Legendre polynomials and $\theta_{ij}$ is the angle between particle momenta.

(iv) The directivity $D = \frac{|\sum_i \vec{p}_{T,i}|}{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}|} \in [0,1]$.

Let $N_{ch}$ denote the charged-particle multiplicity of an event. Consider applying a two-dimensional event-selection cut of the form $\{N_{ch}\geq N_{\min}\}\cap\{X \in I\}$, where $X$ is one of the above event-shape variables and $I$ is an interval chosen to enforce near azimuthal isotropy.

Question: Does there exist such a two-dimensional selection $(N_{ch},X)$ that, at any fixed value of $N_{ch}$, reliably isolates a sub-ensemble of events whose single-particle azimuthal distribution $dN/d\varphi$ is nearly uniform (soft, isotropic), as opposed to events dominated by hard back-to-back jet structures, given that the marginal distributions of $X$ remain broad even at the largest accessible multiplicities?

The Equivalence Principle (EP) asserts the local indistinguishability between the effects of a uniform gravitational field and those of a uniformly accelerated reference frame; equivalently, in its weak form, it states that the inertial mass and the gravitational (passive and active) mass of any test body coincide, so that the trajectories of freely falling bodies in a given gravitational field are independent of their internal composition and mass.

Address the following questions concerning the status of this principle when gravity is combined with quantum theory:

(a) Is the Equivalence Principle universally valid in nature, or can it fail in regimes where gravitational and quantum effects are simultaneously relevant?

(b) Suppose that the Equivalence Principle holds exactly at the classical level (i.e., for classical point particles and classical fields on a classical spacetime). Can it nevertheless be violated at the quantum level, for example through the dynamics of quantum test particles, quantum fields, or quantum superpositions of mass/energy states propagating in a gravitational background?

(c) Is the Equivalence Principle, formulated in a precise operational way, logically consistent with the principles of Quantum Mechanics (linearity, superposition, the standard formalism of observables and states) when one attempts to incorporate gravitation alongside the other fundamental interactions in a unified quantum framework?

Provide a definitive resolution of (a)–(c), either by exhibiting a consistent formulation of the Equivalence Principle compatible with Quantum Mechanics in a unified theory, or by identifying an unavoidable mechanism by which the principle must be violated at the quantum level.

Consider the phase diagram of strongly interacting matter parameterized by temperature $T$ and baryon chemical potential $\mu_B$. Statistical-thermal model fits to hadron yield ratios measured in heavy-ion collisions at various energies populate a chemical-freeze-out curve in the $(T,\mu_B)$ plane. Along this curve, for $\mu_B \ll M_N$ (the nucleon mass) the thermodynamic degrees of freedom are dominated by mesons, while for larger $\mu_B$ baryonic degrees of freedom dominate. Define $(T_H,\mu_H)$ as the transitional point on this freeze-out curve where the baryonic contribution to the thermodynamics surpasses the mesonic contribution; statistical-model fits place it in the region $\mu_H \in [350,400]$ MeV, $T_H \in [150,160]$ MeV.

Independently, large-$N_c$ analyses of QCD predict a phase structure with three distinct regions — a confined hadronic phase, a deconfined quark–gluon plasma phase, and a quarkyonic phase (in which the pressure scales as $p\sim N_c$, intermediate between $p\sim N_c^0$ for a hadron gas and $p\sim N_c^2$ for the QGP) — that meet at a triple point in the $(T,\mu_B)$ plane. Extending this picture to the physical case $N_c=3$ yields a conjectured finite-$N_c$ triple point.

Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision in which two nuclei (possibly the heaviest available, e.g. Pb or Au) collide at ultra-relativistic energies, producing a small, spatially highly non-homogeneous, rapidly evolving strongly interacting system. After the initial impact the system passes through several stages (e.g. pre-equilibrium dynamics, a possibly thermalized quark–gluon plasma phase, hadronization, and a hadronic rescattering/freeze-out phase). The only experimentally accessible information consists of the momenta, identities, and correlations of the hadrons, leptons, and photons that reach detectors in the final state, together with electromagnetic radiation emitted during the evolution.

Develop a quantitative framework — including a set of final-state observables and an inversion procedure — that allows one to reconstruct, from these final-state particles and electromagnetic radiation alone, detailed information about the dynamics (equation of state, transport coefficients such as shear and bulk viscosity, thermalization time, expansion profile) and properties (temperature, energy density, chemical composition) of each successive stage of the post-initial evolution of the collision, while consistently accounting for the small system size, large initial-state spatial inhomogeneities and event-by-event fluctuations, and the strongly non-equilibrium dynamical character of the evolution.

Consider high-energy hadronic collisions of three types: nucleus-nucleus (A-A), proton-nucleus (p-A), and proton-proton (pp). For each collision event, define the impact parameter b as the transverse distance between the centers of the incoming objects, the number of wounded nucleons N_part as the number of nucleons that undergo at least one inelastic interaction (computed in a Glauber Monte Carlo model), and the charged-particle multiplicity N_ch as the number of produced charged hadrons in a fixed pseudorapidity window. Centrality classes are defined as percentiles of the N_ch distribution. Assume that nucleon-nucleon charged-particle multiplicities follow a negative binomial distribution, and that A-A multiplicity distributions can be fitted by a Glauber-based ancestor model from which a relatively narrow correlation between b and N_ch is obtained.

(a) Provide a quantitative framework that relates b, N_part, and N_ch consistently across A-A, p-A, and pp collisions, characterizing the conditional distributions P(b | N_ch), P(N_part | b), and P(N_ch | N_part, b) for each system.

(b) In p-A collisions, quantify how broad the correlation between N_part and b is compared to A-A, and determine to what extent (and under which selection observables) a meaningful centrality / impact-parameter selection is possible.

(c) For pp collisions, where there is no direct experimental access to b, determine whether (and how) the dependence of observables on the nucleon-level impact parameter can be inferred from the dependence on N_ch, given that the geometry-multiplicity interplay is complex.

(d) Establish under what conditions a direct comparison of pp, p-Pb, and Pb-Pb observables at fixed N_ch (or fixed centrality percentile) is physically meaningful, and provide the appropriate rescaling or matching prescription that should replace naive multiplicity-based comparisons.

Background. A tuple of univariate distributions $F_1,\dots,F_n$ is called jointly mixable if there exist random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ defined on a common probability space such that $X_i\sim F_i$ for each $i$ and the sum $X_1+\cdots+X_n$ is almost surely equal to a constant. When $F_1=\cdots=F_n=F$, the distribution $F$ is called $n$-completely mixable.

Problem. Replace the additive aggregation function $S(x_1,\dots,x_n)=x_1+\cdots+x_n$ by a general measurable function $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ (or more generally $\Phi:\mathcal{X}^n\to\mathcal{Y}$ for a suitable measurable space). Say that distributions $F_1,\dots,F_n$ are $\Phi$-mixable if there exist random variables $X_i\sim F_i$ on a common probability space with $\Phi(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ almost surely constant.

(a) Identify the classes of functions $\Phi$ for which $\Phi$-mixability yields a non-trivial and useful theory (e.g., functions invariant under permutations of coordinates, continuous, monotone in each argument, or Schur-concave/convex aggregations such as $\max$, $\min$, products, $L^p$-norms, or quasi-arithmetic means $\phi^{-1}\!\big(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum\phi(x_i)\big)$).

(b) For such classes, give a characterization (necessary and sufficient conditions on $F_1,\dots,F_n$) for $\Phi$-mixability, generalizing known characterizations available for $\Phi=S$ (e.g., the mean condition and the variance/length conditions for monotone marginal densities).

(c) Determine the analogue of the "center" (the almost-sure constant value of $\Phi(X_1,\dots,X_n)$) and the set of admissible centers.

No general theory characterizing $\Phi$-mixability for arbitrary aggregation functions $\Phi$ replacing the sum appears in the literature. Some related generalizations exist (e.g., joint mixability with center, and unrelated "Φ-mixability" in online learning by Reid et al., 2015), but a systematic answer to which alternative multivariate aggregation functions yield a useful mixability theory and how to characterize them remains, to current knowledge, open.

Let $G$ be a finite connected graph with vertex set $V(G)$, order $n = |V(G)|$, and maximum degree $\Delta(G)$. For each vertex $v \in V(G)$, let $N[v]$ denote the closed neighborhood of $v$, namely $\{v\} \cup \{u : u \text{ is adjacent to } v\}$. A function $f : V(G) \to \{-1, 1\}$ is called negative if
$$\sum_{u \in N[v]} f(u) \le 1 \quad \text{for every } v \in V(G).$$
A negative function $f$ is called maximal if there is no negative function $g \ne f$ such that $g(v) \ge f(v)$ for every $v \in V(G)$. Define the lower against number
$$\beta_N^*(G) = \min\Bigl\{\sum_{v \in V(G)} f(v) : f \text{ is a maximal negative function on } G\Bigr\}.$$
Determine the sharp lower bound for $\beta_N^*(G)$ over all finite connected graphs $G$, expressed as a function of the order $n$ and the maximum degree $\Delta(G)$, and characterize when equality holds.

In high-energy proton-proton (pp) collisions at the LHC, transverse momentum (p_T) distributions of identified light hadrons (π±, K±, p, p̄) at mid-rapidity (|y| < 0.5), measured in bins of charged-particle multiplicity, exhibit a progressive depletion of heavier species relative to lighter ones at low p_T as multiplicity increases. Simultaneous fits of these spectra with the Boltzmann–Gibbs Blast-Wave model — characterized by a kinetic freeze-out temperature T_kin, an average transverse expansion (radial flow) velocity ⟨β_T⟩, and a transverse-velocity profile exponent n — yield multiplicity-dependent parameters whose trends mimic those extracted in nucleus–nucleus (A–A) collisions, suggesting collective-type behavior in high-multiplicity pp events.

Formulate and carry out a quantitative program that extends such collective-type analyses to heavy-flavor hadrons (open-charm hadrons such as D⁰, D±, D_s, Λ_c and charmonia such as J/ψ, ψ(2S), as well as open-beauty states) in pp collisions at center-of-mass energies a factor of two beyond 7 TeV (i.e. around 13–14 TeV) with substantially higher integrated luminosity. Specifically:

(i) Measure the multiplicity-differential p_T spectra and yields of the above heavy-flavor hadrons at mid-rapidity in pp collisions, and fit them simultaneously (together with light-flavor spectra) with a Blast-Wave-type parameterization
   dN/(p_T dp_T) ∝ ∫₀^R r dr · m_T I₀(p_T sinh ρ / T_kin) K₁(m_T cosh ρ / T_kin),
   with ρ(r) = tanh⁻¹(β_T(r)) and β_T(r) = β_s (r/R)^n, extracting (T_kin, ⟨β_T⟩, n) and their evolution with charged-particle multiplicity.

(ii) Quantify whether heavy-flavor hadrons participate in the same collective transverse expansion as light hadrons in pp collisions, by comparing the heavy-flavor-inferred (T_kin, ⟨β_T⟩) with those obtained from light hadrons at matched multiplicities.

(iii) Perform a systematic comparison of the multiplicity-dependent heavy-flavor blast-wave parameters, nuclear-modification-type ratios, and azimuthal anisotropy coefficients (v_2, v_3) in pp collisions with the corresponding observables in A–A collisions at similar charged-particle multiplicities, and assess to what extent the apparent collectivity in small systems extends to the heavy-flavor sector.

The problem is to determine whether and how heavy-flavor production in high-multiplicity pp collisions exhibits collective behavior consistent with that observed in A–A collisions, within a unified Blast-Wave / hydrodynamic framework.

Subsequent LHC measurements (ALICE, CMS, LHCb at 13 TeV) have reported multiplicity-dependent enhancement of D-meson and J/ψ production in pp collisions, and non-zero v_2 for D mesons in high-multiplicity pp/p–Pb events, indicating partial progress. Let m, n be positive integers and let (a_{i,j})_{1 ≤ i ≤ m, 1 ≤ j ≤ n} be a given matrix of positive real numbers. Interpret a_{i,j} as the time taken by worker i to perform production step j; there are m workers available for each of the n steps. An assignment is a tuple (σ_1, …, σ_n) of permutations σ_j ∈ S_m, where σ_j(i) denotes which worker is assigned to step j on equipment i. The total time spent on equipment i is

  T_i(σ_1, …, σ_n) = ∑_{j=1}^n a_{σ_j(i), j},

and the makespan of the assignment is

  M(σ_1, …, σ_n) = max_{1 ≤ i ≤ m} T_i(σ_1, …, σ_n).

Problems:
(a) Characterize the assignments (σ_1*, …, σ_n*) ∈ (S_m)^n that minimize M(σ_1, …, σ_n).
(b) Provide an algorithm that computes such an optimal arrangement (σ_1*, …, σ_n*) for given input (a_{i,j}).

In particular, identify structural properties of optimal arrangements (e.g., relation to "completely mixable" or "jointly mixable" rearrangements of the columns of (a_{i,j})) and determine the computational complexity of finding one.

Let n ≥ 3 be an integer. A distribution function F on ℝ is called n-completely mixable with center μ ∈ ℝ if there exist random variables X_1, …, X_n, each with distribution F, such that
   X_1 + X_2 + ⋯ + X_n = nμ   almost surely.
Denote by M_n(μ) the set of all distribution functions on ℝ that are n-completely mixable with center μ.

More generally, an n-tuple (F_1, …, F_n) of one-dimensional distribution functions is called jointly mixable with joint center K ∈ ℝ if there exist random variables X_1, …, X_n with X_i ∼ F_i for each i such that
   X_1 + X_2 + ⋯ + X_n = K   almost surely.
Denote by J_n(K) the set of all such n-tuples.

For n = 1 the sets are trivial (only point masses), and for n = 2 the set M_2(μ) consists exactly of the distributions symmetric about μ, with a corresponding characterization of J_2(K).

Problem: For each integer n ≥ 3, give a complete characterization of the set M_n(μ) of one-dimensional distributions that are n-completely mixable with center μ, and equivalently of the set J_n(K) of n-tuples of one-dimensional distributions that are jointly mixable with joint center K.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The full characterization of n-completely mixable distributions and of jointly mixable n-tuples for n ≥ 3 is widely cited as an open problem in the complete mixability literature. Sufficient conditions (e.g., symmetric unimodal densities, concave densities, monotone densities under moment conditions) and detection algorithms have been developed, but no complete characterization is known. Recent works (e.g., on centers of probability measures and detection of mixability) extend partial results without resolving the general characterization.

Setup. A two-player bimatrix game is specified by a pair of real m×n payoff matrices (A,B): if the row player plays a mixed strategy x ∈ Δ_m and the column player plays y ∈ Δ_n (where Δ_k denotes the simplex of probability vectors in R^k), the row player's expected payoff is x^T A y and the column player's is x^T B y. A Nash equilibrium (NE) is a pair (x,y) such that no player can strictly improve by unilateral deviation.

A bimatrix game (A,B) is symmetric if m = n and B = A^T. For a symmetric game, a symmetric Nash equilibrium is a NE of the form (x,x); every symmetric bimatrix game admits at least one symmetric NE.

The rank of a bimatrix game (A,B) is defined as rank(A+B). Thus a symmetric game (A,A^T) has rank k when rank(A+A^T) = k.

Problem. For each k ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}, determine the computational complexity of the following problem: given a symmetric bimatrix game (A,A^T) with integer (or rational) entries satisfying rank(A+A^T) = k, compute a symmetric Nash equilibrium of (A,A^T).

In particular, for each such k, decide whether this problem is solvable in polynomial time, is PPAD-complete, or has some intermediate complexity.

Let m, n be positive integers and let A = (a_{i,j}) be an m×n matrix of nonnegative real numbers. Let S_m denote the symmetric group on {1,…,m}. For permutations σ_1,…,σ_n ∈ S_m, form the m×n matrix whose (i,j) entry is a_{σ_j(i),j}, and consider the maximum row sum

  M(σ_1,…,σ_n) = max_{1 ≤ i ≤ m} ∑_{j=1}^n a_{σ_j(i), j}.

Define
  T^*(A) = min_{σ_1,…,σ_n ∈ S_m} M(σ_1,…,σ_n).

Since rearranging the columns leaves the total sum invariant, one always has
  T^*(A) ≥ (1/m) ∑_{i=1}^m ∑_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}.

(a) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the matrix A under which the equality
  T^*(A) = (1/m) ∑_{i=1}^m ∑_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}
holds (i.e., the average lower bound is attained).

(b) Provide an effective method (algorithm or closed-form characterization) to compute T^*(A) for an arbitrary nonnegative matrix A.

In inclusive quasi-elastic (QE) electron-nucleus scattering, the four-momentum transfer to the nucleus is fully determined event by event from the measured momentum of the scattered electron, giving the three-momentum transfer q and the energy transfer ω. Using these variables, scaling analyses (first-kind and second-kind scaling, the scaling function f(ψ′) of the SuperScaling Approach, and Rosenbluth-separated longitudinal and transverse responses R_L(q,ω), R_T(q,ω)) have been extracted, and the role of short-range nucleon-nucleon correlations — high-momentum pairs involving roughly 20% of the nucleons, responsible for the well-known enhancement of the transverse response — has been quantified.

In charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino-nucleus scattering ν_ℓ + A → ℓ^- + X (and the antineutrino analogue), the incident neutrino energy E_ν is not known on an event-by-event basis: only the outgoing charged lepton's momentum and angle are directly measured, while E_ν is distributed according to a broad flux Φ(E_ν). Consequently, the values of q and ω cannot be reconstructed event by event without an additional model assumption.

Problem. Develop a framework that allows the scaling functions, Rosenbluth-separated nuclear responses, and short-range correlation information extracted from inclusive electron QE data to be used quantitatively to predict the flux-folded inclusive CCQE double differential cross section

  d²σ/(dT_ℓ d cos θ_ℓ) = ∫ dE_ν Φ(E_ν) · d²σ(E_ν, T_ℓ, cos θ_ℓ)/(dT_ℓ d cos θ_ℓ),

in a way that does not require event-by-event knowledge of (q, ω). Specifically, construct an explicit prescription that (i) maps the electron-scattering scaling function and transverse-enhancement contribution into the five weak nuclear response functions entering CCQE, (ii) properly incorporates the broad neutrino flux through integration over E_ν with the kinematically allowed (q, ω) consistent with the measured lepton kinematics, and (iii) yields predictions that simultaneously reproduce existing electron QE scaling data and CCQE neutrino and antineutrino cross sections on nuclear targets such as ¹²C, ⁴⁰Ar, and ⁵⁶Fe.

Consider charged-current quasi-elastic-like (CCQE-like) scattering of muon neutrinos on a carbon (¹²C) target, with the incoming neutrino flux corresponding to that of the MiniBooNE experiment. Two independent nuclear-physics calculations of this process — both based on the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) applied to a relativistic Fermi gas / local Fermi gas description of the nucleus, supplemented with a two-particle–two-hole (2p–2h) contribution arising from meson-exchange currents and short-range correlations — are performed:

(i) the Martini et al. RPA + 2p–2h calculation, and
(ii) the IFIC/Nieves et al. RPA + 2p–2h calculation.

When their predicted flux-integrated double-differential and total CCQE-like cross sections are compared, the genuine one-body (1p–1h) RPA contributions agree reasonably well, but the 2p–2h contributions differ by approximately a factor of two.

Problem. Identify and quantitatively account for the origin of this factor-of-two discrepancy between the two RPA-based 2p–2h predictions for ν_μ–¹²C CCQE-like scattering integrated over the MiniBooNE flux. In particular, determine whether an unresolved enhancement of the axial nuclear response in the 2p–2h channel — beyond the vector and axial-vector meson-exchange-current contributions explicitly included — is responsible for this difference, by isolating the contributions of (a) the longitudinal/transverse axial response, (b) the meson-exchange-current diagrams retained or omitted in each calculation, (c) short-range correlation contributions, and (d) the treatment of Δ-resonance propagation and in-medium width.

Consider neutrino charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) scattering on a carbon target, in which an incoming muon neutrino interacts with a bound nucleon via W-boson exchange producing a muon and a recoiling nucleon. The hadronic vertex is parameterized (within the dipole ansatz) by an axial form factor with a single free parameter, the axial mass M_A, which fixes the Q^2-dependence and overall normalization of the elementary cross section. Two classes of measurements yield apparently inconsistent extractions of M_A from CCQE-like event samples on carbon:

(i) At mean neutrino energies near 1 GeV, an analysis of CCQE-like absolute differential cross sections per nucleon on carbon is well described only by an effective axial mass M_A^{eff} ≈ 1.35 GeV, both in shape (Q^2 distribution) and in absolute rate.

(ii) At neutrino energies above 3 GeV, an analysis of CCQE events on carbon yields M_A ≈ 1.06 ± 0.06 GeV, consistent with extractions from light-target (deuterium) data.

A candidate explanation is that, in addition to genuine 1p1h quasi-elastic scattering, multinucleon (np-nh, in particular 2p2h or two-particle–two-hole meson-exchange-current) processes contribute to the CCQE-like sample at the lower energy and inflate the apparent M_A.

Provide a quantitative theoretical and experimental account that simultaneously reproduces both data sets, by addressing the following:

(a) Determine, within a controlled nuclear-model framework valid across the full range from ≈ 0.5 GeV to ≈ 10 GeV neutrino energy (e.g., RPA-based or equivalent treatments of nuclear correlations together with explicit 2p2h contributions), the energy dependence of the multinucleon contribution to the inclusive CCQE-like cross section on carbon, and decide whether this contribution is significantly smaller (relative to the genuine 1p1h CCQE rate) at neutrino energies above 3 GeV than at energies near 1 GeV.

(b) Determine whether the topological selection (constraints on observed charged-track multiplicity, including proton multiplicity) and kinematic selection (cuts on transverse momentum imbalance and missing energy) used in the high-energy CCQE measurement preferentially remove events in which 2p2h dynamics distort the muon kinematics or produce additional ejected protons, and quantify the resulting bias on the extracted axial mass.

(c) Combining (a) and (b), establish whether a single value of the nucleon axial mass M_A close to the deuterium value (≈ 1.03 GeV) together with multinucleon dynamics can simultaneously reproduce the absolute CCQE-like cross section at ≈ 1 GeV on carbon and the high-energy (>3 GeV) extraction of M_A on carbon.

The tension is widely attributed to multinucleon (2p2h) contributions enhancing the low-energy carbon cross section while leaving the deuterium-based axial mass near 1.03 GeV. RPA + 2p2h calculations (Nieves et al., Martini et al.) and SuSAv2-MEC approaches reproduce both MiniBooNE and (approximately) NOMAD cross sections, but quantitative agreement on the energy dependence of 2p2h and on the impact of NOMAD's selection cuts remains incomplete; combined NCE+CCQE analyses do not fully support multinucleon contributions large enough to remove the normalization tension. Consider neutrino–nucleus scattering at energies relevant to accelerator-based oscillation experiments (roughly 0.2–10 GeV), and focus on neutral-current (NC) processes whose final state contains a single photon and no charged leptons. Such NC γ events constitute an irreducible background to electron-neutrino appearance searches because a single photon shower is experimentally hard to distinguish from an electron shower.

Standard contributions to NC single-photon production include:
(i) NC excitation of baryon resonances (most importantly the Δ(1232)) followed by radiative decay,
(ii) non-resonant nucleon Born terms,
(iii) coherent single-photon production on nuclei,
(iv) anomaly-mediated contributions arising from the Wess–Zumino–Witten term, in particular the ωZγ vertex coupling the ω vector meson to the Z boson and a photon, whose strength is fixed by the chiral anomaly but whose hadronic form factors and off-shell behavior carry large theoretical uncertainty.

Problem. Determine, both theoretically and experimentally, the size and kinematic distributions of the remaining NC single-photon production mechanisms—especially the anomalous ωZγ contribution—on nuclear targets used in current and near-future oscillation experiments (argon, carbon, hydrocarbon, water/CH). Specifically:

(a) Provide a theoretically robust calculation of the anomalous ωZγ contribution to the NC 1γ cross section differential in photon energy and angle on the nucleon and on nuclei, with controlled uncertainties on the vector-meson form factors, off-shell extrapolations, and nuclear effects.

(b) Identify direct experimental measurements—using liquid-argon time projection chambers such as MicroBooNE, the MINERνA detector, and the ND280 near detector of T2K, or comparable detectors—of the NC 1γ inclusive and exclusive cross sections (including coherent and incoherent channels) that are sufficient to constrain these mechanisms to a level adequate for νe appearance analyses.

(c) Combine (a) and (b) to demonstrate that the NC single-photon background to νe appearance is controlled with quantified, sub-dominant systematic uncertainty.

Substantial experimental progress has been made: in 2025 MicroBooNE released an inclusive search for anomalous single-photon production (arXiv:2502.06064), an enhanced search for NC Δ radiative single-photon production (arXiv:2502.05750), and the first search for NC coherent single-photon production (arXiv:2502.06091). Consider an accelerator-based neutrino experiment in which a primary proton beam impinges on a fixed target, producing secondary hadrons (predominantly pions and kaons) that decay in a magnetic-focused decay pipe to yield a neutrino beam (e.g., a NuMI-style configuration). The absolute neutrino flux Φ(E_ν) at the near and far detectors is predicted by a Monte Carlo simulation that convolves: (i) the primary proton beam optics and targeting, (ii) the alignment and geometry of the focusing horns and decay volume, (iii) hadron production cross sections from the primary p+target interaction, and (iv) secondary and tertiary re-interactions of hadrons in target, horn, and surrounding materials. Empirically, different simulation chains based on the same external hadron production data sets produce absolute flux predictions that disagree by up to roughly 20%.

Determine a concrete program — specifying (a) the set of dedicated hadron-production measurements (kinematic coverage in (x_F, p_T), target materials and thicknesses, including thin- and thick-target data sufficient to constrain secondary and tertiary interactions), (b) the in situ beam-line instrumentation and monitoring required (proton beam position, profile, intensity; horn current and alignment; target alignment; muon monitor responses), and (c) the common simulation conventions (interaction models, re-weighting prescriptions, error propagation methods, treatment of correlations) — such that the absolute neutrino flux uncertainty σ(Φ)/Φ at the relevant experimental energies can be demonstrably reduced below 5%. In particular, identify which of the listed sources (primary hadron production, secondary/tertiary interactions, proton beam optics, beam-line alignment) becomes the dominant systematic once primary hadron production is precisely measured, and quantify how the ~20% spread among existing predictions can be reconciled.

Reaching sub-5% absolute flux uncertainty in accelerator neutrino beams remains an active and open challenge. Modern long-baseline experiments (T2K, NOvA, MINERvA) currently report absolute flux uncertainties at the ~5–10% level, with ongoing efforts (e.g., NA61/SHINE replica-target measurements, EMPHATIC, and PPFX for NuMI) aimed at further reductions. Consider charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino–nucleus scattering experiments, in which a neutrino scatters off a nuclear target producing a charged lepton and (nominally) a single nucleon, but where the actual experimental signature is defined by detector-level observables (e.g., presence of a charged lepton, hadronic activity cuts, and reconstructed kinematics) rather than by the underlying interaction process. Different theoretical and experimental communities (neutrino physics, electron-scattering physics) use the terms "quasi-elastic" and "final state interactions" in inequivalent ways, so the mapping between measured cross sections and theoretically calculable quantities is ambiguous.

Formulate a standardized reporting prescription for CCQE measurements that achieves all of the following:

1. A precise, detector-level definition of the event selection (signal definition) specified purely in terms of observable final-state particles, kinematic thresholds, and acceptance, without reference to any particular interaction model.

2. A precise specification of the reported observables (e.g., differential cross sections in chosen kinematic variables) together with their bin definitions, kinematic ranges, and acceptance corrections, such that the reported quantities are model-independent in the sense that any theoretical model can compute them directly from first principles given the incoming neutrino flux.

3. A complete, quantitative description of the incoming neutrino flux (central value plus correlated uncertainties) sufficient for a theorist to fold any predicted cross section against the flux without further assumptions.

4. A clear translation table or operational definition relating the experimentally reported "CCQE" signal to the terminology used in the electron-scattering community and in nuclear theory, so that comparisons across neutrino theory, electron-scattering theory, and experimental data are unambiguous.

Provide such a prescription, and demonstrate that any two experiments adhering to it produce results that can be directly and unambiguously compared to each other and to theoretical predictions.

representations.normalized:
Consider a Random Phase Approximation (RPA) framework for modeling charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino–nucleus scattering on a nuclear target. In such a framework, the inclusive nuclear response is decomposed into longitudinal and transverse pieces of the vector (in particular, the transverse magnetic) response and of the axial response, and the leptonic probe couples to a hadronic current acting on nuclear states. A widely used simplification proceeds under the following two assumptions:

(A) The transverse magnetic response R_T^{(V)} and the transverse axial response R_T^{(A)} are taken to be identical, motivated only by the formal similarity of the non-relativistic reductions of their associated one-body operators, both proportional to (σ × q̂) τ_±.

(B) The nuclear current is taken as a purely one-body operator, and all hadronic final states (including those arising in two-particle–two-hole excitations) are represented as plane waves, which forces a regularization of otherwise divergent two-body phase-space integrals.

The problem is: formulate a theoretically justified replacement for assumptions (A) and (B) within an RPA-based calculation of the CCQE-like cross section that
  (i) treats the transverse magnetic response and the transverse axial response as genuinely distinct, accounting for the known differences between pion-exchange (meson-exchange current) corrections on the vector and axial-vector currents;
  (ii) ensures exact conservation of the vector current (CVC) at the level of the many-body matrix elements actually used (i.e., is consistent under the addition of two-body currents required by current conservation when the one-body current alone fails to be conserved); and
  (iii) replaces the plane-wave description of the hadronic final states by distorted/interacting final states (e.g., final-state interactions or properly antisymmetrized correlated states) so that the two-body integrals entering the response are finite without ad hoc cutoffs,
while still reproducing the inclusive CCQE-like cross-section data on a nuclear target such as ^{12}C in the kinematic regime of the MiniBooNE experiment.

In neutrino-nucleus charged-current and neutral-current quasielastic scattering on light/medium nuclei (e.g., carbon), the inclusive nuclear response can be decomposed into vector, axial, and vector-axial pieces, and further into longitudinal and transverse components with respect to the three-momentum transfer q. When two-body meson-exchange (and related) currents are added to the one-body current, the transverse vector response is known to be enhanced. The question concerns the corresponding axial transverse response.

Provide:

(a) A clear identification of the physical mechanism(s) (e.g., Δ-isobar excitation, pion-in-flight and contact terms, short-range correlations dressing one-body currents, interference between one-body and two-body amplitudes in the 1p1h sector, genuine 2p2h contributions) that produce an enhancement of the purely axial transverse response function R_T^{AA}(q,ω) and of the axial-vector interference response R_T^{VA}(q,ω) in CCQE and NCQE scattering on a nucleus such as ^{12}C.

(b) Quantitative estimates, as functions of the three-momentum transfer |q| and energy transfer ω across the kinematic regime relevant for accelerator neutrino experiments (|q| up to ~1 GeV), of the size of this axial transverse enhancement relative to the impulse-approximation (one-body) result, including its sign and its model dependence.

(c) For each of the principal theoretical frameworks used to predict CCQE/NCQE cross sections — Random Phase Approximation (RPA), Relativistic Mean Field (RMF), and SuperScaling Approach (SuSA/SuSAv2) — an explicit statement of which assumptions about vector and axial transverse enhancements are built into the framework, together with quantitative tests against ab initio calculations (e.g., Green's Function Monte Carlo on light nuclei) demonstrating whether or not those assumptions reproduce the axial transverse enhancement.

Determine the origin, magnitude (as a function of q and ω), and inter-model variability of the axial transverse response enhancement from two-body currents, and state precise criteria under which RPA, RMF, and SuSA predictions for CCQE on carbon are consistent with the underlying enhancement.

Subsequent work has made substantial progress but no full consensus exists. Recent calculations attribute much of the transverse (including axial) enhancement to interference between meson-exchange currents and short-range correlations acting on high-momentum nucleon pairs, while pure relativistic Fermi-gas treatments without SRC can yield a reduction. Different frameworks (RPA, RMF/SuSAv2, GFMC, factorized 2p2h) still disagree quantitatively on the axial transverse enhancement magnitude, so the question is partially solved.

representations.normalized:
Consider the description of charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino-nucleus scattering on nuclear targets within two relativistic many-body frameworks:

1. The Relativistic Mean Field (RMF) approach, in which the bound and outgoing nucleons are treated as solutions of a Dirac equation with strong scalar and vector mean-field potentials, and final-state interactions of the knocked-out nucleon are encoded by the same (real) RMF potential used for the bound state.

2. The Relativistic Green's Function (RGF) approach, in which the inclusive cross section is expressed via the single-particle Green's function with a complex relativistic optical potential (e.g. EDAI, EDAD1, EDAD2 parametrizations fitted to elastic proton-nucleus scattering); the imaginary part, which would represent loss of flux to inelastic channels in exclusive processes, is reinstated in the inclusive sum so as to redistribute strength among all open channels.

Develop a theoretical framework that achieves all of the following simultaneously:

(a) Identify, from an underlying microscopic many-body theory (such as Green's Function Monte Carlo or a comparable ab initio nuclear structure calculation), the precise dynamical content that an effective RMF final-state interaction must encode, and derive constraints that uniquely fix the appropriate RMF potential to be used for inclusive CCQE observables, removing the present latitude in its choice.

(b) Construct, or characterize, a phenomenological relativistic optical potential that satisfies the dispersion relations linking its real and imaginary parts over the full energy range relevant to accelerator-based neutrino experiments, so that the RGF prediction for inclusive CCQE cross sections is determined unambiguously from elastic nucleon-nucleus phenomenology rather than depending on the choice among inequivalent fits.

(c) Quantitatively decompose the enhancement of the inclusive CCQE cross section produced by the RGF model relative to impulse-approximation (IA) models into contributions from genuine single-nucleon final-state interaction effects, two- and multi-nucleon emission (meson-exchange currents and short-range correlations), and non-nucleonic channels (e.g. pion production followed by absorption), and reconcile this decomposition with independent calculations of those individual mechanisms.

State and prove (or otherwise rigorously establish) the conditions under which (a)–(c) hold consistently within a single relativistic many-body description of inclusive lepton-nucleus scattering.

The question concerns long-standing theoretical ambiguities in modeling inclusive CCQE neutrino-nucleus scattering with RMF and RGF approaches. Subsequent literature (Meucci, Giusti, and collaborators; Gonzalez-Jimenez et al.) continues to compare RMF/RGF with different optical potentials (EDAI, EDAD) against MiniBooNE/T2K/MINERvA data, and ab initio (GFMC, spectral function, SuSAv2) calculations have refined but not eliminated the ambiguity in the choice of RMF/optical potential or fully decomposed the RGF enhancement into 2p2h and non-nucleonic contributions. representations.normalized:
Consider charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino-nucleus scattering, in which an incoming neutrino interacts with a bound nucleon inside a target nucleus via the exchange of a W boson, producing a charged lepton and a struck nucleon. After the primary electroweak interaction, the outgoing hadrons must propagate through the residual nuclear medium, where they may rescatter, be absorbed, charge-exchange, or produce additional hadrons; these processes are collectively called final-state interactions (FSI) and reshape the exclusive hadronic final state (in particular proton multiplicities, momenta, and angular distributions) actually observed in fine-grained tracking detectors and liquid-argon time-projection chambers.

A formally complete quantum-mechanical treatment of FSI in the exclusive CCQE channel would require introducing a large number of presently unknown nuclear transition form factors, which is not feasible in practice. Existing implementations in neutrino Monte Carlo event generators (e.g. intranuclear cascade models) reproduce inclusive observables reasonably well but exhibit documented shortcomings when confronted with proton-emission observables.

Problem: Devise a tractable, theoretically well-founded, and experimentally reliable prescription for FSI that
(i) can be implemented inside neutrino event generators on an event-by-event basis to produce exclusive hadronic final states for CCQE interactions on nuclear targets,
(ii) avoids the need to introduce an intractable number of unknown form factors,
(iii) is consistent with constraints from electron-nucleus scattering data on the same nuclei, and
(iv) reproduces measured proton kinematic distributions (multiplicities, momenta, angles, and transverse-kinematic-imbalance variables) in CCQE-like neutrino-nucleus events to within experimental uncertainties.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space. Denote by $\mathcal{F}_{(X,\mathcal{A})}$ the class of all $\mathcal{A}$-measurable functions $f:X\to[0,1]$, and by $\mathcal{M}_{(X,\mathcal{A})}$ the class of capacities $\mu:\mathcal{A}\to[0,1]$, i.e., set functions that are nondecreasing, satisfy $\mu(\emptyset)=0$ and $\mu(X)=1$. A semicopula is a function $S:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$ that is nondecreasing in each coordinate and has $1$ as a neutral element (i.e., $S(1,x)=S(x,1)=x$ for all $x\in[0,1]$). For a semicopula $S$, define the smallest semicopula-based integral
$$ I_S(\mu,f) \;=\; \sup_{t\in[0,1]} S\bigl(t,\;\mu(\{x\in X:f(x)\ge t\})\bigr). $$
Characterize all semicopulas $S$ for which the translation-invariance property
$$ I_S(\mu,f+a) \;=\; I_S(\mu,f)+a $$
holds for every measurable space $(X,\mathcal{A})$, every capacity $\mu\in\mathcal{M}_{(X,\mathcal{A})}$, every $f\in\mathcal{F}_{(X,\mathcal{A})}$, and every $a\in[0,1]$ such that $f+a$ still takes values in $[0,1]$.

The problem (posed by Hutník) has been solved: the only semicopula for which the smallest semicopula-based integral is translation invariant in the stated sense is the Łukasiewicz t-norm $S(x,y)=\max(x+y-1,0)$. This characterization is established in the zbMATH-indexed work titled "The solution of Hutník's open problem."

Consider the problem of transferring sophisticated neutrino–nucleus scattering calculations into Monte Carlo neutrino event generators used to simulate experimental data. Such calculations include: (i) differential cross-section tables computed in the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) for charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) and related processes; (ii) precomputed hadronic tensors W^{μν}(q,ω) tabulated as functions of energy transfer ω and momentum transfer q, from which inclusive cross sections may be reconstructed by contraction with the leptonic tensor; and (iii) ab initio nuclear-structure outputs such as Green's Function Monte Carlo (GFMC) response functions, which are too computationally expensive to evaluate inside a generator at run time.

Develop a general framework that addresses the following questions:

1. Specify a standardized data format and interpolation scheme by which precomputed hadronic tensors and RPA differential cross-section tables on (E_ν, q, ω) (or equivalent kinematic) grids can be ingested by a neutrino event generator so as to reproduce the underlying inclusive predictions to a prescribed numerical accuracy.

2. Provide a method for propagating theoretical uncertainties (e.g. those arising from nuclear form factors, two-body current contributions, RPA correlation parameters, and nuclear-model variants) through the tabulated input into event-by-event reweighting factors usable in experimental analyses.

3. Prescribe how to supplement an inclusive calculation, which yields only the lepton kinematics, with a model for the exclusive hadronic final state (nucleon multiplicities, momenta, and intrinsic excitations) consistent with energy–momentum conservation and the underlying nuclear response, including for calculations such as GFMC where only inclusive responses are computed.

State precise consistency conditions the framework must satisfy and demonstrate, by mathematical construction or by a worked example for one such calculation, that all three requirements can be met simultaneously.

Let the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) be enumerated as ρ_n = β(n) + iγ(n), n ≥ 0, with γ(n) > 0 listed in non-decreasing order. Recall that a sequence (x_n) of real numbers is said to be uniformly distributed modulo 1 if for every 0 ≤ a < b ≤ 1,
   lim_{N→∞} (1/N) #{ n < N : {x_n} ∈ [a,b) } = b − a,
where {x} denotes the fractional part of x.

Recall further that an infinite binary sequence is called (Martin-Löf) random if it passes every recursively enumerable statistical test of randomness; an arbitrary sequence of real numbers is said to form a random sequence if a natural binary encoding of it (e.g., the binary expansions of its terms) yields a Martin-Löf random sequence.

Suppose that for every positive real number z ≠ 1 the sequence
   ( (log z)/(2π) · γ(n) )_{n ≥ 0}
is uniformly distributed modulo 1. Does it follow that the sequence (γ(n))_{n ≥ 0} of imaginary parts of the non-trivial zeros of ζ(s) forms a random sequence in the sense of algorithmic randomness?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

A technical report by Calude, Salomaa, and Roblot ("Zeros of Riemann's Zeta Function Are Uniformly Distributed, But Not Random") argues that, although the imaginary parts of the non-trivial zeros of ζ are conjecturally uniformly distributed modulo 1 in the stated sense, this sequence is not algorithmically random; the zeros are computable (e.g., to arbitrary precision by known algorithms), so the sequence cannot be Martin-Löf random. Thus the implication asked about fails: uniform distribution does not entail algorithmic randomness for these zeros.

A discipline is called quasi-empirical if its methodology resembles that of the empirical sciences (such as physics): conjectures are tested against examples and computational evidence, hypotheses may be adopted on the basis of their explanatory or predictive power rather than from formal proof alone, and theories are subject to revision in light of new evidence. By contrast, the classical view holds that mathematics proceeds purely deductively, with theorems established only by rigorous proof from accepted axioms.

Question: Is mathematics quasi-empirical? That is, taking into account phenomena such as the incompleteness theorems, algorithmic randomness, the practical role of computer experimentation and probabilistic reasoning in mathematical discovery, and the existence of plausible but unproved hypotheses (e.g., axioms adopted for their consequences), should mathematical research be conducted in a manner more like physics — accepting and using mathematical statements on the basis of empirical/heuristic evidence rather than insisting exclusively on formal proof?

Background. The (prefix-free) Chaitin–Kolmogorov complexity H(x) of a finite binary string x is defined as the length of a shortest input p to a fixed universal prefix-free Turing machine U such that U(p) halts and outputs x; equivalently H(x) = min{|p| : U(p) = x}. This quantity is defined only for finite strings, since it relies on the universal machine halting after finitely many steps.

Problem. Develop a satisfactory notion of algorithmic complexity H(α) for infinite binary sequences α ∈ {0,1}^ω that extends the finite-string theory and shares its principal invariance, coding, and information-theoretic properties (e.g., machine-independence up to additive constants, a counting/Kraft inequality, a coherent relation to randomness of α, and consistent behavior under prefixes so that H(α) governs H(α↾n) as n → ∞). Two approaches are to be investigated and compared:

(a) Non-terminating computations: define H(α) using programs for the universal prefix-free machine that never halt but, while running forever, produce α as their (monotone) output, possibly via a transfinite or limit notion of program length and convergence.

(b) Infinite-time computational models: define H(α) using computational devices that consume and produce infinite strings in finite "physical" time, such as cellular automata acting on Z, real-valued computable functions in the BSS or computable-analysis sense, or infinite-time Turing machines, and use the size/description of such devices to measure complexity.

Determine, for at least one such formalization in each of (a) and (b), whether the resulting H(·) is well-defined up to an additive constant, prove its basic properties, characterize the sequences α with H(α) "small" or "maximal," and clarify the precise relationship between the two approaches and existing notions (plain, prefix, monotone, a-priori, and process complexity of finite prefixes; Martin-Löf and Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness).

Background. Fix the binary alphabet {0,1}. For a finite binary string x of length n, the (plain) Kolmogorov complexity C(x) is the length of a shortest input to a fixed universal Turing machine that outputs x. A finite string x of length n is called Kolmogorov random (with deficiency d) if C(x) ≥ n − d. For infinite binary sequences, write 2^ω for Cantor space with the uniform (fair-coin) measure. An infinite sequence X ∈ 2^ω is Martin-Löf random if it passes every Martin-Löf test, i.e. for every uniformly computably enumerable sequence (U_n) of open subsets of 2^ω with μ(U_n) ≤ 2^{−n}, one has X ∉ ⋂_n U_n.

A (partial) computable map F : 2^ω → 2^ω (defined on a set of full uniform measure) is said to preserve randomness if F(X) is Martin-Löf random whenever X is Martin-Löf random. Analogously, a computable function f mapping finite strings to finite strings is said to preserve Kolmogorov randomness if there is a constant c such that C(f(x)) ≥ |f(x)| − c whenever C(x) ≥ |x| − O(1).

Problem. Characterize the transformations that preserve randomness in each of the following senses, and clarify the relationship between the two notions:
(a) Describe necessary and sufficient conditions on a (partial) computable function F : 2^ω → 2^ω under which F(X) is Martin-Löf random for every Martin-Löf random X.
(b) Describe necessary and sufficient conditions on a computable function f on finite binary strings under which f preserves Kolmogorov randomness in the sense above.
(c) Determine the structural and measure-theoretic properties (e.g. measure preservation, almost-everywhere computability, layerwise computability) that characterize these classes of transformations, and determine to what extent the finite and infinite versions correspond.

The general study of randomness-preserving transformations has produced several substantive results — for example, Shen's theorem that almost-everywhere computable measure-preserving maps preserve Martin-Löf randomness (and in fact every ML-random point has an ML-random preimage), as well as work on layerwise computability and on continuous transformations of 2-random sequences. For an isolated rotating neutron star (pulsar) with angular velocity Ω(t), define the observational braking index by

  n = Ω Ω̈ / (Ω̇)²,

equivalently obtained from a spin-down law Ω̇ = −K Ω^n with K constant. The standard canonical torque mechanisms predict the following discrete values: n = 1 for a pure relativistic particle wind, n = 3 for pure magnetic dipole radiation in vacuum (the MDR model), and n = 5 for pure magnetic quadrupole radiation. Observationally, however, several isolated pulsars have measured braking indices, accurate to within a few percent or better, lying strictly between these predictions, in the approximate range 1 < n < 2.8.

Problem: Construct a physical spin-down model for an isolated pulsar — specifying the torque(s), magnetospheric configuration, and any time evolution of relevant quantities (such as magnetic field strength, magnetic inclination angle, moment of inertia, or particle outflow) — that yields, in a self-consistent way, braking indices continuously taking values in the observed range 1 < n < 2.8, and that quantitatively reproduces the precisely measured n values of the known isolated pulsars without requiring fine-tuning beyond what is astrophysically justified.

Let $U$ be a fixed universal Turing machine and let $V$ be a fixed universal prefix-free Turing machine (i.e., a universal machine whose domain is a prefix-free subset of $\{0,1\}^*$). For a finite binary string $\sigma\in\{0,1\}^*$ of length $n$, define the plain Kolmogorov complexity
$$C(\sigma)=\min\{|p|:U(p)=\sigma\}$$
and the prefix-free (Chaitin) complexity
$$K(\sigma)=\min\{|p|:V(p)=\sigma\}.$$
Fix a constant $c\ge 0$. Call $\sigma$ Kolmogorov $c$-random if $C(\sigma)\ge n-c$, and Chaitin $c$-random if $K(\sigma)\ge n-c$.

It is known that every Chaitin random string is Kolmogorov random (up to an additive constant), but the converse fails: there exist strings that are Kolmogorov random yet not Chaitin random.

Problem. Identify and rigorously formulate natural ``randomness'' properties $P$ on finite binary strings such that:
(i) every Chaitin random string satisfies $P$ (uniformly in the randomness deficiency), and
(ii) there exist Kolmogorov random strings that fail to satisfy $P$.

In other words, exhibit intrinsic combinatorial, statistical, or computability-theoretic features that distinguish Chaitin randomness from Kolmogorov randomness on finite strings.

Consider an isolated, rotating neutron star (pulsar) with angular frequency Ω whose spin-down is governed by a torque of the form

    Ω̇ = −C Ω^n,

where n is the braking index and the torque coefficient C is proportional to μ² sin²α, with μ the magnetic dipole moment of the star and α the inclination angle between the magnetic moment and the rotation axis. The canonical magnetic-dipole-radiation model gives n = 3, but observations of several young pulsars yield steady-state braking indices strictly less than 3.

Determine whether, and by what mechanism, the quantities entering C — namely μ (and the underlying interior/exterior magnetic-field structure), sin α, plus additional contributions to the spin-down torque from non-dipolar field components, plasma outflow and magnetospheric currents, and rotationally driven internal effects (such as phase transitions, evolving density profiles, and superfluid components) — evolve as the pulsar spins down so as to produce a measured braking index n < 3. Specifically, identify a physically consistent time evolution of μ, α, and/or the magnetospheric/internal structure that quantitatively reproduces n < 3 for isolated pulsars while remaining compatible with their observed long-term timing behavior.

representations.normalized:
Constructive mathematics is, informally, ordinary mathematics together with the principle that "existence equals computability": every existence claim must be witnessed by an algorithm that produces the asserted object. Within this framework, constructive proofs yield programs, and constructive objects (real numbers, functions, sequences, structures, etc.) are presented as algorithms together with moduli of convergence or other effectivity data.

Traditionally, the complexity of such constructive constructions has been analyzed through "dynamic" measures such as time and space resource bounds on the programs that realize them. A complementary, less developed viewpoint is provided by program-size (Kolmogorov / algorithmic information) complexity: the length, in bits, of the shortest program (in a fixed universal description language) that realizes a given constructive object or carries out a given constructive proof.

Develop a systematic theory of constructive mathematics from the viewpoint of program-size complexity. Concretely:

1. Formulate a precise notion of program-size complexity K(X) of a constructive object X (for instance, a constructive real, a constructive function on a constructive metric space, or an effectively presented algebraic structure), via the length of the shortest program that, when run in a fixed universal model, outputs (or computes arbitrarily good approximations to) X.

2. Extend this to a notion of program-size complexity of a constructive proof, viewed as a program extracted via the "proofs as programs" / realizability correspondence, and study how proof-theoretic transformations (cut elimination, normalization, double-negation translation, A-translation, etc.) affect program size.

3. Investigate, for representative theorems and constructions of constructive analysis, algebra, and topology, the program-size complexity of the canonical constructive witnesses, and prove nontrivial upper and lower bounds.

4. Identify analogues, in the program-size setting, of classical results about dynamic complexities of constructive objects, and establish trade-offs between program size and time/space resources for constructive realizers.

The task is to carry out such a study and obtain meaningful structural results.

Let Ω(t) > 0 denote the rotational angular frequency of an isolated rotating neutron star, and consider the polynomial spin-down model

    Ω̇(t) = −s(t) Ω(t) − r(t) Ω(t)^3 − g(t) Ω(t)^5,

where s(t), r(t), g(t) are nonnegative time-dependent coefficients representing, respectively, a particle-wind torque, a magnetic-dipole-radiation torque, and a (mass) quadrupole gravitational-radiation torque. For such a model define the (instantaneous) braking index by

    n(t) := Ω(t) Ω̈(t) / Ω̇(t)^2.

Address the following questions:

(a) Show that, for slowly rotating pulsars (Ω small enough that the Ω^5 term is negligible) and under the assumption that s, r are slowly varying compared with Ω, the model can be made consistent with any observed braking index n ∈ ℝ by an appropriate choice of the pair (s(t), r(t)), and characterize the family of such pairs (s,r) that fit a given finite set of measurements {(Ω_i, Ω̇_i, Ω̈_i)}.

(b) Determine to what extent the combination of s(t) and r(t) extracted in (a) constrains the surface magnetic-field strength B, given the standard magnetic-dipole relation r(t) ∝ B(t)^2 (with explicit proportionality constants depending on stellar moment of inertia and geometry), without assuming any prior evolution law for B or for the stellar composition.

(c) For rapidly rotating pulsars, where the Ω^5 term is non-negligible, decide whether the three coefficients (s(t), r(t), g(t)) can be uniquely identified from rotational observables (Ω, Ω̇, Ω̈, and higher derivatives), and identify what additional physical inputs (e.g. relating g(t) to the mass-quadrupole ellipticity) are needed for unique reconstruction.

The problem is to establish whether this polynomial ansatz provides a fitting framework for known low-frequency braking-index measurements without invoking detailed magnetic-field or composition evolution, and to determine its predictive power at high frequencies.

Recall that Gödel's incompleteness theorems state that any consistent, effectively axiomatized formal system that is sufficiently strong to encode elementary arithmetic is necessarily incomplete: there exist true arithmetical statements that cannot be proved within the system. Algorithmic information theory strengthens this through Chaitin's theorem, which exhibits, for each such formal system T, a constant c_T such that T cannot prove any statement of the form "K(x) > c_T", where K denotes Kolmogorov (prefix-free) complexity; thus almost all true incompressibility facts about finite binary strings are unprovable in T.

Question: In the actual practice of mathematics, should the phenomenon of incompleteness — in its classical Gödelian form and in its sharpened algorithmic-information-theoretic form — be regarded as a fundamental and serious constraint that genuinely limits what working mathematicians can hope to establish from any fixed axiomatic foundation, or is it instead a peripheral curiosity (a "red herring") that does not meaningfully obstruct mathematical practice? Provide a justified position, including either (a) compelling examples of natural, non-metamathematical mathematical statements whose unprovability from standard foundations (e.g., ZFC) demonstrates that incompleteness is a genuine working constraint, or (b) principled reasons explaining why such phenomena, although logically present, do not in fact constrain ordinary mathematical activity.

Background. Fix some reasonable formalization of "model of computation" (for example, a class of Turing machines with input and output tapes) together with an associated time-complexity measure t_M(x), defined as the number of steps that machine M takes on input x before halting. For each machine M in the model, define the time-bounded descriptive complexity

  C_M(x) := min{ |p| : M(p) = x },

and the time cost of producing x by M as t_M(x) (the running time of M on the shortest, or any specified, program p that outputs x).

The classical Invariance Theorem of Kolmogorov complexity states: there exists a machine U in the model (a "universal" machine) such that for every machine M there is a constant c_M with

  C_U(x) ≤ C_M(x) + c_M  for all finite strings x.

Question. Does there exist a model of computation, together with a time-complexity measure t, in which an analogous invariance theorem holds for time complexity? Concretely: is there a model containing a distinguished machine U such that for every machine M in the model there is a constant c_M (or, more generally, a fixed function depending only on M) with

  t_U(x) ≤ t_M(x) + c_M  for all x

(or some similarly tight, machine-independent bound), so that the time required by U to produce any output is, up to an additive constant, no worse than the time required by any other machine in the model to produce the same output?

Let U be a universal monotone Turing machine that may run forever, reading bits from a one-way input tape and writing bits to a one-way output tape. For an infinite binary sequence X ∈ {0,1}^ω, define the program-size (monotone) complexity of X by

  KM(X) = inf{ |p| : p ∈ {0,1}^* and U on input p eventually outputs every finite prefix of X },

and more generally, for a finite string x, KM(x) = inf{ |p| : U(p) outputs a string having x as a prefix }. Define the algorithmic probability that U produces (a sequence extending) x by

  P(x) = Σ { 2^{-|p|} : U(p) outputs a string with prefix x },

and for an infinite sequence X, P(X) is given by the corresponding measure-theoretic quantity on the cylinder generated by prefixes of X.

Develop a systematic theory of the program-size complexity KM for infinite computations and, in particular, establish precise quantitative relationships between KM and the algorithmic probability P in this infinite setting. Specifically, determine in what sense and under what hypotheses an analogue of the coding theorem

  KM(X) = -log_2 P(X) + O(1)

(or its appropriate refinements, e.g. with logarithmic correction terms) holds for infinite sequences X, and characterize the class of infinite sequences for which such an identity is meaningful.

A binary string is an element of $\{0,1\}^{<\omega}$, and a binary sequence is an element of $\{0,1\}^{\omega}$. The (prefix-free) Kolmogorov complexity $K(\sigma)$ of a finite binary string $\sigma$ is the length of a shortest input on which a fixed universal prefix-free Turing machine outputs $\sigma$. A finite binary string $\sigma$ of length $n$ is called Kolmogorov random (with parameter $c$) if $K(\sigma) \geq n - c$. An infinite binary sequence $X \in \{0,1\}^{\omega}$ is called Martin-Löf random if there is a constant $c$ such that for every $n$, $K(X\!estriction\! n) \geq n - c$; equivalently, $X$ is not contained in any effectively presented null $G_\delta$ set.

A computable binary operation on strings is a total computable map $F : \{0,1\}^{<\omega} 	imes \{0,1\}^{<\omega} 	o \{0,1\}^{<\omega}$, and a computable binary operation on sequences is a total Turing functional $G : \{0,1\}^{\omega} 	imes \{0,1\}^{\omega} 	o \{0,1\}^{\omega}$.

Provide a characterization (necessary and sufficient conditions on $F$, respectively $G$) of those computable binary operations that preserve algorithmic randomness, in each of the following two senses:

(a) For strings: identify all $F$ such that there exists a constant $c'$ with the property that, whenever $\sigma$ and $	au$ are Kolmogorov random binary strings (with some fixed parameter $c$) of equal length $n$, the output $F(\sigma,	au)$ is also Kolmogorov random with parameter $c'$ (and of comparable length).

(b) For sequences: identify all $G$ such that whenever $X$ and $Y$ are Martin-Löf random binary sequences (possibly with some independence or relative randomness assumption to be specified), the output $G(X,Y)$ is also Martin-Löf random.

In particular, classify which such operations exist beyond the trivial examples (projections, bitwise XOR with one argument fixed to a computable sequence, the join $X \oplus Y$, etc.).

The general problem of characterizing binary operations preserving algorithmic randomness of strings/sequences appears to remain open. Partial results are known: van Lambalgen's theorem characterizes when the join $X\oplus Y$ is Martin-Löf random (iff $X$ is ML-random and $Y$ is ML-random relative to $X$), and almost-everywhere computable measure-preserving transformations preserve ML-, Schnorr-, and Kurtz-randomness. No general classification of randomness-preserving binary operations was found in the surveyed literature.

Let $f: (\mathbb{C}^{n+1}, 0) \to (\mathbb{C}, 0)$ be a holomorphic germ defining an isolated hypersurface singularity of Milnor number $\mu$, and assume the singularity is non-simple. Fix a Milnor representative and let $B_\varepsilon \subset \mathbb{C}^{n+1}$ be a small ball, and let $\Lambda$ be a base of a miniversal deformation $F(x,\lambda)$ of $f$. For a generic $\lambda \in \Lambda$ the function $F(\cdot,\lambda)$ on $B_\varepsilon$ is Morse with $\mu$ distinct critical values. The Lyashko–Looijenga submersion $LL$ assigns to such $\lambda$ the unordered $\mu$-tuple of critical values of $F(\cdot,\lambda)$ in $\mathbb{C}$.

Given a distinguished system of paths in the target connecting two of the critical values $c_i, c_j$ to a common point (with all other critical values held fixed along the way), the corresponding collision is said to be liftable through $LL$ to $B_\varepsilon$ if the path of unordered critical-value tuples can be lifted to a path in (the appropriate stratum of) $\Lambda$ within a fixed neighborhood of the origin. To each Morse critical point one associates a vanishing cycle in the Milnor fiber, and any two such cycles have a well-defined intersection index in $\{0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots\}$.

It is known that if the two vanishing cycles associated to $c_i$ and $c_j$ have intersection index $\pm 2$, then the collision of $c_i$ and $c_j$ along the chosen paths cannot be lifted to $B_\varepsilon$ via $LL$.

Question: Are there further refined obstructions to the liftability of partial critical-value collisions through $LL$? In particular, prove or disprove: if the intersection index of the two vanishing cycles associated to $c_i$ and $c_j$ equals $0$ or $\pm 1$, then the collision of $c_i$ and $c_j$ (with all other critical values fixed) can always be lifted to $B_\varepsilon$ via the Lyashko–Looijenga submersion.
