Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space and let $f:X\to X$ be a continuous map, defining a discrete-time dynamical system $\{f^n\}_{n\ge 0}$. Recall the following definitions:

(a) $f$ has sensitive dependence on initial conditions if there exists $\delta>0$ such that for every $x\in X$ and every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ there exist $y\in U$ and $n\ge 0$ with $d(f^n(x),f^n(y))>\delta$.

(b) $f$ is topologically transitive if for every pair of nonempty open sets $U,V\subseteq X$ there exists $n\ge 0$ with $f^n(U)\cap V\neq\emptyset$.

(c) $f$ has dense periodic points if $\{x\in X: \exists n\ge 1,\, f^n(x)=x\}$ is dense in $X$.

A system is called chaotic (in the sense of Devaney) when it satisfies (a), (b), and (c).

Recall also the Chaitin (prefix-free Kolmogorov) complexity $H(s)$ of a finite binary string $s$, defined as the length of the shortest input to a fixed universal prefix-free Turing machine that outputs $s$, and the corresponding notion of algorithmic randomness for infinite binary sequences (a sequence $\omega$ is Chaitin/Martin-Löf random if there is a constant $c$ with $H(\omega\!\restriction\!n)\ge n-c$ for all $n$).

Problem. Provide a characterization of deterministic chaos (Devaney chaos, or sensitivity to initial conditions together with topological transitivity and density of periodic points) for continuous maps $f:X\to X$ on a compact metric space in terms of Chaitin complexity. Specifically, identify a natural way to encode trajectories $\{f^n(x)\}_{n\ge 0}$ as infinite binary sequences and determine the precise relationship between the chaotic behavior of $f$ and the Chaitin complexity (or algorithmic randomness) of the resulting sequences for typical initial conditions $x\in X$.

The Andrews–Curtis conjecture remains a well-known open problem in combinatorial group theory as of 2025. Let $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,\mathbb{R}^n,0)\to(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{R},0)$ be a real isolated function singularity, and let $F:(\mathbb{C}^n\times\mathbb{C}^k,\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^k,0)\to(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{R},0)$ be a real (mini-versal) deformation of $f$ depending on parameters in $\mathbb{R}^k$. Inside $\mathbb{R}^k$, the real total discriminant — i.e. the union of parameter values for which the corresponding function is non-Morse together with parameter values for which $0$ is a critical value — separates $\mathbb{R}^k$ into open chambers. Crossing a wall of this discriminant from one chamber to a neighboring one induces a "surgery" on the combinatorial data of a real Morsification (the collection of real critical values, the intersection matrix on the vanishing cycles, and the additional set of topological invariants of a real Morsification).

For a non-simple real singularity, one may consider purely formal surgeries on this combinatorial data (collections of critical values endowed with their intersection matrix and the additional real Morsification invariants), and one may compose such formal surgeries in arbitrary finite chains. Call such a chain realizable if it arises from an actual continuous path in $\mathbb{R}^k$ avoiding generic strata of the discriminant.

Let $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,\mathbb{R}^n,0)\to(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{R},0)$ be a real isolated function singularity, and let $F:(\mathbb{C}^n\times\mathbb{C}^k,\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^k,0)\to(\mathbb{C},\mathbb{R},0)$ be a real (mini-versal) deformation of $f$ depending on parameters in $\mathbb{R}^k$. Inside $\mathbb{R}^k$, the real total discriminant — i.e. the union of parameter values for which the corresponding function is non-Morse together with parameter values for which $0$ is a critical value — separates $\mathbb{R}^k$ into open chambers. Crossing a wall of this discriminant from one chamber to a neighboring one induces a "surgery" on the combinatorial data of a real Morsification (the collection of real critical values, the intersection matrix on the vanishing cycles, and the additional set of topological invariants of a real Morsification).

For a non-simple real singularity, one may consider purely formal surgeries on this combinatorial data (collections of critical values endowed with their intersection matrix and the additional real Morsification invariants), and one may compose such formal surgeries in arbitrary finite chains. Call such a chain realizable if it arises from an actual continuous path in $\mathbb{R}^k$ avoiding generic strata of the discriminant.

Determine the obstructions that decide whether a given chain of formal surgeries on the combinatorial data of a real Morsification of a non-simple real singularity is realizable by an actual path in the real parameter space $\mathbb{R}^k$.

An enumeration algorithm for such chains of formal surgeries was implemented (Vassiliev, 2002), and computational checks for all corank-2 singularities with Milnor number ≤ 11 found no non-realizable formal surgery, but no general theorem identifying the obstructions has been published. No subsequent work resolving the obstruction question for non-simple real singularities was located.

Develop a theory of algorithmic information (Kolmogorov complexity, randomness, and related notions) for bi-infinite sequences indexed by the integers, and more generally for elements of constructive complete partial orders (constructive cpo's). Specifically:

(a) Define and study analogues of plain and prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity, Martin-Löf randomness, and effective dimension for elements of the space of bi-infinite sequences over a finite alphabet, and more generally for the points of an effectively given (constructive) cpo.

(b) Investigate whether bi-infinite cellular automata — i.e., shift-commuting continuous maps on the space of bi-infinite sequences — can serve as a natural class of computational models for this theory, and characterize the algorithmic randomness, complexity-preservation, and information-theoretic properties of such automata.

The task is to produce a coherent framework giving definitions, basic invariance theorems, and characterizations of randomness and complexity in this bi-infinite / cpo setting that parallel the classical theory for one-sided infinite sequences computed by Turing machines.

A connected CW 2-complex K is called aspherical if its second homotopy group π₂(K) vanishes (equivalently, its universal cover is contractible, since K is 2-dimensional). Given a group presentation ⟨X | R⟩ for a group G = F/N, where F is the free group on X and N is the normal closure of the set R ⊂ F of relators, the associated presentation 2-complex K has one 0-cell, one 1-cell for each generator in X, and one 2-cell attached along each relator in R. The relation module of the presentation is the abelianization N/[N,N], regarded as a left ℤG-module via conjugation in F.

Question: Is every connected subcomplex of an aspherical CW 2-complex itself aspherical? Equivalently, if G admits an aspherical presentation ⟨X | R⟩ whose relation module N/[N,N] is a free ℤG-module, must every presentation ⟨X | R'⟩ obtained by retaining only a subset R' ⊆ R of the relators also have an aspherical presentation 2-complex?

representations.normalized: Algorithmic information theory studies the quantitative properties of finite and infinite binary strings using notions from computability theory. Its central objects include: (i) the (plain or prefix-free) Kolmogorov complexity C(x) (resp. K(x)) of a finite binary string x, defined as the length of a shortest input to a fixed universal (prefix-free) Turing machine that outputs x; (ii) conditional complexity K(x | y); (iii) algorithmic mutual information I(x : y) = K(x) + K(y) − K(x, y); (iv) Martin-Löf randomness for infinite binary sequences; and (v) related notions such as algorithmic probability and the halting probability Ω.\n\nProblem. Provide an axiomatic foundation for algorithmic information theory. That is, formulate a finite (or otherwise natural and recursively enumerable) list of axioms, in a precisely specified formal language, that characterizes the basic functions of the theory — for example a complexity-like function K : {0,1}* → ℕ together with the conditional version K(· | ·) — uniquely up to an additive constant, and from which the standard laws of the subject (the invariance theorem, the coding theorem, symmetry of information K(x, y) = K(x) + K(y | x) + O(log), the conservation inequalities for mutual information, and the basic theorems on Martin-Löf randomness) can be derived as theorems. Equivalently: identify a complete set of axioms whose models are exactly the (equivalence classes of) prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity functions, and develop the resulting theory purely from these axioms.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of giving an axiomatic foundation for algorithmic information theory is a well-known open challenge posed by Chaitin. While partial axiomatic treatments have been proposed (e.g., by Calude, Shen, and others, characterizing Kolmogorov complexity by properties such as enumerability from above, the counting condition, and universality), no widely accepted complete axiomatization of the full theory (including randomness and mutual information) has emerged. The problem is generally still considered open.

A one-relator group is a group given by a presentation of the form
G = ⟨ x_1, x_2, …, x_n | r ⟩,
where r is a single nontrivial reduced word in the free group F(x_1,…,x_n). The conjugacy problem for a finitely presented group G asks for an algorithm that, given any two words u and v in the generators and their inverses, decides whether the elements they represent are conjugate in G; that is, whether there exists g ∈ G with g u g^{-1} = v.

Question: Does there exist a uniform algorithm that solves the conjugacy problem for every one-relator group? Equivalently, is the conjugacy problem decidable for every group admitting a presentation with a single defining relation?

The conjugacy problem for arbitrary one-relator groups is widely regarded as still open. It is known to be decidable in important special cases (e.g., one-relator groups with torsion, by B. B. Newman; and various classes such as certain HNN-extension/ascending cases handled in recent work), but no general algorithm is known. Recent surveys on the theory of one-relator groups (2025) continue to list it as an outstanding open problem.

Consider the 6-dimensional real parameter space P consisting of pairs (a,b) where a(x,y) and b(x,y) are real polynomials in two variables of degree at most 1, i.e. a(x,y) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 y and b(x,y) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 y. For each (a,b) ∈ P, define the polynomial system

  f_{a}(x,y) = x^2 - y^2 + a(x,y),
  g_{b}(x,y) = xy + b(x,y),

and let R(a,b) ⊂ R^2 denote the (finite, generically) set of common real roots of f_a and g_b.

Fix a real number ε > 0. An ε-approximate continuous root selector over an open set U ⊂ P is a continuous map φ : U → R^2 such that for every (a,b) ∈ U there exists p ∈ R(a,b) with ‖φ(a,b) − p‖ < ε.

Define the ε-approximate covering number N(ε) of the family {(f_a, g_b) : (a,b) ∈ P} to be the smallest positive integer N such that there exists an open cover P = U_1 ∪ U_2 ∪ ⋯ ∪ U_N together with continuous ε-approximate root selectors φ_i : U_i → R^2 for each i = 1,…,N.

Determine N(ε) (in particular, its dependence on ε for sufficiently small ε > 0), or determine sharp upper and lower bounds for N(ε).

Background and setup. For a finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, let $S(\mathcal{H})$ denote the set of pure quantum states (unit vectors up to global phase). Fix a universal quantum Turing machine $U$ acting on classical descriptions, and for $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ define the quantum algorithmic information (quantum Kolmogorov complexity) of a pure state $|\psi\rangle \in S(\mathcal{H})$ by
$$ K_q^{\varepsilon}(|\psi\rangle) \;=\; \min\bigl\{\, |p| : p \in \{0,1\}^* ,\; \langle \psi | U(p) \rangle \langle U(p) | \psi \rangle \ge 1-\varepsilon \,\bigr\}, $$
where $|p|$ denotes the bit-length of the classical program $p$. (Equivalent variants based on quantum descriptions or prefix-free machines may also be considered.)

Let $T$ be a recursively axiomatizable, sound formal theory containing enough arithmetic to formalize statements of the form "$K_q^{\varepsilon}(|\psi\rangle) \ge n$", where $|\psi\rangle$ is presented through a finite classical specification (e.g., as an algebraic state vector or as the output of a fixed preparation circuit description).

Problem. Establish quantitative incompleteness theorems for the determination of quantum algorithmic information. Specifically:

(a) Prove that there exists a constant $c_T$, depending only on $T$ and $U$, such that for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and every classically describable pure state $|\psi\rangle$, the theory $T$ cannot prove the statement "$K_q^{\varepsilon}(|\psi\rangle) > c_T$"; in particular, only finitely many true lower bounds on $K_q^{\varepsilon}$ are provable in $T$.

(b) Identify an analogue of Chaitin's $\Omega$ in the quantum setting: construct a (classically describable) quantum object whose quantum algorithmic information content is algorithmically random and not determinable beyond finitely many bits in any such $T$.

(c) Determine to what extent these incompleteness phenomena depend on the chosen variant of quantum Kolmogorov complexity (classical-description-based vs. quantum-description-based) and on the fidelity parameter $\varepsilon$.

Let $\{0,1\}^*$ denote the set of finite binary strings and $\{0,1\}^\infty$ the set of infinite binary sequences. For a string $x\in\{0,1\}^*$, let $K(x)$ denote its prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity. A finite string $x$ of length $n$ is called (Kolmogorov) random if $K(x)\geq n - O(1)$, and an infinite sequence $X\in\{0,1\}^\infty$ is called Martin-Löf random if there is a constant $c$ such that $K(X\!\upharpoonright\!n)\geq n-c$ for all $n$.

Develop a mathematical theory of the "symmetry" of random strings and random sequences. Concretely:

(a) Propose a precise definition of what it means for a finite string $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ or an infinite sequence $X\in\{0,1\}^\infty$ to possess a symmetry. For instance, given a group $G$ acting on $\{0,1\}^n$ (e.g. by cyclic shifts, reflections, bit-flips, or coordinate permutations), define a quantitative notion of $G$-symmetry of $x$ — such as the size of the stabilizer, the minimum edit distance from $x$ to a $G$-fixed point, or the deficiency in Kolmogorov complexity $n - K(x)$ relative to symmetry-respecting descriptions — and analogously for infinite sequences under shift or other group actions.

(b) Using such a definition, determine whether random strings and Martin-Löf random sequences must lack symmetry: prove or disprove that for every fixed nontrivial group action $G$, every Kolmogorov random string (resp. Martin-Löf random sequence) is asymmetric in the proposed sense, with quantitative bounds on the degree of asymmetry.

(c) Conversely, decide whether the absence of symmetry can serve as a sufficient condition, or at least a necessary symptom, of non-randomness: characterize the relationship between asymmetry and randomness, and in particular determine whether there exist non-random strings/sequences that are nevertheless maximally asymmetric.

The question is posed as an open research direction in algorithmic information theory. status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

This is a special case of Tarski's problem on the elementary equivalence of nonabelian free groups. It was solved affirmatively, independently by Z. Sela (in a long series of papers, "Diophantine geometry over groups I–VII") and by O. Kharlampovich and A. Myasnikov ("Elementary theory of free non-abelian groups", J. Algebra, 2006): all nonabelian free groups of finite rank have the same elementary theory, so in particular $\mathrm{Th}(F_2) = \mathrm{Th}(F_3)$.

Let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a compact domain with smooth algebraic boundary $\Sigma$ of degree $\geq 3$, and assume $n$ is odd. For a generic affine hyperplane $H \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, define the cut-volume function $V(H)$ to be the $n$-dimensional volume of one of the two parts into which $H$ divides $D$, considered as a (multivalued) function on the space of affine hyperplanes.

A point $p$ of the complexification $\Sigma_{\mathbb{C}} \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ is called a non-degenerate parabolic point if the second fundamental form of $\Sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$ at $p$ is degenerate but its kernel is one-dimensional and transverse, in the standard non-degeneracy sense. A generic cuspidal edge is the standard codimension-one singularity that may occur on $\Sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$ in place of a parabolic point.

It is known that, in odd dimension $n$, if $V$ is algebraic then $\Sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$ has neither non-degenerate parabolic points nor generic cuspidal edges.

Question (two parts):

(a) Is it true that for every compact domain $D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n$ odd) with smooth algebraic boundary $\Sigma$ of degree $\geq 3$, the complexification $\Sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$ must contain at least one non-degenerate parabolic point or at least one generic cuspidal edge?

(b) If (a) fails, determine an enlarged finite list $\mathcal{L}$ of singularity types — each type obstructing algebraicity of $V$ — such that for every such $\Sigma$ the complexification $\Sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$ unavoidably contains a singularity of some type in $\mathcal{L}$.

Let strings be finite binary words over $\{0,1\}^*$. Fix a universal (prefix or plain) Turing machine and let $K(\cdot)$ and $K(\cdot\mid\cdot)$ denote the corresponding (plain or prefix) Kolmogorov complexity. The standard "degree of randomness" of a string $x$ of length $n$ measures how close $K(x)$ is to its maximum possible value among strings of length $n$ (so that $x$ is random when $K(x)$ is close to $n = \log\,2^n$).

Generalize this notion to randomness relative to an arbitrary finite set of strings. Concretely, for a finite set $M\subseteq\{0,1\}^*$ with $|M|=m$ and for $x\in M$, propose a definition of "randomness of $x$ with respect to $M$" (a randomness degree, or randomness deficiency, $d(x\mid M)$) such that the following properties hold:

1. When $M=\{0,1\}^n$ is the set of all strings of length $n$, the definition reduces to the usual degree of randomness of a string of length $n$.
2. Whenever $M$ can be specified by a program of length negligible compared with $\log m$ (i.e., $K(M)=o(\log m)$), almost all elements $x\in M$ should have $K(x)$ close to $\log m$ and hence be random with respect to $M$.
3. The number of $x\in M$ that fail to be random with respect to $M$ (those whose complexity falls noticeably below $\log m$) is small, with explicit counting bounds in terms of the deficiency level.

Provide such a definition, and prove the corresponding existence/counting statements making (2) and (3) precise.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The notion of randomness deficiency of a string with respect to a finite set is now standard in algorithmic information theory. One defines $d(x\mid M)=\log|M|-K(x\mid M)$ (or, in a related variant, $\log|M|-K(x)+K(M)$); this reduces to the usual randomness notion when $M=\{0,1\}^n$, and a simple counting argument shows that the fraction of $x\in M$ with deficiency at least $k$ is at most $2^{-k}$, so when $K(M)$ is negligible compared with $\log|M|$ almost all elements of $M$ have complexity close to $\log|M|$. Detailed treatments appear in the monograph of Shen, Uspensky and Vereshchagin (AMS Surveys 220) and in the textbook of Li and Vitányi.

Let $\mathcal{P}(d;N)$ denote the space of real polynomials of degree $\le d$ in $N$ variables, and consider the open subset whose elements define smooth real algebraic hypersurfaces $V_f = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^N : f(x) = 0\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ (or its projective compactification). For a smooth hypersurface $V \subset \mathbb{R}^N$, define the linear–Morse complexity
$$\mu_{\mathrm{lin}}(V) := \min_{\ell} \#\{\text{critical points of } \ell|_V\},$$
where the minimum is taken over all linear functions $\ell : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}$ whose restriction $\ell|_V$ is a Morse function. Along a generic one-parameter family $\{V_t\}_{t \in [0,1]}$ of hypersurfaces, the value of $\mu_{\mathrm{lin}}$ may change either by a topological surgery of $V_t$ (a Morse modification of the hypersurface) or by a bifurcation of the projective dual variety of $V_t$ (a degeneration of the family of linear restrictions, e.g. a tangency or a coincidence of critical values).

Call a generic path $\{V_t\}_{t \in [0,1]}$ from a hypersurface $V_0$ to a "trivial" hypersurface $V_1$ (e.g. an empty set, a sphere, or a hyperplane) a greedy simplification if at every parameter value $t^* \in [0,1]$ at which a topological surgery or a bifurcation of the dual variety occurs and affects $\mu_{\mathrm{lin}}$, the complexity strictly decreases:
$$\mu_{\mathrm{lin}}(V_{t^*+\varepsilon}) < \mu_{\mathrm{lin}}(V_{t^*-\varepsilon}) \quad \text{for small } \varepsilon > 0.$$

Question: Is it true that every smooth hypersurface $V_0$ defined by an element of $\mathcal{P}(d;N)$ can be connected to a trivial hypersurface by such a greedy-simplification path, i.e., one along which every relevant topological surgery and every relevant bifurcation of the dual variety strictly decreases the linear-Morse complexity $\mu_{\mathrm{lin}}$?

A group G is said to have exponent n (where n is a positive integer) if x^n = 1 for every x in G, and n is the least such positive integer. A group G is called locally finite if every finitely generated subgroup of G is finite. The Burnside problem asks: for which positive integers n is every group of exponent n locally finite? Equivalently, for which n is the free Burnside group B(m, n) (the freest m-generator group of exponent n) finite for every positive integer m?

It is classically known that every group of exponent n is locally finite when n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}. Determine, for each of the exponents n = 5, n = 8, n = 9, and n = 12, whether every group of exponent n is locally finite (equivalently, whether B(m, n) is finite for every m, with particular interest in the case m = 2).

Let $f:(\mathbb{R}^n,0)\to(\mathbb{R},0)$ be a smooth (or analytic) function germ with $df(0)=0$ and finite Milnor number $\mu(f)$. A real Morsification of $f$ is a real deformation $f_t$ of $f$ (lying in a versal deformation of $f$) such that, for $t\neq 0$ small, $f_t$ has only nondegenerate (Morse) critical points, all of whose critical values are real and distinct. Denote by $\#\mathrm{Crit}_{\mathbb{R}}(f_t)$ the number of real critical points of $f_t$, and define
$$\rho(f) := \min\{\#\mathrm{Crit}_{\mathbb{R}}(f_t) : f_t \text{ is a real Morsification of } f\}.$$
Inside the base of a versal deformation of $f$, the discriminant has codimension-one strata, and a generic real path crosses such strata transversally; the simplest real bifurcation along such a path is an $A_2$ Morse surgery, in which two real Morse critical points are created or destroyed (or, more generally, the number of real critical points changes by $\pm 2$).

Question: Given any real Morsification $f_0$ of $f$, does there exist a generic real path $\{f_t\}_{t\in[0,1]}$ in the base of a versal deformation of $f$, joining $f_0$ to a real Morsification $f_1$ with exactly $\rho(f)$ real critical points, such that along the path every $A_2$ Morse surgery strictly decreases the number of real critical points (i.e. the function $t\mapsto \#\mathrm{Crit}_{\mathbb{R}}(f_t)$ is monotonically non-increasing)?

Let $F_n$ denote the free group of finite rank $n$, given by a fixed free basis. For an automorphism $\varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$, the fixed subgroup is
$$\mathrm{Fix}(\varphi) = \{w \in F_n : \varphi(w) = w\}.$$
By a theorem of Bestvina–Handel, $\mathrm{Fix}(\varphi)$ is finitely generated of rank at most $n$.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, on input an automorphism $\varphi$ of $F_n$ specified by the images of the basis elements, decides whether $\mathrm{Fix}(\varphi)$ is nontrivial, i.e. whether $\varphi$ has a nontrivial fixed point in $F_n$?

Bogopolski and Maslakova gave an algorithm that, given an automorphism of a finite-rank free group, computes a basis of its fixed subgroup (using train-track methods following Bestvina–Handel). In particular this decides whether the fixed subgroup is nontrivial. Mutanguha later extended this to endomorphisms of free groups.

A one-relator group is a group given by a presentation $G = \langle x_1, \ldots, x_n \mid r \rangle$ with a single defining relator $r$, a nontrivial cyclically reduced word in the free group $F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. For integers $m, n \neq 0$, the Baumslag–Solitar group is $BS(m,n) = \langle a, b \mid b a^m b^{-1} = a^n \rangle$. A finitely generated group is called word hyperbolic (Gromov hyperbolic) if its Cayley graph, with respect to some (equivalently, any) finite generating set, is a $\delta$-hyperbolic metric space for some $\delta \geq 0$.

Question: Must every one-relator group that contains no subgroup isomorphic to a Baumslag–Solitar group $BS(m,n)$ (for some $m, n \neq 0$) be word hyperbolic?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The general question is widely cited as an open problem in combinatorial/geometric group theory. Partial progress includes: one-relator groups with torsion are known to be hyperbolic (Newman); Louder–Wilton proved that one-relator groups with negative immersions are hyperbolic (later strengthened by Linton), and CSA characterizations rule out certain BS subgroups. The full conjecture for torsion-free one-relator groups remains unresolved.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question was raised by V. Shpilrain. The case of rank 2 was settled affirmatively by Shpilrain and independently by S. Ivanov, and the general finite-rank case was resolved affirmatively by Donghi Lee ("Endomorphisms of free groups that preserve automorphic orbits", J. Algebra, 2002, and related work), showing that any endomorphism of a finite-rank free group that maps every primitive element to a primitive element is an automorphism.

Determine whether $\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ is representation rigid in this sense. That is: is it true that for every $n \geq 2$ and every $d \geq 1$, the automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ admits only finitely many equivalence classes of irreducible complex representations of dimension $d$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question, attributed to H. Bass, asks whether Aut(F_n) is representation rigid. Humphries' result that braid groups are not representation rigid implies Aut(F_2) is not rigid, giving a negative answer for n=2. The status for general n ≥ 3 does not appear to be fully settled, though work of Grunewald–Lubotzky and others has produced rich families of representations. Overall the problem is partially resolved.

Equivalently, recall that the braid group on $4$ strands is the group
$$B_4 = \langle \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3 \mid \sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_1 = \sigma_2\sigma_1\sigma_2,\ \sigma_2\sigma_3\sigma_2 = \sigma_3\sigma_2\sigma_3,\ \sigma_1\sigma_3 = \sigma_3\sigma_1 \rangle,$$
and it is known that $\mathrm{Aut}(F_2)$ is linear if and only if $B_4$ is linear.

Determine whether $\mathrm{Aut}(F_2)$ is linear; equivalently, determine whether $B_4$ admits a faithful finite-dimensional representation over some field.

Let $F_2$ denote the free group of rank $2$, and let $\mathrm{Aut}(F_2)$ denote its automorphism group. A group $G$ is called linear if there exists a field $K$ and a positive integer $n$ such that $G$ admits a faithful representation $G \hookrightarrow GL_n(K)$. Equivalently, recall that the braid group on $4$ strands is the group
$$B_4 = \langle \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3 \mid \sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_1 = \sigma_2\sigma_1\sigma_2,\ \sigma_2\sigma_3\sigma_2 = \sigma_3\sigma_2\sigma_3,\ \sigma_1\sigma_3 = \sigma_3\sigma_1 \rangle,$$
and it is known that $\mathrm{Aut}(F_2)$ is linear if and only if $B_4$ is linear.

Determine whether $\mathrm{Aut}(F_2)$ is linear; equivalently, determine whether $B_4$ admits a faithful finite-dimensional representation over some field.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem is solved affirmatively. Daan Krammer first proved that the Lawrence–Krammer representation of B_4 is faithful, establishing linearity of B_4 (and hence of Aut(F_2)). Stephen Bigelow then extended faithfulness to all B_n, and Krammer subsequently gave a purely algebraic proof for all n. Thus Aut(F_2) is linear.

Let $F_2^5$ denote the normal subgroup of $F_2$ generated by all fifth powers $\{w^5 : w \in F_2\}$ (equivalently, the set of elements expressible as a product of fifth powers of elements of $F_2$ and their conjugates; in fact $F_2^5$ coincides with the verbal subgroup of $F_2$ given by the word $x^5$, which equals the set of products of fifth powers).

Determine whether the iterated commutator
$$[x,y,y,y,y,y,y]$$
(of weight $7$, with $y$ appearing six times) belongs to $F_2^5$; equivalently, whether $[x,y,y,y,y,y,y]$ can be written as a product of fifth powers of elements of $F_2$.

The question is closely tied to the structure of the free Burnside group $B(2,5) = F_2/F_2^5$, whose finiteness is itself a long-standing open problem. status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is the classical Kaplansky zero-divisor conjecture. As of 2025 it remains open: it is known to hold for residually torsion-free elementary amenable groups and other special classes, but no general proof or counterexample is known. The related Kaplansky unit conjecture was disproved by Gardam in 2021, but this does not resolve the zero-divisor conjecture.

The question (due to Bergman) was completely answered by Snopce, Tanushevski and Zalesskii in "Retracts of free groups and a question of Bergman" (IMRN, 2022). They prove that the answer is YES when the subgroup S has rank at most 2, and NO in general: for every m ≥ 3, 1 ≤ k ≤ n−1, there exist a subgroup H of F_n of rank m and a retract R of F_n of rank k such that H ∩ R is not a retract of H.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The Tits alternative for $\mathrm{Out}(F_n)$ was established by Bestvina, Feighn, and Handel in two papers (Annals of Math. 151 (2000) and Annals of Math. 161 (2005)): every subgroup of $\mathrm{Out}(F_n)$ either contains a non-abelian free group or is virtually abelian (in particular virtually solvable). A group $H$ is called linear if there exists a field $k$ and a positive integer $d$ such that $H$ embeds as a subgroup of the general linear group $GL_d(k)$.

Question: Is the free uniquely divisible group $F_{\mathbb{Q}}$ (of rank $n \geq 2$) linear?

Doron Puder (2014, J. London Math. Soc., "Growth of primitive elements in free groups") established the exponential growth rate: the number of primitive elements of length k in F_n grows like (2n-3)^k for n ≥ 3, and like √3^k for n = 2 (in the cyclic-word setting, with related results for words). $$\mathrm{Fix}(\varphi)=\{w\in F_n : \varphi(w)=w\}$$
for its fixed subgroup. Recall that every subgroup of a free group is itself free, and the rank of a free group is the cardinality of any free basis.

Let $S\le F_n$ be a subgroup of finite rank. Decide whether the inequality
$$\mathrm{rank}\big(\mathrm{Fix}(\varphi)\cap S\big)\;\le\;\mathrm{rank}(S)$$
holds for every such endomorphism $\varphi$ and every finite-rank subgroup $S$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The inequality is known to hold when $\varphi$ is an automorphism (Bestvina–Handel, settling the Scott conjecture, gives $\mathrm{rank}(\mathrm{Fix}(\varphi))\le n$, with the relative version following by graph pullback) and more generally when $\varphi$ is an injective endomorphism (Dicks–Ventura). The general (possibly non-injective) endomorphism case, posed by Dicks and Ventura and listed as a standing open problem in compilations of open problems in combinatorial group theory, does not appear to have been resolved in full generality; recent work of Mutanguha and others on stable images and fixed subgroups of free group endomorphisms makes parts tractable but does not settle the relative rank inequality for arbitrary endomorphisms and arbitrary finite-rank subgroups.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Work of Kharlampovich and Myasnikov on definable sets in free groups (building on quantifier-elimination type results for the elementary theory of nonabelian free groups, also developed by Sela) shows that the only proper definable subgroups of a nonabelian free group $F$ are the cyclic ones; in particular, the commutator subgroup $[F,F]$ — being a proper nonabelian (and noncyclic) subgroup — is not first-order definable in $F$. This resolves Malcev's question in the negative.

Consider a protein–protein interaction network G = (V, E) representing the membrane subinteractome of a eukaryotic cell (e.g., yeast), where vertices V are membrane proteins and edges E are pairwise physical interactions, possibly weighted by interaction confidence. A membrane complex is a subset C ⊆ V whose proteins assemble together; complexes are to be predicted by clustering G.

Suppose that, in addition to the static graph G, two further sources of biological information are available:

1. Chaperone information: a partial mapping χ: V → 2^H assigning to each protein a set of molecular chaperones (from a chaperone set H) known to assist its folding or assembly.

2. Time information: a partial function τ that, for certain proteins or interactions, gives temporal data describing the order or timing of assembly events and dynamic exchange of subunits during complex formation. The function τ may be specified as timestamps τ: V → ℝ_{≥0}, as a partial order on E, or as exchange-rate annotations on edges.

The problem is twofold:

(a) Identify concrete experimental or database-derivable sources from which the temporal data τ for membrane-complex assembly and dynamic subunit exchange can, in principle, be obtained.

Consider a protein–protein interaction network G = (V, E) representing the membrane subinteractome of a eukaryotic cell (e.g., yeast), where vertices V are membrane proteins and edges E are pairwise physical interactions, possibly weighted by interaction confidence. A membrane complex is a subset C ⊆ V whose proteins assemble together; complexes are to be predicted by clustering G.

Suppose that, in addition to the static graph G, two further sources of biological information are available:

1. Chaperone information: a partial mapping χ: V → 2^H assigning to each protein a set of molecular chaperones (from a chaperone set H) known to assist its folding or assembly.

2. Time information: a partial function τ that, for certain proteins or interactions, gives temporal data describing the order or timing of assembly events and dynamic exchange of subunits during complex formation. The function τ may be specified as timestamps τ: V → ℝ_{≥0}, as a partial order on E, or as exchange-rate annotations on edges.

The problem is twofold:

(a) Identify concrete experimental or database-derivable sources from which the temporal data τ for membrane-complex assembly and dynamic subunit exchange can, in principle, be obtained.

(b) Formulate a clustering algorithm A that takes as input (G, χ, τ) and outputs a collection of predicted membrane complexes {C_1, …, C_k} together with a predicted assembly schedule for each C_i, such that the use of τ and χ provably (or empirically) improves complex identification compared with clustering G alone. Specify the objective function optimized by A and how χ and τ enter the objective or the constraints.

Develop a computational framework for systematically characterizing complex-formation relationships between membrane proteins and soluble proteins. Concretely, given (i) a set M of proteins annotated as integral or peripheral membrane proteins, (ii) a set S of soluble proteins, and (iii) heterogeneous experimental and predicted data sources (e.g., affinity-purification mass-spectrometry interaction data, co-fractionation profiles, structural models, sequence- and domain-based features, and subcellular localization annotations), design and validate computational analyses that:

1. Infer which heteromeric complexes contain both membrane and soluble subunits, distinguishing transient from stable associations.
2. Identify recurrent interaction motifs (e.g., specific domains, transmembrane-region-adjacent interfaces, lipid-anchor mediated contacts) that mediate membrane–soluble subunit coupling.
3. Provide a probabilistic model assigning each candidate (m, s) pair with m ∈ M and s ∈ S a calibrated score for participating in a common complex, together with rigorous benchmarking on curated reference complexes that explicitly include membrane components.
4. Quantify and correct biases introduced by the under-representation of membrane proteins in standard interaction-detection assays.

Specify the algorithmic methodology, the evaluation metrics, and the gold-standard datasets used, and analyze the asymptotic and statistical properties of the resulting predictor.

This is Remeslennikov's question on absolute profinite rigidity of finitely generated free groups. It remains open in general. Partial results exist: free groups are profinitely rigid among themselves, the property has been verified for finitely generated residually free groups (and certain extensions with abelian hierarchies), and finitely generated free metabelian groups have been shown to be profinitely rigid, but the original question for free groups versus arbitrary finitely generated residually finite groups is still unresolved as of 2024–2025.

A one-relator group is a group given by a presentation of the form $G = \langle x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \mid r \rangle$, where $r$ is a single nontrivial element of the free group $F_n$ on the generators $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. The group $G$ is said to be a one-relator group with torsion if $r = w^k$ for some element $w \in F_n$ that is not a proper power and some integer $k \geq 2$ (in which case $G$ contains an element of order $k$). A group $G$ is called residually finite if for every nontrivial element $g \in G$ there exists a homomorphism $\varphi : G \to Q$ onto a finite group $Q$ such that $\varphi(g) \neq 1$.

Question: Is every one-relator group with torsion residually finite?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

This is Baumslag's residual finiteness conjecture for one-relator groups with torsion. It was resolved affirmatively by Daniel Wise, who proved that one-relator groups with torsion are virtually compact special, hence residually finite (in fact, this follows by combining the small-cancellation/hyperbolicity of such groups with Wise's theorem that hyperbolic virtually special groups are residually finite).

Define the lower central series of $F$ recursively by $\gamma_1(F) = F$ and $\gamma_{k+1}(F) = [\gamma_k(F), F]$ for $k \ge 1$. Define basic commutators in $X$ and their weights as follows (the standard Hall ordering): the elements $x_1, \dots, x_r$ are the basic commutators of weight $1$, ordered $x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_r$. Assuming the basic commutators of weight less than $w$ have been defined and totally ordered so that commutators of smaller weight precede those of larger weight, the basic commutators of weight $w$ are the commutators $[u,v]$ where $u$ and $v$ are basic commutators with $\mathrm{wt}(u) + \mathrm{wt}(v) = w$, $u > v$, and, if $u = [u_1, u_2]$, then $v \ge u_2$. Basic commutators of weight $w$ are ordered after all basic commutators of weight $<w$ in any fixed total order extending these constraints.

Question: For every integer $c \ge 1$, is $\gamma_c(F)$ equal to the normal closure in $F$ of the set of basic commutators of weight exactly $c$?

Basic commutators of weight $w$ are ordered after all basic commutators of weight $<w$ in any fixed total order extending these constraints.

Question: For every integer $c \ge 1$, is $\gamma_c(F)$ equal to the normal closure in $F$ of the set of basic commutators of weight exactly $c$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question (attributed to Charles Sims) is known to have a positive answer for c ≤ 5, and partial results are known: γ_n(F) is the normal closure of basic commutators of weights n through 2n−4, and for rank-2 free groups γ_6(F) is the normal closure of basic commutators of weights 6 and 7. The general case appears to remain open.

A one-relator group is a group given by a finite presentation of the form
G = ⟨ x_1, x_2, …, x_n | r ⟩,
where r is a single nonempty word in the free group F(x_1,…,x_n). The word problem for G asks, given a word w in the generators x_1^{±1},…,x_n^{±1}, to decide whether w represents the identity element of G. By a classical theorem of Magnus, the word problem is decidable for every one-relator group.

Question: Does there exist, for every one-relator group G, an algorithm that solves the word problem of G in time bounded by a quadratic function of the length |w| of the input word w? More weakly, is there always such an algorithm running in time polynomial in |w|?

Let $F$ be a finitely generated free group with free basis $X$, let $[F,F]$ denote its commutator subgroup, and let $r \in [F,F]$ be a non-trivial element (equivalently, a freely reduced word in $X^{\pm 1}$ whose exponent sum on each generator is zero). Let $R$ be the normal closure of $r$ in $F$, and consider the one-relator group $G = F/R$.

Recall that a finitely generated group $H$ with finite generating set $A$ is called automatic if there exists a regular language $L \subseteq (A \cup A^{-1})^*$ surjecting onto $H$ such that:
(i) for every word $w \in L$ representing $h \in H$, the path in the Cayley graph of $H$ from $1$ to $h$ traced by $w$ is a quasi-geodesic; and
(ii) for each $a \in A \cup A^{-1} \cup \{1\}$, the set of pairs $(u,v) \in L \times L$ with $u \cdot a =_H v$ is recognized by a synchronous two-tape finite automaton.

Question: Must every such one-relator group $G = F/R$ with relator $r \in [F,F]$ be automatic?

Gardam and Woodhouse (Proc. This resolves the general question of automaticity of one-relator groups in the negative; the construction provides counterexamples even within the class of one-relator groups whose relator lies in the commutator subgroup, so not every such $G=F/R$ with $r\in[F,F]$ is automatic.

A group $G$ is called equationally Noetherian if for every positive integer $n$ and every (possibly infinite) system of equations $S \subseteq G * F_n$ in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with coefficients in $G$ (where $F_n$ is the free group on $x_1,\dots,x_n$), there exists a finite subsystem $S_0 \subseteq S$ such that the solution sets in $G^n$ satisfy $V_G(S) = V_G(S_0)$.

Question: Suppose $A$ and $B$ are two equationally Noetherian groups. Is their free product $A * B$ necessarily equationally Noetherian?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been answered affirmatively. It is known (with a proof attributed to Sela, and further results by Groves–Hull and others on acylindrically hyperbolic groups) that the free product of two equationally Noetherian groups is again equationally Noetherian; more generally, the class of equationally Noetherian groups is closed under finite free products.

representations.normalization_method: unicode-preserving newline and trailing-whitespace normalization v1
representations.normalized:
Setup. Work in the complex projective plane $\mathbb{P}^2 = \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C})$. A reduced plane curve $C \subset \mathbb{P}^2$ of degree $6$ is called a sextic of torus type if its defining polynomial $F$ can be written as $F = F_2^3 + F_3^2$, where $F_2, F_3 \in \mathbb{C}[x,y,z]$ are homogeneous of degrees $2$ and $3$ respectively. The singularities of $C$ are recorded by their ADE-types; the configuration $2E_6 + A_5 + A_2$ means $C$ has exactly two singular points of type $E_6$, one of type $A_5$, and one of type $A_2$.

It is known that within the moduli of irreducible projective sextics of torus type with the prescribed singularity configuration $2E_6 + A_5 + A_2$, there are exactly two complex equisingular components, and they are interchanged by the action of $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$. Pick smooth representatives $C_+$ and $C_-$ defined over a number field, conjugate to each other by a non-trivial Galois automorphism. A pair of plane curves $(C_+, C_-)$ is called an arithmetic Zariski pair if $C_+$ and $C_-$ are Galois conjugate but the topological pairs $(\mathbb{P}^2, C_+)$ and $(\mathbb{P}^2, C_-)$ are not homeomorphic.

Question. Do $C_+$ and $C_-$ form an arithmetic Zariski pair? Equivalently, is it true that there is no homeomorphism $\mathbb{P}^2 \to \mathbb{P}^2$ sending $C_+$ onto $C_-$, given that $\pi_1(\mathbb{P}^2 \setminus C_+) \cong \pi_1(\mathbb{P}^2 \setminus C_-)$?

representations.normalized:
Consider the Eyral–Oka sextic curves: a Galois-conjugate pair of complex projective plane curves of degree 6 defined over a number field, sharing the same combinatorial type of singularities (in particular containing two singular points of type E6 and singular points of type A2). For each curve in the pair, one may choose a projection from a smooth point onto a generic line and obtain a braid monodromy factorization in the braid group of the corresponding fiber; equivalence of two such factorizations is generated by Hurwitz moves and global conjugation, and equivalence is a topological invariant of the embedded curve.

Beyond the classical projection from a generic smooth point, one obtains further candidate arithmetic Zariski pairs by projecting from the singular points of the curves:
(i) projection from a singular point of type E6 (the symmetry exchanging the two E6 points makes the choice immaterial), and
(ii) projection from a singular point of type A2.

In each of cases (i) and (ii), the two curves are strongly real, so their braid monodromy factorizations can be computed explicitly.

Prove that in each of these two cases the resulting braid monodromy factorizations of the conjugate curves are not equivalent (under Hurwitz equivalence and global conjugation), thereby establishing that the pairs of curves obtained via these projections form genuine (topologically non-equivalent) arithmetic Zariski pairs.

Let $K \subset S^3$ be a tame knot, and let $G_K = \pi_1(S^3 \setminus K)$ denote its knot group. A group $H$ is called free-by-cyclic if it fits into a short exact sequence
$$1 \to F \to H \to \mathbb{Z} \to 1,$$
where $F$ is a free group (of finite or infinite rank). A group $G$ is called virtually free-by-cyclic if it contains a finite-index subgroup that is free-by-cyclic.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question appears in the standard list of open problems in combinatorial group theory and is not recorded as resolved. Recent work (2023–2024) on virtually free-by-cyclic groups develops homological criteria and proves the property for various classes (e.g., one-relator groups with torsion, certain hyperbolic virtually compact special groups), but does not settle the question for all knot groups. No source found claims a proof or a counterexample for general knot groups.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Finitely generated groups discriminated by a free group are exactly the limit groups (finitely generated fully residually free groups). It is a theorem (independently due to Kharlampovich–Myasnikov and Sela) that every limit group admits a hierarchical decomposition built from free abelian groups and surface groups via free products and amalgamations over $\mathbb{Z}$, which implies that limit groups are finitely presented. Hence the answer is yes.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question, posed by Gromov, of whether every word-hyperbolic group is residually finite remains a well-known open problem in geometric group theory. It is equivalent to asking whether every non-trivial hyperbolic group has a non-trivial finite quotient, and to whether every hyperbolic group is virtually torsion-free. Partial results are known (e.g., cubulated/QCERF hyperbolic groups are residually finite), but no general resolution has been established.

Let $S$ be a semigroup. For a subset $A \subseteq S$, define
$$\Delta(A) = \{x \in S : xA \cap A \neq \emptyset\}.$$
For subsets $X, B \subseteq S$, define
$$X^{-1}B = \bigcup_{x \in X}\{y \in S : xy \in B\}.$$
When $B \subseteq S$ satisfies $S^{-1}B = S$, define the covering number
$$\mathrm{cov}\,B = \min\{|X| : X \subseteq S \text{ and } S = X^{-1}B\}.$$
Let $n \geq 1$ be an integer and let $\mathcal{P} = \{A_1, \dots, A_n\}$ be a partition of $S$ into $n$ nonempty cells. Must there exist a cell $A \in \mathcal{P}$ such that $S^{-1}\Delta(A) = S$ and $\mathrm{cov}\,\Delta(A) \leq n$?

(It is known that the answer is affirmative when $S$ is finite, and when $n = 2$.)

A finitely generated group $G$ with finite generating set $A$ (closed under inversion) is called biautomatic if there exists a regular language $L \subseteq A^*$ such that:
(i) the natural map $L \to G$ is surjective;

A finitely generated group is called (Gromov-)hyperbolic if its Cayley graph is a $\delta$-hyperbolic metric space for some $\delta \ge 0$, equivalently, all geodesic triangles are $\delta$-thin.

For an integer $n \ge 6$ and a positive real parameter $r > 0$, consider the Chebyshev-type minimax approximation problem on the interval $[-1,1]$:
$$E_n(r) \;=\; \min_{b_0,b_1,\dots,b_{n-2}\in\mathbb{R}} \; \max_{x\in[-1,1]} \; \bigl|\, x^n + r\,x^{n-1} - (b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2 + \cdots + b_{n-2} x^{n-2})\,\bigr|.$$
That is, given the leading two terms $x^n + r x^{n-1}$, find the polynomial $B(x) = b_0 + b_1 x + \cdots + b_{n-2} x^{n-2}$ of degree at most $n-2$ that best approximates $x^n + r x^{n-1}$ in the uniform (sup) norm on $[-1,1]$.

The task is, working in the first-order theory of the real numbers, to perform quantifier elimination on the formula expressing the optimal value $E_n(r)$ and the optimal coefficients $b_0,\dots,b_{n-2}$ as functions of $r$, and to obtain by computer an explicit closed-form (semi-algebraic) description of the optimal $B$ and of $E_n(r)$ for $n \ge 6$. Equivalently, produce explicit algebraic expressions (as piecewise algebraic functions of $r$) for the coefficients $b_i(r)$ of the best approximant and for the minimax error.

The problem (often called Zolotarev's / Solotareff's problem, posed as a quantifier-elimination challenge by Collins in 1992) has been solved by general quantifier-elimination tools (e.g., qepcad) only for small degrees: a complete explicit semi-algebraic solution is known for n ≤ 4, and partial results (e.g., explicit form for n = 5, where the associated relation curve has genus 1) have been obtained via algebraic-geometric methods using curve parametrization. For general n ≥ 6, no complete closed-form solution by quantifier elimination has been reported; the problem remains a challenge benchmark.

Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with a finite generating set $A$, and let $A^*$ denote the set of finite words over $A \cup A^{-1}$. The group $G$ is said to be automatic if there exist a regular language $L \subseteq A^*$ (the language of normal forms) such that:
(i) the natural map $L \to G$ sending a word to the group element it represents is surjective;
(ii) for every generator $a \in A \cup A^{-1} \cup \{1\}$, the set
$$L_a = \{(u,v) \in L \times L : u \cdot a =_G v\}$$
is recognizable by a synchronous two-tape finite-state automaton (equivalently, the relation $L_a$ is regular in the sense of automatic structures).

A subgroup $H \le G$ is called a retract of $G$ if there exists a group homomorphism $r : G \to H$ such that $r(h) = h$ for every $h \in H$ (equivalently, $H$ is the image of an idempotent endomorphism of $G$).

Question: Is every retract of an automatic group itself automatic? That is, if $G$ is automatic and $H \le G$ is a retract of $G$, must $H$ admit an automatic structure?

Construct a public-key cryptosystem whose key generation, encryption, and decryption procedures are based on Diophantine linear algebra (i.e., on solving systems of linear equations and/or congruences over the integers, including problems such as computing Hermite or Smith normal forms, integer kernel/image bases, and integer solutions to A x = b modulo various moduli), and whose security can be rigorously based on a computational problem in this setting. The cryptosystem must satisfy the following requirements:

1. Correctness: legitimate decryption recovers the plaintext with overwhelming probability.
2. Efficiency: key generation, encryption, and decryption run in time polynomial in the security parameter.
3. Security: no probabilistic polynomial-time adversary can break the scheme (e.g., distinguish ciphertexts or recover the secret key) with non-negligible advantage. In particular, the security must not be reducible to, nor breakable by, known lattice basis reduction algorithms (such as LLL and its block variants like BKZ); that is, an adversary equipped with polynomial-time lattice reduction oracles for lattices of dimension polynomial in the security parameter must still be unable to break the scheme.

Provide such a cryptosystem together with a proof of security under a clearly stated, plausible hardness assumption from Diophantine linear algebra that is not known to be solvable by lattice basis reduction.

A subgroup $H \leq G$ has finite index if the set of cosets $G/H$ is finite, and $H$ is proper if $H \neq G$.

Let G be a group. For each n ≥ 1, regard a system of equations in n variables over G as a subset S ⊆ G * F_n, where F_n is the free group on x_1, …, x_n. A solution of S in G is a homomorphism φ: G * F_n → G that restricts to the identity on G and satisfies φ(s) = 1 for every s ∈ S. Two systems S, S' ⊆ G * F_n are equivalent if they have the same set of solutions in G. The group G is called equationally noetherian if for every n ≥ 1 and every system S ⊆ G * F_n there exists a finite subset S_0 ⊆ S such that S and S_0 are equivalent.

A finitely generated group G is called word-hyperbolic (in the sense of Gromov) if its Cayley graph with respect to some (equivalently, any) finite generating set is a δ-hyperbolic metric space for some δ ≥ 0.

Let $K$ be a field. Suppose we are given an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ which, on input a matrix $A \in K^{m \times n}$ and a vector $y \in K^n$, computes the matrix-vector product $A \cdot y \in K^m$ using at most $T(m,n)$ arithmetic operations in $K$ and at most $S(m,n)$ auxiliary space (i.e., space beyond that occupied by the input $A$, $y$ and the output).

The classical transposition principle (Tellegen's principle) shows that, when $\mathcal{A}$ is a linear straight-line program, one can transform it into an algorithm computing $A^{T} \cdot z$ for $z \in K^m$ using $O(T(m,n))$ arithmetic operations; however, the standard transformation may blow up the auxiliary space.

Problem: Provide a general construction that, given $\mathcal{A}$ as above, produces an algorithm computing $A^{T} \cdot z$ for any input $z \in K^m$ using simultaneously
- $O(T(m,n))$ arithmetic operations in $K$, and
- $O(S(m,n))$ auxiliary space.

The construction must be effective and applicable to practical problems (i.e., not merely an abstract simulation that destroys implementability).

The simultaneous time- and space-preserving transposition principle is widely cited as an open problem in symbolic computation. Consider the perturbed sine-Gordon equation

    ε u_{xxt}(x,t) + u_{xx}(x,t) − u_{tt}(x,t) − a u_t(x,t) = sin(u(x,t)) − γ,

where u(x,t) ∈ ℝ represents the phase difference between the wave functions of two superconductors separated by a thin insulating layer, ε > 0 and a > 0 are dissipation parameters modeling, respectively, longitudinal (surface) losses and shunt (in-line) losses across the junction, and γ ∈ ℝ is a normalized constant current bias.

Let the spatial domain be a bounded interval (or, more generally, a one-dimensional region) Ω = (−L, L) ⊂ ℝ partitioned into a finite collection of open subintervals Ω₁, …, Ω_N separated by interface points {x_1, …, x_{N−1}} ⊂ Ω. On each subdomain Ω_k the equation above holds, possibly with subdomain-dependent coefficients (ε_k, a_k, γ_k) modeling alternating "window" and "passive" regions of a window Josephson junction. At each interface point x_j impose interface (transmission) conditions of the form

    [u]_{x_j} := u(x_j^+, t) − u(x_j^−, t) = 0,
    [β u_x]_{x_j} := β(x_j^+) u_x(x_j^+, t) − β(x_j^−) u_x(x_j^−, t) = h_j(t),

where β(x) > 0 is a piecewise constant coefficient (encoding the differing junction characteristics on the two sides of the interface) and h_j(t) accounts for the action of an external magnetic field at the interface. Boundary conditions of the form u_x(±L, t) = H_±(t) (Neumann data corresponding to an applied magnetic field) and initial conditions u(x,0) = u_0(x), u_t(x,0) = u_1(x) are prescribed.

Formulate this initial-boundary-value problem with interface conditions rigorously and analyze it: in particular, establish existence, uniqueness, regularity, and continuous dependence on the data (ε, a, γ, β, h_j, H_±, u_0, u_1) of a solution u, and study the long-time qualitative behavior (e.g., stability of equilibria, propagation of fluxons across the interfaces) of the resulting phase dynamics.

Let $n\geq 2$ and let $P_n$ denote the pure braid group on $n$ strands, that is, the kernel of the natural surjection from the braid group $B_n$ onto the symmetric group $S_n$. Let $R = \mathbb{Z}[t_1^{\pm 1}, \ldots, t_n^{\pm 1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in $n$ commuting variables. The Gassner representation is the homomorphism
$$G_n : P_n \longrightarrow GL_n(R)$$
obtained as follows: identify $P_n$ with the fundamental group of the configuration space of $n$ ordered distinct points in the plane (based at a fixed configuration), and consider the action of $P_n$ on the first homology of the universal abelian cover of the punctured disk with $n$ punctures; choosing a basis yields an $n\times n$ matrix with entries in $R$ for each pure braid (after reduction one obtains an $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ "reduced" version, and faithfulness of either form is equivalent).

Question: Is $G_n$ injective for every $n \geq 2$? Equivalently, is the Gassner representation of the pure braid group $P_n$ faithful for all $n$?

Consider the third-order parabolic equation modeling phase dynamics in a Josephson junction,
  ε(φ_t − φ_xxt) − φ_xx + γ sin φ + α φ_t = f(x,t),   (x,t) ∈ (0,L) × (0,T),
where ε, α, γ > 0 and φ(x,t) denotes the phase difference of the macroscopic wave functions across the junction. Consider also the FitzHugh–Nagumo reaction–diffusion system
  u_t = D u_xx + u(u − a)(1 − u) − v + I(x,t),
  v_t = b u − c v,   (x,t) ∈ (0,L) × (0,T),
with 0 < a < 1, b, c, D > 0, where u(x,t) represents the membrane potential of a nerve axon at position x and time t and v(x,t) is a recovery variable modeling the transmembrane current.

Formulate Robin boundary value problems for both systems, namely conditions of the form
  α₁ φ(0,t) + β₁ φ_x(0,t) = g₁(t),   α₂ φ(L,t) + β₂ φ_x(L,t) = g₂(t),
and analogous Robin conditions on (u, v), with prescribed initial data, and develop a unified analytic theory (existence, uniqueness, regularity, a priori estimates, asymptotic behavior, and dependence on parameters) that exploits the equivalence under continuous parameter variations between the third-order Josephson equation and the FitzHugh–Nagumo system, in order to derive results applicable to the propagation of nerve impulses and related biological phenomena.

Consider the perturbed sine-Gordon equation modelling fluxon dynamics in a Josephson junction subject to an applied magnetic field parallel to the plane of the dielectric barrier:

(A)  ε u_{xxt} + u_{xx} − u_{tt} − a u_t = sin(u) − γ − b cos(k x),

posed for (x,t) ∈ (0,L) × (0,∞), with prescribed initial data u(x,0), u_t(x,0) and suitable boundary conditions at x = 0, L. Here ε > 0 is a small dissipative parameter, a > 0 is a normal-current dissipation coefficient, γ ∈ ℝ is the normalized bias current, b ∈ ℝ represents the magnitude of an applied magnetic field parallel to the dielectric barrier, and k > 0 is a wavenumber.

Consider also the microshort/annular variant

(B)  ε u_{xxt} + u_{xx} − u_{tt} − a u_t = [1 − δ(x) μ] sin(u) − γ − b cos(k x),

where δ(x) is the Dirac distribution at a point representing a localized microshort and μ ∈ ℝ is the current density associated with that microshort, possibly together with the presence of a gap in the vacuum chamber (modelled by an additional spatial discontinuity in the coefficients).

Questions:
(i) Establish well-posedness (existence, uniqueness and continuous dependence on data) for classical or weak solutions of equations (A) and (B) in suitable functional spaces.
(ii) Derive a priori energy-type estimates and pointwise/asymptotic-in-time bounds for the solution u and its derivatives in terms of ε, a, γ, b, k, μ and the data, analogous to those known for the standard perturbed sine-Gordon equation ε u_{xxt} + u_{xx} − u_{tt} − a u_t = sin(u) − γ.
(iii) Analyze the singular limit ε → 0⁺ and obtain uniform-in-ε estimates for both (A) and (B), including the case in which a gap in the vacuum chamber is incorporated into the model.

A geodesic metric space $(X,d)$ is said to be CAT($\kappa$) if every geodesic triangle in $X$ (with perimeter less than $2\pi/\sqrt{\kappa}$ when $\kappa>0$) is "thinner" than a comparison triangle of the same side lengths in the model surface $M_\kappa^2$ of constant curvature $\kappa$; precisely, for any geodesic triangle $\Delta$ in $X$ with vertices $x,y,z$ and any comparison triangle $\bar\Delta\subset M_\kappa^2$ with the same side lengths, and for any two points $p,q$ on the sides of $\Delta$ with corresponding points $\bar p,\bar q$ on $\bar\Delta$, one has $d(p,q)\le d_{M_\kappa^2}(\bar p,\bar q)$.

A finitely generated group $G$ is called (Gromov) hyperbolic if its Cayley graph (with respect to some, equivalently any, finite generating set) is $\delta$-hyperbolic for some $\delta\ge 0$, meaning that every geodesic triangle has each side contained in the $\delta$-neighborhood of the union of the other two.

An action of $G$ on a metric space $X$ by isometries is called geometric (i.e., properly discontinuously and cocompactly) if it is properly discontinuous and the quotient $X/G$ is compact.

Question: Does every Gromov hyperbolic group $G$ admit a geometric action by isometries on some CAT($\kappa$) space for some real number $\kappa<0$?

Recent work by Chen, Kordek, and Margalit (2019, revised 2023) gives a complete classification of endomorphisms of $B_4$, and classifies homomorphisms $B_n\to B_{2n}$ for $n\ge 5$, indicating significant progress on the structure of homomorphisms between braid groups. Consider the linear third-order parabolic operator with variable coefficients
\[
L\,u \;=\; \varepsilon(x,t)\,u_{xxt} \;-\; u_{tt} \;+\; u_{xx} \;-\; \alpha(x,t)\,u_{t},
\]
and the associated semilinear equation modeling an exponentially shaped Josephson junction with variable coefficients
\[
\varepsilon(x,t)\,u_{xxt} \;+\; u_{xx} \;-\; u_{tt} \;-\; \varepsilon(x,t)\,\lambda(x,t)\,u_{xt} \;-\; \lambda(x,t)\,u_{x} \;-\; a(x,t,u)\,u_{t} \;=\; \sin u,
\]
posed for $(x,t)\in(0,1)\times(0,T)$ with prescribed initial data $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$, $u_t(x,0)=u_1(x)$ and boundary conditions (e.g. Dirichlet, Neumann, or periodic) on $x=0,1$. Here $\varepsilon,\alpha,\lambda$ are given strictly positive smooth functions of $(x,t)$ (no longer required to be constant), and the damping coefficient $a$ may depend on the unknown phase $u$, with the prototypical phase-dependent choice $a(u)=1-\cos u$.

Develop a qualitative theory for these operators and equations with nonconstant coefficients. Specifically:
(i) prove existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence on the data for the corresponding initial-boundary value problems;
(ii) construct a fundamental solution (or Green's function) for the variable-coefficient operator $L$ above and establish its sign, decay, and regularity properties;
(iii) derive a priori estimates ensuring boundedness of solutions, and analyze their asymptotic behavior as $t\to\infty$ (including stability of equilibria and dissipative properties);
(iv) treat in particular the phase-dependent damping case $a=1-\cos u$.

Let G be a finitely generated group with finite generating set A, and let A* denote the free monoid on A ∪ A^{-1}. A combing of G is a section σ: G → A* of the natural evaluation map (so σ(g) is a word representing g for every g ∈ G) such that the family {σ(g) : g ∈ G} satisfies the synchronous fellow-traveller property: there exists a constant K ≥ 0 such that for all g, h ∈ G with d_A(g, h) ≤ 1 (in the word metric), and for every t ≥ 0,
   d_A( σ(g)(t), σ(h)(t) ) ≤ K,
where σ(g)(t) denotes the element of G obtained by reading the first t letters of σ(g) (with σ(g)(t) := g once t exceeds the length of σ(g)). The group G is called combable if it admits such a combing for some finite generating set.

The group G is called automatic if, in addition, there exists a finite generating set and a combing σ such that the language L = {σ(g) : g ∈ G} ⊂ A* is a regular language (i.e., recognized by some finite-state automaton).

Question: Is every combable group automatic?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has a negative answer. Bridson constructed synchronously combable groups whose Dehn function is cubic (in particular, strictly greater than quadratic). Since every automatic group satisfies a quadratic isoperimetric inequality, such groups are combable but not automatic, resolving the question in the negative.

Let $n \geq 4$ be an integer, and let $B_n$ denote the Artin braid group on $n$ strands, given by the presentation
$$B_n = \langle \sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_{n-1} \mid \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \text{ for } 1 \leq i \leq n-2,\ \sigma_i \sigma_j = \sigma_j \sigma_i \text{ for } |i-j| \geq 2 \rangle.$$
A factor group (quotient group) of $B_n$ is any group of the form $B_n / N$ where $N$ is a normal subgroup of $B_n$. Such a factor group is called proper if $N \neq \{1\}$, torsion-free if it has no nontrivial elements of finite order, and nonabelian if it is not abelian.

Question: Does there exist a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq B_n$ with $N \neq \{1\}$ such that the quotient $B_n / N$ is both torsion-free and nonabelian?

For a massive star (initial mass ≳ 10 M☉), two independent methods are used to estimate its current mass:

1. The evolutionary mass M_evol, obtained by placing the star at its measured effective temperature and luminosity on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram and reading off the mass from a grid of stellar evolutionary tracks (which may include rotational mixing, overshooting, and prescribed mass loss).

2. The spectroscopic mass M_spec, obtained from a quantitative non-LTE stellar-atmosphere analysis of the star's spectrum, which yields the surface gravity log g and effective temperature T_eff; together with the radius R inferred from luminosity and T_eff, this gives M_spec = g R² / G.

Empirically, in samples of OB stars in the Milky Way, the Large Magellanic Cloud, and the Small Magellanic Cloud, these two estimates disagree systematically: even after incorporating line blanketing in the atmosphere models and rotational mixing in the evolutionary models, residual differences |M_evol − M_spec| / M_evol of order 20%–50% persist, generally in the sense that M_evol > M_spec (the "mass discrepancy").

Problem. Identify the physical or modeling ingredient(s) — for instance, prescriptions for mass loss, internal mixing, convective core boundary treatment, binarity and mass transfer, magnetic fields, micro/macroturbulence in atmosphere modeling, treatment of the wind/photosphere transition, or other effects — whose inclusion (or correction) in the evolutionary tracks and/or in the atmosphere analyses is necessary and sufficient to bring M_evol and M_spec into statistical agreement across the Milky Way, LMC, and SMC samples. Equivalently, determine whether the residual 20%–50% discrepancy reflects a genuine deficiency of stellar evolution theory, of stellar atmosphere theory, of the observational inputs (T_eff, log g, L, distance), or some combination thereof.

Recent literature continues to report a residual systematic difference between evolutionary and spectroscopic masses of OB-type and red supergiant stars. A 2018 A&A study of Galactic O-type stars finds the mass discrepancy persists and varies with luminosity/mass regime; a 2024 study of red supergiants at subsolar metallicity proposes that intrinsically hotter temperatures (lower TiO opacity) can largely reconcile the masses for that subclass, but no single ingredient has been shown to remove the discrepancy uniformly across MW/LMC/SMC OB-star samples. Let $G$ be a word-hyperbolic group with a fixed finite generating set $S$, and let $d_S$ denote the associated word metric on the Cayley graph of $G$. A subgroup $H \le G$ is called:

- **quasiconvex** if there exists a constant $K \ge 0$ such that every geodesic in the Cayley graph between two elements of $H$ stays within the $K$-neighborhood of $H$;
- **malnormal** if for every $g \in G \setminus H$, one has $gHg^{-1} \cap H = \{1\}$.

Question: Suppose $H$ is a finitely generated malnormal subgroup of the hyperbolic group $G$. Must $H$ be quasiconvex in $G$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question (often attributed to Bestvina) is widely cited as an open problem in geometric group theory. Partial results are known: quasiconvex subgroups of hyperbolic groups have finite height (Gitik–Mitra–Rips–Sageev), and finitely generated malnormal subgroups of one-ended hyperbolic right-angled Coxeter groups are quasiconvex. However, no proof or counterexample is known in the general hyperbolic-group setting.

representations.normalized:
Red supergiants (RSGs) are evolved massive stars whose effective temperatures T_eff are commonly estimated by two largely independent observational techniques:

(i) fitting the strengths and shapes of TiO molecular absorption bands in the optical spectrum using model stellar atmospheres, and

(ii) fitting the broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) and/or applying the Far-Infrared Flux Method (FIFM), which rely on continuum fluxes formed in deeper atmospheric layers.

In practice these two approaches yield systematically different T_eff for the same RSGs, with TiO-based temperatures being several hundred Kelvin cooler than SED/FIFM-based temperatures. TiO bands form high in the atmosphere, where opacities, density/temperature stratification, and three-dimensional (convective/granulation) effects are expected to be large, while the continuum forms much deeper.

Problem. Determine the correct effective-temperature scale of red supergiants and provide a physically consistent revision of stellar-atmosphere and stellar-evolution models that simultaneously:

(a) reconciles the TiO-band temperatures with the SED and far-infrared continuum temperatures (specifying the role of upper-atmosphere opacity, non-LTE effects, hydrodynamic structure, and 3D granulation in the line-forming region of TiO);

(b) yields a quantitative prediction of the coolest T_eff a red supergiant can attain on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, and clarifies the dependence of this lower T_eff limit on the convective-overshooting parameter (and other mixing prescriptions) used in evolutionary tracks for massive stars.

Provide either a definitive unified T_eff scale calibrated against both diagnostics, or a rigorous demonstration of which atmospheric/evolutionary modelling assumptions must be modified to remove the discrepancy.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The discrepancy between TiO-band and SED/far-infrared temperature scales for red supergiants is well established and partially understood: 3D granulation and upper-atmosphere effects in the TiO line-forming region are widely identified as the dominant cause, and recent (2018, 2021, 2024) studies (e.g. LTE T_eff scales for Magellanic Cloud RSGs, line-depth-ratio diagnostics, and subsolar-metallicity RSG surveys) have refined and partially calibrated SED-based temperature scales and proposed empirical J−Ks color–temperature relations to bring TiO temperatures into agreement with evolutionary tracks. However, a fully consistent atmosphere+evolution model that resolves the discrepancy and pins down the coolest attainable T_eff (and its overshooting dependence) has not yet been agreed upon, so the question is best characterized as partially solved.

For an integer $n \geq 1$, let $B_n$ denote the Artin braid group on $n$ strands, which is the group with generators $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \dots, \sigma_{n-1}$ subject to the relations
$$\sigma_i \sigma_j = \sigma_j \sigma_i \quad \text{whenever } |i-j| \geq 2,$$
$$\sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \quad \text{for } 1 \leq i \leq n-2.$$
A linear representation of a group $G$ is a homomorphism $\rho : G \to \mathrm{GL}_d(K)$ for some integer $d \geq 1$ and some field $K$. The representation is called faithful if $\rho$ is injective.

Question: For every integer $n \geq 1$, does the braid group $B_n$ admit a faithful linear representation over some field?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem is solved positively. Bigelow (2001) and Krammer (2000, 2002) independently proved that the braid groups $B_n$ are linear for all $n$, by showing the Lawrence–Krammer representation is faithful.

Let $r > 2$ and $c \geq 2$ be integers. Let $N_{r,c}$ denote the free nilpotent group of rank $r$ and nilpotency class $c$; that is, $N_{r,c} = F_r / \gamma_{c+1}(F_r)$, where $F_r$ is the free group of rank $r$ and $\gamma_{c+1}(F_r)$ is the $(c+1)$-st term of its lower central series. Let $\mathrm{Aut}(N_{r,c})$ denote the group of all automorphisms of $N_{r,c}$, and define the fixed-point subgroup
$$\mathrm{Fix}(\mathrm{Aut}(N_{r,c})) := \{\, g \in N_{r,c} : \varphi(g) = g \text{ for every } \varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(N_{r,c}) \,\}.$$
Prove or disprove: $\mathrm{Fix}(\mathrm{Aut}(N_{r,c})) = \{1\}$ for every $r > 2$ and every $c \geq 2$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Web searches did not surface a definitive resolution of the question of whether the subgroup of elements fixed by every automorphism of a free nilpotent group of rank greater than 2 is trivial. Related results address fixed points of specific (e.g. Frobenius, central, or finite-order) automorphisms, but no source clearly settles this problem in full generality.

representations.normalized:
Consider hot, massive O-type stars whose stellar winds are believed to be driven by radiation pressure on metal lines (the standard radiatively driven wind theory). The theory predicts a quantitative scaling of the modified wind momentum

  D_mom = M_dot · v_inf · sqrt(R/R_sun)

with stellar luminosity and metallicity Z, namely log D_mom = x log(L/L_sun) + log D_0(Z), with D_0 decreasing as Z decreases. Empirical determinations of D_mom for O-type stars in the very low-metallicity dwarf galaxies IC 1613, WLM, and NGC 3109 — whose nebular oxygen abundances lie roughly between one-tenth and one-seventh of the solar value — have been reported to lie systematically above the theoretical prediction, suggesting either (a) a breakdown of radiatively driven wind theory at very low metallicity, or (b) the onset of an additional wind-driving mechanism not contained in the standard theory.

A competing explanation attributes the apparent excess to systematics: overestimated terminal wind velocities v_inf inferred from limited UV/optical diagnostics, and the use of oxygen as the metallicity proxy together with an assumed solar α/Fe ratio, when in fact these galaxies may possess a subsolar α/Fe ratio so that the iron-group abundance (which dominates radiative line driving) is higher than the oxygen-based estimate suggests.

Question: At metallicities Z ≈ Z_sun/10 to Z_sun/7, does standard radiatively driven wind theory genuinely fail to predict the observed wind momenta of O-type stars, or are the reported discrepancies fully accounted for by measurement systematics in v_inf and by abundance assumptions (in particular the assumed α/Fe ratio)? Equivalently, after correcting for these systematics, do the empirical wind momenta of O stars in IC 1613, WLM, and NGC 3109 lie on the extrapolation of the modified-wind-momentum–luminosity–metallicity relation predicted by line-driven wind theory?

Subsequent work, in particular Bouret et al. (MNRAS 449, 1545, 2015, "No breakdown of the radiatively driven wind theory in low-metallicity environments") and FUV (HST-COS) analyses of OB stars in IC 1613, argues that the apparent excess wind momenta originate from overestimated terminal velocities and from underestimated metallicities (subsolar α/Fe), and that empirical mass-loss rates are consistent with line-driven wind predictions, i.e. no breakdown. However, sample sizes remain small and the question of an additional driving mechanism at very low Z is not definitively excluded across all luminosity regimes; thus the issue is partially resolved rather than fully closed.

Let $B_n$ denote the braid group on $n$ strands, with standard Artin generators $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ subject to the relations $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$. The (reduced) Burau representation is the homomorphism $\beta_n:B_n\to GL_{n-1}(\mathbb{Z}[t,t^{-1}])$ defined on generators by the standard $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrices over the ring of Laurent polynomials in one variable $t$ obtained from the action of $B_n$ on the homology of the infinite cyclic cover of the $n$-punctured disk.

Determine whether $\beta_n$ is faithful (i.e., injective) in each of the following two cases:
(a) $n=4$;
(b) $n=5$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The case n=5 was settled by Bigelow (1999), who proved the Burau representation of B_5 is not faithful; this also implies non-faithfulness for all n≥5. The case n=4 remains open as of recent work; partial results show faithfulness up to large complexity bounds and "almost everywhere" faithfulness, but no full proof or disproof is known.

A group $G$ is called locally nilpotent if every finitely generated subgroup of $G$ is nilpotent. The group $G$ is called torsion-free if it has no non-identity elements of finite order.

Question: Is it true that every locally nilpotent group is a homomorphic image of some torsion-free locally nilpotent group? That is, for every locally nilpotent group $G$, does there exist a torsion-free locally nilpotent group $H$ together with a surjective group homomorphism $H \twoheadrightarrow G$?
