representations.normalized:
Early-type massive stars (spectral types O and early B) frequently show surface abundance patterns indicative of nuclear-processed material, in particular enhanced helium and altered carbon, nitrogen and oxygen (CNO) ratios consistent with partial CNO-cycle processing. Several physical mechanisms are known to be capable of dredging such material from the stellar interior to the photosphere, including: (i) rotational mixing driven by meridional circulation and shear instabilities in differentially rotating radiative envelopes; (ii) mass and angular-momentum exchange in close binary systems (Roche-lobe overflow, tidal mixing, mergers); (iii) magnetic braking and large-scale magnetic-field effects that alter internal angular-momentum transport and mixing; and (iv) other internal instabilities (e.g. gravity-wave transport, semiconvection, thermohaline mixing). To first order, all of these processes can reproduce qualitatively similar surface helium and CNO enrichment patterns.

Problem. Identify a set of second-order observational diagnostics — for example, quantitative correlations between stellar parameters (surface abundances, projected rotational velocity v sin i, mass, luminosity, surface gravity, magnetic-field strength, binary status, age) or characteristic time scales of enrichment — that can unambiguously and consistently discriminate among rotational mixing, binary interaction, magnetic effects, and internal instabilities as the dominant mechanism responsible for surface chemical enrichment in early massive stars.

As of recent literature on massive-star evolution and large spectroscopic surveys (e.g., VLT-FLAMES, IACOB, BLOeM), the relative contributions of rotational mixing, binarity, and magnetism to surface CNO/He enrichment remain debated and no single diagnostic has been established to disentangle them definitively.

Let $n \geq 2$ and let $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}[t, t^{-1}]$ denote the ring of Laurent polynomials in one variable with integer coefficients. The (unreduced) Burau representation of the braid group $B_n$ on $n$ strands is the homomorphism $\rho_n : B_n \to \mathrm{GL}_n(\Lambda)$ defined on the standard Artin generators $\sigma_i$ ($1 \le i \le n-1$) by sending $\sigma_i$ to the block-diagonal matrix
$$\rho_n(\sigma_i) = I_{i-1} \oplus \begin{pmatrix} 1-t & t \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \oplus I_{n-i-1}.$$
The reduced Burau representation $\bar{\rho}_n : B_n \to \mathrm{GL}_{n-1}(\Lambda)$ is obtained from $\rho_n$ by restricting to an invariant $(n-1)$-dimensional summand.

Problem. Give necessary and sufficient conditions on a square matrix $M \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\Lambda)$ (respectively $M \in \mathrm{GL}_{n-1}(\Lambda)$) for $M$ to lie in the image of $\rho_n$ (respectively $\bar{\rho}_n$); equivalently, characterize intrinsically those matrices over $\Lambda$ that arise as the Burau matrix of some braid in $B_n$.

No intrinsic characterization of the image of the Burau representation appears in the literature. The representation is known to be faithful for n ≤ 3, non-faithful for n ≥ 5 (Bigelow, Long–Paton), and the case n = 4 is itself still open. Recent work (e.g., Salter on linear-central filtrations and the image of the Burau representation) gives partial information about the image but does not provide a complete set of necessary and sufficient conditions. The problem appears to remain open.

A group is finitely generated if it is generated, as a group, by some finite subset.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, given a finite presentation of a finitely generated nilpotent group $G$, decides whether $G$ is directly indecomposable?

representations.normalized:
Spectral lines observed in massive O- and B-type stars exhibit a non-thermal broadening component, conventionally called macroturbulent broadening, which is in excess of thermal Doppler broadening, natural broadening, collisional broadening, and rotational broadening, and which is empirically modeled by convolving the intrinsic line profile with a (typically radial-tangential) velocity distribution of characteristic amplitude of order tens of km/s. The physical mechanism producing this broadening is not established. Candidate mechanisms include: (i) collective effects of high-order, low-degree heat-driven (kappa-mechanism) gravity-mode pulsations excited in the stellar envelope; (ii) turbulent pressure fluctuations generated by subsurface convective layers associated with the iron opacity bump; and (iii) coherent and stochastic surface velocity fields produced by convection-driven internal gravity waves propagating from the convective core (or from subsurface convection zones) to the photosphere.

Determine the physical origin of macroturbulent line broadening in massive O- and B-type stars across the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. Specifically, decide whether a single mechanism among (i)–(iii) is dominant throughout the OB regime, or whether different mechanisms dominate in distinct regions of the parameter space spanned by mass, evolutionary stage, and surface gravity; and in the latter case, identify the boundaries in this parameter space and the relative contributions of each mechanism to the observed macroturbulent velocity.

Recent observational and modeling work (notably the 2024 A&A study from the ESO UVES/FEROS Large Programs of TESS OB pulsators) provides evidence that kappa-driven gravity-mode pulsations alone cannot explain macroturbulence in high-mass stars, that subsurface iron-opacity-bump convection (FeCZ) correlates with macroturbulent velocities for stars above ~30 M⊙, and that internal gravity waves are favored for stars below ~12 M⊙, with both contributing in the intermediate range. The problem is therefore partially resolved: a regime-dependent picture is emerging, but a definitive, quantitative attribution across all OB stars remains open.

Let $p$ be a prime, $L = \mathbb{F}_q$ with $q = p^n$, and let $\psi\colon L \to \mathbb{C}^\times$ be the canonical additive character $\psi(x) = \exp(2\pi i\,\mathrm{Tr}_{L/\mathbb{F}_p}(x)/p)$. For an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$ (so that $x \mapsto x^s$ is a permutation of $L$), define the Weil sum
$$W_{L,s}(a) \;=\; \sum_{x \in L} \psi(x^s - a x), \qquad a \in L.$$
The reduced spectrum of $W_{L,s}$ is the set $\{\,W_{L,s}(a) : a \in L^\times\,\}$ of distinct values taken on the nonzero elements. Call $s$ $k$-valued (over $L$) when this reduced spectrum has exactly $k$ elements. An exponent $s$ is called singular if $s \equiv p^j \pmod{q-1}$ for some $j$ would fail (precise standard definition: $s$ is degenerate/non-singular if $s$ is a power of $p$ modulo $q-1$; otherwise non-degenerate; "singular" is taken in the sense used for three-valued spectra).

It is known (three-valued theorem) that if $s$ is three-valued then $s$ is singular, $s \equiv 1 \pmod{p-1}$, and the reduced spectrum $\{0, A, B\}$ consists of rational integers.

Problem: Establish an analogous structural theorem for four-valued exponents. Specifically, determine which congruence conditions on $s$ (modulo $p-1$ or otherwise), which singularity/non-degeneracy conditions, and which arithmetic restrictions on the four values of the reduced spectrum (e.g. integrality or rationality) must hold whenever $s$ is four-valued over $L$.

Katz and Wong (2023/2024) established a rationality result for four-valued Weil spectra: if the spectrum has exactly four values, then all four are rational integers, with the sole exception of $L=\mathbb{F}_5$ and $s \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. This addresses the integrality aspect of the analogue, but the full structural analogue (congruence on $s$ modulo $p-1$ and singularity in the same form as the three-valued theorem) is not fully resolved.

A group $G$ is called metabelian if its commutator subgroup $[G,G]$ is abelian, equivalently, if $G$ admits a normal abelian subgroup $A$ with $G/A$ abelian. A group is finitely presented if it is isomorphic to $\langle X \mid R\rangle$ for some finite set $X$ of generators and finite set $R$ of relators.

The isomorphism problem for a class $\mathcal{C}$ of finitely presented groups asks for an algorithm which, given two finite presentations $\langle X_1 \mid R_1\rangle$ and $\langle X_2 \mid R_2\rangle$ both defining groups in $\mathcal{C}$, decides in finite time whether the two groups they present are isomorphic.

Question: Does there exist such an algorithm when $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of all finitely presented metabelian groups? In other words, is the isomorphism problem decidable for finitely presented metabelian groups?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The decidability of the isomorphism problem for finitely presented metabelian groups is widely cited as an open problem. Surveys list it among the major open algorithmic questions in combinatorial group theory; the isomorphism problem has been fully resolved for nilpotent, hyperbolic, and limit groups, but not for the metabelian class. Partial progress exists for specific families (e.g., residually nilpotent metabelian groups, free metabelian recognition), but the general problem remains unresolved.

Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $L=\mathbb{F}_p$ be the prime field of order $p$, and let $s$ be an integer with $\gcd(s, p-1)=1$ (an invertible exponent). For $u,v\in L$, define
$$N(u,v) = \#\{(x,y)\in L\times L : x+y=u,\ x^s+y^s=v\}.$$
Call $s$ "nice" if, as $v$ ranges over $L\setminus\{1\}$, the multiset $\{N(1,v)\}$ takes at most three distinct values.

Declare two exponents $s, s'$ equivalent (write $s\approx s'$) if $s'\equiv p^j s \pmod{p-1}$ for some integer $j\ge 0$ (a Frobenius twist; trivial in the prime-field case) or $s s' \equiv 1 \pmod{p-1}$ (inversion), and take the equivalence relation generated by these.

Two "paradigmatic" families of nice exponents are known explicitly (corresponding to standard quadratic-type and other classical constructions giving three-valued $N(1,\cdot)$).

Question: Prove or disprove that for every odd prime $p$, every nice exponent $s$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $s\not\approx 1$ is equivalent (under the relation above) to a member of one of these paradigmatic families.

Let $B_n$ denote the Artin braid group on $n$ strands, with standard presentation generated by $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{n-1}$ subject to the braid relations $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$ for $1\le i\le n-2$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i$ for $|i-j|\ge 2$. Let $[B_n,B_n]$ denote the commutator subgroup of $B_n$. A group homomorphism $\varphi:[B_n,B_n]\to[B_n,B_n]$ is called an endomorphism of $[B_n,B_n]$, and is said to be nontrivial if its image is not the trivial subgroup. We say that $\varphi$ extends to an endomorphism of $B_n$ if there exists a homomorphism $\Phi:B_n\to B_n$ such that $\Phi$ restricted to $[B_n,B_n]$ equals $\varphi$ (in particular this requires $\Phi([B_n,B_n])\subseteq [B_n,B_n]$).

Question: For every integer $n\ge 4$, does every nontrivial endomorphism of $[B_n,B_n]$ extend to an endomorphism of $B_n$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Kordek (Bull. London Math. Soc., 2022) classified homomorphisms from $[B_n,B_n]$ to $B_n$ for $n\ge 7$, showing in particular that every nontrivial such homomorphism extends to an endomorphism (in fact an automorphism) of $B_n$. Related work by Chen–Kordek–Margalit handles further homomorphism rigidity results. The cases $n=4,5,6$ do not appear to be fully settled by these results, so the question in full generality for all $n\ge 4$ remains only partially resolved.

It is a theorem (due to Gersten–Holt–Riley) that every finitely generated nilpotent group of class c has Dehn function bounded above by n^{c+1}, and the Dehn function is known to be polynomial (more precisely, equivalent to n^d for some integer d). Hamkins (1998) showed that every group's transfinite automorphism tower terminates, but this does not directly settle the finite-stage question for finitely generated torsion-free nilpotent groups. Kassabov later proved Baumslag's conjecture in the special case of finitely generated free nilpotent groups, giving an explicit bound on the height of the tower in terms of rank and nilpotency class. The general question for arbitrary finitely generated torsion-free nilpotent groups appears not to have been fully resolved.

The problem appears to be partially resolved. Timoshenko settled the metabelian case ($d=2$) affirmatively. Gupta and Shpilrain proved triviality of the center for solvable groups of arbitrary derived length under the additional hypothesis that the relator is not a proper power modulo any term of the derived series. status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general question of whether the direct product of two finitely generated Hopfian groups is Hopfian is well known to have a negative answer in general, but the restriction to finitely generated solvable Hopfian groups appears to remain open. In the variety of metabelian groups (groups $G$ satisfying $[[G,G],[G,G]]=1$), a group $P$ is called projective if for every surjective homomorphism $\pi:A\twoheadrightarrow B$ between metabelian groups and every homomorphism $f:P\to B$, there exists a homomorphism $\tilde f:P\to A$ with $\pi\circ\tilde f=f$. The rank of a metabelian group is the minimal cardinality of a generating set. A free metabelian group of rank $\kappa$ is the free object of rank $\kappa$ in the variety of metabelian groups.

Question: Is every projective object of infinite countable rank in the variety of metabelian groups necessarily a free metabelian group?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem appears in the well-known list of open problems in combinatorial group theory (problem M4, attributed to P. Hall) maintained on Shpilrain's problems page and in Baumslag's compilations. The finite-rank case is known to be answered affirmatively, but the countably-infinite-rank case is listed as still open in the second edition of these problem lists.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

A theorem of Göbel and Paras (Illinois J. Math., 1998) shows that for every group $H$ there exists a torsion-free metabelian group $G$ with trivial center such that $\mathrm{Out}(G)\cong H$. Hence no group $H$ fails to be realized in this way, resolving the question in the negative.

representations.normalized:
Consider an isolated rotating neutron star ("pulsar") whose spin angular frequency Ω(t) decreases in time according to a braking law of the form

  dΩ/dt = −K(Ω, t) Ω^p,

so that the dimensionless braking index is defined by

  n = Ω Ω̈ / (Ω̇)^2.

In the canonical magnetic-dipole-radiation model, the star is modeled as a rigid sphere with constant moment of inertia I, constant magnetic dipole moment m, and constant inclination angle α between m and the rotation axis, giving the spin-down torque I Ω̇ ∝ −m^2 sin^2(α) Ω^3 and hence the canonical value n = 3.

Allowing the moment of inertia I(Ω) to vary with rotation through centrifugal deformation of a relativistic star yields a corrected braking index that depends on dI/dΩ. Numerical studies of realistic equations of state show that for spin frequencies ν = Ω/(2π) below roughly 160 Hz, the rotation-induced change in I is too small to shift n appreciably from 3, even for the most easily deformed (low-mass, soft-equation-of-state) configurations.

The observed sample of isolated pulsars with reliably measured braking indices lies in the low-frequency range ν ≈ 1–30 Hz, yet exhibits braking indices spread over a wide interval (notably values significantly below 3 and in some cases above 3) that cannot be accounted for by the I(Ω) mechanism alone.

Problem: Identify which physical parameter(s) entering the braking torque — for example, the magnetic dipole magnitude m, the inclination angle α, the effective magnetospheric/plasma-loading coefficient, the multipolar structure of the magnetic field, or other torque ingredients — must vary with frequency (or with time) at these low spin frequencies, and determine a quantitatively consistent prescription for their evolution that reproduces the observed range of braking indices for pulsars with ν ≈ 1–30 Hz.

The question of which torque parameters must evolve to explain anomalous braking indices of slowly rotating isolated pulsars remains an active research topic. Subsequent works propose various partial mechanisms (e.g., a two-dipole model with a migrating/growing dipole, magnetospheric/plasma effects, wobble models, oscillation damping, hierarchical Bayesian population fits), but no single, observationally validated prescription has been established. A finitely generated group $G$ is called word hyperbolic if its Cayley graph (with respect to some, equivalently any, finite generating set) is a Gromov-hyperbolic metric space. A finite presentation $\langle X \mid R\rangle$ of $G$ is called a Dehn presentation if for every nontrivial word $w$ in $X \cup X^{-1}$ representing the identity in $G$, there exist a relator $r \in R$ (cyclically reduced) and a factorization $r = uv$ such that $w$ contains $u$ as a subword and $|v| < |u|$; equivalently, the word problem can be solved by iteratively replacing such subwords $u$ by $v^{-1}$, strictly decreasing the length at every step. It is a theorem of Gromov that a finitely presented group is word hyperbolic if and only if it admits a Dehn presentation.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, given as input an arbitrary finite presentation $\langle X \mid R\rangle$ of a word hyperbolic group $G$ (not assumed to be a Dehn presentation), produces in time polynomial in the total length of the input a Dehn presentation for $G$?

Fix an integer $d \geq 2$ and let $\mathcal{S}_d$ denote the variety of all groups whose derived series terminates at the trivial subgroup in at most $d$ steps (i.e., solvable groups of derived length at most $d$). For a free group $F$ on a finite set $X$ in this variety (the relatively free group of rank $|X|$ in $\mathcal{S}_d$) and a single element $r \in F$, let $G = F/\langle\langle r \rangle\rangle$ be the one-relator group in the variety $\mathcal{S}_d$, where $\langle\langle r \rangle\rangle$ is the normal closure of $r$ in $F$. The word problem for $G$ asks for an algorithm that, on input a word $w$ in the generators $X$ and their inverses, decides whether $w$ represents the identity element of $G$.

Question: For every fixed $d \geq 2$, and for every choice of finite generating set $X$ and relator $r$, is the word problem for the one-relator group $G$ in the variety $\mathcal{S}_d$ uniformly solvable?

Consider an isolated, rotating, magnetized neutron star whose angular frequency Ω evolves under a combination of spin-down torques. Define the braking index by

  n = Ω · Ω̈ / Ω̇²,

so that a single power-law torque Ω̇ ∝ −Ω^k yields n = k. Assume the total spin-down torque is a sum of (i) a magnetic dipole radiation (MDR) contribution with intrinsic braking index n = 3, (ii) a relativistic particle-wind contribution with intrinsic braking index n = 1, and (iii) possibly a quadrupole-radiation contribution with intrinsic braking index n = 5. The magnitude of each torque depends on the surface magnetic field B(t), which may itself evolve in time, and the wind and dipole torques share this dependence on B(t).

Determine, as a function of the observed braking index n_obs ∈ (1, 3), what fraction f_w of the instantaneous rotational energy-loss rate (or equivalently of the spin-down torque) is contributed by the relativistic particle wind, given the coupling of the wind torque to the same magnetic-field evolution that affects the dipole torque. Equivalently, given a model in which

  −I Ω Ω̇ = L_dip(B,Ω) + L_wind(B,Ω),

with L_dip producing intrinsic n = 3 and L_wind producing intrinsic n = 1, derive the relation between n_obs, the ratio L_wind/L_dip, and the magnetic-field decay/growth law dB/dt, and use it to quantify the wind's contribution for pulsars whose measured braking indices fall between roughly 1 and 3.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question of quantifying the relativistic particle-wind contribution to pulsar spin-down has been actively studied. Combined dipole-plus-wind torque models yield braking indices in the observed 1 < n < 3 range, and explicit decompositions have been computed for individual pulsars: e.g., for the Crab pulsar a particle-wind component is estimated to contribute ~25% of the rotational energy-loss rate, and for several pulsars wind and dipole contributions have been found to be of comparable magnitude. However, no single universal formula uniquely fixes the wind fraction across all pulsars because the result depends on assumed magnetic-field evolution and wind luminosity scaling, so the broader question remains only partially resolved.

Let $k \geq 2$ and $d \geq 1$ be integers. Let $F_k$ denote the free group of rank $k$, and define its derived series by $F_k^{(0)} = F_k$ and $F_k^{(i+1)} = [F_k^{(i)}, F_k^{(i)}]$ for $i \geq 0$. The free solvable group of rank $k$ and derived length $d$ is the quotient $S_{k,d} := F_k / F_k^{(d)}$. Its commutator subgroup $[S_{k,d}, S_{k,d}]$ consists of all finite products of commutators $[a,b] = a^{-1}b^{-1}ab$ with $a,b \in S_{k,d}$. For an element $g \in [S_{k,d}, S_{k,d}]$, define its commutator length $\mathrm{cl}(g)$ to be the least integer $n \geq 0$ such that $g$ can be written as a product of $n$ commutators in $S_{k,d}$. The commutator width of $S_{k,d}$ is $\mathrm{cw}(S_{k,d}) := \sup_{g \in [S_{k,d}, S_{k,d}]} \mathrm{cl}(g) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \cup \{\infty\}$.

Question: Does there exist, for each pair $(k,d)$ with $k \geq 2$ and $d \geq 2$, a finite integer $N(k,d)$ such that $\mathrm{cw}(S_{k,d}) \leq N(k,d)$? Equivalently, is every element of the commutator subgroup of $S_{k,d}$ a product of at most $N(k,d)$ commutators?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question is classical (often attributed as a problem of Kargapolov). It is known via results of Allambergenov and Romankov that for rank $k \geq 2$ and derived length $d \geq 3$, the free solvable group $S_{k,d}$ has infinite commutator width, so no such bound $N(k,d)$ exists in general. Web sources confirm that finitely generated solvable groups can have infinite commutator width and that commutator widths of free solvable groups have been studied with such negative results in the literature.

Let $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,0)	o(\mathbb{C},0)$ be an isolated hypersurface singularity that is not simple (i.e., not of ADE type), with Milnor number $\mu$. Fix a small disc $D\subset\mathbb{C}$ around $0$ and a configuration of $\mu$ distinct points $z_1,\dots,z_\mu\in D\setminus\{0\}$, together with a distinguished system of non-intersecting paths $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_\mu$ in $D$ joining $0$ to $z_1,\dots,z_\mu$ respectively (an "easy" distinguished path system).

A Morsification of $f$ with these critical values is a holomorphic perturbation $f_\lambda$ of $f$ all of whose critical points are nondegenerate and whose critical values are exactly $z_1,\dots,z_\mu$. To each such $f_\lambda$ and the chosen path system there is associated, via vanishing cycles transported along the paths $\gamma_i$ to a regular fiber over $0$, a Dynkin diagram (a graph on $\mu$ vertices encoding the intersection form of the vanishing cycles).

Let $\Delta_0$ denote the Dynkin diagram obtained from a fixed initial Morsification with the prescribed critical values and path system. The braid group $\pi_1(B(D,\mu))$ of $\mu$-point configurations in $D$ acts formally on diagrams by Picard–Lefschetz transformations: each braid $\ell$ produces, by purely combinatorial substitution of the Picard–Lefschetz formulas applied vertex-by-vertex, a new graph $\ell\cdot\Delta_0$ on $\mu$ vertices. Call any graph obtained from $\Delta_0$ by some sequence of such formal Picard–Lefschetz moves a formally reachable Dynkin diagram. Call a graph realizable if it is the actual Dynkin diagram of some Morsification $f_{\lambda'}$ of $f$ with the same critical values $z_1,\dots,z_\mu$ and the same path system $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_\mu$.

Problem. Determine, for non-simple singularities $f$, the set of formally reachable Dynkin diagrams that are not realizable; that is, characterize those Dynkin graphs that arise from the initial diagram $\Delta_0$ by formal braid Picard–Lefschetz moves but never occur as the Dynkin diagram of any Morsification of $f$ with the same critical values and the same distinguished path system.

A group $G$ is solvable of derived length at most $d$ if its derived series $G = G^{(0)} \supseteq G^{(1)} \supseteq \cdots$, defined by $G^{(i+1)} = [G^{(i)}, G^{(i)}]$, satisfies $G^{(d)} = \{1\}$. For an integer $r \geq 2$ and $d \geq 1$, the free solvable group $S_{r,d}$ of rank $r$ and derived length $d$ is the quotient $F_r / F_r^{(d)}$, where $F_r$ is the free group of rank $r$. A group is finitely presented if it admits a presentation with finitely many generators and finitely many defining relators.

Question: Does there exist a finitely presented solvable group $H$ that contains a subgroup isomorphic to the free solvable group $S_{r,3}$ of derived length $3$ for some (equivalently, every) $r \geq 2$?

representations.normalized:
Let $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$ be a holomorphic function germ with an isolated critical point at the origin, of Milnor number $\mu<\infty$. Consider a miniversal deformation $F:(\mathbb{C}^n\times\mathbb{C}^\mu,0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$ of $f$ with base $B\cong(\mathbb{C}^\mu,0)$. The $\mu$-constant stratum $\Sigma_\mu\subset B$ is the germ of points $t\in B$ such that the singularity of $F(\cdot,t)$ at its critical locus has total Milnor number equal to $\mu$ (equivalently, the singularity does not split).

For a generic point $t\in B$ the function $F(\cdot,t)$ is Morse with $\mu$ distinct critical values, and the homology of its Milnor fiber carries a basis of vanishing cycles $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_\mu\in H_{n-1}(\text{Milnor fiber};\mathbb{Z})$ together with the Seifert/intersection form $\langle\delta_i,\delta_j\rangle$. The Lyashko–Looijenga map $LL:B\to\mathrm{Sym}^\mu(\mathbb{C})$ sends $t$ to the unordered tuple of critical values of $F(\cdot,t)$. A "collision" of two critical values $c_i,c_j$ corresponds to a path along which the corresponding vanishing cycles $\delta_i,\delta_j$ can be made to coincide; such a collision is "prohibited" (forced to land in $\Sigma_\mu$) when the intersection-form data of $\delta_i,\delta_j$ (e.g. $\langle\delta_i,\delta_j\rangle=\pm 2$) makes their merging incompatible with the singularity remaining a collection of $A_1$ points.

Problem: Produce general lower bounds for $\dim\Sigma_\mu$ purely in terms of the intersection form on the lattice of vanishing cycles. More precisely, formulate and prove a statement of the following type: if one can exhibit $k$ "independent" collisions of critical values that are prohibited by the intersection-form data, then
$$\dim_0 \Sigma_\mu \;\ge\; k,$$
by showing that each prohibited collision, when forced, produces an independent direction in $B$ along which the deformation approaches $\Sigma_\mu$. Give a precise notion of "independent prohibited collisions" in terms of the intersection form for which this bound holds.

Consider the Tower of Hanoi with four pegs. A state assigns finitely many discs of pairwise distinct sizes to pegs, with the constraint that on each peg the discs are stacked so that no disc lies on top of a strictly smaller disc. A legal move takes the topmost disc of one peg and places it on another peg, again subject to the constraint that no disc is placed on a smaller one. A perfect state is one in which all n discs are stacked on a single peg (necessarily in decreasing order of size from bottom to top).

Define the following "P2 subproblem" on four pegs: starting from a perfect state with all n discs on one peg, transform it via legal moves into a final state in which the n discs are distributed among exactly two specified target pegs (different from each other), in any legal arrangement; minimize the total number of moves.

The "split strategy" for this subproblem is: choose an integer k with 0 ≤ k ≤ n, and
(i) using all four pegs, move the top k smallest discs from the source peg to one of the auxiliary pegs in an optimal perfect-to-perfect four-peg Tower of Hanoi solution;
(ii) leaving those k smaller discs untouched on that peg, treat the remaining three pegs as a three-peg Tower of Hanoi instance and move the bottom n − k largest discs to one of the two target pegs using the optimal three-peg solution (which uses 2^{n−k} − 1 moves);
finally, choose k to minimize the total move count.

Question: Is the split strategy always optimal for this four-peg P2 subproblem? Equivalently, for every n ≥ 0, does the minimum number of legal moves required to take a perfect state of n discs to a state in which the discs occupy exactly two prescribed pegs equal the minimum, over k ∈ {0, 1, …, n}, of (optimal four-peg perfect-to-perfect cost for k discs) + (2^{n−k} − 1)?

The classical Frame–Stewart conjecture for the four-peg perfect-to-perfect Tower of Hanoi was settled by Bousch in 2014, but the analogous split-strategy optimality for the variant in which the goal is to redistribute n discs from one peg onto two specified pegs (the "P2" subproblem) is described as the most interesting open problem about the Tower of Hanoi in the standard monograph on the subject, and no proof or disproof appears in the recent literature surveyed.

Setup. Let f:(ℝⁿ,0)→(ℝ,0) be a real-analytic function germ with an isolated critical point at the origin and corank 2 (i.e., the Hessian of f at 0 has rank n−2). Let μ(f) denote its Milnor number, and let F:(ℝⁿ×ℝᵏ,0)→(ℝ,0) be a (mini-)versal deformation of f. As parameters vary in the base of F, the critical points and critical values of the fiber functions undergo bifurcations (Morse births/deaths, collisions of critical values, etc.); these bifurcations can be encoded combinatorially as "surgeries" on the labelled set of real critical points and their critical values, producing chains of formal surgeries between Morsifications of f. Call a formal surgery realizable if it can be realized by an actual one-parameter family inside the versal deformation F.

Experimental observation. For every real function singularity of corank 2 with Milnor number μ ≤ 11, an exhaustive algorithmic enumeration of all chains of formal surgeries connecting Morsifications has, in every case examined, found that every formal surgery encountered along such a chain is in fact realizable by a surgery of functions in the versal deformation.

Problem. Prove or disprove the following statement at the level of a theorem: for every real function germ of corank 2 with isolated critical point and Milnor number μ ≤ 11, every formal surgery occurring in a chain of formal surgeries between Morsifications is realizable by a surgery of functions in its versal deformation.

$$f_a(x,y) = x^2 - y^2 + a(x,y), \qquad g_b(x,y) = xy + b(x,y),$$
where $a(x,y)$ and $b(x,y)$ range over all real polynomials of degree at most $1$ (so $V \cong \mathbb{R}^6$, parametrized by the coefficients of $a$ and $b$). For every $(a,b) \in V$, the system
$$\{f_a(x,y) = 0,\ g_b(x,y) = 0\}$$
has either $2$ or $4$ solutions in $\mathbb{R}^2$, counted with multiplicities.

Define the covering number $N$ as the minimal positive integer $k$ such that there exist open sets $U_1, \dots, U_k$ with $\bigcup_{i=1}^k U_i = \mathbb{R}^6$ and continuous maps $\varphi_i : U_i \to \mathbb{R}^2$ with the property that, for every $(a,b) \in U_i$, the point $\varphi_i(a,b)$ is a solution of the system $\{f_a = 0,\ g_b = 0\}$.

It is known that $N \geq 2$ (this lower bound follows from embedding the complex equation $z^2 = A$, whose covering number over the complex parameter $A$ is $2$). Determine the exact value of $N$. In particular, is $N = 2$?

Let $\mathbb{R}^d$ denote the parameter space of monic real polynomials of degree $d$ in one variable,
$$f_a(x) = x^d + a_1 x^{d-1} + \cdots + a_{d-1} x + a_d, \qquad a=(a_1,\dots,a_d)\in\mathbb{R}^d.$$
For a parameter $a\in\mathbb{R}^d$, an "exact solution" is a real number $x$ with $f_a(x)=0$, and (for any fixed tolerance $\varepsilon>0$) an "approximate solution" is a real $x$ with $|f_a(x)|<\varepsilon$. Given a subset $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, a continuous choice of solutions on $U$ is a continuous function $s:U\to\mathbb{R}$ such that, for every $a\in U$, $s(a)$ is an exact (respectively approximate) solution of $f_a$.

Define the (exact, resp. approximate) covering number $N_d^{\mathrm{exact}}$ (resp. $N_d^{\mathrm{appr}}(\varepsilon)$) to be the smallest integer $N$ such that the locus $\{a\in\mathbb{R}^d : f_a \text{ has at least one real root}\}$ (resp. all of $\mathbb{R}^d$ in the approximate case) can be covered by $N$ open subsets $U_1,\dots,U_N$, on each of which there exists a continuous choice of solutions.

Determine these covering numbers $N_d^{\mathrm{exact}}$ and $N_d^{\mathrm{appr}}(\varepsilon)$ for every $d\ge 2$, and more generally formulate and compute the analogous covering numbers for systems of polynomial equations of given degrees in any number of real variables, where one continuously selects an exact or approximate common solution over the parameter space of coefficients.

Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a compact domain with smooth boundary $\partial K$. For each affine hyperplane $H \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ that meets the interior of $K$, the hyperplane divides $K$ into two parts; let $V_+(H)$ and $V_-(H)$ denote the $n$-dimensional Lebesgue volumes of these two parts (so $V_+(H)+V_-(H)=\mathrm{vol}(K)$). Parametrize the space of affine hyperplanes by coefficients $(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_n)$ via $H=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n : a_0+a_1x_1+\dots+a_nx_n=0\}$. The (two-valued) function $H\mapsto\{V_+(H),V_-(H)\}$ is called algebraic if each branch satisfies a nontrivial polynomial equation $P(V,a_0,\dots,a_n)=0$ with real coefficients. It is classical that when $n$ is odd and $\partial K$ is an ellipsoid (quadric), this volume-cut function is algebraic.

Question: Do there exist smooth hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$, other than quadrics in odd-dimensional spaces, bounding a compact domain $K$ for which the volume cut from $K$ by any affine hyperplane is an algebraic function of the hyperplane?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

For even $n$, it has been proved (Vassiliev, generalizing Newton's lemma) that no smooth algebraically integrable bodies exist. The odd-dimensional case remains open: ellipsoids are the only known examples, but Vassiliev and others have constructed locally algebraically integrable bodies and "algebroidally integrable" candidates in odd dimensions, whose global algebraicity is not established. Recent surveys (Agranovsky–Bolotov–Koldobsky–Vassiliev–Yagudin, 2023) describe the problem as still partially open in odd dimensions.

Fix natural numbers $d$ and $N$, and let $P(d;N)$ denote the space of smooth real algebraic hypersurfaces of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ (i.e., the open subset of the projectivization of the space of real polynomials of degree $\le d$ in $N$ variables consisting of those polynomials whose zero set in $\mathbb{R}^N$ is a smooth hypersurface). Call a hypersurface in $P(d;N)$ trivial if it is empty (allowed only when $d$ is even) or, when $d$ is odd, if it is ambient-isotopic in $\mathbb{R}^N$ to the standard unknotted hyperplane $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$.

Fix a natural measure of topological complexity $c\colon P(d;N)\to \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ whose absolute minimum is attained exactly on the trivial hypersurfaces; for definiteness one may take $c$ to be either the total Betti number (sum of dimensions of the $\mathbb{Z}/2$-homology groups) of the hypersurface, or the minimal number of critical points of a Morse function on it.

A generic path in $P(d;N)$ crosses the discriminant transversely, and each such crossing modifies the hypersurface by a Morse surgery. Question: is it true that every hypersurface in $P(d;N)$ can be connected to a trivial hypersurface by a generic path in $P(d;N)$ along which every Morse surgery strictly decreases $c$? Equivalently, does there exist a nontrivial hypersurface in $P(d;N)$ such that every Morse surgery applied to it (via a generic short arc in $P(d;N)$ leaving its connected component) leaves $c$ unchanged or increases it?

Let $\mathbb{R}^N$ be equipped with coordinates and let $P(d;N)$ denote the (finite-dimensional) real vector space of real polynomials in $N$ variables of degree at most $d$. For a polynomial $f\in P(d;N)$ whose zero set $V(f)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N:f(x)=0\}$ is a smooth (nonsingular) hypersurface, define the topological complexity $T(f)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ of $V(f)$ to be the sum of its Betti numbers (with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients), or any equivalent reasonable measure of topological complexity. Call a hypersurface "trivial" if it is empty or isotopic to a standard sphere/affine subspace, i.e. has the smallest possible complexity in its connected component of the space of nonsingular hypersurfaces.

The discriminant $\Sigma\subset P(d;N)$ is the closed subset of polynomials whose zero set is singular. A continuous path $\gamma:[0,1]\to P(d;N)$ is called generic if it meets $\Sigma$ transversally at finitely many interior points (so all but finitely many $\gamma(t)$ define smooth hypersurfaces).

Suppose that there exist nonsingular hypersurfaces in $P(d;N)$ which cannot be simplified to a trivial one in a strictly complexity-decreasing manner along generic paths (failure of greedy simplification). For each value $T\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, define
$$F(T) = \min\bigl\{ F\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} : \text{every smooth } f\in P(d;N) \text{ with } T(f)=T \text{ admits a generic path in } P(d;N) \text{ from } f \text{ to a trivial polynomial along which } T(\gamma(t))\le F \text{ for all } t \text{ with } \gamma(t)\notin\Sigma\bigr\}.$$

Provide an explicit upper bound for the function $T\mapsto F(T)$ (depending on $d$ and $N$).

Let f : (ℝⁿ, 0) → (ℝ, 0) be a smooth real function germ with df(0) = 0 and finite Milnor number (i.e. the complexification of f has an isolated critical point at the origin). A real Morsification of f is a smooth deformation f_t (t ∈ [0,1], f_0 = f) such that for some small t > 0 the function f_t has only nondegenerate (Morse) critical points in a small neighborhood of 0 ∈ ℝⁿ. Let ρ(f) denote the minimal possible number of real critical points of f_t in a small fixed neighborhood of 0, taken over all real Morsifications of f.

Two natural lower bounds for ρ(f) are:
 (a) |ind₀(grad f)|, the absolute value of the index at 0 of the gradient vector field of f;
 (b) the Smale number of the relative homology group
        H_*(f⁻¹((−∞, ε]), f⁻¹((−∞, −ε]); ℤ)
     for sufficiently small ε > 0, defined as the sum over all degrees of (rank of the free part) + 2·(minimal number of generators of the torsion subgroup).

It is clear that (a) ≤ (b) ≤ ρ(f). Address the following:

1. Can the inequality (a) < (b) be strict for some f?
2. Do the two bounds (a) and (b) coincide for every function germ of corank 2 (i.e. when the Hessian of f at 0 has rank n − 2)?
3. Can the relative homology group H_*(f⁻¹((−∞, ε]), f⁻¹((−∞, −ε]); ℤ) have nontrivial torsion?
4. Is the lower bound (b) always sharp, i.e. does ρ(f) equal the Smale number of this relative homology group for every such germ f?

Background. For a polynomial $f:\mathbb{C}	o\mathbb{C}$ of degree $n$ with a simple root $z_0$, let $d$ denote the minimal distance from $z_0$ to the other roots of $f$. A classical sharp estimate states that the disk of radius $c\,d/n^{2n-1}$ (more precisely, the $d^{2n-1}$-type neighborhood) centered at $z_0$ is contained in the convergence domain of the one-dimensional Newton iteration $z\mapsto z-f(z)/f'(z)$ converging to $z_0$, and that this estimate cannot be improved as a universal function of $d$ and $n$ alone.

Now consider the multidimensional Newton method for systems of polynomial equations. Let $F=(f_1,\dots,f_N):\mathbb{C}^N	o\mathbb{C}^N$ be a polynomial map with components of degrees $n_1,\dots,n_N$, and let $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}^N$ be a nondegenerate (simple) zero of $F$, i.e.\ $F(\zeta)=0$ and $DF(\zeta)$ is invertible. The Newton iteration is $z_{k+1}=z_k-DF(z_k)^{-1}F(z_k)$, and the convergence domain of $\zeta$ is the set of starting points $z_0$ from which this iteration is well-defined for all $k$ and converges to $\zeta$.

Problem. Define a natural geometric quantity $d=d(F,\zeta)$ measuring the separation of $\zeta$ from the other zeros of $F$ (and, if needed, from the singular locus of $F$), and produce a universal lower bound — depending only on $d$, the degrees $n_1,\dots,n_N$, and the dimension $N$ — for the radius of a neighborhood of $\zeta$ entirely contained in the convergence domain of the multidimensional Newton iteration. The bound should be the multidimensional analogue of the one-dimensional sharp estimate above, and ideally should not be improvable as a universal function of these parameters.

Background. For a polynomial $f:\mathbb{C}	o\mathbb{C}$ of degree $n$ with a simple root $z_0$, let $d$ denote the minimal distance from $z_0$ to the other roots of $f$. A classical sharp estimate states that the disk of radius $c\,d/n^{2n-1}$ (more precisely, the $d^{2n-1}$-type neighborhood) centered at $z_0$ is contained in the convergence domain of the one-dimensional Newton iteration $z\mapsto z-f(z)/f'(z)$ converging to $z_0$, and that this estimate cannot be improved as a universal function of $d$ and $n$ alone.

Now consider the multidimensional Newton method for systems of polynomial equations. Let $F=(f_1,\dots,f_N):\mathbb{C}^N	o\mathbb{C}^N$ be a polynomial map with components of degrees $n_1,\dots,n_N$, and let $\zeta\in\mathbb{C}^N$ be a nondegenerate (simple) zero of $F$, i.e.\ $F(\zeta)=0$ and $DF(\zeta)$ is invertible. The Newton iteration is $z_{k+1}=z_k-DF(z_k)^{-1}F(z_k)$, and the convergence domain of $\zeta$ is the set of starting points $z_0$ from which this iteration is well-defined for all $k$ and converges to $\zeta$.

Problem. Define a natural geometric quantity $d=d(F,\zeta)$ measuring the separation of $\zeta$ from the other zeros of $F$ (and, if needed, from the singular locus of $F$), and produce a universal lower bound — depending only on $d$, the degrees $n_1,\dots,n_N$, and the dimension $N$ — for the radius of a neighborhood of $\zeta$ entirely contained in the convergence domain of the multidimensional Newton iteration. The bound should be the multidimensional analogue of the one-dimensional sharp estimate above, and ideally should not be improvable as a universal function of these parameters.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Web search returned no source providing the analogue of the sharp one-dimensional Reshetnyak-type universal estimate (depending only on root separation and degrees) for the radius of the convergence domain of the Shub–Smale multidimensional Newton method. Existing results (Smale's α-theory, point estimates, projective Newton method) give convergence criteria of a different nature rather than a sharp universal bound in terms of the geometric separation of zeros. The problem appears to remain open.

Let G = (V, E, w) be a weighted undirected graph representing a protein–protein interaction network, where V is the set of all proteins, E ⊆ V × V is the set of pairwise interactions, and w : E → [0, 1] assigns each interaction a confidence score. Let M ⊆ V be a designated subset of nodes (the membrane proteins), and let S = V \ M (the soluble proteins). Define the membrane subinteractome as the induced subgraph G[M] = (M, E_M, w|_{E_M}) where E_M = { (u, v) ∈ E : u, v ∈ M }. Assume G[M] is sparse, in the sense that |E_M| = O(|M|) and the average degree in G[M] is small relative to that in G.

The task is to design and rigorously justify a filtering procedure F that takes as input the network G together with the partition (M, S) and outputs a refined edge set E_M^* ⊆ E_M (with associated refined confidences) intended to retain true membrane–membrane interactions while removing spurious ones. Specifically:

(a) Formulate a precise filtering criterion F(G, M) → E_M^* that is suitable when the candidate edge set E_M is already sparse, so that aggressive thresholding on w alone may discard true positives.

(b) Determine whether F should depend only on the induced subgraph G[M] (i.e., F(G[M]) → E_M^*), or whether it should also use information from the rest of G — namely the soluble subgraph G[S], the bipartite cross-edges between M and S, or global topological/statistical features of G — and quantify in what regimes (e.g., as a function of network density, score noise model, or proportion |M|/|V|) each choice yields better precision/recall trade-offs.

Provide either an algorithm together with a theoretical performance guarantee (for example, bounds on expected false-positive and false-negative rates under a stated random graph or noisy-observation model of interactome data), or a proof that no such filter can simultaneously achieve specified precision and recall thresholds using only G[M].

This is a methodological open question about filtering membrane protein subinteractomes. Searches reveal ongoing work on integrating membrane-specific and global interactome information (e.g., subcellular-localization-aware confidence scoring and methods such as STRING, MINT, and membrane-focused integrators), but no consensus or definitive theoretical resolution exists for sparse membrane subinteractome filtering. Consider the problem of computationally predicting protein complexes from a protein–protein interaction (PPI) network, modeled as a weighted graph G = (V, E, w), where vertices V represent proteins, edges E represent observed pairwise interactions, and weights w: E → [0,1] represent interaction reliabilities. A "protein complex" is typically defined as a subset C ⊆ V whose members co-assemble as a functional unit. Standard prediction methods output a collection {C_1, …, C_k} of pairwise (largely) disjoint or only mildly overlapping subsets of V intended to represent the distinct complexes in the cell.

Now suppose that for certain complexes — in particular, membrane-associated complexes — there is a phenomenon of "dynamic exchange": proteins transiently associate with and dissociate from an otherwise stable core, so that at different times or in different cellular contexts the same nominal complex is realized as several different but related subsets S_1, S_2, …, S_m ⊆ V (the "isoforms" of the complex), each sharing a common core but differing in their peripheral/transient members.

Question: Design and justify a computational prediction framework that, taking as input the weighted PPI graph G (possibly augmented with temporal, conditional, or localization annotations), outputs for each underlying complex a family {S_1, …, S_m} of alternative compositional forms rather than a single subset C, and that provably (or empirically, under a stated benchmark and evaluation metric) recovers known dynamically exchanging complexes better than methods returning a single fixed subset per complex. In particular, formulate:
(a) a precise mathematical model of a "dynamic complex" as an equivalence class or family of vertex subsets sharing a designated core;
(b) an algorithm that, given G, enumerates such families; and
(c) an evaluation metric comparing a predicted family {S_1, …, S_m} against a gold-standard family {T_1, …, T_n} of known isoforms.

Determine whether such a framework can be devised so that it strictly outperforms (under the chosen metric) the best single-subset prediction methods on benchmarks of membrane complexes exhibiting dynamic exchange.

The detection of multiple alternative ("isoform") compositions of dynamically exchanging protein complexes from PPI networks remains an open challenge in computational systems biology. While several methods (e.g., DECAFF, CMC, ClusterONE, dynamic/temporal PPI clustering approaches) attempt to handle overlap and temporal variation, no consensus framework reliably recovers families of alternative forms of the same complex, particularly for membrane complexes, and recent reviews continue to list it as an unresolved problem.

Consider the task of computationally predicting membrane protein complexes from a protein–protein interaction network or similar data, producing a collection of predicted putative complexes (subsets of proteins hypothesized to form a complex). Suppose that the set of experimentally confirmed (bona fide) membrane protein complexes available as a gold-standard reference is very small, so that standard supervised evaluation metrics (e.g., precision, recall, F-measure, or maximum matching ratio against a reference catalogue) are statistically unreliable. At the same time, many predicted putative complexes may themselves be biologically meaningful candidates worthy of experimental validation, and they may include currently unannotated proteins to which functional roles could be assigned through guilt-by-association.

Formulate a principled evaluation framework for assessing the quality of predicted membrane protein complexes under these conditions. The framework should:

1. Define quantitative scoring criteria that do not rely solely on overlap with a small reference catalogue of known complexes, e.g., by incorporating internal coherence measures (topological cohesiveness, co-localization in the membrane, co-expression, shared GO annotations, evolutionary conservation of co-occurrence).
2. Specify how to combine multiple lines of indirect evidence into a confidence score for each predicted complex, with calibrated uncertainty.
3. Provide a procedure for prioritizing predicted complexes for prospective experimental validation, accounting for the possibility that confirmed predictions extend, rather than match, the reference set.
4. Specify how unannotated proteins occurring in high-confidence predicted complexes should be assigned tentative functional roles, with statistical control of false annotation rates.
5. Demonstrate that the evaluation framework is well-defined, reproducible, and consistent in the limit as the reference catalogue grows, and is robust to the bias induced by the scarcity of known membrane complexes.

Construct such a framework and justify its theoretical properties.

A membrane protein complex is a multi-subunit assembly embedded in a cellular membrane, formed by sequential incorporation of intermediate subassemblies (intermediaries). Empirical studies indicate that this assembly proceeds in an ordered fashion, with chaperone proteins guiding the process so as to suppress the appearance of off-pathway or unwanted intermediaries. One proposed explanation is that the ordering serves as a protective mechanism, shielding the cell from intermediaries that would be harmful if they accumulated, but the underlying biological rationale remains unsettled.

Provide a mechanistic explanation, supported by a quantitative or model-based argument, for why membrane complexes assemble through a strictly ordered sequence of chaperone-assisted intermediaries. In particular, identify and justify the functional purpose (e.g., cytoprotection against toxic intermediates, kinetic efficiency, fidelity of stoichiometry, or another principle) that makes ordered, chaperone-mediated assembly preferable to unordered assembly pathways for membrane-embedded multi-subunit complexes.

The question is a biological/biophysical open problem about why membrane protein complexes assemble in a strict, chaperone-mediated order. Reviews on membrane complex biogenesis (e.g., respiratory chain supercomplex assembly, photosystem assembly) continue to discuss ordered assembly and chaperone roles as an active research area without a definitive, generally accepted explanation; cytoprotection against reactive intermediates is one hypothesis among several. No web search was performed in this response, so the status is reported based on the framing of the problem as openly unresolved.

Let $T=(V,E)$ be a finite tree and let $K$ be a positive integer. A complete $K$-coloring of $T$ is a map $c:V\to\{1,2,\dots,K\}$ satisfying:
(i) for every edge $\{u,v\}\in E$, $c(u)\neq c(v)$ (properness); and
(ii) for every pair $i\neq j$ in $\{1,2,\dots,K\}$, there exists an edge $\{u,v\}\in E$ with $\{c(u),c(v)\}=\{i,j\}$.

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem: given $(T,K)$ as input, decide whether $T$ admits a complete $K$-coloring.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The decision problem of whether a tree admits a complete K-coloring (i.e., whether the achromatic number of a tree is at least K) was shown to be NP-complete by Cairnie and Edwards (and independently by Manlove and McDiarmid). Polynomial-time algorithms are known for restricted subclasses, e.g., trees of bounded maximum degree.

Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph. A complete K-coloring of G is a function c : V → {1, 2, …, K} such that:
(i) c(u) ≠ c(v) whenever {u, v} ∈ E (proper coloring), and
(ii) for every pair of distinct colors i, j ∈ {1, …, K}, there exists at least one edge {u, v} ∈ E with {c(u), c(v)} = {i, j}.
The achromatic number ψ(G) is the largest integer K for which G admits a complete K-coloring.

It is known that computing ψ(G) is NP-hard in general, and remains NP-hard when G is restricted to be a tree. Characterize the classes of finite trees for which the achromatic number can be determined by a polynomial-time algorithm. In particular, identify natural structural classes 𝒞 of trees (for example, defined by bounds on degree, diameter, depth, caterpillar-like structure, or similar parameters) such that there exists an algorithm computing ψ(T) for every T ∈ 𝒞 in time polynomial in |V(T)|.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The achromatic number problem is NP-hard for general trees. Polynomial-time algorithms are known for some restricted tree classes, notably trees of bounded maximum degree (Chaudhary & Vishwanathan; Bodlaender; et al.), and for complements of trees. The broader question of characterizing all tree classes admitting polynomial-time algorithms remains an active area, so the problem is partially solved.

Work in the framework of classical computability theory on $\omega$. For a set $X \subseteq \omega$, let $X'$ denote its Turing jump. A Turing degree $\mathbf{d}$ is said to be of PA degree relative to $\emptyset'$ if it computes a $\{0,1\}$-valued total function that is diagonally non-computable relative to $\emptyset'$ (equivalently, $\mathbf{d}$ computes a complete consistent extension of Peano Arithmetic augmented with $\emptyset'$ as an oracle). A set $A \subseteq \omega$ is $\Delta^0_2$ if both $A$ and its complement $\overline{A} = \omega \setminus A$ are limits of computable sequences (equivalently, $A \leq_T \emptyset'$).

Question: Does there exist a $\Delta^0_2$ set $A \subseteq \omega$ such that for every infinite set $H \subseteq \omega$ with $H \subseteq A$ or $H \subseteq \overline{A}$, the Turing jump $H'$ has PA degree relative to $\emptyset'$?

A set $A \subseteq \omega$ is $\Delta^0_2$ if both $A$ and its complement $\overline{A} = \omega \setminus A$ are limits of computable sequences (equivalently, $A \leq_T \emptyset'$).

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question appears to be answered negatively by Monin and Patey's paper "Pigeons do not jump high" (Advances in Mathematics, 2019). They prove that for every set $A$ (in particular every $\Delta^0_2$ set) there is an infinite subset of $A$ or of its complement whose jump is not of high degree. Since any degree that is PA relative to $\emptyset'$ computes $\emptyset''$ and is therefore high, no such $\Delta^0_2$ set $A$ exists.

Background and definitions. Let C₊ and C₋ be a pair of complex projective plane curves in ℙ²(ℂ) whose defining homogeneous polynomials are Galois-conjugate to each other over a quadratic number field K ⊂ ℂ (so that, in particular, C₊ and C₋ have the same combinatorial type of singularities). Suppose moreover that there exist projective lines L₊, L₋ ⊂ ℙ², each defined over the same conjugate copies of K, such that L₊ (resp. L₋) is associated with C₊ (resp. C₋) by a fixed geometric construction (e.g. a distinguished tangent line through a prescribed singular point), and assume that the following two properties hold:

(i) The complements ℙ² ∖ (C₊ ∪ L₊) and ℙ² ∖ (C₋ ∪ L₋) are analytically (hence topologically) isomorphic; one such analytic isomorphism is induced by a Cremona transformation of ℙ².

(ii) No Cremona transformation realising the isomorphism in (i) extends to a homeomorphism of pairs (ℙ², C₊ ∪ L₊) → (ℙ², C₋ ∪ L₋).

Recall that an ordered pair of reduced curves (D₊, D₋) in ℙ² with the same combinatorics is called a Zariski pair if there is no homeomorphism of pairs (ℙ², D₊) → (ℙ², D₋), and is called a complement-equivalent Zariski pair if in addition the complements ℙ² ∖ D₊ and ℙ² ∖ D₋ are homeomorphic.

Question. Under the hypotheses (i) and (ii) above, do the pairs (ℙ², C₊ ∪ L₊) and (ℙ², C₋ ∪ L₋) form a complement-equivalent Zariski pair? Equivalently, although their complements are homeomorphic, is it true that there is no homeomorphism of pairs (ℙ², C₊ ∪ L₊) → (ℙ², C₋ ∪ L₋) carrying C₊ ∪ L₊ onto C₋ ∪ L₋?

\[
B \;=\; \{\,x_i\cdot x_j = x_k : i,j,k\in\{1,\dots,6\}\,\}\;\cup\;\{\,x_j! = x_k : j,k\in\{1,\dots,6\},\ j\neq k\,\}.
\]
A subsystem of $B$ is any subset $S\subseteq B$. By a solution of $S$ we mean a tuple $(x_1,\dots,x_6)\in(\mathbb{Z}_{>0})^6$ of positive integers satisfying every equation in $S$ simultaneously.

Decide whether the following statement holds: for every subsystem $S\subseteq B$ that has only finitely many solutions in positive integers, every solution $(x_1,\dots,x_6)$ of $S$ satisfies
\[
x_1,\dots,x_6 \;\le\; (24!)!.
\]

Let $G$ be a group and let $n$ be a positive integer. Suppose $\mathcal{P} = \{A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n\}$ is a partition of $G$ into $n$ nonempty cells (so $G = A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_n$ and the cells are pairwise disjoint). For a subset $A \subseteq G$, define the difference set
$$AA^{-1} := \{ab^{-1} : a, b \in A\}.$$
For a subset $F \subseteq G$, write $FAA^{-1} := \{fc : f \in F,\ c \in AA^{-1}\}$.

Question: Must there exist a cell $A \in \mathcal{P}$ and a subset $F \subseteq G$ with $|F| \le n$ such that
$$G = F\,A\,A^{-1}?$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem was posed by Protasov in 1995 (Kourovka Notebook, Problem 13.44) and remains open in general. Affirmative partial answers are known: for amenable groups (in particular, finite groups), for partitions with $n \le 3$, for normal partitions (where $x^{-1}Ax = A$ for all cells $A$ and $x \in G$), and a related weakened form $G = F A A^{-1} A$ with $|F| \le n$ has been established. The Kourovka Notebook continues to list it among unsolved problems.

Fix a norm ‖·‖ on the coefficient vectors of bivariate polynomials (for instance, the ℓ¹, ℓ², or ℓ^∞ norm on the vector of coefficients indexed by monomials up to a given total degree).

Given as input a polynomial f(x, y) ∈ ℚ[x, y] (specified by its coefficients in some standard encoding) and a rational tolerance ε ∈ ℚ_{≥0}, design an algorithm that decides, in time polynomial in the total degree of f and in the bit size of the coefficients of f and of ε, whether there exists a polynomial f̂(x, y) ∈ ℂ[x, y] such that:
  (i) f̂ admits a nontrivial factorization f̂ = g · h with g, h ∈ ℂ[x, y] and deg(g), deg(h) ≥ 1; and
  (ii) ‖f − f̂‖ ≤ ε.

Either provide such a polynomial-time decision procedure, or prove that no such procedure exists (under suitable complexity-theoretic assumptions).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The decision problem of detecting the existence of a nontrivially factorable bivariate complex polynomial within ε of a given rational polynomial, in time polynomial in the degree and coefficient size, appears to remain open. Existing literature provides numerical/approximate factorization algorithms (Gao–Kaltofen–May–Yang–Zhi, Corless–Galligo–Kotsireas–Watt, Chèze–Galligo) and reductions for exact factorization, but no known polynomial-time algorithm settles the decision problem with guaranteed worst-case complexity bounds.

Consider a family of dynamical systems parametrized by a control parameter $c \in \mathbb{R}$ such that the dynamics admit three qualitatively distinct regimes: an ordered regime ($c < c^*$), a critical regime ($c = c^*$), and a disordered (chaotic) regime ($c > c^*$). For each system, the dynamic repertoire is encoded by an attractor landscape $\mathcal{A}(c)$ (the collection of attractors together with their basins under the deterministic or stochastic update rule).

Let $\mathcal{T}$ denote a class of tasks. A task $T \in \mathcal{T}$ comes equipped with a fitness function
$$F_T : \mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R},$$
that assigns to each attractor landscape a real-valued performance score quantifying how effectively the system accomplishes $T$. The environment is modeled as a stochastic process $\{E_t\}_{t \ge 0}$ taking values in a space of task instances, characterized by:
(i) a correlation length $\xi$ describing spatial/structural correlations of the fitness landscape over the configuration space,
(ii) a temporal rate of change $r$ at which $E_t$ evolves, and
(iii) an amplitude $\Delta$ measuring the magnitude of environmental variations.

An evolutionary dynamics is a Markov process on the parameter $c$ whose stationary distribution $\pi_{T,\xi,r,\Delta}(c)$ concentrates around values of $c$ that maximize the long-run expected fitness $\mathbb{E}[F_{E_t}(\mathcal{A}(c))]$.

Problem. Determine, as a function of the task class $\mathcal{T}$ and the parameters $(\xi, r, \Delta)$, the set
$$\mathcal{C} := \{ (T,\xi,r,\Delta) : \pi_{T,\xi,r,\Delta} 	ext{ is concentrated at } c = c^* \}.$$
That is, characterize precisely the task features and the landscape/environmental parameters $(\xi, r, \Delta)$ for which evolutionary dynamics select the critical regime over the ordered or disordered regimes, and provide explicit conditions (inequalities or threshold relations) separating the regions of parameter space where ordered, critical, or disordered systems are evolutionarily favored.

The question of when evolutionary dynamics select critical systems remains an active and unresolved research direction. Subsequent literature on criticality in biological and adaptive systems (e.g., works by Hidalgo, Grigera, Munoz and others on "information-based fitness and the emergence of criticality") provides partial results in specific models, showing criticality can be advantageous in variable environments, but no general characterization in terms of task class and environmental parameters has been established.

Let $K$ be a field (typically $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$, or $\mathbb{C}$) and let $I = \langle f_1, \dots, f_s \rangle \subset K[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ be a polynomial ideal, with a fixed monomial order $\prec$. Recall that a Gröbner basis of $I$ with respect to $\prec$ is a finite generating set $G \subset I$ such that the leading monomials of elements of $G$ generate the leading-monomial ideal of $I$.

Develop algorithms that compute Gröbner bases of $I$ approximately by means of iterative numerical system-solving methods (for example, Gauss–Seidel iteration, conjugate gradient iteration, Newton iteration, or related iterative schemes), with the following requirements:

1. The algorithms must be compatible with standard floating-point numerical software (i.e., usable in inexact-arithmetic environments rather than requiring exact rational/symbolic arithmetic throughout).

2. For some classes of input ideals, the algorithms must compute a Gröbner basis (or a usable approximation thereof) faster than algorithms based on exact arithmetic.

3. The algorithms must still recover the underlying structural/combinatorial information of the Gröbner basis (such as the leading-term structure, the staircase, and the support of the basis polynomials), for instance by combining the numerical iterations with modular-arithmetic techniques.

Produce such methods together with a precise convergence analysis and a description of the classes of ideals for which the resulting numerical-iterative Gröbner basis computation is provably faster than purely exact-arithmetic computation, while still certifying the correct combinatorial structure of the basis.

Consider the design of artificial adaptive systems (for example, recurrent neural networks, reservoir computers, spiking networks, cellular automata, or Boolean networks used for learning tasks). A dynamical system is said to be at (or near) dynamical criticality if its parameters place it on the boundary between an ordered regime, where perturbations decay, and a chaotic regime, where perturbations grow exponentially; equivalently, the maximal Lyapunov exponent (or an analogous order parameter, such as the Derrida sensitivity for discrete systems) is close to zero, and observables typically display power-law correlations and a balance between robustness and flexibility.

Formulate and resolve the following design-principle question. Let 𝒮 be a parameterized class of artificial dynamical systems intended to perform learning or computation, and let 𝒞(s) be a quantitative measure of how close s ∈ 𝒮 is to dynamical criticality (or to a property strongly correlated with criticality, such as maximal dynamical complexity, vanishing Lyapunov exponent, or maximal mutual information between input history and internal state). Determine whether there exists a task-independent objective functional based solely on 𝒞 (and not on any task-specific fitness function) such that:

(a) optimizing 𝒞 over 𝒮 by an automatic procedure (e.g. evolutionary search, gradient descent, or self-organization) yields systems whose performance on a broad family of learning or computational tasks is competitive with, or superior to, systems obtained by directly optimizing task-specific fitness functions; and

(b) the evolutionary advantages attributed to critical dynamical systems observed in natural systems can be rigorously shown to transfer to such automatically designed artificial systems, in the sense of provable bounds (or strong empirical universality) relating proximity to criticality 𝒞(s) and task-general performance.

Equivalently: is dynamical criticality a viable, general-purpose, task-independent design criterion for automatically generating artificial learning systems, replacing or complementing ad hoc task-specific fitness functions?

(b) the evolutionary advantages attributed to critical dynamical systems observed in natural systems can be rigorously shown to transfer to such automatically designed artificial systems, in the sense of provable bounds (or strong empirical universality) relating proximity to criticality 𝒞(s) and task-general performance.

Equivalently: is dynamical criticality a viable, general-purpose, task-independent design criterion for automatically generating artificial learning systems, replacing or complementing ad hoc task-specific fitness functions?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question remains an active research direction without a definitive resolution. Multiple recent works (edge-of-chaos initialization in deep nets, reservoir computing at criticality, mean-field tuning of spiking networks, neuromorphic nanowire networks, asynchronous critical systems) provide partial evidence that proximity to criticality enhances computational capacity and trainability, and propose automatic tuning schemes. However, no general theorem or universally accepted task-independent design criterion based solely on criticality has been established; criticality often requires fine-tuning and its universality as a stand-alone design principle is still debated.

1. Components implementing symbolic algorithms (e.g., polynomial arithmetic, Gröbner basis computation, factorization, simplification, integration, linear algebra over symbolic domains, etc.) can be specified abstractly in terms of the algebraic structures they operate on (rings, fields, modules, ideals, polynomial domains, etc.) and combined generically without rewriting code for each concrete instantiation.

3. The methodology must be practical enough to be widely adopted in actual software development for symbolic mathematics, not merely a theoretical specification.

The problem is to produce such a methodology, demonstrate its feasibility through implementations, and establish it as a de facto standard for symbolic computation software.

In the study of circumstellar discs around young stellar objects, a "transition disc" is defined (for the purposes of this problem) as a protoplanetary disc whose spectral energy distribution shows only stellar photospheric emission from the near-infrared through the mid-infrared, indicating the absence of warm dust in the inner regions, while exhibiting strong far-infrared excess from an outer dusty disc. A "pre-transition disc" is defined as a disc that otherwise resembles a transition disc (i.e., has a large dust-depleted gap and a substantial outer disc) but additionally retains either (a) a small amount of optically thin dust within the inner cavity, or (b) a radially thin optically thick inner wall located near the dust sublimation (dust-destruction) front, producing measurable near-infrared excess.

Question: Are pre-transition discs (as defined above) evolutionary precursors of transition discs? More precisely, does there exist a continuous evolutionary pathway by which a typical pre-transition disc loses its remaining inner optically thin dust and/or its narrow optically thick inner wall to become a transition disc whose spectral energy distribution shows only photospheric emission from the near-infrared out to the mid-infrared? Provide observational, theoretical, or model-based evidence either establishing or ruling out such an evolutionary connection.

Background and definitions. An elementary function over an interval is one obtained from rational functions of the variable by finitely many applications of field operations, exponentials, logarithms, and algebraic extensions. The classical Risch algorithm is a decision procedure that, given an elementary function f(x) in a suitable differential field, decides whether f has an elementary antiderivative and, if so, returns one such antiderivative F satisfying F'(x) = f(x). However, the antiderivatives F produced by the Risch algorithm need not be continuous on the whole natural domain of f: typical outputs may exhibit removable jump discontinuities at branch cuts of logarithms, arctangents, or algebraic radicals, even when a continuous antiderivative on a larger connected domain exists.

Problem. Either:
(a) Provide an algorithm — either a modification of the Risch algorithm or a replacement — that, given an elementary function f, returns an antiderivative F of f which is continuous on a domain of maximum extent (i.e., on every connected component of the natural domain of f, F should be continuous, and the domain on which F is defined and continuous should be maximal in a precisely formulated sense); or
(b) Give a precise and clear description of the largest class C of functions (elementary or otherwise) for which continuous antidifferentiation can be performed by an efficient algorithm, together with such an algorithm.

The solution must include a rigorous correctness proof, and ideally a complete implementation in a major computer algebra system so that it is available for general use.

No general algorithm or implementation is known that always produces antiderivatives continuous on domains of maximum extent for elementary functions, nor is there a sharp characterization of the largest function class admitting efficient continuous antidifferentiation. The problem appears to remain open.

Consider the population of protoplanetary transition discs characterized by (i) low millimetre continuum fluxes and (ii) small inner cavities ("holes") whose existence has been inferred indirectly by fitting parametric models to the unresolved spectral energy distribution (SED), rather than from spatially resolved imaging. Such objects are widely conjectured to represent discs that are genuinely undergoing dispersal of their primordial gas-and-dust content (as opposed to discs hosting massive embedded planets or large dust traps). Determine, by means of high-resolution direct imaging in dust continuum and gas tracers (e.g. resolved sub-millimetre/millimetre interferometric observations and resolved molecular-line observations) the following for this specific subpopulation:

(a) Whether the inner dust cavities inferred from SED modelling are confirmed when the discs are imaged at resolutions sufficient to resolve the predicted hole radius; that is, quantify the dust surface density profile Σ_dust(r) inside the SED-inferred hole radius R_hole and decide whether Σ_dust(r) is consistent with a true depleted cavity or with a continuous, unbroken distribution.

(b) Whether any non-axisymmetric structure (e.g. azimuthal asymmetries, lopsided dust concentrations, spiral features) is present in the dust or gas distribution within or near the cavity, and characterise its amplitude and morphology.

(c) The amount of gas remaining inside the cavities, expressed as a gas surface density profile Σ_gas(r) for r < R_hole and an integrated gas mass M_gas(r < R_hole), together with the gas-to-dust ratio in the cavity region.

Provide quantitative constraints (or upper limits) on Σ_dust(r), Σ_gas(r), the gas-to-dust ratio, and any asymmetry contrast for this low-mm-flux, small-hole subclass of transition discs.

Consider the perturbed sine-Gordon equation
\[
\varepsilon\, u_{xxt} + u_{xx} - u_{tt} - a\, u_t \;=\; \sin u - \gamma,
\]
posed for $(x,t)$ in a bounded spatial domain modeling a window Josephson junction (a one-dimensional junction with prescribed boundary/interface conditions of mixed type at the endpoints), where $a>0$ is a shunt-loss coefficient, $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ is a normalized bias current, and $\varepsilon \ge 0$ is a parameter measuring longitudinal (surface) losses. The third-order term $\varepsilon\, u_{xxt}$ is viscous/dissipative; when $\varepsilon = 0$ the equation reduces to a standard window-Josephson-junction model.

The task: for $\varepsilon > 0$, derive quantitative estimates of the diffusive (smoothing/dissipative) effects produced by the term $\varepsilon\, u_{xxt}$. Specifically, give explicit bounds (in terms of $\varepsilon$, $a$, $\gamma$, the domain size, and the initial-boundary data) that:

1. Compare a solution $u^\varepsilon$ of the equation above to the corresponding solution $u^0$ of the limiting equation obtained by setting $\varepsilon = 0$, providing convergence rates as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$ in suitable Sobolev norms.
2. Quantify the parabolic regularization induced by the $\varepsilon\, u_{xxt}$ term (e.g., gain of spatial regularity, decay of high-frequency modes, or smoothing of initial data).
3. Describe how the long-time dynamics, dissipation rates, and energy decay are modified by the presence of $\varepsilon\, u_{xxt}$ relative to the case $\varepsilon = 0$.

Consider the nonlinear partial differential equation
   ε u_{xxt} + u_{xx} − u_{tt} − ε λ u_{xt} − λ u_{x} − a u_{t} = sin(u),
where ε > 0, a > 0 and λ ∈ ℝ are fixed constants, posed on a bounded spatial interval (say x ∈ (0, L)) for t > 0, supplemented by initial data u(x,0) = h_0(x), u_t(x,0) = h_1(x). For Dirichlet boundary conditions u(0,t) = g_1(t), u(L,t) = g_2(t), it is known that one can perform an asymptotic analysis showing that the influence of the boundary perturbations g_1, g_2 on the solution becomes null or remains bounded as t → ∞.

Problem: Extend this asymptotic analysis of boundary perturbations to the same equation under
 (a) Neumann boundary conditions u_x(0,t) = g_1(t), u_x(L,t) = g_2(t), and
 (b) mixed boundary conditions (Dirichlet at one endpoint, Neumann at the other).
Specifically, derive a priori estimates and long-time asymptotic estimates that quantify, for these boundary-value formulations, the long-time effect of the boundary disturbances g_1, g_2 on the solution u(x,t).

Consider the parabolic integro-differential operator
  L_R u(x,t) := u_t(x,t) - ε u_xx(x,t) + a u(x,t) + b ∫_0^t e^{-β(t-τ)} u(x,τ) dτ,
acting on sufficiently regular functions u(x,t) with x in a real interval (e.g. the whole line or a strip) and t ≥ 0, and consider the associated Cauchy or initial-boundary value problems for the equation
  L_R u = F(x,t,u),
with prescribed initial datum u(x,0) and (when applicable) boundary data, where F is a given (possibly nonlinear) source term. Existing well-posedness, fundamental-solution, and asymptotic analyses of L_R (including the construction of an explicit kernel involving Bessel functions of the first kind) are carried out under the standing assumption that the four parameters a, b, ε, β are all strictly positive real numbers. The problem is to extend the analysis of the operator L_R—construction of fundamental solutions, a priori estimates, well-posedness theorems, qualitative properties (such as maximum principles, regularity, and large-time behavior), and explicit asymptotic formulas—to arbitrary real values of the parameters a, b, ε, β (allowing zero or negative values), thereby covering models that fall outside the positivity regime.

Consider a model of a gaseous protoplanetary disc around a young star in which a giant planet, embedded in the disc, opens an annular gap by exerting tidal torques on the surrounding gas. The disc is termed a "transition disc" if it exhibits a characteristic spectral energy distribution showing a deficit of near- and mid-infrared emission (indicating an inner cavity or hole) together with strong (sub-)millimetre continuum emission from cold outer dust. Define the "hole size" as the radius of the inner cavity carved by the planet, and call a transition disc "mm-bright" if its millimetre continuum flux exceeds a fixed threshold typical of the brightest observed sources. Within standard viscous disc theory coupled with Type I/II planetary migration, a gap-opening planet generally migrates inward on a timescale comparable to or shorter than the disc lifetime, while continuing to accrete gas through the gap. Empirically, mm-bright transition discs with small hole sizes (e.g. cavity radius less than about 10 AU) and simultaneously high accretion rates are essentially absent from observed samples, whereas mm-bright transition discs with large holes are common.

Construct a self-consistent disc–planet evolution model (specifying the surface-density evolution, viscous α, planet migration prescription, gas accretion across the gap, and dust dynamics determining mm flux) such that:

(a) a giant planet capable of producing an mm-bright transition disc with a large hole does not subsequently migrate inward into the regime of small holes while the disc remains mm-bright and accreting; or

(b) the observational transition-disc signature (infrared deficit together with high mm flux) reliably disappears before the planet–disc system would otherwise populate the empirically forbidden region of high mm flux, small hole, and ongoing accretion.

Determine quantitative conditions on the disc and planet parameters under which (a) or (b) holds, and demonstrate that the resulting predicted population of transition discs is consistent with the observed scarcity of accreting, mm-bright, small-hole systems.
