representations.normalized: Determine the true upper limit on the initial (zero-age main sequence) mass of an individual star that can form in nature. Specifically: (1) Earlier statistical analyses of the stellar mass function in the Arches cluster pointed to a sharp cutoff near 150 solar masses. (2) Spectroscopic and atmospheric modeling of the brightest stars (a1, a2, a3, c) in the core of R136 in 30 Doradus yields inferred initial masses in the range 160–320 solar masses. (3) The binary system R144 in 30 Doradus has an estimated total present-day mass of 200–300 solar masses, with an inferred initial system mass possibly as large as 400 solar masses, implying at least one component near 200 solar masses at birth. The problem is to decide whether masses above 150 solar masses are physically real for single stars, or whether they are artifacts of (a) dependence on stellar atmosphere and evolution models, (b) calibration uncertainties in luminosity, temperature, and mass-loss rates, and (c) unresolved multiplicity (i.e., apparent very massive "stars" actually being close binaries or merger products). Provide a quantitative determination of the maximum birth mass of an individual star, accounting for these systematics.

The question remains open as of recent literature. Spectroscopic re-analyses of R136 stars (notably R136a1) have revised estimates downward to roughly 150–230 solar masses, but values still exceed the canonical 150 solar-mass limit. representations.normalized:
In the study of circumstellar dust discs around young stellar objects, a "transition disc" is conventionally identified by a deficit of near- and/or mid-infrared excess in its spectral energy distribution (SED), interpreted as a depletion of small dust within an inner cavity. High-resolution millimetre interferometric imaging has, however, revealed objects (such as MWC 758 and WSB 60) whose SEDs look indistinguishable from those of "primordial" (full) discs — i.e. they show no near-infrared deficit — yet whose resolved millimetre continuum images exhibit a large central cavity in the large (mm-sized) dust grains.

Address the following questions:

(a) Do such objects (primordial-looking SED together with a resolved large mm-wavelength cavity in the large dust component) constitute a statistically significant hidden population among Class II circumstellar discs, rather than isolated peculiar cases?

(b) If such a population exists, determine whether it is physically related to the canonical transition-disc classes (those identified by infrared SED deficits and/or by resolved mm cavities accompanied by an SED deficit). Specifically, decide which of the following evolutionary relationships best describes them:
  (i) precursors that subsequently develop into infrared-deficient transition discs;
  (ii) contemporaneous counterparts representing a parallel manifestation of the same physical mechanism (e.g. dust filtration, planet-disc interaction, photoevaporation) but with differing small-dust content in the inner disc;
  (iii) descendants representing a later evolutionary stage of previously infrared-deficient transition discs after replenishment of small inner dust.

Provide observational and/or theoretical criteria (e.g. occurrence rates, accretion rates, stellar ages, inner-disc gas/small-dust content, scattered-light morphology) that would discriminate among (i)–(iii).

Determine the correct effective-temperature scale T_eff(spectral type, luminosity class) of O-type stars as a function of host-galaxy metallicity, with particular focus on galaxies beyond the Magellanic Clouds. Specifically:

1. Establish how the O-star T_eff scale depends on metallicity Z, testing the conjecture that the scale becomes systematically hotter as Z decreases, while accounting for and properly controlling: (a) small-number statistics in the spectroscopic samples available for each galaxy, (b) the limited signal-to-noise of faint-star spectra in distant galaxies, and (c) the dependence of derived parameters on the choice of stellar atmosphere code.

2. Assess and quantify the systematic uncertainty introduced by the fact that current calibrations rely essentially on two non-LTE, line-blanketed, expanding-atmosphere codes — FASTWIND and CMFGEN — which share similar physical assumptions (treatment of NLTE, line blanketing, spherical extension, mass loss). Determine whether the inferred T_eff values would change significantly if alternative independent atmosphere codes with different physical approximations were employed.

3. Extend the calibration into the low-metallicity regime characteristic of dwarf galaxies in and beyond the Local Group, providing an empirical T_eff scale and quantitative comparison between galaxies of differing Z that is robust against the sampling biases above.

The problem is to deliver such a calibrated, code-independent, statistics-controlled effective-temperature scale for O-type stars across the metallicity range spanned by the Milky Way, the Magellanic Clouds, and lower-metallicity galaxies beyond them.

The literature shows partial progress: empirical T_eff scales for O stars in the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds (Massey et al. 2004, 2005, 2009; Martins et al. 2005) have established that lower-metallicity O dwarfs are several thousand K hotter than Galactic counterparts. More recent work using FASTWIND combined with genetic-algorithm fitting has begun characterizing massive stars in sub-SMC-metallicity Local Group dwarf galaxies. However, the calibration still depends almost exclusively on FASTWIND and CMFGEN (which share similar physics), samples beyond the Magellanic Clouds remain small, and a fully code-independent, statistics-controlled T_eff–Z calibration has not been delivered. The problem therefore appears still open.

Consider the semilinear parabolic Cauchy problem
  u_t - Δu = |u|^{p-1} u - b |∇u|^q,    (t,x) ∈ (0,∞) × R^N,
  u(0,x) = u_0(x),                      x ∈ R^N,
where N ≥ 1, p > 1, q ≥ 1, and b > 0. Recall that for the pure reaction-diffusion equation u_t - Δu = |u|^{p-1} u on R^N, the Fujita exponent p_c = 1 + 2/N has the property that every nontrivial nonnegative solution blows up in finite time when 1 < p ≤ p_c, while for p > p_c there exist nontrivial nonnegative global-in-time solutions (and blow-up solutions also exist).

Restrict to the scaling-critical balance q = 2p/(p+1), so that the reaction and gradient-damping terms share the same parabolic scaling, and assume b > 0 is sufficiently small. Determine whether there exists a Fujita-type critical exponent p^* = p^*(N,b) ∈ (1, ∞] such that:
  (i) for every 1 < p < p^* (with q = 2p/(p+1)), no nontrivial nonnegative global classical solution of the above equation exists; and
  (ii) for every p > p^*, nontrivial nonnegative global solutions do exist (for suitable initial data).
If such an exponent exists, identify it; otherwise, describe the dichotomy structure of the global existence/blow-up regimes.

Consider radiatively driven winds of hot, massive (OB-type) stars. Two empirical discrepancies with current theoretical predictions are observed:

(i) In the modified wind momentum–luminosity relation, defined by D_mom = Ṁ v_∞ (R/R_⊙)^{1/2} as a function of stellar luminosity L, the observationally inferred relation lies systematically offset (vertically shifted) from the theoretically predicted relation across stars of different host-galaxy metallicities.

(ii) Below a limiting stellar luminosity (the "weak-wind" regime, roughly log(L/L_⊙) ≲ 5.2), empirically inferred mass-loss rates Ṁ fall orders of magnitude below the theoretical predictions of line-driven wind theory.

Several physical effects are candidate contributors to these mismatches:
 - Microclumping: small-scale optically thin density inhomogeneities in the wind, parameterized by a clumping factor f_cl = ⟨ρ²⟩/⟨ρ⟩², which causes ρ²-sensitive diagnostics (e.g. Hα recombination, free–free radio emission) to overestimate Ṁ when treated as smooth.
 - Macroclumping / porosity: large-scale optically thick clumps that allow radiation to escape through low-density channels, weakening the apparent strength of resonance lines and biasing Ṁ determinations.

Consider radiatively driven winds of hot, massive (OB-type) stars. Two empirical discrepancies with current theoretical predictions are observed:

(i) In the modified wind momentum–luminosity relation, defined by D_mom = Ṁ v_∞ (R/R_⊙)^{1/2} as a function of stellar luminosity L, the observationally inferred relation lies systematically offset (vertically shifted) from the theoretically predicted relation across stars of different host-galaxy metallicities.

(ii) Below a limiting stellar luminosity (the "weak-wind" regime, roughly log(L/L_⊙) ≲ 5.2), empirically inferred mass-loss rates Ṁ fall orders of magnitude below the theoretical predictions of line-driven wind theory.

Several physical effects are candidate contributors to these mismatches:
 - Microclumping: small-scale optically thin density inhomogeneities in the wind, parameterized by a clumping factor f_cl = ⟨ρ²⟩/⟨ρ⟩², which causes ρ²-sensitive diagnostics (e.g. Hα recombination, free–free radio emission) to overestimate Ṁ when treated as smooth.
 - Macroclumping / porosity: large-scale optically thick clumps that allow radiation to escape through low-density channels, weakening the apparent strength of resonance lines and biasing Ṁ determinations.
 - Inadequacy of the classical Hα diagnostic in the small-Ṁ regime, where the line becomes insensitive to mass loss and additional diagnostics (UV resonance lines, X-rays, IR/radio continua) are required.

Problem. Quantitatively determine the individual contributions of microclumping, macroclumping/porosity, and Hα diagnostic limitations to the observed vertical offset in the wind momentum–luminosity relation and to the weak-wind discrepancy at low luminosity, and prescribe a self-consistent treatment of these effects that yields reliable empirical mass-loss rates Ṁ(L, Z) reconciled with theoretical line-driven-wind predictions across the full luminosity and metallicity range of OB stars.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent (2024) analyses of OB-star winds in the Galaxy and Magellanic Clouds confirm that the weak-wind problem persists below log(L/L_⊙) ≈ 5.2, with empirical mass-loss rates orders of magnitude below theoretical line-driven predictions. Studies show high but variable clumping factors, evidence for porosity effects, and metallicity- and luminosity-dependent wind structure that complicates Hα-based diagnostics. The relative contributions of microclumping, macroclumping/porosity, and Hα limitations are still being disentangled, with no consensus prescription yet for fully reconciling empirical and theoretical mass-loss relations.

representations.normalized:
Consider the semilinear parabolic equation
  u_t − Δu = |u|^{p−1} u − b |∇u|^q,    (t,x) ∈ (0,T) × R^N,
with N ≥ 1, p > 1, q > 1, and b > 0. Choose the scaling-invariant exponent q = 2p/(p+1), so that the equation is invariant under the rescaling u_λ(t,x) = λ^{2/(p−1)} u(λ^2 t, λ x).

A backward self-similar blowup solution at time T > 0 is a solution of the form
  u(t,x) = (T − t)^{−1/(p−1)} W( x / (T − t)^{1/2} ),
where the profile W : R^N → R satisfies the elliptic equation
  ΔW − (1/2) y · ∇W − W/(p−1) + |W|^{p−1} W − b |∇W|^q = 0,    y ∈ R^N.

It is known that for every N ≥ 1 and every b ∈ (0,2) there exists some p_0 = p_0(b,N) > 1 (defined non-explicitly through a limiting argument) such that for every p ∈ (1, p_0) the profile equation admits a solution W that is positive, of class C^2, radially symmetric, and radially decreasing on R^N.

Answer the following:
(a) Determine the actual set of admissible exponents p > 1 for which such positive, radial, radially decreasing self-similar profiles exist.
(b) Decide whether the existence statement can be extended to all p > 1 and all b > 0.
(c) For each fixed admissible pair (p,b,N), decide whether the positive radial self-similar profile W is unique.
(d) In the critical case q = 2p/(p+1), decide whether every blowup of (positive) solutions of the equation is asymptotically described by such a self-similar profile, or whether qualitatively different blowup behaviors can occur.

representations.normalized:
In the standard theory of single-star stellar evolution, stars with initial masses roughly between 8 M☉ and 25–30 M☉ are expected to end their lives as red supergiants (RSGs) and to explode as hydrogen-rich (Type II-P) core-collapse supernovae. However, direct identifications of progenitor stars in pre-explosion imaging of nearby Type II-P supernovae yield inferred initial masses lying only in the range 8 ± 1 M☉ to about 16–17 M☉, with no confirmed progenitor having an initial mass close to 25 M☉. This deficit of high-mass RSG progenitors is known as the "red supergiant problem."

Provide a quantitative astrophysical resolution of the following: For single, approximately solar-metallicity massive stars in the initial mass range ≈17–30 M☉ that pass through a red supergiant phase, determine which mechanism — (a) substantially enhanced RSG mass loss that strips the hydrogen envelope and shifts the progenitor off the RSG branch before core collapse, (b) "dark" (failed) core collapse directly into a black hole producing no luminous supernova or only a very faint transient, or (c) some other evolutionary channel (e.g., obscuration by circumstellar dust, binary interactions, or specific compactness-dependent explodability) — is responsible for the absence of identified high-mass RSG progenitors. The required answer should specify the operating mechanism(s), the mass thresholds at which each becomes dominant, and demonstrate consistency with observed Type II-P progenitor mass distributions, supernova rates, and compact-remnant mass functions.

representations.normalized:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a smoothly bounded domain (or, when $n=1$, a bounded interval), and consider the semilinear parabolic problem with absorbing gradient term
$$
\begin{cases}
 u_t - \Delta u = |u|^{p-1}u - b\,|\nabla u|^q, & x \in \Omega,\ t > 0,\\
 u = 0, & x \in \partial\Omega,\ t > 0,\\
 u(\cdot,0) = \varphi, & x \in \Omega,
\end{cases}
$$
where $p > 1$, $b > 0$, and $q > 1$. A classical solution $u$ is called global if its maximal existence time satisfies $T^*(\varphi) = \infty$; it is called bounded if $\sup_{t \ge 0} \|u(t)\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} < \infty$, and unbounded global otherwise.

It is known that in the one-dimensional case $\Omega = (0,L)$ with the special exponent $q = 2$ and $p > 2$, there exists $b = b_0(L) > 0$ and infinitely many initial data $\varphi$ producing nondecreasing-in-time, global, $L^\infty$-unbounded solutions.

Question. In the intermediate exponent range
$$
\frac{2p}{p+1} < q < p, \qquad q \neq 2,
$$
(in dimension $n \ge 1$, excluding the already-known case $q=2$ on an interval): must every global classical solution remain bounded, or can unbounded global solutions occur for some choice of $\Omega$, $b$, and $\varphi$? Provide a complete classification of boundedness versus unboundedness of global solutions in this regime.

representations.normalized:
Massive main-sequence stars (initial masses ≳ 15 M☉, spectral type O) that rotate sufficiently rapidly are predicted by stellar-evolution theory to undergo "chemically homogeneous evolution": rotationally induced internal mixing keeps the hydrogen abundance profile essentially uniform throughout the star, so that as hydrogen is consumed in the core the star evolves bluewards and upwards from the Zero Age Main Sequence in the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram (rather than redwards as in standard, non-homogeneous evolution), with strongly enhanced surface helium and CNO-processed nitrogen abundances appearing already during core hydrogen burning.

Observations of O-type stars in the Milky Way and in the 30 Doradus region of the Large Magellanic Cloud reveal projected rotational velocities v sin i large enough that, according to current rotating stellar-evolution models, a non-negligible subpopulation should be evolving homogeneously.

Problem. Determine whether the most rapidly rotating Galactic and Large Magellanic Cloud O stars actually undergo chemically homogeneous evolution. Specifically:

(a) Identify a set of necessary and sufficient observational signatures — combining position in the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, projected rotational velocity, surface helium mass fraction Y, surface N/C and N/O abundance ratios, and (where applicable) binary properties — whose simultaneous occurrence in an individual star would constitute unambiguous evidence that the star is on a chemically homogeneous evolutionary track rather than a standard rotating-evolution track.

(b) Decide, on the basis of currently available samples of rapid rotators with v sin i at the high end of the observed distribution, whether any such star meets these criteria, thereby establishing or ruling out the existence of the chemically homogeneous evolutionary channel for single massive stars at Galactic and LMC metallicities.

Subsequent observational work has produced suggestive but not conclusive evidence for chemically homogeneous evolution at Galactic/LMC/SMC metallicities. Examples include the young, nitrogen-enriched O2 III(f*) star MPG 355 in SMC cluster NGC 346 interpreted as homogeneously evolving, ON2 III stars near the ZAMS with large N/C ratios, and a correlation in LMC O stars between high surface helium enrichment and the mass discrepancy. Quasi-CHE candidates have also been claimed up to solar metallicity. Theoretical interest has surged since the LIGO black-hole-merger detections, but a definitive, unambiguous identification of single-star CHE in MW/LMC rapid rotators is still lacking, so the question remains only partially resolved.

Let $p>1$ and $q>1$ with $q\ge p$. For an unbounded smooth domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$, define the inradius
$$\rho(\Omega)=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)=\sup\{r>0:\Omega \text{ contains a ball of radius } r\}.$$
Consider the semilinear parabolic Dirichlet problem
$$
\begin{cases}
u_t-\Delta u = u^{p}+|\nabla u|^{q}, & x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\
u(x,t)=0, & x\in\partial\Omega,\ t>0,\\
u(x,0)=\varphi(x)\ge 0, & x\in\Omega,
\end{cases}
$$
with nonnegative initial data $\varphi\in L^\infty(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ vanishing on $\partial\Omega$. Let $u$ denote the maximal classical nonnegative solution defined on $[0,T^*)$, with $T^*\in(0,\infty]$ the maximal existence time. Call $u$ an "unbounded global solution" if $T^*=\infty$ and $\lim_{t\to\infty}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}=\infty$.

Question: Assuming $\rho(\Omega)=\infty$ and $q\ge p$, does there always exist an initial datum $\varphi$ for which the corresponding solution is an unbounded global solution (rather than blowing up in finite time)?

Massive stars (initial masses roughly above 20 solar masses) may, after exhausting hydrogen in the core, evolve through a red supergiant (RSG) phase and, in some non-standard evolutionary scenarios, return blueward across the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram via a "blue loop," reappearing as B-type supergiants (post-RSG B supergiants). Such post-RSG objects are predicted to differ from pre-RSG B supergiants in two observable ways: (i) their surfaces should display strongly enhanced CNO-cycle products (in particular elevated N/C and N/O ratios) due to dredge-up during the RSG phase, and (ii) because of strong angular momentum loss while in the RSG phase, they should rotate substantially more slowly than pre-RSG B supergiants, with projected rotational velocities v sin i at or below about 5 km/s.

Address the following:

(a) Do post-RSG blue loops actually occur in nature and produce a distinct, observationally identifiable population of Galactic B-type supergiants, separate from the pre-RSG B supergiants?

(b) Among current candidate post-RSG B supergiants—identified, for instance, through pulsational properties consistent with a post-RSG interior structure—the measured surface CNO abundance enhancements are smaller than those predicted by non-standard evolutionary calculations including blue loops. Can the post-RSG blue-loop scenario, possibly with refined input physics, account for this quantitative mismatch between observed and predicted surface abundances?

(c) Does the population of B supergiants split into two kinematically distinct groups in v sin i, with the post-RSG group concentrated at very low rotational velocities (≲ 5 km/s), as required to confirm the scenario?

Recent stellar-evolution work continues to predict two distinct B-supergiant populations (pre-RSG and post-RSG via blue loops) with differing CNO surface abundances and rotation rates, but observational confirmation remains incomplete: candidate post-RSG B supergiants still show smaller CNO enhancements than non-standard models predict, and the very low v sin i (≲ 5 km/s) measurements needed to discriminate the two populations are at the edge of current capabilities. Recent results (e.g., merger-origin blue supergiants, ongoing studies of α Cygni variables) add alternative channels but do not settle the question.

representations.normalized:
Consider the Cauchy problem on the whole Euclidean space:
  u_t - Δu = u^p - |∇u|^q,    (t,x) ∈ (0,T*) × R^N,
  u(0,x) = φ(x),               x ∈ R^N,
where p > 1, q ≥ p, and φ ≥ 0 is a sufficiently smooth, bounded initial datum. Let u be the (classical) maximal solution defined on the maximal existence interval [0,T*), with T* ∈ (0, ∞]. Assume that u is unbounded, i.e. limsup_{t → T*^-} ‖u(t,·)‖_{L^∞(R^N)} = ∞.

Define the (extended) blow-up set
  E := { x_0 ∈ R^N ∪ {∞} : there exist sequences x_n → x_0 in R^N ∪ {∞} and t_n → T*^- with u(t_n, x_n) → ∞ }.

It is known that under these hypotheses one has the dichotomy E = R^N ∪ {∞} or E = {∞}, and that the first alternative E = R^N ∪ {∞} is realized by some choices of φ (with T* = ∞, the solution diverging at every spatial point as t → ∞).

Question: Does there exist an initial datum φ for which the second alternative occurs, namely E = {∞}? Equivalently, is there a choice of φ such that the corresponding solution u becomes unbounded only by escaping to spatial infinity, while remaining locally bounded in space-time on every compact subset of R^N × [0,T*)?

The question is listed as an open problem in the recent survey on parabolic equations with gradient nonlinearities. A web search did not turn up any subsequent paper resolving the existence of an initial datum on R^N (with q ≥ p) for which the blow-up set is exactly {∞}; related literature (Souplet and coauthors, Quittner–Souplet monograph) discusses the dichotomy and examples of E = R^N ∪ {∞}, but not a construction or refutation of the E = {∞} case.

Let $\mathscr{H}^1$ denote the Hardy space of Dirichlet series defined as the completion of the space of Dirichlet polynomials $\sum_{n=1}^N a_n n^{-s}$ under the norm
$$\Big\| \sum_{n=1}^N a_n n^{-s} \Big\|_{\mathscr{H}^1} \;=\; \int_{\mathbb{T}^\infty} \Big| \sum_{n=1}^N a_n \chi(n) \Big|\, d\mu(\chi),$$
where $\mathbb{T}^\infty$ is the infinite-dimensional torus equipped with normalized Haar measure $\mu$, and where each character $\chi: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{T}$ is the completely multiplicative function determined by $\chi(p) = z_p$ (with $z_p$ the coordinate of $\chi$ corresponding to the prime $p$). For each integer $N \geq 1$, define the partial sum of the Riemann zeta function
$$F_N(s) \;=\; \sum_{n=1}^N n^{-s}.$$
Determine whether
$$\| F_N \|_{\mathscr{H}^1} \;=\; o\!\left(\sqrt{N}\right) \qquad \text{as } N \to \infty.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The closely related randomized version, in which $n^{-s}$ is replaced by a Steinhaus random multiplicative function, was resolved by A. Harper, who proved better-than-square-root cancellation $\mathbb{E}\big|\sum_{n\le N} f(n)\big| \asymp \sqrt{N}/(\log\log N)^{1/4}$. However, the deterministic question for $\|F_N\|_{\mathscr{H}^1}$ — i.e., for the average of $|\sum_{n\le N}\chi(n)|$ over all completely multiplicative characters $\chi$ — does not appear to have been resolved; only partial estimates and lower bounds are available, and the problem is still listed as open in surveys of Hardy spaces of Dirichlet series.

[{"title": "Moments of random multiplicative functions, I: Low moments, better than squareroot cancellation, and critical multiplicative chaos", "url": "https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/forum-of-mathematics-pi/article/moments-of-random-multiplicative-functions-i-low-moments-better-than-squareroot-cancellation-and-critical-multiplicative-chaos/A7B32F8285B07AE15700F02E997B233F", "snippet": "Harper proves E|sum_{n<=x} f(n)| asymp sqrt(x)/(log log x)^{1/4}, confirming better-than-square-root cancellation conjectured by Helson in the random setting.", "claim": "The randomized version of Helson's conjecture is solved by Harper."}, {"title": "Helson's problem for sums of a random multiplicative function (Bondarenko–Seip)", "url": "https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematika/article/abs/helsons-problem-for-sums-of-a-random-multiplicative-function/01FC5EBBB3992C5795F3CDA48F818D73", "snippet": "Lower bounds for small moments of sums of a random multiplicative function as progress toward Helson's conjecture.", "claim": "Prior partial progress focused on the random analogue."}, {"title": "Hardy spaces of Dirichlet series and the Riemann zeta function (Seip lecture notes)", "url": "https://www.um.es/beca/NoLiFA/charlas/talk_Seip_NoLiFA.pdf", "snippet": "Discusses the deterministic H^1 norm of partial sums of zeta and lists the o(sqrt N) question as open.", "claim": "The deterministic Helson problem about ||F_N||_{H^1} = o(sqrt N) remains open."}]

In a relativistic heavy-ion collision, a dense, rapidly expanding and fluctuating medium (the quark-gluon plasma) is produced. Hard partonic scatterings inside this medium produce pairs of high-energy partons that fragment into collimated sprays of hadrons (jets), approximately back-to-back in the transverse plane by momentum conservation. As these jets traverse the medium they lose energy and are modified, a phenomenon known as jet quenching. The goal of jet tomography is to use the measured attenuation and modification of such jets to reconstruct spatial and dynamical properties of the medium, in analogy with x-ray tomography of a static body by a controlled beam.

Unlike an idealized tomography setup, a heavy-ion collision is characterized by:
(i) the absence of an externally controlled, mono-energetic, penetrating probe beam — the probes are produced internally with a broad spectrum of energies, flavors, and production points sampled by the nuclear overlap geometry;
(ii) the absence of a fully established, first-principles dynamical theory of in-medium parton energy loss valid across all relevant energy scales and coupling regimes; and
(iii) the absence of a static, homogeneous background — the medium expands hydrodynamically, cools, and exhibits event-by-event geometric and quantum fluctuations.

Problem. Formulate a mathematically and physically reliable jet-tomography program for heavy-ion collisions: namely, specify a procedure that, taking as input experimentally measurable jet observables (such as nuclear modification factors, di-jet asymmetries, jet substructure, and azimuthal anisotropies) together with a model of the fluctuating, evolving medium and a model of in-medium energy loss, produces quantitative reconstructions of medium properties (such as the local transport coefficient $\hat{q}(x,t)$, temperature, and density profiles) with controlled and demonstrably non-misleading systematic and statistical uncertainties, in spite of the three obstacles above.

Consider high transverse-momentum partons (jets) traversing the hot, deconfined QCD medium produced in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The nuclear modification factor R_AA(p_T) is defined as the ratio of the measured charged-hadron transverse-momentum spectrum in nucleus-nucleus collisions to the spectrum in proton-proton collisions at the same center-of-mass energy, scaled by the average number of binary nucleon-nucleon collisions.

A "conformal AdS/CFT energy-loss scenario" is one in which the medium is modeled by a strongly coupled conformal field theory (e.g. N=4 super Yang-Mills) with a fixed (non-running) jet-medium coupling, leading via the gauge/gravity correspondence to an energy-loss law of the form dE/dx ∝ x^2 (path-length squared) for a light quark or gluon traversing the medium. Because the underlying theory is conformal, no additional scale enters and the coupling does not run with p_T.

Question: Under such a conformal AdS/CFT energy-loss scenario, the predicted R_AA(p_T) at LHC energies (Pb–Pb collisions at center-of-mass energies of several TeV per nucleon pair) is approximately flat as a function of p_T at high p_T. The measured R_AA(p_T) at LHC, however, exhibits a pronounced rising slope with p_T. Determine whether the conformal AdS/CFT energy-loss scenario, with its fixed jet-medium coupling and squared-path-length dependence, is compatible with the observed rapid rise of R_AA(p_T) in LHC data, or whether it is excluded by these measurements.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question is treated as resolved in the heavy-ion phenomenology literature: comparisons of conformal AdS/CFT energy-loss predictions (fixed coupling, dE/dx ∝ x^2) with LHC R_AA(p_T) measurements show overquenching and a flat shape inconsistent with the observed rising slope, leading the community to conclude that a strictly conformal AdS scenario is ruled out, while non-conformal/running-coupling holographic extensions remain under study.

representations.normalized:
Consider ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions modeled as a two-component (soft + hard) system. The soft sector describes a low transverse-momentum (low-pT) bulk medium whose transverse geometry in a given centrality class fluctuates event by event; quantify its azimuthal asymmetry by the second-order eccentricity

  e2 = |∫ d²x_⊥ ρ(x_⊥) x_⊥² e^{2iφ}| / ∫ d²x_⊥ ρ(x_⊥) x_⊥²,

where ρ is the initial energy-density distribution in the transverse plane. Within a fixed centrality class, sub-classes of events are selected according to their value of e2 (e.g., the top 1% in e2, or events near the mean of the e2 distribution). The hard sector consists of high-pT partons that traverse the medium and lose energy according to a jet-energy-loss model, producing observable jets characterized by

  – the nuclear modification factor R_AA(pT) = (dN^{AA}/dpT) / (N_coll · dN^{pp}/dpT),
  – the high-pT elliptic flow v2(pT) = ⟨cos[2(φ − Ψ_RP)]⟩ of the hard hadron/jet distribution,

while the soft bulk also produces a low-pT v2.

Within this Soft-Hard Event Engineering framework, determine quantitatively how the choice of low-pT background — specifically (a) using event-by-event fluctuating initial conditions versus a smoothed (event-averaged) initial condition, and (b) restricting to e2-selected sub-samples within a fixed centrality class — affects:

  (i) the high-pT nuclear modification factor R_AA(pT), and
  (ii) the high-pT elliptic flow v2(pT), including its dependence on the mean and width of the low-pT v2 distribution induced by the e2 selection.

In particular, establish whether R_AA is sensitive or insensitive to the e2-eccentricity distribution of the background, and characterize the proportionality (or other functional dependence) between high-pT v2 and low-pT v2 across e2-selected sub-classes, as well as the role of event-by-event background fluctuations in enhancing the high-pT v2.

Studies of Soft-Hard Event Engineering have established (within specific energy-loss models) that R_AA is essentially independent of e2-eccentricity selection within a centrality class, while high-pT v2 is approximately proportional to low-pT v2 and is enhanced by event-by-event fluctuations. These qualitative findings are reproduced in subsequent analyses, but a complete, model-independent quantitative description across all observables and energies remains incomplete, so the broader problem is partially solved.

Consider the microscopic Bohr Hamiltonian formalism for nuclear collective quadrupole motion, in which a five-dimensional collective Schrödinger equation in the shape variables (β, γ) and three Euler angles is derived from a self-consistent mean-field theory (e.g., Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov with a chosen effective interaction) by means of the generator coordinate method (GCM) together with the Gaussian overlap approximation (GOA). Restricting the GCM to zero-quasiparticle generator states and using the GOA effectively imposes an adiabatic approximation: the collective coordinates are decoupled from non-collective (quasiparticle) degrees of freedom, and the resulting Bohr Hamiltonian has the form

  H_coll = T_vib(β,γ) + T_rot(β,γ; Î) + V(β,γ),

with mass parameters and potential V(β,γ) computed microscopically from the mean-field configurations.

When applied to even–even deformed nuclei, this adiabatic microscopic Bohr Hamiltonian systematically predicts excited 0⁺ states (interpreted as β-vibrations or shape-coexisting states) whose excitation energies are too high (typically by about 50%) and whose character is too vibrational. Recent reviews and microscopic-Bohr-Hamiltonian studies (e.g., the five-dimensional collective Hamiltonian derived from EDF mean fields via GCM+GOA) continue to identify the adiabatic restriction to zero-quasiparticle generator states as a known limitation, and the character of low-lying 0⁺ "β-vibrational" states in well-deformed rare-earth nuclei is described as unresolved. representations.normalized:
The Interacting Boson Model (IBM) describes low-lying collective quadrupole excitations of even–even atomic nuclei in terms of two kinds of bosons: an s-boson with angular momentum J=0 and a d-boson with angular momentum J=2, whose creation operators s† and (d†_μ)_{μ=-2,...,2} together with their adjoints and bilinears generate the Lie algebra of U(6). The standard IBM Hamiltonian is built from scalar combinations of these generators, e.g.

H_IBM = ε_d (d†·d̃) + κ Q·Q + κ' L·L + ...,

with a finite set of phenomenological parameters (such as ε_d, κ, κ', and the parameter χ in the quadrupole operator Q_μ = (s†d̃ + d†s)_μ + χ (d†d̃)_μ).

The physical premise of the model is that the s and d bosons represent collective valence-nucleon pairs in spherical single-particle orbitals coupled to total spin 0 and spin 2, respectively, on top of an inert closed-shell core. For nuclei with only a few valence nucleons (or holes) outside a closed shell, one can derive the IBM parameters microscopically from an underlying shell-model nucleon Hamiltonian by mapping collective fermion pair states onto boson states (e.g., via the OAI mapping or generalized seniority schemes).

Problem. Starting solely from the assumption that the s and d bosons represent valence-nucleon pairs in spherical orbitals coupled to angular momentum 0 and 2, give a microscopic derivation, from a realistic nucleonic Hamiltonian acting in the valence shell-model space, of the parameters of the IBM Hamiltonian (including ε_d, the strengths of the boson–boson interaction terms, and χ) that is valid for nuclei lying far from closed shells, i.e., near mid-shell where the number of valence pairs is large and deformed/transitional behaviour dominates. Equivalently, construct an explicit fermion-to-boson mapping procedure whose output IBM parameters reproduce, in a controlled approximation, the low-lying collective spectra and electromagnetic transition rates of mid-shell even–even nuclei.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Microscopic derivations of IBM parameters are well established for nuclei near closed shells (OAI mapping, generalized seniority, broken-pair approaches). For nuclei far in the open shell (mid-shell, strongly deformed), a fully microscopic derivation purely from the shell-model picture of valence pairs has not been achieved; modern approaches instead derive IBM parameters by mapping nuclear energy density functional / mean-field potential energy surfaces onto the IBM, providing a practical but indirect route. Thus the problem is partially solved: parameters can be obtained globally via mean-field mapping, but a direct microscopic derivation from the valence-pair shell-model premise for mid-shell nuclei remains an open issue.

representations.normalized:
Consider an atomic nucleus exhibiting collective rotational motion, modeled as a quantum rotor whose low-lying excited states form a rotational band of angular-momentum eigenstates with quantum numbers I = I_0, I_0+2, I_0+4, .... Treat the rotational wave function as a coherent superposition of orientation states, and define a coherence angle Δψ as the angular resolution to which the orientation of the rotating mean-field shape can be quantum-mechanically defined; the rotational wave function can therefore acquire only a phase ψI/ℏ bounded by this coherence, restricting the number of band members to ΔI ∼ 2/Δψ.

A regular (state) band of finite length is observed to terminate by one of the following mechanisms:
(i) band crossing by an aligned two-quasiparticle configuration (e.g., a pair of high-j neutrons or protons whose intrinsic spins align with the rotation axis);
(ii) quasiparticle alignment within the band itself;
(iii) a transition to magnetic rotation (shears mechanism); or
(iv) band termination, in which the available valence-space angular momentum is exhausted in a non-collective stretched configuration.

Problem. Derive, from microscopic considerations of spontaneous symmetry breaking of rotational symmetry by the nuclear mean field together with the coherence-angle estimate ΔI ∼ 2/Δψ, quantitative criteria expressing the maximum spin I_max (equivalently, the maximum number of band members) that a regular rotational band can sustain before being cut off by each of the mechanisms (i)–(iv). The criteria should relate I_max to intrinsic nuclear parameters (such as the deformation parameter β, the moment of inertia ℐ, single-particle level density at the Fermi surface, pairing gap Δ, and Fermi-surface high-j orbital occupations) and predict, for a given nucleus and configuration, which of the four cutoff mechanisms occurs first.

A targeted web search did not turn up a derivation that unifies the coherence-angle estimate ΔI ∼ 2/Δψ with quantitative spontaneous-symmetry-breaking criteria predicting the cutoff of rotational bands by band crossing, quasiparticle alignment, magnetic rotation, or band termination. The status is best regarded as open.

representations.normalized:
Background and setup. Consider an even–even near-spherical (vibrator-like) atomic nucleus described in a shell-model framework. Its low-lying collective states are organized into approximate quadrupole vibrational multiplets labeled by a phonon number N = 0, 1, 2, …, with each N-phonon multiplet containing several states of definite angular momentum I. The yrast line is the sequence of lowest-energy states for each spin I; for a harmonic vibrator the yrast member of the N-phonon multiplet has spin I = 2N.

The tidal-wave (TW) description treats the yrast vibrational states as a single semiclassical rotating mean-field configuration: a uniformly rotating quadrupole-deformed shape obtained from the self-consistent cranking model, in which angular momentum is generated by increasing the deformation amplitude at (approximately) constant rotational frequency, rather than by increasing the frequency at fixed deformation as in a rigid rotor. In this picture, the yrast E2 transitions B(E2; I → I−2) along the vibrational ground band are reproduced as the classical quadrupole radiation of the rotating mean-field shape.

Empirical/shell-model observation to be modeled. Large-scale shell-model calculations for vibrator-like nuclei (for instance, ⁶²Ni) reveal, in addition to the yrast sequence, a set of comparatively rare but enhanced E2 transitions running parallel to the yrast line: namely, transitions between off-yrast members of successive vibrational multiplets that connect the same non-yrast spin I in the N-phonon multiplet to spin I−2 (or the corresponding off-yrast state) in the (N−1)-phonon multiplet. The remaining off-yrast E2 strengths form a comparatively incoherent (chaotic-looking) background.

Problem. Construct an extension of the tidal-wave approach—still based on semiclassical, self-consistent rotating mean-field configurations (e.g., excited cranking solutions, additional collective or quasiparticle excitations built on top of the tidal wave, or analogous coherent semiclassical modes)—that:

(a) reproduces the yrast tidal-wave description as a special case;
(b) yields a discrete family of additional rotating configurations whose E2 decay pattern reproduces the enhanced off-yrast transitions parallel to the yrast sequence found in shell-model calculations of vibrator-like nuclei such as ⁶²Ni;
(c) explains, within this semiclassical mean-field picture, why the remaining off-yrast E2 strength appears incoherent; and
(d) gives quantitative predictions for excitation energies and B(E2) values of these off-yrast states that agree with the shell-model results.

Does such an extension exist, and if so, formulate it explicitly?

Setup. Work in the ring of symmetric functions in variables x = (x_1, x_2, ...) with coefficients in ℚ(q,t). For coprime integers a, b ≥ 1, let Θ_{a,b} denote the symmetric-function operator associated with the (a,b)-action coming from the elliptic Hall algebra / rectangular Catalan combinatorics, and define the operator-twisted symmetric functions
   f^{(a,b)}_λ(x;q,t) := Θ_{a,b}(f_λ)(1)
for any symmetric function f_λ. In particular, for the hook partition (j+1, 1^k) (one part equal to j+1 and k parts equal to 1), let s_{(j|k)}(x) be the corresponding Schur function and set
   s^{(a,b)}_{(j|k)}(x;q,t) := Θ_{a,b}(s_{(j|k)})(1).

For arbitrary positive integers m, n write (m,n) = (ad, bd) with d = gcd(m,n) and gcd(a,b) = 1, and define
   e_{m,n}(x;q,t) := e^{(a,b)}_d(x;q,t),    h_{m,n}(x;q,t) := h^{(a,b)}_d(x;q,t),
where e_d, h_d are the elementary and complete homogeneous symmetric functions of degree d.

Let α(m,n) be the number of integer lattice points strictly between the line segment from (0,0) to (m,n) and the diagonal-avoiding (m,n)-staircase path lying weakly above this segment, and set
   β := α(m,n) − d + 1,
which equals the number of lattice points that lie between the diagonal-avoiding (m,n)-staircase path and the (m−1,n)-staircase path.

For symmetric functions f, g over ℚ(q,t), write f ⪯_s g if and only if g − f is Schur-positive, i.e., expands in the Schur basis with coefficients in ℕ[q,t].

Question. Prove (or disprove) that the following two Schur-positivity inequalities hold simultaneously:
 (i) For all coprime a, b ≥ 1 and all integers j, k ≥ 0,
     q · (−1)^{j} s^{(a,b)}_{(j+1 \mid k−1)}(x;q,t)  ⪯_s  (−1)^{j−1} s^{(a,b)}_{(j \mid k)}(x;q,t).
 (ii) For all integers m, n ≥ 1, with d = gcd(m,n) and β as above,
     q^{β} · e_{m−1,n}(x;q,t)  ⪯_s  (−qt)^{1−d} · h_{m,n}(x;q,t).

The two Schur-inclusion conjectures concerning hook-indexed and (e,h)-indexed images under the rectangular (a,b)-operators appear to remain open. They are part of a family of Schur-positivity conjectures by F. Bergeron in rectangular Catalan combinatorics; recent surveys (including Bergeron's 2021 monograph on symmetric functions and rectangular Catalan combinatorics) still list such Schur-inclusion problems among unresolved questions, and no proof in the stated generality was found.

representations.normalized:
Work in the ring of symmetric functions over $\mathbb{Q}(q,t)$ with the standard bases $\{e_\lambda\}$ (elementary), $\{h_\lambda\}$ (complete homogeneous), and $\{s_\lambda\}$ (Schur). For coprime integers $a,b \ge 1$ and a positive integer $d$, let $\Theta_{a,b}$ denote the operator on symmetric functions associated with the rectangular $(a,b)$-Catalan setting (the relevant element of the elliptic Hall algebra acting on symmetric functions). Define the "complete seed" specialization
$$h^{(a,b)}_d(x;q,t) := \Theta_{a,b}\bigl(h_d\bigr)(x;q,t),$$
and, for integers $j,k \ge 0$ with $j+k = d-1$, the "hook seed" specialization
$$s^{(a,b)}_{(j\mid k)}(x;q,t) := \Theta_{a,b}\bigl(s_{(j\mid k)}\bigr)(x;q,t),$$
where $(j\mid k)$ denotes the hook partition with arm $j$ and leg $k$ in Frobenius notation, namely $(j+1, 1^{k})$.

For symmetric functions $f,g$, write $f \le_e g$ to mean that $g - f$ is $e$-positive, i.e.\ all coefficients of $g-f$ in the elementary basis $\{e_\lambda\}$ are nonnegative; in particular $0 \le_e f$ means $f$ itself is $e$-positive.

Specialize $t = 1+r$, regarding $q$ and $r$ as formal parameters (so $e$-positivity is asked for as a polynomial in $q,r$ with nonnegative coefficients in the $e$-basis).

Prove or disprove: for every $d \ge 1$, every coprime pair $(a,b)$ with $a,b \ge 1$, and every $j,k \ge 0$ with $j+k = d-1$, both
$$0 \;\le_e\; (-1)^{1-k}\, h^{(a,b)}_d(x;q,1+r),$$
and
$$q\,(-1)^{j}\, s^{(a,b)}_{(j+1\mid k-1)}(x;q,1+r) \;\le_e\; (-1)^{j-1}\, s^{(a,b)}_{(j\mid k)}(x;q,1+r).$$

The question is one of several positivity conjectures formulated for operators in the elliptic Hall algebra acting on symmetric functions (Theta operators, rectangular (a,b)-Catalan setting). Subsequent work by D'Adderio, Romero, and collaborators has resolved various Schur- and e-positivity conjectures in this circle, but no source found explicitly confirms a proof or disproof of the specific e-positivity / e-inclusion statements at t = 1+r for the complete and hook seeds for all coprime (a,b). Status appears unresolved in the literature accessible via the search.

Work in the ring $\Lambda(x)[q,t]$ of symmetric functions in variables $x = (x_1, x_2, \dots)$ over $\mathbb{Q}(q,t)$. Let $\{e_\lambda\}$ denote the elementary basis of $\Lambda$. For two symmetric-function-valued polynomials $A, B$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}[q,t]$, write $A \le_e B$ (the e-positivity order) if $B - A$ expands in the basis $\{e_\lambda\}$ with coefficients lying in $\mathbb{N}[q,t]$.

For positive integers $m, n \ge 1$, let $e_{m,n}(x;q,t)$ and $h_{m,n}(x;q,t)$ denote the symmetric functions associated to the elementary and complete-homogeneous "rectangular" seeds in the rectangular Catalan setting, and set $d = \gcd(m,n)$. Suppose there exist nonnegative integer exponents $\alpha = \alpha(m,n)$ and $\beta = \alpha(m,n) - d + 1$ such that, in the analogous Schur-positivity order $\preceq_s$,
$$q^{\alpha} e_{m-1,n}(x;q,t) \preceq_s e_{m,n}(x;q,t), \qquad q^{\beta} e_{m-1,n}(x;q,t) \preceq_s (-qt)^{1-d}\, h_{m,n}(x;q,t).$$

Now specialize $t = 1+r$ where $r$ is a formal parameter, and write $f(x;q,1+r)$ for this specialization. Prove or disprove that for all integers $m, n \ge 1$,
$$q^{\alpha}\, e_{m-1,n}(x;q,1+r) \;\le_e\; e_{m,n}(x;q,1+r),$$
$$q^{\beta}\, e_{m-1,n}(x;q,1+r) \;\le_e\; (-q(1+r))^{1-d}\, h_{m,n}(x;q,1+r),$$
and provide a combinatorial interpretation of the resulting nonnegative coefficients.

representations.normalized:
Consider an idealized model of a rotating, strongly magnetized neutron star (a pulsar). The star rotates with angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ and is endowed with a strong magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$; the surrounding plasma-filled region (the magnetosphere) supports an electromagnetic field $(\mathbf{E},\mathbf{B})$ that is, away from certain localized regions, well approximated by the force-free condition $\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$. Localized regions where $\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{B}\neq 0$ are called "gaps"; in such regions charged particles are accelerated along magnetic field lines, and energetic particles can initiate electron–positron pair cascades that supply plasma to the magnetosphere. The pulsar also emits coherent radio waves from a "radio source region" that is in general spatially distinct from the gap (acceleration) region.

Determine, from first principles within the framework of relativistic plasma electrodynamics in a rotating dipolar (or more general) magnetic geometry:

1. The location and geometry of the acceleration regions, i.e. the regions of nonzero $\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{B}$, together with their physical properties (extent, electric potential drop, time dependence, and stability).
2. The quantitative relationship between these acceleration regions and the resulting particle acceleration and pair-creation rates.
3. The location of the radio emission region as constrained by the acceleration regions, including a derivation of the mapping (or the lack thereof) between the gap location and the radio source location.

Provide a self-consistent global solution of the magnetospheric electrodynamics that simultaneously specifies the gap structure, the pair-production multiplicity, and the placement of the coherent radio emission region.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The location and properties of pulsar magnetospheric gaps and the connection between acceleration regions and the radio emission region remain open problems in pulsar electrodynamics. Recent global particle-in-cell simulations and analytical work (e.g., Cerutti & Beloborodov reviews, Philippov et al. PIC studies through the mid-2020s) have produced candidate gap structures (polar cap, slot gap, outer gap, current sheet) but no consensus model fixes both the gap locations and the radio source region from first principles.

Consider a rotating, magnetized neutron star (a pulsar) with angular velocity vector ω, and let B(x,t) and E(x,t) denote the electromagnetic fields in its magnetosphere, sourced together with a plasma of charged particles (electrons, positrons, ions). In ideal corotation, the plasma drifts with the perpendicular corotation velocity v_cor⊥ = (ω × x)⊥, the charge density takes the Goldreich–Julian value ρ_GJ = −ε₀ ∇·(v_cor × B), and a particular current density J_req (including a displacement contribution J_disp = ε₀ ∂E/∂t arising from time dependence in an obliquely rotating frame) is required to maintain this configuration self-consistently with Maxwell's equations.

(a) Identify the physical conditions on the local plasma (number densities, available charge carriers, mobility along and across B, pair-creation supply, etc.) under which the magnetospheric plasma is able to supply simultaneously both the required charge density ρ_GJ and the required current density J_req everywhere in the magnetosphere.

(b) Characterize the regime of "current starvation," in which the plasma cannot supply the cross-field component of J_req needed to sustain the time-dependent corotation charge density, and determine where in the magnetosphere this regime is unavoidable.

(c) In regions where current starvation occurs, develop a self-consistent model describing (i) the resulting departure of the plasma flow from corotation v_cor⊥, and (ii) the appearance and structure of regions ("gaps") supporting a nonzero parallel electric field E_∥ = (E·B)/|B|, including its back-reaction on the particle motion, pair production, and the global magnetospheric current circuit.

The problem of a self-consistent treatment of current starvation and parallel-electric-field gaps in pulsar magnetospheres remains open. Recent PIC and Vlasov simulations (e.g., 2024 limit-cycle pair-production models, 2025 1D Vlasov QED-cascade simulations over polar caps) explore aspects of gap dynamics and screening but do not provide a complete global self-consistent analytic model; current starvation continues to be discussed as an unresolved feature of pulsar electrodynamics.

representations.normalized:
Consider a discrete-time dynamical system on a finite set of variables X = {x_1, ..., x_N}, each taking values in a finite alphabet, whose joint dynamics depends on a control parameter that places the system in one of three regimes: an ordered regime (low entropy, frozen or short transient trajectories), a disordered regime (high entropy, near-random trajectories), and a critical regime separating the two (e.g., characterized by power-law distributions of avalanche sizes, diverging correlation length, or maximal mutual information between subsets of variables).

For any subset S ⊆ X observed along a stationary trajectory, define an integration measure I(S) that quantifies the statistical interdependence among the variables in S (for example, the multi-information I(S) = Σ_{x ∈ S} H(x) − H(S), where H denotes Shannon entropy estimated from the observed trajectory). Call S a "tightly integrated subset" if I(S) is significantly larger than what is expected for randomly chosen subsets of the same cardinality under a suitable null model, and consider the partially ordered collection (hierarchy) of such subsets under inclusion.

Question: Do dynamical systems operating in the critical regime exhibit common, distinctive organizational signatures in the structure and hierarchy of their tightly integrated subsets that systematically distinguish them from systems in the ordered and disordered regimes? More precisely, does there exist a quantitative invariant (a function of the family of integrated subsets and their inclusion hierarchy) that:

(a) takes characteristically different values in the ordered, critical, and disordered regimes across a broad class of model dynamical systems (e.g., random Boolean networks, Ising-type spin dynamics, neuronal network models),
(b) can be reliably estimated from finite-length observed trajectories, and
(c) identifies criticality without requiring direct access to the control parameter?

Provide a construction of such an invariant together with rigorous criteria for detecting criticality from the organization of integrated subsets, or prove that no such universal organizational signature exists.

representations.normalized:
A Weak-lined T-Tauri star (WTT) is a young pre-main-sequence star characterised by weak Hα emission (equivalent width below the classical T-Tauri threshold) and little or no detectable gas accretion signatures. A protoplanetary transition disc is a circumstellar disc of primordial gas and dust that exhibits an inner cavity or large gap, interpreted as the late stage of disc dispersal before the disc fully dissipates. A debris disc, in contrast, is an essentially gas-poor disc whose observed dust is secondary, continuously regenerated by collisional grinding of planetesimals.

Consider a WTT that displays a measurable infrared excess above the stellar photosphere but exhibits little or no gas emission (e.g. negligible CO or accretion-related line emission). Determine criteria — based on observable quantities such as fractional infrared luminosity L_IR/L_*, dust mass, spectral energy distribution shape, gas-to-dust ratio upper limits, stellar age, and dust grain properties — that decide whether such an object should be classified as:

(a) a transition disc in the final stage of its protoplanetary lifetime, in which the dust is primordial and the gas has nearly fully dispersed, or

(b) a young debris disc, in which the dust is secondary and is being collisionally replenished from a planetesimal belt.

Provide a classification rule and assess, for the population of WTTs with infrared excesses, which of the two interpretations applies, justifying the answer with quantitative diagnostics.

Consider a WTT that displays a measurable infrared excess above the stellar photosphere but exhibits little or no gas emission (e.g. negligible CO or accretion-related line emission). Determine criteria — based on observable quantities such as fractional infrared luminosity L_IR/L_*, dust mass, spectral energy distribution shape, gas-to-dust ratio upper limits, stellar age, and dust grain properties — that decide whether such an object should be classified as:

(a) a transition disc in the final stage of its protoplanetary lifetime, in which the dust is primordial and the gas has nearly fully dispersed, or

(b) a young debris disc, in which the dust is secondary and is being collisionally replenished from a planetesimal belt.

Provide a classification rule and assess, for the population of WTTs with infrared excesses, which of the two interpretations applies, justifying the answer with quantitative diagnostics.

The classification of WTTs with infrared excess as evolved transition discs vs. young debris discs remains under active investigation. Studies (e.g., Hardy et al. 2015; subsequent ALMA gas/dust surveys) suggest most such WTTs are better described as young debris discs, but no universal observational criterion has been established and individual cases remain ambiguous, so the question is generally regarded as open.

Consider a protoplanetary "transition disc" around a young pre-main-sequence star, modeled as a gaseous disc of solar-type composition with embedded solid grains spanning a wide range of sizes. Assume the disc contains a large central cavity in the millimeter continuum emission, interpreted as arising from a radial pressure maximum (a "dust trap") in the gas at some radius R_mm, where aerodynamic drag concentrates millimeter-sized grains into a narrow outer ring. Smaller (sub-micron to micron) grains are aerodynamically well coupled to the gas and can in principle follow the gas distribution past the pressure maximum.

Define a transition disc to be "mm-bright" if its (sub-)millimeter continuum flux indicates a substantial reservoir of trapped mm-sized dust at radius R_mm. Let R_small denote the characteristic inner truncation radius of the small (micron-sized) grain population, as inferred from scattered-light imaging of the disc surface and from the shape of the spectral energy distribution.

Determine, for the population of mm-bright transition discs, which of the following alternatives correctly describes the typical radial distribution of small dust grains:

(a) R_small ≈ R_mm, i.e. the small grains are removed (or strongly depleted) at essentially the same radius at which the millimeter grains are trapped, so that the cavity is effectively size-independent; or

(b) R_small ≪ R_mm, i.e. the small grains extend significantly inward of the outer mm ring while only the larger grains remain confined to the outer ring, producing a strongly size-dependent cavity structure.

Provide a quantitative criterion (in terms of gas pressure profile, Stokes number of the grains, and turbulent diffusion) that distinguishes the two regimes, and determine which alternative is realized in observed mm-bright transition discs.

Multiple observational and theoretical studies indicate that in many mm-bright transition discs the small (micron-sized) grains extend substantially inward of the mm-grain ring, consistent with size-dependent cavities produced by pressure-bump dust trapping: micron-sized particles can cross the pressure maximum and drift inward while mm-sized grains remain trapped in the outer ring. Consider a population-synthesis model of protoplanetary discs around young stars in which gas is dispersed by a combination of viscous accretion onto the central star and X-ray/EUV photoevaporation driven by stellar high-energy radiation. In such a model, once viscous accretion has dropped sufficiently, photoevaporation opens an inner gap at a few astronomical units, after which the inner disc drains rapidly onto the star and the outer disc is cleared from the inside out. Define a \"transition disc\" as a disc whose spectral energy distribution shows a deficit of near-infrared excess (indicating an inner cavity/hole) while still retaining substantial outer-disc emission. Call such a transition disc \"optically thick with a large hole\" if its hole radius exceeds roughly 20 AU and the remaining outer disc is optically thick at infrared wavelengths, and call it \"non-accreting\" if its accretion rate onto the central star is below about 10^{-11} solar masses per year. Observations indicate that such optically thick, non-accreting transition discs with large holes are extremely rare. Augment the photoevaporation clearing model with possibly an additional rapid outer-disc-clearing mechanism (for instance, a \"thermal sweeping\" instability that propagates outward through a low-density disc once a critical surface-density profile is reached).

Question: Within this class of disc-evolution models, can photoevaporation alone, or photoevaporation supplemented by such a rapid outer-disc-clearing process, be made to clear the outer disc quickly enough after inner-hole formation that the predicted population of optically thick, non-accreting transition discs with large holes is consistent with the observed scarcity of such objects?

representations.normalized:
Consider a protoplanetary "transition" disc around a young pre-main-sequence star, defined as a circumstellar gas-and-dust disc with a large inner cavity (typical radius of order tens of astronomical units) that nevertheless exhibits ongoing accretion of gas onto the central star at observed rates comparable to those of full (non-cavity) discs (typically 10^{-9} to 10^{-7} solar masses per year). Let M_in denote the inferred mass of gas currently residing inside the cavity (as constrained by gas-tracer observations), and let \dot M_acc denote the stellar accretion rate. Define the inner-disc draining time as t_drain = M_in / \dot M_acc. Observations indicate that for many transition discs t_drain ranges from tens to a few thousand years, which is many orders of magnitude shorter than the standard viscous draining timescale t_visc ~ R^2/\nu ~ 10^6 years for cavity radii R of several tens of AU and standard turbulent viscosities \nu. In the extreme case of a system such as IRS 48, the required replenishment timescale is comparable to the local Keplerian orbital period at the cavity radius, which would demand a highly supersonic radial mass flux across the cavity.

Problem: Identify and quantitatively justify a physical mechanism (or combination of mechanisms) that transports gas from the outer disc, across the dust-depleted cavity, into the inner disc on timescales of order t_drain (i.e., 10–10^3 years, in some cases approaching the local orbital timescale), while simultaneously remaining consistent with (i) the maintenance of a strong dust trap at the cavity edge that filters out millimetre-sized grains, (ii) the persistence of the cavity over the observed disc lifetime, and (iii) the observed stellar accretion rates. Equivalently, derive the surface-density and radial-velocity profiles of gas inside the cavity that this mechanism predicts, and show that they reproduce the empirical t_drain values without violating the dust-filtration and longevity constraints.

representations.normalized:
A protoplanetary disc is a rotating disc of gas and dust around a young stellar object. Among such discs, "transition discs" are those whose spectral energy distributions and/or resolved images reveal a substantial inner cavity or gap (typically tens of astronomical units in radius) depleted of small dust, while still retaining an outer dust/gas reservoir. High-resolution imaging (e.g., in the (sub-)millimetre with interferometers, and in scattered light in the near-infrared) has revealed in many transition discs strong non-axisymmetric features, including large-scale azimuthal asymmetries (lopsided "horseshoes" in millimetre continuum), spiral arms, and shadowed regions, in addition to axisymmetric rings.

Question: Are such non-axisymmetric structures statistically and physically distinctive of the transition-disc class, or do they occur with comparable frequency, amplitude, and morphological character in the broader population of "primordial" (non-transition) protoplanetary discs? Equivalently, decide whether the presence of azimuthal asymmetries, spiral arms, and shadow features can serve, by itself, as a diagnostic that uniquely identifies a disc as belonging to the transition-disc phenomenon, or whether these features are generic to protoplanetary discs at large and therefore non-diagnostic without additional information (such as the presence of a resolved inner cavity).

Fix real numbers $p>1$, $b>0$, and $q\in[1,p)$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be a domain that contains a cone
$$\Omega_0=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N:\ x\neq 0,\ x/|x|\in\Sigma\},$$
where $\Sigma$ is a nonempty open subset of the unit sphere $S^{N-1}$. For a nonnegative initial datum $\varphi\in L^\infty(\Omega)\cap C(\overline{\Omega})$ with $\varphi=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, consider the Cauchy–Dirichlet problem
$$u_t-\Delta u=|u|^{p-1}u-b|\nabla u|^q\quad\text{in }\Omega\times(0,T^*),\qquad u=0\ \text{on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T^*),\qquad u(\cdot,0)=\varphi,$$
and let $T^*=T^*(\varphi)\in(0,\infty]$ denote the maximal existence time of the classical solution.

It is known that when $\tfrac{2p}{p+1}\le q<p$ there exists a constant $C=C(\Omega_0)>0$ such that the growth condition
$$\liminf_{\substack{|x|\to\infty\\ x\in\Omega_0}}|x|^{2/(p-1)}\varphi(x)>C\qquad(\ast)$$
implies $T^*<\infty$ (finite-time blowup).

Question: Does the same implication hold throughout the range $1\le q<\tfrac{2p}{p+1}$? That is, does there exist $C=C(\Omega_0)>0$ such that whenever $1\le q<\tfrac{2p}{p+1}$ and $\varphi\ge 0$ satisfies $(\ast)$, the corresponding solution blows up in finite time?

$$u_t - \Delta u = |u|^{p-1}u - b\,|\nabla u|^q, \qquad x\in\Omega,\ t>0,$$

$$p>1, \qquad \frac{2p}{p+1} < q < p.$$

$$\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)} \asymp (T-t)^{-\frac{q}{2(p-q)}} \quad \text{as } t\to T^-,$$

Let $N\ge 1$, $p>1$, $q>1$ with $q\ge p$, and $b>0$. For a (possibly unbounded) domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$, consider the initial-boundary value problem
$$
\begin{cases}
u_t-\Delta u=|u|^{p-1}u-b|\nabla u|^q & \text{in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\
u=0 & \text{on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\\
u(\cdot,0)=\varphi\ge 0 & \text{in }\Omega,
\end{cases}
$$
with $\varphi\in L^\infty(\Omega)\cap C(\overline{\Omega})$ vanishing on $\partial\Omega$, and let $T^*=T^*(\varphi)\in(0,\infty]$ denote the maximal existence time of the classical solution. It is known that $T^*=\infty$ whenever $\Omega$ is bounded, and also whenever $\varphi$ is compactly supported in $\mathbb{R}^N$ (even if $\Omega$ is unbounded).

Question: Does there exist any domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ and any admissible nonnegative initial datum $\varphi$ (necessarily not compactly supported) such that $T^*(\varphi)<\infty$, i.e., the solution undergoes finite-time blowup? Equivalently, can finite-time blowup occur in the regime $q\ge p$, in particular for $\Omega=\mathbb{R}^N$?

Consider the semilinear parabolic equation
  u_t - Δu = |u|^{p-1} u - b |∇u|^q,    x ∈ Ω, t > 0,
with u = 0 on ∂Ω and a smooth initial datum u(·,0) = u_0, where Ω ⊂ ℝ^N is a smooth bounded domain (or Ω = ℝ^N), b > 0 is a fixed constant, p > 1, and q > 1 lies in a range for which there exist classical solutions that are global in time but unbounded (i.e. T_max(u_0) = ∞ and lim sup_{t→∞} ‖u(·,t)‖_{L^∞(Ω)} = ∞).

For such an unbounded global solution u, the only currently known two-sided estimate has the form
  C_1 t ≤ ‖u(·,t)‖_{L^∞(Ω)} ≤ C_2 e^{C_3 t},   t ≥ 1,
for some positive constants C_1, C_2, C_3.

Determine the precise asymptotic grow-up rate of ‖u(·,t)‖_{L^∞(Ω)} as t → ∞: identify an explicit function ϕ(t) (e.g. polynomial, exponential, or another elementary rate) such that
  ‖u(·,t)‖_{L^∞(Ω)} ∼ ϕ(t)  as t → ∞,
thereby sharpening the linear lower bound and the exponential upper bound to an exact asymptotic growth law.

representations.normalized:
In the phenomenology of high transverse-momentum partonic probes ("jets") traversing the quark–gluon plasma produced in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, two competing classes of energy-loss models are commonly considered:

(i) A perturbative-QCD (pQCD)-like model, in which the average energy loss per unit proper path length of the parton through the medium scales linearly with the path length, dE/dτ ∝ τ.

(ii) An AdS/CFT-correspondence-inspired (strongly coupled) model, in which the average energy loss scales quadratically with the path length, dE/dτ ∝ τ².

Two standard observables computed and measured for high-pT hadrons or jets in nucleus–nucleus collisions are:
 • the nuclear modification factor R_AA(pT, centrality), defined as the ratio of the differential yield in AA collisions to the binary-collision-scaled yield in pp collisions;
 • the high-pT elliptic flow coefficient v₂(pT, centrality), the second Fourier coefficient of the azimuthal distribution of high-pT particles relative to the event-plane.

Empirically, when a running (scale-dependent) jet–medium coupling is permitted in the strongly coupled, non-conformal scenario, both the linear (τ) and quadratic (τ²) path-length dependences can be tuned to reproduce simultaneously the measured R_AA and high-pT v₂ at RHIC and LHC energies, so these two observables alone cannot distinguish the two underlying mechanisms.

Problem. Identify an experimentally accessible jet (or high-pT hadron) observable O — for example a function of pT, of jet substructure variables, of azimuthal angle relative to the reaction plane, of jet-correlation or jet–hadron correlation kinematics, or of system-size/centrality dependence — such that the predicted value of O in any pQCD-like model with dE/dτ ∝ τ and the predicted value of O in any non-conformal AdS/CFT-like model with dE/dτ ∝ τ² (with running jet–medium coupling) differ by an amount exceeding plausible theoretical and experimental uncertainties, thereby breaking the degeneracy between the linear and quadratic path-length dependences.

representations.normalized:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, jet quenching is commonly characterized by two observables at high transverse momentum p_T: the nuclear modification factor R_AA(p_T), defined as the ratio of the hadron yield in nucleus-nucleus collisions to the binary-collision-scaled yield in proton-proton collisions, and the elliptic flow coefficient v_2(p_T), the second Fourier coefficient of the azimuthal distribution of produced hadrons relative to the event plane. Energy-loss models historically reproduce R_AA(p_T) but underpredict the measured high-p_T v_2(p_T) by up to a factor of two ("the high-p_T v_2 puzzle").

Consider an energy-loss prescription in which a hard parton of energy E traversing a deconfined medium of local temperature T loses energy at a rate
   dE/dx = − κ(E^2, T) · f(E, T, x, …),
where f encodes the path-length and medium dependence used in a chosen jet-quenching model (e.g. of Bjorken–Bjorken–Müller–Gyulassy type), evolved on top of a hydrodynamic or parton-cascade background describing the bulk medium produced in heavy-ion collisions. Let the jet-medium coupling κ(E^2, T) be a positive function of the parton energy squared and the medium temperature, allowed to be non-monotonic and in particular enhanced near the QCD pseudo-critical temperature T_c ≈ 160 MeV to incorporate non-perturbative effects around the deconfinement transition.

Question: Is there a choice of such an energy- and temperature-dependent jet-medium coupling κ(E^2, T), with non-perturbative enhancement near T_c, that simultaneously reproduces the experimentally measured R_AA(p_T) and high-p_T v_2(p_T) for light-flavor hadrons in heavy-ion collisions, with the simultaneous description being robust against the choice of underlying bulk evolution (viscous hydrodynamics versus parton cascade)?

Consider the Unified Model of collective quadrupole motion in a finite nucleus, in which a small number A of nucleons is described by a Hamiltonian that couples intrinsic quasiparticle degrees of freedom to collective quadrupole shape variables (β, γ) and their conjugate momenta. The model rests on two implicit assumptions: (i) adiabatic separation of scales, requiring that the characteristic collective time T_coll be much larger than the characteristic quasiparticle time T_qp; and (ii) coherence of the collective mode, requiring that a sufficiently large number of nucleons participate coherently in each collective quantum so that the mode behaves as a well-defined bosonic excitation.

Provide a quantitative, non-perturbative formulation that determines the validity limits of this model. Specifically:

1. Derive a precise criterion, expressed in terms of T_coll/T_qp (or equivalently the ratio of collective excitation energy to the two-quasiparticle gap), at which the adiabatic separation breaks down. In particular, characterize the regime T_coll/T_qp ≲ 3 in which adiabaticity fails, and describe how the coupling between quasiparticle and collective degrees of freedom should be treated non-perturbatively in this regime.

2. Define a coherence length (or coherence number) N_coh for the collective quadrupole mode in terms of the underlying nucleonic correlations, and quantify how the granular structure of the collective degrees of freedom—arising from the finite number of correlated nucleons—produces progressive decoherence of the collective modes as the number of excitation quanta n increases. Determine the maximal n for which the collective description remains meaningful as a function of A and N_coh.

3. Combine (1) and (2) into a unified domain-of-validity diagram for the Unified Model, identifying which observables (energies, B(E2) values, branching ratios) remain reliable and which require corrections beyond the adiabatic, coherent approximation.

representations.normalized:
In the Interacting Boson Model (IBM) of nuclear collective motion, low-lying collective excitations of an even-even nucleus are described in terms of a finite system of bosons of two kinds: monopole bosons s (angular momentum 0) and quadrupole bosons d (angular momentum 2). A central postulate of the IBM is that the total boson number N is fixed and equal to half the number of valence nucleons (or valence holes) outside the nearest doubly-magic core. Because each d boson carries angular momentum 2, the maximal yrast spin that can be built from N_d ≤ N quadrupole bosons is I_max = 2N, and the electric-quadrupole transition strengths B(E2; I → I−2) within the ground-state band are predicted to decrease as I approaches this cutoff and to vanish at I = 2N.

Formulate and resolve the following question rigorously:

(a) Does the finite boson-number assumption of the IBM (N = (number of valence nucleons or holes)/2) systematically fail to describe high-spin yrast collectivity in deformed even-even nuclei, in the sense that observed B(E2; I → I−2) values along the ground-state band remain large (and in particular nonzero) for spins I exceeding the IBM cutoff 2N?

(b) Devise a systematic, model-independent experimental test across a representative set of nuclei that compares IBM-predicted B(E2; I → I−2) strengths within the ground-state band against measured values for spins approaching and exceeding the boson-number limit, and determine whether the discrepancy is generic rather than confined to isolated cases.

Provide either a proof that the finite boson-number cutoff is consistent with high-spin yrast B(E2) data (with quantified deviations within experimental uncertainty), or evidence that the cutoff is systematically violated, identifying the class of nuclei in which the failure occurs.

Consider a finite system of A interacting nucleons (protons and neutrons) governed by a realistic two-body (and possibly three-body) nuclear Hamiltonian. Treat the system within a self-consistent mean-field framework in which the nucleons move in an average potential generated by themselves, and consider the cranked (rotating) mean-field approximation: minimize the expectation value of H − ωJ_x in a Slater determinant (or HFB quasiparticle vacuum), where J_x is the angular-momentum projection along a body-fixed axis and ω is a Lagrange multiplier (cranking frequency). Assume that the time scales of collective rotational motion and of single-particle motion are comparable, so that the two are strongly coupled.

In this framework, characterize, in terms of the underlying single-particle structure (shell filling, deformation of the self-consistent mean field, pairing correlations, level density near the Fermi surface, and quasiparticle alignments), the following:

(a) Necessary and sufficient microscopic conditions on a nucleus with given proton and neutron numbers (Z, N) for rotational collective modes — i.e. regular rotational bands of states whose energies depend on angular momentum I approximately as E(I) ≈ I(I+1)/(2𝓘) with a well-defined moment of inertia 𝓘 — to emerge as one moves away from closed-shell (magic) nucleon numbers.

(b) Necessary and sufficient microscopic conditions under which these rotational modes cease to exist (band termination / damping of rotational correlations) as the excitation energy E* increases above the yrast line (the locus of lowest-energy states for each angular momentum I).

Provide a precise criterion, expressible through properties of the self-consistent rotating mean-field solution and its quasiparticle spectrum, that distinguishes the regimes of existence and non-existence of rotational collective motion in both situations (a) and (b).

The microscopic conditions for the onset and damping of nuclear rotational bands remain an active research area. Studies based on cranked mean-field, tilted-axis cranking, and shell-model approaches have given partial answers (e.g., onset of deformation away from magic numbers, rotational damping above the yrast line at E* of a few MeV studied by Døssing, Matsuo, Bracco and others), but no complete microscopic criterion exists. The question is generally regarded as open.

representations.normalized:
Consider a nuclear many-body system whose low-energy dynamics is described by two interacting sectors of degrees of freedom: (i) collective quadrupole degrees of freedom, encoded by the five real shape variables associated with the quadrupole tensor (parameterised, e.g., by the Bohr variables (β, γ) together with three Euler angles), and (ii) quasiparticle degrees of freedom, obtained from a Bogoliubov transformation of single-nucleon creation/annihilation operators acting on a paired Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov vacuum. Let H = H_coll + H_qp + H_coup denote a Hamiltonian on the tensor-product Hilbert space of these two sectors, where H_coup represents a particle–vibration (quadrupole–quasiparticle) coupling.

In the low-level-density adiabatic regime the coupling H_coup can be treated perturbatively (e.g., by quasiparticle–phonon expansions or generator-coordinate-method approximations). Outside this regime — for higher excited states, where level density is large and adiabaticity fails, and for odd-mass (odd-A) nuclei, where a blocked quasiparticle is always present — the coupling becomes strong and perturbation theory diverges; both non-adiabaticity (failure of the Born–Oppenheimer separation between collective and intrinsic motion) and decoherence (loss of phase coherence between collective wave packets due to coupling to the dense quasiparticle background) must be incorporated.

Problem. Devise a mathematically controlled, non-perturbative scheme for diagonalising (or otherwise computing the spectrum and transition matrix elements of) such a coupled collective–quasiparticle Hamiltonian H in the strong-coupling regime applicable to higher-lying excited states and to odd-A nuclei, in a way that simultaneously accommodates non-adiabatic effects and decoherence between the collective and quasiparticle sectors.
