representations.normalized:
Consider a spatially flat string-cosmology background described, in the string frame, by a four-dimensional metric of FRW type
   ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2 δ_{ij} dx^i dx^j
together with a dilaton field φ(t), governed by the lowest-order tree-level string effective action
   S = (1/2) ∫ d^4x √(-g) e^{-φ} [ R + (∂φ)^2 - V(φ) + 16π G L_m ],
where L_m is the Lagrangian of the matter sector. Let H = ȧ/a denote the Hubble rate and write the shifted dilaton φ̄ = φ - 3 ln a. The matter sector is taken to be composed of two perfect fluids with energy densities ρ_1, ρ_2 and barotropic equations of state p_i = (γ_i - 1) ρ_i (i = 1, 2), which are not separately conserved but exchange energy through a coupling Q(t):
   ρ̇_1 + 3 H γ_1 ρ_1 = -Q,   ρ̇_2 + 3 H γ_2 ρ_2 = +Q.
Couple this two-fluid system to the string-cosmology equations (the dilaton equation, the Hamiltonian constraint, and the spatial field equation derived from the action above), allowing Q to belong to a broad family of physically motivated couplings (e.g. Q proportional to H ρ_1, H ρ_2, H(ρ_1+ρ_2), or to combinations of the dilaton time derivative φ̇ with the densities).

Problem. Carry out a complete asymptotic analysis (both at early times t → 0^± and at late times |t| → ∞, on the pre-big-bang and post-big-bang branches) of the resulting dynamical system for (H, φ̇, ρ_1, ρ_2). Determine:
  (a) the full set of asymptotic regimes (fixed points and scaling solutions of H(t), a(t), φ(t), ρ_i(t)) in this two-interacting-fluid setting, classified by (γ_1, γ_2) and by the form of Q;
  (b) which of the asymptotic features known to hold for a single perfect fluid coupled to the string-frame dilaton (e.g. existence of pre-big-bang superinflationary branches, dilaton-driven kinetic regimes, curvature/coupling singularities, and scale-factor duality relations) persist, are deformed, or are destroyed when energy exchange between the two fluids is switched on;
  (c) which qualitative conclusions about the physical viability of flat string cosmology — in particular the genericity of the graceful-exit problem and the structure of the high-curvature/strong-coupling regime — survive in the generalized interacting two-fluid setting.

A web search yields a substantial literature on two interacting fluids with energy exchange in flat FRW cosmologies (including asymptotic and scaling analyses for dark-energy/dark-matter couplings), but no source was found that carries out the requested systematic generalization of the single-fluid asymptotic results specifically within tree-level dilaton-driven string cosmology. Setup. Let M be a smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension 7 with holonomy group equal to the exceptional group G2, and let Ω^{ch}_M denote its smooth chiral de Rham complex, viewed as a sheaf of N=1 superconformal vertex algebras on M. The Shatashvili–Vafa G2 superconformal vertex algebra SV^{G2} is the W-algebra extension of the N=1 superconformal algebra at central charge c = 21/2 generated by fields {L, G, Φ, K, X, M} satisfying the Shatashvili–Vafa OPE relations; in particular it contains a Virasoro field X of central charge c = 7/10 commuting with the remaining N=1 super-Virasoro structure. By a theorem of Rodriguez (here referred to as the "Rodriguez embedding"), the vertex algebra of global sections of Ω^{ch}_M contains two commuting copies of SV^{G2}.

Question. For each of the two copies of SV^{G2} produced by the Rodriguez embedding inside the global sections of Ω^{ch}_M, is the embedded copy a simple vertex algebra? Equivalently, do the embedded copies coincide with the simple quotient of the universal Shatashvili–Vafa vertex algebra at c = 21/2, so that the c = 7/10 Virasoro subalgebra generated by the field X is the unitary tricritical Ising minimal model (a member of the unitary discrete series of Virasoro minimal models)?

Searches surface continuing research on Shatashvili–Vafa G2 algebras, their embeddings into the chiral de Rham complex on G2 manifolds (Rodriguez/Ekstrand–Heluani–Källén–Zabzine), deformations and quantum Hamiltonian reductions, but no source explicitly establishes (or refutes) that the specific copies of SV^{G2} produced by Rodriguez's embedding inside Ω^{ch}_M are simple vertex algebras with the c = 7/10 piece being the unitary tricritical Ising minimal model. representations.normalized:
Consider 11-dimensional supergravity, whose bosonic field content consists of a Lorentzian metric g on an 11-manifold M and a 3-form gauge potential A with 4-form field strength F = dA. The standard two-derivative bosonic action is

  S_0 = (1/2κ²) ∫ ( R ⋆1 − (1/2) F ∧ ⋆F − (1/6) A ∧ F ∧ F ).

Deform this action by adding the Lovelock series of dimensionally continued Euler densities and the higher-order Weyl-curvature invariants that arise as α'-type corrections in M-theory; schematically,

  S = S_0 + ∑_{k≥2} α_k ∫ L_k(R) ⋆1 + ∑_{n≥1} β_n ∫ W_n(C) ⋆1,

where L_k denotes the k-th Lovelock Lagrangian (the dimensionally continued 2k-dimensional Euler density built from the Riemann tensor) and W_n denotes scalar polynomials of degree n in the Weyl tensor C that appear in the known higher-derivative corrections to 11-dimensional supergravity (for example the eight-derivative t_8 t_8 R^4 and ε_{11} ε_{11} R^4 invariants).

Let (g_0, F_0) be an exact cosmological solution of the undeformed equations of motion derived from S_0 — that is, a spatially homogeneous (Bianchi-type or Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker) Lorentzian solution on M = ℝ × N^{10} for some 10-dimensional spatial manifold N — and consider it as a solution of the deformed equations of motion arising from S, treated either as exact or as a perturbative series in the deformation parameters α_k, β_n.

Address the following:

(a) Determine whether (g_0, F_0) is linearly stable as a solution of the equations of motion of S under small perturbations (δg, δA) of the metric and 3-form on M.

(b) Classify all asymptotic modes admitted by (δg, δA) in the late-time and/or large-spatial-distance regime, computing their growth or decay rates as functions of the deformation parameters.

(c) Using the results of (a) and (b), state and prove (or disprove) a no-hair theorem for an inflationary phase of such a deformed 11-dimensional cosmology: namely, that any sufficiently small perturbation of an inflating background solution (g_0, F_0) decays so that the perturbed solution asymptotically approaches the inflationary background.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $2^X$ denote the family of all non-empty closed subsets of $X$. The Wijsman topology $\mathscr{T}_{W(d)}$ on $2^X$ is defined as the weakest topology on $2^X$ for which every distance functional $A \mapsto d(x,A) = \inf_{a\in A} d(x,a)$, with $x \in X$, is continuous (equivalently, the weakest topology making all maps $d(\cdot, A): X \to \mathbb{R}$ vary continuously in $A$). Equip $\omega_1$ and $\omega_1+1$ with their order topologies, and consider the product space $\omega_1 \times (\omega_1+1)$.

Question: If $(X,d)$ is non-separable, must the Wijsman hyperspace $(2^X, \mathscr{T}_{W(d)})$ contain a closed topological copy of $\omega_1 \times (\omega_1+1)$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

The problem is posed as an open question on the Wijsman topology. Searches surface related results showing closed copies of various ordinal-related spaces (e.g., $\omega^{\aleph_1}$, $(\omega_1+1)^{\omega_1}$) embed into Wijsman hyperspaces of non-separable (or locally separable, weight-regular) metric spaces, but no source confirms a solution to this specific embedding question for $\omega_1 \times (\omega_1+1)$ in general non-separable metric spaces. Current status appears unresolved.

Consider a five-dimensional bulk spacetime containing a three-dimensional Robertson–Walker (RW) brane coupled to a bulk scalar field φ. Adopt coordinates (t, x^i, y) with y the transverse coordinate to the brane (located at y = 0), and a metric ansatz of warped form
  ds^2 = a(y)^2 [ -dt^2 + b(t)^2 γ_{ij}(x) dx^i dx^j ] + dy^2,
where γ_{ij} is a maximally symmetric three-metric of spatial curvature k ∈ {-1, 0, +1}, and b(t) is the RW scale factor. The bulk action contains Einstein gravity coupled to a scalar φ(t,y) with potential V(φ) and a brane tension/source term localized at y = 0. The resulting Einstein–scalar system reduces to an autonomous polynomial dynamical system in suitable variables, to which the method of asymptotic splittings can be applied: every formal asymptotic solution is decomposed into a dominant balance plus subdominant corrections expanded in Puiseux/Fuchsian series, and a solution is called "regular" if all such series converge in a neighborhood of the asymptotic regime and produce a finite, geodesically complete bulk geometry containing the brane.

Question:
(a) Do regular asymptotic solutions of this five-dimensional Einstein–scalar system with an RW brane (k = -1, 0, +1) exist, in the sense of the method of asymptotic splittings?
(b) If such regular solutions exist, can any of them implement the self-tuning program for the four-dimensional effective cosmological constant — that is, force the induced four-dimensional curvature on the brane to vanish for a continuous range of values of the brane vacuum energy without fine-tuning of bulk parameters?
(c) How does the role of the spatial curvature k modify the structure of regular asymptotic solutions and their self-tuning capability, compared with the case of a Minkowski brane (b(t) ≡ const, k = 0 with flat induced metric)?

Consider a Robertson–Walker 3-brane embedded in a five-dimensional bulk, with dynamics derived either from a gravi-dilaton string effective action or from its Einstein-frame counterpart. On the brane, take a spatially homogeneous and isotropic metric ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2 g_{ij} dx^i dx^j (with g_{ij} of constant spatial curvature k ∈ {-1,0,1}), a scalar (dilaton) field φ(t) with potential V(φ), and a perfect fluid of energy density ρ(t) and pressure p(t) = (γ-1)ρ(t), γ ∈ ℝ. Allow the scalar field and the fluid to interact through a coupling Q(t), so that the conservation equations take the form
   φ̈ + 3H φ̇ + V'(φ) = Q,
   ρ̇ + 3H γ ρ = -Q φ̇,
where H = ȧ/a, coupled to the modified Friedmann/brane equations induced by the chosen action.

Call an asymptotic behaviour "regular" if every solution (a, φ, ρ) extends smoothly to t → +∞ (resp. is past-complete to t → -∞) without curvature, density, or finite-time blow-up singularities, and the scale factor a(t) avoids both collapse-type and big-rip-type singularities.

Question: Does there exist a choice of coupling Q, potential V, and fluid parameter γ such that the resulting interacting Robertson–Walker brane system possesses regular asymptotics and simultaneously satisfies the following three conditions:
 (1) the induced brane field equations (Friedmann constraint and evolution) are fulfilled for all t in the relevant interval;
 (2) the standard energy conditions (e.g. weak and dominant) hold for the combined scalar–fluid stress-energy on the brane;
 (3) the asymptotic behaviour is compatible with a non-trivial cosmological evolution (i.e. neither the scalar field nor the fluid is identically zero, and the scale factor is non-constant)?

Determine whether such interacting configurations exist, and if so, characterize the admissible couplings Q and parameters (V, γ, k).

Consider a spatially homogeneous cosmological model in four spacetime dimensions whose gravitational sector is governed by a higher-order gravity action of the form
   S = ∫ d^4x √(-g) ( R + ε f(R, R_{μν}R^{μν}, R_{μνρσ}R^{μνρσ}, …) ) + S_matter,
where f is a smooth scalar built from curvature invariants of order higher than two, and ε is a parameter controlling the strength of the higher-order corrections. Assume the matter content is a perfect fluid with a general (constant) equation of state p = w ρ, w ∈ ℝ.

Define the "compactified Milne mod Z₂ × ℝ³" state to be the spacetime obtained from the Milne universe (the future light cone of the origin in (1+1)-Minkowski space, with metric ds² = -dt² + t² dχ², χ ∈ ℝ) by the Z₂ identification χ ~ -χ, taken as a product with flat ℝ³; equivalently, the metric
   ds² = -dt² + t² dχ² + dx₁² + dx₂² + dx₃²,   t > 0,  χ ≥ 0.

Assume the higher-order curvature terms are asymptotically subdominant relative to the Einstein–Hilbert term as t → 0⁺ (i.e. as one approaches the would-be reversal/bounce point).

Question: Does the compactified Milne mod Z₂ × ℝ³ state arise as a global asymptotic attractor of the cosmological dynamics under these assumptions, for general w? If so, characterize the basin of attraction and the range of equations of state w for which this attractor behavior holds.

Let $(\mathbb{R}^{1,n}, \eta)$ denote $(n+1)$-dimensional Minkowski space with the standard flat Lorentzian metric $\eta$. The ambient cosmological construction associates to a Lorentzian manifold $(M, g)$ of dimension $n+1$ an $(n+2)$-dimensional Ricci-flat ambient space $(\widetilde{M}, \widetilde{g})$ in which $(M, g)$ embeds as a conformal class representative, in such a way that the construction depends only on the conformal class $[g]$.

Say that a smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a perturbation of $\eta$ if $g = \eta + h$ for a smooth symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor $h$ which is small in a suitable (e.g. weighted Sobolev) norm sufficient to ensure global nonlinear stability of Minkowski space as a solution of the vacuum Einstein equations. Two perturbations $g_1, g_2$ of $\eta$ are called conformally related if there exists a smooth positive function $\Omega: \mathbb{R}^{n+1} 	o (0, \infty)$ such that $g_2 = \Omega^2 g_1$.

Prove or disprove: for every perturbation $g$ of $\eta$ for which the ambient cosmological construction is admissible (i.e., yields a well-defined Ricci-flat ambient metric on a neighborhood of the embedded copy of $(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, g)$), and for every smooth positive conformal factor $\Omega$ such that $\Omega^2 g$ is again a perturbation of $\eta$ in the above sense, the ambient construction is also admissible for $\Omega^2 g$, and the resulting ambient spaces agree up to the natural diffeomorphism induced by the conformal rescaling. Equivalently, is the ambient cosmological construction stable under arbitrary conformally related perturbations of Minkowski space?

representations.normalized:
Consider a young, energetic rotation-powered pulsar whose magnetosphere accelerates primary electrons that initiate electromagnetic cascades, producing electron–positron pairs. Define the pair multiplicity κ to be the average number of pairs produced per primary electron extracted from the stellar surface, so that the relativistic magnetized wind launched by the pulsar is composed mostly of pairs together with a possible ionic component (with ion-to-electron mass ratio m_i/m_e ≈ 1836). Theoretical cascade models suggest 10^3 ≲ κ ≲ 10^7 for young energetic pulsars.

(a) Determine κ as a function of fundamental pulsar parameters (e.g. spin period P, period derivative Ṗ, surface magnetic field B, magnetic inclination angle, and curvature radius of magnetic field lines), based on a self-consistent model of polar-cap pair cascades.

(b) Using multi-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic modelling of the resulting pulsar wind nebula (the synchrotron-emitting bubble inflated by the pulsar wind into the surrounding medium) compared with multi-wavelength observations, derive constraints on κ that are tight enough to decide whether the inequality κ < m_i/m_e ≈ 10^3–10^4 can hold, in which case an ionic component, although numerically negligible, would carry an energetically dominant fraction of the wind power.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Pair multiplicity in young pulsar magnetospheres remains an active area of investigation. Theoretical cascade work (Timokhin & Harding 2015, 2019) bounds the maximum multiplicity at a few × 10^5 with weak dependence on B and curvature radius, while a 2025 A&A study used H.E.S.S. and LHAASO PWN observations to derive lower limits on κ for several young pulsars. No tight, generally accepted determination of κ has been established, and the question of whether an ion component can be energetically dominant remains unresolved.

representations.normalized:
Consider a relativistic, magnetized pulsar wind terminating in a standing shock (the termination shock, TS) embedded in a pulsar wind nebula. Downstream of the TS, ultra-relativistic electrons and positrons radiate synchrotron emission whose observed spectrum (as in the Crab Nebula) is well fit by an injected isotropic energy distribution of broken power-law form

   N(E) ∝ E^{-p₁}  for E ≲ E_b,
   N(E) ∝ E^{-p₂}  for E ≳ E_b,

with p₁ ≈ 1.5 (radio-emitting low-energy particles), p₂ ≈ 2.2 (optical/X-ray/γ-ray emitting high-energy particles up to a few TeV), and a break around E_b ∼ 100 GeV.

Three candidate acceleration mechanisms operate at or near the TS, each requiring distinct upstream conditions:

(i) Driven magnetic reconnection of the alternating-polarity "striped" component of the wind, requiring a sufficiently large magnetization σ, a striped-wind geometry within a latitude band around the magnetic equator, and high pair multiplicity κ;

(ii) Diffusive shock acceleration (DSA), requiring locally weak magnetization (σ ≪ 1) so that the relativistic shock is quasi-parallel/weakly magnetized, achievable only in sectors where upstream magnetic dissipation is strong;

(iii) Resonant ion-cyclotron absorption, requiring the presence of a relativistic ion component carrying a substantial fraction of the wind's energy at sufficiently high Lorentz factor, whose cyclotron waves downstream resonantly accelerate the pair plasma.

Problem. Determine, within a self-consistent multi-dimensional relativistic MHD model of the pulsar wind and its termination shock, the combination of these mechanisms and the corresponding spatial sectors of the TS (e.g., equatorial striped zone, mid-latitude oblique sectors, polar regions) that simultaneously reproduce:

(a) the flat low-energy slope p₁ ≈ 1.5 of the radio-emitting population,
(b) the steeper high-energy slope p₂ ≈ 2.2 up to multi-TeV energies,
(c) the location of the spectral break E_b,
(d) the inferred total particle injection rate and pair multiplicity, and
(e) consistency with the wind magnetization profile σ(θ) and striped-wind latitude extent inferred from global MHD modelling of the nebular morphology.

Specify which sectors of the TS contribute each spectral component, the required σ(θ), pair multiplicity κ, and ion energy fraction, and whether a single mechanism in different sectors, or a genuine combination of mechanisms, is necessary.

Recent (2024) JWST observations of small-scale torus features provided the first direct observational evidence linking the spectral curvature to acceleration physics at the TS, and phenomenological models (e.g., Fraschetti & Pohl 2017) reproduce the broadband spectrum, but no consensus mechanism (reconnection vs. DSA vs. ion-cyclotron resonance) and no unique sector assignment along the TS has been established within self-consistent multi-D MHD models.

Consider a pulsar wind nebula modeled as a relativistic, ideal magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) flow in three spatial dimensions, in which a cold, ultrarelativistic, magnetized wind from a central pulsar terminates at a strong shock and inflates a magnetized bubble inside an expanding supernova ejecta. The wind is parameterized by a time-dependent spin-down luminosity L(t), a striped/toroidal magnetization parameter σ(θ,t), and a latitude-dependent energy flux. Inside the nebula, the magnetic field is allowed to evolve dynamically, including the development of large-scale current-driven (kink) instabilities of the toroidal field that drive turbulent magnetic dissipation and reconnection. Particles are injected at the termination shock with a broken power-law energy distribution, advected with the flow, and lose energy through adiabatic expansion, synchrotron radiation, and inverse-Compton scattering on the cosmic microwave background, far-infrared dust, and stellar/synchrotron photon fields. Run such a simulation for a physical time comparable to the age of the Crab Nebula (~10^3 yr), long enough that the system enters a self-similar expansion phase.

Determine whether there exists a choice of admissible wind and injection parameters (within ranges consistent with pulsar spin-down, multiwavelength constraints, and the total injected pair multiplicity) such that the resulting simulation simultaneously satisfies all of the following observational constraints for the Crab Nebula:

(i) the volume-averaged interior magnetic-field strength matches the observationally inferred value (≈ 100–300 μG) to within observational uncertainty;
(ii) the synthetic surface-brightness maps reproduce both the optical/X-ray torus and the polar jet at the observed luminosities and morphologies (in particular the torus is not under-luminous and the jets are not over-collimated);
(iii) the integrated photon spectrum from radio through gamma-rays, including the synchrotron component and the inverse-Compton component, agrees with measurements; and
(iv) the inferred total particle content (number of radiating leptons and implied pair multiplicity at the wind termination) is consistent with independent constraints from pulsar magnetospheric models.

State whether such a self-consistent three-dimensional RMHD model of the Crab Nebula exists, or prove that within the stated modeling framework no parameter choice can simultaneously meet (i)–(iv).

Three-dimensional RMHD simulations of the Crab Nebula (e.g., Porth, Komissarov, Keppens; Olmi et al.) successfully reproduce many morphological features (wisps, torus, inner-knot polarization) and randomize the magnetic field to address the sigma problem, but consistently report the volume-averaged interior magnetic field below the observationally inferred value (by factors of ~2), under-luminous torus or jets, and require excess injected particles and steeper spectra to fit the integrated synchrotron spectrum. No published 3D simulation has simultaneously matched the magnetic-field strength, full jet/torus brightness, broadband synchrotron+IC spectrum, and pair-multiplicity constraints, so the question remains open.

representations.normalized:
Consider a classical molecular dynamics framework for studying crystal nucleation from the liquid phase. The system consists of N atoms or molecules whose configurations x ∈ R^{3N} evolve under Newtonian dynamics governed by an interatomic potential U(x), with the liquid maintained at thermodynamic conditions (temperature T, pressure P) where the crystalline phase is thermodynamically favored. Crystal nucleation is a rare event: the time scale for spontaneous formation of a critical crystalline nucleus typically exceeds by many orders of magnitude the time scales accessible to direct numerical integration of the equations of motion. To overcome this, enhanced-sampling techniques (e.g., metadynamics, umbrella sampling, forward flux sampling, transition path sampling, seeding) are used to bias or accelerate exploration of configuration space along chosen collective variables that distinguish liquid-like from crystal-like local environments.

Develop (a) systematically improved interatomic potentials U(x) — whether empirical, machine-learned, or otherwise — that quantitatively reproduce the thermodynamic, structural, and dynamical properties of real liquids and their crystalline polymorphs near coexistence (in particular melting temperatures, surface tensions, diffusion coefficients, and relative phase stabilities), and (b) enhanced-sampling algorithms together with collective variables that yield converged, statistically reliable estimates of nucleation free-energy barriers, nucleation rates J(T,P), and critical-nucleus structures for systems of practical interest (e.g., metals, water and ice polymorphs, molecular crystals, alloys), such that the resulting simulated nucleation rates and pathways agree quantitatively with experimental measurements.

Provide criteria, algorithms, and benchmarks under which both objectives can be met simultaneously for a chosen target liquid.

Consider the homogeneous nucleation of urea crystals from a supersaturated solution, viewed as an activated process along a suitable reaction coordinate joining the homogeneous liquid solution to the crystalline phase. Suppose molecular-dynamics-style sampling of the free-energy landscape produces the following picture:

(i) Pre-critical configurations along the pathway contain disordered (amorphous) molecular aggregates ("precursor clusters") of solute molecules that are denser than the bulk liquid but lack long-range orientational/translational order.

(ii) These amorphous precursor clusters are unstable with respect to the homogeneous liquid: they do not occupy a distinct local minimum of the free energy as a function of the chosen order parameters, but rather lie on the uphill side of a single free-energy barrier.

(iii) The transition-state configuration (the saddle point of the free-energy landscape, i.e. the critical nucleus) already possesses a fully crystalline core surrounded by a thinner disordered shell.

The "two-step nucleation mechanism" is conventionally defined as a pathway in which the system first crosses a barrier into a metastable intermediate phase (e.g. a dense amorphous or liquid-like cluster occupying its own free-energy basin) and only subsequently crosses a second barrier from this intermediate into the crystalline phase.

Question: Under conditions (i)–(iii) above—where the critical nucleus is predominantly crystalline and the amorphous precursors do not constitute a metastable phase with its own free-energy basin but are merely unstable fluctuations of the liquid—does the urea nucleation pathway satisfy the definition of a two-step nucleation mechanism, or must it instead be classified as a single-step (classical-type) nucleation mechanism with a structured transition state? Provide a precise criterion, formulated in terms of the topology of the free-energy landscape (number and depth of intermediate basins along the minimum free-energy path), that unambiguously distinguishes two-step from one-step nucleation in this setting.

The literature on solution crystallization (including urea, glycine, NaCl, and proteins) continues to debate the classification boundary between one-step and two-step nucleation. Consider a relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model of a pulsar wind nebula (PWN), such as the Crab Nebula, in which a central pulsar drives a magnetized relativistic outflow that terminates in a strong shock (the termination shock, TS) before inflating a slowly expanding nebular bubble. Define the wind magnetization parameter

  σ(r) = F_Poynting(r) / F_kinetic(r),

the ratio of the Poynting flux to the particle kinetic-energy flux carried by the wind at radius r from the pulsar. Theoretical pulsar magnetosphere models predict σ ≫ 1 near the light cylinder, while ideal-MHD modeling of the nebula demands σ ≪ 1 just upstream of the termination shock so that the shocked flow can decelerate to match observed expansion speeds.

Within full three-dimensional ideal relativistic MHD (allowing non-axisymmetric instabilities and reconnection of the striped wind), address the following:

(a) Identify and quantify the physical mechanisms by which σ is reduced and/or redistributed between the light-cylinder region (σ ≫ 1) and the upstream side of the termination shock (σ ≪ 1) in the course of the wind's propagation.

(b) Starting from a high-σ pulsar wind (σ ≳ 1) inflow boundary condition, evolve the 3D MHD system long enough to determine whether the resulting time-averaged nebular magnetic-field strength approaches the value B ≈ 200 μG inferred for the Crab Nebula, and whether the synthetic synchrotron and inverse-Compton non-thermal emission spectra computed from the simulated flow and assumed particle distribution agree with multiwavelength observations across radio, optical, X-ray, and γ-ray bands.

Provide either a constructive demonstration (theoretical or numerical) that such consistency can be achieved, or a proof/argument that high-σ 3D MHD evolution cannot simultaneously reproduce these observational constraints.

Three-dimensional relativistic MHD simulations (Porth, Komissarov & Keppens 2013, 2014) showed that kink instability and magnetic dissipation in the nebular volume can accommodate Poynting-dominated pulsar winds with σ up to ~3 while still producing termination-shock sizes and dynamics consistent with the Crab Nebula, which is widely described as a substantial resolution of the classic sigma-problem. However, achieving full quantitative consistency of the average nebular magnetic field (~200 μG) and of synthetic non-thermal emission across all spectral bands within a single high-σ 3D MHD model remains an active area of investigation, so the broader question is best characterized as partially solved.

Consider the Crab Nebula, a pulsar wind nebula powered by a young rotation-powered pulsar that injects a magnetized relativistic wind into the surrounding supernova ejecta, where the wind is decelerated at a termination shock and the shocked plasma fills the nebula and emits synchrotron radiation across the electromagnetic spectrum. Observed synchrotron emission spans from radio, produced by electrons with relatively low Lorentz factors, up to X-rays and gamma rays, produced by electrons with much higher Lorentz factors. By number, the radio-emitting electrons dominate the lepton population of the nebula, but their origin is uncertain.

Three competing scenarios are proposed for the radio-emitting electron population:

(A) Continuous injection: radio-emitting electrons are part of the present-day pulsar wind and are accelerated together with the higher-energy electrons at the termination shock, so that their spatial distribution in the nebula is set by the same advection and diffusion processes acting on the high-energy population.

(B) Distributed reacceleration: radio-emitting electrons originate elsewhere in the nebula (for example, extracted from the cold thermal filaments that pervade the nebula) and are continuously (re)accelerated in situ by interaction with magnetohydrodynamic turbulence, so that they are roughly uniformly distributed throughout the nebular volume.

(C) Relic population: radio-emitting electrons are a fossil population produced during an early, possibly initial, outburst phase of the pulsar, surviving to the present day because their synchrotron cooling times exceed the age of the system.

Determine which of (A), (B), (C) is realized in the Crab Nebula, and identify quantitative observational signatures (such as morphological correlations between radio and higher-frequency emission, polarization patterns, spectral-index maps, or time variability) and predictions from three-dimensional relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations of the pulsar wind nebula that can discriminate among the three scenarios.

Consider the Crab Nebula, a pulsar wind nebula powered by a young rotating neutron star, in which sporadic gamma-ray flares with photon energies extending above ~100 MeV have been observed on timescales of hours to days. Within ideal relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), the electric field magnitude is bounded by the magnetic field magnitude (E ≤ B), and synchrotron emission from particles accelerated under this constraint cuts off at approximately 200 MeV; the observed flare photons therefore require acceleration in regions where the ideal-MHD bound is violated, with a candidate mechanism being stochastic magnetic reconnection in thin current sheets where a non-ideal (reconnection) electric field can accelerate particles to PeV energies. Determine:

(a) the precise spatial location(s) within the Crab Nebula at which the gamma-ray flares are produced — in particular, whether they originate in the termination-shock region, at the base of the polar jet, or elsewhere; and

(b) whether stochastic magnetic reconnection in thin current sheets at such locations can self-consistently accelerate electrons (and/or positrons) to PeV energies, and produce the corresponding synchrotron gamma-ray emission, on the observed flare rise/decay timescales of hours to days, given the inferred local magnetic field strengths and plasma parameters of the nebula.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The exact location of the Crab gamma-ray flare emission and the detailed mechanism by which particles are accelerated to PeV energies on hour-to-day timescales remain unresolved. No optical/X-ray counterpart has been identified, and while relativistic magnetic reconnection (in the termination-shock region or jet base) is the leading candidate and has been shown via PIC and MHD simulations to plausibly produce the required acceleration, current models cannot yet pinpoint the location or fully reproduce flare statistics. Recent reviews continue to list the flare origin as an open question.

representations.normalized:
Heterogeneous crystal nucleation refers to the formation of a crystalline phase from a metastable liquid (or supersaturated/supercooled fluid) in the presence of a foreign interface (e.g., a substrate, impurity, container wall, or another solid surface), where the interface lowers the nucleation barrier compared to homogeneous nucleation in the bulk. In molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, the system is described by a set of atomic positions evolving under classical equations of motion governed by an interatomic potential (force field) U(r_1,...,r_N), and rare-event sampling techniques (e.g., metadynamics, forward-flux sampling, seeding, transition path sampling) are used to estimate nucleation rates J and free-energy barriers ΔG* as functions of thermodynamic conditions (temperature T, pressure p, supersaturation Δμ) and of properties of the foreign interface (chemistry, lattice mismatch, roughness, wettability/contact angle θ, curvature).

Develop a quantitative atomistic simulation framework that simultaneously achieves the following:

(i) Realistic interfaces: prescribe a methodology for performing MD simulations of heterogeneous nucleation in which the substrate/interface is modeled with sufficient atomistic detail (chemical composition, surface termination, defect structure, finite temperature reconstruction, and electrostatic/polarization response) that the resulting nucleation rates and pathways are quantitatively reliable for the chosen force field, including a specification of the minimal interfacial features that the force field must reproduce in order to predict ΔG* and J within a target accuracy.

(ii) Transferable trends: from such simulations, extract general, possibly non-material-specific scaling laws or functional relationships of the form J = J(Δμ, T, X) and ΔG* = ΔG*(Δμ, T, X), where X is a small set of dimensionless interfacial descriptors (e.g., normalized lattice mismatch, contact angle, reduced curvature, interfacial stiffness ratio), such that the laws hold across distinct material systems within a quantified error.

State precisely the descriptors X, the class of force fields and interfaces for which the framework is valid, and prove or provide numerical evidence of the transferability of the resulting trends across at least two structurally and chemically different liquid–substrate systems.

representations.normalized: A three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of a simple graph $G=(V,E)$ assigns to each vertex $v\in V$ an axis-aligned box (a rectangular parallelepiped with integer coordinates) in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with pairwise disjoint interiors, and to each edge $\{u,v\}\in E$ an axis-parallel polygonal route from a point on the surface of the box of $u$ to a point on the surface of the box of $v$. Distinct edge routes may share points only at common endpoints on box surfaces, and an edge route may not pass through the interior of any box. A drawing is called \emph{1-bend} if every edge route consists of at most two axis-parallel segments (i.e., has at most one bend). A drawing is called a \emph{cube-drawing} if every vertex box is a cube. A cube-drawing is called \emph{degree-restricted} if for every vertex $v$ the surface area of its cube is $O(\deg(v))$; equivalently, for the complete graph $K_n$ this means each vertex cube has surface area $O(n)$ (so side length $O(\sqrt{n})$).\n\nQuestion: Does there exist, for every $n$, a 1-bend degree-restricted three-dimensional orthogonal cube-drawing of the complete graph $K_n$?

representations.normalized:
Classical nucleation theory (CNT) models the rate of formation of a new (crystalline) phase from a metastable (supercooled liquid) parent phase by treating an emerging nucleus as a spherical cluster whose free energy of formation is written as the sum of a negative bulk term proportional to its volume (driven by the chemical potential difference Δμ between the two phases) and a positive surface term proportional to its area (governed by an effective interfacial free energy γ). The resulting free-energy barrier ΔG* and the steady-state nucleation rate J = A exp(−ΔG*/kBT) depend on Δμ, γ, the attachment kinetics, and a Zeldovich factor.

Different classes of supercooled liquids (e.g., simple atomic liquids, metallic alloys, network-forming liquids such as water and silica, colloidal suspensions, molecular liquids with complex polymorphism) exhibit qualitatively distinct nucleation behaviors, including non-classical multi-step pathways, pre-critical ordering, polymorph selection, and strongly non-spherical or diffuse interfaces, which are not captured by the standard CNT ansatz.

Question: Does there exist a single universal extension or refinement of classical nucleation theory — together with a corresponding universal enhanced-sampling computational framework — that quantitatively predicts crystal nucleation rates and pathways across all such classes of supercooled liquids and thermodynamic conditions; or is it instead the case that any quantitatively predictive theoretical and computational treatment must necessarily be system-specific, requiring different tailored variants of CNT and different tailored sampling techniques for different classes of systems?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is a broad, conceptual open problem in the theory of crystal nucleation. It is not a precisely formulated mathematical conjecture with a definitive resolution, and current literature continues to develop both system-specific extensions of CNT (e.g., two-step nucleation, non-classical pathways) and specialized enhanced-sampling methods, with no universal framework established. The status is therefore open in the sense that no universal theory has been demonstrated, while the meta-question of whether such universality is even achievable remains debated.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple graph with maximum degree $\Delta$. A *matching* in $G$ is a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint. Given a linear ordering $\pi=(v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n)$ of $V$ and a matching $M\subseteq E$, draw each edge $\{v_i,v_j\}\in M$ (with $i<j$) as the semicircular arc in the upper half-plane connecting positions $i$ and $j$ on a horizontal line; the matching $M$ is said to be *non-crossing with respect to $\pi$* if no two of these arcs cross, equivalently, if there are no two edges $\{v_i,v_j\},\{v_k,v_\ell\}\in M$ with $i<k<j<\ell$.

Decide whether the following holds: there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for every simple graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta$, the edge set $E$ can be partitioned into at most $c\,\Delta$ matchings $M_1,\dots,M_t$ ($t\le c\Delta$) for which there is a single linear ordering $\pi$ of $V$ such that every $M_k$ is non-crossing with respect to $\pi$.

A 3-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of a simple graph G=(V,E) assigns to each vertex v∈V an axis-aligned box with integer coordinates in ℤ³, with pairwise interior-disjoint boxes, and routes each edge uv as a polyline in ℤ³ whose segments are parallel to the coordinate axes, starts on the boundary of the box of u, ends on the boundary of the box of v, is otherwise disjoint from all vertex boxes, and is internally disjoint from every other edge route. A bend of an edge route is an interior point at which the route changes direction. The drawing is called a cube-drawing if every vertex box is an axis-aligned cube (i.e., has the same integer side length in all three directions; possibly different cubes may have different sizes). The volume of a drawing is the number of unit grid cells in the smallest axis-aligned bounding box that contains all vertex boxes and edge routes.

Let Δ(G) denote the maximum degree of G and n=|V(G)|.

Question: Does every simple graph G admit a 3-dimensional orthogonal cube-drawing in which every edge route has at most one bend and whose volume is O(Δ(G)³·n)?

The problem of a complete rigorous mathematical treatment of drop pinch-off for the full incompressible Navier-Stokes free-boundary system with surface tension appears to remain open. Existing rigorous results address related but distinct questions: Eggers-Dupont type one-dimensional asymptotic models with universal scaling laws, formal/numerical universal pinching for axisymmetric free-surface flow, and the construction by Castro-Córdoba-Fefferman-Gancedo-Gómez-Serrano of "splash" singularities for the 2D free-boundary Navier-Stokes equations (a different self-intersection-type singularity). No source found establishes a full rigorous theory of topology-changing pinch-off for the 3D free-boundary Navier-Stokes system with Gibbs-Thompson/Young-Laplace boundary condition.

The inviscid limit problem for incompressible Navier–Stokes with no-slip boundary conditions is widely recognized as a major open problem. Kato (1984) provided an equivalent characterization in terms of vanishing energy dissipation in a thin boundary layer of width O(ν), and many partial results exist (e.g., for analytic data, or under additional assumptions). However, in the physically realistic regime of unstable boundary layers in closed domains, identification of the limiting equations remains open.

abla\cdot u = 0,$$
with viscosity $
u>0$, smooth divergence-free initial data $u_0$ of finite energy, and smooth (say, zero or smooth compactly supported / smooth periodic) external forcing $f$.

A smooth solution is said to exhibit finite-time blowup if there exists $T^*<\infty$ such that the solution $u$ is smooth on $[0,T^*)$ but $\limsup_{t	o T^{*-}}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{H^s}=\infty$ for some $s$ large enough (equivalently, the solution loses regularity at $T^*$).

Question: Does there exist smooth, divergence-free initial data $u_0$ (with $f\equiv 0$, say) of finite energy such that the corresponding solution to the above equations develops finite-time blowup? Equivalently, prove or disprove that for every such initial datum the solution remains smooth for all $t\ge 0$.

The global regularity / finite-time blowup problem for the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and remains open as of 2026. No proof of either global regularity or of finite-time blowup for smooth finite-energy data is known; recent work (e.g., on hypodissipative or generalized models, and Tao's averaged Navier-Stokes blowup result) has provided partial insight but not resolved the original problem.

A three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of a simple graph G = (V, E) assigns to each vertex v ∈ V an axis-aligned box B_v ⊂ ℝ^3 with integer coordinates, such that the boxes have pairwise disjoint interiors. Each edge uv ∈ E is drawn as a polygonal curve made of axis-parallel segments whose endpoints lie on the surfaces of B_u and B_v respectively, with the interior of the curve disjoint from every box and from the other edge curves except at common endpoints. A bend of an edge route is an interior point of the curve where two segments of different axis directions meet. The drawing is called 1-bend if every edge route has at most one bend. The volume of the drawing is the volume of the smallest axis-aligned bounding box containing the union of all vertex boxes and edge routes (equivalently, the product of the side lengths of the integer bounding box).

Question: Let K_n be the complete graph on n vertices. Must every 1-bend three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of K_n have volume Ω(n^3)?

Consider an isotropic diffuse electromagnetic background that, when measured by an observer, exhibits a near-perfect Planck (blackbody) spectrum with characteristic temperature approximately 2.7 K (the so-called 3 K microwave background). Because a smooth blackbody spectrum carries no intrinsic distance information (no spectral lines, no parallax, no standard-candle structure), the spatial distribution of emitting sources along the line of sight cannot be inferred from the spectrum alone.

Determine, on the basis of independent physical arguments and observational constraints, the spatial origin of this radiation. Specifically:

(a) Is the observed 3 K background produced exclusively as a fossil relic emitted in the early universe at very large cosmological distances (i.e. on a last-scattering surface at high redshift), so that essentially none of the locally measured intensity originates from sources within the observable nearby universe?

(b) Or could a non-negligible fraction of the locally observed intensity be generated by sources distributed throughout space, including local and intermediate-distance regions, so that the 3 K background is a more universal radiation field filling space and produced both nearby and at large distances?

Provide quantitative bounds on the fraction of the observed 3 K intensity that may be attributed to local versus distant sources, using whatever constraints (anisotropy structure, polarization, Sunyaev–Zel'dovich distortions, spectral distortions, correlations with large-scale structure, etc.) can break the degeneracy left by the blackbody spectrum.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The mainstream cosmological consensus interprets the 3 K microwave background as a relic of the early universe emitted at the last-scattering surface (z≈1100), supported by its near-perfect blackbody spectrum, anisotropy spectrum, polarization, and Sunyaev–Zel'dovich measurements toward galaxy clusters (which place much of the radiation behind clusters). However, the precise question of whether a non-negligible local or intermediate-distance contribution can be ruled out in a model-independent way—given that a blackbody spectrum alone provides no distance measurement—remains a posed open question in the cited line of inquiry, and no rigorous quantitative upper bound on a possible local component is universally established outside the standard model assumptions.

Let G = (V, E) be a simple graph with n = |V| vertices, m = |E| edges, and maximum degree Δ. A 3-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of G assigns to each vertex v an axis-aligned box in the integer grid Z^3 with pairwise interior-disjoint boxes, and to each edge a polygonal curve composed of axis-parallel segments connecting points on the boundaries of the boxes of its endpoints, such that distinct edges' interiors are disjoint and edges meet boxes only at endpoints. The drawing is called 1-bend if every edge route uses at most one bend (turn). The volume of the drawing is the volume of the smallest axis-aligned bounding box of the entire drawing.

A crossing-free matching of G is a matching M ⊆ E together with a straight-line drawing of the edges of M (in some plane embedding model) so that no two edges of M cross. Suppose the following hypothesis holds:

(H) Every graph G can be edge-decomposed into O(Δ) crossing-free matchings.

Question: Assuming (H), does it follow that every graph G admits a 1-bend 3-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of volume O(m·n)?

Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $A$ be a $K$-algebra (not necessarily commutative or unital).

A $K$-linear map $\delta : A \to A$ is called a $K$-derivation if $\delta(ab) = \delta(a)b + a\delta(b)$ for all $a,b \in A$, and a $K$-$\mathcal{E}$-derivation if $\delta = \mathrm{Id}_A - \phi$ for some $K$-algebra endomorphism $\phi$ of $A$. The map $\delta$ is locally nilpotent if for every $a \in A$ there exists an integer $m \geq 1$ (depending on $a$) such that $\delta^m(a) = 0$.

For $\vartheta \in \{\text{left}, \text{right}, \text{two-sided}\}$, a $K$-subspace $V \subseteq A$ is called a $\vartheta$-Mathieu subspace ($\vartheta$-MS) of $A$ if it satisfies the following property: for every $a \in A$ such that $a^m \in V$ for all sufficiently large $m \geq 1$, and for every $b \in A$, one has
- $ba^m \in V$ for all sufficiently large $m$, when $\vartheta = \text{left}$;
- $a^m b \in V$ for all sufficiently large $m$, when $\vartheta = \text{right}$;
- $ba^m c \in V$ for all $b,c \in A$ and all sufficiently large $m$, when $\vartheta = \text{two-sided}$.

A $\vartheta$-ideal of $A$ means a left ideal, right ideal, or two-sided ideal according to $\vartheta$.

Question: Let $\delta$ be either a locally nilpotent $K$-derivation or a locally nilpotent $K$-$\mathcal{E}$-derivation of $A$. For each $\vartheta \in \{\text{left}, \text{right}, \text{two-sided}\}$ and every $\vartheta$-ideal $I$ of $A$, must the image $\delta(I)$ be a $\vartheta$-Mathieu subspace of $A$?

The general LNED conjecture remains open. Partial affirmative results are known: it has been verified for Laurent polynomial algebras, for algebraic algebras, for bivariate polynomial algebras over one-dimensional UFDs, and for various classes of locally nilpotent derivations of polynomial rings in three variables (rank-two, homogeneous rank-three, rank-one acting on principal ideals). No full resolution has been reported.

\[ \partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u = \Delta u - \nabla p, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0, \]

Rather than classifying admissible initial data $u_0$, consider the space $\mathcal{P}$ of all time-dependent solution paths $t\mapsto u(t,\cdot)$ (e.g., Leray-Hopf weak solutions, or suitable weak/mild solutions in a chosen function space). Define on $\mathcal{P}$ qualitative equivalence classes determined by path properties such as: long-time asymptotic behavior, scaling/self-similar structure, energy-dissipation profile, vorticity alignment, frequency cascade behavior, or topological/geometric features of the trajectory in phase space.

The problem: Does there exist such a classification of solution paths in $\mathcal{P}$ by qualitative properties of the trajectory (rather than by properties of the initial data) that
(i) is preserved or sufficiently controlled under the Navier-Stokes evolution,
(ii) captures enough information about the nonlinear term $(u\cdot\nabla)u$ to distinguish regular paths from potentially singular ones, and
(iii) can be used to establish or refute global regularity for the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations?

Let $u(x,t)$ be a smooth, divergence-free velocity field on $\mathbb{R}^d$ (with $d=2$ or $d=3$) solving either the incompressible Euler equations
\[
\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,
\]
or the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations
\[
\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u + \nabla p = \nu \Delta u, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,
\]
with $\nu>0$. Let $X(a,t)$ denote the Lagrangian flow map defined by $\partial_t X(a,t)=u(X(a,t),t)$, $X(a,0)=a$, and let $A(x,t)$ be the back-to-labels (inverse Lagrangian) map, satisfying $A(X(a,t),t)=a$ and equivalently
\[
\partial_t A + (u\cdot\nabla)A = 0, \qquad A(x,0)=x.
\]
By incompressibility, $A(\cdot,t)$ is volume preserving and $\det(\nabla A)=1$.

Develop an Eulerian theory of mixed Eulerian-Lagrangian quantities built from $u$, $A$, and their derivatives. In particular, identify and analyze nonlinear commutator-type expressions involving the second derivatives $\partial_i\partial_j A^k(x,t)$ (for instance, expressions of schematic form
\[
C^{k}_{ij}[u,A](x,t) := \partial_i\partial_j A^k - (\nabla A)\text{-pullback of the corresponding Eulerian second-derivative object},
\]
and contractions thereof against $\nabla u$, $\nabla^2 u$, or curvature-like tensors of the map $A$) and determine whether such commutator quantities satisfy useful evolution equations, conservation or coercivity properties that can be exploited to obtain new a priori estimates, regularity criteria, or geometric information for the underlying Euler or Navier-Stokes flow.

Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ ($d=2,3$), with viscosity $\nu>0$ and (possibly) a forcing $f$:
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = f, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$
together with appropriate boundary conditions (e.g.\ periodic on the torus $\mathbb{T}^d$, or no-slip on a bounded domain). Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the space of weak (Leray–Hopf) solution paths $u:[0,\infty)\to H$, where $H$ is the standard divergence-free $L^2$ space.

Consider Borel probability measures $\mu$ on a suitable function space $\mathcal{X}$ (e.g.\ $C([0,\infty);H_w)$ or $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$) that are supported on $\mathcal{P}$. One may regard such measures as candidates for describing statistical states of turbulent flow.

Provide a complete mathematical characterization of such measures, including:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Existence:} Construct measures $\mu$ supported on Navier–Stokes solution paths that are physically meaningful (e.g.\ invariant under the flow when applicable, or describing a stationary statistical equilibrium).
\item \textbf{Time dependence:} Determine for which regimes such measures can be chosen time-independent (statistically stationary) versus genuinely time-dependent.
\item \textbf{Uniqueness:} Determine whether, for given parameters $(\nu, f, \Omega, \text{boundary conditions})$, such a measure is unique within natural admissibility classes.
\item \textbf{Symmetries:} Identify which symmetries of the equations (translations, rotations, scaling, parity, etc.) are inherited by $\mu$, and whether spontaneous symmetry breaking can occur.
\item \textbf{Parameter dependence:} Describe the dependence of $\mu$ on $\nu$, on the forcing $f$, and on the geometry of $\Omega$, including limits such as $\nu\to 0$.
\item \textbf{Stability and bifurcations:} Analyze the stability of $\mu$ under perturbations and characterize bifurcations of the family $\{\mu_\lambda\}$ as parameters $\lambda$ vary.
\end{enumerate}

The problem is to give a rigorous mathematical theory answering all of the above.

Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations
\[ \partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0, \]
in a bounded smooth domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ with no-slip boundary condition $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ and forcing or boundary data driving a statistically stationary turbulent regime. Associated to a smooth velocity field $u$ is the Eulerian–Lagrangian "back-to-labels" map $A(x,t)$, defined as the (diffusive) inverse of the Lagrangian trajectory map: in the inviscid case $A$ satisfies $\partial_t A + (u\cdot\nabla)A = 0$ with $A(x,0)=x$, and in the viscous case $A$ solves
\[ \partial_t A + (u\cdot\nabla) A - \nu\Delta A = 0,\qquad A(x,0)=x, \]
so that $A(x,t)$ records the (averaged) initial label of the fluid particle currently at position $x$ at time $t$.

Develop a rigorous theory for the statistics of $A$ in classical boundary-driven Navier–Stokes turbulence. Specifically, obtain rigorous quantitative results (bounds, scaling laws, or exact identities, in suitable averaged or ensemble sense) for:

1. The moments $\mathbb{E}\,|A(x,t)-x|^p$ for $p\ge 1$.
2. The averaged tensor products
\[ \mathbb{E}\,\bigotimes_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(A(x+y_j,t+s_j)-A(x,t)\bigr) \]
for arbitrary $n\ge 1$, spatial increments $y_j\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and temporal increments $s_j\in\mathbb{R}$.
3. The corresponding structure functions, their $L^p$ norms, and the statistics of the spatial derivatives $\nabla A$ (in particular moments of $\nabla A - I$).

Determine, in particular, scaling exponents in the inertial range and dependence on the viscosity $\nu$, with all estimates respecting the no-slip boundary condition.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of rigorously establishing a viscosity-independent positive lower bound on the energy dissipation rate for 3D Navier–Stokes turbulence (the "zeroth law of turbulence" / anomalous dissipation) is widely regarded as a fundamental open problem. Recent work (e.g., Bedrossian–Blumenthal–Punshon-Smith on Lagrangian chaos and dissipation for stochastic Navier–Stokes, and Brué–De Lellis, Armstrong–Vicol on anomalous dissipation for advection–diffusion and forced Navier–Stokes constructions) has established related results in restricted settings, but the general statement under the stated ensemble assumptions remains open.

Consider the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for an ideal fluid with no body force:
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,\qquad u(0,x)=u_0(x),$$
where $u:[0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is the velocity field and $p:[0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$ is the pressure. Assume the initial data $u_0$ is smooth (i.e., $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$), divergence-free, and rapidly decaying (e.g., in the Schwartz class $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$).

Determine whether one of the following holds:

(a) For every such initial datum $u_0$, the corresponding solution $u(t,\cdot)$ exists and remains smooth for all $t\in[0,\infty)$; or

(b) There exists such an initial datum $u_0$ for which the solution develops a finite-time singularity, i.e., there is some $T^*<\infty$ such that $u(t,\cdot)$ cannot be continued as a smooth solution beyond $T^*$.

The blowup problem for the 3D incompressible Euler equations with smooth, rapidly decaying initial data on the whole space $\mathbb{R}^3$ remains open. Substantial recent progress includes Elgindi's finite-time singularity for $C^{1,\alpha}$ (non-smooth) axisymmetric data without swirl, and the Chen–Hou computer-assisted proof (2025, PNAS) of nearly self-similar finite-time blowup for the 3D axisymmetric Euler equations with smooth initial data in a bounded cylindrical domain with boundary. representations.normalized:
Let $X$ be a nonempty set. A function $d: X \times X \to [0,\infty)$ is called a quasimetric on $X$ if it satisfies:
(a) $d(x,y) + d(y,x) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$;
(b) $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$ for all $x,y,z \in X$.
(Note that $d$ need not be symmetric and $d(x,x)$ need not be zero a priori, but (a) forces $d(x,x)=0$.)

For such a space, declare a sequence $\{x_n\} \subset X$ to be Cauchy if $\lim_{n,m\to\infty} d(x_n,x_m) = 0$, and to converge to $x \in X$ if $\lim_{n\to\infty} d(x,x_n) = 0$. Call $(X,d)$ complete if every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges to some point of $X$.

A map $g: X \to X$ is called a contraction if there exists $\lambda \in [0,1)$ such that $d(g(x), g(y)) \le \lambda\, d(x,y)$ for all $x,y \in X$.

Question: Must every contraction $g$ on every complete quasimetric space $(X,d)$ have a fixed point?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem has been resolved in the negative: a contraction on a complete quasimetric space need not have a fixed point. A complete answer (with explicit counterexamples in the dislocated/quasimetric setting) was provided by Choban and Berinde, who exhibit a contractive self-map on a complete dislocated metric space (a quasimetric space in this sense) without any fixed point, and identify additional hypotheses under which a fixed point does exist.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The cosmological origin of the CMB is the consensus interpretation in mainstream cosmology, supported by COBE, WMAP, and Planck data. However, the underlying conceptual question — whether alternative mechanisms can in principle reproduce all CMB observables — remains debated by a minority of researchers (quasi-steady-state cosmology, plasma/thermalization models). No alternative model has been shown to reproduce the full set of CMB observations (blackbody spectrum, acoustic peaks, polarization) as successfully as ΛCDM, but no rigorous no-go result rules out all alternatives. The question is therefore best classified as open in the sense posed.

Consider the cosmic microwave background (CMB), an approximately isotropic blackbody radiation field with present-day temperature T_0 ≈ 2.725 K. Within the standard hot big bang cosmological model, the CMB originates from the epoch of last scattering at redshift z ≈ 1000–1100, and its blackbody temperature scales as T(z) = T_0 (1 + z). The model further predicts unavoidable spectral distortions imprinted during cosmological recombination (the cosmological recombination radiation, coming from bound–bound and free–bound transitions in primordial hydrogen and helium near z ≈ 1000–10000), as well as μ- and y-type distortions from earlier energy injections.

Devise an observational program that decisively establishes — independently of the indirect excitation-temperature method based on fine-structure or rotational lines of CN, neutral/ionized carbon, and CO seen in quasar absorption systems (which can be contaminated by local heating, collisional excitation, and radiative pumping) — that this 2.725 K background is of cosmological primordial origin. Specifically:

(a) Provide a measurement strategy that confirms the linear law T(z) = T_0 (1 + z) at large redshifts (e.g., z ≳ 6) with sufficient accuracy and freedom from astrophysical contamination to discriminate against alternative non-cosmological origin scenarios.

(b) Determine whether the predicted recombination-era spectral distortion signal near z ≈ 1000 can be detected with present or near-future instruments, and either exhibit such a detection or establish a quantitative lower bound on the instrumental sensitivity (in absolute spectral intensity) required to detect it.

A solution consists of either (i) reporting verified observational confirmations satisfying (a) and (b) together, or (ii) proving rigorous obstructions showing that one or both cannot be achieved with current technology.

Part (a) has substantial progress: T(z) measurements via the Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect at z ≲ 1 and via molecular/atomic excitation in quasar absorbers extend to z ~ 3, and a 2021 Nature measurement using H2O absorption pushed a direct CMB temperature determination to z = 6.34, all consistent with T_0(1+z). However, contamination by local excitation processes is still acknowledged. Part (b) remains unresolved: the cosmological recombination line signal has not been detected; proposed missions (PIXIE, PRISTINE, BISOU, Voyage 2050 concepts) target the required ~nK-level sensitivity but no such instrument is yet in operation. Hence the overall question of a decisive primordial-origin verification through these specific signatures is partially solved.

Develop a vulnerability-analysis framework for unmanned aerial system (UAS) networks that explicitly models a UAS as a cyber-physical system composed of four heterogeneous subsystems: (i) the communications subsystem (radio links, networking protocols, ground-control links, swarm communications), (ii) the computation subsystem (onboard processors, flight-control software, autopilot logic), (iii) the sensing subsystem (GPS, IMU, cameras, lidar, environmental sensors), and (iv) the physical airframe subsystem (motors, actuators, power, aerodynamic structure). The framework should satisfy the following requirements:

1. It must represent the cross-couplings and feedback interactions among the four subsystems above, rather than treating the UAS as a standard mobile ad hoc network or as a collection of independent subsystems analyzed in isolation.

2. It must support the identification of vulnerabilities that arise specifically from interactions between heterogeneous subsystems (i.e., vulnerabilities that are not present in any single subsystem in isolation but emerge from their coupling).

3. It must be sufficiently general to apply across the heterogeneous space of UAV architectures and capabilities (varying airframes, sensor suites, autonomy levels, and mission profiles), while still permitting concrete instantiation for a given platform.

Formally describe such a framework, give a rigorous notion of an "interaction-induced vulnerability" within it, and provide an analysis methodology that, given a specific UAS instantiation, enumerates or characterizes the set of interaction-induced vulnerabilities. Demonstrate that the framework captures vulnerabilities that pure ad hoc network models or single-subsystem models provably miss.

Consider an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) equipped with a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver and an inertial sensor suite, moving along an unconstrained three-dimensional trajectory with high translational and angular velocities. The receiver observes a superposition of authentic GNSS signals and adversarial spoofing signals injected by one or more ground- or air-based attackers, where the attacker may control signal power, code phase, Doppler shift, direction of arrival, and polarization. Existing reactive countermeasures (e.g., direction-of-arrival checks, polarization analysis, statistical signal-processing detectors, and beamforming-based suppression) typically rely on assumptions—such as a quasi-stationary platform, a known antenna orientation, or a stable multipath environment—that are violated by the high speeds and full spatial freedom of UAV motion.

Formulate and design a proactive anti-spoofing mechanism for the UAV sensory and navigation subsystem that actively eliminates (rather than merely detects) spoofing components from the received signal, subject to the following requirements:

1. The mechanism must remain valid under arbitrary UAV kinematics, including rapid changes in attitude, position, and velocity.
2. It must not depend on assumptions of antenna orientation stability, ground proximity, or static multipath geometry.
3. It must operate within the size, weight, power, and computational constraints of a typical small UAV platform.
4. It must guarantee, under a precisely stated adversary model (defining attacker power, number of spoofing transmitters, and degree of synchronization with authentic GNSS signals), bounded residual position and timing error after spoofing-signal elimination.

Provide such a design together with a rigorous analysis establishing the conditions on signal geometry, antenna configuration, and processing algorithm under which the proactive elimination is provably effective, or alternatively prove an impossibility result delimiting the regimes in which no such proactive mechanism can succeed.

Consider the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations for a fluid of constant density and kinematic viscosity ν > 0:

  ∂_t u + (u · ∇)u − ν Δu + ∇p = 0,   ∇ · u = 0,

where u(x,t) ∈ ℝ³ is the velocity field and p(x,t) ∈ ℝ is the pressure, posed on one of the following standard spatial domains: the whole space ℝ³ (with appropriate decay at infinity), the three-dimensional torus 𝕋³ (periodic boundary conditions), or a bounded smooth domain Ω ⊂ ℝ³ with the no-slip boundary condition u|_{∂Ω} = 0. There is no external forcing.

A smooth initial velocity is a divergence-free vector field u₀ : domain → ℝ³ belonging to C^∞ (with appropriate decay or boundary compatibility).

Determine the most general class of such smooth divergence-free initial data u(x,0) = u₀(x) for which the corresponding solution (u,p) exists globally in time (for all t > 0) and remains smooth (i.e., u(·,t) ∈ C^∞ for every t > 0).

Equivalently, characterize sharp sufficient conditions on u₀ that guarantee global-in-time smoothness of the resulting Leray solution and rule out any finite-time singularity.

Only partial results exist (small data, axisymmetric without swirl, various conditional/regularity criteria such as Ladyzhenskaya–Prodi–Serrin and Beale–Kato–Majda, and Koch–Tataru small-BMO⁻¹ data), but no general characterization is known.

Consider an unmanned aerial system (UAS) network in which each aircraft participates in an air-traffic-control (ATC) and collision-avoidance subsystem modeled on ADS-B and TCAS. In the baseline model: (i) every aircraft periodically broadcasts in cleartext a state report containing its identifier, position, velocity, and altitude, with no cryptographic authentication or integrity protection; (ii) each aircraft runs a collision-avoidance logic that, upon receiving the broadcasts of nearby aircraft within a surveillance radius, issues resolution advisories (e.g., climb/descend) based only on instantaneous range, closure rate, and time-to-closest-approach thresholds, without forecasting the longer-term joint trajectories induced by the advisories themselves.

Consider an adversary that can (a) eavesdrop on all broadcasts, (b) inject forged broadcasts impersonating arbitrary aircraft identifiers, (c) jam or replay legitimate broadcasts, and (d) coordinate the timing and content of injected reports across multiple ghost tracks. Define a TCAS-induced collision as a configuration of (possibly partially adversarial) traffic such that the advisory logic, applied recursively, drives the legitimate aircraft into a state from which no admissible maneuver avoids loss of separation.

Design a redesigned ATC / collision-avoidance protocol for UAS, together with a precise threat model and formal safety property, satisfying the following requirements:

1. Authenticated broadcast: every state report accepted by a receiver is cryptographically bound to a legitimate aircraft identity, with bounded verification latency compatible with the surveillance update rate.
2. Injection and jamming resilience: under any polynomially bounded adversary of the type above, the probability that a forged or replayed report is accepted, or that suppression of legitimate reports causes an undetected loss of situational awareness, is negligible.
3. Advisory soundness against orchestrated geometries: the advisory-generation logic must incorporate a multi-step predictive model of joint trajectories such that, for any traffic configuration consistent with the authenticated inputs, the issued advisories provably do not drive participating aircraft into a TCAS-induced collision state, or else explicitly signal an unresolvable conflict.
4. Backward interoperability: the protocol must remain interoperable with legacy ADS-B/TCAS-equipped manned aircraft to a specified, precisely stated degree.

Provide the protocol specification, the formal adversary and safety definitions, and proofs (or impossibility results) establishing properties 1–4, including quantitative bounds on bandwidth, latency, and the maximum traffic density under which property 3 can be guaranteed.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of securing ADS-B/TCAS for UAS against unauthenticated broadcasts, false-data injection, and TCAS-induced collisions remains an active and unresolved research area. Multiple proposals exist (lightweight authentication, PKI-based ADS-B, ADS-B encryption, formally verified ACAS X / ACAS Xu using machine-learned or verified lookup tables), but no single protocol has been adopted that simultaneously solves authentication, injection resilience, and provable avoidance of induced-collision geometries for UAS. ACAS Xu addresses some advisory-soundness concerns but not the underlying ADS-B authentication weaknesses.

Consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$,
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu \Delta u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$
for a velocity field $u(t,x)$ and pressure $p(t,x)$, with $\nu>0$. To enforce global-in-time well-posedness and regularity, several classes of regularized models have been proposed:

(a) Hyperviscous models, replacing $-\nu\Delta u$ by $-\nu\Delta u + \mu(-\Delta)^{\alpha} u$ with $\alpha$ sufficiently large (e.g. a bi-Laplacian term $\mu \Delta^2 u$), or other higher-order elliptic dissipation.
(b) Filtered or smoothed models, in which the advecting velocity $u$ in the nonlinearity is replaced by $\overline{u} = \phi_\varepsilon * u$ for some smoothing kernel $\phi_\varepsilon$ (e.g. Leray-$\alpha$, Bardina, NS-$\alpha$ type models).
(c) Models with additional nonlinear regularizing terms.
(d) Galerkin-type projections onto a finite-dimensional subspace that preserve the energy balance.

Each of these modifications introduces a length or order scale not directly justified by macroscopic experiment.

Problem. Determine, on mathematical and physical grounds, which (if any) of these regularizations is the correct choice for modeling macroscopic incompressible fluid flow. In particular: when physical experiments do not exhibit a macroscopic cutoff scale, do different choices of regularization yield genuinely different predictions for macroscopic observables (e.g. statistical quantities of turbulent flow, energy dissipation rate, structure functions), or are the resulting macroscopic theories equivalent in an appropriate limit?

The question of which regularization of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations is appropriate for macroscopic fluid modeling, and whether the choice matters in the absence of a physical macroscopic cutoff, is a long-standing modeling and mathematical open problem. Consider a wireless network of $N$ nodes, each equipped with an antenna array of $M$ elements that performs both direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation and adaptive beamforming. Each node $i$ estimates the angles of arrival $\{\theta_{ij}\}$ of signals from neighbors $j$ using a standard subspace-based estimator (e.g. MUSIC or ESPRIT) applied to the spatial covariance matrix $R_i = \mathbb{E}[x_i x_i^H]$ of received snapshots $x_i \in \mathbb{C}^M$. After DoA estimation, the nodes collaboratively run a distributed beamnulling algorithm: each node $i$ chooses a complex weight vector $w_i \in \mathbb{C}^M$ that places nulls in the directions of identified interferers while maintaining unit gain toward intended neighbors, and these weights are iteratively updated across the network so that the joint pattern $\{w_i\}_{i=1}^N$ converges to a fixed point of the collective null-placement update map $T$.

Suppose an adversary injects jamming signals $s_a(t)$ from one or more locations and is able to shape $s_a(t)$ to mimic the waveform statistics of a chosen legitimate node, thereby contaminating the covariance estimates $R_i$ and influencing the DoA outputs and the inputs to $T$.

(a) Derive necessary and sufficient analytical conditions on (i) the jammer's transmit waveform second-order statistics, (ii) its spatial signature relative to legitimate nodes, and (iii) the array geometry and SNR, under which the adversary can cause each receiver's DoA estimator to either fail to detect a chosen legitimate transmitter or to produce a false DoA pointing at a chosen angle, with prescribed probability.

(b) Model the distributed beamnulling iteration as a discrete dynamical system $w^{(k+1)} = T(w^{(k)}; u^{(k)})$ where $u^{(k)}$ encodes adversarial perturbations to the DoA inputs. Determine feasibility criteria (in terms of the spectral properties of $T$, the perturbation budget $\|u^{(k)}\| \le \varepsilon$, and the network connectivity graph) under which an adversary can drive the trajectory $\{w^{(k)}\}$ toward a fixed point that nulls a maximal set of legitimate links, i.e. yields a maximally disconnected effective communication graph.

(c) Identify countermeasures — formulated as modifications of the update map $T$, of the DoA estimator, or of the protocol — that provably prevent convergence of the perturbed iteration to any fixed point whose induced communication graph is disconnected, and quantify the trade-off between robustness and beamforming gain.

Consider a network of $n$ mobile agents (e.g., unmanned aerial vehicles) operating in $\mathbb{R}^3$, whose positions $x_i(t)\in\mathbb{R}^3$ evolve according to single-integrator or double-integrator dynamics with bounded velocity and acceleration constraints. At each time $t$, the communication topology is modeled by a graph $G(t)=(V,E(t))$ where $V=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $(i,j)\in E(t)$ iff $\|x_i(t)-x_j(t)\|\le R$ for a fixed communication radius $R>0$. A targeted jamming attack is modeled as an adversary that, at time $t$, selects a set $S(t)\subseteq V$ of up to $k$ agents (or a spatial region of radius $\rho$) and removes all edges incident to $S(t)$ from $G(t)$; the attack set $S(t)$ is unknown to the agents and may only be partially observable through noisy local measurements (so detection and localization of the jammer are unreliable).

Define the topological vulnerability of $G(t)$ to $k$-targeted jamming as
$$V_k(G(t)) \;=\; \max_{S\subseteq V,\,|S|\le k}\bigl[\,c(G(t)) - c(G(t)\setminus S)\,\bigr],$$
where $c(\cdot)$ is a connectivity measure such as the algebraic connectivity $\lambda_2$ of the graph Laplacian, or the size of the largest connected component, and $G(t)\setminus S$ denotes removal of all edges incident to $S$.

Design a real-time distributed control law
$$\dot x_i(t) \;=\; u_i\bigl(\{x_j(t)\}_{j\in N_i(t)},\,m_i(t)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\dots,n,$$
where $N_i(t)$ is agent $i$'s current set of neighbors in $G(t)$ and $m_i(t)$ are local (possibly noisy or missing) attack-detection signals, such that:

(i) $G(t)$ remains connected for all $t\ge 0$ in the absence of attacks, and reconnects within a bounded reformation time after any attack;
(ii) the time-averaged vulnerability $\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T V_k(G(t))\,dt$ is minimized over admissible attack strategies $S(\cdot)$;
(iii) mission-level constraints (specified target waypoints or formation shapes for designated agents, kinematic limits, and inter-agent collision avoidance) are satisfied;
(iv) the law is fully distributed, requires no global knowledge of $S(t)$, and is robust to false positives and false negatives in the local detection signals $m_i(t)$.

Provide such an algorithm together with provable guarantees on the reformation time, the achieved vulnerability $V_k$, and the connectivity of $G(t)$, or establish fundamental impossibility/lower bounds relating $(n,k,R,\rho)$ to the achievable vulnerability and reformation time.

The problem of jointly minimizing topological vulnerability and ensuring distributed reformation under unreliable attack detection in UAV/multi-agent networks remains an active research direction. Subsequent work has produced partial results on resilient consensus (e.g., W-MSR-type filters), connectivity-preserving formation control, and robust graph design via algebraic connectivity maximization, but no general distributed algorithm with optimal vulnerability guarantees under unreliable jamming localization is established. The status appears to be open / partially addressed.
