Consider the two-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on the torus $\mathbb{T}^2 = \mathbb{R}^2/\mathbb{Z}^2$,
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu \Delta u + \nabla p = f, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$
with periodic boundary conditions, viscosity $\nu>0$, zero spatial mean, and a time-independent forcing $f \in L^2(\mathbb{T}^2)^2$ with zero mean. It is known that this dynamical system, viewed on the phase space $H = \{u\in L^2(\mathbb{T}^2)^2 : \nabla\cdot u=0,\ \int u =0\}$, possesses a compact global attractor $\mathcal{A}\subset H$ of finite Hausdorff (and fractal) dimension which attracts every trajectory as $t\to\infty$.

An inertial manifold for this system is a finite-dimensional smooth (at least $C^1$) Lipschitz manifold $\mathcal{M}\subset H$ that is (i) positively invariant under the semiflow, (ii) contains the global attractor $\mathcal{A}$, and (iii) attracts every trajectory exponentially fast (the exponential tracking property): for every $u_0\in H$ there exist $v_0\in\mathcal{M}$ and constants $C,\kappa>0$ such that $\|S(t)u_0 - S(t)v_0\|_H \le C e^{-\kappa t}$ for all $t\ge 0$, where $S(t)$ denotes the solution semigroup.

Question: Does there exist an inertial manifold $\mathcal{M}$ for the two-dimensional periodic Navier–Stokes equations as above? Equivalently, is the long-time dynamics on $\mathcal{A}$ conjugate (via a smooth finite-dimensional reduction with exponentially decaying transient infinite-dimensional modes) to a finite-dimensional smooth dynamical system?

Consider an unmanned aerial system (UAS) network, modeled as a flying ad hoc network (FANET): a finite set of mobile nodes (aerial vehicles) whose pairwise communication links evolve over time according to a time-varying graph G(t) = (V, E(t)), with high node mobility producing rapid topology changes and with strict end-to-end latency constraints on packet delivery. A routing mechanism is a distributed algorithm R that, at each time t and for each source–destination pair (s, d), computes a path P_R(s, d, t) ⊆ E(t) used to forward traffic.

Adopt a standard adversarial model in which an attacker controls a subset A ⊂ V of nodes (or can inject a bounded number of external nodes/links) and may perform routing-layer attacks such as black-hole, gray-hole, wormhole, sinkhole, Sybil, rushing, route falsification, and replay attacks. Define security metrics for R, for example:
  (i) packet delivery ratio under attack,
  (ii) probability that an attacker-controlled node lies on P_R(s, d, t),
  (iii) detection latency of malicious behavior,
  (iv) resilience to topology churn rate, defined as the maximum link-change rate per unit time tolerated while preserving (i)–(iii) above thresholds.

Problem. For the class of routing mechanisms proposed for FANET/UAS networks that compute paths in rapidly changing topologies under stringent latency constraints (as opposed to those designed for slower mobile ad hoc networks, MANETs), provide a rigorous, technical security analysis and comparison. Specifically:
  (a) Formalize a uniform threat model and a set of quantitative security metrics suitable to FANET conditions (high mobility, 3D topology, intermittent links, latency bounds).
  (b) For each candidate routing mechanism R, derive analytical or simulation-based bounds on the metrics (i)–(iv) under the threat model of (a), without simply inheriting security assumptions or guarantees established for MANET routing protocols.
  (c) Identify which mechanisms, if any, satisfy a prescribed security level (e.g., delivery ratio ≥ 1 − ε under up to k compromised nodes within latency L) and characterize the trade-offs between latency, mobility tolerance, and security.

Either exhibit such an analysis and comparison, or prove fundamental impossibility results showing that no FANET routing mechanism in a given class can simultaneously meet specified latency and security thresholds under the stated adversary.

Consider an unmanned aerial system (UAS) network, modeled as a flying ad hoc network (FANET): a finite set of mobile nodes (aerial vehicles) whose pairwise communication links evolve over time according to a time-varying graph G(t) = (V, E(t)), with high node mobility producing rapid topology changes and with strict end-to-end latency constraints on packet delivery. A routing mechanism is a distributed algorithm R that, at each time t and for each source–destination pair (s, d), computes a path P_R(s, d, t) ⊆ E(t) used to forward traffic.

Adopt a standard adversarial model in which an attacker controls a subset A ⊂ V of nodes (or can inject a bounded number of external nodes/links) and may perform routing-layer attacks such as black-hole, gray-hole, wormhole, sinkhole, Sybil, rushing, route falsification, and replay attacks. Define security metrics for R, for example:
  (i) packet delivery ratio under attack,
  (ii) probability that an attacker-controlled node lies on P_R(s, d, t),
  (iii) detection latency of malicious behavior,
  (iv) resilience to topology churn rate, defined as the maximum link-change rate per unit time tolerated while preserving (i)–(iii) above thresholds.

Problem. For the class of routing mechanisms proposed for FANET/UAS networks that compute paths in rapidly changing topologies under stringent latency constraints (as opposed to those designed for slower mobile ad hoc networks, MANETs), provide a rigorous, technical security analysis and comparison. Specifically:
  (a) Formalize a uniform threat model and a set of quantitative security metrics suitable to FANET conditions (high mobility, 3D topology, intermittent links, latency bounds).
  (b) For each candidate routing mechanism R, derive analytical or simulation-based bounds on the metrics (i)–(iv) under the threat model of (a), without simply inheriting security assumptions or guarantees established for MANET routing protocols.
  (c) Identify which mechanisms, if any, satisfy a prescribed security level (e.g., delivery ratio ≥ 1 − ε under up to k compromised nodes within latency L) and characterize the trade-offs between latency, mobility tolerance, and security.

Either exhibit such an analysis and comparison, or prove fundamental impossibility results showing that no FANET routing mechanism in a given class can simultaneously meet specified latency and security thresholds under the stated adversary.

Let $B \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a bounded simply connected domain (an obstacle) with smooth boundary, and let $\Omega = \mathbb{R}^3 \setminus \overline{B}$ be the exterior domain. Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u = -\nabla p + \nu \Delta u, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0 \quad \text{in } \Omega,$$
with kinematic viscosity $\nu>0$, no-slip boundary condition $u=0$ on $\partial B$, and prescribed uniform flow at infinity
$$u(x,t) \to U \quad \text{as } |x|\to\infty,$$
for some fixed nonzero constant vector $U \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Define the bulk energy dissipation rate
$$\varepsilon = \limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T \frac{\nu}{|B|}\int_\Omega |\nabla u(x,t)|^2\,dx\,dt$$
(or, equivalently, the time-averaged drag power per unit obstacle volume).

Problem: Establish rigorous, physically realistic upper bounds for $\varepsilon$ in terms of $|U|$, $\nu$, and the geometry of $B$ (e.g. of the form $\varepsilon \le C\, |U|^3/L$ for a characteristic length $L$ of $B$ and a constant $C$ depending only on the shape of $B$), directly from the Navier–Stokes equations without ad hoc closure assumptions.

Consider a network of unmanned aerial systems (UAS) modeled as a time-varying graph G(t) = (V, E(t)), where V is a set of mobile airborne nodes and E(t) is the set of communication links at time t, determined by node positions and a communication-range/channel model. Each node executes a mobile routing protocol that depends on (i) the current topology, (ii) channel availability, and (iii) reported geographical positions {p_i(t)}_{i in V} of all nodes (e.g., as required by position-based routing schemes), and that is designed to converge—within bounded time T*—to a routing state in which every source-destination pair has a valid forwarding path.

Suppose an adversary may simultaneously employ the following capabilities, subject to a budget B that bounds the total magnitude or rate of adversarial actions:
1. Topological perturbation: forcing a subset of nodes to alter their positions or links via exploitation of an adaptive formation-control mechanism (e.g., injecting bounded false control inputs that cause prescribed displacements of cooperating nodes).
2. Jamming: rendering a chosen subset J(t) ⊆ E(t) of links unusable during chosen time intervals.
3. Position-knowledge manipulation: replacing the reported positions p_i(t) of nodes in a chosen subset S ⊆ V by adversarially chosen values \tilde p_i(t) within an allowable deviation bound.

Formalize the following questions:

(a) Feasibility. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on (G(t), the routing protocol, the formation-control law, and the adversarial budget B) under which the adversary can construct a joint strategy combining (1)–(3) that prevents convergence of the routing protocol indefinitely, or that increases its convergence time beyond any prescribed multiple of T*.

(b) Quantitative lower bounds. Derive, as a function of B and structural parameters of G(t), a tight lower bound on the worst-case convergence time achievable by the adversary.

(c) Countermeasures. Design and prove correctness/optimality of a routing or control mechanism (possibly using authenticated position reporting, robust consensus, redundancy, or detection of formation-control anomalies) that guarantees convergence within a bounded time for every adversarial strategy of budget at most B, or characterize the maximal B for which such guarantees are achievable.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold equipped with the Levi-Civita connection, with Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^{i}_{jk}$ in local coordinates $x^1,\dots,x^n$, and let $g^{ij}$ denote the inverse metric. Let $\Omega^{ch}_M$ be the chiral de Rham complex of $M$, the sheaf of vertex superalgebras locally generated, on a coordinate chart with coordinates $\gamma^i$ and conjugate fields $b_i,\varphi^i,\psi_i$ (bosonic and fermionic), in such a way that its weight-zero part recovers $\bigwedge^{\bullet} T^*M$. Define local odd generators
$$e_i^{\pm} \;=\; \psi_i \;\pm\; g_{ij}\,\varphi^{j},$$
and consider, for each smooth $k$-form $\omega \in C^{\infty}(M,\bigwedge^{k} T^*M)$ written locally as
$$\omega = \sum \omega_{i_1\dots i_k}\, dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k},$$
the local expressions
$$J^{\pm}(\omega) \;=\; :\!\omega_{i_1\dots i_k}\,e^{\pm}_{i_1}\cdots e^{\pm}_{i_k}\!: \;+\; (\text{correction terms}),$$
where the correction terms are normally ordered polynomials whose coefficients are given by Bessel-polynomial numbers and involve contractions of $g^{ij}$ with $\Gamma^{l}_{jk}\,\partial\gamma^{m}$ insertions, one such correction being inserted for every increase of two in the form-degree, so that on overlaps of charts the local pieces glue to globally defined sections of $\Omega^{ch}_M$, yielding two embeddings of sheaves of graded vector spaces
$$\bigwedge^{\bullet} T^*M \;\hookrightarrow\; \Omega^{ch}_M,\qquad \omega \mapsto J^{\pm}(\omega).$$

Problem: Provide an intrinsic geometric (coordinate-free) characterization of the maps $\omega \mapsto J^{\pm}(\omega)$. In particular, identify a natural construction—formulated solely in terms of $(M,g)$, the Levi-Civita connection, and the canonical structures of the chiral de Rham complex (such as its $N=1$ or $N=2$ supersymmetric vertex algebra structure, the de Rham/Dirac-type currents, or related geometric operators)—that produces the global sections $J^{\pm}(\omega)$ from $\omega$ without recourse to the explicit local formulas with Bessel-polynomial coefficients and $\Gamma^{l}_{jk} g^{jk}\partial\gamma^{l}$ correction terms.

The literature on the chiral de Rham complex (Ekstrand–Heluani–Källén–Zabzine and subsequent work) shows that on Riemannian manifolds an N=1 superconformal structure exists locally, and in special holonomy cases (Calabi–Yau, hyperkähler, G2) two commuting copies of various superconformal algebras have been constructed on global sections. Let $M$ be a smooth compact 7-manifold with holonomy group contained in $G_2$. Associated to $M$ is the smooth chiral de Rham complex $\Omega^{ch}(M)$, a sheaf of topological vertex algebras with a conformal grading by $L_0$-eigenvalues whose space of global sections $H = \Gamma(M, \Omega^{ch}(M))$ carries the action of an extended chiral algebra associated with $G_2$ holonomy. In particular, $H$ admits a distinguished odd "BRST-type" operator $Q^-_0$ with $(Q^-_0)^2 = 0$ and two commuting Virasoro fields $T^+$ and $X^+$ whose zero modes $L^+_0, X^+_0$ commute with $Q^-_0$.

Suppose one constructs the cohomology $\mathcal{H}(M) := H(H, Q^-_0)$ in such a way that each $L^+_0$-conformal-weight subspace of $\mathcal{H}(M)$ is finite-dimensional. Define the formal series
$$\chi_M(\tau) = q^{-21/48}\,\mathrm{str}_{\mathcal{H}(M)}\, q^{L^+_0}, \qquad q = e^{2\pi i \tau},$$
where $\mathrm{str}$ is the supertrace with respect to the fermionic grading, and the two-variable refinement
$$\chi_M(\tau, z) = q^{-21/48}\,\mathrm{str}_{\mathcal{H}(M)}\, q^{L^+_0} y^{X^+_0}, \qquad y = e^{2\pi i z},$$
obtained from the joint eigenspace decomposition under $L^+_0$ and $X^+_0$.

Determine $\chi_M(\tau)$ (and $\chi_M(\tau,z)$) explicitly in terms of topological invariants of $M$. Establish whether $\chi_M$ provides a $G_2$-analog of the elliptic genus, whether the series converges on the upper half plane $\{\Im\tau > 0\}$, and whether it possesses modular transformation properties under an appropriate subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ (or, in the two-variable case, suitable Jacobi-modular properties).

Let $M$ be a smooth compact $8$-dimensional manifold with holonomy group $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$, and let $\Omega^{ch}_M$ denote its chiral de Rham complex, viewed as a sheaf of vertex superalgebras whose space of global sections (using a smooth model) is $C^\infty(M,\Omega^{ch}_M)$. Assume that the parallel $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$-invariant 4-form on $M$ induces, inside this vertex superalgebra, an action of the Shatashvili–Vafa $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ superconformal vertex algebra $\mathcal{SV}^{\mathrm{Spin}(7)}$, generated by the Virasoro field $L$, an $N=1$ supercurrent, and the additional currents associated with the $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ structure. Let $Q^-_0$ be the zero mode of the BRST current arising from the topological twist of the left-moving $\mathcal{SV}^{\mathrm{Spin}(7)}$ algebra (the standard $A$-type twist analogue for the Shatashvili–Vafa $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ algebra), so that $(Q^-_0)^2 = 0$, and form the cohomology
$$H\bigl(C^\infty(M,\Omega^{ch}_M),\,Q^-_0\bigr).$$
Let $c$ denote the central charge of the left-moving copy of $\mathcal{SV}^{\mathrm{Spin}(7)}$ and let $L_0$ be the energy operator. Decide whether the following statements hold:
(a) The graded dimension
$$\mathrm{tr}_{H(C^\infty(M,\Omega^{ch}_M),\,Q^-_0)}\, q^{L_0 - c/24}$$
is well-defined, i.e.\ each conformal-weight eigenspace of $H(C^\infty(M,\Omega^{ch}_M),\,Q^-_0)$ is finite-dimensional.
(b) This graded dimension equals the elliptic genus of $M$.

Consider a magnetized plasma described on large (inertial-range) scales by the equations of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD): for a single-fluid plasma with mass density ρ, velocity field u, magnetic field B, and pressure p, the equations are

  ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρu) = 0,
  ρ(∂u/∂t + u·∇u) = −∇p + (1/μ₀)(∇×B)×B,
  ∂B/∂t = ∇×(u×B) + η∇²B,
  ∇·B = 0,

together with an equation of state. Turbulence in this regime exhibits a power-law inertial-range cascade. At small scales comparable to the ion Larmor radius r_L = v_⊥/Ω_i (with Ω_i = qB/m_i the ion gyrofrequency) or the ion inertial length d_i = c/ω_pi (with ω_pi the ion plasma frequency), the fluid description fails and kinetic effects governed by the Vlasov–Maxwell system

  ∂f_s/∂t + v·∇f_s + (q_s/m_s)(E + v×B)·∇_v f_s = (∂f_s/∂t)_coll,
  ∇×E = −∂B/∂t,  ∇×B = μ₀ J + (1/c²) ∂E/∂t,

become necessary. Additional complications include: (i) magnetic reconnection events that require at least an approximate treatment of electron-scale physics (e.g. electron inertia, pressure-tensor terms, or Hall MHD with electron contributions); (ii) regions such as the outer heliosphere where collisions are negligible, invalidating closure assumptions of fluid models; and (iii) pickup ions (e.g. from charge exchange with interstellar neutrals) that produce non-Maxwellian, energetically dominant distribution components f_pui(v).

Problem. Construct a mathematical model—either as a hybrid fluid–kinetic system, a reduced gyrokinetic/kinetic-MHD model, or a multi-fluid model with appropriate non-Maxwellian closures—that:

  (a) reduces to standard MHD on scales ≫ max(r_L, d_i);
  (b) captures the transition from the inertial range into the dissipation range across scales ∼ r_L and ∼ d_i, predicting the spectral shape and dissipation mechanism in that range;
  (c) admits magnetic reconnection with electron-scale physics retained at least approximately;
  (d) remains valid in collisionless regimes; and
  (e) self-consistently incorporates an energetically significant non-Maxwellian pickup-ion population.

Prove well-posedness of the resulting system in a suitable functional setting, and identify the conserved quantities, dissipation operators, and predicted energy spectra that connect the MHD inertial range to the kinetic dissipation range.

Consider a collisionless, low-beta (plasma beta β ≪ 1) magnetized plasma intended to model conditions in the solar corona, consisting of protons and electrons in a background magnetic field B₀. Let proton cyclotron (ion-cyclotron) waves propagate (quasi-)parallel to B₀ at frequencies near the proton gyrofrequency Ω_p = eB₀/m_p c. Linear Vlasov–Maxwell theory applied to a Maxwellian proton distribution predicts a cyclotron-resonant damping rate γ_lin > 0 due to wave–particle interaction at the resonance v_∥ = (ω − Ω_p)/k_∥.

Develop a rigorous nonlinear or coarse-grained fluid/kinetic treatment of resonant wave–particle interaction for this system (for example, by including finite-amplitude trapping, quasilinear plateau formation along curved diffusion shells in velocity space, or a coarse-grained fluid closure that retains the dominant resonant physics), and determine whether the effective damping rate γ_eff produced by such a treatment satisfies γ_eff < γ_lin by an amount sufficient to make the wave-energy decay length L_eff = v_g / γ_eff comparable to or larger than the coronal heating scale heights of interest.

The problem is: prove or disprove that nonlinear or coarse-grained treatments of cyclotron-resonant wave–particle interaction in such low-beta plasmas yield a sufficiently reduced effective damping rate that proton cyclotron waves can persist in the solar corona over scales substantially exceeding those predicted by linear theory, thereby requiring a quantitative reevaluation of linear ion-cyclotron damping scenarios.

Consider a small unmanned aerial vehicle whose navigation state x_k ∈ R^n (position, velocity, attitude) is estimated at discrete time k by fusing three sensor streams via a state estimator (e.g., an extended Kalman filter):

1. A Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver producing measurements z_k^G = h_G(x_k) + n_k^G, possibly corrupted by an adversarial spoofing signal a_k^G that gradually drives the receiver's pseudorange solution away from truth while remaining within the innovation-gating threshold τ of the estimator.
2. An inertial measurement unit (IMU) providing high-rate measurements z_k^I = h_I(x_k) + b_k + n_k^I with bias b_k and bounded noise; the IMU has accuracy/cost limits typical of small commercial UAVs.
3. A downward- or forward-looking camera providing optical-flow / visual-odometry measurements z_k^V = h_V(x_k, T_k) + n_k^V, where T_k denotes the texture field of the observed terrain. The camera is subject to two adversarial actions: (i) blinding, modeled by setting z_k^V to a saturation value over a chosen interval, and (ii) terrain-texture deception, modeled by replacing T_k with an adversarial field T_k^* that is either spatially homogeneous or periodically modulated, inducing a controllable bias in the optical-flow estimate.

Assume the closed-loop guidance law u_k = π(x̂_k) drives the UAV toward a reference trajectory using the fused estimate x̂_k.

Address the following:
(a) Feasibility. Characterize, in terms of the gating threshold τ, the IMU bias-instability and noise covariance, and the camera frame rate / resolution, the set of admissible adversarial inputs (a_k^G, blinding schedule, T_k^*) that remain undetected by standard innovation-based fault detectors.
(b) Control-loop impact. Derive bounds on the steady-state and transient deviation of the true state x_k from the reference trajectory induced by such admissible attacks, as a function of attack magnitude and duration.
(c) Mitigation. Propose and analyze a detection / resilient-estimation scheme that, under the accuracy and computational constraints of small UAVs, guarantees a quantifiable reduction in the worst-case deviation of (b) against the joint GNSS-spoofing + camera-blinding + texture-deception attack model.

Provide rigorous feasibility conditions, performance bounds, and mitigation guarantees.

Let M be a smooth manifold of special holonomy (Calabi–Yau, hyperkähler, Spin(7), or G2), and let Ω_ch(M) denote its chiral de Rham complex, the sheaf of vertex superalgebras canonically associated to M. It is known that, depending on the holonomy of M, the vertex algebra of global sections of Ω_ch(M) (or an appropriate variant) contains a copy of one of the following superconformal W-algebras, embedded by an explicit geometric construction using local frames and the metric:

- the N = 2 superconformal algebra (Calabi–Yau case),
- the (small) N = 4 superconformal algebra (hyperkähler case),
- the Shatashvili–Vafa Spin(7) algebra SV^{Spin(7)} (Spin(7) case),
- the Shatashvili–Vafa G2 algebra SV^{G2} (G2 case).

Each of these algebras can independently be realized as a quantum Hamiltonian reduction W_k(g, f) of an affine vertex algebra of a simple Lie superalgebra g at a suitable level k, with respect to a nilpotent (or odd nilpotent) element f, computed as the cohomology of an explicit BRST complex C^•(g, f).

Question. Does there exist a morphism of complexes (of vertex superalgebras)
Φ : C^•(g, f) ⟶ Ω_ch(M),
or, more generally, a morphism from C^•(g, f) into a resolution of Ω_ch(M), such that the induced map on cohomology W_k(g, f) → Ω_ch(M) recovers, in each of the four cases above, exactly the geometric embedding of the corresponding superconformal W-algebra into Ω_ch(M)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

A search reveals work connecting BRST/Hamiltonian reduction to chiral algebras (e.g., the BRST reduction of the chiral Hecke algebra) and confirms that the superconformal algebras inside the chiral de Rham complex of special-holonomy manifolds are W-algebras, but no construction of these embeddings as direct Hamiltonian reductions of an affine vertex algebra into Ω_ch(M) (or a resolution) appears in the literature. The solar chromosphere has temperatures of order a few thousand kelvin, yet the overlying solar corona reaches temperatures in excess of 10^6 K, and a fast solar wind (with speeds of roughly 700–800 km/s near 1 AU) emerges from coronal holes. Standard fluid (hydrodynamic) models of the corona and solar wind, based purely on thermal conduction and pressure gradients, cannot reproduce these observed temperatures and outflow speeds without invoking additional, extended sources of energy and momentum deposition.

Identify and quantitatively characterize the physical mechanism(s) responsible for:

(a) heating the plasma from chromospheric temperatures (~10^3–10^4 K) to coronal temperatures (>10^6 K) against radiative and conductive losses, and

(b) accelerating the solar wind, in particular the fast wind streams above coronal holes, determining its asymptotic speed, temperature, and species-dependent properties (ion vs. electron temperatures, temperature anisotropies, differential streaming).

Specifically, determine which of the candidate mechanisms—including but not limited to (i) damping of Alfvén waves and turbulent cascades of MHD/kinetic Alfvén waves, (ii) magnetic reconnection events (nanoflares, jets, interchange reconnection at coronal-hole boundaries), and (iii) velocity filtration of suprathermal particle distributions—operates, in what proportions, and on what spatial and temporal scales, in a way consistent with all observational constraints (spectroscopic line widths and intensities, in situ plasma and field measurements, particle distribution functions) and theoretical requirements (energy budget, wave generation and dissipation rates, plasma stability).

The coronal heating and solar wind acceleration problem remains an active open question in space plasma physics. Recent Parker Solar Probe results (including 2025 work on a "helicity barrier" in Alfvénic turbulence and on ambipolar-electric-potential-driven acceleration) provide significant new evidence and partial mechanisms, but no single mechanism has been established as the complete explanation, and multiple candidate mechanisms (Alfvén-wave/turbulence damping, reconnection-driven heating, kinetic effects) continue to be investigated.

Consider the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) description of the solar corona, in which the plasma is governed by the ideal/resistive MHD equations coupled to Maxwell's equations, together with a kinetic (Vlasov–Maxwell) description of suprathermal electrons near collisionless shock waves. A coronal mass ejection (CME) is a large-scale eruption of magnetized plasma that detaches from the low corona and propagates into the heliosphere, eventually merging with the ambient solar wind (a continuously expanding plasma outflow from the Sun). A type II solar radio burst is slowly drifting radio emission, observed at a fundamental frequency near the local electron plasma frequency f_p = (1/2π)√(n_e e²/ε₀ m_e) and at its second harmonic 2f_p, produced in association with a collisionless MHD shock wave driven by a CME or flare.

Address the following:

(a) Geometry and evolution of CMEs. Provide a quantitative model of the three-dimensional magnetic and density structure of a coronal mass ejection (e.g., as a flux rope, spheromak, or other topology) and determine, from first-principles MHD, the mechanism and trajectory by which such a structure detaches from the closed coronal magnetic field, escapes the corona, and evolves dynamically into a self-similar or steady-state structure embedded in the ambient solar wind.

(b) Electron acceleration in type II bursts. For a collisionless fast-mode shock with upstream magnetic field B, density n_e, and shock normal angle θ_Bn, determine the spatial region — upstream foreshock, shock ramp, or downstream — in which the suprathermal electron beams responsible for type II radio emission are accelerated, and characterize the acceleration mechanism (e.g., shock drift acceleration, diffusive shock acceleration, or stochastic acceleration).

(c) Radio emission sites. Within the same shock geometry, determine the spatial locations at which the fundamental (near f_p) and second-harmonic (near 2f_p) electromagnetic emissions are generated via plasma-emission processes (Langmuir-wave excitation followed by linear mode conversion and/or nonlinear three-wave coupling L + L' → T at 2f_p and L + S → T at f_p), and predict the resulting source separation and frequency-band ratio.

CME initiation, three-dimensional geometry, and coupling to the solar wind remain active areas of research, with no consensus model; likewise, the precise acceleration site of energetic electrons relative to CME-driven shocks and the location of fundamental vs. harmonic plasma emission in type II bursts are still debated in current heliophysics literature (recent reviews and Parker Solar Probe / Solar Orbiter studies continue to investigate these questions).

Consider an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) modeled as a discrete-time control system equipped with: (i) a communications link L to a ground controller, (ii) a sensor suite S = (s_1, ..., s_n) producing measurements that feed a fault-detection function F : (history of L and S) → {none, temporary, persistent, fatal}, and (iii) a fail-safe policy π that maps detected fault classes to actions: π(temporary) = hover-in-place, π(persistent) = return-to-base, π(fatal) = self-destruct. An adversary is allowed to (a) jam or delay messages on L for arbitrary intervals, and (b) inject bounded but otherwise arbitrary perturbations into a chosen subset of the sensor channels (sensory spoofing), subject to known physical/sensor consistency constraints.

Design the pair (F, π), together with any necessary cryptographic, redundancy-based, or cross-validation mechanisms, such that the following manipulation-resistance properties hold simultaneously:

1. (Soundness under attack) For every admissible adversarial strategy, the probability that F outputs "fatal" when no genuine fatal condition (capture or imminent crash) holds is at most ε_f, and the probability that F outputs "persistent" or "temporary" without a genuine corresponding fault is at most ε_p, ε_t respectively.

2. (Liveness) In the absence of attack, F correctly identifies each genuine fault class within a bounded detection delay Δ.

3. (Exploit resistance) There is no admissible adversarial strategy that, by jamming L or perturbing S within the allowed bounds, can force the UAV into hover-in-place, return-to-base, or self-destruct with probability exceeding the bounds in (1), thereby preventing the adversary from using fail-safe activation as a means to immobilize, redirect, or destroy the UAV.

Formulate a rigorous adversary model, the set of admissible attacks, and the precise meaning of (1)–(3), and either construct (F, π) achieving these guarantees with explicit bounds (ε_f, ε_p, ε_t, Δ), or prove an impossibility result identifying the fundamental tradeoff between detection delay Δ and the achievable false-trigger probabilities under jamming and sensor spoofing.

The problem of designing UAV fault-handling and fail-safe logic that is provably resilient against communications jamming and sensor spoofing is widely recognized as an open research direction in cyber-physical UAS security. While various partial mitigations (encrypted/authenticated links, GPS anti-spoofing, multi-sensor fusion, attack-resilient state estimation) have been proposed, no general framework providing the soundness/liveness/exploit-resistance guarantees described is established in the literature.

Consider a two-species Bose gas in three dimensions described by N_1 bosons of species 1 and N_2 bosons of species 2 with N_1, N_2 → ∞ and N_1/N_2 → c ∈ (0,∞). The Hamiltonian on L^2_sym(ℝ^{3N_1}) ⊗ L^2_sym(ℝ^{3N_2}) is

H_{N_1,N_2} = −∑_{i=1}^{N_1} Δ_{x_i}/(2m_1) − ∑_{j=1}^{N_2} Δ_{y_j}/(2m_2)
 + ∑_{i<i'} N_1^2 V_{11}(N_1(x_i − x_{i'}))
 + ∑_{j<j'} N_2^2 V_{22}(N_2(y_j − y_{j'}))
 + ∑_{i,j} N^2 V_{12}(N(x_i − y_j)),

where N = N_1 + N_2 and the interaction potentials V_{11}, V_{22}, V_{12}: ℝ^3 → ℝ are spherically symmetric and compactly supported (the genuine Gross–Pitaevskii scaling, in which each pair interaction is rescaled by its own particle-number factor so that the effective scattering length is of order 1/N).

Under the additional hypothesis that V_{11}, V_{22}, V_{12} are pointwise non-negative, persistence of two-component Bose–Einstein condensation along the dynamics generated by H_{N_1,N_2} is known: if the initial state is asymptotically a product of two condensates with one-particle orbitals φ_0, ψ_0 ∈ H^1(ℝ^3), then for every t the reduced one-particle density matrices γ^{(1)}_{N_k}(t) of species k = 1,2 converge in trace norm to |φ_t⟩⟨φ_t| and |ψ_t⟩⟨ψ_t|, where (φ_t, ψ_t) solve the coupled Gross–Pitaevskii system

i ∂_t φ_t = −Δφ_t/(2m_1) + 8π a_{11} |φ_t|^2 φ_t + 4π a_{12}(1 + m_1/m_2) |ψ_t|^2 φ_t,
i ∂_t ψ_t = −Δψ_t/(2m_2) + 8π a_{22} |ψ_t|^2 ψ_t + 4π a_{12}(1 + m_2/m_1) |φ_t|^2 ψ_t,

with a_{αβ} the s-wave scattering lengths of V_{αβ}.

Question: Can the non-negativity hypothesis on V_{11}, V_{22}, V_{12} be removed while remaining at the true Gross–Pitaevskii scaling above (i.e., allowing the potentials to take negative values, subject only to suitable stability and regularity conditions ensuring well-posedness), so that persistence of two-component condensation and convergence to the coupled Gross–Pitaevskii system still hold?

For the single-species Gross–Pitaevskii limit, the positivity assumption on the interaction has been removed only in softer (mean-field-like) scaling regimes, while removal at the true GP scaling is still cited as an important open problem. Recent work on the two-component Gross–Pitaevskii equation (e.g., quantitative derivation in the hard-core limit, 2025) does not relax the non-negativity assumption at the genuine GP scaling for the binary Bose gas. No source confirming a derivation without positivity at the true two-component GP scaling was found.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Multiple recent observational and theoretical studies (Parker Solar Probe analyses, Helios–Voyager comparisons, and dedicated MHD turbulence studies) corroborate that outward-propagating Alfvénic fluctuations originate near the Sun and undergo radial dynamical evolution driven by velocity shear between fast and slow streams, stream interaction regions, and proximity to the heliospheric current sheet, where weakened radial magnetic field and transverse gradients reduce Alfvénicity. Shear-driven (Kelvin–Helmholtz-like) nonlinear couplings beyond the Alfvén critical zone are recognized as boosting low-frequency turbulence to observed heliospheric levels. The mechanism is regarded as essentially understood.

Consider a network of highly mobile airborne nodes communicating over wireless links. Each node is equipped with an adaptive radio that, at each time step t = 0, 1, 2, ..., must select a physical-layer configuration

  a_t = (P_t, f_t, m_t, A_t) ∈ 𝒜,

consisting of a transmit power P_t, a carrier frequency f_t, a modulation scheme m_t, and an antenna configuration A_t, drawn from a finite or compact set 𝒜 of admissible configurations. The selection at time t is made on the basis of an environmental observation s_t ∈ 𝒮 (e.g., measured spectrum occupancy, interference, channel quality, geometry). The true environment state x_t ∈ 𝒳 evolves according to an unknown, possibly non-stationary process, and the observation is produced by

  s_t = h(x_t) + e_t,

where e_t is an adversarial perturbation chosen by an attacker who knows the policy π : 𝒮 → 𝒜 and aims to drive the radio into configurations that minimize a communication utility U(a_t, x_t) (e.g., throughput, link reliability, or jam-resistance). Impose the following operational constraints:

(i) Rapid channel variation: the environment x_t can change significantly between consecutive decision epochs, so any window over which a "normal" baseline could be estimated for anomaly detection has length at most W, where W is too small for classical statistical change-point or outlier detection to achieve a prescribed false-alarm/missed-detection trade-off.

(ii) Low-overhead requirement: the policy π must be computable using at most B bits of side information per decision and incur at most a fraction ρ of the link capacity for control/redundancy traffic, with B and ρ small.

(iii) Hostile deployment: real-time collaborative sensing among nodes is limited; each node may exchange messages with at most k neighbors per epoch, and any subset of up to c nodes may be compromised and report arbitrary values.

Problem. Design a decision rule π : 𝒮 → 𝒜 (possibly randomized and history-dependent) and prove guarantees of the following form: for every adversary strategy producing perturbations {e_t} subject to a budget ‖e_t‖ ≤ ε, and for every admissible environment trajectory {x_t},

  (1/T) Σ_{t=1}^T 𝔼[U(π(s_t), x_t)]  ≥  U* − g(ε, W, B, ρ, k, c, T),

where U* = sup_{a∈𝒜} (1/T) Σ_t U(a, x_t) is the best fixed-configuration utility in hindsight and g is an explicit function tending to 0 as the constraints relax. Equivalently, characterize the optimal trade-off between robustness to adversarial environmental inputs and the constraints (i)–(iii), and exhibit a concrete adaptive-radio algorithm achieving it for UAS-like airborne networks, where cognitive-radio-style anomaly detection and distributed-sensing countermeasures fail to provide such a guarantee.

Consider a system of $N$ identical bosons in $\mathbb{R}^3$ described by the Hamiltonian
$$H_N = \sum_{j=1}^{N} (-\Delta_{x_j}) + \sum_{1 \le i < j \le N} N^2 V(N(x_i - x_j)),$$
acting on the symmetric subspace of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^{3N})$, where $V \ge 0$ is a sufficiently regular, compactly supported, spherically symmetric two-body potential, and let $a > 0$ denote the scattering length of $V$ (so that $N^2 V(N\,\cdot)$ is the Gross-Pitaevskii scaling). Let $\psi_{N,t} = e^{-iH_N t}\psi_{N,0}$ denote the many-body Schrödinger evolution starting from an initial state $\psi_{N,0}$ exhibiting complete Bose-Einstein condensation into a one-particle wave function $\varphi_0 \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^3)$ with $\|\varphi_0\|_{L^2} = 1$, in the sense that the one-particle reduced density matrix $\gamma_{N,0}^{(1)}$ satisfies $\gamma_{N,0}^{(1)} \to |\varphi_0\rangle\langle\varphi_0|$ as $N \to \infty$.

Prove that for every fixed $t \in \mathbb{R}$ the one-particle reduced density matrix $\gamma_{N,t}^{(1)}$ of $\psi_{N,t}$ converges, as $N \to \infty$, to $|u_t\rangle\langle u_t|$, where $u_t$ is the solution of the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger (Gross-Pitaevskii) equation
$$i\partial_t u_t = -\Delta u_t + 8\pi a\, |u_t|^2 u_t, \qquad u_{t=0} = \varphi_0.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The rigorous derivation of the cubic Gross-Pitaevskii equation from many-body bosonic quantum dynamics in the Gross-Pitaevskii scaling was solved by Erdős, Schlein, and Yau (2006–2010) using the BBGKY hierarchy. Subsequent work by Pickl, Benedikter–de Oliveira–Schlein, and others provided alternative proofs and explicit convergence rates. The problem is considered solved.

Consider a network of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) operating as a formation in three-dimensional space. Each UAV $i$ has a position $p_i(t)\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and an attitude (orientation) described by a rotation $R_i(t)\in SO(3)$ encoding roll, pitch, and yaw. Each UAV carries a finite set of fixed directional antennas; antenna $a$ on UAV $i$ has a body-frame boresight direction $u_{i,a}\in S^2$ and a beam pattern $G_{i,a}:S^2\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. The set of essential radio links $\mathcal{L}$ includes air-to-ground (ATG) links to fixed ground stations $g_k\in\mathbb{R}^3$ as well as air-to-air links between UAVs. A link $\ell=(i,a)\to(j,b)$ is considered functional at time $t$ only if the relative geometry satisfies a connectivity predicate
$$C_\ell(p_i,R_i,p_j,R_j)=\big[\,G_{i,a}(R_i^{-1}\hat d_{ij})\cdot G_{j,b}(R_j^{-1}\hat d_{ji}) \ge \tau_\ell\,\big],$$
where $\hat d_{ij}$ is the unit vector from $i$ to $j$ and $\tau_\ell>0$ a threshold. Certain attitudes (e.g., a half-roll or a steep climb) cause $C_\ell=0$ for the ATG link because the ground-pointing antenna no longer faces the ground station.

An adversary employs a jammer whose position and power can be adapted over time. The defenders use a spatial-retreat policy $\pi$: a (possibly randomized) feedback map from the observed jamming signal history to a target reformation $(p_i'(t),R_i'(t))_i$. The adversary observes the resulting motion and attitude responses and may adapt its jamming strategy to drive the formation into attitudes for which $C_\ell=0$ on essential links.

Formulate and solve the following: design a class of spatial-retreat policies $\pi$ for UAV formations with fixed antenna placements such that, for every adaptive adversary strategy in a specified class, the expected fraction of time during which all essential links in $\mathcal{L}$ remain functional is maximized (or stays above a guaranteed threshold). In particular, characterize necessary and sufficient conditions on the antenna geometry $\{u_{i,a},G_{i,a}\}$, the formation kinematic constraints, and the policy $\pi$ under which no observation-based adversary can force the reformation into attitudes that break ATG or other essential links, and provide constructive policies achieving these guarantees.

Consider a high-mobility wireless network of N mobile nodes (e.g., aerial vehicles) modeled as a time-varying graph G(t) = (V, E(t)) on a node set V with |V| = N, in which each directed edge (u,v) ∈ E(t) carries packet traffic with a per-hop forwarding delay D_{uv}(t). An external passive adversary observes only the times and locations of transmissions (not their contents) and attempts to reconstruct E(t) by a timing-analysis / correlation attack: for each ordered pair (u,v), the adversary computes a statistic such as the cross-correlation of the transmission point processes at u and v across a small candidate delay window, and declares (u,v) ∈ Ê(t) when the statistic exceeds a threshold τ. The defender may employ three combinable countermeasures:

(i) Delay randomization: at each forwarding hop, add an independent random delay X_{uv} drawn from a distribution F supported on [0, Δ_max], subject to an end-to-end latency constraint E[Σ X] ≤ L on every routed path.

(ii) Decoy transmissions: each node u may emit additional dummy packets according to an independent point process N_u^{decoy} with rate λ_u^{decoy}, contributing an aggregate bandwidth/energy overhead B = Σ_u c_u λ_u^{decoy}.

(iii) Topology control: the defender chooses node positions / transmission powers so that, jointly with the decoy schedule, the observable spatial-temporal traffic distribution {(t_i, x_i)} appears statistically homogeneous over the deployment region to the adversary, inducing artificial correlations between all node pairs.

Let A(F, {λ_u^{decoy}}, topology) denote the adversary's edge-recovery accuracy (e.g., F1-score of Ê(t) versus E(t)).

Determine, under the latency budget L, decoy-overhead budget B, and mobility constraints:
(a) Feasibility: characterize necessary and sufficient conditions on (L, B, N, mobility model) under which there exists a defense strategy achieving A ≤ ε for a prescribed ε > 0.
(b) Overhead: derive tight lower and upper bounds on the minimum decoy rate Σ λ_u^{decoy} (and bandwidth/energy) needed to guarantee A ≤ ε.
(c) Optimal implementation: identify the joint distribution F*, decoy intensities {λ_u^{decoy*}}, and topology-control rule that minimize A subject to the latency and overhead constraints, and quantify the resulting trade-off curve between A, L, and B.

Consider an Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) network modeled as a time-varying directed graph G(t) = (V, E(t)) whose vertices are airborne nodes and whose edges represent wireless links with limited bandwidth and stringent end-to-end latency constraints. A set of flows F = {(s_i, d_i, r_i, L_i)} is to be routed, where (s_i, d_i) is a source–destination pair, r_i is a required throughput, and L_i is a maximum tolerable end-to-end delay. A passive global adversary observes per-link traffic patterns (timing, volume, and direction of packets) and attempts to infer (i) which packets belong to a common flow and (ii) the source–destination pair of each flow; formally, the adversary outputs a posterior distribution over flow assignments and over (s, d) pairs given its observations.

Routing-layer defenses are modeled by augmenting any feasible multi-flow routing R with two mechanisms:
1. Mixing: at selected relay nodes, packets from different flows are batched, reordered, and possibly delayed by up to τ before forwarding;
2. Decoy transmissions: dummy packets are injected along chosen paths at rate ρ to obscure traffic patterns.

Let A(R, τ, ρ) denote the adversary's advantage, defined as the total-variation distance between its posterior on (flow, source-destination) assignments and the uniform prior. Let C(R, τ, ρ) denote the induced cost, including added latency, bandwidth overhead, and energy.

Address the following:
(a) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on G(t), F, and the per-link capacity/latency budgets under which there exists a defense (R, τ, ρ) satisfying A(R, τ, ρ) ≤ ε while every flow meets its throughput r_i and delay L_i (feasibility).
(b) Characterize the Pareto frontier of (A, C) and design a defense (R*, τ*, ρ*) that minimizes C subject to A ≤ ε and all flow QoS constraints; equivalently, solve

   min_{R, τ, ρ}  C(R, τ, ρ)   s.t.   A(R, τ, ρ) ≤ ε,  end-to-end delay of flow i ≤ L_i,  throughput of flow i ≥ r_i  for all i.

(c) Provide tight lower bounds on the unavoidable overhead C as a function of ε, the network topology, and the flow set, and exhibit defenses achieving these bounds (or show they cannot be achieved).

Let $M$ be a smooth compact Riemannian manifold of special holonomy (for instance with holonomy contained in $G_2$, $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$, or more generally one of the entries of Berger's list other than the $\mathrm{SU}(n)$/Calabi–Yau case) and let $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$ denote the smooth ($C^\infty$) chiral de Rham complex of $M$, viewed as a sheaf of $N=1$ topological vertex superalgebras on $M$.

Carry out, or determine whether one can carry out, the following construction:

(1) Construct on $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$ two commuting superconformal vertex algebra structures (a "left-moving" and a "right-moving" copy) extending the standard $N=1$ structure, where the extended algebra on each side is the superconformal algebra associated to the holonomy group of $M$ (e.g. the Shatashvili–Vafa $G_2$ algebra in the $G_2$ case, or the analogous $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ algebra).

(2) Take the space of global sections $\Gamma(M,\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M)$ (rather than sheaf cohomology) and then take BRST cohomology with respect to a chosen nilpotent BRST current built from the left-moving superconformal structure, obtaining a $\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$-graded vertex operator superalgebra $H_M$ whose conformal-weight homogeneous components are finite dimensional.

(3) Decompose $H_M$, and its graded dimension (super)trace

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold and let $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}(M)$ denote its smooth chiral de Rham complex, the sheaf of vertex superalgebras built locally from the bc–βγ system whose generators in a coordinate chart are bosonic fields $b^i, a_i$ and fermionic fields $\phi^i, \psi_i$ (with $i=1,\dots,\dim M$). On flat space the standard Boson–Fermion superconformal algebra contains odd generators
$$G^+_{\text{flat}} = \psi_i \partial b^i, \qquad G^-_{\text{flat}} = \phi^i a_i .$$
For a general Riemannian metric $g_{ij}$ with inverse $g^{ij}$ and Levi-Civita Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^k_{ij}$, define local odd sections $G^\pm$ on a coordinate chart by adding to the flat expressions correction terms involving $g_{ij}$, $g^{ij}$, $\Gamma^k_{ij}$, and a cubic fermionic term, in the standard way that produces an $N=2$-type pair of supercurrents at the level of formal local generators.

Question: Determine a topological or geometric invariant of $(M,g)$ (a characteristic class or curvature-type obstruction on $M$) whose vanishing is a necessary and sufficient condition for the local expressions $G^+$ and $G^-$ to patch together into globally defined sections of $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}(M)$.

Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the set of finite words over $A$, viewed as the infinite rooted prefix tree $T(A)$ in which the root is the empty word $\varepsilon$ and the children of a node $u\in A^*$ are the words $ua$ for $a\in A$. For a (finite or infinite) word $w$ over $A$, let $\mathrm{Pref}(w)\subseteq A^*$ denote the set of all prefixes of $w$ (including $\varepsilon$). Given a family $\mathcal{W}$ of words, the subtree of $T(A)$ generated by $\mathcal{W}$ is defined as the subtree
$$S(\mathcal{W}) \;=\; \bigcup_{w\in\mathcal{W}} \mathrm{Pref}(w),$$
endowed with the induced tree structure from $T(A)$. For a single word $w$, write $S(w):=S(\{w\})$, and more generally allow constructions in which a word $w$ "generates" an associated subtree of $T(A)$ via a fixed prefix-closure procedure (for instance, the subtree consisting of all prefixes of all conjugates, or all prefixes of all factors, of $w$).

Question: Does there exist a sequence of words $(w_n)_{n\ge 1}$ over a fixed finite alphabet $A$, with $|A|\ge 2$, such that the subtree generated by each $w_n$ is finite, but the size (number of nodes) of the subtree generated by $w_n$ tends to infinity as $n\to\infty$? Equivalently: can words generate arbitrarily large finite subtrees of the prefix tree?

Let $M$ be a smooth $7$-manifold equipped with a torsion-free $G_2$-structure (i.e., a Riemannian metric with holonomy contained in $G_2$). Let $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$ denote the smooth chiral de Rham complex on $M$, viewed as a sheaf of $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$-graded (by conformal weight) topological vertex algebras whose weight-zero part recovers the ordinary de Rham complex of $M$. Recall that on Calabi–Yau manifolds (where the holonomy is contained in $SU(n)$, giving an $N=2$ superconformal structure) and on hyperkähler manifolds (giving an $N=4$ structure), one can define a "half-twist" BRST differential $Q^-_0$ on $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$ whose cohomology sheaf and whose cohomology on global sections both have finite-dimensional conformal-weight spaces.

On a $G_2$-manifold $M$, the vertex algebra of smooth global sections $C^\infty(M,\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M)$ has infinite-dimensional conformal-weight spaces. The Shatashvili–Vafa $G_2$ superconformal algebra acts on $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$, providing a natural analogue of the supersymmetry data used in the $N=2$ and $N=4$ cases.

Question: Does there exist an odd derivation (BRST-type differential) $Q^-_0$ on $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$, analogous to the half-twist differential of the Calabi–Yau and hyperkähler cases, such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item the cohomology sheaf $H(\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M, Q^-_0)$ has finite-dimensional conformal-weight spaces, and
\item the cohomology $H(C^\infty(M,\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M), Q^-_0)$ of the vertex algebra of global sections also has finite-dimensional conformal-weight spaces?
\end{enumerate}

Let $M$ be a closed 7-dimensional Riemannian manifold with holonomy group $G_2$, equipped with its parallel $G_2$-invariant 3-form $\varphi$ and its Hodge dual 4-form $\psi=\ast\varphi$. Let $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$ denote the chiral de Rham complex of $M$, viewed as a sheaf of $N=1$ superconformal vertex algebras whose space of global sections $V(M)=H^0(M,\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M)$ carries a natural $N=1$ superconformal structure of central charge $c=21/2$.

The Shatashvili–Vafa $G_2$ superconformal algebra $\mathrm{SV}^{G_2}$ is the $N=1$ vertex algebra at central charge $c=21/2$ generated by the Virasoro field $L$, its superpartner $G$, a primary field $\Phi$ of conformal weight $3/2$ (the bosonic $G_2$ field) and its superpartner $X$ of weight $2$, subject to the Shatashvili–Vafa OPE relations.

Rodriguez's theorem provides two distinguished sections $\Phi^{\pm}\in V(M)$, built from $\varphi$ and $\psi$, that generate two mutually commuting copies $\mathrm{SV}^{G_2}_{\pm}\subset V(M)$ of the Shatashvili–Vafa $G_2$ algebra at $c=21/2$.

Question. Does there exist a fermionic, square-zero, weight-one BRST-type differential $Q^-_0$ on $V(M)$ (canonically associated with the $G_2$-structure on $M$) such that all of the following hold simultaneously?

(a) $[Q^-_0,\,\mathrm{SV}^{G_2}_{+}]=0$, so that one of the two Shatashvili–Vafa copies survives in the cohomology $H^\ast(V(M),Q^-_0)$ as a vertex subalgebra isomorphic to $\mathrm{SV}^{G_2}$.

(b) The cohomology $H^\ast(V(M),Q^-_0)$ decomposes, as a graded $\mathrm{SV}^{G_2}$-module, into a direct sum of irreducible $\mathrm{SV}^{G_2}$-representations:
$$H^\ast(V(M),Q^-_0)\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{\lambda} N_\lambda(M)\otimes L_\lambda,$$
where $\{L_\lambda\}$ is the set of irreducible $\mathrm{SV}^{G_2}$-modules and $N_\lambda(M)$ are the multiplicity spaces.

(c) The generating series of graded dimensions of the multiplicity spaces,
$$Z_M(\tau)\;=\;\sum_{\lambda} \big(\dim_q N_\lambda(M)\big)\,\mathrm{ch}_{L_\lambda}(\tau),$$
or equivalently the formal series $\sum_\lambda \dim_q N_\lambda(M)\cdot e_\lambda$ assembling the multiplicities, is a mock modular form canonically attached to $M$ (consistent with the expectation that $\mathrm{SV}^{G_2}$ characters arise via Hamiltonian reduction of $\widehat{\mathfrak{osp}}(4|2)$ at level $k=1/3$ and are mock modular, while the full character of $H^\ast(V(M),Q^-_0)$ is modular).

abla^{LC}\psi = 0$ for the Levi-Civita connection). Let $\Omega^{ch}_M$ denote the (smooth) chiral de Rham complex of $M$, i.e. the sheaf of topological vertex superalgebras constructed by Malikov–Schechtman–Vaintrob in its smooth/Riemannian incarnation, and let $C^\infty(M, \Omega^{ch}_M)$ be its vertex superalgebra of global sections.

Let $SV^{\mathrm{Spin}(7)}$ denote the Shatashvili–Vafa $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ superconformal vertex algebra: the (unique up to isomorphism) extension of the $N=1$ superconformal vertex algebra at central charge $c=12$ by a primary field of conformal weight $2$ (and its superpartner of weight $5/2$) satisfying the Shatashvili–Vafa OPE relations associated with the $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ four-form.

Prove or disprove the following: there exist two global sections $X^+, X^- \in C^\infty(M, \Omega^{ch}_M)$, naturally associated with the parallel four-form $\psi$, such that the vertex subalgebras generated by $X^+$ and by $X^-$ are each isomorphic to $SV^{\mathrm{Spin}(7)}$ at central charge $c=12$, and such that these two subalgebras commute with each other (i.e. all OPEs between fields of the first and fields of the second are regular).

The analogous conjecture in the $G_2$ case was proven by Ekstrand–Heluani–Källén–Zabzine and subsequent work (e.g. Heluani–Rodríguez Díaz, "G_2 holonomy manifolds are superconformal"). Let $\mathfrak{osp}(3|2)$ denote the basic classical Lie superalgebra of type $B(1,1)$, and consider its affinization $\widehat{\mathfrak{osp}}(3|2)$ at level $k=1/3$. Apply the quantum Hamiltonian reduction (Drinfeld–Sokolov–Kac–Wakimoto reduction) associated to a principal odd nilpotent element of $\mathfrak{osp}(3|2)$ to the affine vertex superalgebra at this level; the resulting $W$-superalgebra is the Shatashvili–Vafa Spin(7) superconformal algebra $\mathcal{SW}(3/2,2)$ at central charge $c=12$, an extension of the $N=1$ superconformal algebra by a primary supercurrent of conformal weight $3/2$ and a primary field of conformal weight $2$.

For an irreducible highest-weight module $L(\lambda)$ over $\widehat{\mathfrak{osp}}(3|2)$ at level $1/3$ with appropriate (admissible) highest weight $\lambda$, let $\chi_{L(\lambda)}(\tau,z)$ denote its (super)character, and let $H(\chi_{L(\lambda)})$ denote the character of the reduced module obtained by applying the Kac–Wakimoto character formula for quantum Hamiltonian reduction (which produces, in general, expressions involving mock theta functions).

On the other side, there is a conjectural list of (super)characters of unitary irreducible highest-weight representations of $\mathcal{SW}(3/2,2)$ at $c=12$ that arises in the decomposition of the elliptic genus of compact eight-dimensional manifolds of Spin(7) holonomy.

Question: Is every conjectural unitary character in this Spin(7) list of the form $H(\chi_{L(\lambda)})$ for some admissible highest weight $\lambda$ of $\widehat{\mathfrak{osp}}(3|2)$ at level $k=1/3$, i.e., are these characters obtained via the Kac–Wakimoto quantum Hamiltonian reduction procedure from characters of $\widehat{\mathfrak{osp}}(3|2)$ at level $1/3$?

Let $M$ be a smooth compact 8-manifold with holonomy group $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$, and let $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$ denote its smooth chiral de Rham complex (the sheaf of vertex algebras introduced by Malikov–Schechtman–Vaintrob, considered with its natural global sections forming a vertex superalgebra). Assume that the conjectural extension of the Shatashvili–Vafa-type construction to the $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ setting endows $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$ with a distinguished Virasoro vertex subalgebra $\mathrm{Vir}_{1/2}$ of central charge $c=1/2$, generated by a chiral analogue of the $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$-invariant Cayley 4-form. Recall that the $c=1/2$ Virasoro vertex operator algebra has exactly three irreducible unitary representations, with lowest conformal weights $0$, $1/16$, and $1/2$, and is itself a unitary rational vertex operator algebra precisely when realized inside an appropriate ambient vertex algebra in which it acts semisimply.

Question: Is the vertex algebra produced by this $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ chiral construction irreducible in such a way that the embedded copy of $\mathrm{Vir}_{1/2}$ is a unitary vertex operator algebra and $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$ decomposes as a direct sum of irreducible $\mathrm{Vir}_{1/2}$-modules (so that the associated topological twist of $\Omega^{\mathrm{ch}}_M$ along this $c=1/2$ minimal model structure is well-defined)?

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional simple Lie superalgebra, $f \in \mathfrak{g}$ a nilpotent even element, and $k \in \mathbb{C}$ a level. Denote by $W^k(\mathfrak{g}, f)$ the affine W-algebra obtained by the quantum Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction of the affine vertex superalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}$ at level $k$ associated to $f$. When $f = f_{\min}$ is a minimal nilpotent, write $W^k_{\min}(\mathfrak{g}) := W^k(\mathfrak{g}, f_{\min})$; when $f = f_{\mathrm{prin}}$ is principal, $W^k(\mathfrak{g}, f_{\mathrm{prin}})$ denotes the (super)principal W-algebra.

Two families of vertex superalgebras arise in connection with Riemannian manifolds of special holonomy:

(A) The supersymmetry algebras acting on the chiral de Rham complex of a manifold with reduced holonomy. Concretely, these are the $N=2$ superconformal algebra (Kähler holonomy $U(n)$), the small $N=4$ superconformal algebra (hyperkähler holonomy $\mathrm{Sp}(n)$), the Shatashvili–Vafa $G_2$ algebra $SV^{G_2}$, and the Shatashvili–Vafa $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ algebra $SV^{\mathrm{Spin}(7)}$. Each of these can be realized as a (super)principal or minimal W-algebra $W^k(\mathfrak{g}, f)$ for an explicit pair $(\mathfrak{g}, f)$ and specific level $k$.

(B) The minimal W-algebras $W^k_{\min}(\mathfrak{g}')$ whose strong generators of low conformal weight reproduce, on a suitable cotangent-fiber representation, the holonomy Lie algebras associated to the same special holonomy groups ($U(n)$, $\mathrm{Sp}(n)$, $G_2$, $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$).

Problem: Determine the precise vertex-algebraic relationship between the family (A) and the family (B). In particular, for each holonomy class, exhibit an explicit homomorphism, embedding, conformal extension, coset, or quantum Hamiltonian reduction relating the corresponding minimal W-algebra in (B) to the supersymmetry algebra in (A) acting on the chiral de Rham complex, and identify the levels for which such a relation holds.

Consider a system of $N$ identical bosons in $\mathbb{R}^3$, each with internal spin degree of freedom $F=1$, so that the one-particle Hilbert space is $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{C}^3)$ and the $N$-body state space is the symmetric tensor product $\bigotimes_{\mathrm{sym}}^N L^2(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{C}^3)$. Let the many-body Hamiltonian have the mean-field form
$$H_N \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^N \big(-\Delta_{x_i} + U(x_i)\big) \;+\; \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}\Big(V_0(x_i-x_j)\,\mathbb{1} \;+\; V_1(x_i-x_j)\,\mathbf{F}_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf{F}_j\Big),$$
where $V_0,V_1:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$ are spatial two-body interactions, $\mathbf{F}=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ are the spin-1 angular momentum matrices acting on $\mathbb{C}^3$, and $\mathbf{F}_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf{F}_j=\sum_{a}F_a^{(i)}F_a^{(j)}$ is the spin–spin coupling. Consider initial states exhibiting complete Bose–Einstein condensation onto a one-particle spinor $\Phi_0=(\phi_{+1,0},\phi_{0,0},\phi_{-1,0})\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{C}^3)$ with $\|\Phi_0\|_{L^2}=1$, in the sense that the one-body reduced density matrix $\gamma_N^{(1)}(0)$ converges to $|\Phi_0\rangle\langle\Phi_0|$ as $N\to\infty$.

Formally, the conjectured effective dynamics is the three-component nonlinear Schrödinger system for $\Phi=(\phi_{+1},\phi_0,\phi_{-1})$,
$$i\partial_t \phi_m \;=\; (-\Delta+U)\phi_m \;+\; (V_0*\rho)\,\phi_m \;+\; \sum_{a\in\{x,y,z\}}\big(V_1*\langle F_a\rangle\big)\,\big(F_a\Phi\big)_m,\qquad m\in\{+1,0,-1\},$$
where $\rho(x)=\sum_m|\phi_m(x)|^2$ and $\langle F_a\rangle(x)=\langle\Phi(x),F_a\Phi(x)\rangle_{\mathbb{C}^3}$, with initial datum $\Phi(0)=\Phi_0$.

Problem. Prove that, under suitable hypotheses on $V_0$, $V_1$, and $U$, for each fixed time $t\ge 0$ the one-body reduced density matrix $\gamma_N^{(1)}(t)$ of the solution of the Schrödinger equation $i\partial_t\Psi_N = H_N\Psi_N$ converges in trace norm, as $N\to\infty$, to $|\Phi(t)\rangle\langle\Phi(t)|$, where $\Phi(t)$ solves the coupled spin-1 system above with initial datum $\Phi_0$. Equivalently, rigorously derive the spin-1 spinor effective nonlinear Schrödinger system from the many-body quantum dynamics in the mean-field limit.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

A rigorous derivation of the effective three-component nonlinear Schrödinger system for spin-1 spinor Bose–Einstein condensates from the many-body quantum dynamics in the mean-field scaling was carried out by Michelangeli and Olgiati (2018, arXiv:1803.05410), who proved convergence of the one-body reduced density matrix to the projection onto the solution of the coupled spinor system, with quantitative bounds. representations.normalized:
Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) is the gauge theory of the strong interaction with gauge group SU(3) and quark matter fields. Its thermodynamic equilibrium states, parametrized by temperature T and baryon chemical potential μ_B, are believed to organize into a phase diagram containing a low-(T,μ_B) hadron-gas phase (color-confined, chiral-symmetry-broken) and a high-(T,μ_B) quark-gluon-plasma phase (deconfined, approximately chirally symmetric). At μ_B = 0 lattice QCD establishes that the transition between these two phases is an analytic crossover. At larger μ_B, in the regime accessible to low- and intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions, the nature of the transition is not rigorously established.

Determine, within QCD at finite temperature and finite baryon chemical potential:

(a) Does there exist a region of the (T, μ_B) plane in which the transition between the quark-gluon-plasma phase and the hadron-gas phase is a genuine first-order thermodynamic phase transition (i.e., a curve of coexisting phases across which thermodynamic quantities such as the energy density and the baryon density are discontinuous)?

(b) If such a first-order transition line exists, does it terminate at a critical endpoint — a point (T_c, μ_B^c) at which the transition becomes second order — and if so, locate this point and characterize its universality class.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The existence and location of a QCD first-order transition line at finite baryon chemical potential and an associated critical endpoint remain open as of 2025. The STAR Beam Energy Scan program at RHIC has not produced a definitive signal in collisions at √s_NN ≥ 7.7 GeV, and lower-energy data plus future experiments (FAIR/CBM) are still needed. Theoretical work continues to model the conjectured first-order region and critical point, but neither lattice QCD nor experiment has confirmed or excluded their existence.

representations.normalized:
Heavy-ion collisions at high beam energies are well described by hybrid frameworks that combine relativistic viscous hydrodynamics for a hot, near-equilibrium quark–gluon plasma core with a hadronic transport (Boltzmann-type) afterburner for the dilute hadronic stage, while collisions at low beam energies are well described by purely hadronic transport. At intermediate beam energies, neither limit is uniformly valid: parts of the system may be sufficiently dense and thermalized to warrant a hydrodynamic description, while other parts remain dilute and far from equilibrium.

Construct a single dynamical framework that smoothly interpolates between these two regimes and apply it consistently throughout an intermediate-energy collision. Concretely:

1. Define a coupling scheme in which a viscous-hydrodynamic core is dynamically embedded in a hadronic-transport "corona" (or, dually, in which localized hydrodynamic "bubbles" are embedded inside a global hadronic-transport calculation), with explicit, energy- and momentum-conserving criteria (e.g.\ local energy density, thermalization, or Knudsen-number thresholds) that determine which cells are evolved hydrodynamically and which kinetically, together with prescriptions for converting between fluid and particle degrees of freedom in both directions.

2. Incorporate a finite-baryon-density QCD equation of state that includes a phase transition and a critical point, and couple the hydrodynamic evolution to the dynamics of the associated order parameter (e.g.\ via stochastic/fluctuating hydrodynamics or a Langevin equation for a sigma-like field) so that critical fluctuations and non-equilibrium effects near the critical point — including memory effects, finite relaxation times, and possible spinodal decomposition through a first-order transition — are treated consistently.

3. Demonstrate that the resulting framework reproduces the high-energy hybrid limit and the low-energy pure-transport limit as appropriate, and yields well-defined, observable predictions (e.g.\ particle spectra, flow harmonics, and cumulants of conserved-charge fluctuations) across the full intermediate-energy range.

Provide such a construction, or prove obstructions to its existence.

Consider intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions in the regime where a hydrodynamic description of the produced matter is potentially applicable only after a finite stage of non-equilibrium evolution. Model the collision dynamics by a transport approach that includes partonic degrees of freedom (e.g., a Boltzmann-type kinetic evolution with parton-parton scatterings, possibly supplemented by hadronic channels), coupled to an eventual switch to a relativistic viscous-hydrodynamic description of the evolving energy-momentum tensor T^{μν}(x).

Quantitatively determine, as a function of the collision energy √s_{NN} in the intermediate-energy range, the minimum amount of explicitly non-equilibrium evolution (characterized, for instance, by a proper-time interval τ_{neq}, an inverse Knudsen number, or a measure of the anisotropy of T^{μν} such as the pressure ratio P_L/P_T) that must be retained in the transport stage before a hydrodynamic description becomes valid, in the sense that observables (e.g., anisotropic flow coefficients v_n, transverse momentum spectra, particle yields) computed with the hybrid transport+hydrodynamic scheme become insensitive to the switching criterion within prescribed tolerances. In particular, characterize this required non-equilibrium duration in transport frameworks that incorporate partonic degrees of freedom.

representations.normalized:
In high-energy heavy-ion collisions, the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) is an effective field theory description of the small Bjorken-x part of a high-energy hadron's or nucleus's wavefunction, in which the gluon density saturates at a characteristic transverse scale Q_s (the saturation scale). Standard CGC initial-condition models for the early stages of nuclear collisions (e.g., the McLerran–Venugopalan model and its IP-Glasma–type implementations) are formulated as effectively two-dimensional (transverse-plane) descriptions in the high-energy / boost-invariant limit, with the longitudinal (rapidity) dynamics either absent or treated only perturbatively.

Address the following:

(a) Construct an extension of the CGC initial-state framework for nuclear collisions that is fully three-dimensional, i.e., that consistently incorporates non-trivial longitudinal (rapidity) dependence of the color sources and of the resulting classical Yang–Mills gluon fields, going beyond the boost-invariant 2D transverse description. Specify how the rapidity-dependent color-charge correlators, the JIMWLK/BK-type evolution in x, and the matching to subsequent hydrodynamic evolution are to be formulated.

(b) Determine the range of collision energies √s_NN (per nucleon pair) for which the saturation assumptions underlying the CGC effective theory — namely the existence of a hard saturation scale Q_s with Q_s ≫ Λ_QCD so that α_s(Q_s) ≪ 1, and the dominance of high-occupation-number classical gluon fields at small x — remain quantitatively valid for collisions of heavy nuclei. In particular, identify a lower bound (or characterize the breakdown) on √s_NN below which the CGC/saturation picture ceases to be a controlled approximation for modeling the initial state.

Consider the three-fluid hydrodynamic description of an intermediate-energy heavy-ion collision, in which the matter produced in the collision is modeled by three coupled relativistic fluids: a baryon-rich projectile fluid (p), a baryon-rich target fluid (t), and a baryon-free fireball fluid (f) of newly produced particles. Each fluid α ∈ {p, t, f} carries an energy–momentum tensor T_α^{μν} and (for α = p, t) a baryon four-current N_α^μ, evolving according to

   ∂_μ T_α^{μν} = S_α^{ν},     ∂_μ N_α^{μ} = J_α,

where the source terms S_α^{ν} and J_α encode the local exchange of energy, momentum, and baryon number between the projectile/target fluids and the fireball fluid (with ∑_α S_α^{ν} = 0 and J_p + J_t = 0, since the fireball carries zero net baryon number). The source terms are typically modeled through cross-section-weighted nucleon–nucleon interaction rates that decelerate the projectile and target streams and feed the fireball.

Question: Can such source terms in three-fluid hydrodynamics, with two baryon-rich projectile and target fluids generating a baryon-free fireball fluid, provide a quantitatively correct microscopic mechanism that explains the observed pattern of baryon deposition (i.e., the rapidity distribution and stopping of net baryon number) in heavy-ion collisions at intermediate beam energies (roughly the range covered by RHIC beam energy scan and lower)?

representations.normalized:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the produced fireball is commonly modeled as a system that approaches local thermal and chemical equilibrium and then undergoes chemical freeze-out (when inelastic processes that change particle abundances cease) followed by kinetic freeze-out (when elastic rescattering ceases). Under the standard statistical-hadronisation picture, all hadron species are assumed to chemically freeze out at a common temperature T_ch and baryochemical potential μ_B, so that measured yields are described by a single thermal distribution. However, because different hadron species couple to the surrounding hadronic medium through reaction channels with widely varying cross sections, in principle each species s should decouple at its own effective temperature T_s and time τ_s.

Formulate and answer the following question quantitatively:

Can species-dependent, out-of-equilibrium signatures and a particle-specific freeze-out hierarchy {(T_s, τ_s)} be identified and measured precisely enough — for instance through deviations of measured particle ratios (such as p/π, K/π, Λ/π, Ξ/π, Ω/π, φ/π, and resonance-to-stable ratios like K*/K and ρ/π) from a single common-freeze-out thermal fit, and through the centrality, system-size, and √s_NN dependence of these deviations — to reconstruct the dynamics of hadronisation, in the sense of determining for each hadron species the dominant inelastic reaction channels, the corresponding hadronic cross sections, and the resulting decoupling temperature and time? In particular, quantify the magnitude of the freeze-out hierarchy effect for each species, and determine whether currently available or foreseen experimental observables suffice to invert these measurements into a reconstruction of the hadronisation dynamics.

Subsequent ALICE measurements and theoretical work support baryon–antibaryon annihilation in the hadronic phase as the leading explanation for the suppressed p/π ratio at LHC, with hadronic transport codes (UrQMD, EPOS, SMASH) reproducing both the proton suppression and resonance ratios while preserving hyperon yields. In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the spectrum of "direct" photons (i.e., inclusive photons after subtraction of the decay-photon background) above the prompt/perturbative component exhibits an approximately exponential low-momentum excess whose inverse slope T_eff is, in a model-dependent way, related to an effective initial temperature T_0 of the produced quark–gluon plasma (the relation involves space-time averaging over the fireball evolution and a blue-shift due to collective flow). Measured inverse slopes are approximately 200 MeV in Au+Au collisions at RHIC top energy and approximately 300 MeV in Pb+Pb collisions at LHC energies, suggesting initial temperatures in the range T_0 ≈ 300–500 MeV, well above the deconfinement temperature T_c ≈ 155 MeV.

Question: Does the effective initial temperature T_0 inferred from the direct-photon excess strictly increase from RHIC to LHC collision energies? Concretely, by combining (i) higher-precision experimental direct-photon spectra (with reduced statistical and systematic uncertainties) and (ii) theoretical calculations of thermal photon emission that incorporate medium-modified photon production rates together with state-of-the-art (3+1)-dimensional viscous hydrodynamic / hybrid space-time evolutions of the fireball, can one establish at a statistically significant level that T_0(LHC) > T_0(RHIC)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

ALICE has measured an inverse slope of 304 ± 51 MeV in Pb+Pb at the LHC, larger than the PHENIX value of 221 ± 19 MeV in Au+Au at RHIC, which is consistent with an increase of the inferred initial temperature from RHIC to LHC. PHENIX has subsequently released higher-precision low-momentum photon results, and theoretical work using medium-modified rates and modern hydrodynamic evolutions has progressed. Consider strongly interacting matter described by Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the SU(3) gauge theory of quarks and gluons, in thermal equilibrium characterized by a temperature T and a net-baryon number density n_B (equivalently, a baryon chemical potential μ_B). The QCD phase diagram in the (T, μ_B) plane is conjectured to contain a hadronic phase at low T and low μ_B, a quark–gluon plasma phase at high T, and possibly a first-order chiral/deconfinement transition line at large μ_B terminating at a critical end-point.

In heavy-ion collision experiments performed by colliding gold nuclei at center-of-mass energies per nucleon pair √s_{NN} ranging from approximately 7.7 GeV up to 200 GeV (a beam energy scan), a hot dense fireball of strongly interacting matter is produced and subsequently expands and cools.

Determine, as functions of √s_{NN} in the above range:
(a) The temperature T(√s_{NN}) and net-baryon-density n_B(√s_{NN}) (or equivalently μ_B(√s_{NN})) characterizing the thermodynamic state of the produced matter at the relevant stages of its evolution (in particular at the time when bulk thermodynamic properties are imprinted on observables).
(b) The microscopic degrees of freedom that provide the appropriate effective description of QCD matter at those values of (T, μ_B): for example, deconfined quarks and gluons, hadronic resonances, or some intermediate/critical degrees of freedom near a possible QCD critical point.

Provide quantitative trajectories in the (T, μ_B) plane and identify the dominant degrees of freedom along these trajectories.

representations.normalized:
In the context of ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the ρ meson (a vector meson of mass ≈ 770 MeV and vacuum width ≈ 150 MeV) is observed via dilepton production to undergo substantial broadening, and possibly "melting," when propagating through hot hadronic matter at temperatures near the QCD pseudocritical temperature T_c ≈ 155 MeV. Independently, lattice and effective-theory studies indicate that QCD chiral symmetry, spontaneously broken in vacuum, is approximately restored at high temperature, so that chiral partners (e.g. the ρ and a₁ vector–axial-vector channels) should become degenerate in the chirally symmetric phase.

(a) Provide a rigorous theoretical derivation, starting from the QCD Lagrangian or a controlled effective field theory of it, that connects the in-medium spectral function of the isovector vector current (whose low-mass strength is dominated by the ρ) to order parameters of chiral symmetry restoration such as the quark condensate ⟨q̄q⟩(T) and the difference of vector and axial-vector chiral susceptibilities. In particular, establish quantitatively whether the experimentally observed broadening/melting of the ρ spectral function in hot hadronic matter implies—and is implied by—the restoration of SU(2)_L × SU(2)_R chiral symmetry, going beyond the level of conjecture (e.g. Weinberg-type and QCD sum-rule arguments) to a controlled derivation.

(b) Formulate observables in dilepton spectra (low-mass region dominated by the ρ; intermediate-mass region 1.0 ≲ M ≲ 3.0 GeV sensitive to thermal radiation and charm) measurable in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and LHC energies, as well as in proton–proton and proton–nucleus collisions, that would discriminate whether the collective phenomena (e.g. azimuthal anisotropies, ridge correlations) seen in high-multiplicity small systems are accompanied by the formation of a thermalized, chirally (partially) restored medium analogous to that produced in heavy-ion collisions.

The problem is to (i) supply the theoretical connection in (a) and (ii) identify and analyze the dilepton observables in (b) that would resolve the small-system question.

Consider Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the SU(3) gauge theory of quarks and gluons, in thermal equilibrium at temperature $T>0$ and baryon chemical potential $\mu_B \in \mathbb{R}$. For such a state, the energy–momentum tensor $T^{\mu
u}$ near equilibrium admits a hydrodynamic expansion in which the dissipative (viscous) part is, to first order in gradients of the fluid velocity $u^\mu$, characterized by two transport coefficients: the shear viscosity $\eta(T,\mu_B)$ and the bulk viscosity $\zeta(T,\mu_B)$. Let $s(T,\mu_B)$ denote the equilibrium entropy density.

Determine, as functions of $(T,\mu_B)$ throughout the QCD phase diagram (in particular across the crossover/transition region between the hadron-resonance phase and the quark–gluon plasma), the dimensionless ratios
$$\frac{\eta}{s}(T,\mu_B), \qquad \frac{\zeta}{s}(T,\mu_B).$$
Provide a first-principles characterization of these transport-to-entropy ratios for QCD matter at finite temperature and finite baryon chemical potential.
