Let $\Sigma=\{0,1,2\}$ be a three-letter alphabet. A finite word $w\in\Sigma^*$ is called square-free if it contains no nonempty factor of the form $uu$. Let $T$ be the rooted tree whose vertices are all ternary square-free words, in which the root is the empty word and the parent of any nonempty square-free word $w$ is obtained by deleting the last letter of $w$ (so the children of $w$ are exactly the square-free words of the form $wa$ with $a\in\Sigma$). The level (or index) of a vertex $w$ equals its length $|w|$.

For a vertex $v$ of $T$, the subtree $T(v)$ rooted at $v$ consists of $v$ together with all its descendants. Call $T(v)$ a minimal subtree if $v$ has a unique child in $T$ that itself has a unique child, and so on — equivalently, $T(v)$ is a non-branching path emanating from $v$ that ends at a leaf or at the first descendant of $v$ which has at least two children. The index of such a minimal subtree is the level of its root $v$.

Prove or disprove: there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for every minimal subtree of $T$ of index $n$, the number of vertices in this subtree is at most $C\log n$ (for all sufficiently large $n$). In other words, the size of any minimal subtree of index $n$ in $T$ is $O(\log n)$.

Setup. Let $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$ be the binary alphabet, and let $\Sigma^*$ (resp. $\Sigma^\omega$) denote the set of finite (resp. one-sided infinite) words over $\Sigma$. For a finite word $w \in \Sigma^*$, the Parikh vector of $w$ is $\Psi(w) = (|w|_0, |w|_1)$, where $|w|_a$ denotes the number of occurrences of the letter $a$ in $w$. Two finite words $u,v$ are abelian equivalent, written $u \sim_a v$, if $\Psi(u) = \Psi(v)$ (equivalently, $v$ is a permutation of the letters of $u$).

An abelian cube is a non-empty word of the form $u_1 u_2 u_3$ with $u_1 \sim_a u_2 \sim_a u_3$; the common length $|u_1| = |u_2| = |u_3|$ is called the abelian period of the cube. An infinite word $w \in \Sigma^\omega$ is said to avoid abelian cubes of abelian period at least $p$ if no factor of $w$ is an abelian cube whose abelian period is $\geq p$.

Problem. Does there exist an integer $p \geq 1$ and an infinite word $w \in \{0,1\}^\omega$ such that $w$ contains no factor that is an abelian cube of abelian period at least $p$? In other words, can long abelian cubes be avoided on a two-letter alphabet?

An infinite word $w \in \Sigma^\omega$ is said to avoid abelian cubes of abelian period at least $p$ if no factor of $w$ is an abelian cube whose abelian period is $\geq p$.

Problem. Does there exist an integer $p \geq 1$ and an infinite word $w \in \{0,1\}^\omega$ such that $w$ contains no factor that is an abelian cube of abelian period at least $p$? In other words, can long abelian cubes be avoided on a two-letter alphabet?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Rao and Rosenfeld (Avoidability of long k-abelian repetitions, Math. Comp. 2016) settled this negatively: every infinite binary word contains abelian cubes of abelian period at least 2, so long abelian cubes cannot be avoided over a two-letter alphabet. (However, weaker variants such as k-abelian cubes for k ≥ 3 are avoidable on binary alphabets, by Mercaş–Saarela and subsequent work.)

Setting. Let A and B be finite alphabets, and let A* denote the free monoid of finite words over A, with concatenation as product and the empty word as identity. The Parikh vector of a word w in A* is the vector in N^A whose a-th coordinate counts the occurrences of the letter a in w. Two words u, v in A* are abelian equivalent (written u ~_ab v) when they have the same Parikh vector. For an integer k >= 2, an abelian k-power is a word of the form w_1 w_2 ... w_k with w_1 ~_ab w_2 ~_ab ... ~_ab w_k and w_1 nonempty. A word is abelian k-power-free if it contains no abelian k-power as a factor. A morphism h : A* -> B* is said to preserve abelian k-power-freeness (or to be abelian k-power-free) if, for every abelian k-power-free word w in A*, the word h(w) in B* is again abelian k-power-free.

Background problem (P). Develop effective methods to decide, for given alphabets A, B, integers k >= 2, and a morphism h : A* -> B*, whether h preserves abelian k-power-freeness, and to construct families of such morphisms. Equivalently, identify a finite, computable "candidate set" C(h, k) of words in A* such that h preserves abelian k-power-freeness if and only if h(w) is abelian k-power-free for every w in C(h, k).

Problem. Design and rigorously analyze efficient heuristics that, given alphabets A, B, an integer k >= 2, and a morphism h : A* -> B*, produce a tractable candidate set C(h, k) suitable for testing whether h preserves abelian k-power-freeness. The heuristics should:
(i) come with an explicit construction of C(h, k) and a proof that membership in C(h, k) for all relevant test words is sufficient (and, ideally, necessary) for h to preserve abelian k-power-freeness;
(ii) yield bounds on |C(h, k)| and on the lengths of words in C(h, k) in terms of |A|, |B|, k, and the maximum length of h(a) for a in A;
(iii) be implementable so as to make problem (P) computationally feasible for parameter ranges of practical interest, in particular for small alphabets and small k.

Provide such heuristics, prove their correctness and bounds, and demonstrate their efficiency.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. For words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$, we write the following derivation relations:

- Suffix square completion: $u \Rightarrow_{ssc} ux$ whenever $u$ has a suffix of the form $yx$ with $|y|=|x|\ge 1$ (so that $yx$ is a square $xx$, equivalently $u$ ends with a square whose second half is $x$).
- Prefix square completion: $u \Rightarrow_{psc} xu$ whenever $u$ has a prefix of the form $xy$ that forms a square $xx$, i.e. $y=x$.

The prefix–suffix square completion relation $\Rightarrow_{pssc}$ is the union of $\Rightarrow_{ssc}$ and $\Rightarrow_{psc}$. For a starting word $w_0\in\Sigma^*$, let $\mathrm{PSSC}^*(w_0)$ denote the set of all (finite or infinite) words obtainable from $w_0$ by iterating $\Rightarrow_{pssc}$.

A word $w\in\Sigma^\omega\cup\Sigma^*$ is called cube-free if it contains no factor of the form $xxx$ with $x\in\Sigma^+$. Note that any word obtained from $w_0$ by a non-trivial sequence of prefix–suffix square completion steps necessarily contains squares.

Question. Does there exist a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, a starting word $w_0\in\Sigma^*$, and an infinite derivation $w_0 \Rightarrow_{pssc} w_1 \Rightarrow_{pssc} w_2 \Rightarrow_{pssc} \cdots$ producing an infinite word $w\in\Sigma^\omega$ such that $w$ is cube-free (and, by the nature of the operation, every sufficiently long prefix of $w$ contains squares)?

Determine the minimal integer $k$ with $2<k<6$ (i.e. $k\in\{3,4,5\}$) such that there exists an infinite word over $\Sigma_3$ avoiding all abelian squares of period at least $k$.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$. For a word $w \in \Sigma^*$, define the prefix square completion of $w$ as the set
$$P(w) = \{uw : w = uv \text{ with } u \in \Sigma^+\},$$
i.e., the words obtained by prepending to $w$ a non-empty prefix of $w$ (so that $w$ acquires a square as a prefix). Symmetrically, define the suffix square completion
$$S(w) = \{wv : w = uv \text{ with } v \in \Sigma^+\}.$$
The prefix-suffix square completion of $w$ is $\mathrm{PS}(w) = P(w) \cup S(w)$. Extend $\mathrm{PS}$ to languages by $\mathrm{PS}(L) = \bigcup_{w \in L} \mathrm{PS}(w)$, and define the iterated prefix-suffix square completion of an initial language $L_0 \subseteq \Sigma^*$ by
$$\mathrm{PS}^*(L_0) = \bigcup_{n \geq 0} \mathrm{PS}^n(L_0), \qquad \mathrm{PS}^0(L_0) = L_0,\ \mathrm{PS}^{n+1}(L_0) = L_0 \cup \mathrm{PS}(\mathrm{PS}^n(L_0)).$$

Investigate the structural and language-theoretic properties of the family of languages $\mathrm{PS}^*(L_0)$ as $L_0$ ranges over distinguished classes of initial languages. In particular:

1. Characterize $\mathrm{PS}^*(\{w\})$ for a singleton initial set, and determine in which level of the Chomsky hierarchy (regular, context-free, context-sensitive) this language always lies.
2. Determine whether the class of regular languages is closed under the operator $L_0 \mapsto \mathrm{PS}^*(L_0)$; if not, characterize precisely those regular $L_0$ for which $\mathrm{PS}^*(L_0)$ is regular.
3. Address the analogous closure questions when $L_0$ is taken to be finite, or context-free.
4. Provide decision algorithms (with complexity bounds) for membership, emptiness, and equivalence problems for languages of the form $\mathrm{PS}^*(L_0)$ when $L_0$ is finite or regular.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$. A morphism is a map $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ satisfying $h(uv)=h(u)h(v)$. The incidence (Parikh) matrix of $h$ on $\Sigma=\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}$ is the $k\times k$ integer matrix $M_h$ whose $(i,j)$ entry is the number of occurrences of $a_i$ in $h(a_j)$. An infinite word $w\in\Sigma^\omega$ is a fixed point of $h$ if $h(w)=w$.

Two finite words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$ are abelian equivalent if each letter of $\Sigma$ occurs the same number of times in $u$ as in $v$. A nonempty word of the form $uv$ with $u$ abelian equivalent to $v$ is called an abelian square. An infinite word $w$ is abelian-square-free if no factor (contiguous subword) of $w$ is an abelian square.

Question: Does there exist an alphabet $\Sigma$ with $|\Sigma|=5$ and a morphism $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ such that
(i) the incidence matrix $M_h$ has at least two eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity) whose modulus is strictly less than $1$, and
(ii) $h$ admits an infinite fixed point that is abelian-square-free?

Otherwise w avoids p in the abelian sense. A pattern p is said to be avoidable in the abelian sense if there exists a finite alphabet A and an infinite word w ∈ A^ω such that every finite factor of w avoids p in the abelian sense.

A pattern is a word p = p_1 p_2 ... p_n over an alphabet of variables E = {0, 1, 2, ...}. A word w ∈ A* is said to encounter the pattern p in the abelian sense if there exist non-empty words h_1, h_2, ..., h_n ∈ A* such that:
 (i) w contains h_1 h_2 ... h_n as a factor, and
 (ii) for all i, j ∈ {1, ..., n}, if p_i = p_j then h_i ~_ab h_j.
Otherwise w avoids p in the abelian sense. A pattern p is said to be avoidable in the abelian sense if there exists a finite alphabet A and an infinite word w ∈ A^ω such that every finite factor of w avoids p in the abelian sense.

Determine, for each of the following six patterns, whether it is avoidable in the abelian sense:
 p_1 = 0 1 0 2 0 3 1 2,
 p_2 = 0 1 0 2 0 3 2 1,
 p_3 = 0 1 0 2 1 3 0 3,
 p_4 = 0 1 0 2 3 0 3 1,
 p_5 = 0 1 0 2 0 3 0 1 3,
 p_6 = 0 1 0 2 1 3 0 2 0.

Setup. Let A be a finite alphabet and A* the free monoid of finite words over A. For a word w ∈ A*, the Parikh vector ψ(w) records the multiplicity of each letter of A in w. Two words u, v ∈ A* are abelian equivalent, written u ~_ab v, if ψ(u) = ψ(v) (equivalently, v is a permutation of u).

A pattern is a word p over a (variable) alphabet E = {x_1, …, x_n} of n letters. A word w over an alphabet A is said to encounter p in the abelian sense if there exists a non-erasing morphism h: E* → A* such that the word h(p) appears as a factor of w with the property dictated by abelian occurrence: more precisely, w contains a factor of the form w_1 w_2 … w_k, where p = x_{i_1} x_{i_2} … x_{i_k}, each w_j is a non-empty word over A, and whenever i_j = i_{j'} we have w_j ~_ab w_{j'}. Otherwise, w is said to avoid p in the abelian sense, or to be p-free in the abelian sense.

The pattern p is called abelian avoidable if there exists a finite alphabet A and an infinite word w over A that avoids p in the abelian sense.

The Zimin words Z_n are defined recursively over the alphabet {x_1, x_2, …} by Z_1 = x_1 and Z_{n+1} = Z_n x_{n+1} Z_n. Thus Z_2 = x_1 x_2 x_1, Z_3 = x_1 x_2 x_1 x_3 x_1 x_2 x_1, and so on.

Question. Prove or disprove the following: for every pattern p over an alphabet of exactly n letters, p is abelian avoidable if and only if the Zimin word Z_n is p-free in the abelian sense.

A characterization of abelian (un)avoidable patterns analogous to the Zimin/Bean–Ehrenfeucht–McNulty theorem for ordinary unavoidability is widely cited as still missing. Surveys and recent works on abelian pattern avoidance (e.g., the classification of 3-letter patterns and partial results for 4-letter and binary patterns) state that abelian unavoidability still lacks a Zimin-style characterization, and several 4-letter patterns remain undecided. Setup. Let A be a finite alphabet of size n ≥ 2. Two finite words u,v ∈ A* are said to be abelian equivalent (written u ~_ab v) if they have the same length and, for every letter a ∈ A, the number of occurrences of a in u equals the number of occurrences of a in v.

For a real number α > 1, an abelian α-power is a finite word w that can be written w = u_1 u_2 … u_k v, where u_1 ~_ab u_2 ~_ab … ~_ab u_k, the words u_i are nonempty of common length p, v is a prefix of some word abelian-equivalent to u_1, and (kp + |v|)/p = α. An infinite word x ∈ A^ω is said to avoid abelian α-powers (or abelian β-powers for every β > α) if no factor of x is an abelian β-power for any β > α.

Define the abelian repetition threshold of an n-letter alphabet by
    ART(n) = inf { α > 1 : there exists an infinite word over an n-letter alphabet that avoids abelian β-powers for every β > α }.

Define an analogous threshold DART(r), where one restricts attention to abelian powers in which the lengths of consecutive abelian-equivalent blocks are all distinct (so-called "distinct abelian powers"): DART(r) is the corresponding infimal exponent over alphabets of size r.

Problem. Determine the exact value of ART(n) for every integer n ≥ 2, and determine the exact value of DART(r) for every integer r ≥ 2.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The exact values of the abelian repetition threshold ART(n) remain unknown. Samsonov and Shur (2012) proved lower bounds ART(2) ≥ 11/3, ART(3) ≥ 2, ART(4) ≥ 9/5, ART(k) ≥ (k−2)/(k−3) for k ≥ 5, and conjectured these to be tight. Subsequent work (Petrova–Shur, 2022) showed the Samsonov–Shur bounds are not tight for k = 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and proposed a revised conjecture, leaving the exact values open. The closely related distinct-abelian variant remains likewise unresolved.

An infinite word $w = w_0 w_1 w_2 \cdots$ over a finite alphabet $A$ is called an Arnoux–Rauzy word if for every length $n \geq 0$ it has exactly one left special factor and exactly one right special factor of length $n$, and each of these special factors can be extended (on the appropriate side) by every letter of $A$ to yield another factor of $w$. For a positive integer $C$, the word $w$ is said to be $C$-balanced if for every letter $a \in A$ and every pair of factors $u, v$ of $w$ with $|u| = |v|$, one has $\bigl||u|_a - |v|_a\bigr| \leq C$, where $|x|_a$ denotes the number of occurrences of the letter $a$ in $x$. The balance of $w$ is the smallest such $C$ (or $\infty$ if no such $C$ exists).

Problem. Given an integer $C \geq 1$ and an alphabet $A$ of size $k \geq 3$, give an explicit characterization (for instance in terms of the directive sequence in the Arnoux–Rauzy substitution system) of all Arnoux–Rauzy words over $A$ whose balance is exactly $C$ (equivalently, of all $C$-balanced Arnoux–Rauzy words).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Partial results are known. It has been shown that not every Arnoux–Rauzy word is C-balanced for some constant C: there exist Arnoux–Rauzy words with infinite imbalance. Sufficient conditions for C-balancedness are known, and the question for 2-balanced ternary Arnoux–Rauzy words has been studied; in particular, the set of directive-sequence prefixes producing 2-balanced ternary Arnoux–Rauzy words has been shown not to form a rational language, ruling out simple automatic characterizations. A complete characterization of Arnoux–Rauzy words with a given balance remains open.

Let $F$ be a (possibly infinite) set of finite words over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$. An $F$-factorization of a finite word $w \in \Sigma^*$ is a decomposition $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$ such that each factor $u_i$ belongs to $F$. Various decision and computation problems associated to $F$-factorizations (such as: deciding whether a given input word $w$ admits an $F$-factorization, counting the number of $F$-factorizations, or producing an explicit one when it exists) are known to be solvable in polynomial time in $|w|$ for several natural classes of sets $F$ (for instance when $F$ is given by a finite automaton, by a regular expression, or by other suitably effective descriptions).

The task is the following: for each such problem about $F$-factorizations that is known to admit a polynomial-time algorithm, design an explicit and efficient algorithm. More precisely, develop algorithms whose running time has small polynomial degree (and good dependence on the description size of $F$) for the polynomial-time-solvable instances of $F$-factorization problems, improving upon merely showing membership in $\mathrm{P}$.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the set of all finite words over $\Sigma$. For a positive integer $k$, two words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$ are said to be $k$-abelian equivalent, written $u\sim_k v$, if for every word $w\in\Sigma^*$ with $|w|\le k$, the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $v$ (equivalently, $u$ and $v$ have the same length and, for $|w|\le k$, the same factor counts).

For an integer $n\ge 2$, call a non-empty word $u\in\Sigma^*$ a $k$-abelian-$n$-power if it admits a factorization $u=u_1u_2\cdots u_n$ with $u_i\sim_k u_{i+1}$ for every $i\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w}\in\Sigma^{\mathbb{N}}$ is said to avoid $k$-abelian-$n$-powers if no non-empty factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is a $k$-abelian-$n$-power.

Problem. Determine, for each pair of integers $k\ge 1$ and $n\ge 2$, the smallest size of an alphabet $\Sigma$ over which there exists an infinite word avoiding $k$-abelian-$n$-powers, and decide for which triples $(k,n,|\Sigma|)$ such an infinite word exists.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the set of all finite words over $\Sigma$. For a positive integer $k$, two words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$ are said to be $k$-abelian equivalent, written $u\sim_k v$, if for every word $w\in\Sigma^*$ with $|w|\le k$, the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $v$ (equivalently, $u$ and $v$ have the same length and, for $|w|\le k$, the same factor counts).

For an integer $n\ge 2$, call a non-empty word $u\in\Sigma^*$ a $k$-abelian-$n$-power if it admits a factorization $u=u_1u_2\cdots u_n$ with $u_i\sim_k u_{i+1}$ for every $i\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w}\in\Sigma^{\mathbb{N}}$ is said to avoid $k$-abelian-$n$-powers if no non-empty factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is a $k$-abelian-$n$-power.

Problem. Determine, for each pair of integers $k\ge 1$ and $n\ge 2$, the smallest size of an alphabet $\Sigma$ over which there exists an infinite word avoiding $k$-abelian-$n$-powers, and decide for which triples $(k,n,|\Sigma|)$ such an infinite word exists.

Rao in the WORDS open-problems compilation, does not appear to be fully resolved in the available literature; partial results on long k-abelian repetitions appear in work of Rao and Rosenfeld.

Let A be a finite alphabet and consider words (finite or infinite sequences) over A. For a finite word w, write |w| for its length. Two finite words u and v are said to be abelian-equivalent if v is a permutation of u (equivalently, every letter of A occurs the same number of times in u as in v).

A factor of the form uv occurring inside a word, where u and v are abelian-equivalent, is called an abelian-square; a factor uvw with u, v, w pairwise abelian-equivalent is called an abelian-cube. The integer |u| is called the (abelian) period of the repetition. An infinite word is said to avoid such repetitions of period at least 2 if no factor of the form uv (resp. uvw) with |u| ≥ 2 and the abelian-equivalence condition occurs in it.

Answer the following two questions:

(1) Does there exist an infinite word over a 3-letter alphabet that contains no factor of the form uv with |u| ≥ 2 such that u and v are abelian-equivalent?

(2) Does there exist an infinite word over a 2-letter alphabet that contains no factor of the form uvw with |u| ≥ 2 such that u, v, w are pairwise abelian-equivalent?

Let A be a finite alphabet and let F ⊆ A^+ be a language of nonempty words. An F-factorization of an infinite word w ∈ A^ω is a factorization w = u_1 u_2 u_3 ⋯ with each u_i ∈ F. Such a factorization is called regular (resp. context-free) if the language F is regular (resp. context-free).

An F-factorization w = u_1 u_2 ⋯ is said to possess the synchronization property with parameters (n, k) (where n, k are positive integers) if, for every factor v of w of length at least n, there exist indices i ≤ j such that v contains the block u_i u_{i+1} ⋯ u_j as a factor and j − i + 1 ≥ k; equivalently, knowing any sufficiently long factor of w determines a portion of the factorization unambiguously up to a bounded shift. We say F (together with w) "possesses the synchronization property" if there exist some parameters (n, k) for which the property holds.

Determine the computational complexity of each of the following decision problems:

(1) Given a regular language F (specified, e.g., by a finite automaton) and an infinite word w admitting an F-factorization, decide whether the factorization possesses the synchronization property for some (unspecified) parameters n, k.

(2) The same question when F is given as a context-free language (specified by a context-free grammar or pushdown automaton).

In both cases the parameters of synchronization are not part of the input.

Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the free monoid of finite words over $A$. For a finite set $X \subseteq A^*$, the (combinatorial) rank $r(X)$ is defined as
$$r(X) = \min\{|F| : F \subseteq A^*,\ X \subseteq F^*\}.$$
A bi-infinite word over $A$ is a sequence $w = (w_i)_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ with $w_i \in A$. Such a $w$ is called periodic if there exists a positive integer $p$ with $w_{i+p} = w_i$ for all $i \in \mathbb{Z}$, and non-periodic otherwise. An $X$-factorization of $w$ is a way of writing $w$ as a bi-infinite concatenation of elements of $X$, i.e., a strictly increasing bi-infinite sequence of integers $(n_j)_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}$ such that for every $j$ the word $w_{n_j} w_{n_j+1} \cdots w_{n_{j+1}-1}$ belongs to $X$. Two $X$-factorizations are called disjoint if the sets of cut points $\{n_j\}$ are disjoint.

Suppose $w$ is a non-periodic bi-infinite word that admits $k$ pairwise disjoint $X$-factorizations, where $k \le |X|$. Decide whether it is necessarily true that
$$r(X) \le |X| - k + 1.$$

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. A morphism is a map $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ with $h(uv)=h(u)h(v)$. A morphism $h$ is prolongable on a letter $a\in\Sigma$ if $h(a)=au$ for some $u\in\Sigma^+$ with $h^n(u)\neq\varepsilon$ for all $n\geq 0$; in this case the iteration $h^\omega(a)=\lim_{n\to\infty}h^n(a)\in\Sigma^\mathbb{N}$ is a pure morphic infinite word. A morphic word is the image $g(h^\omega(a))$ under a coding (letter-to-letter morphism) $g:\Sigma\to\Delta$.

Two finite words $u,v\in\Delta^*$ are abelian equivalent, written $u\sim_{ab} v$, if $|u|_c=|v|_c$ for every letter $c\in\Delta$ (equal Parikh vectors). For an integer $k\geq 2$, an abelian $k$-power is a nonempty word of the form $u_1u_2\cdots u_k$ with $u_1\sim_{ab} u_2\sim_{ab}\cdots\sim_{ab} u_k$. An infinite word $w$ avoids abelian $k$-powers if no factor of $w$ is an abelian $k$-power; it avoids long abelian $k$-powers if only finitely many factors of $w$ are abelian $k$-powers (equivalently, all sufficiently long factors are abelian-$k$-power-free).

Problem. Provide an algorithm which, given as input a morphism $h$, a letter $a$ on which $h$ is prolongable, a coding $g$, and an integer $k\geq 2$, decides:
(a) whether the morphic word $g(h^\omega(a))$ avoids abelian $k$-powers; and
(b) whether $g(h^\omega(a))$ avoids long abelian $k$-powers.
Equivalently, determine whether the abelian-power-avoidance problem for morphic words is decidable in full generality, or exhibit a class of morphisms for which the question is undecidable.

Let Σ be a finite alphabet and Σ⁺ the set of nonempty finite words over Σ. For a word w ∈ Σ⁺, let p(w) denote the smallest period of w, i.e., the least positive integer p such that w[i] = w[i+p] for all valid indices i.

Each X-factorization determines a set of "cut positions" in w (the positions between consecutive factors xᵢ, xᵢ₊₁, viewed as integers in {1, …, |w|−1}). Two X-factorizations of w are called disjoint if their sets of cut positions are disjoint (equivalently, they do not share a common factorization point inside w).

The combinatorial rank r(X) of a finite set X ⊆ Σ⁺ is defined as
   r(X) = min { |F| : F ⊆ Σ⁺ and X ⊆ F* },
where F* denotes the submonoid generated by F.

Question. Suppose w ∈ Σ⁺ and X ⊆ Σ⁺ satisfies p(x) < p(w) for every x ∈ X. Is it true that w admits at most |X| + 1 − r(X) pairwise disjoint X-factorizations?

An abelian square is a nonempty word of the form $uv$ where $v$ is a permutation (rearrangement) of the letters of $u$, i.e., $u$ and $v$ have the same Parikh vector. An infinite word $w$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ is called abelian-square-free if no factor of $w$ is an abelian square. A morphism $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ is called abelian-square-free if $h(w)$ is abelian-square-free whenever $w$ is, and in particular iterating $h$ on a suitable letter produces an abelian-square-free infinite word.

In 1992, Keränen exhibited a uniform morphism $g:\{a,b,c,d\}^*\to\{a,b,c,d\}^*$ of length $|g(a)|=|g(b)|=|g(c)|=|g(d)|=85$ which is abelian-square-free, thereby proving that abelian squares are avoidable over a four-letter alphabet.

Problem: Construct an abelian-square-free morphism on the four-letter alphabet $\{a,b,c,d\}$ that is simpler than Keränen's $85$-uniform morphism (for example, of strictly smaller uniform length, or with a substantially simpler combinatorial description), or prove that no such simpler morphism exists.

In 1992, Keränen exhibited a uniform morphism $g:\{a,b,c,d\}^*\to\{a,b,c,d\}^*$ of length $|g(a)|=|g(b)|=|g(c)|=|g(d)|=85$ which is abelian-square-free, thereby proving that abelian squares are avoidable over a four-letter alphabet.

Problem: Construct an abelian-square-free morphism on the four-letter alphabet $\{a,b,c,d\}$ that is simpler than Keränen's $85$-uniform morphism (for example, of strictly smaller uniform length, or with a substantially simpler combinatorial description), or prove that no such simpler morphism exists.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Searches indicate that constructions of abelian-square-free morphisms over four letters remain rare and difficult; subsequent works (e.g., a 98-uniform morphism by Carpi, and DT0L-language constructions) have produced alternative or related morphisms but no widely accepted "simpler" replacement for Keränen's 85-uniform morphism has been established. The problem of finding a genuinely simpler abelian-square-free morphism on four letters appears to remain open.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet with $|\Sigma|\ge 2$, and let $\Xi=\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ be a finite set of $n$ unknowns. A word equation over $\Sigma$ with unknowns in $\Xi$ is a pair $(u,v)\in (\Sigma\cup\Xi)^*\times(\Sigma\cup\Xi)^*$, usually written $u=v$. A solution of such an equation is a morphism $\varphi:(\Sigma\cup\Xi)^*\to\Sigma^*$ that fixes every letter of $\Sigma$ and satisfies $\varphi(u)=\varphi(v)$. Two systems of word equations (possibly infinite) over the same set of unknowns are called equivalent if they have exactly the same set of solutions. A subsystem of a system $(S)$ is any subset of the equations of $(S)$.

By the Ehrenfeucht compactness property (proved by Albert and Lawrence, and independently by Guba), every system $(S)$ of word equations on finitely many unknowns over a free monoid $\Sigma^*$ is equivalent to some finite subsystem of itself.

Question: Does there exist a positive integer $k=k(n)$, depending only on the number $n$ of unknowns, such that every system $(S)$ of word equations in $n$ unknowns over $\Sigma^*$ is equivalent to one of its subsystems consisting of at most $k$ equations?

The Ehrenfeucht compactness property guarantees a finite equivalent subsystem, but no explicit upper bound on the size of such a subsystem in terms of the number of unknowns is known for $n\ge 3$. Background and notation. Fix an integer k ≥ 2 and consider infinite words over a k-letter alphabet Σ_k = {1, …, k}. For a rational number r > 1, an r-power is a word of the form x = u^n v where v is a (possibly empty) prefix of u and |x|/|u| = r. A word w is r⁺-free if it contains no factor that is an r'-power with r' > r. The repetition threshold over k letters is RT(k) = k/(k−1) for k ≥ 5 (Dejean's theorem), so an infinite (k/(k−1))⁺-free word over k letters exists. For an infinite word w = w_1 w_2 w_3 … and a letter a ∈ Σ_k, the frequency of a in w is

  freq_w(a) = lim_{n→∞} #{i ≤ n : w_i = a} / n,

provided the limit exists.

Problem. Prove or disprove the following two statements.

(i) For every integer k ≥ 5, there exists an infinite (k/(k−1))⁺-free word over a k-letter alphabet in which some letter has frequency exactly 1/(k+1).

(ii) For every integer k ≥ 6, there exists an infinite (k/(k−1))⁺-free word over a k-letter alphabet in which some letter has frequency exactly 1/(k−1).

Let $x$ be an infinite word over a finite alphabet $A$, and let $p_x(n)$ denote its factor complexity, i.e. the number of distinct factors of $x$ of length $n$. It is known that the condition $p_x(n) = O(n)$ (linear factor complexity) is equivalent to the existence of a finite set $S$ of factors of $x$ of bounded complexity such that every factor of $x$ can be written as a concatenation of two elements of $S$.

An $S$-adic representation of an infinite word $x$ consists of a finite set $\Sigma = \{\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_k\}$ of substitutions $\sigma_i : A_i^* \to A_{i-1}^*$ together with an infinite directive sequence $(\sigma_{i_n})_{n \geq 1}$ and a sequence of letters such that $x = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sigma_{i_1} \sigma_{i_2} \cdots \sigma_{i_n}(a_n)$, possibly subject to combinatorial rules constraining which compositions $\sigma_{i_n} \sigma_{i_{n+1}}$ are admissible.

Problem: Produce a characterization of the class of infinite words $x$ with $p_x(n) = O(n)$ in terms of an $S$-adic system of representation, i.e. exhibit a finite set of substitutions together with explicit rules governing their admissible compositions, such that an infinite word has linear factor complexity if and only if it admits an $S$-adic representation by these substitutions following these rules.

Let $\sigma$ be a primitive substitution on a finite alphabet $\mathcal{A}=\{a_1,\dots,a_d\}$, and let $u$ be an infinite fixed point of $\sigma$. The incidence matrix $M_\sigma$ of $\sigma$ is the $d\times d$ matrix whose $(i,j)$-entry counts the occurrences of $a_i$ in $\sigma(a_j)$. For a finite factor $w$ of $u$, write $|w|_a$ for the number of occurrences of the letter $a\in\mathcal{A}$ in $w$. The balance function of $u$ is
$$B_u(n)=\max\big\{\,\big||w|_a-|w'|_a\big| : a\in\mathcal{A},\ w,w'\text{ factors of }u,\ |w|=|w'|=n\,\big\}.$$
The asymptotic growth of $B_u(n)$ is governed by the spectrum (eigenvalues) of $M_\sigma$, in particular by the second largest eigenvalue modulus relative to the Perron eigenvalue.

Construct an explicit primitive substitution $\sigma$ together with a modification $\tilde\sigma$ (for instance by a power, by a conjugation, or by another natural transformation that alters the non-Perron part of the spectrum of the incidence matrix) such that the change in the spectrum produces a genuinely significant change in the balance properties of the corresponding fixed points—e.g., transforming a bounded balance function into an unbounded one, or changing the asymptotic order of growth of $B_u(n)$ from one regime to another (logarithmic, polynomial $n^\alpha$ with a different exponent $\alpha$, etc.). Provide such an example and prove that the balance behavior changes as claimed.

Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $A^+$ the set of nonempty finite words over $A$. Let $F = (f_i)_{i \in I}$ be a fixed indexed family of nonempty words over $A$ (a "factor set"). An $F$-factorization of a word $w \in A^+$ is a finite sequence of indices $(i_1, i_2, \dots, i_n) \in I^n$ such that $w = f_{i_1} f_{i_2} \cdots f_{i_n}$. Such an $F$-factorization is called regular if the sequence of indices $(i_1, \dots, i_n)$ is non-increasing with respect to a fixed total order on $I$ (equivalently, the indices appear in a fixed canonical order, as in Lyndon-type factorizations). Among all regular $F$-factorizations of a given word $w$, define the minimal (respectively maximal) regular $F$-factorization to be one whose length $n$ (the number of indices in the sequence) is smallest (respectively largest).

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input a word $w \in A^+$ (and the family $F$, when not fixed), computes the minimal regular $F$-factorization of $w$ and the maximal regular $F$-factorization of $w$ in time polynomial in the length of $w$?

Among all regular $F$-factorizations of a given word $w$, define the minimal (respectively maximal) regular $F$-factorization to be one whose length $n$ (the number of indices in the sequence) is smallest (respectively largest).

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input a word $w \in A^+$ (and the family $F$, when not fixed), computes the minimal regular $F$-factorization of $w$ and the maximal regular $F$-factorization of $w$ in time polynomial in the length of $w$?

Background and definitions. Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $A^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $A$. A factorization of a word $w \in A^*$ over a language $F \subseteq A^*$ is a sequence $(u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k)$ with each $u_i \in F$ and $u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k = w$. Given a language $F \subseteq A^+$, the F-factorization problem associates to every word $w$ the set of all factorizations of $w$ over $F$. The factorization $F$ is said to be:
- complete if every word in $A^*$ admits at least one factorization over $F$;
- unique if every word in $A^*$ admits at most one factorization over $F$.

A language $F$ is said to be specified by a deterministic (pushdown) automaton if it is the language accepted by such an automaton, and by a linear context-free grammar if it is generated by a context-free grammar in which every production has at most one nonterminal in its right-hand side.

Question. Determine whether each of the following decision problems is decidable or undecidable:
(a) Given a context-free language $F \subseteq A^+$ specified by a deterministic pushdown automaton, decide whether the $F$-factorization is complete; and the analogous problem for uniqueness.
(b) Given a context-free language $F \subseteq A^+$ specified by a linear context-free grammar, decide whether the $F$-factorization is complete; and the analogous problem for uniqueness.

Let α ∈ (0,1) be an irrational number with simple continued fraction expansion α = [0; a_1, a_2, a_3, …], and let (q_n)_{n≥0} be the sequence of denominators of its convergents, defined by q_0 = 1, q_1 = a_1, and q_{n+1} = a_{n+1} q_n + q_{n-1} for n ≥ 1. Define
   Π(α) = { r·q_{n} + q_{n-1} : n ≥ 0, 1 ≤ r ≤ a_{n+1} } ∪ {q_0}.

A Sturmian word with slope α is an infinite word t over a two-letter alphabet {0,1} of the form
   t_n = ⌊(n+1)α + ρ⌋ − ⌊nα + ρ⌋   (n ≥ 0)
for some ρ ∈ ℝ (or its analogue with ⌈·⌉). A factor of t is any finite word that occurs as a contiguous block t_i t_{i+1} … t_{i+ℓ−1}. The least period of a nonempty finite word w = w_1 w_2 … w_ℓ is the smallest positive integer p such that w_i = w_{i+p} for all 1 ≤ i ≤ ℓ − p.

Prove or disprove: for every nonempty factor w of t, the least period of w belongs to Π(α).

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, written additively, and let $A \subseteq G$ be a nonempty subset. For positive integers $h$ and $s$, define the following sumsets.

Unrestricted sumsets:
- $hA = \{a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_h : a_i \in A\}$ (with repetitions allowed),
- $[0,s]A = \bigcup_{h=0}^{s} hA$ (with $0A = \{0\}$),
- $\langle A\rangle = \bigcup_{h \ge 0} hA$, the subgroup generated by $A$.

Unrestricted signed sumsets:
- $h_{\pm}A = \{\varepsilon_1 a_1 + \cdots + \varepsilon_h a_h : a_i \in A,\ \varepsilon_i \in \{+1,-1\}\}$,
- $[0,s]_{\pm}A = \bigcup_{h=0}^{s} h_{\pm}A$.

Restricted sumsets:
- $h\hat{\,}A = \{a_{i_1} + \cdots + a_{i_h} : 1 \le i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_h \le |A|\}$ (sums of $h$ distinct elements of $A$),
- $[0,s]\hat{\,}A = \bigcup_{h=0}^{s} h\hat{\,}A$,
- $\Sigma A = \bigcup_{h=0}^{|A|} h\hat{\,}A$, the set of all subset sums of $A$.

Restricted signed sumsets:
- $h\hat{\,}_{\pm}A = \{\varepsilon_1 a_{i_1} + \cdots + \varepsilon_h a_{i_h} : 1 \le i_1 < \cdots < i_h \le |A|,\ \varepsilon_j \in \{+1,-1\}\}$,
- $[0,s]\hat{\,}_{\pm}A = \bigcup_{h=0}^{s} h\hat{\,}_{\pm}A$,
- $\Sigma_{\pm}A = \bigcup_{h=0}^{|A|} h\hat{\,}_{\pm}A$.

A subset $A \subseteq G$ is said to span $G$ under one of these operations if the corresponding sumset equals $G$. Define the spanning-threshold functions
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi(G,h) &= \min\{|A| : A \subseteq G,\ hA = G\}, \\
\varphi(G,[0,s]) &= \min\{|A| : A \subseteq G,\ [0,s]A = G\}, \\
\varphi(G,\mathbb{N}_0) &= \min\{|A| : A \subseteq G,\ \langle A\rangle = G\},
\end{aligned}
\]
and analogously $\varphi_{\pm}(G,\cdot)$, $\hat{\varphi}(G,\cdot)$, and $\hat{\varphi}_{\pm}(G,\cdot)$ using the signed, restricted, and restricted-signed sumset operations defined above.

Problem: For every finite abelian group $G$ and all parameters $h,s \ge 1$, determine exact formulas for the twelve spanning-threshold quantities
\[
\varphi(G,h),\ \varphi(G,[0,s]),\ \varphi(G,\mathbb{N}_0),\ \varphi_{\pm}(G,h),\ \varphi_{\pm}(G,[0,s]),\ \varphi_{\pm}(G,\mathbb{N}_0),
\]
\[
\hat{\varphi}(G,h),\ \hat{\varphi}(G,[0,s]),\ \hat{\varphi}(G,\mathbb{N}_0),\ \hat{\varphi}_{\pm}(G,h),\ \hat{\varphi}_{\pm}(G,[0,s]),\ \hat{\varphi}_{\pm}(G,\mathbb{N}_0),
\]
and, where possible, characterize the extremal subsets $A \subseteq G$ that achieve these minima.

Setup. Let $A$ be a finite alphabet. An infinite word $x \in A^{\mathbb N}$ is said to be quasiperiodic if there exists a finite nonempty word $q \in A^+$ (called a quasiperiod of $x$) such that every position of $x$ lies inside some occurrence of $q$ in $x$; equivalently, $x$ is covered by occurrences of $q$. An infinite word that is not quasiperiodic is called non-quasiperiodic.

A morphism is a map $f : A^* \to A^*$ satisfying $f(uv) = f(u)f(v)$ for all $u,v \in A^*$; it extends in the natural way to infinite words $A^{\mathbb N}$. A morphism $f$ is said to be:
- strongly quasiperiodic if $f(x)$ is quasiperiodic for every infinite word $x \in A^{\mathbb N}$;
- weakly quasiperiodic if $f(x)$ is quasiperiodic for at least one non-quasiperiodic infinite word $x \in A^{\mathbb N}$.

A morphism $f$ is said to generate a quasiperiodic infinite word if there is a letter $a \in A$ such that $f(a)$ begins with $a$, the iterates $f^n(a)$ converge (in the usual prefix sense) to an infinite word $f^\omega(a) \in A^{\mathbb N}$, and this infinite word $f^\omega(a)$ is quasiperiodic. Here $f(a)$ is said to be a power of $a$ if $f(a) = a^k$ for some integer $k \ge 1$.

Question. Let $f : A^* \to A^*$ be a morphism that generates a quasiperiodic infinite word $f^\omega(a)$, where $a \in A$ is the generating letter. Suppose that $f(a)$ is not a power of $a$. Is it then true that $f$ is weakly quasiperiodic, i.e., that there exists at least one non-quasiperiodic infinite word $x \in A^{\mathbb N}$ such that $f(x)$ is quasiperiodic?

Let $\Xi = \{x_1, x_2, x_3\}$ be a set of three unknowns and let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. A word equation over $\Xi$ is a pair $(u,v) \in \Xi^* \times \Xi^*$, usually written $u = v$. A solution is a morphism $h : \Xi^* \to \Sigma^*$ such that $h(u) = h(v)$. A solution $h$ is called periodic if there exists a word $w \in \Sigma^*$ such that $h(x_1), h(x_2), h(x_3) \in w^*$; otherwise it is called non-periodic.

A system $S$ of word equations over $\Xi$ is independent if it is not equivalent (i.e., does not have the same set of solutions) to any of its proper subsystems.

Question: Does there exist an independent system consisting of exactly three word equations in the three unknowns $x_1, x_2, x_3$ that admits a non-periodic solution $h : \Xi^* \to \Sigma^*$?

The problem appears still open. Recent surveys on independent systems of word equations (e.g., "Independent Systems of Word Equations: From Ehrenfeucht to Eighteen", 2019) report that for three unknowns the maximal size of an independent system is bounded above by 18, but it is conjectured to be 2; the existence of an independent system of three equations in three unknowns with a non-periodic solution remains an open question, related to work of Czeizler and Karhumäki.

Let $ho:\mathbb{R}^3	o\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ be the one-electron density of a molecular system in its ground (or a stationary) state, assumed smooth away from a finite set of nuclear positions $\{R_\alpha\}\subset\mathbb{R}^3$. Consider the gradient vector field $
ablaho$. A point $p$ is a critical point of rank 3 and signature $-3$ (a $(3,-3)$ attractor) if $
ablaho(p)=0$ and the Hessian of $ho$ at $p$ has three negative eigenvalues; in molecular systems these attractors coincide with the nuclear positions $R_\alpha$. The basin $\Omega_\alpha$ of an attractor $R_\alpha$ is the set of points whose gradient trajectory of $
ablaho$ terminates at $R_\alpha$. The boundary $\partial\Omega_\alpha$ is an interatomic surface satisfying the local zero-flux condition
$$
ablaho(r)\cdot n(r)=0\qquad	ext{for all }r\in\partial\Omega_\alpha,$$
where $n(r)$ is the outward unit normal. A region $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ whose boundary satisfies the same zero-flux equation is called a net-zero-flux basin. The collection of topological atoms $\{\Omega_\alpha\}$ is one such partition, but there exist many other net-zero-flux basins (called quantum divided basins) that are not topological atoms; in particular some such regions contain no nucleus.

Problem. Provide a mathematical principle, formulated intrinsically from the one-electron density and the framework of subsystem quantum mechanics, that singles out the topological atoms $\{\Omega_\alpha\}$ uniquely among all regions of $\mathbb{R}^3$ whose boundaries satisfy the zero-flux equation $
ablaho\cdot n=0$. Equivalently, identify an additional condition (or variational/topological characterization) that, together with the local zero-flux condition, has the topological atoms as its only solutions, and thereby explains why topological atoms—rather than arbitrary net-zero-flux basins—are the physically natural quantum subsystems in the quantum theory of atoms in molecules.

The question of providing a rigorous mathematical principle that uniquely characterizes topological (Bader) atoms among the infinite family of net-zero-flux basins (quantum divided basins) appears to remain open. Existing literature acknowledges that the local zero-flux equation admits many spurious solutions (some without nuclei) and that a rigorous definition of topological atoms requires supplementing it with an auxiliary condition; informal "naturalness" criteria (containing exactly one nucleus, simplest gradient-flow basins) are invoked, but no universally accepted derivation from first principles of subsystem quantum mechanics has been established.

Consider a non-relativistic molecular system consisting of $M$ fixed point-like nuclei with positive charges $\{Z_A\}_{A=1}^M$ at positions $\{\mathbf{R}_A\}_{A=1}^M$ and $N$ electrons, governed by the Hamiltonian
$$ H_{\mathrm{Coul}} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_i^2 - \sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{A=1}^M \frac{Z_A}{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{R}_A|} + \sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}_j|}, $$
with associated ground-state wavefunction $\Psi$ and one-electron density
$$ \rho(\mathbf{r}) = N\int |\Psi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{r}_N)|^2\, d\mathbf{r}_2\cdots d\mathbf{r}_N. $$
The gradient vector field $\nabla\rho$ partitions $\mathbb{R}^3$ into basins associated with its attractors (the asymptotic limits of integral curves of $\nabla\rho$). Empirically, for Coulombic molecular systems the attractors of $\nabla\rho$ coincide (with rare exceptions) with the nuclear positions $\{\mathbf{R}_A\}$, giving rise to the notion of a topological atom. By contrast, for a "Hookean" model in which the electron–nucleus Coulomb attractions $-Z_A/|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{R}_A|$ are replaced by harmonic potentials $\tfrac{1}{2}k|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{R}_A|^2$ (e.g., Hookean $\mathrm{H}_2^+$), the resulting density may possess a single attractor located between the nuclei rather than one attractor at each nucleus.

Provide a rigorous mathematical mechanism — for example, in terms of the Kato cusp condition, analytic structure of $\rho$ near the nuclei, or properties of the electron–nucleus interaction kernel — that explains why, for the Coulombic Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{Coul}}$, the nuclei are necessarily (or generically) the attractors of $\nabla\rho$, while the substitution of Coulomb attractions by harmonic attractions can destroy this property. Equivalently, characterize precisely how the singular $1/r$ form of the electron–nucleus interaction determines the critical-point structure and basin decomposition of the one-electron density so that the topological atom emerges naturally.

Let $\rho:\mathbb{R}^3\to[0,\infty)$ denote the ground-state one-electron density of an $N$-electron molecular system with a fixed configuration of $M$ nuclei at positions $R_1,\dots,R_M\in\mathbb{R}^3$. For an external one-body potential $v:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$, let $\rho_v$ denote the resulting ground-state one-electron density (assumed to exist and be sufficiently smooth so that its critical points and gradient flow are well defined). The topology of $\rho_v$ is the structure consisting of the set of critical points of $\rho_v$ classified by Morse index, together with the gradient-flow cell decomposition of $\mathbb{R}^3$ induced by $-\nabla\rho_v$ (i.e., the partition into "topological atoms" and the network of bond, ring, and cage critical points connecting them).

Consider the point-charge Coulomb external potential
$$v_{\text{pt}}(r) \;=\; -\sum_{A=1}^{M}\frac{Z_A}{|r-R_A|},$$
and let $\mathcal{V}$ be a class of "marginally modified" external potentials with the same nuclear positions $R_1,\dots,R_M$ and charges $Z_1,\dots,Z_M$, including in particular the finite-nucleus models in which each Coulomb singularity is replaced by a smooth potential generated by a finite nuclear charge distribution (e.g., Gaussian or uniform-ball nuclear models).

Problem. Prove or disprove: for every $v\in\mathcal{V}$, the topology of $\rho_v$ (in the sense above) is the same as the topology of $\rho_{v_{\text{pt}}}$. More precisely, establish a precise notion of "marginal modification" of the external potential under which the homeomorphism type of the gradient-flow cell decomposition of $\rho_v$, together with the number and Morse indices of its critical points, is invariant; and use this to extend the critical-distance explanation of the naturalness of topological atoms from the point-charge Coulomb case to this larger class of external potentials.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $w \in \Sigma^*$ be a finite word of length $n$. Two words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$ are said to be Abelian-equivalent, written $u \sim_a v$, if $|u|=|v|$ and for every letter $a \in \Sigma$ the number of occurrences of $a$ in $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $a$ in $v$. A factor $f$ of $w$ is called an Abelian square if $f = uv$ with $u \sim_a v$ (equivalently, $|u|=|v|$ and $u$ and $v$ have the same Parikh vector). Two Abelian squares $u_1 v_1$ and $u_2 v_2$ (with $u_i \sim_a v_i$) are said to be Abelian-equivalent (or "equivalent as Abelian squares") if $u_1 \sim_a u_2$ (which then forces $v_1 \sim_a v_2$ as well). Let $\mathrm{ASQ}(w)$ denote the number of pairwise Abelian-inequivalent Abelian squares occurring as factors of $w$.

Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant $C > 0$ such that for every finite alphabet $\Sigma$ and every word $w \in \Sigma^*$ of length $n \ge 1$,
$$\mathrm{ASQ}(w) \le C\, n\sqrt{n}.$$

The known lower bound for the maximum number of Abelian-inequivalent Abelian squares in a binary word of length n is Ω(n^{1.5}/log n), established by Kociumaka, Radoszewski, Rytter and Waleń (2014/2016). No matching upper bound of order O(n√n) has been published; the conjectured O(n^{1.5}) upper bound remains open according to surveys and follow-up work on nonstandard squares.

The question of defining an origin-independent topological atomic energy for non-Coulombic, inhomogeneous, or marginally modified potentials is posed as an open problem in the foundations of QTAIM. Subsequent literature on QTAIM (including extensions to relativistic, finite-nucleus, and magnetic-interaction settings) acknowledges that the subsystem virial theorem fails to deliver origin independence outside the strictly Coulombic case, and no general resolution satisfying all the standard requirements appears in the published literature; the problem is therefore considered open.

Fix an integer $m \geq 2$. Let $X_0 \geq 0$ be a non-negative, non-constant random variable, and define recursively
$$X_{n+1} = \big(X_n^{(1)} + X_n^{(2)} + \cdots + X_n^{(m)} - 1\big)_+, \qquad n \geq 0,$$
where $X_n^{(1)}, \dots, X_n^{(m)}$ are independent copies of $X_n$ and $x_+ := \max(x,0)$. Since $mE(X_n) - 1 \leq E(X_{n+1}) \leq mE(X_n)$, the limit
$$F_\infty := \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{E(X_n)}{m^n}$$
exists in $[0, \infty)$.

Consider the parametric family of initial laws
$$P_{X_0} = (1-p)\,\delta_0 + p\,P_{Y_0},$$
where $Y_0$ is a fixed positive random variable and $p \in [0,1]$ is a parameter. Write $F_\infty(p)$ for the resulting free energy. Since $p \mapsto F_\infty(p)$ is non-decreasing, there exists a critical threshold $p_c \in [0,1]$ such that $F_\infty(p) = 0$ for $p < p_c$ and $F_\infty(p) > 0$ for $p > p_c$.

Assume $p_c > 0$ (and possibly impose additional integrability conditions on $Y_0$). Determine whether there exists a constant $K \in (0, \infty)$ such that
$$F_\infty(p) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{K + o(1)}{(p - p_c)^{1/2}}\right) \qquad \text{as } p \downarrow p_c.$$

The conjecture was proved in 2019–2021 by Chen, Dagard, Derrida, Hu, Lifshits and Shi (Annals of Probability, 2021), under a suitable integrability assumption on the initial distribution: the free energy vanishes at the transition with the predicted essential singularity of exponent 1/2. Let $\psi$ be the (normalized, antisymmetric) electronic wavefunction of an $N$-electron molecular system, and let $ho:\mathbb{R}^3	o[0,\infty)$ be its associated one-electron density,
$$ho(\mathbf{r})=N\int |\psi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}_2,\dots,\mathbf{r}_N)|^2\,d\mathbf{r}_2\cdots d\mathbf{r}_N.$$
A topological atom $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ is defined as a basin of attraction of the gradient vector field $
ablaho$, equivalently a maximal open region whose boundary $\partial\Omega$ satisfies the zero-flux condition
$$
ablaho(\mathbf{r})\cdot \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r})=0\quad	ext{for all }\mathbf{r}\in\partial\Omega,$$
where $\mathbf{n}$ is the outward unit normal. For a quantum mechanical observable represented by an operator $\hat{A}$ acting on $N$-electron wavefunctions, the corresponding atomic property is
$$M_\Omega[\psi]=\int_\Omega \langle\psi|\hat{A}|\psiangle_\Omega\,d\mathbf{r},$$
where $\langle\cdotangle_\Omega$ denotes the appropriate basin-restricted expectation density.

Question. Does there exist (i) an explicit functional $F_{\hat{A}}[ho|_\Omega]$ of the one-electron density restricted to a topological atom $\Omega$, or alternatively (ii) a well-posed variational principle with Euler–Lagrange equations whose stationary points yield $ho|_\Omega$ (or some other atomic function $f_\Omega$ from which atomic properties may be reconstructed), such that for every quantum observable $\hat{A}$ in a suitable class one has $M_\Omega[\psi]=F_{\hat{A}}[ho|_\Omega]$ (respectively, $M_\Omega[\psi]$ is computable from the variational solution)? Construct such a functional or variational principle, or prove that none exists.

No explicit density functional for topological-atom properties or a fully successful basin-restricted variational principle appears to have been established. Let $\rho:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be the (sufficiently smooth) one-electron charge density of a stationary molecular state, and consider the gradient vector field $\nabla\rho$. A topological atom (atomic basin) $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ is a connected open region whose boundary $\partial\Omega$ consists of interatomic zero-flux surfaces, i.e. surfaces $S$ on which
$$\nabla\rho(\mathbf{r})\cdot\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}) = 0 \quad \text{for every } \mathbf{r}\in S,$$
where $\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r})$ is the unit outward normal at $\mathbf{r}$. For a one-electron Hermitian operator $\hat{A}$, define the basin property
$$A(\Omega) = \int_{\Omega} \rho_A(\mathbf{r})\,d\mathbf{r},$$
where $\rho_A$ is the corresponding property density derived from the molecular wavefunction, and the associated current $\mathbf{j}_A$ on $\partial\Omega$ via the subsystem hypervirial relations.

Question. Do the interatomic zero-flux surfaces act as a "hologram" for topological atoms, in the precise sense that for a sufficiently broad class of one-electron observables $\hat{A}$ the basin property $A(\Omega)$ is determined entirely by the restriction of $\rho$ and of the relevant currents $\mathbf{j}_A$ to the boundary $\partial\Omega$ (without requiring knowledge of $\rho_A$ throughout the three-dimensional interior of $\Omega$)? Equivalently, characterize the class of operators and the boundary data on $\partial\Omega$ that suffice to reconstruct the corresponding bulk basin properties.

representations.normalized:
Background. The Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) partitions a molecule's three-dimensional space using the gradient vector field of the (single-particle) electron density ρ(r). A topological atom Ω is a basin of attraction of ∇ρ associated with a nuclear critical point; distinct basins are separated by interatomic surfaces S, which are the two-dimensional separatrices of the gradient flow, characterized by the zero-flux condition

  ∇ρ(r) · n(r) = 0   for all r ∈ S,

where n(r) is the unit normal to S. For a quantum-mechanical observable with one-particle density operator Ô, its atomic property on Ω is defined by the volume integral

  A(Ω) = ∫_Ω ⟨Ô⟩(r) dr.

Problem. Develop a "boundary-only" (holographic) reformulation of QTAIM with the following precise requirements:

(a) Provide a constructive procedure that, given only the geometric data of the interatomic surface ∂Ω (its embedding in ℝ³, its induced metric, second fundamental form, and the restriction of ρ and its derivatives to ∂Ω), expresses every atomic property A(Ω) of interest (such as electronic population, kinetic energy, dipole and higher multipole moments, virial quantities) as an integral over ∂Ω alone, with no recourse to integration over the three-dimensional basin.

(b) Prove that the resulting surface functionals reproduce the standard three-dimensional QTAIM atomic properties for arbitrary molecular electron densities satisfying the zero-flux boundary condition, and identify the minimal differential-geometric data on ∂Ω (e.g., principal curvatures, mean and Gaussian curvatures, geodesics, intrinsic Laplacian) that suffice for this reduction.

(c) Characterize the analytical differential geometry of QTAIM interatomic surfaces (regularity, curvature bounds, topology, behavior at bond critical points and at infinity) needed to make the reduction in (a)–(b) rigorous and computationally practical.

Determine whether such a boundary-only formulation exists, and if so, exhibit it explicitly.

representations.normalized:
In standard quantum mechanics, a closed system is described by a Hilbert space H, a state (a unit vector or density operator on H), and observables (self-adjoint operators on H), with dynamics generated by a Hamiltonian. The notion of a "subsystem" — a proper part of a larger quantum system together with its complementary "environment" — is not uniquely specified by these axioms: there is no canonical prescription that, given an interacting many-electron system (e.g. a molecule with nuclear configuration fixed in the Born–Oppenheimer approximation, described by an antisymmetric N-electron wavefunction Ψ on R^{3N} together with the one-electron density ρ(r) and the one-body and pair densities derived from Ψ), singles out a decomposition of the total Hilbert space, or of physical space R^3, into a subsystem and its environment in a way that yields well-defined, additive subsystem observables (kinetic energy, potential energy, charge, etc.).

The Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) supplies one such prescription: it partitions R^3 into disjoint open regions Ω (atomic basins) bounded by zero-flux surfaces of the gradient field of the electron density,
   ∇ρ(r) · n(r) = 0  for all r ∈ ∂Ω,
where n(r) is the outward unit normal to ∂Ω. On each such region one defines subsystem observables by integrating appropriate densities over Ω, and a subsystem variational principle (an analogue of Schwinger's principle of stationary action restricted to Ω) is postulated as an additional axiom on top of the axioms of quantum mechanics.

Formulate, within a precise mathematical framework, a set of principles and axioms governing the notion of a quantum subsystem of an interacting N-particle quantum system that
(a) reduces to the standard axioms of quantum mechanics when the subsystem is taken to be the whole system;
(b) selects, from the set of admissible spatial or Hilbert-space decompositions, those which carry well-defined additive observables and a self-consistent subsystem dynamics (or stationary-action principle);
(c) contains the QTAIM zero-flux partitioning and its associated subsystem variational principle as a special case, while admitting natural extensions (for example to open quantum systems, to time-dependent and relativistic settings, to alternative scalar fields replacing ρ, and to non-disjoint or fuzzy partitions).

Determine whether such a system of principles can be formulated, prove its internal consistency, and characterize the class of admissible subsystem decompositions it singles out.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group and let $A \subseteq G$ be a subset of size $m=|A|$. For a positive integer $h$, define the following sumsets:

- Unrestricted sumset: $hA = \{a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_h : a_i \in A\}$, with maximum possible cardinality $\binom{m+h-1}{h}$ (the number of multisets of size $h$ from $m$ elements).
- Unrestricted signed sumset: $h_\pm A = \{\varepsilon_1 a_1 + \cdots + \varepsilon_h a_h : a_i \in A,\ \varepsilon_i \in \{+1,-1\}\}$, with maximum cardinality $c(h,m) := \sum_{k=0}^{h}\binom{m+k-1}{k}\cdot[\text{signed multiset count}]$ (the number of signed multisets of size $h$ from $m$ elements).
- Restricted sumset: $\hat{h}A = \{a_{i_1}+\cdots+a_{i_h} : 1\le i_1<\cdots<i_h\le m\}$, with maximum cardinality $\binom{m}{h}$.
- Restricted signed sumset: $\hat{h}_\pm A = \{\varepsilon_1 a_{i_1}+\cdots+\varepsilon_h a_{i_h} : 1\le i_1<\cdots<i_h\le m,\ \varepsilon_j\in\{\pm 1\}\}$, with maximum cardinality $\binom{m}{h}2^h$.

For $s\ge 0$ define the cumulative versions $[0,s]A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{s} hA$, $[0,s]_\pm A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{s} h_\pm A$, $[0,s]\hat{}A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{s}\hat{h}A$, $[0,s]\hat{}_\pm A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{s}\hat{h}_\pm A$, and the full subset-sum sets $\Sigma A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{m}\hat{h}A$ and $\Sigma_\pm A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{m}\hat{h}_\pm A$.

A set $A$ is called Sidon-type for the corresponding operation if its sumset attains the maximum possible cardinality listed above (so all formal sums are distinct in $G$). Define:

$$\sigma(G,h)=\max\{|A|:|hA|=\tbinom{m+h-1}{h}\},\quad \sigma(G,[0,s])=\max\{|A|:|[0,s]A|=\tbinom{m+s}{s}\},$$
$$\sigma_\pm(G,h)=\max\{|A|:|h_\pm A|=c(h,m)\},\quad \sigma_\pm(G,[0,s])=\max\{|A|:|[0,s]_\pm A|=\textstyle\sum_{h=0}^{s} c(h,m)\},$$
$$\hat\sigma(G,h)=\max\{|A|:|\hat h A|=\tbinom{m}{h}\},\quad \hat\sigma(G,[0,s])=\max\{|A|:|[0,s]\hat{}A|=\textstyle\sum_{h=0}^{s}\binom{m}{h}\},$$
$$\hat\sigma(G,\mathbb{N}_0)=\max\{|A|:|\Sigma A|=2^m\},$$
$$\hat\sigma_\pm(G,h)=\max\{|A|:|\hat h_\pm A|=\tbinom{m}{h}2^h\},\quad \hat\sigma_\pm(G,[0,s])=\max\{|A|:|[0,s]\hat{}_\pm A|=\textstyle\sum_{h=0}^{s}\binom{m}{h}2^h\},$$
$$\hat\sigma_\pm(G,\mathbb{N}_0)=\max\{|A|:|\Sigma_\pm A|=3^m\}.$$

Determine, as functions of the structure of $G$ and the parameters $h$ and $s$, the values of all ten Sidon-type quantities above, and characterize the extremal sets attaining these maxima.

The classical critical number χ̂(G,ℕ₀) (subset-sum spanning) for finite abelian groups was settled in a series of works culminating around 2007–2009 (Gao–Hamidoune, Freeze–Gao–Geroldinger, and others). Model an inflated spherical ball as a thin elastic membrane of radius $R$, wall thickness $h$, Young's modulus $E$, and Poisson ratio $
u$, enclosing a gas at regulated absolute internal pressure $P$ (gauge pressure $P - P_{	ext{atm}}$). The ball, of total mass $m$, impacts a rigid planar surface (or is struck by a rigid implement) with normal incoming speed $v_0$.

During impact, model the contact mechanics so that the contact force $F(t)$, the contact duration $	au$, the maximum deformation $\delta_{\max}$, the coefficient of restitution $e$, and the peak deceleration $a_{\max}$ can each be expressed as functions of $(P, R, h, E, 
u, m, v_0)$.

Define two functionals on the regulated pressure $P$ (with all other parameters fixed by the sport):

1. A "playability" functional $\mathcal{F}(P)$ that increases with the speed and liveliness of the rebound, e.g.
$$\mathcal{F}(P) = e(P) \cdot v_{\text{rebound}}(P) / \tau(P),$$
or any monotone surrogate measuring how fast and dynamic the resulting game is.

2. An "injury risk" functional $\mathcal{R}(P)$ that increases with the impulsive load delivered to a target (a head, a hand, etc.) per impact and accumulates over repetitive impacts, e.g.
$$\mathcal{R}(P) = \big(\max_t F(t;P)\big)^{\alpha} \cdot \big(a_{\max}(P)\big)^{\beta}$$
for suitable exponents $\alpha, \beta > 0$ derived from a chosen biomechanical injury criterion.

The problem is:

(a) Derive, from first principles of membrane elasticity coupled to the gas equation of state, explicit (possibly asymptotic) expressions for $F(t)$, $\tau$, $\delta_{\max}$, $e$, and $a_{\max}$ as functions of $P$ in the regimes where pressure-induced membrane tension dominates and where bending/elastic stiffness dominates.

(b) Using these expressions, determine the optimal regulated pressure
$$P^* = \arg\max_{P > P_{\text{atm}}} \big[\mathcal{F}(P) - \lambda \, \mathcal{R}(P)\big]$$
for a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda > 0$ encoding the fun-versus-risk trade-off, and characterize how $P^*$ scales with $(R, h, E, m, v_0)$.

(c) Decide whether the empirically prescribed inflation-pressure ranges across major sports (e.g. basketball, soccer, volleyball, rugby, tennis) are consistent with the values of $P^*$ predicted by the model in (b), thereby confirming or refuting the hypothesis that regulated inflation pressures correspond to a fun/risk optimum.

Consider the normal impact of a hollow or inflated spherical ball with a rigid surface. Define the dimensionless storage number St as the ratio of elastic energy stored in the shell to that stored in the enclosed gas during deformation, so that St ≫ 1 corresponds to a shell-dominated ball (e.g. a table-tennis ball, where the shell elasticity stores essentially all the deformation energy) and St ≪ 1 corresponds to a gas-dominated inflated ball (e.g. a basketball, where the gas pressure stores essentially all the deformation energy and the shell behaves as an inertial membrane). Let A denote the characteristic amplitude and f the characteristic frequency of post-impact vibrations of the shell/membrane, and let M denote the ball mass. Model the kinetic energy carried by such vibrations as E_{d,vib} ≈ (1/2) M (2π f A)^2 (or an appropriate modal generalization), and compare it with the kinetic energy lost in the collision (the difference between incoming and rebound translational kinetic energies).

Question: Can the transfer of translational kinetic energy into shell vibrations (St ≫ 1) or into inflated-membrane vibrations (St ≪ 1) quantitatively account for the measured energy dissipation in such impacts? Specifically:
(a) Derive, for each regime, the expected relations between A, f, the geometric and material parameters of the ball (radius, shell thickness, Young's modulus, surface density, internal gas pressure), and the impact velocity.
(b) Determine whether the resulting amplitudes and frequencies are large enough so that E_{d,vib} matches the experimentally observed dissipated energy, and identify in which of the two regimes (shell-elastic vs. gas-elastic membrane) vibrational losses can or cannot be the dominant dissipation mechanism.

Consider a non-relativistic free atom with N electrons and a single nucleus of charge Z>0 located at the origin in R^3, governed by the standard many-electron Schrödinger Hamiltonian
  H = -∑_{i=1}^N (1/2)Δ_i  - ∑_{i=1}^N Z/|r_i| + ∑_{1≤i<j≤N} 1/|r_i - r_j|,
acting on the antisymmetric subspace of L^2((R^3×{↑,↓})^N). Let Ψ_0 be a (normalized) ground-state wavefunction of H, and define the one-electron density
  ρ(r) = N ∑_{σ_1,...,σ_N} ∫_{R^{3(N-1)}} |Ψ_0(r,σ_1; r_2,σ_2; ... ; r_N,σ_N)|^2 dr_2 ... dr_N.

Prove (or disprove) the following two statements about ρ:

(a) The function ρ has exactly one attractor (i.e. local maximum) on R^3, located at the position of the nucleus r=0, and this critical point is non-degenerate of Morse type (3,−3) (the Hessian of ρ at 0 has three negative eigenvalues).

(b) The density ρ is radially monotonically decreasing away from the nucleus: along every ray emanating from the origin, ρ is a strictly decreasing function of the distance |r|. Equivalently, the spherically averaged density ρ̄(r) = (4π)^{-1} ∫_{S^2} ρ(rω) dω satisfies dρ̄/dr < 0 for r>0, and moreover ρ itself decreases on every radial direction.

Establish (a) and (b) as theorems derived from the underlying many-body quantum mechanics, rather than as numerically observed regularities.

The conjecture that the ground-state one-electron density of a free atom is monotonically decreasing along every ray from the nucleus (and has its unique maximum, of (3,−3) type, at the nucleus) is a long-standing open problem. Rigorous results are known only in special cases: it holds rigorously for hydrogen and for one-electron systems whose external potential increases monotonically from the nucleus, and partial/sufficient conditions have been derived for two-electron and many-electron systems (e.g. Ayers 2003, Angulo–Dehesa 1991). The general many-electron case remains unproven.

Consider an inflated elastic ball (a thin membrane enclosing a gas at pressure above atmospheric) that is dropped onto a rigid horizontal surface and bounces. During impact, a portion of the kinetic energy is dissipated, and one candidate mechanism is dissipation inside the gas itself, namely:

(i) irreversible compression of the gas,
(ii) viscous friction within the gas flow generated by the deformation of the ball, and
(iii) non-reversible thermodynamic transformations of gas components such as condensation/evaporation of water vapour.

Formulate and answer the following question quantitatively. Let T_0 denote the equilibrium gas temperature inside the ball before the impact and T_eq the equilibrium gas temperature after the ball has come to rest following the bounce (after pressure equilibration but before significant thermal exchange with the surroundings). Let E_kin be the kinetic energy lost by the ball during the impact (difference between kinetic energies just before and just after the bounce).

(a) Is the fraction of E_kin dissipated by irreversible processes inside the enclosed gas a significant (non-negligible) part of the total impact dissipation?

(b) Does T_eq exceed T_0, and if so by how much, as a function of the impact velocity, ball geometry, internal pressure, and gas composition?

(c) How does this dissipated fraction depend on the gas filling the ball, when the gas is varied among water-vapour-saturated air, dry air, pure diatomic nitrogen N_2, and monoatomic helium He?

Provide a model (for example, computing the internal gas flow during deformation and the work of viscous stresses, together with the thermodynamic cycle followed by the gas) that predicts (a)–(c), and compare its predictions with the corresponding measurements (e.g. fast-response thermocouple recordings of the internal temperature evolution).

Consider a non-relativistic Coulombic molecular system with N electrons and q clamped nuclei located at positions R_1,...,R_q in R^3, with nuclear charges Z_1,...,Z_q > 0. The electronic Hamiltonian (in atomic units) is

  H = -1/2 sum_{i=1}^N Δ_{r_i} - sum_{i=1}^N sum_{A=1}^q Z_A/|r_i - R_A| + sum_{1<=i<j<=N} 1/|r_i - r_j| + sum_{1<=A<B<=q} Z_A Z_B/|R_A - R_B|.

Let Ψ be a normalized ground-state wavefunction of H (with the nuclear positions fixed as parameters), and let

  ρ(r; R_1,...,R_q) = N ∫ |Ψ(r, r_2,...,r_N)|^2 ds dr_2 ... dr_N

be the associated one-electron density on R^3, where the spin coordinate s and the electron coordinates r_2,...,r_N are integrated out. A point r* ∈ R^3 is called a critical point of ρ if ∇ρ(r*) = 0; it is of type (3,-3) (a local maximum / "attractor") if the Hessian of ρ at r* is negative definite. A nuclear (3,-3) critical point is one located at some R_A; any other (3,-3) critical point is called a non-nuclear attractor.

Question: Prove or disprove the following conjecture.

(a) For every pair of nuclei (A,B) there exists a critical internuclear distance d^c_{AB} > 0 such that, whenever |R_A - R_B| > d^c_{AB} for all 1 <= A < B <= q, the gradient field of ρ has exactly q critical points of type (3,-3), and these are precisely the nuclear positions R_1,...,R_q (in particular, ρ has no non-nuclear attractors).

(b) Formulate in mathematically precise terms, and prove, the statement that for "most" molecules the equilibrium internuclear distances (the local minimizers of the Born–Oppenheimer total energy as a function of (R_1,...,R_q)) exceed the corresponding critical distances d^c_{AB}.

Consider a molecule modeled in the Born–Oppenheimer approximation as a quantum system of N electrons in the field of fixed nuclei, with associated electronic state described by a density operator ρ on the antisymmetric Fock/Hilbert space, and with one-electron density ρ(r) = N ∫|Ψ|² dτ' that is partitioned in real space according to the Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM): each topological atom Ω is the basin of attraction in the gradient vector field ∇ρ(r) of a nuclear maximum, with interatomic surfaces S(Ω) satisfying the zero-flux condition ∇ρ(r)·n(r) = 0 for all r ∈ S(Ω).

Adopt the framework of open quantum systems, in which a subsystem A coupled to an environment E is described by a reduced density operator ρ_A = Tr_E ρ_{AE} obtained by partial trace, together with an associated dynamical map (e.g., a completely positive trace-preserving evolution or a Lindblad-type master equation) governing its effective dynamics.

Problem. Develop a rigorous formalism in which a topological atom Ω ⊂ ℝ³ (an open spatial subsystem with permeable, zero-flux boundary, exchanging electrons and energy with its complement Ω' in the molecule) is treated as an open quantum subsystem, and use this formalism to give an efficient state specification of the topological atom. Specifically:

(a) Define an appropriate reduced state ρ_Ω that encodes the quantum state of the electrons confined to (or associated with) the basin Ω, obtained by an analogue of the partial trace over the degrees of freedom in Ω', and show that it reproduces the standard QTAIM observables (atomic populations, kinetic and potential energy contributions, atomic multipole moments) as expectation values Tr(ρ_Ω O_Ω) of suitable operators O_Ω restricted to Ω.

(b) Derive the effective (possibly non-unitary) dynamical equation governing ρ_Ω that accounts for the exchange of electrons and energy across the interatomic surface S(Ω), and identify the conditions under which this evolution admits a Markovian (Lindblad) form.

(c) Determine whether such an open-system description provides a more efficient and physically faithful state specification of the topological atom than the standard QTAIM characterization, and, in particular, whether it resolves the issue of inferring atomic properties from a well-defined subsystem state rather than from spatially restricted integrals over the total molecular wavefunction.

Setting. Let ρ : ℝ³ → ℝ_{≥0} be the (one-electron) electron density of a molecular system, viewed as a smooth scalar field with isolated nuclear maxima. The Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) partitions ℝ³ into disjoint open "topological atoms" Ω_A, where each Ω_A is the basin of attraction (under the gradient flow of ρ) of a nuclear critical point. Each basin is bounded by an interatomic surface S_A consisting of points where the gradient ∇ρ is tangent to the surface, i.e. ∇ρ · n = 0, with n the outward unit normal (the zero-flux boundary condition).

For a quantum-mechanical observable represented by an operator O, the average value over the topological atom Ω_A is ⟨O⟩_A = ∫_{Ω_A} ρ_O(r) dr for an appropriate density ρ_O derived from the system's wavefunction. The subsystem hypervirial theorem states that for a wide class of observables, ⟨O⟩_A can be reconstructed from a "property current" J_O on S_A via a Gauss-like identity of the form
   ⟨O⟩_A = ∮_{S_A} J_O · n dS,
i.e. the basin property is recoverable purely from boundary data (a "holographic" relation).

However, certain properties of topological atoms are not known to admit such a representation. Two important examples are:
 (i) the atomic energy E(Ω_A), defined via the kinetic energy density and an appropriate share of the potential energy of Ω_A;
 (ii) the (de)localization indices λ(Ω_A) and δ(Ω_A, Ω_B), defined for a state with one- and two-electron density matrices ρ₁, ρ₂ by
   δ(Ω_A, Ω_B) = -2 ∫_{Ω_A} ∫_{Ω_B} [ρ₂(r₁,r₂) - ρ(r₁)ρ(r₂)] dr₁ dr₂,
   λ(Ω_A) = δ(Ω_A, Ω_A)/2,
which measure electron sharing between basins.

Problem. Establish (or disprove) a general Gauss-like theorem for topological atoms that strictly extends the subsystem hypervirial theorem and applies to every conceivable property ⟨O⟩_A of a topological atom Ω_A. More precisely: for any reasonable atomic property functional F[ρ, ρ₁, ρ₂, …](Ω_A) — including in particular the atomic energy E(Ω_A), the localization index λ(Ω_A), and the delocalization indices δ(Ω_A, Ω_B) — exhibit a vector (or tensor) field J_F constructible from the wavefunction, defined on (a neighborhood of) S_A, such that
   F(Ω_A) = ∮_{S_A} J_F · n dS,
thereby realizing a fully holographic principle in which all properties of a topological atom are determined by data on its interatomic surface; or else prove that no such universal boundary representation can exist.

Setup. In the Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM), a molecular system is described by a smooth, everywhere-positive electron density ρ : ℝ³ → ℝ_{>0} obtained from the underlying many-electron wavefunction. A topological atom Ω ⊂ ℝ³ is defined as a basin of the gradient vector field ∇ρ: namely, Ω is a maximal open subset of ℝ³ such that every integral curve of ∇ρ starting in Ω terminates at the same nuclear critical point (a local maximum of ρ). Equivalently, Ω is bounded by a zero-flux surface S = ∂Ω satisfying ∇ρ(r) · n(r) = 0 for every r ∈ S, where n is the outward unit normal. To each one-electron property A is associated a property current j_A on ℝ³, derived from the wavefunction, whose integral fluxes through ∂Ω determine the atomic contribution of Ω to A.

Problem. Determine whether QTAIM, viewed either as a theory of the pair (ρ, {j_A}) or as a theory of its topological atoms Ω, admits a non-trivial dual formulation. In particular, decide each of the following:

(a) Does there exist a non-Euclidean Riemannian (or more general) manifold (M, g), depending functorially on (ℝ³, ρ), and a density ρ̃ on M corresponding to a free (non-interacting) atom, such that the topological atom (Ω, ρ|_Ω) in Euclidean three-space is isomorphic — under a precisely specified equivalence of densities, currents, and basin/zero-flux structures — to (M, ρ̃)? Construct such a duality, or prove that no such non-trivial correspondence exists.

(b) Does there exist a stationary non-equilibrium thermodynamic open system, with a well-defined boundary geometry and boundary flows, such that the property currents {j_A} of a topological atom Ω are equivalent (as vector fields with associated conserved fluxes) to the boundary flows of this thermodynamic system, in a way that recovers all QTAIM atomic observables? Either exhibit such a correspondence or prove its impossibility.

A non-trivial dual is required to give a bijection on observables that is not merely a tautological relabeling.

representations.normalized:
In the quantum theory of atoms in molecules, a molecular system is described by its (scalar) one-electron charge density ρ: ℝ³ → ℝ_{≥0}, a smooth function whose critical points (where ∇ρ = 0) are classified by the signature of the Hessian into nuclear attractors (3,−3), bond critical points (3,−1), ring critical points (3,+1), and cage critical points (3,+3). Atomic basins are defined as the connected regions of the gradient field ∇ρ bounded by zero-flux surfaces (surfaces S satisfying ∇ρ(r)·n(r)=0 for all r ∈ S). As nuclear coordinates evolve along a reaction path R(t), the critical points of ρ(·;R(t)) migrate continuously in ℝ³ (away from catastrophe events).

The problem is to formulate a "liquid (continuum) model" for the dynamics of the charge density ρ in which:

1. The migrating critical points {x_k(t)} of ρ(·;R(t)) are treated as transported by an effective velocity field on a viscous medium, governed by a constitutive law of the form
   η(ρ,∇ρ,…) · ẋ_k(t) = F_k[ρ, R, Ṙ],
   where η is a scalar (or tensorial) viscosity functional taken as the principal parameter of the model and F_k is a force functional derivable from the energetic and topological structure of ρ.

2. The model reproduces, in appropriate limits, the established mechanics of the charge density (continuity equation for ρ, atomic-basin force and virial theorems, and stationarity of zero-flux surfaces), and yields a closed evolution equation for ρ along nuclear motion compatible with the catastrophe set of QTAIM.
