In the quantum theory of atoms in molecules, a molecular system is described by its (scalar) one-electron charge density ρ: ℝ³ → ℝ_{≥0}, a smooth function whose critical points (where ∇ρ = 0) are classified by the signature of the Hessian into nuclear attractors (3,−3), bond critical points (3,−1), ring critical points (3,+1), and cage critical points (3,+3). Atomic basins are defined as the connected regions of the gradient field ∇ρ bounded by zero-flux surfaces (surfaces S satisfying ∇ρ(r)·n(r)=0 for all r ∈ S). As nuclear coordinates evolve along a reaction path R(t), the critical points of ρ(·;R(t)) migrate continuously in ℝ³ (away from catastrophe events).

The problem is to formulate a "liquid (continuum) model" for the dynamics of the charge density ρ in which:

1. The migrating critical points {x_k(t)} of ρ(·;R(t)) are treated as transported by an effective velocity field on a viscous medium, governed by a constitutive law of the form
   η(ρ,∇ρ,…) · ẋ_k(t) = F_k[ρ, R, Ṙ],
   where η is a scalar (or tensorial) viscosity functional taken as the principal parameter of the model and F_k is a force functional derivable from the energetic and topological structure of ρ.

2. The model reproduces, in appropriate limits, the established mechanics of the charge density (continuity equation for ρ, atomic-basin force and virial theorems, and stationarity of zero-flux surfaces), and yields a closed evolution equation for ρ along nuclear motion compatible with the catastrophe set of QTAIM.

Construct such a model with a precisely defined viscosity functional η, derive the corresponding equations of motion for ρ and for its critical points, and use it to address at least one of the following standing problems: (a) prediction of bifurcation thresholds at which bond/ring/cage critical points coalesce or annihilate, (b) quantitative characterization of "structural stability" of molecular graphs under nuclear displacement, and (c) extension of the mechanics of the charge density to a complete dynamical theory consistent with the underlying quantum stress-tensor field.

Determine whether such a viscosity-based liquid model of the charge density exists with the above properties, and exhibit it explicitly, or prove that no such consistent model can be formulated within the QTAIM framework.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is a programmatic open problem about formulating a new "liquid/viscous" continuum model for the QTAIM charge density. No subsequent work appears to have constructed such a model with viscosity as principal parameter; the broader program of completing the mechanics of the charge density remains open in the QTAIM literature.

Consider the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), a reinforcement-learning benchmark in which an agent interacts with Atari 2600 games through a deterministic simulator (the emulator) that, at each discrete time step t, takes the current RAM/screen state s_t and an action a_t from a finite action set A and returns the next state s_{t+1}, a reward r_t, and a terminal flag. A learned model of an ALE game is a function M (typically parameterized by a neural network or other learned representation) that, given a state representation and an action, predicts the next state representation and reward, and which can be iterated to produce rollouts of length H by feeding its own predictions back as input.

Design and analyze a learned model M of Atari 2600 games in the ALE satisfying simultaneously the following three properties:

1. (Long-horizon accuracy.) The expected prediction error of M over rollouts of horizon H grows sufficiently slowly with H that compounding errors do not render the model useless for planning at horizons relevant to control on representative ALE titles.

2. (Computational efficiency.) The wall-clock cost per simulated step of M is no larger than that of the Stella emulator itself, so that using M for planning yields a strict speed advantage over planning directly with the emulator.

3. (Robust planning under model error.) Provide a planning algorithm that, when paired with such an imperfect M, achieves performance on a broad suite of ALE games that is competitive with, or better than, planning algorithms that have access to the exact emulator under matched compute budgets, despite errors in M that compound over time.

Equivalently: exhibit a learned model and an associated planning procedure for the ALE that is fast (faster than the emulator), accurate over long rollouts, and effective for planning even when the model is imperfect; or prove that no such combination can exist under stated computational/statistical assumptions.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Substantial progress has been made since the problem was posed. SimPLe (Kaiser et al., ICLR 2020) demonstrated successful planning with a learned video model in the ALE, mitigating compounding error via short rollouts. MuZero (Schrittwieser et al., 2019/2020) achieved state-of-the-art Atari performance by planning with a learned latent model, and DreamerV2/V3 (Hafner et al., 2020/2023) attained human-level Atari performance using learned world models. These works address long-horizon accuracy and planning under imperfect models, though achieving a learned model that is simultaneously faster than the Stella emulator, accurate over long rollouts, and robust for planning across all ALE titles remains not fully resolved; hence partially solved.

Consider the normal impact of an inflated elastic ball (e.g. a sports ball, modeled as a thin pressurized spherical shell of radius R filled with gas at internal pressure p, mass m) striking a flat rigid surface at vertical velocity V. As the ball deforms against the surface, a circular contact patch forms whose radius l(t) grows in time; from the geometry of a sphere indented by a depth x = Vt, one has l(t) ≈ √(2Rx) so that the lateral expansion velocity of the ball–ground–air contact line is

  dl/dt ≈ V √(R/(2x)),

which diverges as x → 0+. While dl/dt exceeds the speed of sound c_s in the surrounding air, a shock wave is emitted from the contact line, and once dl/dt < c_s ordinary acoustic radiation continues.

Problem. Derive a quantitative estimate of the total energy E_sound radiated as sound and shock waves into the surrounding air during a single normal impact, expressed in terms of the impact parameters (V, R, m, ambient air density ρ_air and sound speed c_s, and any relevant material/pressure parameters). In particular:

(a) determine the contribution from the supersonic regime dl/dt > c_s, where shock-wave dissipation occurs along the moving contact line, and the contribution from the subsonic acoustic radiation regime;

(b) compare E_sound with the typical total kinetic energy lost in such an impact (of order ΔE ∼ (1/2) m V² with restitution losses on the order of tens of joules for a standard sports ball), and decide whether sound/shock-wave radiation is a negligible contribution to the overall energy budget of the impact.

Provide the scaling laws, the explicit estimate, and the criterion under which the inequality E_sound ≪ ΔE holds.

Consider the Arcade Learning Environment, a benchmark in which a reinforcement-learning agent interacts with a suite of Atari 2600 games. Each game is modeled as a Markov decision process M = (S, A, P, R, γ) where S is a set of screen-derived states, A is a finite set of joystick actions, P is a stochastic transition kernel, R is a scalar reward, and γ ∈ (0,1) is a discount factor. Given a finite collection of source games {M_1, …, M_k} on which the agent has been trained and a target game M_t drawn from the same suite, define the sample complexity N(M_t; ε) as the minimum number of environment interactions required for the agent to attain expected return within ε of an optimum-policy baseline.

Design and analyze a transfer-learning procedure T that, taking as input the agent's experience on {M_1, …, M_k}, produces an initialization for learning on M_t such that:

1. (Positive transfer.) For target games M_t that are similar to some source games, N(M_t; ε) under T is provably smaller than N(M_t; ε) when learning from scratch.

2. (Loose analogy.) The reduction in sample complexity persists when the source and target games share only abstract structural features (e.g., common object dynamics or shared reward semantics) rather than near-identical visual or mechanical structure.

3. (Avoidance of negative transfer.) T includes an automatic, data-driven mechanism that decides, for each candidate source M_i, whether using its experience accelerates or harms learning on M_t, discarding or down-weighting sources that would cause N(M_t; ε) to increase relative to learning from scratch.

4. (Disentangled transfer.) T transfers representation (a state-encoding map φ: S → R^d) and policy (a mapping π: S → Δ(A) or value function Q: S × A → R) as separable components, rather than as a single monolithic pretrained network, and allows either component to be transferred independently.

Provide such a procedure together with theoretical or empirical guarantees on each of the four properties across the Atari suite.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Transfer across Atari games remains an active, unresolved research direction. Methods such as Actor-Mimic, Progressive Networks, PathNet, policy distillation, and more recent multi-task agents (e.g., Multi-Game Decision Transformer, Gato) demonstrate partial successes, but no published method simultaneously (i) automatically detects and avoids negative transfer, (ii) handles only loosely analogous games, and (iii) cleanly disentangles representation from policy transfer with guarantees. The combined problem as stated is therefore still considered open.

Consider a thin-walled inflated spherical ball (a pressurized elastic shell) of mass $m$, outer radius $R$, shell thickness $h$, and internal gauge pressure $P$, made of a viscoelastic material (e.g., synthetic rubber) with high-strain-rate dynamic viscosity $\eta(\dot\varepsilon)$ for strain rates $\dot\varepsilon \in [10^2, 10^3]\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The ball impacts a rigid flat surface normally with pre-impact speed $U_0$ and rebounds with speed $U_1$; define the coefficient of restitution $e = U_1/U_0$. During contact, the shell undergoes rapid bending and local flattening over a contact patch, producing viscous dissipation $E_{\mathrm{visc}}$ in the shell material in addition to other loss channels (aerodynamic, acoustic, internal-gas, substrate).

(a) Derive a quantitative model that expresses the energy $E_{\mathrm{visc}}$ dissipated by viscoelastic bending and deformation of the shell during a single normal impact as an explicit function of the parameters $(m, R, h, P, U_0, \eta)$, including the dependence on the effective strain-rate spectrum induced by the impact.

(b) Using this model, determine the contribution $\Delta(1-e^2)_{\mathrm{shell}}$ of shell viscoelastic dissipation to $1 - e^2$, and characterize how this contribution depends on shell thickness $h$ in the limit $h \to 0$ (in particular, decide whether $\Delta(1-e^2)_{\mathrm{shell}} \to 0$).

(c) Extend the model to a shell composed of $N$ bonded layers with individual thicknesses $h_i$ and viscosities $\eta_i$, and incorporate the effect of seams (stitched or glued joints of total length $L_s$ and characteristic compliance differing from the bulk shell), and predict how multilayer construction and seams modify $e$ relative to a homogeneous single-layer shell of the same total thickness, mass, radius, and internal pressure.

Provide closed-form scaling laws and, for a basketball-like configuration ($m \approx 0.6\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R \approx 0.12\,\mathrm{m}$, $U_0 = 16\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\eta \sim 0.2\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$), compute $E_{\mathrm{visc}}$.

Consider three families of polynomials defined by three-term recurrence relations and the initial condition P_0 = 1, P_{-1} = 0, as follows.

(A) A continuous four-parameter family $\{H_n(z;\mu,\nu,\alpha,\theta)\}_{n\geq 0}$ of polynomials in the real variable $z\in\mathbb{R}$, depending on parameters $\mu,\nu,\alpha,\theta$, satisfying a symmetric three-term recurrence
$$z\,H_n(z) = a_n\,H_{n+1}(z) + b_n\,H_n(z) + a_{n-1}\,H_{n-1}(z),$$
with prescribed coefficients $a_n=a_n(\mu,\nu,\alpha,\theta)$ and $b_n=b_n(\mu,\nu,\alpha,\theta)$ depending on the four parameters.

(B) A discrete four-parameter family $\{h_n(k;\mu,\nu,\alpha,\beta)\}_{n\geq 0}$ associated with a countably infinite spectrum indexed by $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$, defined by an analogous three-term recurrence with prescribed coefficients depending on $\mu,\nu,\alpha,\beta$.

(C) A discrete four-parameter family $\{g_n(k;\mu,\nu,\beta,N)\}_{n=0}^{N}$ associated with a finite spectrum of size $N+1$, defined by an analogous three-term recurrence with prescribed coefficients depending on $\mu,\nu,\beta,N$.

For each of these three families, derive a complete analytic description starting from the recurrence and initial values. Specifically, determine in closed form (for example in terms of generalized hypergeometric functions ${}_pF_q$):
1. the orthogonality measure / weight function with respect to which the family is orthogonal,
2. a generating function $\sum_{n\geq 0} H_n(z)\,t^n/c_n$ (or its discrete analogue),
3. the asymptotic behaviour of the polynomials as $n\to\infty$,
4. the orthogonality relations and the normalization constants,
5. a Rodrigues-type formula expressing $P_n$ via repeated differences/derivatives of the weight,
6. forward and backward shift operator relations,
7. the distribution and asymptotics of the zeros,
8. an explicit closed-form representation of $P_n$ (e.g. as a hypergeometric function).

Consider the normal impact of an inflated spherical ball of mass m, undeformed radius R_0, and internal inflation pressure P_0 against a rigid flat surface, with initial impact speed U_0. Let x(t) denote the indentation (compression) of the ball at time t, and let \dot{x}(t) be the indentation speed. A proposed model for the dissipative force acting on the ball during contact is

   F_d(t) = - m \dot{x}(t)^2 / (2 R_0).

Under this model the equation of motion of the ball's center of mass during contact is m \ddot{x} = F_{el}(x, P_0) + F_d, where F_{el} is the (conservative) elastic restoring force arising from membrane deformation and pressurization.

Resolve the following:

(a) Provide a microscopic physical mechanism (for example, excitation of shell vibrational modes, internal acoustic radiation, viscoelastic membrane losses, or gas-dynamic dissipation) that derives, from first principles, a dissipative force of the form F_d = - m \dot{x}^2 / (2 R_0) for an inflated elastic shell impacting a rigid wall, and identify the regime of inflation pressure, shell stiffness, and impact velocity in which such a derivation is valid.

(b) Using this model, compute the coefficient of restitution

   e(U_0, P_0, \text{shell parameters}) = |\dot{x}(t_f)| / U_0,

where t_f is the moment of separation, and determine whether its predicted dependence on U_0, P_0, and the mechanical parameters of the shell (Young's modulus, thickness, areal density) agrees with systematic experimental measurements of e obtained by varying inflation pressure and shell characteristics over a broad range.

Decide whether the momentum-flux dissipation law F_d = - m \dot{x}^2 / (2 R_0) is a physically valid description of energy loss in inflated-ball impacts.

Consider a family of polynomials $\{\widetilde{W}_n(z^2;\kappa,\tau,\eta,\xi)\}_{n\geq 0}$ in the variable $z^2$, depending on real parameters $\kappa,\tau,\eta,\xi$, defined by initial conditions $\widetilde{W}_0=1$, $\widetilde{W}_{-1}=0$ together with a deformed three-term recursion relation of the form
$$z^2\,\widetilde{W}_n(z^2) = A_n\,\widetilde{W}_{n+1}(z^2) + B_n\,\widetilde{W}_n(z^2) + C_n\,\widetilde{W}_{n-1}(z^2),$$
where the coefficients $A_n, B_n, C_n$ are explicit rational functions of $n$ and the parameters $(\kappa,\tau,\eta,\xi)$ that reduce, in a limiting case, to those of the classical Wilson polynomials, but in the deformed case introduce a Heun-type modification (so that the family is sometimes called the Racah–Heun polynomial family).

Determine the analytic structure of $\widetilde{W}_n(z^2;\kappa,\tau,\eta,\xi)$. Specifically:

1. Find an explicit closed-form representation (e.g., in terms of (generalized) hypergeometric functions or Heun functions) for $\widetilde{W}_n(z^2;\kappa,\tau,\eta,\xi)$.
2. Determine a positive weight function $\rho(z^2;\kappa,\tau,\eta,\xi)$ (continuous, discrete, or mixed) with respect to which the polynomials are orthogonal, and write the corresponding orthogonality relation.
3. Derive a generating function $\sum_{n\geq 0} \widetilde{W}_n(z^2;\kappa,\tau,\eta,\xi)\, t^n / c_n$ for an appropriate normalization sequence $c_n$.
4. Establish the asymptotic behavior of $\widetilde{W}_n$ as $n\to\infty$ and as $|z|\to\infty$.
5. Provide a Rodrigues-type formula expressing $\widetilde{W}_n$ via repeated application of a divided-difference (or shift) operator to a product of Pochhammer-type factors.
6. Identify forward and backward shift operators $\mathcal{F}$, $\mathcal{B}$ in the variable $z$ such that $\mathcal{F}\,\widetilde{W}_n = \lambda_n\,\widetilde{W}_{n-1}^{(+)}$ and $\mathcal{B}\,\widetilde{W}_n^{(+)} = \mu_n\,\widetilde{W}_{n+1}$ for suitable parameter-shifted families and constants $\lambda_n,\mu_n$.
7. Locate the zeros of $\widetilde{W}_n$ in the complex plane and describe their interlacing and asymptotic distribution.

Consider an American football modeled as a prolate-spheroidal inflated elastic shell containing air at gauge pressure $P$, gripped, thrown, and caught by a player. Develop a mechanical model of (i) the grip phase, in which the quarterback's fingers compress the ball and tangential friction must prevent slip during the launching motion, and (ii) the catching phase, in which the ball impacts a receiver's hands and either is retained or rebounds elastically. The model should incorporate the dependence of the ball's local surface stiffness, contact area, and coefficient of restitution on the internal pressure $P$.

(a) Show analytically how the maximum tangential force transmitted to the ball during the launch and the rebound velocity during the catch depend on $P$, and explain in mechanical terms why decreasing $P$ below the regulation value facilitates both launching and receiving the ball.

(b) Using realistic parameters for an NFL football (mass, dimensions, shell elastic moduli, regulation pressure range, throw and catch velocities), compute a quantitative estimate of the performance benefit — for instance, the increase in probability of a successful catch, the reduction in fumble probability, or the increase in effective grip force — obtained when the gauge pressure is reduced from the regulation lower limit (about 12.5 psi) to the under-inflated values (about 10.5–11.5 psi) reported in the 2015 AFC Championship "Deflategate" incident.

Consider a sequential interaction between a learning agent and one or more other agents in a stochastic environment. Formally, let the environment be described by a partially observable stochastic game with state space S, joint action space A = A_1 × ... × A_n, transition kernel T(s' | s, a), and, for the learning agent, an observation kernel O(o | s, a) over an observation space Ω. At each time step t the learning agent receives only an observation o_t ∈ Ω that may (i) reveal the underlying environment state s_t only partially or noisily, and (ii) reveal the actions a_{-i,t} of the other agents only partially, noisily, or not at all (some action coordinates may be missing). The learning agent does not have access to the observation kernel O and cannot obtain the conditional probabilities of observations from prior domain knowledge.

Each other agent j is assumed to act according to an unknown stationary (or history-dependent) policy π_j mapping its own interaction history to a distribution over A_j. The behaviour model of agent j is the policy π_j (or a sufficient parametrization thereof).

Develop and rigorously analyze a procedure by which the learning agent, using only its sequence of observations (o_1, o_2, …) and its own actions, produces an estimator π̂_j of each other agent's policy π_j such that:

1. The estimator is consistent or has provable error bounds with respect to a suitable distance on policies (for example expected total-variation distance between π̂_j(· | h) and π_j(· | h) under the induced state-history distribution), despite incomplete, noisy, or missing observations of states and of other agents' actions.

2. The procedure does not require the observation kernel O or any prior specification of observation probabilities, but instead either jointly identifies (O, π_j) from data up to an explicitly characterized identifiability class, or yields policy estimates that are invariant to the unknown O within such a class.

3. The procedure's sample and computational complexity, and its identifiability assumptions on (S, A, T, O, π_j), are explicitly stated.

State precise conditions on the partially observable stochastic game under which such an estimator exists, and construct an algorithm achieving these guarantees, or prove impossibility results delimiting when behaviour-model reconstruction under unknown observation probabilities is infeasible.

Consider an autonomous decision-making agent A interacting in an environment that produces, at each time step t, a high-dimensional observation x_t ∈ X ⊆ R^n (which may encode the full interaction history up to time t and/or a high-dimensional state description). Another agent B chooses actions a_t ∈ A according to a stochastic policy π(a_t | f(x_t)), where f : X → R^k is an unknown projection onto an unknown subset S ⊆ {1, …, n} of size k ≪ n of the available factors; that is, B's action distribution depends only on the coordinates in S, while remaining factors are statistically irrelevant to π given S.

A observes a stream of pairs (x_t, a_t) generated by B's interaction with the environment. A does not know S, does not know k, and is not given an a priori list of candidate subsets. Exhaustively enumerating all 2^n subsets of {1, …, n}, or learning a separate model for each, is infeasible.

Design and analyze an algorithm that, from the observed data, identifies (with high probability) the relevant subset S — equivalently, recovers the support of B's policy dependence — using a number of samples and a runtime that scale polynomially in n and in 1/ε for an accuracy parameter ε on the resulting predictive policy, and that does not rely on (i) prior knowledge of S, (ii) an explicit enumeration of all candidate factors, or (iii) brute-force combinatorial search over subsets. Provide provable guarantees on sample complexity, computational complexity, and recovery accuracy under stated assumptions on π and on the distribution of x_t.

Consider an open multiagent system defined as follows. Let $\mathcal{A}_t$ denote a finite but variable set of agents present at discrete time $t \in \mathbb{N}$. Agents may join the system (i.e., be added to $\mathcal{A}_t$) or leave it (i.e., be removed from $\mathcal{A}_t$) at arbitrary times without issuing any notification to other agents. The cardinality $|\mathcal{A}_t|$ is therefore time-varying and unknown a priori. Each agent $i \in \mathcal{A}_t$ has an internal decision-making policy $\pi_i$, drawn from some (possibly unknown) class $\Pi$, which it uses to choose actions based on its observations of the environment and of other agents.

A modelling agent $m$ interacts in this system over time and seeks to maintain, for each other agent $j$ it currently encounters, a model $\hat{\pi}_j$ that approximates $\pi_j$ in a way that is useful for predicting $j$'s future actions. In addition, suppose that $m$ has previously interacted in a sequence of related open systems $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_{k}$, and has accumulated knowledge $K$ (e.g., learned models, priors over $\Pi$, or behavioural features) from those past systems that might be transferable to a new system $S_{k+1}$.

Problem: Design a modelling method for $m$ that
(i) is computationally efficient (polynomial-time per interaction step in the current number of observed agents and observation history length),
(ii) handles the unbounded and time-varying number of agents, including agents that newly appear without prior interaction history and agents that disappear permanently or temporarily,
(iii) produces models $\hat{\pi}_j$ whose predictive accuracy converges, in a precise sense to be specified, toward the true $\pi_j$ as observations of $j$ accumulate, and
(iv) systematically transfers the prior knowledge $K$ from $S_1, \ldots, S_k$ into $S_{k+1}$ so as to improve modelling performance on agents in $S_{k+1}$ relative to learning from scratch.

Provide such a method together with formal guarantees on its efficiency, accuracy, and transfer benefit, or establish impossibility results delimiting what guarantees are achievable.

(i) is computationally efficient (polynomial-time per interaction step in the current number of observed agents and observation history length),
(ii) handles the unbounded and time-varying number of agents, including agents that newly appear without prior interaction history and agents that disappear permanently or temporarily,
(iii) produces models $\hat{\pi}_j$ whose predictive accuracy converges, in a precise sense to be specified, toward the true $\pi_j$ as observations of $j$ accumulate, and
(iv) systematically transfers the prior knowledge $K$ from $S_1, \ldots, S_k$ into $S_{k+1}$ so as to improve modelling performance on agents in $S_{k+1}$ relative to learning from scratch.

Provide such a method together with formal guarantees on its efficiency, accuracy, and transfer benefit, or establish impossibility results delimiting what guarantees are achievable.

Modelling agents in open multiagent systems is widely characterized in the literature as an unresolved research challenge. Subsequent work (e.g., interactive POMDP extensions for open systems by Chandrasekaran et al., and ongoing research on ad hoc teamwork and open ad hoc teamwork by Stone, Albrecht, and collaborators through the early 2020s) has produced partial methods but no general efficient solution with transfer guarantees. The problem remains open.

The weak cosmic censorship conjecture remains a major open problem in mathematical general relativity. Christodoulou proved a version for the spherically symmetric Einstein–scalar-field system in 1999, but the general (non-symmetric) conjecture is unresolved. Recent work (e.g., Dafermos–Luk on the C^0 formulation of strong cosmic censorship, and various counterexamples in higher dimensions or with specific matter) continues to refine the question, but no general proof exists.

Consider the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), a reinforcement learning benchmark consisting of a large suite of Atari 2600 games. Each game is modeled as a Markov decision process whose state at time t is given by a raw screen observation s_t (a 210×160 array of pixels with a 128-color palette, optionally stacked over several recent frames), whose action set A is a finite subset of the 18 Atari joystick/button combinations, and whose reward r_t is the per-step change in the in-game score. A general agent is a single learning algorithm (with one fixed set of hyperparameters) that, given only (s_t, r_t, a_t) interaction traces, must learn to play every game in the suite.

Design and analyze a learning procedure that produces an internal representation φ: S → R^d (with d, the architecture, and the training objective fixed across games) and a policy π based on φ such that all of the following hold simultaneously:

1. (Generality) The same algorithm and hyperparameters are used for every game in the ALE; no per-game feature engineering or tuning is permitted.

2. (Sample efficiency) The number of environment interactions required to reach human-level performance on a representative set of ALE games is substantially smaller than the tens of millions of frames required by standard deep Q-network (DQN) style methods. Quantify the achievable sample complexity and prove or empirically establish a separation from the DQN baseline.

3. (Sparse-reward exploration) On games in which extrinsic reward is encountered only after long action sequences—exemplified by Montezuma's Revenge—the procedure must, with high probability, convert isolated reward events into a policy that obtains those rewards consistently, rather than failing to propagate the signal.

State precise assumptions on the environment (e.g., determinism vs. stochasticity, frame-skip, episode termination) under which the guarantees in (2) and (3) hold, and either (a) exhibit an algorithm meeting all three criteria with provable or rigorously measured guarantees, or (b) prove an impossibility result showing that no algorithm satisfying (1) can simultaneously achieve (2) and (3) within a specified sample budget.

Consider the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), a benchmark suite of Atari 2600 games in which a reinforcement learning agent at each discrete time step observes a frame (or short stack of frames) of raw pixel input, selects one of 18 joystick/button actions, and receives a scalar reward equal to the change in the game's score. Within this benchmark, certain games — including Montezuma's Revenge, Private Eye, Pitfall!, and Tennis — exhibit reward signals that are extremely delayed (thousands of primitive actions may pass before any nonzero reward), sparse, or initially negative/deceptive (the agent receives only negative rewards before discovering any positive ones).

Restrict attention to model-free reinforcement learning agents that use parametric function approximation (e.g., deep neural networks) over the raw observation space and that learn a policy or value function via stochastic interaction with the environment, without access to a learned or hand-coded forward model of the game dynamics, without expert demonstrations, and without game-specific prior knowledge.

Problem. Design and analyze such a model-free function-approximation agent together with an exploration mechanism — possibly based on (i) commitment to temporally extended actions or options at a higher level of abstraction than single joystick inputs, and/or (ii) an intrinsic motivation reward signal that drives the agent to continue exploring when extrinsic scoring appears infeasible — that, using only environment interactions and within a sample budget comparable to standard ALE evaluation protocols, reliably discovers the delayed/sparse/deceptive extrinsic rewards in games such as Montezuma's Revenge, Private Eye, Pitfall!, and Tennis, and attains performance competitive with human play across all of these games simultaneously.

Substantial progress has been made since the problem was posed. DeepMind's Agent57 (2020) is the first agent to surpass the human baseline on all 57 Atari games, including Montezuma's Revenge, Pitfall!, Private Eye, and Tennis, using a model-free distributed agent with a family of intrinsic-motivation policies. Consider the standard reinforcement learning setting in which an agent interacts with a Markov decision process (MDP) M = (S, A, P, r, γ) with state space S, action space A, transition kernel P(s' | s, a), reward function r(s, a), and discount factor γ ∈ [0, 1). The agent's goal is to learn a policy π: S → Δ(A) maximizing the expected discounted return E[∑_{t≥0} γ^t r(s_t, a_t)]. In the off-policy setting, value functions or policies for a target policy π are estimated from trajectories produced by behavior policies μ that may differ substantially from π, and value functions Q_θ: S × A → ℝ are represented by a parameterized function approximator (e.g., a neural network) with parameters θ.

Design an off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm with parameterized function approximation that simultaneously satisfies all of the following requirements, when applied to high-dimensional control tasks of the difficulty of Atari 2600 games (large discrete action spaces, raw image observations, long horizons):

1. Stability: the parameter iterates θ_t generated by the algorithm provably do not diverge under standard regularity assumptions on the function approximator and the data-generating distribution, even when the behavior policy μ differs significantly from the target policy π.

2. Theoretical guarantees that match empirical behavior: the algorithm admits a convergence (or boundedness) analysis whose hypotheses and conclusions actually explain the observed empirical performance, rather than holding only in regimes (e.g., linear function approximation, on-policy sampling) that are absent in practice.

3. Sample reuse: the algorithm can reliably and efficiently reuse transitions (s, a, r, s') generated by behavior policies μ that are very different from the current target policy π, without performance collapse.

4. No reliance on stabilizing heuristics: the algorithm does not require an experience replay buffer or a separately maintained target network solely as a mechanism to prevent divergence; any use of such components must be justified beyond merely ensuring non-divergence.

Either construct such an algorithm and prove it meets requirements 1–4 while demonstrating empirical performance competitive with state-of-the-art off-policy methods on a benchmark suite of high-dimensional control tasks, or prove that no algorithm satisfying all four requirements simultaneously can exist within a specified class of function approximators and sampling regimes.

Consider an autonomous agent A operating in a multi-agent environment that contains one or more other agents. To act effectively, A must maintain models of the other agents that may capture diverse aspects of their behavior and cognition, including:

(i) Policy reconstruction: estimating another agent's mapping from observation/state histories to action distributions.
(ii) Type-based reasoning: maintaining a (Bayesian) belief over a discrete set of candidate behavioral types and updating it from observed actions.
(iii) Classification: assigning observed agents to behavioral or strategic categories based on features of their interaction history.
(iv) Plan recognition: inferring the goals and (hierarchical) plans of another agent from partial action sequences.
(v) Recursive / epistemic reasoning: representing nested beliefs of the form "A believes that B believes that A believes …" up to some finite depth, as in interactive POMDPs or epistemic logic.
(vi) Graphical models: representing dependencies among agents' actions, types, goals, and observations via probabilistic graphical structures.

Currently, each of these modelling capabilities is typically realized by a distinct formalism, and integrations are achieved only through loose modular pipelines in which the outputs of one component are fed as inputs to another.

Problem. Design a single mathematical representation together with an associated inference and learning procedure for an agent A such that:

(a) The representation simultaneously instantiates all of the capabilities (i)–(vi) above as special cases or as marginal/derived quantities of one underlying model.
(b) Inference performed for any one capability automatically updates the quantities relevant to the others, so that the modelling processes inform one another synergistically rather than independently.
(c) The framework admits a well-defined semantics (e.g., as a probabilistic or decision-theoretic model), permits tractable approximate inference, and reduces, in appropriate limiting cases, to each of the standard formalisms underlying (i)–(vi).

Either construct such a unified representation and prove that it satisfies (a)–(c), or prove that no representation satisfying (a)–(c) can exist under stated assumptions.

Consider a sequential interaction between a modelling agent A and another agent B, both acting in a shared environment formalized as a stochastic game. At each time step t, agent A selects an action a_t from a finite action set, observes B's action b_t and an environment state s_t, and maintains a probabilistic model M_t over B's policy (a mapping from histories to action distributions). Agent A wishes to perform exploratory actions that yield information about B's policy — that is, actions that reduce the entropy or uncertainty of M_t with respect to B's true (unknown) policy π_B — while satisfying the following constraints:

(i) Safety: the exploratory actions chosen by A must not perturb B's future behaviour in ways that change π_B beyond a prescribed tolerance, i.e. for some predefined divergence measure D and threshold ε ≥ 0, the policy of B conditional on having observed A's exploratory history must satisfy D(π_B^{after} ∥ π_B^{baseline}) ≤ ε, where π_B^{baseline} denotes B's policy in the absence of the exploratory perturbation.

(ii) Tractability: the algorithm used by A to select exploratory actions must run in time polynomial in the size of the state and action spaces and the planning horizon, ruling out exhaustive look-ahead over the joint state-action tree.

Design an action-selection rule (or characterize the existence of one) for agent A that maximizes a measure of expected information gain about π_B over a finite horizon T, subject to the safety constraint (i) and the computational constraint (ii), and provide formal guarantees on its information-gain efficiency relative to the unconstrained Bayes-optimal exploration strategy.

Consider an autonomous agent operating in a real-time environment in which the available computational budget per decision cycle is largely consumed by perception, communication, planning, physics simulation, and rendering. Suppose the agent must additionally maintain models of one or more other agents acting in the same environment, where an agent model is a function that, given a history of observations of another agent's behavior, produces a predictive representation (for example, a policy, type distribution, or belief state) used to inform the modelling agent's own decisions.

Develop and analyze general-purpose algorithmic techniques—such as specialized data structures, parallel or distributed architectures, and incremental update schemes that process only newly arrived observations rather than recomputing from full histories—that allow such agent-modelling methods to be implemented with worst-case per-step time and memory complexity small enough to fit within the residual computational budget of a real application. Specifically:

1. Formalize a model of the per-step computational budget and of the agent-modelling task (input: stream of observations of other agents; output: updated predictive model).
2. Identify which classes of agent-modelling methods admit incremental update algorithms whose per-step cost is independent of the length of the observation history, and characterize the achievable trade-offs between update cost, memory, and predictive accuracy.
3. Provide implementations and asymptotic and empirical analyses showing that the resulting methods remain efficient enough to be deployed alongside the other resource-intensive components listed above.

Consider the standard framework of multi-agent modelling in which an autonomous agent maintains predictive models of other agents' behaviour. Formally, let an environment be described by a state space S, a finite set of agents I, and for each agent i a set of actions A_i. A standard agent model is a mapping π_i : H → Δ(A_i) from interaction histories H (sequences of states and joint actions) to distributions over A_i, with the implicit assumption that each action a ∈ A_i is instantaneous, i.e. its effect on the state is realized in a single discrete time step.

Now drop the instantaneous-action assumption: each action a ∈ A_i has a duration d(a) > 0 (possibly stochastic, possibly state-dependent), during which the agent is committed to a, the action's effect is spread over multiple time steps, and the action may be interrupted. Observations available to the modelling agent consist of state trajectories (s_t)_{t≥0} together possibly with partial action labels.

The problem is to determine:

(a) Precisely which formal modifications must be made to existing classes of agent-modelling methods (e.g. policy reconstruction, type-based reasoning, plan recognition, recursive reasoning, group modelling) so that they remain well-defined, consistent, and predictively accurate when the modelled agents execute temporally extended actions with the above semantics; and

(b) Whether the problem of inferring such temporally extended actions should be handled inside the agent-modelling layer itself (i.e. by enlarging the hypothesis space of π_i to include duration-aware policies over options or semi-Markov decision processes) or whether it should be factored out as a separate lower-level activity-recognition problem that maps raw state trajectories to a sequence of completed extended actions, whose output then feeds an unmodified instantaneous-action modeller.

Provide a rigorous comparison of the two architectural choices in terms of identifiability of the agent's policy, sample complexity of learning, and predictive accuracy under interruption and concurrency of extended actions.

Construct a mathematically rigorous and physically consistent theory of quantum gravity that satisfies all of the following requirements:

1. In an appropriate classical (large-scale, low-energy) limit, the theory reproduces the predictions of Einstein's general relativity, in which spacetime is modeled by a smooth pseudo-Riemannian 4-manifold (M, g) of Lorentzian signature whose metric g satisfies the Einstein field equations
   R_{μν} − (1/2) R g_{μν} + Λ g_{μν} = (8πG/c^4) T_{μν},
where R_{μν} is the Ricci tensor, R the scalar curvature, Λ the cosmological constant, G Newton's constant, c the speed of light, and T_{μν} the stress–energy tensor.

2. In the appropriate flat-spacetime / weak-gravity limit, the theory reproduces the predictions of relativistic quantum mechanics and quantum field theory, including unitary time evolution of states in a (suitably defined) Hilbert space and the standard probabilistic interpretation of quantum measurements.

3. The theory remains mathematically well-defined and predictive in regimes in which gravitational and quantum effects are simultaneously non-negligible (for example, near black-hole horizons and cosmological singularities, and at energies approaching the Planck scale E_P = √(ℏ c^5 / G)). In particular, it must give finite, well-defined answers to questions involving the gravitational behavior of quantum matter and the quantum behavior of the gravitational field.

4. The theory is internally consistent: its mathematical formulation is free of pathologies such as uncontrolled ultraviolet divergences, anomalies obstructing fundamental symmetries it claims to preserve, and logical contradictions (e.g., violations of unitarity arising from gravitational effects such as black-hole formation and evaporation).

Provide such a theory together with a precise mathematical formulation, or prove that no such theory can exist.

Consider an autonomous agent A interacting with one or more other agents in a (possibly partially observable, stochastic) multi-agent environment. Agent A maintains a modelling apparatus consisting of three layers: (i) a modelling method M (an algorithm that maps observed interaction histories to predictions about other agents' behaviour), (ii) a model class C (the parametric or structural family of hypotheses M searches over), and (iii) a model space S (the space of possible model classes A could in principle entertain). Let h_t denote the interaction history available to A at time t, and let τ denote the task or objective A is pursuing.

Define a notion of task-oriented adequacy as a relation Adeq(M, C, S; h_t, τ) that may be strictly weaker than predictive correctness; for example, Adeq could require only that the predictions induced by (M, C) suffice for A to choose actions whose expected return on task τ is within ε of optimal, or that they correctly rank a relevant subset of candidate actions.

Design, and prove guarantees for, an introspective procedure I executable by A that, on the basis of h_t and τ alone (without privileged access to the true models of the other agents), accomplishes the following:

1. Detection: decides whether the current triple (M, C, S) satisfies Adeq(·; h_t, τ);
2. Diagnosis: when adequacy fails, identifies which layer (the method M, the class C, or the space S) is responsible and characterises in what way the current model is inadequate or misleading;
3. Revision: autonomously produces a revised triple (M', C', S') and provides a criterion under which the revision improves task-oriented adequacy, together with conditions ensuring that the iterative application of I converges (in a precise sense to be specified) to a triple satisfying Adeq.

Formalise the notion of adequacy, the introspection operator I, and the revision dynamics, and determine whether such a procedure with provable detection, diagnosis, and revision guarantees exists for general multi-agent interaction settings, or identify the structural assumptions on the environment, the task τ, and the model space S under which it does.

representations.normalized:
In relativistic heavy-ion collisions at intermediate center-of-mass energies (in particular, energies of the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron, √s_NN ≈ 6–17 GeV, and below), an enhancement of strange-hadron yields per participating nucleon is observed relative to elementary nucleon–nucleon collisions. Two qualitatively distinct classes of mechanisms could in principle account for this enhancement:

(a) Partonic mechanisms, in which strangeness is produced in a deconfined quark–gluon medium (e.g. via gluon–gluon fusion gg → s s̄ in a thermalized partonic phase).

(b) Purely hadronic mechanisms acting in a dense hadronic medium, including multi-step inelastic hadronic reactions, formation and decay of baryonic and mesonic resonances, and multi-meson fusion processes such as n π → K K̄ Y or analogous many-body channels that open the strangeness-conservation phase space without requiring partonic degrees of freedom.

Quantify, within a well-defined hadronic transport or thermal framework that excludes partonic degrees of freedom, the fraction of the experimentally observed strangeness enhancement (for representative observables such as the K⁺/π⁺ ratio, the Λ, Ξ, and Ω yields per participant, and the Wróblewski factor λ_s) at SPS energies and below that can be generated solely by hadronic-medium mechanisms of type (b). Specifically, determine whether multi-step hadronic reactions, resonance excitation, and multi-meson fusion processes are sufficient — without invoking a partonic phase — to reproduce the magnitude and the energy dependence of the measured strangeness enhancement in this energy regime.

Recent literature (e.g., 2025 NA61/SHINE updates and EPOS4 small-system studies) continues to investigate the relative role of hadronic versus partonic mechanisms in strangeness enhancement at SPS and lower energies. representations.normalized:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the yields of hadrons containing strange quarks (such as kaons, Λ, Ξ, and Ω baryons), normalized to non-strange hadron production and to nucleon-nucleon reference data, are observed to be enhanced relative to expectations from elementary proton–proton collisions at low multiplicity. This phenomenon is known as strangeness enhancement. A long-standing theoretical proposal attributes this enhancement to the formation of a deconfined, thermalized state of quarks and gluons—the quark–gluon plasma (QGP)—in which the suppression of strange-quark pair production due to the strange-quark mass is lifted by partonic processes (notably gluon fusion gg → s s̄) and by chemical equilibration at the partonic level. Competing purely hadronic explanations (e.g., canonical suppression of strangeness in small systems, hadronic rescattering, string-junction or rope-hadronization mechanisms, color-reconnection enhancements) can also produce the observed pattern of yield ratios without invoking a deconfined phase.

Problem: Provide an experimental observable, or a combination of observables together with a quantitative analysis, that establishes a direct and unambiguous causal link between the observed strangeness enhancement in heavy-ion collisions and the formation of a quark–gluon plasma, in such a way that all viable purely hadronic mechanisms are excluded as the dominant origin of the enhancement. The criterion of success is to identify a measurement (or set of measurements) whose outcome is predicted by QGP formation but cannot be reproduced by any consistent hadronic-phase model with comparable agreement to data.

Recent work (Strangeness in Quark Matter 2024 and related Quark Matter proceedings) shows that strangeness enhancement, originally proposed as a QGP signature, is also observed in high-multiplicity pp and p–Pb collisions where QGP formation is not established, and is partly reproduced by hadronic models (color reconnection, ropes, canonical suppression). Let $\Lambda = \{\lambda_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of pairwise distinct complex numbers with $0 \notin \Lambda$ and $\lambda_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$. Let $a > 0$ and consider the segment $X = [-a,a] \subset \mathbb{R}$. Let $C[-a,a]$ denote the Banach space of continuous complex-valued functions on $[-a,a]$ with the uniform norm. The exponential system associated to $\Lambda$ is
$$\operatorname{Exp}\Lambda = \{e^{\lambda_n z} : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \subset C[-a,a].$$
We say that $\operatorname{Exp}\Lambda$ is complete in $C[-a,a]$ if the closure of its linear span in $C[-a,a]$ equals $C[-a,a]$.

Problem. Find a precise necessary and sufficient condition, expressed through a suitable notion of density of the sequence $\Lambda$ and the geometry of the segment $[-a,a]$ (in particular its length $2a$), characterizing exactly those sequences $\Lambda$ for which $\operatorname{Exp}\Lambda$ is complete in $C[-a,a]$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of finding an exact density-type criterion for completeness of complex exponential systems on a real segment is a classical long-standing open problem. Known results (Beurling–Malliavin, Levinson, Koosis, Redheffer) give sharp criteria for completeness "up to a finite number of exponentials" or in weighted/Paley–Wiener settings, but no exact characterization of completeness in $C[-a,a]$ is known. Recent surveys continue to list it as open.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Lorentzian 4-manifold satisfying the Einstein field equations. The geodesic hypothesis asserts that a sufficiently small, freely falling test body moves along a timelike geodesic of $(M,g)$.

Formulate and prove a rigorous theorem that justifies this hypothesis. Specifically, give a precise mathematical sense in which the following statement holds: as the size, mass, and self-gravitational backreaction of a material body tend to zero (for instance via a one-parameter family of solutions of the Einstein equations coupled to suitable matter—e.g. a perfect fluid, dust, or a nonlinear Klein–Gordon field—with support concentrating on a timelike curve $\gamma\subset M$), the curve $\gamma$ along which the body's energy concentrates must be a timelike geodesic of the background metric $g$.

The problem is to obtain such a derivation that
(i) starts from the full nonlinear Einstein equations (so that gravitational self-interaction/backreaction is consistently incorporated rather than postulated away),
(ii) avoids ad hoc regularization of singular point-particle stress–energy, and
(iii) yields the geodesic equation for $\gamma$ as a rigorously proved theorem in the negligible-mass limit.

Several rigorous results exist that justify the geodesic hypothesis in restricted settings: Geroch–Jang-type theorems for shrinking world tubes of matter, the Gralla–Wald (2008) rigorous derivation of the motion (and self-force) of a small body via one-parameter families of solutions to Einstein's equations, and Y. Choquet-Bruhat / Stuart / J. Wong-type derivations using concentrated Klein–Gordon matter (e.g. Stuart, Comm. Math. Phys. 2014). However, a fully general theorem covering arbitrary small self-gravitating bodies in generic spacetimes is not established, so the problem is best described as partially solved.

Consider relativistic collisions of hadronic and nuclear systems (for example pp, p–Pb, and Pb–Pb at LHC energies) in which one measures, at mid-rapidity, the charged-particle pseudorapidity density dN_ch/dη and the yield ratios of strange hadrons (e.g. K_S^0, Λ, Ξ, Ω) to charged pions, π. Within the statistical hadronization framework, the so-called "strangeness enhancement" with increasing event activity is commonly modeled by a transition from a canonical ensemble (with exact conservation of strangeness over a correlation volume V_0) to a grand-canonical ensemble; the canonical suppression factors depend explicitly on V_0.

Empirically, the strange-to-pion yield ratios are observed to grow smoothly as a function of ⟨dN_ch/dη⟩ across collision systems and energies, suggesting a single underlying control parameter related to the effective reaction volume.

Problem. Determine whether, for the multiplicity dependence of strange-to-pion yield ratios, the mapping (collision system, centrality, energy) ↦ ⟨dN_ch/dη⟩ ↦ V_0 is a sufficient statistic for the observed strangeness production. Concretely:

(a) Specify a quantitative relation V_0 = V_0(⟨dN_ch/dη⟩) such that all measured strange-to-pion ratios collapse onto a single universal curve as a function of V_0 alone (or equivalently of ⟨dN_ch/dη⟩), independent of collision system and energy.

(b) If no such universal collapse holds, identify additional observables O_1, O_2, … (such as event-shape variables like sphericity or transverse spherocity, mean transverse momentum, the transverse-energy density dE_T/dη, the underlying-event activity, the number of multi-parton interactions, or initial-state geometric quantities) which must be included so that the strange-to-pion ratios become a function f(⟨dN_ch/dη⟩, O_1, O_2, …) that is universal across systems.

Provide either a proof of universality in (a) under stated assumptions, or a demonstration in (b) that a specific additional observable produces a system-size dependence of strangeness production not captured by ⟨dN_ch/dη⟩ and V_0 alone.

Let G ⊂ ℂ be an unbounded convex domain containing the ray [0, +∞), and let Clos G denote its closure. For x ∈ [0, +∞) set
   d_G(x) = sup{ |z − z′| : z, z′ ∈ G, Re z = Re z′ = x },
and define the width of G by
   d_G = lim_{x → +∞} d_G(x),
assuming this limit is finite (the finite-width case).

Find a necessary and sufficient condition on Λ — not assuming that Λ is separated from the imaginary axis (i.e., not assuming inf_n |Re λ_n| > 0) — characterizing exactly when Exp Λ is complete in H(Clos G).

Let $(M,g)$ be a $D$-dimensional Lorentzian manifold with $D\ge 5$ that is a smooth, asymptotically flat, stationary solution of the vacuum Einstein equations $\mathrm{Ric}(g)=0$, and suppose $(M,g)$ contains a regular event horizon (so that $(M,g)$ is a stationary, asymptotically flat, vacuum black-hole spacetime). In four dimensions, the classical no-hair/uniqueness theorems imply that any such spacetime is, up to isometry, a Kerr solution and is therefore characterized by its mass and angular momentum. In higher dimensions $D\ge 5$ this fails: explicit families such as the Myers–Perry black holes and the Emparan–Reall black ring (with horizon topology $S^1\times S^2$ in $D=5$) show that mass and angular momenta alone do not determine the solution, and horizon topology is not restricted to spheres.

Problem: Provide a complete classification, up to isometry, of all stationary, asymptotically flat, regular vacuum black-hole solutions in dimension $D\ge 5$, and identify a finite set of geometric/topological invariants (such as mass, angular momenta, horizon topology, and rod/interval structure on the orbit space) that uniquely determine each such solution. Equivalently, prove a uniqueness theorem of the form: any two stationary asymptotically flat vacuum black holes in $D\ge 5$ with the same chosen invariants are isometric, and exhibit the full list of allowed invariant data.

The general classification of stationary asymptotically flat vacuum black holes in dimension D≥5 remains open. Four-dimensional uniqueness fails in higher dimensions, as shown by the Emparan–Reall black ring coexisting with Myers–Perry solutions. Substantial partial results exist: in D=5, uniqueness has been proven within the class of stationary, asymptotically flat vacuum solutions admitting two commuting axial Killing vectors (Hollands–Yazadjiev and others), where the rod/interval structure together with mass and angular momenta determines the solution. The problem is unresolved without such symmetry assumptions and in D≥6.

Consider proton–proton (pp) collisions at LHC center-of-mass energies, in which event samples are classified by charged-particle multiplicity at midrapidity. For each multiplicity class, define the integrated yield ratios of strange hadron species to charged pions, in particular K/π, Λ/π, Ξ/π, and Ω/π. The grand-canonical limit of a thermal/statistical hadronization model predicts a fixed equilibrium value for each such ratio (independent of system size once canonical suppression is fully lifted).

Question: As the charged-particle multiplicity in pp collisions is pushed to very high values (so that the system size is large enough for canonical strangeness suppression to be effectively removed and the grand-canonical limit to be approached), do the strange-hadron-to-pion ratios saturate at the grand-canonical equilibrium values, or do some of them — most notably Ω/π, the ratio involving the most strange baryon — continue to rise with multiplicity rather than leveling off? Determine experimentally and/or theoretically whether saturation occurs for all strange species, or whether multi-strange species exhibit a continued increase beyond the grand-canonical prediction.

The literature describes the completeness problem for exponential systems on a general compact convex set $K\subset\mathbb{C}$ with nonempty interior as a long-standing open problem. representations.normalized:
In low-energy heavy-ion collisions (e.g., Ni+Ni or Au+Au at beam energies on the order of 1–2 AGeV), kaons are produced inside a hot, dense hadronic medium and subsequently decouple ("freeze out") from it. Because of strangeness-exchange reactions available to K− but not to K+, the kaon–nucleon cross sections satisfy σ(K−N) > σ(K+N), so K− mesons should rescatter more strongly with surrounding nucleons than K+ mesons. Under the hypothesis of "sequential freeze-out," this asymmetry implies that K+ and K− decouple from the medium at different times and under different thermodynamic conditions, which would manifest, for instance, in differing inverse-slope parameters of their transverse-mass spectra, differing polar emission patterns, or a centrality- and system-size-independent K−/K+ ratio.

Question: Does experimental data from low-energy heavy-ion collisions provide evidence supporting this sequential freeze-out scenario for the two kaon species K+ and K−, attributable to their different cross sections with nucleons?

representations.normalized:
The φ meson is a vector meson with valence quark content s s̄, so its net strangeness quantum number is S = 0. In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, however, the φ meson exhibits features typically associated with particles carrying nonzero strangeness:

(a) Its enhancement factor (the ratio of its yield per participant nucleon in nucleus–nucleus collisions to that in elementary proton–proton or proton–nucleus collisions, as a function of centrality and collision energy) lies between the enhancement factors observed for the singly strange Λ (|S| = 1) and the doubly strange Ξ (|S| = 2), as if the φ carried an effective strangeness in the range 1–2.

(b) The width of the φ rapidity distribution dN_φ/dy as a function of center-of-mass energy √s_NN broadens with increasing energy faster than the corresponding rapidity widths of the pion and of the charged kaons K⁺ and K⁻, a behavior that is difficult to reconcile with simple kaon-coalescence (K K̄ → φ) as the dominant production mechanism.

Provide a quantitative dynamical mechanism for φ-meson production and propagation in the hot and dense medium created in heavy-ion collisions that simultaneously explains, from first principles or from a controlled effective theory of QCD matter:

1. why the φ enhancement pattern with centrality and √s_NN tracks that of strange (rather than non-strange) hadrons despite the φ having S = 0, and
2. the observed energy dependence of the rapidity-distribution width of the φ relative to those of π, K⁺, and K⁻.

The anomalous strangeness-like behavior of the φ meson and the energy dependence of its rapidity-distribution width in heavy-ion collisions remain unresolved. Consider the Einstein field equations governing the evolution of a spatially inhomogeneous spacetime toward a spacelike singularity. The BKL (Belinskii–Khalatnikov–Lifshitz) heuristic predicts that, generically, the approach to such a singularity is asymptotically local: each spatial point evolves independently in an oscillatory Kasner-like manner described by Bianchi type I and II vacuum models. Numerical and heuristic studies suggest, however, that on certain spatial surfaces the asymptotic-locality picture breaks down through the formation of so-called "spike" structures — spatial features where the Kasner exponents fail to vary continuously and the dynamics is described by inhomogeneous (rather than purely local) vacuum models.

Formulate and prove the following:

(a) Show rigorously that, for a generic class of solutions of the vacuum Einstein equations (suitably defined, e.g. on a spatial manifold of T^3 topology with no symmetry assumptions) approaching a spacelike singularity, spike structures necessarily occur on a non-empty set of spatial points.

(b) Determine the effect of these spike structures on the asymptotic behavior of the metric near the singularity, and incorporate them into a complete mathematical description (statement and proof) of generic singularity formation, including the modification of the BKL local-Kasner asymptotics that they induce.

  dp/dr = -G [ε(r)+p(r)][m(r)+4πr³p(r)/c²] / (r² c² [1 - 2Gm(r)/(rc²)]),
  dm/dr = 4π r² ε(r)/c²,

with energy density ε(r) and pressure p(r) related by an equation of state (EoS) p = p(ε). Suppose that, at sufficiently high baryon density, the matter composition includes not only nucleons (n,p), leptons (e⁻,μ⁻), and possibly mesons, but also hyperons (Λ, Σ⁻,⁰,⁺, Ξ⁻,⁰), with their populations determined by chemical equilibrium under weak interactions and electric charge neutrality. Let the baryon–baryon interactions be specified by two‑body and three‑body (YN, YY, NNY, NYY, YYY) potentials whose parameters are constrained by available hypernuclear binding energies and scattering data.

Quantify, with rigorous bounds, the extent to which present and conceivable improvements in the empirically determined hyperon–nucleon and hyperon–hyperon interactions (including three-body forces in hypernuclear matter) can raise the maximum gravitational mass M_max of the resulting TOV mass–radius sequence. Specifically, determine whether the inclusion of hyperons in beta‑equilibrated dense matter is compatible with M_max ≥ 2 M_⊙, and characterize the class of admissible YN/YY interaction models (consistent with hypernuclear data) for which this lower bound on M_max is achieved. Provide quantitative estimates of the achievable shift ΔM_max as a function of the uncertainty bands of the hyperonic potentials.

Let ³_ΛH denote the hypertriton, the lightest known hypernucleus, consisting of a proton, a neutron, and a Λ bound by the strong interaction; its mesonic weak decay proceeds predominantly through the Λ inside the bound state, with measurable mean lifetime τ(³_ΛH).

Define the in-medium modification of hyperon properties as any change in the effective mass, width, coupling constants, or weak-decay rate of a Λ embedded in nuclear matter or in a finite nucleus, relative to its free-space values, attributable to interactions with the surrounding nucleons (e.g. Pauli blocking of final-state nucleons, ΛN → NN nonmesonic channels, mean-field shifts, and pion final-state interactions).

Question: Are the properties of a Λ hyperon modified when it is bound inside a nucleus or immersed in nuclear matter? Concretely, do precise measurements and a fully consistent theoretical treatment establish that τ(³_ΛH) differs from τ_Λ by an amount that cannot be explained solely by the trivial kinematics of a weakly bound Λ (and the associated Λ separation energy B_Λ in ³_ΛH together with pion final-state interactions and nucleon Pauli blocking), thereby indicating a genuine medium modification of hyperon properties?

representations.normalized:
Consider the following idealized setup in non-relativistic quantum mechanics. Let S be a quantum system with two-dimensional Hilbert space H_S, and let O and P be two observers, each modeled as a quantum system with Hilbert spaces H_O and H_P respectively, equipped with pointer observables. Suppose S is prepared in a superposition |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ ∈ H_S with |α|^2 + |β|^2 = 1, and O performs a (von Neumann) measurement of the observable with eigenstates {|0⟩,|1⟩} via a unitary interaction U_{SO} on H_S ⊗ H_O that takes |i⟩|ready⟩_O ↦ |i⟩|i⟩_O. Consider two descriptions of this process:

(E) From O's perspective: after the interaction, S is in a definite eigenstate |i⟩ with probability |⟨i|ψ⟩|^2, and O has recorded the corresponding outcome.

(E′) From a third observer P's perspective who has not interacted with S or O: the joint system S+O is in the entangled pure state α|0⟩|0⟩_O + β|1⟩|1⟩_O on H_S ⊗ H_O, with no definite outcome assigned.

The "third person problem" asserts that the apparent discrepancy between (E) and (E′) forces one to adopt a relational interpretation in which quantum states must be relativized to a specifying observer (i.e. there is no observer-independent state of S+O).

Question: When the measurement interaction, the physical correlations underlying "recording an outcome", and the dynamical role of decoherence and of P's potential further interactions are all specified without ambiguity, does the difference between the descriptions (E) and (E′) provide a genuine logical or physical justification for the claim that quantum states must be fundamentally relativized to observers? Equivalently, can one construct a sharpened, unambiguous formulation of the measurement process in which (E) and (E′) are mutually consistent statements about the same observer-independent quantum state, thereby defeating the argument; or can it be shown that any such sharpening necessarily preserves a genuine inequivalence between (E) and (E′) that compels relativization?

representations.normalized:
Consider a quantum interpretation (call it R) characterized by the doctrine that the values of physical quantities, and the states ascribing them, are not observer-independent: every physical fact is relative to a particular observer/system pair. Consider an EPR–Bell scenario consisting of two spatially separated observers A and B who perform measurements with settings a, b on a spin-singlet (or analogous entangled) pair, obtaining outcomes x, y. Following Jarrett's decomposition, write Bell's locality condition as the conjunction of:

 (PI) Parameter Independence: P(x | a, b, λ) = P(x | a, λ) and P(y | a, b, λ) = P(y | b, λ);
 (OI) Outcome Independence: P(x | a, b, y, λ) = P(x | a, b, λ) and P(y | a, b, x, λ) = P(y | a, b, λ),

where λ denotes whatever complete specification of the state of the pair the interpretation admits. Standard quantum-mechanical predictions for entangled pairs satisfy PI but violate OI.

Question: Does interpretation R, by virtue of denying observer-independent properties alone, succeed in preserving Bell-locality (PI ∧ OI) in EPR–Bell scenarios? Equivalently, must any such interpretation that reproduces the standard quantum probabilities still accept some form of non-local dependence reflected in the violation of outcome independence, despite parameter independence being preserved?

representations.normalized:
In classical general relativity, consider one-parameter families of asymptotically flat initial data $(g_{ab}(p), K_{ab}(p), \Phi(p))$ for the Einstein equations coupled to some matter model (e.g., a massless scalar field, a perfect fluid, or pure vacuum gravitational waves), parametrized smoothly by a real parameter $p$, such that for sufficiently small $p$ the maximal Cauchy development disperses to flat space, while for sufficiently large $p$ it contains a black hole. Numerical evidence (originating with spherically symmetric massless scalar collapse) suggests that there is a critical value $p_*$ at which:

(i) (Universality) the late-time near-threshold evolution approaches a unique critical spacetime $Z_*$ depending only on the matter model, not on the family;
(ii) (Self-similarity) $Z_*$ is either continuously self-similar (admits a homothetic Killing vector) or discretely self-similar (invariant under a discrete rescaling $(\tau,x)\mapsto(\tau-\Delta,x)$ for a universal echoing period $\Delta$);
(iii) (Scaling) for supercritical data $p>p_*$ near $p_*$, the mass of the resulting black hole obeys $M_{\rm BH}\propto (p-p_*)^{\gamma}$ for a universal critical exponent $\gamma$ depending only on the matter model.

Provide a rigorous mathematical formulation and proof of this picture. In particular:

(a) Formulate precisely, within the Cauchy problem for the Einstein(–matter) system, the notion of the black hole threshold as a codimension-one set in a suitable space of initial data, and the notion of a critical solution as a codimension-one attractor (an attracting fixed point of the renormalization-group-type flow on the threshold surface).
(b) Prove existence, uniqueness, and the conjectured (continuous or discrete) self-similar symmetry of such critical solutions for at least one nontrivial matter model.
(c) Establish the universal mass-scaling law $M_{\rm BH}\sim (p-p_*)^{\gamma}$, deriving $\gamma$ from the spectrum of the linearization of the renormalization flow about the critical solution.
(d) Determine to what extent these phenomena persist beyond spherical symmetry, and in particular whether they occur at the threshold of vacuum gravitational collapse, where the formation of a naked singularity at threshold would constitute a codimension-one failure of cosmic censorship.

representations.normalization_method: unicode-preserving newline and trailing-whitespace normalization v1
representations.normalized:
Setup. Let $A \in \mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{R})$ have $n$ real eigenvalues whose absolute values are pairwise distinct, and let $C_1,\dots,C_{2^n}$ denote the connected components of $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{n} \pi_i$, where $\pi_1,\dots,\pi_n$ are the $n$ eigenhyperplanes of $A$ (the invariant hyperplanes, each spanned by $n-1$ of the eigenvectors). For each component $C_k$, the Klein sail $S_k$ is defined as the boundary of the convex hull of the nonzero integer points $C_k \cap \mathbb{Z}^n \setminus \{0\}$. Each sail is a (generally infinite) polyhedral surface whose two-dimensional and higher-dimensional cells are convex integer polyhedra called the faces of the sail.

Two integer polyhedra $P, Q \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ are called integer-equivalent if there exists $g \in \mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Z}) \ltimes \mathbb{Z}^n$ (an affine integer transformation) with $g(P) = Q$.

Problem. Construct an adequate complete invariant for the integer-equivalence classes of those convex integer polyhedra that arise as faces of Klein sails of operators $A$ as above. That is, exhibit an explicitly computable invariant $\mathcal{I}(P)$, defined for every convex integer polyhedron $P$, such that:
(i) for any two faces $P, Q$ of (possibly different) Klein sails, $\mathcal{I}(P) = \mathcal{I}(Q)$ if and only if $P$ and $Q$ are integer-equivalent;
(ii) the invariant $\mathcal{I}$ admits a finite combinatorial description.

Reviews of strangeness production in heavy-ion collisions and the ongoing programs at the SPS energy scan, RHIC Beam Energy Scan (BES-I and BES-II), NA61/SHINE, HADES, and the future CBM/FAIR and NICA experiments indicate that whether a distinct onset of strangeness enhancement exists between low and intermediate collision energies remains an unresolved experimental and theoretical question, with hadronic medium effects making its identification difficult. No conclusive resolution has been reported.

Let $A \in GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix all of whose eigenvalues are real, distinct, and nonzero, with $n$ one-dimensional invariant subspaces $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ in general position with respect to the coordinate hyperplanes. The complement $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus (\ell_1 \cup \dots \cup \ell_n)$ has $2^n$ open simplicial cones; for each such cone $C$, the boundary of the convex hull $\operatorname{conv}(C \cap \mathbb{Z}^n \setminus \{0\})$ is a polyhedral surface called a sail of the multidimensional continued fraction associated with $A$. Faces of sails are integer-equivalence classes of bounded faces of these polyhedra (two faces being equivalent if related by an element of $GL(n,\mathbb{Z})$ preserving the cone structure).

In dimension $n=2$, the classical Gauss–Kuzmin theorem gives, for almost every real $\alpha$, the asymptotic frequency
$$\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{\#\{1\le k\le N : a_k(\alpha) = m\}}{N} = \log_2\!\left(1 + \frac{1}{m(m+2)}\right),$$
where $a_k(\alpha)$ are the partial quotients (equivalently, integer lengths of edges of the one-dimensional sail).

Problem. For $n \ge 3$, develop a generalized Gauss–Kuzmin distribution describing the asymptotic frequencies of integer-congruence classes of faces appearing in sails of multidimensional continued fractions. More precisely, define a natural notion of asymptotic frequency for face types of sails (for instance, with respect to an invariant measure on the space of multidimensional continued fractions, such as the Möbius measure on the manifold of $n$-dimensional simplicial cones), prove its existence, and compute or characterize this distribution explicitly for face types of sails.

The problem of establishing a generalized Gauss–Kuzmin distribution for faces of multidimensional sails appears to remain open. Partial progress has been made via the geometric approach using invariant Möbius measures (e.g., Karpenkov's work on Möbius measures and Gauss–Kuzmin face statistics), but a full ergodic-theoretic generalization of the Gauss map suitable for face statistics of sails in dimension $\ge 3$ is still considered a hard open problem.

representations.normalized:
In heavy-ion collisions at center-of-mass energies below the elementary nucleon-nucleon production threshold for a given strange hadron ("sub-threshold" energies), measurements yield surprisingly large production of doubly strange and hidden-strange hadrons. In particular, in Ar+KCl collisions at E_lab ≈ 1.76 A GeV, the ratio Ξ⁻/(Λ + Σ⁰) is observed to be much larger than the expectation of statistical hadronization (thermal) models, and the ratio φ/K⁻ rises dramatically as the collision energy decreases towards very low energies.

Provide a quantitative microscopic mechanism (for example, multi-step strangeness-exchange reactions of the type Ȳ + B → Ξ + K, Y + Y → Ξ + N, decays of high-mass baryon resonances into φN or Ξ-containing channels, in-medium modifications of strange-particle properties, or other dynamical processes), implemented within a transport or thermal framework, that simultaneously reproduces:
(a) the absolute Ξ⁻ yield and the measured Ξ⁻/(Λ + Σ⁰) ratio at sub-threshold beam energies, and
(b) the energy dependence of the φ/K⁻ ratio, including its strong rise toward sub-threshold energies,
together with the yields of singly strange hadrons (K⁺, K⁻, Λ, Σ) at the same energies, while remaining consistent with elementary p+p and p+A constraints.

Determine whether such a mechanism, supported by present data, accounts for these dramatic sub-threshold enhancements, or identify what additional physics is required.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent literature (HADES experimental reviews, transport-model studies, and a 2023 EPJA systematics paper on strange-hadron yields near threshold) indicates that while strangeness-exchange channels (Ȳ+B, Y+Y → Ξ+K) and proposed high-mass resonance decay channels into φN and Ξ partially explain the sub-threshold Ξ⁻ and φ enhancements seen in Ar+KCl at 1.76 A GeV, no single model simultaneously and quantitatively reproduces the Ξ⁻/(Λ+Σ⁰) and φ/K⁻ ratios together with all singly-strange yields. Standard calculations underpredict the Ξ⁻/Λ/K⁺ ratio by factors of several. The question is therefore still considered open.

representations.normalized:
Consider high-energy hadronic and nuclear collisions of three types: proton–proton (pp), proton–nucleus (pA), and nucleus–nucleus (AA), performed at a range of center-of-mass energies. For each collision event class, define the charged-particle multiplicity density at midrapidity, dN_ch/dη, measured in a fixed pseudorapidity window around η = 0. For each event class, also measure the yields (per inelastic event) of strange and multi-strange hadrons (e.g., K_S^0, Λ, Ξ^-, Ω^-) and form their ratios to pion yields, which quantify strangeness production.

Question: Does the charged-particle multiplicity density dN_ch/dη serve as a universal scaling variable for the system-size and energy dependence of strangeness production? More precisely, when the strange-hadron-to-pion yield ratios are plotted as functions of dN_ch/dη, do the data points obtained from pp, pA, and AA collisions across different collision energies fall on a single common curve, independent of the colliding system and the collision energy?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Experimental measurements (notably ALICE) show that strange-to-pion yield ratios increase smoothly with dN_ch/dη from low-multiplicity pp through p–Pb and into Pb–Pb, with similar trends across systems, suggesting an approximate universal scaling at LHC energies. However, the question of whether this scaling is truly universal across all energies (including RHIC and lower-energy data) remains under investigation, and deviations have been reported, so the question is partially addressed rather than fully resolved.
