representations.normalized:
Consider relativistic heavy-ion (and small-system) collisions in which strange hadrons are produced and described by a statistical-thermal (hadron resonance gas) model. In this framework, exact conservation of the strangeness quantum number in a sub-volume V₀ leads to a canonical partition function whose strange-particle yields are suppressed relative to the grand-canonical limit, with a suppression factor that becomes more pronounced as the strangeness content |S| of the hadron species increases. As V₀ grows (parameterized experimentally by the charged-particle multiplicity dN_ch/dη), the canonical description is expected to smoothly approach the grand-canonical limit, producing a "strangeness hierarchy" in which the relative volume (multiplicity) dependence of yield ratios to pions becomes progressively steeper for hadrons of higher |S| (e.g., |S|=1 for K and Λ, |S|=2 for Ξ, |S|=3 for Ω).

Question: Across all available center-of-mass collision energies (from low-energy fixed-target through RHIC and LHC, and across system sizes from pp through p-A to A-A), do the measured multiplicity dependences of strange-to-nonstrange particle yield ratios quantitatively follow the canonical-to-grand-canonical transition predicted by the statistical-thermal model, including the expected ordering in which the slope of the multiplicity dependence increases monotonically with the strangeness content of the hadron?

Studies after 2017 (e.g., Vovchenko et al., 2009.04844) show that the canonical statistical model with strict local strangeness conservation qualitatively reproduces the observed strangeness hierarchy and the trend toward grand-canonical saturation at high multiplicities, but quantitatively over-suppresses (multi-)strange baryons at low multiplicities unless additional ingredients (S-matrix/phase-shift corrections, modified correlation volume) are introduced. The picture works approximately at LHC energies but discrepancies remain at low energies and small systems, so the question is partially settled rather than fully confirmed.

representations.normalized:
In relativistic heavy-ion collisions at low center-of-mass energies (roughly a few GeV per nucleon pair), the produced fireball is dominated by a dense hadronic medium rather than a deconfined partonic phase. Strange hadrons (e.g., kaons K^+, K^-, K^0, hyperons Λ, Σ, Ξ, and the φ meson) are produced near or below their elementary nucleon-nucleon thresholds and subsequently propagate through this hadronic medium, where their production cross sections, in-medium self-energies (mass shifts and widths), strangeness-exchange reactions (such as YN ↔ KN, K̄N ↔ πY), and rescattering/absorption all influence the observable yields, spectra, and flow.

Provide a quantitatively predictive theoretical description of the production and propagation of strange hadrons in low-energy heavy-ion collisions that:
(i) specifies the elementary and secondary production channels (including multi-step and sub-threshold mechanisms) together with their cross sections;
(ii) incorporates the in-medium modifications of strange-hadron properties (effective masses, widths, dispersion relations) in dense baryonic matter;
(iii) describes the transport and final-state interactions (including strangeness exchange, regeneration, and absorption); and
(iv) simultaneously reproduces, within a single consistent framework, the measured yields, transverse-momentum spectra, rapidity distributions, and collective flow (directed v1 and elliptic v2) of K^+, K^-, Λ, Ξ, and φ across the available low-energy heavy-ion data.

Determine whether such a consistent description currently exists, or identify the missing physical ingredients required to obtain it.

representations.normalized:
Consider relativistic heavy-ion collisions at low center-of-mass energies per nucleon pair (roughly in the range $\sqrt{s_{NN}} \lesssim 10$ GeV), in which a hot and dense hadronic medium is produced and subsequently freezes out into observable hadrons, including strange hadrons such as kaons, hyperons, and multi-strange baryons. The statistical hadronization model postulates that, at chemical freeze-out, the abundances of all hadron species $i$ are determined entirely by a small set of macroscopic thermodynamic parameters — typically a temperature $T$, a baryochemical potential $\mu_B$, a strangeness chemical potential $\mu_S$, an electric charge chemical potential $\mu_Q$, and a fireball volume $V$ (with possible canonical suppression factors for exactly conserved quantum numbers in small systems) — through the grand-canonical (or canonical) partition function of an ideal hadron resonance gas:
$$\langle N_i \rangle \;=\; \frac{V g_i}{2\pi^2}\int_0^\infty \frac{p^2\,dp}{\exp\!\big[(\sqrt{p^2+m_i^2}-\mu_i)/T\big] \pm 1}, \qquad \mu_i = B_i\mu_B + S_i\mu_S + Q_i\mu_Q.$$

Question: At low collision energies in the regime described above, does the produced hadronic medium behave as a macroscopic thermodynamic system whose particle yields — including those of strange hadrons of every strangeness content — are fully and consistently described by a single choice of statistical-model parameters $(T,\mu_B,\mu_S,\mu_Q,V)$ within experimental uncertainties? Equivalently, are all observed low-energy strangeness production phenomena (such as energy-dependent $K^+/\pi^+$ and $\Lambda/\pi$ ratios, multi-strange baryon yields, and possible canonical strangeness suppression) accounted for by such a statistical description, or do there exist robust strangeness observables at low energies that fall outside any consistent statistical-hadronization fit?

The question of whether the statistical hadronization model fully describes hadron (and especially strange hadron) production at low collision energies remains an active and unresolved topic. Recent reviews and HADES/STAR-FXT/NA61 results continue to report deviations (e.g., in $K^+/\pi^+$, $\Xi$ and $\Omega$ yields, and the need for canonical suppression or non-equilibrium strangeness fugacity $\gamma_S$), indicating the issue is still open.

Consider the s-wave low-energy scattering of two Λ hyperons, parameterized in the effective range expansion by a scattering length a₀ and effective range r_eff via k cot δ(k) = 1/a₀ + (1/2) r_eff k² + O(k⁴), where δ(k) is the s-wave phase shift at relative momentum k. In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the two-Λ correlation function C(k) is related to the source function S(r) and the relative wave function ψ_k(r) by the Koonin–Pratt formula C(k) = ∫ d³r S(r) |ψ_k(r)|², where ψ_k incorporates quantum statistics, the strong ΛΛ interaction (treated, e.g., via the Lednický–Lyuboshitz analytic formula), and feed-down/residual-source corrections. Two independent analyses of the same Au+Au √s_NN = 200 GeV ΛΛ correlation data have produced conflicting conclusions about the sign of the interaction: one inferring a weakly repulsive ΛΛ interaction and the other a weakly attractive ΛΛ interaction.

In high-energy heavy-ion collisions, light (anti-)nuclei and hypernuclei are produced and their integrated yields are typically described by the statistical (thermal) hadronization model, in which particle abundances are fixed at chemical freeze-out at a temperature T_chem on the order of 155 MeV. The hypertriton ³_ΛH is an extremely weakly bound object: it consists of a Λ hyperon bound to a deuteron with a Λ separation energy of only about 130 keV (total binding energy ≈ 2.35 MeV including the deuteron), giving an rms radius of order 10 fm — much larger than the typical inter-hadron spacing in the fireball at freeze-out, and a binding energy orders of magnitude smaller than T_chem.

Naively, such a fragile cluster cannot survive in a hot hadronic medium of temperature T_chem ≫ B(³_ΛH) (the so-called "snowball in hell" situation). Nevertheless, experimental measurements of (anti-)hypertriton yields in Pb–Pb and Au–Au collisions are well reproduced by statistical-model predictions that use the vacuum mass and assume formation at chemical freeze-out.

Provide a quantitative theoretical explanation of this fact: derive, from a microscopic or effective description of the expanding hadronic system, why the chemical-freeze-out statistical model accurately predicts the yield of very weakly bound hypernuclei such as ³_ΛH despite B(³_ΛH) ≪ T_chem, and identify the dynamical mechanism that fixes their abundance at (or near) chemical freeze-out values.

Relational Quantum Mechanics (RQM) is an interpretation of quantum theory which denies that physical systems possess observer-independent quantum states. Instead, the quantum state of a system S is defined only relative to a second physical system O that interacts with (or "observes") S; different observing systems may simultaneously assign different states to the same system S, and there is no privileged absolute state. The "third person problem" arises when one considers an external observer P who describes the joint system S+O: P's account of the values realized in S relative to O can come into tension with O's own account of those values, raising the question of how to reconcile the different observer-relative descriptions and what physical content the relativization carries.

Problem. Provide a precise explication of the relativization of quantum states to observing systems in RQM and determine what explanatory role this relativization plays. Specifically:

(a) Formulate, in a mathematically explicit framework (e.g., specifying for each ordered pair (S,O) of physical systems a state-assignment map and rules governing how distinct assignments relative to different observers O, O', P, ... are related), what it means for a quantum state to be "relative to" an observer.

(b) Using this framework, analyze the third person problem: given a system S, an observer O that has interacted with S, and a further observer P describing S+O, state and justify consistency conditions that the state assignments relative to O and relative to P must satisfy, and exhibit whether such conditions can be met without reintroducing observer-independent facts.

(c) Identify in precise terms the explanatory or predictive surplus, if any, that relativization provides over a non-relational description of quantum phenomena (in particular regarding measurement outcomes, the quantum-to-classical transition, and locality/Bell-type correlations), or else show that relativization amounts to a redescription with no additional explanatory content.

Decide whether RQM, so formulated, genuinely advances the understanding of quantum phenomena, or whether the relativization of states fails to perform substantive explanatory work.

Within the interpretational framework of Relational Quantum Mechanics (RQM)—in which the state of a physical system S is not absolute but is defined only relative to another system O acting as an "observer," and in which all physical systems (including observers) are to be treated quantum mechanically on equal footing—provide a justified account of the state reduction (collapse) process associated with measurement. Specifically, determine whether RQM can:

(i) explain the occurrence of definite, observer-relative outcomes in a measurement interaction between two quantum systems S and O without presupposing an unexplained collapse postulate inherited from standard quantum mechanics;

(ii) resolve the "third person" problem, i.e., reconcile the descriptions given by an external observer E who treats the joint S+O system unitarily (and would therefore assign an entangled, non-collapsed state) with the description relative to O (for which a definite outcome has occurred); and

(iii) thereby resolve the measurement problem stricto sensu, rather than merely re-labeling quantum states with observer indices while leaving the physical mechanism of state reduction unaccounted for.

Either supply such a justified account, or prove that no consistent account satisfying (i)–(iii) is possible within the axioms of RQM.

Setup. Let $C \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a simplicial cone with apex at the origin whose $n$ edges are spanned by vectors in general position with respect to the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^n$ (i.e., the edges do not lie in any rational hyperplane other than those containing them). The sail of $C$ is the boundary of the convex hull of $(C \cap \mathbb{Z}^n) \setminus \{0\}$; the collection of sails associated to all $2^n$ connected components of $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \bigcup H_i$ (where $H_i$ are the $n$ hyperplanes spanning the faces of $C$) is the $n$-dimensional continued fraction in the sense of Klein associated to $C$.

Two cones $C_1, C_2$ are said to be integer congruent if there exists an affine transformation $A \in \mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Z}) \ltimes \mathbb{Z}^n$ such that $A(C_1) = C_2$.

Problem. Construct an adequate complete invariant of such simplicial cones up to integer congruence; that is, exhibit a computable invariant $I(\cdot)$ (for instance, of combinatorial-geometric type generalizing the Lagrange–LLS sequence of an integer angle in dimension two) such that for any two cones $C_1, C_2$ as above,
$$I(C_1) = I(C_2) \iff C_1 \text{ and } C_2 \text{ are integer congruent}.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No publication appears to provide a complete integer-congruence invariant for cones in the multidimensional Klein continued-fraction setting. While in dimension two the LLS sequence gives a complete invariant of integer angles, in higher dimensions only partial invariants (face combinatorics, integer areas/volumes, edge lengths and statistical characteristics studied since Arnold) are known. Let $C \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be a simplicial cone with apex at the origin bounded by $n+1$ hyperplanes in general position with respect to the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$ (i.e., none of the bounding hyperplanes contains a nonzero lattice point). The associated Klein sail is the boundary of the convex hull
$$\operatorname{Sail}(C) \;=\; \partial igl(\operatorname{conv}(C \cap \mathbb{Z}^{n+1} \setminus \{0\}) igr),$$
which is an $n$-dimensional generalized polyhedral surface. Its faces (compact convex lattice polytopes of dimensions $0,1,\dots,n$) are called the faces of the sail. Two faces are said to be of the same combinatorial type if they are equivalent under the action of the affine group $\operatorname{GL}(n+1,\mathbb{Z}) \ltimes \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$ on lattice polytopes (equivalently, if there is a lattice-affine bijection between them).

Problem: Classify all combinatorial types of faces (in the lattice/affine equivalence sense above) that can occur as faces of some Klein sail $\operatorname{Sail}(C)$ arising from an $(n+1)$-dimensional simplicial cone in general position with the lattice. In particular, determine which lattice polytopes (up to $\operatorname{GL}\ltimes\mathbb{Z}$ equivalence) are realizable as faces of sails of Klein polyhedra associated with multidimensional geometric continued fractions.

A discrete group $\Gamma$ is said to have Kazhdan's property (T) (equivalently, to be a Kazhdan group) if every unitary representation of $\Gamma$ on a Hilbert space that has almost-invariant unit vectors must have a nonzero invariant vector; equivalently, the trivial representation is isolated in the unitary dual of $\Gamma$. Let $\mathrm{Homeo}_+([0,1])$ denote the group of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of the closed interval $[0,1]$ (those fixing the endpoints).

Question: Does there exist a nontrivial (and therefore necessarily infinite) Kazhdan group $\Gamma$ that admits a faithful homomorphism $\Gamma \to \mathrm{Homeo}_+([0,1])$? Equivalently, is there a nontrivial group with Kazhdan's property (T) acting effectively by orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of the interval?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is widely cited as open. Background and setup. Let $A \in \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ be a hyperbolic matrix with three real, distinct, irrational eigenvalues, and let $\pi_1, \pi_2, \pi_3 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be the three eigenplanes through the origin spanned by pairs of eigenvectors. The complement $\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus (\pi_1 \cup \pi_2 \cup \pi_3)$ has eight open simplicial cones. For each such cone $C$, the boundary of the convex hull of the nonzero integer points of $\overline{C}$ is a polyhedral surface called a sail; the union of the eight sails is the (two-dimensional) Klein continued fraction associated with $A$. The subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ commuting with $A$ contains a free abelian subgroup of rank $2$ (by the Dirichlet unit theorem) which acts freely and properly discontinuously on each sail; the quotient of a sail by this action is a compact $2$-torus tiled by the images of the faces, edges, and vertices of the sail. This tiled torus is called the torus decomposition of the periodic two-dimensional continued fraction.

Problem. Give a complete classification (combinatorial description) of all tilings of the $2$-torus by convex polygons that arise as torus decompositions of periodic two-dimensional continued fractions in the sense above. Equivalently, characterize precisely which combinatorial torus tilings can be realized by the quotient of some sail of some hyperbolic $A \in \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ under the action of its associated rank-$2$ unit group.

Let $\Delta(x, u, u_{(1)}, \ldots, u_{(k)}) = 0$ be a system of partial differential equations for an unknown function $u : \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R}^m$, where $u_{(j)}$ denotes the collection of $j$-th order partial derivatives of $u$. A (classical Lie point) infinitesimal symmetry of the system is a vector field
$$ X = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \xi^i(x,u)\,\partial_{x^i} + \sum_{\alpha=1}^{m} \eta^\alpha(x,u)\,\partial_{u^\alpha} $$
whose $k$-th prolongation $\mathrm{pr}^{(k)} X$ annihilates $\Delta$ on the solution variety $\{\Delta = 0\}$. Imposing this condition and equating coefficients of independent monomials in the derivatives of $u$ yields a linear system of partial differential equations in the unknown coefficient functions $\xi^i$ and $\eta^\alpha$, called the determining system. For PDEs with a high degree of symmetry, this determining system is typically large and overdetermined (having many more equations than unknowns), and reducing it to a standard form (e.g., by differential elimination, the Cartan–Kuranishi prolongation–projection procedure, or differential Gröbner/Janet-type bases) is computationally expensive.

Problem. Develop effective algorithms for completely solving the overdetermined linear systems of partial differential equations that arise as the determining systems for the (point, contact, or generalized) symmetries of partial differential equations admitting large symmetry algebras. The algorithms should:

1. Reduce a given overdetermined linear PDE system to an involutive (passive) form of finite type whenever possible, with explicit complexity bounds.
2. Determine the structure (dimension, Levi decomposition, structure constants) of the resulting symmetry Lie algebra without requiring the closed-form integration of the system.
3. Produce, when possible, explicit closed-form general solutions of the determining equations, identifying all functional and constant parameters.
4. Handle systems containing arbitrary functions/parameters (classification problems) by automatically splitting into all inequivalent branches.

Provide a rigorous specification, correctness proof, and termination/complexity analysis of such an algorithm, or prove obstructions to its existence.

Consider equations whose unknowns are functions $u(n,t)$ (or $u(n,m)$) of one or more discrete variables $n,m\in\mathbb{Z}$ and possibly continuous variables $t\in\mathbb{R}$, of the general form
$$F igl(n,t,\{u(n+i,t)\},\{\partial_t^j u(n+i,t)\} igr)=0$$
for differential-difference equations, or
$$F igl(n,m,\{u(n+i,m+j)\} igr)=0$$
for purely difference equations, where the shift operator $S$ acts by $S u(n,\cdot)=u(n+1,\cdot)$.

Several inequivalent notions of a ``symmetry'' of such an equation appear in the literature, including:

1. Continuous Lie point symmetries acting on the continuous variables and on the dependent variable, with the discrete index $n$ held fixed.
2. Generalized (Lie–Bäcklund) symmetries given by evolutionary vector fields $\mathbf{v}_Q=Q\,\partial_u$ with characteristic $Q$ depending on shifts $S^k u$ and derivatives, whose prolongation annihilates $F$ on the solution manifold.
3. Symmetries arising as compatible flows in an integrable hierarchy (master symmetries, recursion operators, Lax-pair generated symmetries).
4. Discrete/point transformations of the lattice variables themselves, including transformations mixing $n$ and $u$.
5. Symmetries defined via formal pseudo-difference operators, or via the variational/Lagrangian framework for difference equations.

The problem is the following:

(a) Establish precise relationships between these distinct notions of symmetry for differential-difference and difference equations, identifying when they coincide, when one is strictly stronger, and how the corresponding symmetry algebras or groups embed into one another.

(b) Formulate, if possible, a single standard definition of a symmetry of a differential-difference (respectively, difference) equation that specializes to each of the above notions in the appropriate limit and that reduces to the classical definition of a symmetry of a differential equation in the continuum limit.

For integers $k \geq 2$ and $d \geq 2$, let $\mathcal{H}_d(\mathbb{P}^k)$ denote the space of holomorphic endomorphisms of the complex projective space $\mathbb{P}^k$ of algebraic degree $d$, equipped with its natural complex-manifold (parameter) structure and Lebesgue-class measure. For $f \in \mathcal{H}_d(\mathbb{P}^k)$, an attracting periodic point is a periodic point $p$ of period $n$ such that all eigenvalues of $Df^n(p)$ have modulus strictly less than $1$; the basin of attraction of such a point is called a sink of $f$. Define
$$\mathcal{F} = \{ f \in \mathcal{H}_d(\mathbb{P}^k) : f \text{ has infinitely many sinks} \}.$$
It is known that $\mathcal{F}$ is nonempty when $k \geq 2$ (via the Newhouse phenomenon of persistent homoclinic tangencies). Determine whether $\mathcal{F}$ can have nonempty interior in $\mathcal{H}_d(\mathbb{P}^k)$, and whether $\mathcal{F}$ can have positive Lebesgue measure.

$$f(z,w) = (p(z) + aw,\; bz),$$
where $a,b \in \mathbb{C}$ with $ab \neq 0$ and $p$ is a polynomial of degree $d \geq 2$. Assume that the origin $0 \in \mathbb{C}^2$ is an attracting fixed point of $f$, and let
$$\Omega = \{q \in \mathbb{C}^2 : f^n(q) \to 0 \text{ as } n \to \infty\}$$
denote its basin of attraction. It is known that $\Omega$ is a Fatou–Bieberbach domain, i.e. $\Omega$ is biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^2$ but $\Omega \neq \mathbb{C}^2$. Let $M$ be a connected complex manifold of complex dimension $2$. Suppose there exists a sequence of injective holomorphic maps $\varphi_n : B \to M$, where $B \subset \mathbb{C}^2$ denotes the open unit ball, such that
\[
\varphi_n(B) \subset \varphi_{n+1}(B) \quad \text{for all } n, \qquad M = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \varphi_n(B).
\]
Assume in addition that the Kobayashi pseudometric $K_M$ vanishes identically on $M$. Must $M$ be biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^2$?

(Background motivating the question: Let $F : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}^n$ be a biholomorphism and let $K \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a hyperbolic invariant set of saddle type whose stable dimension equals $2$. For $p \in K$, the stable manifold $W^s(p)$ is an increasing union of biholomorphic images of the unit ball on which the Kobayashi pseudometric vanishes identically; one asks whether $W^s(p)$ must be biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^2$. This is known when $p$ is a periodic saddle point.)

representations.normalized:
Consider the symplectic map of $\mathbb{C}^2$ defined by
$$H(z,w) = (f(z) - w,\; z),$$
where $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ is an entire function with $f(0)=0$. Then $H(0,0)=(0,0)$, and a direct computation shows that the eigenvalues of the differential $H'(0,0)$ are of the form $e^{\pm i\theta}$ for some $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$ (determined by $f'(0)$). Because the eigenvalues are inverses of each other on the unit circle, infinitely many resonance relations $\lambda_1^{a}\lambda_2^{b}=\lambda_j$ (with $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$, $a+b\geq 2$, $j\in\{1,2\}$) hold, leading to an infinite family of formal compatibility conditions for normalization.

A Siegel domain (rotation domain) for $H$ at the fixed point $(0,0)$ is an open neighborhood $U$ of $(0,0)$ that is invariant under $H$, on which some subsequence of the iterates $H^{n_k}$ converges, uniformly on compact subsets of $U$, to the identity map of $U$.

Problem: Construct an entire function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ with $f(0)=0$ such that the associated symplectic Hénon-type map $H(z,w)=(f(z)-w, z)$ admits a Siegel domain at the fixed point $(0,0)$, or show that no such entire $f$ exists.

Let $k\ge 2$ and let $f:\mathbb{P}^k	o\mathbb{P}^k$ be a holomorphic endomorphism (a holomorphic self-map of complex projective $k$-space, necessarily of some algebraic degree $d\ge 2$). The Fatou set $F(f)$ is the largest open subset of $\mathbb{P}^k$ on which the iterates $\{f^n\}_{n\ge 1}$ form a normal family; its connected components are called the Fatou components of $f$. A Fatou component $U$ is called invariant if $f(U)=U$.

Suppose $U$ is an invariant Fatou component of $f$ such that for every $z\in U$ the orbit $f^n(z)$ accumulates only on the boundary $\partial U$ (equivalently, every limit map of a convergent subsequence of $\{f^n|_U\}$ takes values in $\partial U$). A point $p\in\mathbb{P}^k$ is said to be a parabolic fixed point of $f$ if $f(p)=p$ and at least one eigenvalue of the differential $df_p$ is a root of unity (in particular, not all eigenvalues lie strictly inside the unit disk).

Question: Must there exist a parabolic fixed point of $f$ on $\partial U$?

More generally, give a complete classification of the invariant (and periodic) Fatou components of holomorphic endomorphisms of $\mathbb{P}^k$ for $k\ge 2$, extending the one-dimensional classification of Fatou for $k=1$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The classification of (periodic) Fatou components for holomorphic endomorphisms of $\mathbb{P}^k$ with $k\ge 2$ is a long-standing open problem. The one-dimensional case was settled by Fatou, but in higher dimension only partial results are known: a near-complete classification of invariant Fatou components has been obtained for moderately dissipative Hénon maps (Lyubich–Peters), and partial Sullivan-type non-wandering theorems have been proved for certain polynomial skew products, while wandering Fatou components have been constructed in dimension two (Astorg–Buff–Dujardin–Peters–Raissy). The general question on $\mathbb{P}^k$, including the existence of a parabolic fixed point on $\partial U$ when iterates tend to the boundary, appears to remain open.

The nonwandering set $\Omega(f)$ is defined as the set of points $p \in \mathbb{P}^k$ such that for every neighborhood $U$ of $p$, there exists an integer $n \geq 1$ with $f^n(U) \cap U \neq \emptyset$.

Define a Siegel analytic set for $f$ to be a closed analytic subset $X$ of some open set $V \subset \mathbb{P}^k$ such that there is a subsequence $n_i \to \infty$ for which the iterates $f^{n_i}|_X$ converge to the identity $\mathrm{Id}_X$ uniformly on compact subsets of $X$.

(a) Is $\Omega(f)$ equal to the closure of the union of the periodic points of $f$ together with all Siegel analytic sets of $f$?

(b) For holomorphic (entire) self-maps $f: \mathbb{C}^2 \to \mathbb{C}^2$, does there exist a counterexample to the analogous statement?

Background. Let $\Delta(x,u,u^{(k)})=0$ denote a system of partial differential equations for a function $u(x)$ of independent variables $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, where $u^{(k)}$ denotes the collection of partial derivatives of $u$ up to order $k$. The classical Lie group (infinitesimal) method seeks one-parameter groups of point transformations
$$\tilde x_i = x_i+\varepsilon\,\xi_i(x,u)+O(\varepsilon^2),\qquad \tilde u = u+\varepsilon\,\eta(x,u)+O(\varepsilon^2),$$
whose prolongation leaves the equation invariant on its solution manifold. Invariance of $\Delta=0$ under the prolonged vector field $\mathbf v=\sum_i\xi_i\partial_{x_i}+\eta\,\partial_u$ yields the determining equations for $(\xi_i,\eta)$; the resulting symmetry algebra produces group-invariant (similarity) reductions of $\Delta=0$ to systems with fewer independent variables.

Generalized procedures (the nonclassical method of Bluman and Cole, the direct method of Clarkson and Kruskal, and their further extensions) impose the symmetry condition only on the joint solution set of $\Delta=0$ and an invariant-surface condition $\xi_i u_{x_i}=\eta$, and can produce similarity reductions of $\Delta=0$ that do not arise from any classical Lie point symmetry of $\Delta$.

Problem. Formulate an effective a priori criterion, expressible directly in terms of the partial differential equation $\Delta(x,u,u^{(k)})=0$ itself (its coefficients, structure, or invariants), that decides — without performing the explicit reduction computation — whether $\Delta=0$ admits symmetry reductions that cannot be obtained by the classical Lie group method, and hence for which a generalized (nonclassical, direct, or related) approach is genuinely required.

Let f : ℂ^k → ℂ^k be a polynomial map of topological degree d_t that extends to a holomorphic endomorphism of the complex projective space ℙ^k, and let ω be the Fubini–Study (Kähler) form on ℙ^k. It is known that the sequence of normalized pull-backs (f^n)*ω^k / d_t^{nk} converges to a mixing probability measure μ, the unique measure of maximal entropy of f, whose support S_μ is contained in the non-wandering set Ω(f) and contains a dense set of repelling periodic points.

Recall that the Hausdorff dimension of a Borel probability measure ν is
   dim_H(ν) := inf { dim_H(B) : B Borel, ν(B) = 1 }.

For k = 1 (polynomial P on ℂ), μ coincides with the harmonic measure at ∞ of the filled Julia set K_P = { z ∈ ℂ : (P^n(z))_n is bounded }, and the theorems of Makarov and Bishop–Jones–Wolff yield dim_H(μ) = 1.

Address the following questions:

(a) Is the support S_μ open in the non-wandering set Ω(f)? (The case where S_μ is hyperbolic is known.)

(b) How does the one-dimensional dimension result extend to polynomial maps on ℂ^k that are holomorphic on ℙ^k? More generally, determine the Hausdorff dimension dim_H(μ) for an arbitrary holomorphic endomorphism f of ℙ^k.

(c) For the family of small perturbations f_{ε,δ}(z, w) = (z^2 + ε w, w^2 + δ z) on ℂ^2 (or ℙ^2), characterize the parameters (ε, δ) for which the maximal entropy measure μ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.

Significant partial progress is known. Berteloot–Dupont and Dupont showed that Lattès endomorphisms are the only holomorphic endomorphisms of ℙ^k whose maximal entropy measure is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and that they are characterized by the maximality of dim_H(μ) (equivalently minimality of Lyapunov exponents). representations.normalized:
Consider a boundary value problem consisting of a (system of) differential equation(s)
   E(x, u, u_x, u_xx, ...) = 0
posed on a domain Ω ⊂ ℝ^n with boundary conditions
   B_i(x, u, u_x, ...) = 0  on  Γ_i ⊂ ∂Ω,  i = 1, ..., k.

The classical Lie symmetry approach to such a problem requires that one seek a one-parameter Lie group of point transformations
   x* = x + ε ξ(x,u) + O(ε^2),   u* = u + ε η(x,u) + O(ε^2),
whose infinitesimal generator X = ξ·∂_x + η·∂_u (suitably prolonged) leaves invariant simultaneously:
 (i) the differential equation E = 0,
 (ii) each boundary manifold Γ_i, and
 (iii) each boundary condition B_i = 0 on Γ_i.

This simultaneous-invariance requirement is typically very restrictive and admits only few (often none) nontrivial symmetries even when the underlying equation possesses a rich symmetry algebra.

Problem. Develop a general, systematic procedure for applying symmetry methods to boundary value problems that goes beyond the classical requirement of joint invariance of the equation and all boundary conditions under a single one-parameter Lie group. Specifically, formulate a framework — for example by constructing auxiliary differential equations satisfied by all solutions of a designated subset of the boundary conditions but not by all solutions of E = 0, by allowing symmetries that map solutions of the boundary value problem to solutions while not preserving the boundary conditions individually, or by another mechanism — that
 (a) reduces, in a constructive algorithmic way, to determining symmetries of the boundary value problem (in the sense of mapping solutions to solutions),
 (b) recovers the classical jointly-invariant symmetries as a special case, and
 (c) is capable of producing additional, genuinely new symmetries useful for obtaining exact or invariant solutions of boundary value problems for broad classes of equations and domains.

Recent literature (e.g., Bluman's monographs, Hydon's work on initial-value problems, and articles on Lie symmetries of nonlinear boundary value problems) develops partial techniques — weaker invariance requirements, conditional symmetries, and case-by-case algorithms — but no fully general procedure replacing the classical joint-invariance requirement is known. Surveys explicitly note the lack of a general method for constructing auxiliary equations satisfied by the boundary conditions but not by the full PDE, leaving the question open.

Let $f:\mathbb{P}^k\to\mathbb{P}^k$ be a holomorphic endomorphism of algebraic degree $d\geq 2$, and let $T$ denote its Green current, that is, the unique positive closed $(1,1)$-current of mass $1$ satisfying $f^*T=d\,T$, obtained as the limit $T=\lim_{n\to\infty} d^{-n}(f^n)^*\omega$ for $\omega$ the Fubini–Study form. Recall that $T$ is said to be extremal in the cone of positive closed $(1,1)$-currents of mass $1$ on $\mathbb{P}^k$ if whenever $T=\tfrac{1}{2}(S_1+S_2)$ with $S_1,S_2$ positive closed $(1,1)$-currents of mass $1$, one has $S_1=S_2=T$.

Characterize the holomorphic endomorphisms $f$ of $\mathbb{P}^k$ for which the Green current $T$ is extremal.

Known facts to be incorporated into the characterization:
(a) If $f$ is given in homogeneous coordinates $[z_1:\cdots:z_k:t]$ by
$$f([z_1:\cdots:z_k:t]) = [P_1(z,t):\cdots:P_k(z,t):t^d],$$
where each $P_j$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$ in $(z_1,\dots,z_k,t)$ containing no monomial that is a pure power of $t$, then $T$ is extremal.
(b) For Ueda-type examples the Green current need not be extremal; in particular, for the map on $\mathbb{P}^2$ given by $[z:w:t]\mapsto[z^2:w^2-2zt:t^2]$, the Green current $T$ is not extremal.

Provide necessary and sufficient conditions on $f$ for the extremality of $T$.

A general characterization of when the Green current of a holomorphic endomorphism of P^k is extremal does not appear in the literature. Partial results are known: extremality holds for skew products of the stated form, and Jonsson observed non-extremality for Ueda-type examples such as [z^2:w^2-2zt:t^2]. Recent work studies regularity for "semi-extremal" endomorphisms of P^2, which suggests the full characterization remains open.

Background. For a partial differential equation $\Delta(x,u^{(n)})=0$ with independent variables $x=(x_1,\dots,x_p)$ and dependent variable $u$, the classical Lie symmetry method seeks one-parameter groups of point transformations leaving the equation invariant; the corresponding infinitesimal generator $X=\sum_i \xi_i(x,u)\partial_{x_i}+\eta(x,u)\partial_u$ is determined by linear determining equations. The nonclassical (conditional) symmetry method of Bluman and Cole augments the system $\Delta=0$ with the invariant surface condition $Q[u]:=\sum_i \xi_i(x,u)u_{x_i}-\eta(x,u)=0$ and requires invariance only of the joint system $\{\Delta=0,\,Q=0\}$ together with its differential consequences; the resulting determining equations for $(\xi_i,\eta)$ are nonlinear, and the associated $Q$-conditional symmetries yield reductions to lower-dimensional equations and exact solutions not obtainable by classical symmetries.

Setup. Let $u_n(t)$ (or $u_{n,m}$) denote a function defined on a lattice indexed by integers $n$ (and $m$), and consider:
(a) a differential-difference equation of the form
$$F\bigl(t,n,u_n,u_{n\pm 1},\dots,u_{n\pm k},\dot u_n,\dot u_{n\pm 1},\dots,\ddot u_n,\dots\bigr)=0,$$
(b) a (purely) difference equation of the form
$$G\bigl(n,m,u_{n+i,m+j}\bigr)_{(i,j)\in S}=0$$
on a multidimensional lattice, where $S$ is a finite stencil.

Problem. Develop a systematic theory of nonclassical (conditional) symmetry reductions for differential-difference equations and for difference equations. In particular:

1. Formulate an analogue of the invariant surface condition $Q[u]=0$ appropriate for shift operators on a lattice, and derive the corresponding nonclassical determining equations for differential-difference and difference equations.

2. Establish algorithmic procedures (and, where possible, closed-form criteria) for solving these nonlinear determining systems and for constructing the resulting symmetry reductions to lower-dimensional differential-difference, difference, or ordinary differential/difference equations.

3. Apply the framework to obtain new exact solutions of representative integrable and non-integrable differential-difference and difference equations (such as the Toda lattice, Volterra lattice, discrete KdV, and discrete sine-Gordon equations) that are not accessible via classical Lie point symmetries.

4. Clarify the relationship between the resulting nonclassical lattice symmetries and known notions such as generalized symmetries, master symmetries, and continuous limits to nonclassical symmetries of the corresponding partial differential equations.

Background and setup. Let $\Delta(x,u^{(n)})=0$ be a partial differential equation for an unknown function $u(x)$, $x=(x^1,\dots,x^p)$, where $u^{(n)}$ denotes $u$ together with all its partial derivatives up to order $n$. Two notions of symmetry are recalled.

(a) Generalized (Lie–Bäcklund) symmetry. An evolutionary vector field $\mathbf{v}_Q = Q(x,u^{(k)})\,\partial_u$, with characteristic $Q$ depending on $x$, $u$, and derivatives of $u$ up to some finite order, is a generalized symmetry of $\Delta=0$ if its prolongation satisfies
$$\operatorname{pr}\mathbf{v}_Q[\Delta]\big|_{\Delta=0}=0,$$
i.e. the symmetry condition holds on the solution manifold of $\Delta=0$ together with all its differential consequences.

(b) Nonclassical (conditional) symmetry. An evolutionary vector field $\mathbf{v}_Q$ is a nonclassical symmetry of $\Delta=0$ if its prolongation annihilates $\Delta$ on the joint solution manifold of the system
$$\Delta = 0, \qquad Q = 0,$$
together with all differential consequences of both equations. Equivalently, $\operatorname{pr}\mathbf{v}_Q[\Delta]$ vanishes modulo $\Delta$, $Q$, and their derivatives. When $Q$ is restricted to be linear in first derivatives of $u$ (the classical Bluman–Cole point case), this recovers the usual notion of nonclassical point symmetry.

Let $f: \mathbb{C}^2 \to \mathbb{C}^2$ be a complex Hénon map, i.e., a finite composition of maps of the form $(x,y) \mapsto (p(x) - ay, x)$ with $p$ a polynomial of degree at least $2$ and $a \in \mathbb{C}^*$. Write the $n$-th iterate as $f^n = (g_n, h_n)$, where $g_n, h_n : \mathbb{C}^2 \to \mathbb{C}$ are the coordinate projections of $f^n$. Let $J^+$ denote the forward Julia set of $f$ (the boundary of the set of points whose forward orbits are bounded), and let $\mu$ be the unique maximal-entropy invariant measure of $f$, with support $S_\mu = J^+ \cap J^-$ (the closure of the saddle periodic points).

Determine whether there exists a Hénon map $f$ as above and a point $p = (x,y) \in S_\mu$ such that for every $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ and every $q \in S_\mu$, there is an integer $n \geq 0$ for which
$$\|g_n(p) - g_n(q)\| < \varepsilon,$$
where only the first ($x$-)coordinate of the iterates is used to measure distance. (It is known that the analogous statement with $\|f^n(p) - f^n(q)\| < \varepsilon$ replacing $\|g_n(p) - g_n(q)\| < \varepsilon$ has no such $p$.)

Let $\Delta(x, u, u_{(1)}, \dots, u_{(k)}) = 0$ be a system of differential equations for an unknown function $u(x)$, where $x = (x^1, \dots, x^n)$ are independent variables and $u_{(j)}$ denotes the collection of all partial derivatives of $u$ of order $j$. A common strategy for producing special (e.g., invariant, similarity, separable, or otherwise structured) solutions is to append to $\Delta = 0$ one or more auxiliary differential constraints $\Phi(x, u, u_{(1)}, \dots, u_{(m)}) = 0$, or to substitute an ansatz $u = F(x, \phi_1(\xi_1), \dots, \phi_r(\xi_r))$ of a prescribed functional form, and then to solve the overdetermined system that results.

Develop an a priori criterion (intrinsic to the differential equation $\Delta = 0$, without first attempting the reduction) that determines:

(a) which differential constraints $\Phi = 0$, when adjoined to $\Delta = 0$, yield a compatible overdetermined system whose general solution is nontrivial and explicitly computable; and

(b) which ansatz choices for $u$ reduce $\Delta = 0$ to a system of equations whose solutions can be found in closed form (or by a finite, effective procedure).

Equivalently, characterize, in terms of structural invariants of $\Delta$ (such as its symmetry algebra, conservation laws, integrability properties, or geometric data of its associated jet-space submanifold), the set of useful differential constraints and computationally tractable ansätze.

Let $k\ge 1$ and write coordinates on $\mathbb{C}^{2k}$ as $(z_1,\dots,z_k,w_1,\dots,w_k)$, where $z_j = x_j + i x'_j$ and $w_j = y_j + i y'_j$ with $x_j,x'_j,y_j,y'_j\in\mathbb{R}$. Let $\omega = \sum_{j=1}^{k} dz_j\wedge dw_j$ be the standard holomorphic symplectic form on $\mathbb{C}^{2k}$, and identify $\mathbb{R}^{2k}\subset\mathbb{C}^{2k}$ with the totally real subspace $\{x'_j = 0,\ y'_j = 0,\ j=1,\dots,k\}$, with real coordinates $(x,y)=(x_1,\dots,x_k,y_1,\dots,y_k)$.

Let $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{R}}$ denote the class of holomorphic symplectomorphisms $f:\mathbb{C}^{2k}\to\mathbb{C}^{2k}$ (i.e. biholomorphisms with $f^{*}\omega = \omega$) that preserve $\mathbb{R}^{2k}$, meaning $f(\mathbb{R}^{2k})=\mathbb{R}^{2k}$. Endow $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{R}}$ with the Whitney fine topology; with this topology $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a Baire space.

For $f\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{R}}$ define the real filled Julia set
$$K^{\mathbb{R}}_f \;:=\; \{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2k}\;:\; \{f^n(x,y)\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\text{ is bounded in }\mathbb{R}^{2k}\}.$$

Prove that the set
$$\mathcal{S}'_{\mathbb{R}} \;:=\; \{f\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{R}}\;:\; K^{\mathbb{R}}_f\text{ has empty interior in }\mathbb{R}^{2k}\}$$
is a $G_\delta$ dense subset of $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{R}}$.

Let $X_{\mathbb{C}}$ be a projective variety over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $f: X_{\mathbb{C}} \to X_{\mathbb{C}}$ be an endomorphism. Say that $f$ has "large dynamics" if, for instance, $f$ has positive topological entropy, or equivalently the first dynamical degree $\lambda_1(f) > 1$, or more generally if $f$ admits a "large" non-wandering set. Suppose that $X$ is defined over a number field $k$ with $[k:\mathbb{Q}] < \infty$, and that $f$ is also defined over $k$, so that one may speak of the set of $k$-rational points $X(k)$.

Question: Does the largeness of the dynamics of $f$ force the set of rational points $X(k)$ (possibly after replacing $k$ by a finite extension) to be "large" in $X_{\mathbb{C}}$? In particular, must $X(\bar{\mathbb{Q}})$ be Zariski dense in $X_{\mathbb{C}}$? More broadly, prove that the existence of an endomorphism $f$ with large dynamics on $X$ implies non-trivial arithmetic properties of $X(k)$ (such as potential density of rational points).

Bost and closely related to potential density conjectures (Campana, Harris–Tschinkel) and to the Zariski dense orbit and Kawaguchi–Silverman conjectures, remains open in general. Let $\mathbb{P}^2$ denote the complex projective plane. A compact set $K \subset \mathbb{P}^2$ is said to be laminated by smooth holomorphic curves if $K$ admits a lamination structure whose leaves are smooth (immersed) holomorphic curves; equivalently, every point of $K$ has a neighborhood in $K$ biholomorphic to a product $T \times \mathbb{D}$, where $T$ is a topological transversal and $\{t\} \times \mathbb{D}$ corresponds to a holomorphic disk lying in a leaf.

Question: Does there exist a compact set $K \subset \mathbb{P}^2$ which is laminated by smooth holomorphic curves and which is not itself a (compact) algebraic curve?

Equivalently (in the related foliation form): Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a holomorphic foliation (with singularities) on $\mathbb{P}^2$, and let $\mathrm{Sing}\,\mathcal{F}$ denote its (non-empty) singular set. Must the closure $\overline{L}$ of every leaf $L$ of $\mathcal{F}$ intersect $\mathrm{Sing}\,\mathcal{F}$? (If not, then $\overline{L}\setminus L$ would provide a non-trivial compact set in $\mathbb{P}^2$ laminated by smooth holomorphic curves.)

It is known that:
(a) Analogous compact laminated sets that are not algebraic do exist in $\mathbb{P}^3$.
(b) There is no closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $\mathbb{P}^2$ directed by such a lamination, except when the lamination is itself a compact algebraic curve (i.e., if locally the current has the form $\int d\mu(\theta)\,[V_\theta]$ with $V_\theta$ the leaves, then the lamination must be a compact curve).

Determine whether such a non-algebraic compact lamination in $\mathbb{P}^2$ can exist.

The existence of a non-trivial minimal set / non-algebraic compact lamination by holomorphic curves for a holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb{P}^2$ remains a well-known open problem. There exist unique positive closed (1,1)-currents T^+ and T^- of mass 1 supported on J^+ and J^- respectively. Set μ = T^+ ∧ T^-, the canonical invariant measure of f, and J* = supp(μ). Let Ω(f) denote the nonwandering set of f, which satisfies Ω(f) ⊆ K.

(a) Determine the precise inclusion relations among Ω(f), J, and J*. In particular, is it always the case that J* = J = Ω(f), or can these sets differ?

(b) Characterize, among all generalized Hénon maps, those for which f is uniformly hyperbolic on Ω(f).

Let $F:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^2$ be a biholomorphism (in particular, one may consider a Hénon map of the form $F(z,w)=(p(z)-aw,z)$ with $p$ a polynomial of degree at least $2$ and $a\in\mathbb{C}^*$). Suppose $F$ has a fixed point $p_0$ at which the differential $dF_{p_0}$ has eigenvalues $e^{2\pi i\alpha_1}, e^{2\pi i\alpha_2}$ with $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ irrational, and $F$ is locally linearizable at $p_0$. A Siegel domain for $F$ is a maximal connected open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}^2$ containing $p_0$ on which $F$ is conjugate, by a biholomorphism, to a linear rotation, i.e., the iterates $\{F^n|_\Omega\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}$ form a normal family with limits also injective and the closure of $\{F^n|_\Omega\}$ in $\mathrm{Hol}(\Omega,\mathbb{C}^2)$ is a compact group acting transitively.

Question: Can such a Siegel domain $\Omega$ have boundary $\partial\Omega$ that is strongly pseudoconvex (i.e., $\partial\Omega$ is a $C^2$ hypersurface near each of its points and the Levi form of any local defining function is positive definite on the complex tangent space)?

For an integer $N\ge 1$, let
$$D_N=\Bigl\{z=(z_1,\dots,z_N)\in\mathbb{C}^N:\sum_{j=1}^{N}|z_j|<1\Bigr\}$$
denote the open unit ball with respect to the $\ell^1$-norm in $\mathbb{C}^N$, and let
$$D_N^{2}=\Bigl\{z\in\mathbb{C}^N:\sum_{j=1}^{N}|z_j|^2<1\Bigr\}$$
denote the open Euclidean unit ball in $\mathbb{C}^N$. Let $C^{(0,1)}(D_N)$ denote the space of continuous $(0,1)$-forms on $D_N$ (continuous on the closure, with continuous coefficients), and let $\bar{\partial}$ denote the Cauchy–Riemann operator. Use the supremum norm $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ on $D_N$ for both functions and forms (with the form norm being the sup over $D_N$ of the maximum of the moduli of the coefficients).

Prove or disprove the following: there exists an absolute constant $C>0$ (independent of the dimension $N$) such that for every $N\ge 1$ and every $\bar{\partial}$-closed form $f\in C^{(0,1)}(D_N)$ there exists $u\in C(\overline{D_N})$ satisfying
$$\bar{\partial} u = f\quad\text{on } D_N,\qquad \|u\|_\infty\le C\,\|f\|_\infty.$$
Establish (or refute) the analogous statement with $D_N$ replaced by the Euclidean ball $D_N^{2}$.

Setup. A Reinhardt domain in $\mathbb{C}^k$ is an open connected subset $D\subset\mathbb{C}^k$ that is invariant under the standard torus action $(z_1,\dots,z_k)\mapsto(e^{i\theta_1}z_1,\dots,e^{i\theta_k}z_k)$ for all $(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k)\in\mathbb{R}^k$.

Given a holomorphic self-map $f$ of either $\mathbb{C}^k$ (an automorphism) or of $\mathbb{P}^k$ (an endomorphism of degree at least $2$), and a fixed point (or periodic point) $p$ of $f$, the Siegel domain associated with $f$ at $p$ is, by definition, the connected component containing $p$ of the open set
$$\{z : (f^n(z))_{n\ge 0}\text{ is well-defined and converges to }p\text{ uniformly on a neighborhood of }z\},$$
i.e. the basin of attraction (or, in the indifferent linearizable case, the maximal Siegel/rotation domain) on which the dynamics of $f$ is conjugate to a linear or rotational normal form.

Problem. Classify, up to biholomorphism, all Reinhardt domains $D\subset\mathbb{C}^k$ that arise as Siegel domains in the above sense, namely those Reinhardt domains $D$ for which there exists either an automorphism of $\mathbb{C}^k$ or an endomorphism of $\mathbb{P}^k$ such that some Siegel domain associated to it is biholomorphic to $D$.

Consider the Chirikov standard map on the cylinder T × R, defined by
  R(θ, p) = (θ + pT/m, p + K sin(θ + pT/m)),
where T, m, K > 0 are fixed parameters and θ ∈ R/2πZ, p ∈ R. Set k = KmT.

(Classical part.) Prove that whenever k > 1, almost every orbit (with respect to Lebesgue measure on T × R) of the iterated map R is unbounded, i.e. for almost every initial condition (θ₀, p₀) the sequence of momenta of R^n(θ₀, p₀) is unbounded as n → ∞.

(Quantum part.) For ℏ > 0, regard a state ψ ∈ L²([0, 2π]) as a Fourier series ψ = Σ_{n∈Z} c_n e^{inθ}. Define the one-step quantum evolution operator
  R̂(ψ) = e^{−iK cos θ / ℏ} · Σ_{n∈Z} e^{−iℏn²T/(2m)} c_n e^{inθ}.
Let R̂^k(ψ) = Σ_n c_n^{(k)} e^{inθ} denote its k-th iterate. Show that, generically (i.e. avoiding a resonant set of parameters (ℏ, T, m, K)), the dynamics exhibits dynamical localization: for every initial state ψ there exists a constant C = C(ψ) < ∞ such that
  Σ_{|n| ≤ C} |c_n^{(k)}|² > 1/2  for every k ≥ 0.

Both parts are widely regarded as long-standing open problems. The classical claim that almost every orbit of the Chirikov standard map is unbounded for sufficiently large nonlinearity parameter is a well-known open conjecture (often attributed to Sinai), with positive Lyapunov exponents on a positive-measure set unproven. Dynamical localization for the quantum kicked rotor is also open in the deterministic setting; rigorous proofs exist only for simplified or random models (Bourgain, Jitomirskaya, and others). No proof of either statement in the form stated has appeared.

Let $K \subset X \setminus \{0\}$ be a compact set such that $0 \in \widehat{K}$, and let $L \subset X$ be a compact set containing $K$ in its relative interior (with respect to $X$).

Question: Does $\widehat{L}$ necessarily contain a neighborhood of $0$ in $X$?

Equivalently (Runge formulation): suppose $(\Omega_t)_{t \in (-1,1)}$ is a continuously increasing family of Stein open subsets of $X$ (i.e. $\Omega_{t_1} \subset \Omega_{t_2}$ whenever $t_1 \le t_2$, with appropriate continuity) such that $0 \notin \Omega_t$ for all $t \le 0$ and $0 \in \Omega_t$ for all $t > 0$. Let $X \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a complex analytic set containing the origin $0$, and assume that $0$ is an isolated normal singularity of $X$. For a compact subset $E \subset \mathbb{C}^n$, denote by $\widehat{E}$ its polynomially convex hull, i.e. $\widehat{E} = \{z \in \mathbb{C}^n : |p(z)| \le \sup_E |p| \text{ for every polynomial } p \in \mathbb{C}[z_1,\ldots,z_n]\}$.

Let $K \subset X \setminus \{0\}$ be a compact set such that $0 \in \widehat{K}$, and let $L \subset X$ be a compact set containing $K$ in its relative interior (with respect to $X$).

Question: Does $\widehat{L}$ necessarily contain a neighborhood of $0$ in $X$?

Equivalently (Runge formulation): suppose $(\Omega_t)_{t \in (-1,1)}$ is a continuously increasing family of Stein open subsets of $X$ (i.e. $\Omega_{t_1} \subset \Omega_{t_2}$ whenever $t_1 \le t_2$, with appropriate continuity) such that $0 \notin \Omega_t$ for all $t \le 0$ and $0 \in \Omega_t$ for all $t > 0$. Is $\Omega_{t_1}$ Runge in $\Omega_{t_2}$ (meaning that every holomorphic function on $\Omega_{t_1}$ can be approximated, uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega_{t_1}$, by holomorphic functions on $\Omega_{t_2}$) whenever $t_1 \le 0 < t_2$?

Let $f$ be either a holomorphic endomorphism of the complex projective space $\mathbb{P}^k$ ($k\ge 1$) or a holomorphic automorphism of $\mathbb{C}^k$. Suppose that $p$ is an attracting fixed point of $f$ (i.e. $f(p)=p$ and all eigenvalues of $Df(p)$ have modulus strictly less than $1$), and let \[ \Omega \;=\; \{\,z : f^n(z)\to p \text{ as } n\to\infty\,\} \] be its basin of attraction, an open connected set with boundary $\partial\Omega$. Fix a Riemannian distance $\mathrm{dist}(\cdot,\cdot)$ (the Fubini–Study distance in the projective case, the Euclidean distance in the affine case). For $\delta>0$ define the "annular" region
\[ \Omega^{*}_{\delta} \;=\; \{\,q\in\Omega : \mathrm{dist}(q,\partial\Omega)>\delta \text{ and } \mathrm{dist}(q,p)>\delta\,\}. \]

Problem. Find an explicit function $N(\delta)=N(f,p,\delta)$, depending effectively on $f$, $p$, and $\delta$, with the following property: for every $q\in\Omega^{*}_{\delta}$ the forward orbit segment $\{q, f(q), f^{2}(q), \dots, f^{N(\delta)}(q)\}$ is not entirely contained in $\Omega^{*}_{\delta}$; equivalently, within at most $N(\delta)$ iterations every such point either approaches the fixed point $p$ to within distance $\delta$ or moves to within distance $\delta$ of $\partial\Omega$. Provide concrete quantitative estimates for $N(\delta)$, e.g. for the model map $f(z,w)=(z^{2}+\varepsilon w,\,z)$ on $\mathbb{C}^{2}$ with $p=0$.

Let $M$ be a connected complex manifold and $\Omega \Subset M$ a relatively compact open subset whose boundary $\partial\Omega$ is connected. Assume $M$ is not of the form $\Delta^* \times N$ where $\Delta^* = \{z\in\mathbb{C}:0<|z|<1\}$ and $N$ is a compact complex manifold.

(a) Identify natural geometric or cohomological conditions on the pair $(M,\Omega)$ under which every holomorphic function $f$ defined on some open neighborhood of $\partial\Omega$ in $M$ admits a holomorphic extension either to all of $\Omega$ or to all of $M\setminus\overline{\Omega}$.

(b) Identify natural conditions under which the same conclusion holds when $f$ is merely assumed to be a CR function on $\partial\Omega$ (i.e., a function annihilated by the tangential Cauchy–Riemann operator on the smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$), so that $f$ extends as a holomorphic function to one side of $\partial\Omega$.

It is known that the conclusion of (a) holds whenever $\Omega$ is Stein, and that for $M=\mathbb{P}^k$ every $C^1$ CR function on $\partial\Omega$ extends holomorphically to one side. Determine, beyond these cases, the most general natural hypotheses on $M$ and $\Omega$ guaranteeing such one-sided holomorphic extension of holomorphic, respectively CR, boundary data.

Let $M$ be a complex manifold and let $f : M \to M$ be a holomorphic self-map. Recall the following standard notions:

- A point $p \in M$ is periodic of period $k \geq 1$ if $f^k(p) = p$. Such a periodic point is called repelling if all eigenvalues of the differential $Df^k(p)$ have modulus strictly greater than $1$, and a saddle if $Df^k(p)$ has at least one eigenvalue of modulus $>1$ and at least one of modulus $<1$ (this requires $\dim_{\mathbb C} M \geq 2$).
- The non-wandering set $\Omega(f)$ consists of all $x \in M$ such that for every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ there exist arbitrarily large integers $n$ with $f^n(U) \cap U \neq \emptyset$.
- When $M = \mathbb C^n$, the forward orbit $\{f^k(p)\}_{k \geq 0}$ of a point $p$ is called oscillating if it has a subsequence that remains uniformly bounded in $\mathbb C^n$ and another subsequence that tends to $\infty$.

Address the following questions:

(a) Is the closure of the set of repelling periodic points of $f$ always open in $\Omega(f)$?

(b) In the special case where $M = \mathbb C^n$ and $f$ is an entire holomorphic self-map, does (a) admit a counterexample?

(c) For a holomorphic self-map $f$ of $\mathbb C^n$, can there exist a sequence of points whose orbits are oscillating and which converges to a repelling periodic point of $f$?

(d) For a holomorphic self-map $f$ of $\mathbb C^2$, can there exist a sequence of saddle periodic points converging to a repelling periodic point of $f$? (Note that for biholomorphisms this is impossible, since under the inverse map a repelling point becomes attracting.)

Work in the complex projective space $\mathbb{P}^3 = \mathbb{P}^3(\mathbb{C})$. Recall that a domain $M$ with smooth boundary inside a complex surface (i.e., a smooth complex 2-dimensional manifold) $V$ is called strictly pseudoconvex if at every boundary point $p \in \partial M$ there is a smooth defining function $\rho$ for $M$ near $p$ (with $M = \{\rho < 0\}$ and $d\rho \neq 0$ on $\partial M$) such that the Levi form of $\rho$, namely the restriction of the complex Hessian $\partial \overline{\partial} \rho$ to the complex tangent space $T^{1,0}_p \partial M$, is positive definite. By a compact Riemann surface in $\mathbb{P}^3$ we mean a (nonempty) compact complex 1-dimensional analytic subvariety of $\mathbb{P}^3$ (equivalently, a holomorphic image of a compact Riemann surface inside $\mathbb{P}^3$).
\medskip

(a) Construct (or prove the existence of) a smooth complex algebraic surface $V \subset \mathbb{P}^3$ and a strictly pseudoconvex domain $M \subset V$ with smooth boundary $\partial M$ such that $M \cap C \neq \emptyset$ for every compact Riemann surface $C \subset \mathbb{P}^3$.

\medskip

(b) Let $V \subset \mathbb{P}^3$ be an algebraic hypersurface, and let $M \subset V$ be a strictly pseudoconvex domain. Does there exist a compact Riemann surface $S \subset \mathbb{P}^3$ such that $S \cap V \subset V \setminus M$ (equivalently, $S \cap M = \emptyset$)?

Let $f:\mathbb{P}^k\to\mathbb{P}^k$ be a holomorphic endomorphism of the complex projective space $\mathbb{P}^k$ of algebraic degree $d\ge 2$. Define the Fatou set of $f$ to be the maximal open subset of $\mathbb{P}^k$ on which the iterates $\{f^n\}_{n\ge 1}$ form a locally equicontinuous family, and define the Julia set $J=J(f)$ to be the complement of the Fatou set. Let $\omega$ be the Fubini–Study Kähler form on $\mathbb{P}^k$, and let
$$T=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{(f^n)^*\omega}{d^n}$$
be the Green positive closed $(1,1)$-current of $f$; one has $J=\operatorname{supp}(T)$. The equilibrium (measure of maximal entropy) is $\mu=T^k$. The nonwandering set $\Omega(f|_J)$ of the restriction $f|_J:J\to J$ is the set of points $x\in J$ such that for every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ in $J$ there exists $n\ge 1$ with $f^n(U)\cap U\neq\emptyset$. Set
$$J_0:=\Omega(f|_J).$$
For $k=1$ one has $J\subset J_0$, but for $k\ge 2$ in general $J_0\subsetneq J$.

(a) Determine what can be said about the Hausdorff dimensions of $J$, of $J_0$, and of $J\setminus J_0$.

(b) Describe the set $J_0\setminus\operatorname{supp}(\mu)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether every compact totally real n-submanifold of C^n bounds a holomorphic Riemann surface (smooth up to the boundary) appears to remain open in general. Gromov established existence of holomorphic discs in the Lagrangian case (for suitable Kähler forms), and Duval–Sibony related rational convexity to a Lagrangian condition; Duval has results in special cases such as totally real tori unknotted in the sphere. There are known examples of totally real submanifolds without attached holomorphic discs, but the existence of a bounding Riemann surface (of unspecified genus) in the general totally real case is not established.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Let $f:\mathbb{P}^k\to\mathbb{P}^k$ ($k>1$) be a holomorphic endomorphism. A closed set $A\subset\mathbb{P}^k$ is called attracting if there exists an open neighborhood $U=U(A)$ with $f(\overline{U})\subset U$ and $A=\bigcap_{n\ge 0}f^n(U)$. An attracting set $A$ is called an attractor if the dynamics $f|_A$ admits a dense orbit (alternatively, is chain transitive, meaning that for every $\delta>0$ the $\delta$-pseudo-orbits of $f|_A$ are dense). The attractor is called non-trivial if it is neither a (single) periodic orbit nor the whole space $\mathbb{P}^k$.

Consider holomorphic families $(f_c)_{c\in\Lambda}$ of endomorphisms of $\mathbb{P}^2$ parametrized by a complex manifold $\Lambda$.

(a) Show that non-trivial attractors are robust in $\mathbb{P}^2$: namely, exhibit such families $(f_c)$ for which the set
$$\{c\in\Lambda : f_c \text{ has a non-trivial attractor}\}$$
has positive Lebesgue measure in $\Lambda$.

(b) For such non-trivial attractors $A=A_c\subset\mathbb{P}^2$, give effective estimates (upper and/or lower bounds) for the Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H(A_c)$.

A generalized Hénon map is a polynomial biholomorphism of $\mathbb{C}^2$ obtained as a finite composition of Hénon maps of the form $(z,w)\mapsto (p(z)-aw, z)$ with $p$ a polynomial of degree $\geq 2$ and $a\neq 0$. For such a map $f:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^2$, let $K^{\pm}=\{p\in\mathbb{C}^2:\{f^{\pm n}(p)\}_{n\geq 0}\text{ is bounded}\}$, $J^{\pm}=\partial K^{\pm}$, and define the forward/backward Julia sets accordingly.

Consider a generalized Hénon map of the form
$$f(z,w)=(e^{i\theta}z,\;e^{-i\theta}w)+\text{higher order terms},$$
so that the origin is a fixed point at which the differential has eigenvalues $e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}$ on the $z$- and $w$-axes respectively, with $\theta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus 2\pi\mathbb{Q}$.

Determine an explicit diophantine condition on $\theta$ (a condition of the form $|q\theta - 2\pi p| \geq C/|q|^{\tau}$ for all $p\in\mathbb{Z}$, $q\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$, with appropriate constants $C>0$ and $\tau\geq 1$, or equivalent) which guarantees that $f$ admits two Siegel discs $D_1,D_2\subset J^+\cap J^-$ both passing through the origin, with $D_1$ tangent to the $z$-axis at $0$ and $D_2$ tangent to the $w$-axis at $0$. Here a Siegel disc is an $f$-invariant injectively immersed holomorphic disc on which $f$ is holomorphically conjugate to an irrational rotation.

Let $\Sigma \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a smooth real analytic hypersurface of finite type (in the sense of D'Angelo, i.e., the maximum order of contact of complex analytic curves with $\Sigma$ at each point is finite). A holomorphic vector field on a neighborhood of $\Sigma$ is an expression
$$X = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_j(z)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial z_j},$$
where the coefficients $a_1,\dots,a_n$ are holomorphic functions. Say that $X$ is tangent to $\Sigma$ if its real part $\Re X = \tfrac{1}{2}(X + \overline{X})$ is tangent to $\Sigma$ as a real vector field at every point of $\Sigma$ (equivalently, the local one-parameter family of biholomorphisms generated by $\Re X$ preserves $\Sigma$).

Problem. Classify all holomorphic vector fields $X$ which are tangent (in the above sense) to a real analytic hypersurface $\Sigma$ of finite type, and use this classification to classify the hypersurfaces $\Sigma$ which admit such nontrivial tangent holomorphic vector fields.

Hilbert's sixth problem: Provide a complete mathematical treatment of the axioms of physics. Specifically, accomplish the following two tasks.

(i) Develop an axiomatic foundation of probability theory together with the corresponding limit theorems (laws of large numbers, central limit theorems, ergodic theorems, etc.) in a form suitable to serve as a rigorous foundation for statistical physics, including classical statistical mechanics and its extensions.

(ii) Develop a rigorous mathematical theory of the limiting processes that lead from an atomistic (microscopic) description of matter — for example, a system of N interacting classical particles evolving according to Newton's equations of motion — to the macroscopic laws of motion of continua, such as the compressible Euler equations, the incompressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations, and other equations of continuum mechanics. This is to be carried out through the appropriate scaling limits (e.g., the Boltzmann–Grad limit producing kinetic equations of Boltzmann type, followed by hydrodynamic limits producing fluid equations), with full mathematical rigor and under physically meaningful hypotheses on the underlying particle dynamics.

Part (i) on the axiomatic foundation of probability is widely regarded as solved by Kolmogorov's 1933 measure-theoretic axiomatization together with the classical limit theorems. Part (ii) on the rigorous derivation of continuum equations from atomistic dynamics has seen major progress, including the recent 2025 work of Deng, Hani, and Ma deriving the compressible Euler and incompressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations from hard-sphere Newtonian dynamics via the Boltzmann equation, though this work has drawn critical commentary regarding its physical scope (dilute-gas regime, molecular chaos assumption) and the full program of axiomatizing physics remains incomplete.

Let $\{0,1\}^*$ denote the set of all finite binary strings. A language is a subset $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$. A deterministic Turing machine $M$ is said to decide $L$ in polynomial time if there exists a polynomial $p$ such that, for every input $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, $M$ halts after at most $p(|x|)$ steps and accepts if and only if $x \in L$. The class $\mathbf{P}$ is the set of all languages decidable by some deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.

The class $\mathbf{NP}$ is the set of all languages $L$ for which there exist a polynomial $q$ and a language $V \in \mathbf{P}$ such that
$$L = \{ x \in \{0,1\}^* : \exists\, y \in \{0,1\}^* 	ext{ with } |y| \le q(|x|) 	ext{ and } (x,y) \in V \}.$$
Intuitively, $\mathbf{NP}$ consists of those decision problems whose "yes"-instances admit a certificate verifiable in polynomial time.

Question: Is $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{NP}$? Either prove that every language in $\mathbf{NP}$ belongs to $\mathbf{P}$, or exhibit a language in $\mathbf{NP}$ that provably does not belong to $\mathbf{P}$.

Let $f : \mathbb{P}^k \to \mathbb{P}^k$ be a holomorphic endomorphism of degree at least $2$ on complex projective space, and let $K \subset \mathbb{P}^k$ be a hyperbolic set for $f$ (a compact, $f$-invariant set on which the tangent bundle admits a continuous $Df$-invariant splitting $T\mathbb{P}^k|_K = E^s \oplus E^u$ with $Df$ uniformly contracting on $E^s$ and uniformly expanding on $E^u$). Assume $K$ is a solenoid in the sense that $f|_K$ is conjugate to the shift on a solenoidal inverse limit, and that the stable direction has complex dimension $2$, i.e. $\dim_{\mathbb{C}} E^s = 2$.

(a) Construct, or describe a general procedure to construct, a closed positive $(2,2)$-current $T^s$ on a neighborhood of $K$ that is "stable" in the sense of being directed by the stable distribution $E^s$ along $K$ and invariant (up to a multiplicative constant) under pullback by $f$.

(b) For a point $x \in K$, let $W^s(x)$ denote the global stable manifold of $x$, which is an injectively immersed complex submanifold of $\mathbb{P}^k$ of complex dimension $2$. Determine whether each stable leaf $W^s(x)$ is biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^2$.

In the classical Arrow–Debreu model of general equilibrium, an exchange economy consists of finitely many agents trading finitely many commodities, where each agent has preferences and an initial endowment; this gives rise to an aggregate excess demand function $Z : \mathbb{R}^{\ell}_{++} \to \mathbb{R}^{\ell}$ on the strictly positive price orthant satisfying Walras' law $p \cdot Z(p) = 0$ and homogeneity of degree zero. A price vector $p^*$ is an equilibrium if $Z(p^*) \le 0$. The standard theory establishes existence (and, generically, finiteness) of such equilibria but treats only the static equilibrium notion.

Problem: Develop a mathematical extension of the general equilibrium model that incorporates an explicit price-adjustment dynamics—i.e., a well-posed dynamical system on the price space (such as a flow or differential inclusion driven by excess demand, or a more general learning/tâtonnement-type process)—with the following properties:

(i) Equilibria of the static general equilibrium model are equilibria (rest points) of the dynamics.

(ii) The dynamics is defined and economically meaningful for a generic class of excess demand functions (i.e., not requiring gross substitutability, the weak axiom of revealed preference, or other restrictive assumptions known to be sufficient for convergence of classical tâtonnement).

(iii) For (almost) every excess demand function in this generic class, trajectories of the dynamics converge to an equilibrium price vector from (almost) every initial price.

Provide such a model, together with a proof of global (generic) convergence, or otherwise establish obstructions to its existence.

Within the standard ΛCDM cosmological framework, globular clusters (GCs) are dense, gravitationally bound stellar systems containing typically 10^4–10^6 stars, observed in essentially all sufficiently massive galaxies. The epoch of reionization, during which intergalactic hydrogen was ionized by the first luminous sources, is observationally inferred to have ended near redshift z ≈ 6 (about 12.8 Gyr ago). The cosmic star-formation rate density is observed to peak near redshift z ≈ 2 (about 10 Gyr ago).

Determine which of the following statements correctly describes the dominant formation epoch of the present-day globular cluster population:

(a) Most globular clusters formed more than 12.8 Gyr ago, i.e. at redshift z ≳ 6 prior to the end of reionization, in which case their young, dense, massive-star populations may have contributed appreciably to the ionizing photon budget that reionized the universe; or

(b) Most globular clusters formed substantially later, near the peak of the cosmic star-formation history at z ≈ 2 (∼10 Gyr ago), and therefore did not play a significant role in cosmic reionization.

Provide a quantitative determination, supported by stellar-age measurements of Galactic and extragalactic GCs and by cosmological models of cluster formation, of the fraction of today's GC population that originated in each of these two epochs, and assess whether GCs (or their progenitors) could have contributed nontrivially to reionization.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Recent literature, including JWST observations of high-redshift GC candidates (e.g., the Sparkler) and 2024–2025 model comparison studies, supports a two-epoch picture: roughly half of the old GC population (ages ≳12 Gyr) formed at z ≳ 6 in dwarf-galaxy progenitors and likely contributed to reionization, while a substantial fraction of GCs formed later near z ≈ 2–3. The question is therefore not a strict either/or; both channels appear to operate, though precise fractions and the exact contribution of GC progenitors to the reionizing photon budget remain debated.

Consider the Newtonian N-body problem: N point particles with masses m_1,...,m_N > 0 in R^3 evolve according to
  m_i x_i''(t) = sum_{j != i} G m_i m_j (x_j - x_i)/|x_j - x_i|^3,
with initial positions x_i(0) ∈ R^3 (mutually distinct) and initial velocities v_i(0) ∈ R^3. A singularity at time T < ∞ is a maximal solution that cannot be continued past T. It is called a collision singularity if the limit positions exist with at least two coinciding, and a non-collision singularity otherwise (equivalently, some particle escapes to spatial infinity in finite time or oscillates without limit).

Solve both of the following:

(A) Prove that the set of initial conditions (x_1(0),...,x_N(0), v_1(0),...,v_N(0)) in the phase space (for which the configuration is non-collisional) that fail to yield a global-in-time solution has Lebesgue measure zero.

(B) Determine for which N ≥ 2 there exist non-collision singularities in the Newtonian N-body problem.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Part (B) (Painlevé's conjecture on existence of non-collision singularities) has been established: Xia (1992) proved existence for N ≥ 5, and Xue (2014/2020) proved it for the planar N = 4 case. The global regularity of the $\bar\partial$-equation on weakly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb{P}^n$ is a long-standing problem. Each such GC was formed at some earlier epoch either (i) "in situ," meaning its formation site at the time of formation lay within the virial radius (or main potential well) of the progenitor that evolved into the present-day host galaxy, or (ii) "ex situ," meaning its formation site lay within a distinct satellite/progenitor galaxy that was subsequently accreted and merged into the present-day host. Determine, as a function of host-galaxy mass and assembly history, the relative fractions of in-situ versus ex-situ formed globular clusters in the present-day GC system. In particular, decide whether the present-day GC population of a typical galaxy is dominated by the in-situ channel, dominated by the ex-situ channel, or is a mixture whose proportions are governed quantitatively by the host's merger and accretion history, and characterize that dependence.

Develop a comprehensive mathematical theory describing the long-time (asymptotic) behavior of dynamical systems — including finite-dimensional flows and infinite-dimensional systems arising from partial differential equations such as the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a bounded domain or torus in three dimensions. The desired theory should:

1. Provide rigorous tools to classify and characterize attractors, invariant measures, and statistical limits for general nonlinear dissipative dynamical systems as time tends to infinity.

2. Yield a rigorous mathematical theory of the onset of turbulence: identify and analyze the sequence of bifurcations and transitions (e.g., loss of stability of laminar solutions, emergence of complex/chaotic regimes) by which solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations (or comparable model systems) pass from regular flow to turbulent flow as a control parameter such as the Reynolds number increases.

3. Yield a rigorous mathematical theory of fully developed turbulence: derive from first principles the statistical laws of high-Reynolds-number turbulent flows, including, for instance, the existence of a universal inertial-range energy spectrum, Kolmogorov-type scaling laws, anomalous dissipation, intermittency, and the structure of invariant measures supported on turbulent regimes.

Produce such a unified theory, or prove rigorous theorems establishing its principal components.

Resolve the following three problems in ergodic theory of statistical mechanics:

(A) Ergodicity of gases with soft cores. Consider a classical system of N point particles in a box (or in ℝ^d) interacting via a smooth pair potential V: ℝ^d → ℝ that is finite at the origin (a "soft core"), with Hamiltonian H(q,p) = Σ_i |p_i|²/(2m) + Σ_{i<j} V(q_i − q_j). Show that the Hamiltonian flow on a constant-energy surface is ergodic with respect to the microcanonical (Liouville) measure for generic such V (and, in particular, for natural classes of soft-core potentials).

(B) Approach to equilibrium. For a suitable infinite-volume dynamical system of classical or quantum statistical mechanics (e.g. an infinite ideal or interacting gas, or a quantum lattice/continuous system), starting from a non-equilibrium initial state μ_0, prove that the time-evolved state μ_t converges, as t → ∞, to an equilibrium (Gibbs) state in an appropriate topology, and give a rigorous derivation of irreversible macroscopic behavior from the underlying reversible microscopic dynamics.

(C) Asymptotic abelianness for quantum Heisenberg dynamics. Let A be the quasi-local C*-algebra of the quantum Heisenberg model on Z^d (d ≥ 2) built from spin-s operators at each site, with formal Hamiltonian H = −Σ_{⟨x,y⟩} J S_x · S_y, and let α_t denote the corresponding time evolution on A. Prove that the dynamics is asymptotically abelian in the sense that, for every pair A, B ∈ A of strictly local observables,
   lim_{t → ∞} ‖[α_t(A), B]‖ = 0,
or, in a weaker formulation, that this commutator tends to zero in some natural (e.g. weak, mean ergodic, or state-dependent) sense.

These three problems form Barry Simon's problem BS2 from his lists of open problems in mathematical physics. No general resolution is reported: ergodicity for soft-core interacting gases remains unknown, a fully rigorous derivation of approach to equilibrium from Hamiltonian/quantum dynamics is a long-standing open problem, and asymptotic abelianness for the quantum Heisenberg dynamics is established only in restricted settings (e.g. strong asymptotic abelianness is known for certain entropic K-systems, but not for Heisenberg dynamics in general).

Globular clusters (GCs) are gravitationally bound, dense stellar systems with typical masses in the range 10^4–10^6 solar masses, half-light radii of a few parsecs, and stellar densities comparable to those of young and intermediate-age massive star clusters observed forming today in starburst environments and galaxy mergers. Observationally, GC populations exhibit a number of well-characterized properties, including: (i) a near-universal GC luminosity/mass function (peaked around ~2×10^5 solar masses); (ii) systematic correlations between total GC system mass (or number) and host-galaxy properties such as stellar mass, halo mass, and morphological type; (iii) characteristic color/metallicity bimodality; (iv) specific frequencies that vary with host environment; and (v) multiple stellar populations within individual GCs. Young and intermediate-age massive clusters share many physical properties (mass, size, density, single- or multi-population stellar content) with old GCs.

Formulate and assess the following question precisely: Does there exist a single, universal physical model of massive star cluster formation — applicable across cosmic time and not requiring a distinct formation channel restricted to the early Universe — that simultaneously reproduces (a) the full set of observed statistical properties of old globular cluster populations, (b) the empirical scaling relations between these populations and their host-galaxy properties, and (c) the observed properties of young and intermediate-age massive star clusters? Equivalently: can old globular clusters be explained as the high-redshift, long-surviving tail of the same massive cluster formation process operating in galaxies today, with no special early-Universe-only mechanism invoked?
