status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of a single universal model for massive cluster formation that accounts for both old globular clusters and young/intermediate-age massive clusters remains an active area of investigation. Recent reviews (e.g., Krumholz, McKee & Bland-Hawthorn 2019; Forbes et al. 2018; Adamo et al. 2020; and E-MOSAICS-based studies by Kruijssen, Pfeffer and collaborators 2019–2024) advocate and partly implement a "universal" cluster formation framework embedded in cosmological galaxy formation, achieving substantial success in reproducing many GC scaling relations. However, no consensus has been reached: open issues remain regarding GC mass function evolution, multiple populations, metal-poor GC formation efficiency, and the need (or not) for distinct high-redshift conditions. The problem is therefore best characterized as open / partially addressed.

Place quantum field theory on a rigorous mathematical footing by achieving at least one of the following four goals.

(A) Construction of QCD. Give a precise mathematical construction of quantum chromodynamics, the non-abelian gauge theory with gauge group SU(3) coupled to quark fields, on four-dimensional Minkowski (or Euclidean) space-time. The construction must produce a quantum field theory satisfying a suitable set of axioms (e.g. the Wightman or Osterwalder–Schrader axioms, suitably adapted to gauge theories), with the expected particle content and symmetries.

(B) Renormalizable but not super-renormalizable QFT. Construct any nontrivial quantum field theory in some space-time dimension that is renormalizable but not super-renormalizable, in the sense that the theory's interaction is dimensionless (marginal) rather than having positive mass dimension. The constructed theory must be nontrivial (i.e., not a (generalized) free field) and must satisfy a precise set of axioms for a relativistic quantum field theory.

(C) Inconsistency of QED. Prove that quantum electrodynamics—the U(1) gauge theory coupled to a Dirac spinor field in four-dimensional space-time—cannot be realized as a nontrivial mathematically consistent quantum field theory satisfying the Wightman (or equivalent) axioms.

(D) Nonexistence of nontrivial lattice continuum limit. Prove that no nontrivial continuum limit exists for a lattice-regularized quantum field theory in the relevant case (for example, a φ⁴ theory in four space-time dimensions): that is, prove that every sequence of lattice cutoff theories whose lattice spacing tends to zero, with parameters tuned to approach a critical point, converges only to a (generalized) free field.

Provide a complete mathematical proof for at least one of (A), (B), (C), or (D).

Place quantum field theory on a rigorous mathematical footing by achieving at least one of the following four goals.

(A) Construction of QCD. Give a precise mathematical construction of quantum chromodynamics, the non-abelian gauge theory with gauge group SU(3) coupled to quark fields, on four-dimensional Minkowski (or Euclidean) space-time. The construction must produce a quantum field theory satisfying a suitable set of axioms (e.g. the Wightman or Osterwalder–Schrader axioms, suitably adapted to gauge theories), with the expected particle content and symmetries.

(B) Renormalizable but not super-renormalizable QFT. Construct any nontrivial quantum field theory in some space-time dimension that is renormalizable but not super-renormalizable, in the sense that the theory's interaction is dimensionless (marginal) rather than having positive mass dimension. The constructed theory must be nontrivial (i.e., not a (generalized) free field) and must satisfy a precise set of axioms for a relativistic quantum field theory.

(C) Inconsistency of QED. Prove that quantum electrodynamics—the U(1) gauge theory coupled to a Dirac spinor field in four-dimensional space-time—cannot be realized as a nontrivial mathematically consistent quantum field theory satisfying the Wightman (or equivalent) axioms.

(D) Nonexistence of nontrivial lattice continuum limit. Prove that no nontrivial continuum limit exists for a lattice-regularized quantum field theory in the relevant case (for example, a φ⁴ theory in four space-time dimensions): that is, prove that every sequence of lattice cutoff theories whose lattice spacing tends to zero, with parameters tuned to approach a critical point, converges only to a (generalized) free field.

Provide a complete mathematical proof for at least one of (A), (B), (C), or (D).

All four sub-problems remain open. Constructive QFT has not yet produced a rigorous construction of QCD or any nontrivial strictly renormalizable (not super-renormalizable) 4D theory; recent results (e.g., Aizenman–Duminil-Copin 2021) prove triviality of φ⁴ in four dimensions, which is progress toward (D) for that specific model but does not settle the full problem. The Clay Yang–Mills Millennium Problem (a closely related subproblem) remains unsolved.

Let $1 \le p < n-1$ and let $T$ be a positive closed current of bidimension $(p,p)$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$. Recall that a current $T$ of bidimension $(p,p)$ is positive closed if $dT = 0$ and $\langle T, \alpha_1 \wedge \bar\alpha_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha_p \wedge \bar\alpha_p\rangle \ge 0$ for every choice of smooth $(1,0)$-forms $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_p$ with compact support. To any $p$-dimensional irreducible analytic subvariety $V \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ one associates the integration current $[V]$, which is a positive closed current of bidimension $(p,p)$.

(a) Does there exist a sequence of positive closed currents of the form $T_j = \sum_i c_{j,i} [V_{j,i}]$, where each $V_{j,i}$ is a $p$-dimensional analytic subvariety of $\mathbb{C}^n$ and $c_{j,i} > 0$, such that $T_j \to T$ weakly as currents?

(b) If such an approximation exists, can the sequence be chosen so that, in addition, the supports $\bigcup_i V_{j,i}$ converge to $\operatorname{Supp} T$ in the Hausdorff metric (on compact subsets of $\mathbb{C}^n$)?

(The case $p = n-1$ is classical and is excluded.)

Approximation of positive closed $(1,1)$-currents (i.e. bidimension $(n-1,n-1)$) by analytic divisors is classical (Demailly, with refinements by Duval–Sibony and Guedj). Consider a population of globular clusters (gravitationally bound stellar systems) forming inside galaxies at high redshift (z ≳ 2) across the full range of host galaxy masses. Each cluster is characterized by a mass M and a half-mass radius r_h, and the population has an initial mass function dN/dM that is approximately a power law (e.g. dN/dM ∝ M^{-2}) at the time of formation. As the clusters orbit through the dense interstellar medium (ISM) of their host galaxies, they experience tidal shocks from encounters with giant molecular clouds and other dense gas substructures. A tidal shock transfers energy to a cluster, causing mass loss at a rate that depends on the local ISM density ρ_ISM, the cluster's internal density, and its size, with shock-driven mass loss rate scaling roughly as dM/dt ∝ -M ρ_ISM^2 r_h^3 / (some internal energy scale), and with cluster radii adjusting in response to shocks (e.g. as in models where r_h decreases following each shock). After several Gyr of such evolution, the surviving cluster mass function dN/dM is observed today to be peaked near M ≈ 2×10^5 M_⊙ (the universal "turnover" of the globular cluster mass function), independent of host galaxy properties.

Question: Is the interstellar medium density ρ_ISM(z, M_gal) attained in high-redshift galaxies large enough — uniformly across the full range of galaxy masses M_gal — for tidal shocks alone to evolve the initial power-law cluster mass function into the observed peaked mass function with the universal turnover, rather than achieving this only in a restricted subset of galactic environments (e.g. only in the most gas-rich or most massive systems)?

Let $S^4$ denote the four-dimensional sphere equipped with the standard round metric, and let $P \to S^4$ be a principal $G$-bundle for a compact semisimple Lie group $G$ (e.g. $G = SU(2)$). For a connection $A$ on $P$ with curvature 2-form $F_A$ taking values in the adjoint bundle, the Yang-Mills functional is
$$\mathrm{YM}(A) = \int_{S^4} |F_A|^2 \, d\mathrm{vol}.$$
A connection $A$ is called a Yang-Mills field (or Yang-Mills connection) if it is a critical point of $\mathrm{YM}$, equivalently if it satisfies the Yang-Mills equation $d_A^* F_A = 0$ together with the Bianchi identity $d_A F_A = 0$. Using the Hodge star operator $*$ on 2-forms over $S^4$, the connection $A$ is called self-dual if $*F_A = F_A$ and anti-self-dual if $*F_A = -F_A$.

Decide whether the following statement is true: every Yang-Mills field on $S^4$ is either self-dual or anti-self-dual.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The conjecture is false. Sibner, Sibner, and Uhlenbeck (1989) constructed non-minimal Yang-Mills connections on the trivial SU(2)-bundle over $S^4$ that are neither self-dual nor anti-self-dual. Further non-self-dual Yang-Mills connections were produced by Sadun-Segert, Parker, and others on SU(2)-bundles over $S^4$ with various Chern numbers. Thus the proposed assertion does not hold.

Let $S^4$ denote the round 4-sphere, and let $G$ be a compact simple Lie group. Fix a principal $G$-bundle $P \to S^4$, whose topological type is classified by its second Chern number (Pontryagin number) $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. A connection $A$ on $P$ is called self-dual (an instanton) if its curvature 2-form $F_A$ satisfies $*F_A = F_A$, where $*$ is the Hodge star induced by the round metric on $S^4$. Let $\mathcal{M}_k(G)$ denote the moduli space of self-dual connections on $P$ modulo gauge equivalence.

Prove that, for every fixed Pontryagin number $k$, the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_k(G)$ is connected.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

For classical gauge groups, the ADHM construction parametrizes self-dual connections on $S^4$ by a connected algebraic variety, and Donaldson established that the moduli space for $G=SU(2)$ at charge $k=1$ is diffeomorphic to an open 5-ball (hence connected); analogous connectedness results follow from ADHM data for $SU(N)$, $Sp(n)$, $SO(N)$. A fully general proof covering all compact simple Lie groups (including exceptional groups) is not as widely cited; the question is listed among Yau's problems and is regarded as essentially known for classical groups but not uniformly settled for all gauge groups.

Let $X$ be a (possibly singular) Stein complex analytic space, and let $\Omega \Subset X$ be a relatively compact open subset. Assume that for every boundary point $p \in \partial \Omega$ there exists an open neighborhood $U = U(p) \subset X$ of $p$ such that $U \cap \Omega$ is a Stein space. Must $\Omega$ itself be a Stein space?

(Recall that a complex space $Y$ is Stein if it is holomorphically convex and holomorphically separable, equivalently, if it admits a strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. The question asks whether local Steinness at boundary points propagates to global Steinness of $\Omega$ when the ambient Stein space $X$ is allowed to have singularities.)

A globular cluster is a gravitationally bound, approximately spherical collection of stars; "old" globular clusters are those whose stellar populations have ages comparable to the age of the Universe (typically ≳10 Gyr). For a population of such clusters formed in (or around) a host galaxy, the cluster initial mass function (CIMF) is the differential distribution dN/dM giving the number of clusters formed per unit mass M at the time of their formation, before any subsequent dynamical evolution, mass loss, or destruction.

Two competing hypotheses for the CIMF of old globular clusters are:

(i) A pure power law of the form dN/dM ∝ M^{-β} (with β typically near 2) extending from some low-mass cutoff up to a high-mass cutoff, with no intrinsic preferred mass scale.

(ii) A distribution with a characteristic (preferred) mass scale, for instance a Schechter-like form dN/dM ∝ M^{-β} exp(-M/M_*) or a log-normal form dN/d log M ∝ exp(-(log M - log M_c)^2 / (2σ^2)), in which a turnover or peak mass M_* (or M_c) is imprinted at formation rather than produced by later dynamical evolution.

The problem is the following:

Determine the functional form of the initial mass function of old globular clusters. Specifically:

(a) Decide whether the CIMF is best described by a featureless power law or by a distribution possessing an intrinsic preferred mass scale at formation.

(b) Determine how the answer to (a) depends on properties of the host-galaxy environment, such as host-galaxy stellar mass, morphology, metallicity, and the gas-pressure / density conditions at the epoch of cluster formation; in particular, characterize whether and how parameters such as β, M_*, M_c, or σ vary systematically with these host-galaxy properties.

Consider the vacuum Einstein field equations $R_{\mu\nu}=0$ (or with matter sources) on a four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold, and the two standard families of asymptotic approximation schemes used to construct approximate solutions:

(a) The post-Minkowskian (PM) expansion, in which the metric is expanded around the flat Minkowski metric as a formal power series in Newton's constant $G$:
$$g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+\sum_{n\geq 1}G^{n}\,h^{(n)}_{\mu\nu},$$
the coefficients $h^{(n)}_{\mu\nu}$ being determined iteratively by solving linearized Einstein equations on Minkowski space with sources built from lower-order coefficients.

(b) The post-Newtonian (PN) expansion, in which (for slowly moving, weakly self-gravitating sources with characteristic velocity $v\ll c$) the metric is expanded in inverse powers of the speed of light $c$:
$$g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+\sum_{n\geq 2}c^{-n}\,k^{(n)}_{\mu\nu},$$
valid in the near zone of the source (distances small compared with the characteristic wavelength of emitted gravitational radiation).

The problem is to determine rigorously the range of validity of these two asymptotic expansions. Specifically:

1. Identify precise conditions on the initial data, matter content, and spacetime region under which the formal series above provide genuine asymptotic approximations (in a mathematically precise sense, e.g. Poincaré-asymptotic) to actual solutions of the Einstein equations.

2. Establish quantitative error bounds: for a truncation at order $N$, give estimates of the form $\|g_{\mu\nu}-g^{(N)}_{\mu\nu}\|\le C_N\,\varepsilon^{N+1}$ in suitable function-space norms, on explicit spacetime domains, where $\varepsilon$ is $G$ or $1/c$ as appropriate.

3. Determine the maximal spacetime region (in terms of distance from the source, time interval, and strength of the gravitational field) on which each expansion remains a faithful approximation, and clarify the matching between the near-zone PN expansion and the far-zone PM expansion.

Consider the vacuum Einstein field equations $R_{\mu\nu}=0$ (or with matter sources) on a four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold, and the two standard families of asymptotic approximation schemes used to construct approximate solutions:

(a) The post-Minkowskian (PM) expansion, in which the metric is expanded around the flat Minkowski metric as a formal power series in Newton's constant $G$:
$$g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+\sum_{n\geq 1}G^{n}\,h^{(n)}_{\mu\nu},$$
the coefficients $h^{(n)}_{\mu\nu}$ being determined iteratively by solving linearized Einstein equations on Minkowski space with sources built from lower-order coefficients.

(b) The post-Newtonian (PN) expansion, in which (for slowly moving, weakly self-gravitating sources with characteristic velocity $v\ll c$) the metric is expanded in inverse powers of the speed of light $c$:
$$g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+\sum_{n\geq 2}c^{-n}\,k^{(n)}_{\mu\nu},$$
valid in the near zone of the source (distances small compared with the characteristic wavelength of emitted gravitational radiation).

The problem is to determine rigorously the range of validity of these two asymptotic expansions. Specifically:

1. Identify precise conditions on the initial data, matter content, and spacetime region under which the formal series above provide genuine asymptotic approximations (in a mathematically precise sense, e.g. Poincaré-asymptotic) to actual solutions of the Einstein equations.

2. Establish quantitative error bounds: for a truncation at order $N$, give estimates of the form $\|g_{\mu\nu}-g^{(N)}_{\mu\nu}\|\le C_N\,\varepsilon^{N+1}$ in suitable function-space norms, on explicit spacetime domains, where $\varepsilon$ is $G$ or $1/c$ as appropriate.

3. Determine the maximal spacetime region (in terms of distance from the source, time interval, and strength of the gravitational field) on which each expansion remains a faithful approximation, and clarify the matching between the near-zone PN expansion and the far-zone PM expansion.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The rigorous range of validity of post-Newtonian and post-Minkowskian expansions for solutions of Einstein's equations remains an open problem. While Damour–Schäfer and others showed PN expansions are asymptotic in a formal sense, divergences appear from 4PN order in harmonic coordinates, and no global rigorous error estimates or matched-asymptotic theorems are established. Recent reviews (Blanchet's Living Reviews on PN theory, 2024) and works on resummation (2025) continue to treat validity and convergence as unresolved.

Give a rigorous mathematical proof that Newtonian gravity arises as a well-defined limit of general relativity. Concretely: introduce a one-parameter family of Lorentzian spacetimes $(M, g_\lambda, T_\lambda)$, indexed by a parameter $\lambda \geq 0$ (interpreted as $1/c^2$, where $c$ is the speed of light), each satisfying the Einstein field equations
$$\mathrm{Ric}(g_\lambda) - \tfrac{1}{2} R(g_\lambda)\, g_\lambda = 8\pi\, T_\lambda$$
for $\lambda > 0$, where $T_\lambda$ is a suitable matter stress-energy tensor. Formulate precise regularity, asymptotic, and matter conditions on the family $\{(M, g_\lambda, T_\lambda)\}_{\lambda > 0}$ under which, as $\lambda \to 0^+$, the metrics, connections, and matter fields converge (in an appropriate topology) to a limiting structure $(M, h, t, \nabla, \rho)$ describing a Newton–Cartan / Newtonian spacetime, where:
- $t : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is an absolute time function with level sets being spacelike hypersurfaces,
- $h$ is a degenerate "spatial" cometric of signature $(0,+,+,+)$ with kernel spanned by $dt$,
- $\nabla$ is a torsion-free connection compatible with $t$ and $h$,
- $\rho : M \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ is a mass density,
and the limiting structure satisfies the Newton–Cartan field equation
$$\mathrm{Ric}(\nabla) = 4\pi\rho\, dt \otimes dt$$
together with the appropriate Trautman/Newton curvature conditions. Prove the existence of nontrivial families realizing such a limit (beyond known special examples), and establish convergence theorems guaranteeing that solutions of the Einstein equations reduce, in this limit, to solutions of Newtonian gravity.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Ehlers's frame theory provides a rigorous framework for the Newtonian limit, and a number of partial results exist: examples of one-parameter families of relativistic spacetimes with a Newtonian limit have been constructed (e.g., Lottermoser, Rendall, Oliynyk, Heilig), and post-Newtonian expansions have been justified rigorously in various settings. However, a fully general rigorous existence theorem for families of solutions of Einstein's equations converging to arbitrary Newtonian spacetimes is not yet established, so the problem is widely regarded as only partially solved.

A real hypersurface M in a complex manifold X is called Levi flat if it is locally foliated by complex hypersurfaces of X (equivalently, its Levi form vanishes identically where M is smooth enough for the Levi form to be defined). A topological Levi flat hypersurface is a topological hypersurface that is locally a graph and is locally a disjoint union of holomorphic discs.

(a) Does there exist a C^2 Levi flat hypersurface in the complex projective plane P^2(C)?

(b) Does there exist a topological Levi flat hypersurface in P^2(C), in the sense above (a topological hypersurface that locally is a graph and locally a disjoint union of holomorphic discs)?

(c) Classify all C^∞ Levi flat hypersurfaces in a complex torus C^n / Λ (where Λ is a lattice of rank 2n), i.e. give a complete description of every smooth real hypersurface admitting a foliation by complex hypersurfaces of the torus.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The non-existence of real-analytic Levi-flat hypersurfaces in P^2 is established (Lins Neto, Siu). However, the question of existence of C^2 (and more generally smooth or merely topological) Levi-flat hypersurfaces in P^2 remains an open problem; recent surveys (2025) continue to list it as one of the central open questions in the area. Classification of C^∞ Levi-flat hypersurfaces in complex tori is also not completely resolved.

Consider the system of dwarf satellite galaxies surrounding the giant elliptical galaxy Centaurus A. For each candidate satellite, let its three-dimensional position relative to Centaurus A be determined by sky coordinates together with an accurate distance measurement (e.g., from the tip of the red giant branch), and let membership in the system be defined by such distance-confirmed proximity to Centaurus A. Given the full set of confirmed members with reliable 3D positions:

(a) Determine whether the spatial distribution of the satellites is best described, in a statistically preferred sense, as (i) two distinct, approximately parallel thin planes, or (ii) a single, similarly oriented but thicker plane.

(b) Compute the resulting three-dimensional plane parameters: the normal vector (orientation), the root-mean-square thickness perpendicular to the best-fit plane(s), the in-plane radial extent (semi-major and semi-minor axes), the axis ratios c/a and b/a of the satellite distribution, and the offset of each plane from Centaurus A.

State which of (i) or (ii) is preferred under a chosen model-selection criterion, and report the corresponding plane parameters together with their uncertainties.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent analyses incorporating newly discovered and distance-confirmed satellites favor a single, thicker plane (the Centaurus A satellite plane, CASP) over the originally proposed double-planar structure, with measured rms height ~130 kpc and rms semi-major axis ~330 kpc, nearly orthogonal to the Cen A dust lane and showing coherent line-of-sight velocity patterns suggesting co-rotation. However, complete 3D characterization still depends on obtaining accurate distances for additional candidate satellites, so the question is partially resolved rather than definitively closed.

Let $(M^4, g)$ be a cosmological spacetime, meaning a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian 4-manifold admitting a compact Cauchy hypersurface. Assume that $(M, g)$ satisfies the timelike convergence condition, i.e., the Ricci tensor satisfies $\mathrm{Ric}(v, v) \geq 0$ for every timelike vector $v \in TM$. Prove that one of the following holds:

(a) $(M, g)$ is timelike geodesically incomplete; or

(b) $(M, g)$ splits isometrically as a metric product $(\mathbb{R} \times M^3,\, -dt^2 \oplus h)$, where $(M^3, h)$ is a compact Riemannian 3-manifold (so the spacetime is static).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Known as Bartnik's splitting conjecture (1988). It has been proven under various additional hypotheses (e.g., existence of timelike lines, S-ray condition, level set condition, presence of a CMC Cauchy surface, or a timelike conformal Killing field), but remains open in full generality as of recent surveys and papers (e.g., 2018–2023).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No exact closed-form solution of Einstein's equations describing two orbiting bodies is known. The two-body problem in general relativity is treated only approximately (post-Newtonian expansions, numerical relativity, effective-one-body methods). The expectation, supported by the existence of gravitational-wave emission, is that bound two-body configurations are not stationary and must inspiral, but no rigorous proof of nonexistence of an exact stationary two-body solution in vacuum Einstein gravity exists. The problem remains open.

Let $n \geq 2$ and let $\mathbb{P}^n$ denote complex projective space equipped with the Fubini–Study Hermitian metric. Let $\mathcal{A}_{n-1}$ denote the space of smooth (closed) analytic subvarieties of pure dimension $n-1$ in $\mathbb{P}^n$. For a subvariety $V \in \mathcal{A}_{n-1}$, define its intrinsic diameter $\operatorname{diam}(V)$ to be the diameter of $V$ as a Riemannian manifold with respect to the Hermitian metric induced on $V$ by the Fubini–Study metric of $\mathbb{P}^n$.

It is known that for $n=2$ there exists a sequence of smooth Riemann surfaces $(V_j) \subset \mathcal{A}_1$ in $\mathbb{P}^2$ with
$$\sup_{j} \operatorname{diam}(V_j) \;=\; +\infty.$$

Question: For $n > 2$, does there exist a sequence $(V_j) \subset \mathcal{A}_{n-1}$ of smooth pure $(n-1)$-dimensional analytic subvarieties of $\mathbb{P}^n$ such that
$$\sup_{j} \operatorname{diam}(V_j) \;=\; +\infty,$$
where again the diameter is taken with respect to the induced Hermitian metric?

Consider the satellite galaxy systems observed around the Milky Way, the Andromeda galaxy (M31), and Centaurus A. In each of these three host systems, a substantial fraction of the known satellite galaxies are observed to lie close to a common thin plane (with axis ratios of the satellite spatial distribution that are highly flattened) and to share coherent orbital motion in the sense that their line-of-sight or proper-motion velocities are consistent with a common rotational sense within that plane.

Within the standard cosmological framework (ΛCDM), let p denote the probability that a randomly chosen Milky-Way-like or M31-like host in a cosmological N-body or hydrodynamical simulation possesses a satellite system at least as spatially flattened and at least as kinematically coherent as the corresponding observed system. Current simulation studies indicate p ≲ 1/200 for each of the three observed configurations.

Question: Determine whether the simultaneous occurrence of such extreme, kinematically coherent satellite planes around all three nearby, well-studied hosts can be reconciled with ΛCDM (and with any dark-matter model predicting similar satellite spatial distributions and orbital properties, such as warm or self-interacting dark matter) through refinements in the modeling of structure formation and satellite accretion in cosmological simulations (e.g., baryonic physics, resolution, host selection, environmental effects, group infall, satellite pairing). Equivalently: decide whether the observed mismatch between the frequency of such planes in observations and in simulations reflects incomplete simulation modeling, or instead constitutes a genuine falsification of the ΛCDM paradigm at the scale of satellite galaxy systems.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question remains actively debated as of 2025. Some studies (e.g., Sawala et al. 2023 in Nature Astronomy; Uzeirbegovic et al. 2024 in MNRAS) argue the Milky Way's satellite plane is transient and statistically consistent with ΛCDM once selection and time-evolution effects are modeled, and recent TNG50-based work reports kinematically persistent planes more frequently than earlier simulations suggested. Counter-analyses (e.g., A&A 694 L4, 2025; Pawlowski and collaborators) dispute these claims, finding that satellite systems as extreme as those observed around the Milky Way, M31, and Centaurus A remain rare in ΛCDM simulations and that the tension persists. Let $M$ be a smooth complex projective manifold and let $\Omega \subsetneq M$ be a proper open subset. Assume that $\Omega$ is locally Stein at the boundary, i.e. every point $p \in \partial \Omega$ has an open neighborhood $U$ in $M$ such that $U \cap \Omega$ is a Stein open subset of $M$. Assume in addition that $\partial \Omega$ contains at least one strongly pseudoconvex boundary point (a point $p \in \partial \Omega$ admitting a $C^2$ defining function whose Levi form is positive definite on the holomorphic tangent space to $\partial\Omega$ at $p$).

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions under which $\Omega$ is holomorphically convex, i.e. for every compact subset $K \subset \Omega$ the holomorphic hull
$$\widehat{K}_{\Omega} = \{z \in \Omega : |f(z)| \le \sup_{K} |f| \text{ for all } f \in \mathcal{O}(\Omega)\}$$
is again a compact subset of $\Omega$.

(Note: without the strongly pseudoconvex point hypothesis, Grauert's example of a Levi-flat domain $\{(z,w) \in \mathbb{C}^2/\Lambda : a < \mathrm{Re}(z + \alpha w) < b\}$ on a complex torus, with $\alpha \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$, gives a locally Stein proper open subset of a projective manifold on which all global holomorphic functions are constant, hence not holomorphically convex.)

The Levi problem on general complex manifolds remains an active area: while affirmative for Stein manifolds, $\mathbb{CP}^n$, and certain Kähler settings, classical counterexamples (Grauert, and refinements with real-analytic or strictly pseudoconvex boundary points) show that locally Stein open subsets of compact complex manifolds need not be holomorphically convex. A complete characterization of when a locally Stein proper open subset of a smooth projective manifold with at least one strongly pseudoconvex boundary point is holomorphically convex does not appear to be established in the literature surveyed.

Consider the formation of dwarf satellite galaxies around a host galaxy such as the Milky Way or Andromeda within the standard cosmological framework. Observations reveal that a significant fraction of the luminous satellites of these hosts lie in thin, kinematically coherent, co-rotating planar structures (e.g., the Vast Polar Structure of the Milky Way and the Great Plane of Andromeda), each containing on the order of a dozen or more members within a flattened spatial distribution and sharing a common orbital sense.

One hypothesized formation channel is "group infall," in which several satellites are accreted simultaneously as members of a previously bound galaxy group; satellites infalling as a group naturally share an orbital plane and direction. However, in standard cosmological simulations the typical infalling groups around Milky Way-mass hosts contain too few luminous dwarfs, and multiple separate groups generically infall along uncorrelated directions and at uncorrelated times, so this channel is found to produce planes resembling the observed ones much less frequently than required.

Problem. Identify a physical mechanism (or prove that none can exist within the standard cosmological model) with the following properties:

(a) It preferentially populates a small subset of infalling groups with unusually large numbers (≳10) of luminous dwarf satellite galaxies, while leaving the bulk of groups with the low luminous-dwarf occupation predicted by standard galaxy-formation models;

(b) It causes several such richly populated groups to be accreted by a host halo on nearly the same orbital plane, in the same orbital direction, and at approximately the same cosmic time;

(c) Acting together, (a) and (b) raise the predicted frequency of thin, co-rotating satellite planes (with parameters comparable to the observed Vast Polar Structure and Great Plane of Andromeda) to a level consistent with observation.

Either exhibit such a mechanism, derived from plausible environmental, baryonic, or dynamical conditions during group formation and accretion, and quantify the resulting plane-formation statistics, or rigorously demonstrate that no mechanism within the standard cosmological framework can simultaneously satisfy (a)–(c).

Let (M, g, k) be an asymptotically flat initial data set for the Einstein equations of general relativity. That is, M is a 3-dimensional smooth manifold equipped with a complete Riemannian metric g and a symmetric (0,2)-tensor k (the second fundamental form of M as a spacelike hypersurface in a Lorentzian spacetime), such that outside a compact set M is diffeomorphic to the complement of a ball in R^3 and g and k satisfy standard asymptotic flatness decay conditions ensuring that the ADM mass m_ADM is well defined. Assume the dominant energy condition: the energy density μ = (1/2)(R(g) + (tr_g k)^2 − |k|_g^2) and the momentum density J = div_g(k − (tr_g k) g) satisfy μ ≥ |J|_g pointwise.

Let A denote the area of the outermost apparent horizon in (M, g, k) (the outermost surface on which the future-outgoing null expansion vanishes, viewed as the boundary of the trapped region).

The Penrose inequality asserts that
   m_ADM ≥ sqrt( A / (16π) ).

Problem: Either prove this inequality in the full generality stated above (without symmetry, time-symmetry, maximality of the slice, or other restrictive assumptions on the initial data), or exhibit an asymptotically flat initial data set satisfying the dominant energy condition for which the inequality fails.

A Stein Riemann surface is a connected one-dimensional complex manifold $X$ that is Stein; equivalently, $X$ is a non-compact (open) connected Riemann surface, since every open Riemann surface is Stein. A holomorphic map $f \colon X \to \mathbb{C}^2$ is called a proper holomorphic embedding (equivalently, $f(X)$ is a closed complex submanifold of $\mathbb{C}^2$) if $f$ is a holomorphic immersion, $f$ is injective, and the preimage $f^{-1}(K)$ of every compact set $K \subset \mathbb{C}^2$ is compact in $X$.

Question: Does every Stein (i.e. open) Riemann surface $X$ admit a proper holomorphic embedding into $\mathbb{C}^2$ as a closed complex submanifold?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is a long-standing open problem in complex analysis. Substantial partial results exist (e.g., Kasahara–Nishino, Laufer, Alexander for special cases; Globevnik–Stensønes for finitely connected planar domains; Černe–Forstnerič and Forstnerič–Wold for various classes of bordered Riemann surfaces), but the general question for all open Riemann surfaces remains unsolved as of recent surveys.

Tidal dwarf galaxies (TDGs) are dwarf galaxies formed out of baryonic tidal debris ejected during interactions between larger galaxies; under the standard cold dark matter paradigm such objects are expected to be essentially free of dark matter, while in Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) the gravitational acceleration follows a non-Newtonian law of the form a ≈ √(a_N · a_0) for accelerations a_N below a critical scale a_0 ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m s⁻², producing apparent mass discrepancies and asymptotically flat rotation curves even without dark matter.

Determine the true dynamical state of young tidal dwarf galaxies. Specifically, decide which of the following holds for young TDGs as a class:

(a) They exhibit apparent mass discrepancies and asymptotically flat rotation curves quantitatively consistent with the predictions of MOND (including, where relevant, the external field effect of the host galaxy);

(b) They follow purely Newtonian dynamics with no apparent mass discrepancy beyond their baryonic content; or

(c) They are not in sufficient dynamical equilibrium (their internal orbital times being comparable to or longer than the time elapsed since their formation) for either interpretation to be tested reliably.

Provide an observational and/or theoretical resolution that distinguishes among (a), (b), and (c), thereby establishing whether TDGs can reproduce the observed dynamical behavior of ordinary dwarf satellite galaxies.

Let $(\mathcal{M}, g_{M,a})$ denote the Kerr family of Lorentzian 4-manifolds, parametrized by mass $M>0$ and angular momentum parameter $a$ with $|a|<M$ (the subextremal range). Each $g_{M,a}$ is a smooth, stationary, axisymmetric solution of the vacuum Einstein equations $\mathrm{Ric}(g)=0$ containing a rotating black hole region bounded by an event horizon.

Consider the Cauchy problem for the vacuum Einstein equations with initial data $(\Sigma_0, \bar g_0, k_0)$, where $\Sigma_0$ is a smooth asymptotically flat spacelike hypersurface, $\bar g_0$ a Riemannian metric, and $k_0$ a symmetric 2-tensor on $\Sigma_0$ satisfying the Einstein constraint equations. Assume $(\bar g_0, k_0)$ is a sufficiently small smooth perturbation (in a suitable weighted Sobolev norm) of the induced data on a Cauchy hypersurface of a fixed subextremal Kerr spacetime $g_{M_0, a_0}$ with $|a_0|<M_0$.

Prove that the maximal globally hyperbolic vacuum development of such data possesses a complete future null infinity, that its exterior region is geodesically complete up to the event horizon, and that on this exterior it asymptotically converges (in a suitable sense) to a member $g_{M_\infty, a_\infty}$ of the Kerr family with parameters close to $(M_0, a_0)$ and $|a_\infty| < M_\infty$.

Nonlinear stability of slowly rotating Kerr black holes (|a|/M ≪ 1) was established in a series of works by Klainerman–Szeftel, Giorgi–Klainerman–Szeftel, and Shen, with key wave equation estimates appearing around 2022. Hintz and collaborators have obtained conditional/linear stability results, including linear stability for slowly rotating Kerr (2025) and conditional nonlinear stability of Kerr–de Sitter in the full subextremal range. The full nonlinear stability of subextremal Kerr (without smallness of a/M) remains open as of 2026.

Let $\Omega, V \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be bounded open sets, and let $f: \Omega \to V$ be a biholomorphic mapping. Address the following questions about boundary regularity of $f$:

(a) If both $\partial \Omega$ and $\partial V$ are real-analytic ($C^\omega$), must $f$ extend continuously to $\overline{\Omega}$?

(b) If both $\partial \Omega$ and $\partial V$ are $C^\infty$-smooth, must $f$ extend continuously (or smoothly) to $\overline{\Omega}$?

(c) Do there exist bounded pseudoconvex domains $\Omega, V \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ with smooth boundary and a biholomorphism $f: \Omega \to V$ that does not extend smoothly to $\overline{\Omega}$?

A specific local model whose geometry is to be analyzed in connection with these questions is the domain
$$\{(z_0,z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4) \in \mathbb{C}^5 : (\operatorname{Re} z_0 + |z_1|^2 - |z_2|^2)^2 + \operatorname{Re} z_4 < 0\}.$$

Note: in (a) and (b) the domains $\Omega, V$ are not assumed to be pseudoconvex.

For pseudoconvex domains with real-analytic boundary, biholomorphisms (and proper holomorphic mappings) are known to extend holomorphically across the boundary, by results of Diederich–Fornæss, Baouendi–Jacobowitz–Treves, and Baouendi–Rothschild. Fefferman's theorem handles the smooth strictly pseudoconvex case. However, the general questions for arbitrary (not necessarily pseudoconvex) bounded domains with real-analytic or $C^\infty$ boundary, and the question of existence of biholomorphisms between smooth pseudoconvex domains failing to extend smoothly, remain open. No verified resolution of these specific questions or analysis of the indicated local model was found.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be a domain with real analytic boundary, and let $p \in \partial\Omega$ be a boundary point of finite type (in the sense of D'Angelo) such that $p$ does not lie in the envelope of holomorphy of $\Omega$. Denote by $F_\Omega(q, X)$ the infinitesimal Kobayashi metric of $\Omega$, defined for $q \in \Omega$ and $X \in \mathbb{C}^n$ by
$$F_\Omega(q, X) = \inf\{|\alpha| : \exists\, f : \mathbb{D} \to \Omega \text{ holomorphic with } f(0) = q,\ \alpha f'(0) = X\},$$
where $\mathbb{D}$ is the unit disc. Does there exist $\varepsilon > 0$ and a neighborhood $U$ of $p$ such that
$$F_\Omega(q, X) \geq |X|\, |p - q|^{\varepsilon}$$
for all $q \in \Omega \cap U$ and all $X \in \mathbb{C}^n$? Such a lower bound would imply that any proper holomorphic map $\Omega \to \Omega'$ extends continuously to $\overline{\Omega}$ near $p$.

Let $\mathbb{B}^n \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ denote the open unit ball, and let $H \subset \mathbb{B}^n$ be a smooth ($C^\infty$) real hypersurface of finite type (in the sense of D'Angelo) passing through the origin $0$. Let $\{X_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of closed complex-analytic subvarieties of $\mathbb{B}^n$ such that $0 \in X_k \cap H$ for every $k$. Define the cluster set of the sequence $\{X_k\}$ to be
$$\mathrm{Cl}(\{X_k\}) := \bigcap_{N \geq 1} \overline{\bigcup_{k \geq N} X_k},$$
i.e., the set of all limit points in $\mathbb{B}^n$ of sequences $\{x_k\}$ with $x_k \in X_k$.

Question: Can it happen that $\mathrm{Cl}(\{X_k\}) \subset H$?

(Remark: When $H$ is pseudoconvex, every boundary point of $H$ admits a local plurisubharmonic barrier, and a standard argument then shows that the cluster set cannot be contained in $H$. The problem asks whether the same conclusion holds in the absence of the pseudoconvexity assumption, only assuming that $H$ is a smooth hypersurface of finite type.)

In observations of compact, massive star clusters (with masses comparable to Galactic globular clusters, i.e. roughly 10^5 solar masses or greater, and half-light radii of a few parsecs), the chemical-abundance pattern known as "multiple stellar populations" — characterized by star-to-star variations in light elements such as He, C, N, O, Na, Mg, and Al within a single cluster — is found in all sufficiently old clusters but appears to be absent in clusters younger than approximately 2 Gyr. Determine the physical cause of this approximately 2 Gyr age threshold for the onset of detectable multiple stellar populations in compact, massive star clusters. In particular, decide between the following two alternatives (or identify another mechanism):

(a) Ancient globular clusters formed through a physically distinct channel (operative only at high redshift, z ≳ 0.17) that produced multiple populations, while younger massive clusters form through a different channel that does not.

(b) The same formation pathway operates at all cosmic epochs, and the apparent threshold reflects a stellar-evolution or stellar-mass dependence of the observable abundance signatures (for example, the signature being detectable only in stars below a certain initial mass, which corresponds to a cluster age of roughly 2 Gyr on the red giant branch, or an as-yet-unidentified evolutionary effect tied to stellar rotation, magnetic fields, or surface convection).

Provide a quantitative model that reproduces the threshold and predicts which younger clusters should or should not display the signature.

Stellar clusters in galaxies are subject to dynamical mass loss processes (two-body relaxation driven evaporation, tidal shocks from interactions with the galactic potential and giant molecular clouds, and stellar evolution mass loss) that, over a Hubble time t_H ≈ 13.8 Gyr, impose a minimum initial mass M_surv below which an initially bound cluster cannot survive as a gravitationally bound system. Independently, observations of old Galactic and extragalactic globular clusters reveal that essentially every cluster more massive than some threshold M_MP exhibits multiple stellar populations (light-element abundance variations such as the Na–O and Mg–Al anti-correlations and He spreads), while clusters less massive than M_MP appear chemically homogeneous; M_MP is empirically of order 10^4–10^5 M_⊙, comparable to the value inferred for M_surv.

Question: Is the approximate equality M_surv ≈ M_MP merely a numerical coincidence between two independent mass scales (one set by long-term dynamical evolution in galactic tidal fields, the other set by the conditions for self-enrichment or retention of polluted ejecta during the cluster's earliest phase), or does it arise as a necessary consequence of common underlying physics linking the formation conditions that allow multiple populations to develop to the structural/dynamical conditions that allow a cluster to survive for a Hubble time? Formulate and justify a physical mechanism (or prove the absence of one) that would force M_surv = M_MP up to a factor of order unity, independent of host-galaxy environment.

Let n ≥ 2 and d ≥ 3 be integers, and work over the complex numbers. Denote by S^d(ℂ^n)* the space of homogeneous forms of degree d on ℂ^n, and let X_n^d ⊂ S^d(ℂ^n)* be the open subset consisting of forms f with nonvanishing discriminant (equivalently, forms defining smooth hypersurfaces in ℙ^{n-1}). For f ∈ X_n^d, the gradient ∇f = (∂f/∂x_1, …, ∂f/∂x_n) is an n-tuple of forms of degree d−1 on ℂ^n that form a regular sequence; thus ∇ defines a morphism X_n^d → Z_n^{d-1}, where Z_n^{d-1} ⊂ (S^{d-1}(ℂ^n)*)^n is the variety of n-tuples of degree-(d−1) forms forming a regular sequence. Passing to projectivizations and taking the GIT quotient by the natural SL_n-action, one obtains the induced "projective gradient map"

ℙ∇ : ℙX_n^d / SL_n  ⟶  ℙZ_n^{d-1} // SL_n.

It is known that ℙ∇ is a finite injective morphism. Prove that, for every n ≥ 2 and d ≥ 3, the (closed) image of ℙ∇ is a normal subvariety of ℙZ_n^{d-1} // SL_n.

(By Zariski's Main Theorem, normality of the image would imply that ℙ∇ is an isomorphism onto its image.)

In the cosmological context of hierarchical galaxy assembly, globular clusters (GCs) are dense, gravitationally bound stellar systems with masses typically in the range 10^4–10^6 solar masses, formed predominantly at high redshift. Their present-day (z = 0) population is characterized by observable properties such as the GC mass function, the specific frequency per host galaxy, the spatial and metallicity distributions, and the bimodality between metal-poor and metal-rich subpopulations. Galaxy mergers — major and minor — drive bursts of star formation, can assemble unusually massive giant molecular clouds (GMCs) with masses exceeding 10^7 solar masses through high gas surface densities and turbulent compression, and also produce strong tidal fields that accelerate cluster disruption.

Provide a quantitative determination of the net role played by galaxy mergers in shaping the z = 0 globular-cluster population. Specifically, decide which of the following best describes the merger contribution, and quantify the relative weights of the underlying mechanisms:

(a) Mergers act primarily as a secondary enhancer, boosting GC formation efficiency in high-redshift gas-rich discs where conditions for cluster formation (high pressure, high gas surface density, high turbulent Mach number) are already favorable, without being themselves a necessary ingredient.

(b) Mergers contribute essentially by assembling especially massive GMCs whose collapse produces the most massive bound clusters that survive to z = 0, so that without merger-induced cloud assembly the high-mass end of the present-day GC mass function would not be reproduced.

(c) Mergers increase cluster destruction (through enhanced tidal shocks, disc shocking, and dynamical friction in remnants) sufficiently that their net contribution to the surviving z = 0 GC population is modest, i.e., enhanced formation is largely cancelled by enhanced disruption.

The problem is to quantify, in a cosmological galaxy-formation framework that self-consistently models cluster formation in dense gas and subsequent dynamical evolution, the fractional contribution of merger-triggered formation to the surviving z = 0 GC mass function, specific frequency, metallicity distribution, and spatial distribution, and to identify which of (a), (b), (c) — or which combination — is realized.

representations.normalized: Consider a quantum field theory on a curved spacetime background that contains a black hole formed by gravitational collapse from an initial pure quantum state. According to Hawking's semiclassical analysis, the black hole emits thermal radiation (Hawking radiation) and eventually evaporates completely. The resulting radiation appears to be in a mixed thermal state, suggesting that an initially pure quantum state evolves into a mixed state, in apparent violation of the unitarity of quantum mechanics. The black hole information paradox asks: does the process of black hole formation and complete evaporation preserve quantum information (i.e., is the overall evolution unitary), and if so, by what precise mechanism is the information carried out, encoded, or recovered from the Hawking radiation? Provide a mathematically consistent framework — compatible with both general relativity in the appropriate regime and the principles of quantum mechanics — that resolves this apparent conflict, including a derivation of how the von Neumann entropy of the radiation evolves (the Page curve) and an explicit account of how correlations between early and late Hawking radiation arise or how information otherwise escapes, or alternatively, demonstrate rigorously that unitarity must be abandoned.

In the framework of general relativity coupled to quantum field theory, the Einstein field equations with a cosmological constant Λ read

  R_{μν} − (1/2) g_{μν} R + Λ g_{μν} = 8πG T_{μν},

where g_{μν} is the spacetime metric, R_{μν} the Ricci tensor, R its trace, G Newton's constant, and T_{μν} the stress-energy tensor of matter. Observations of the accelerated expansion of the universe yield an effective value Λ_obs corresponding to a vacuum energy density ρ_Λ ≈ 10^{−47} GeV^4. A naive quantum field theoretic estimate of the zero-point energy of the Standard Model fields, regulated at the Planck scale M_P, gives a vacuum energy density ρ_vac ∼ M_P^4 ≈ 10^{72} GeV^4, exceeding ρ_Λ by roughly 120 orders of magnitude.

(a) Provide a mathematically consistent dynamical or symmetry-based mechanism, within a well-defined effective field theory coupled to gravity, that explains why the observed vacuum energy density entering the gravitational field equations is ρ_Λ ≈ 10^{−47} GeV^4 rather than the natural QFT estimate ∼ M_P^4.

(b) Within the same framework, characterize mathematically the "dark energy" component sourcing the observed late-time accelerated expansion: specify its equation of state w = p/ρ (allowing possible time dependence w(z) as a function of redshift z) and derive it from first principles, distinguishing whether it is a true cosmological constant (w = −1 exactly) or a dynamical field (e.g. quintessence with a scalar potential V(φ)) and giving the corresponding evolution equations.

Consider the Andromeda galaxy (M31) and the subset of 15 of its satellite galaxies that lie in a thin, near-edge-on (as seen from the Milky Way) planar configuration known as the Great Plane of Andromeda (GPoA). These on-plane satellites are observed to have line-of-sight velocities (relative to M31) that are spatially correlated in a manner consistent with coherent rotation about M31: satellites on one side of M31 systematically recede while those on the opposite side systematically approach.

For each on-plane satellite, decompose its three-dimensional velocity vector relative to M31 into a component lying within the GPoA and a component perpendicular to the GPoA. Determine, using precise astrometric proper-motion measurements, whether the perpendicular components of the velocities of the on-plane GPoA satellites are statistically consistent with zero (so that their full 3D motions are largely confined to the plane and the GPoA is a genuine rotationally supported plane of satellites), or whether significant perpendicular motions exist (so that the observed line-of-sight kinematic correlation is only a projected, edge-on signature rather than evidence of a true rotating plane).

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a singular holomorphic foliation by curves on the complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$ (in particular, one may take $n=2$). By definition, $\mathcal{F}$ is given by an open cover $\{U_i\}$ of $\mathbb{CP}^n$ together with holomorphic vector fields $X_i$ on $U_i$, with isolated zeros, such that on each overlap $U_i\cap U_j$ one has $X_i = g_{ij} X_j$ for some nowhere-vanishing holomorphic function $g_{ij}$. The singular set $\mathrm{Sing}(\mathcal{F})$ is the (finite) set of zeros of these local vector fields. Off $\mathrm{Sing}(\mathcal{F})$, the integral curves of the $X_i$ glue into a holomorphic foliation whose maximal connected immersed holomorphic curves are called the leaves of $\mathcal{F}$.

Question: Must every leaf $L$ of $\mathcal{F}$ have a singular point of $\mathcal{F}$ in its closure? Equivalently, does $\overline{L}\cap\mathrm{Sing}(\mathcal{F})\neq\varnothing$ hold for every leaf $L$?

In the framework of classical general relativity coupled to a scalar inflaton field $\phi$ with potential $V(\phi)$ (for instance a slow-roll potential supporting an inflationary regime), consider initial data for the Einstein–scalar field system specified on a Cauchy hypersurface. Such initial data consist of a Riemannian 3-metric $h_{ij}$, its conjugate momentum (extrinsic curvature) $K_{ij}$, and initial values $(\phi, \dot\phi)$ for the scalar field, subject to the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints. Equip the space of admissible initial data with a natural measure or notion of genericity (for example a measure on the constraint surface, or a topological notion such as openness and density in a suitable function-space topology).

Say that a solution "undergoes inflation" if its future Cauchy development contains a sufficiently long epoch (e.g. at least 60 e-folds) of accelerated expansion ($\ddot{a}/a > 0$ in a suitable averaged sense for inhomogeneous spacetimes).

Problem: Determine, quantitatively, how generic the set of initial data leading to inflation is within the full space of admissible initial data. In particular, characterize this set with respect to a chosen measure or topology, and decide whether inflation occurs for a generic (e.g. full-measure, or open and dense) subset of initial conditions, including those that are strongly inhomogeneous and anisotropic.

Consider a large sample of host galaxies, each surrounded by satellite galaxies for which line-of-sight velocities (relative to the host) are measured. For each host, identify diametrically opposed satellite pairs by selecting pairs that lie on opposite sides of the host within a small opening-angle tolerance and within a chosen projected radius. Define the velocity correlation statistic that counts the fraction of such pairs whose line-of-sight velocities (measured relative to the host) have opposite signs (anti-correlated) versus the same sign (correlated). Empirically, in current Sloan Digital Sky Survey samples, an excess of anti-correlated pairs has been observed; this excess has been interpreted as implying that more than 50% of satellites around typical hosts lie in co-orbiting (rotationally supported) planar structures.

Question: Assemble a substantially larger sample of host galaxies with spectroscopically measured satellite line-of-sight velocities, and rigorously test whether the observed excess of anti-correlated diametrically opposed satellite pairs:

(a) is statistically robust under variation of selection criteria, in particular the projected-radius cut and the opening-angle tolerance defining "diametrically opposed"; and

(b) genuinely implies that a substantial fraction (≳ 50%) of satellites belong to thin, rotationally coherent co-orbiting planes,

or whether instead the signal is consistent with isotropic or mildly anisotropic satellite distributions plus selection effects, so that the inferred prevalence of rotating planes of satellites around external hosts is an artifact of limited sample size and selection choices rather than evidence for ubiquitous co-orbiting planes.

Let $R$ be a finite-dimensional associative real algebra equipped with an involution (anti-automorphism of order two) extended coefficient-wise to an involution $\gamma$ on the polynomial ring $R[t]$, where $t$ is a central indeterminate. Define $R^\gamma[t] = \{C \in R[t] : \gamma(C)\,C = C\,\gamma(C) \in \mathbb{R}[t]\}$ and call $
u(C) := \gamma(C)C \in \mathbb{R}[t]$ the norm polynomial of $C$. For $C \in R^\gamma[t]$ monic of degree $n \ge 1$ with $\gcd$ of real polynomial factors trivial (i.e. mrpf $C = 1$), consider the following recursive procedure (gfactor):

1. Choose a monic real quadratic factor $M$ of $
u(C)$.
2. Compute the left remainder $S = \mathrm{lrem}(C, M) \in R[t]$ of degree at most $1$.
3. Find an element $h \in R$ (the "constant zero" $\mathrm{czero}(C, M)$) such that $S(h) = 0$ and $h$ is a zero of $C$ from the right.
4. Perform the right division $C = (t - h) C'$ and recurse on $C'$.

Over division rings (such as $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{H}$) this algorithm is known to terminate and to produce a complete factorization $C = (t-h_1)(t-h_2)\cdots(t-h_n)$ into monic linear factors. When $R$ is a more general finite-dimensional associative real involutive algebra (so that non-invertible nonzero elements may exist), determine:

(a) Necessary and sufficient conditions on $C$ (and on the chosen sequence of quadratic factors of $
u(C)$) for the algorithm to succeed in producing a linear-factor factorization.

(b) An effective decision procedure that, given $C \in R^\gamma[t]$, determines whether $C$ admits a factorization into monic linear factors $(t - h_i)$ with $h_i \in R$, even in cases where the algorithm fails for some — or all — orderings of the quadratic factors of $
u(C)$.

Consider the space of singular holomorphic foliations of a fixed degree $d \geq 2$ on the complex projective plane $\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C})$. Such a foliation $\mathcal{F}$ is given, in homogeneous coordinates, by a polynomial vector field (up to multiples of the radial field) and has a finite singular set $\mathrm{Sing}(\mathcal{F})$; outside $\mathrm{Sing}(\mathcal{F})$ the foliation partitions $\mathbb{P}^2 \setminus \mathrm{Sing}(\mathcal{F})$ into immersed Riemann surfaces called leaves. The space of degree-$d$ foliations on $\mathbb{P}^2$ is itself a complex projective space, so one may speak of properties holding for a generic (i.e. on a residual or full-measure subset) foliation.

Determine the topology of a generic leaf for a generic holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C})$. More precisely, describe the homeomorphism type (e.g. genus, number of ends, fundamental group) of the leaf through a generic point $p \in \mathbb{P}^2$ for a foliation $\mathcal{F}$ chosen generically in the space of degree-$d$ foliations.

The topology of generic leaves of a generic holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb{P}^2$ is widely cited as an open basic question in the theory of holomorphic foliations. Partial results exist in related settings: for generic foliations on Stein manifolds, Firsova showed all but countably many leaves are contractible (the rest cylinders), and for $\mathbb{P}^k$ it is known generic leaves are hyperbolic (covered by the disk). However, the precise topological classification of generic leaves on $\mathbb{P}^2$ remains unresolved.

Consider singular holomorphic foliations by curves on the complex projective plane $\mathbb{P}^2$. Such a foliation $\mathcal{F}$ of degree $d \geq 2$ is given, in homogeneous coordinates, by a holomorphic vector field (or equivalently a section of a suitable twisted tangent bundle) whose zero set is a finite singular set $\mathrm{Sing}(\mathcal{F})$; on the complement $\mathbb{P}^2 \setminus \mathrm{Sing}(\mathcal{F})$, $\mathcal{F}$ defines a smooth one-dimensional holomorphic foliation, whose maximal connected immersed integral curves are called the leaves of $\mathcal{F}$. The space $\mathcal{F}_d$ of degree-$d$ foliations on $\mathbb{P}^2$ is naturally a Zariski-open subset of a complex projective space, and a property is said to hold for a generic foliation of degree $d$ if it holds on a countable intersection of dense open subsets (or, in stronger formulations, on a Zariski-open dense subset) of $\mathcal{F}_d$.

Question: Is it true that, for every degree $d \geq 2$, a generic foliation $\mathcal{F} \in \mathcal{F}_d$ has the property that every leaf (or, at least, every leaf outside a meager set of leaves) is dense in $\mathbb{P}^2$?

Consider a Milky-Way-like host galaxy (a dark matter halo of mass on the order of 10^12 solar masses) onto which satellite (dwarf) galaxies are accreted from the surrounding cosmic web. Suppose that satellite accretion is preferentially channeled along the large-scale filaments of the cosmic web that intersect the host halo. Determine whether such filamentary accretion, taken on its own (i.e., in the absence of additional mechanisms such as group infall, baryonic dissipation, or specific halo-shape dynamics), can simultaneously reproduce the two observed properties of the satellite system around such a host:

(i) Spatial thinness: the satellite distribution lies within a planar structure of root-mean-square thickness only about 20–30 kpc, despite the host halo having a virial radius of order 200–300 kpc.

(ii) Orbital coherence: a large fraction of the satellites possess orbital angular momentum vectors that are mutually closely aligned and point in the same sense, indicating coherent (co-)rotation within the plane.

In particular, address whether filamentary infall can yield such a thin plane given that the typical transverse extent of cosmic filaments at these scales is comparable to or larger than the host halo, and whether it can imprint a high, coherently oriented angular momentum on the satellite population in the realistic situation where two or more filaments feed the host or where filament orientations evolve over cosmic time.

Let $\mathbb{H}$ denote the algebra of real quaternions and let $\mathbb{DH} = \mathbb{H}[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$ denote the algebra of dual quaternions, where $\varepsilon$ commutes with $\mathbb{H}$. For a polynomial $C = P + \varepsilon Q \in \mathbb{DH}[t]$ with $P, Q \in \mathbb{H}[t]$, write $C^* = P^* + \varepsilon Q^*$ for the polynomial obtained by quaternion conjugation of coefficients. The norm polynomial is $C C^* \in \mathbb{DH}[t]$; $C$ is called a motion polynomial if $CC^* \in \mathbb{R}[t]$. Let $\mathrm{mrpf}(P)$ denote the maximal real polynomial factor of $P \in \mathbb{H}[t]$, i.e. the monic polynomial in $\mathbb{R}[t]$ of largest degree dividing $P$ on both sides. A motion polynomial $C = P + \varepsilon Q$ is called bounded if $\mathrm{mrpf}(P)$ has no real zeros, and unbounded otherwise. A factorization of $C$ is an expression $C = (t - h_1)(t - h_2)\cdots(t - h_n) \cdot r(t)$ with $h_i \in \mathbb{DH}$ and $r(t) \in \mathbb{R}[t]$.

It is known that bounded motion polynomials always become factorable after multiplication by a suitable real polynomial. For unbounded motion polynomials, factorability is not guaranteed even after such multiplication.

Characterize the set of unbounded motion polynomials $C \in \mathbb{DH}[t]$ for which at least one of the following operations produces a factorable motion polynomial:
(a) multiplication by a real polynomial $S \in \mathbb{R}[t]$, yielding $CS$;
(b) multiplication by a quaternion polynomial $D \in \mathbb{H}[t]$, yielding $CD$ (or $DC$);
(c) rational reparameterization $t \mapsto A(t)/B(t)$ with $A, B \in \mathbb{R}[t]$, yielding $B^{\deg C} C(A/B)$.

That is, give necessary and sufficient conditions on $C$ for each of (a), (b), (c) to be possible, and describe the resulting class of "factorizable" unbounded motion polynomials.

Let $M$ be a compact Kähler manifold and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a (possibly singular) holomorphic foliation by Riemann surfaces on $M$, with singular set $E$ consisting of isolated points. A singularity $p\in E$ is said to be linearizable if, in suitable local holomorphic coordinates centered at $p$, the foliation is defined by a linear vector field whose linear part is diagonalizable; otherwise $p$ is called non-linearizable.

Let $T$ be an extremal positive $dd^c$-closed current on $M$ directed by $\mathcal{F}$ (i.e., $T\wedge \omega = 0$ for any $(1,0)$-form $\omega$ vanishing on the tangent bundle of $\mathcal{F}$ on $M\setminus E$), and assume that $T$ gives full mass to the union of hyperbolic leaves of $\mathcal{F}$. For a point $a$ on a hyperbolic leaf $L_a$, fix a universal covering map $\varphi_a:\mathbb{D}\to L_a$ with $\varphi_a(0)=a$, where $\mathbb{D}$ is the unit disc. For $0<r<1$, define the Nevanlinna current
$$\tau_r^a \;=\; \frac{1}{T_r(a)}\,(\varphi_a)_*\!\Big(\log\tfrac{r}{|\zeta|}\,[\mathbb{D}_r]\Big),$$
where $\mathbb{D}_r=\{|\zeta|<r\}$ and $T_r(a)$ is the area-type normalization that makes $\tau_r^a$ a probability current.

It is known that, when all singularities of $\mathcal{F}$ are linearizable, one has $\tau_r^a \to T$ as $r\to 1$ in the sense of currents, for $T$-almost every $a\in M$.

Question: Does the same convergence $\tau_r^a\to T$ for $T$-almost every $a$ continue to hold when $\mathcal{F}$ is allowed to have non-linearizable singularities?

representations.normalized:
Consider Lambda-Cold-Dark-Matter cosmological simulations of Milky-Way-like host halos together with their populations of satellite (sub-halo) galaxies on spatial scales of order a few hundred kiloparsecs. The "planes of satellite galaxies" phenomenon refers to observed satellite systems (around the Milky Way and M31, and reported around Centaurus A) whose member galaxies are spatially confined to a thin, flattened configuration and additionally exhibit kinematic coherence in the form of a substantial fraction of co-orbiting members (clustered orbital pole directions). In dark-matter-only simulations, sub-halo systems matching simultaneously the observed degree of spatial flattening and the observed degree of orbital coherence occur with very low frequency.

Question: Do baryonic or hydrodynamical processes incorporated into galaxy-formation simulations (for example, gas cooling, star formation, supernova and AGN feedback, reionisation, ram-pressure stripping, tidal stripping enhanced by a baryonic disk, or selection effects induced by the luminous-satellite/sub-halo connection) materially increase the frequency of simulated satellite systems that simultaneously reproduce both the spatial thinness and the kinematic coherence of the observed satellite planes, beyond the frequency obtained in dark-matter-only simulations? If yes, identify a concrete physical mechanism that produces such an enhancement of phase-space coherence on hundreds-of-kiloparsec scales, as opposed to merely modifying internal satellite structure or radial concentration.

representations.normalized:
A singular Lagrangian fibration is a surjective map φ: M → B from a symplectic manifold (M, ω) onto a (possibly stratified) base B whose generic fibers are Lagrangian submanifolds and whose singular fibers occur over a stratified subset of B; via the action coordinates of Arnold–Liouville, the regular part of B inherits an integral-affine structure that extends to a "singular integral-affine structure" on the stratified base. Two such bases (B, A) and (B′, A′) are called affinely equivalent (as stratified spaces with singular integral-affine structures) if there is a homeomorphism B → B′ that restricts to an isomorphism of stratifications and pulls back the singular integral-affine structure on B′ to that on B. Two singular Lagrangian fibrations φ: M → B and φ′: M′ → B′ are called fiberwise symplectomorphic if there exist a symplectomorphism Φ: M → M′ and a stratified homeomorphism ψ: B → B′ with φ′ ∘ Φ = ψ ∘ φ.

Problem: Identify additional hypotheses on the singular Lagrangian fibrations φ: M → B and φ′: M′ → B′ (for instance restrictions on the types of allowed singularities, on the topology or monodromy of the fibration, on global invariants such as Chern/Lagrangian classes, or on the existence of sections) under which the following statement becomes a rigorous theorem:

If (B, A) and (B′, A′) are affinely equivalent as stratified spaces with singular integral-affine structures, then φ and φ′ are fiberwise symplectomorphic.

Determine the minimal/natural such additional assumptions and produce a precise theorem with a proof, or exhibit counterexamples delimiting the result.

The principle is known to hold in the toric case and in dimension two (Dufour–Molino–Toulet's classification via affine Reeb graphs), and for "simple" semitoric systems (with at most one focus-focus pinch per fiber). Identifying the precise additional assumptions remains an active line of research, with recent work (2024–2025) on classifying affine structures with focus-focus singularities and on singular Lagrangian fibrations.

For 0 < r < 1, let D(r) ⊂ D be the disc of radius r and define the area

Define the associated Ahlfors current

where [D(r)] is the current of integration over D(r).

Question: Does σ_r^a converge (weakly, as currents) to T as r → 1, for T-almost every base point a ∈ X?

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a (singular) holomorphic foliation by Riemann surfaces on a compact complex manifold, and let $T$ be a harmonic (i.e., $dd^c$-closed) positive current of bi-degree $(1,1)$ directed by $\mathcal{F}$. For a (non-singular) leaf $L$ of $\mathcal{F}$ that is hyperbolic, fix a base point $a \in L$ and let $\varphi_a:\mathbb{D}\to L$ be a universal covering map of $L$ with $\varphi_a(0)=a$, where $\mathbb{D}\subset\mathbb{C}$ denotes the unit disc. Pulling back a Hermitian metric $\omega$ on the ambient manifold to $\mathbb{D}$ via $\varphi_a$, define the Nevanlinna characteristic of the leaf by
$$T(r) \;=\; \int_0^r \frac{dt}{t}\int_{|z|<t}\varphi_a^*\omega, \qquad 0<r<1.$$
It is known that for $T$-almost every leaf $L$ there exists a constant $c=c(a)>0$ such that
$$T(r) \;\geq\; c\,\log\frac{1}{1-r} \qquad \text{for } r \text{ sufficiently close to } 1.$$
Question: Does this lower bound hold for every (hyperbolic) leaf of $\mathcal{F}$? In particular, does it hold for every leaf when $\mathcal{F}$ admits no diffuse $dd^c$-closed positive current directed by it?

representations.normalized: Background and definitions. A "plane of satellite galaxies" is a configuration in which a substantial fraction of the satellite galaxies orbiting a host galaxy is observed to lie within a thin, flattened, and kinematically coherent (co-rotating) spatial structure, rather than being distributed isotropically. A "tidal dwarf galaxy" (TDG) is a gravitationally bound dwarf galaxy that forms from material (gas and stars) pulled out into a tidal tail during a close encounter or merger between two larger galaxies; because TDGs form within a common tidal structure, they are predicted to share a coherent kinematic plane. A host galaxy is said to have a "quiet merger history" if it has not undergone any major galaxy–galaxy encounter or merger over a cosmologically significant past interval (so that no major tidal tail capable of spawning a population of TDGs has been produced); an "isolated" host has no nearby massive companion at the present epoch.\n\nProblem. Under the hypothesis that the observed planes of satellite galaxies around host galaxies are produced by the tidal-dwarf-galaxy formation channel — namely, that the satellites making up such a plane are TDGs born from a past major interaction of the host with another massive galaxy — determine whether this hypothesis is consistent with the broader population of host galaxies. Specifically, decide the following empirical question: among isolated host galaxies whose merger histories contain no major galaxy encounter, are coherent planes of satellite galaxies (i) absent or rare, as predicted by the TDG hypothesis, or (ii) common, in which case the TDG channel must be rejected as a viable universal origin of planes of satellites? Provide either an observational determination of the frequency of satellite planes around merger-quiet isolated hosts, or a theoretical argument that constrains it, sufficient to confirm or falsify the TDG hypothesis as the origin of planes of satellites.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The TDG origin of satellite planes remains an actively debated and unresolved hypothesis. Let $(M^{2n}, \omega)$ be a symplectic manifold equipped with a completely integrable Hamiltonian system, i.e. a smooth map $F = (f_1, \dots, f_n) : M \to \mathbb{R}^n$ whose components Poisson-commute and are functionally independent on an open dense subset. Let $L_0 \subset M$ be a compact singular fiber of $F$, and assume that on a neighbourhood $U$ of $L_0$ one has explicit local action variables $I_1, \dots, I_n$ defined on the regular part of $U$, each of which admits a decomposition
$$I_k(h) = I_k^{\mathrm{reg}}(h) + I_k^{\mathrm{sing}}(h),$$
where $h = (h_1, \dots, h_n)$ are coordinates on the base centered at the critical value $F(L_0) = 0$, $I_k^{\mathrm{reg}}$ extends smoothly across $h = 0$, and $I_k^{\mathrm{sing}}$ encodes the non-smooth contribution coming from the singular fiber.

Recall that a critical point $p \in L_0$ is non-degenerate of hyperbolic type if, in Williamson's classification, the quadratic part of $F$ at $p$ contains a hyperbolic block $f = xy$ (in suitable Darboux coordinates). It is known that for $n = 1$ a non-degenerate hyperbolic singular fiber produces a singular part of the form
$$I^{\mathrm{sing}}(h) = c\, h \ln |h| + o(h \ln |h|), \qquad c \neq 0.$$

Question: For arbitrary $n \geq 2$, is it possible to recover the topological type of the singular fiber $L_0$ (or at least to distinguish between distinct topological types of non-degenerate singularities) from the asymptotic behaviour of $I_1^{\mathrm{sing}}, \dots, I_n^{\mathrm{sing}}$ as $h \to 0$? In particular, is the asymptotic
$$I_k^{\mathrm{sing}}(h) \sim c_k\, h \ln |h|$$
along an appropriate transverse direction a characterization of non-degenerate hyperbolic singularities among non-degenerate singular fibers of integrable systems with $n$ degrees of freedom?

Let $\mathbb{P}^2$ denote the complex projective plane, and fix an affine chart $\mathbb{C}^2 \subset \mathbb{P}^2$ with coordinates $(z,w)$. For an integer $d \geq 1$, define:

(a) $\mathcal{A}_d$ to be the space of singular holomorphic foliations on $\mathbb{P}^2$ given in the affine chart $\mathbb{C}^2$ by a polynomial vector field
$$Z = P(z,w)\frac{\partial}{\partial z} + Q(z,w)\frac{\partial}{\partial w}, \qquad \max(\deg P, \deg Q) = d;$$

(b) $\mathcal{B}_d$ to be the space of singular holomorphic foliations on $\mathbb{P}^2$ of degree $d$ (i.e., the foliations whose tangencies with a generic line in $\mathbb{P}^2$ form a divisor of degree $d$).

Each space carries a natural structure of a (Zariski-open subset of a) complex projective space, and hence a notion of "generic" foliation (i.e., belonging to a countable intersection of Zariski-open dense subsets). For a foliation $\mathcal{F}$ in either space, a leaf $L$ of $\mathcal{F}$ is a maximal connected immersed Riemann surface tangent to $\mathcal{F}$ off the singular set; "generic leaf" means a leaf outside an exceptional set of leaves of measure/Baire-meager type (e.g., all leaves outside a countable union).

Question: For a generic foliation $\mathcal{F} \in \mathcal{A}_d$ (respectively, $\mathcal{F} \in \mathcal{B}_d$), is a generic leaf of $\mathcal{F}$ biholomorphic to the open unit disc $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z|<1\}$?

Background and setup. Let $(M,\omega)$ be a connected symplectic 4-manifold and let $F=(J,H)\colon M\to\mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth map with Poisson-commuting components $\{J,H\}=0$, so that $F$ defines a completely integrable system with two degrees of freedom. A point $p\in M$ is a singular point of $F$ if $dF(p)$ has rank $<2$. A rank-$0$ singular point $p$ is called non-degenerate if the Hessians $d^2J(p)$ and $d^2H(p)$ span a Cartan subalgebra of the Lie algebra $\mathrm{sp}(T_pM,\omega_p)$ of quadratic Hamiltonians on $(T_pM,\omega_p)$. By Williamson's theorem, the local model at such a point is, in suitable symplectic Darboux coordinates, a direct sum of blocks of four possible types: elliptic ($q^2+p^2$), hyperbolic ($qp$), focus–focus (a pair of complex-conjugate eigenvalues), and regular. A non-degenerate rank-$1$ singularity is similarly classified by a single block of elliptic or hyperbolic type.

A semitoric system is a 4-dimensional integrable system $F=(J,H)$ such that:
(i) $J$ is proper and generates an effective Hamiltonian $S^1$-action on $M$;
(ii) every singular point of $F$ is non-degenerate;
(iii) no singular point of $F$ has a hyperbolic block.

Under these conditions, a complete symplectic classification of semitoric systems is known: each system is classified, up to isomorphism, by a list of five symplectic invariants (the number of focus–focus values, the Taylor-series invariant at each focus–focus singularity, the polygon invariant, the height invariant, and the twisting-index invariant).

Problem. Extend the symplectic classification of semitoric systems $F=(J,H)$ to the larger class of integrable systems satisfying conditions (i) and (ii) above, but allowing condition (iii) to fail: i.e., produce a complete set of symplectic invariants, together with an existence/uniqueness theorem, that classifies (up to isomorphism) all 4-dimensional integrable systems $F=(J,H)$ for which $J$ is proper and generates an effective Hamiltonian $S^1$-action and all singularities of $F$ are non-degenerate, including those with hyperbolic blocks.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The real-analytic case has been resolved negatively: there is no closed real-analytic Levi-flat hypersurface in $\mathbb{P}^2$ (Cerveau, Lins Neto). For higher dimensions $\mathbb{P}^n$, $n\geq 3$, nonexistence is known also in the smooth ($C^\infty$) category (Siu and others). The smooth case in $\mathbb{P}^2$ remains a well-known open problem; recent partial results include nonexistence under additional symmetry assumptions (e.g., homogeneous Levi-flat hypersurfaces).

Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold equipped with a holomorphic foliation (possibly with singularities) $\mathcal{F}$, or more generally a holomorphic lamination, which is minimal in the sense that every leaf is dense in $X$. A positive current $T$ of bidimension $(1,1)$ on $X$ is said to be directed by $\mathcal{F}$ if, on every flow box, $T$ is a combination of integration currents along the plaques weighted by a positive transverse measure. The current $T$ is called $dd^c$-closed if $dd^c T = 0$, and closed if $dT = 0$. The current $T$ is extremal in the cone of positive $dd^c$-closed directed currents if it cannot be written as a non-trivial convex combination of two non-proportional such currents. Two positive currents are mutually singular if their trace measures are mutually singular Borel measures on $X$.

Construct an example of a compact complex manifold $X$ together with a holomorphic minimal foliation (respectively, a holomorphic minimal lamination) on $X$ admitting uncountably many mutually singular extremal positive directed $dd^c$-closed currents, none of which are closed.
